title: Rep. Grijalva Reacts to Discovery of Ancestral Remains at Organ Pipe Amid Border Wall Construction
text:
Rep. Grijalva is preparing legislation to repeal DHS’ waiver authority and void existing waivers that bypass protections for Tribal sovereignty, sacred sites, and ancestral lands.

Tucson, Arizona — Congresswoman Adelita S. Grijalva released the below statement following reports about the discovery of Native American ancestral remains at Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument in Arizona, where border wall contractors have bulldozed through ancestral lands, disturbed native vegetation and unearthed human remains.

“This is an outrage. For months, Tribal leaders and elders have warned DHS about the devastating consequences of bulldozing through their ancestral lands, beginning with the destruction of the Las Playas Intaglio. For months, those warnings have fallen on deaf ears. Now, we are seeing exactly what they feared: sacred sites destroyed and burial grounds desecrated.

This is precisely why we must end DHS’ sweeping authority to waive laws designed to protect Tribal sovereignty, sacred sites, and environmentally sensitive lands. I will be introducing legislation to repeal that authority and void existing waivers that have allowed DHS to ignore these protections and carelessly bulldoze through much of our southern border.”

The discovery is the latest in a series of devastating impacts to culturally and historically significant sites along the southern border. It comes after the destruction of the Las Playas Intaglio, a sacred cultural site dating back at least 6,500 years. O’odham elders are also worried about damage to Quitobaquito Springs, an ecologically and culturally significant site.

title: Moore, Chu Reintroduce EITC Age Parity Act to Expand Tax Credit to Younger and Older Workers
text:
Representative Gwen Moore (WI-04) and Representative Judy Chu (CA-28) introduced the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC) Age Parity Act to eliminate a barrier preventing younger and older workers without children from accessing the EITC.

Last year, 24 million workers and families received the credit, pulling millions out of poverty. But under current law, workers under the age of 25 and over the age of 65 without children are not eligible for the credit. The EITC Age Parity Act expands this credit’s eligibility so these workers can finally receive permanent support.

“At a time when American families and workers are struggling with higher costs for just about everything, our tax laws should not be taxing workers into poverty. That is why I have long championed updates to the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC), one of our nation’s largest anti-poverty tools. While the American Rescue Plan Act made important changes to the EITC, including allowing younger and older adults without children to benefit from this refundable credit, those temporary changes expired, depriving some of our most vulnerable workers of critical assistance. The EITC Age Parity Act would permanently allow younger and older workers to benefit from the EITC, a crucial first step in ensuring that our tax code can better serve all our workers,” said Rep. Moore.

“The EITC is one of the most impactful and transformative anti-poverty tools we have at our disposal. Unfortunately, arbitrary age limits exclude millions of hardworking Americans who could benefit from it greatly,” said Rep. Chu. “Right now, a 23-year-old stocking shelves and a 66-year-old still working to make ends meet, neither with children at home, are shut out of the EITC for no reason other than their age. I’m proud to reintroduce the EITC Age Parity Act with Rep. Moore to lift more families out of poverty and put more money back in the pockets of millions of workers.”

title: Congressman Harris Applauds Start of Honga River Dredging in Dorchester County
text:
WASHINGTON, DC — Today, Congressman Andy Harris, M.D. (MD-01) announced that the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) Baltimore District has begun dredging the Honga River in Dorchester County.

The project will remove approximately 342,000 cubic yards of sediment, with dredging expected to continue through March 2027. Dredged material will be placed at Barren Island as part of the Mid-Chesapeake Bay Island Ecosystem Restoration Project.

Statement from Congressman Harris:

“Thank you to the Army Corps of Engineers for working closely with South Dorchester County community leaders and local watermen to get the Honga River dredging project underway. This is a strong example of the federal government listening to local concerns and working with the community to see a much-needed project through.”

title: Himes Statement on Revolution Wind Reaching Full Commercial Operation
text:
Bridgeport, CT – Today, Congressman Jim Himes (CT-04) released the following statement:

“The completion of Revolution Wind is an important step towards bringing down rising energy costs across the Connecticut. This project will power 350,000 homes and, beginning in 2028, save customers $500 million annually. I’m glad to see this project become fully operational despite repeated attempts by the Trump Administration to shut it down. With the war in Iran driving up energy prices across the country, we should be making it easier to bring new sources of electricity online, not putting obstacles in their way. I am grateful to my colleagues at the federal, state, and local levels for their continued advocacy on this issue.”

title: Hoyer Statement Calling for the Immediate Delivery of Military Assistance to Ukraine
text:
WASHINGTON, DC – Today, Congressman Steny H. Hoyer (MD-05) released the following statement to continue urging the Pentagon to ensure immediate delivery of the $400 million in defense material that was authorized in the FY2026 National Defense Authorization Act for the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative:

“I learned yesterday from Ukrainian officials that the $400 million in military assistance Congress appropriated more than eight months ago has still not been delivered.

“Ukraine is in a fight for freedom and its future. Its heroic soldiers have been struggling for four-and-a-half years to repel Russia’s criminal invasion, facing innumerable hardships on the battlefield. Civilians in Kyiv, Odesa, and other cities have had to live under the constant threat of aerial attacks and power outages in the depths of winter. The impact of this assistance is not theoretical. It is practical and essential.

“I am urging the Pentagon to do everything it can to complete the paperwork for the delivery of this $400 million in military equipment right away. It will save soldiers’ lives, it will protect civilians, and it will help bring about the victory that must be this war’s end."

title: Boston Globe: Clark and House Democratic leadership made history and won the majority. Now they face the real test: how to use it.
text:
As Revere Representative Katherine Clark stepped up to address a room of roughly four dozen volunteers in one of Pennsylvania’s purplest suburbs one week before Election Day, she opened with a question: “Are you ready to win?”

It’s hard to believe Clark or any of the cheering supporters could fathom in that moment the magnitude of the victory that indeed came to pass on Tuesday.

Riding into January on a blue wave of historic proportions, Clark is widely expected to be the majority leader in a new Democratic majority so large that any talk of factional strife has been swept away along with dozens of Republican members of Congress. But after their celebrations, Democrats will face a stark reality: the hard part of their jobs is just beginning.

Polling this year, which turned out to be fairly accurate, made clear that although voters were supporting Democrats, they still had misgivings about the party and were placing only tentative trust in their leadership. Clark and her fellow Democratic leaders will have two years under Trump’s White House to prove to voters that the trust wasn’t misplaced, as the party eyes what many consider to be the real goal for Democrats: winning the presidency and full control of Congress in 2028.

Clark has been the House whip alongside minority leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York and the third-ranking Democrat Pete Aguilar of California, since they were chosen by peers in 2022. Come January they’ll be promoted to the majority for the first time, with Jeffries expected to become the first Black speaker, Clark the first woman majority leader, and Aguilar the first Latino majority whip. With that newly minted majority, they will have to navigate an ideologically diverse new caucus.

Along with a swath of battleground candidates who flipped dozens of seats, Democrats will welcome a new crop of progressives who ran unabashedly to the left. Many of those lawmakers successfully defeated incumbent Democrats in primaries by adopting positions that have proven divisive flashpoints for Democrats, including pledging to abolish Immigration and Customs Enforcement and being sharply critical of Israel in support of Palestinians.

The leadership team will have a comfortable enough majority that a small group of defections won’t matter for many votes, but they will still have to navigate the existential question of which ideological vision would best serve the mandate they received from voters. Clark, who will hand off whip duties to Aguilar, will control the floor schedule and manage which legislation gets a vote. And they’ll have to do it under the reality that delivering tangible results could be elusive — Trump has already telegraphed he’ll freely exercise his veto power and ignore congressional investigations.

At that campaign event in Pennsylvania’s politically purple Bucks County last week, a race in which the Democrats’ recruit Bob Harvie managed to topple a five-term moderate Republican, Clark brushed aside “ideological labels” and told the Globe that the leadership team is preparing by focusing on delivering on their pledges to be “affordability Democrats.”

“We are going to have, I hope, a very big coalition to bring together,” Clark said. “But I think we have shown in the minority that those core values of fighting for the people in our communities are the ones that draw Democrats together, and I think that’s going to be our source of strength.”

That has been the message of the leadership team post-election, an insistence that they are ready to make life better for Americans.

“This is a change election and we understand as House Democrats that we need to deliver dramatic change,” Jeffries said in his victory speech. At a news conference Wednesday, Jeffries and Clark delivered the same message, saying affordability would be their number one focus.

“The agenda, we cannot wait to get this big caucus together and help set that,” Clark said. “Every week when we come to the floor, it is going to be the people of this country who are going to be the focus of the work we do, and the campaign promises made are going to be promises kept.”

But there were few specifics. The leaders pledged to pass legislation rolling back Republicans’ Medicaid cuts and to reinstate subsidies for insurance plans through Obamacare. Beyond that, Jeffries pledged the caucus would come up with more plans through five “working groups,”on health care (which he noted would be co-led by leading progressive New York Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez), on housing, gas and groceries, goods and utilities, and caregiving.

In many ways, progressives and moderates were echoing the same refrain this election cycle. Melat Kiros, one of the newly elected lawmakers who associates with the far-left Democratic Socialists of America and defeated a longtime incumbent Democrat in a primary, declared in her victory speech that voters had delivered a mandate to take on entrenched Washington interests and money in politics.

“No one knows better how fragile this system they’ve created is than the billionaires,” Kiros said. “This campaign proved that we know our collective power and we are coming to fight back.”

The message echoed almost identically even for Senate candidates who flipped deep red states, including South Carolina’s Annie Andrews and Texas’s James Talarico.

“We just proved that all the money in the world is no match for the people of Texas,” Talarico said in his victory speech. “And we just sent a message to every billionaire megadonor, every trillionaire megadonor, every corrupt defender of this broken political system — in this state, in this country, power belongs to the people.”

“South Carolina . . . you have shown the nation that in this era of partisan divides, of vitriol and name calling, in a politics dominated by billionaires and special interest groups and insiders in Washington. D.C., that we will not bow down,” Andrews said.

In many ways, the commonality between the swing candidates and the progressives was a villainization of Washington insiders who take corporate donations, a criticism Democratic leadership (who have to fill the party coffers) will itself have to face.

As Harvie went door knocking in middle- and working-class Levittown after Clark’s appearance at his campaign headquarters, he made a similar pitch. After pledging to end the war in Iran, fight tariffs, and bring down costs, Harvie told the voters who opened their doors that he refused corporate PAC money and wanted to ban members of Congress from trading stocks — a comment that had more than one voter nodding along.

At a breakfast meeting the next morning of a local Yardley-Morrisville chapter of Indivisible, a left-leaning grass-roots organization that at times wars with Democratic leaders, the potential signs that Democrats could actually be the big tent they strive to be were there.

Jennifer Marsh, one of the group’s organizers who developed a social media campaign in support of Harvie, said she was a longtime supporter of staunch progressive Vermont independent Senator Bernie Sanders, who perhaps on policy wouldn’t line up neatly with Harvie. But she saw no daylight with him because his background spoke volumes to her.

“When I look at the parties, I see one represented by billionaires and one represented by teachers and social workers, like Bob Harvie was a teacher,” said Marsh, a 63-year-old retired art director from Lower Makefield. “I believe the Democratic Party has to swing back toward that, and I believe Bob Harvie does too.”

Marsh was working alongside another local activist, Doug Moyer, a 65-year-old retired Education Testing Services employee and former longtime Republican who became a Democrat in 2015. But despite his close friendship and activism work with Marsh, Moyer said he feared the party will be “swayed by the allure of the progressive” and “lose twice as many moderate centrist independents.”

He said the key to keeping the coalition will be appearing steady to voters.

“Both parties make mistakes, but it’s very clear to me if you’re reasonable, objective, not living in a bubble, which party is insane, or which party is more reasonable,” Moyer said. “Yes, we have extremists in our party, the far progressive left, but they’re a tiny percentage compared to the number of crazy extremists in the other party.”

—

title: CBS: Katherine Clark of Massachusetts will be first woman to serve as House majority leader, Hakeem Jeffries says
text:
Massachusetts Congresswoman Katherine Clark is set to make history as the first woman to become a majority leader in Congress, the leader of the House Democrats said Wednesday.

Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, widely expected to be elected the next speaker of the House after Democrats won big in the 2026 midterm elections, introduced Clark at a news conference as “the next majority leader of the House of Representatives” and “someone who will be the first woman to ever serve in that position in our 250-year journey.”

Clark, the current House minority whip who lives in Revere, was elected to Congress in 2013 to replace now-Sen. Ed Markey. The 63-year-old said she was proud to “make history” as part of the new majority.

“In the words of the great Dolly Parton, it’s been a long hard fight, but I see a brand new day a-dawning,” Clark said.

Clark has been outspoken about childcare issues, introducing the Babies Act in 2022 to support new mothers with more access to birth centers and midwives. She also bashed President Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill” last year, calling it “incredibly cruel” for making cuts to Medicaid and food stamps.

Clark still needs to be elected by her House colleagues to become majority leader in the new Congress. She said Wednesday that Americans are trusting her party to do more than just “damage control” on the Trump administration.

“They have entrusted a Democratic Congress to lead us forward to something better, to make their lives easier,” she said.

Clark on Thursday officially declared her intent to run for majority leader in a letter to other Democratic representatives.

“My priority will be ensuring that every corner of our Caucus is heard and empowered to have a role in the policymaking process,” Clark wrote. “At every decision point, I intend to work closely with you to understand the needs of your district and maximize your ability to deliver for your constituents.”

Steve Kerrigan, chair of the Massachusetts Democratic Party, has known Clark since she first ran to be on the Melrose School Committee back in 2001.

“It’s huge. The last time we’ve had someone at that height in House leadership was Tip O’Neill and that was decades ago,” Kerrigan said. “I am excited for the world to get to know the really incredibly special person she is and the great leader that she is.”

WBZ-TV political analyst Jon Keller said Clark as majority leader could mean millions of dollars in funding for Massachusetts.

“That’s an area where during the last two years of the Trump administration we have really been hurt by cuts and federal research grants and other funding sources,” Keller said.

Congresswoman Clark’s office did not return WBZ’s request for an interview.

—

title: CommonWealth Beacon: A former state lawmaker, Clark now ready to help set US House agenda
text:
US REP. KATHERINE CLARK and fellow Democrats eyeing leadership roles in the US House and Senate will be busy over the next several weeks solidifying an agenda they hope will help the party hold onto, and possibly expand, its base of support over the next few years.

Top Democrats agree their agenda will focus on ways to lower costs including reversing Medicaid cuts and opposing tariffs proposed by President Donald Trump.

Asked by a reporter on Wednesday about priorities, New York Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, who is favored to become the next House speaker, said “we have been focused relentlessly on dealing with the affordability crisis and driving down the high cost of living.”

That includes extending Affordable Care Act premium tax credits that expired last year, lifting Trump’s tariffs, reversing cuts to Medicaid and ending the “reckless and costly war” that has driven up gas prices.

“We ran as affordability Democrats, and every single campaign had that at its center: lower costs, make sure every American has health care when and where they need it, that they can afford and hold those who are enriching themselves through corruption at taxpayers’ expense accountable and that’s exactly what we’re going to do,” Clark said during a press conference on Wednesday.

“The priority, the agenda – we cannot wait to get this big caucus together and help set that with the speaker’s vision and guidance. But I can tell you this: that every week when we come to the floor, it is going to be the people of this country who are going to be the focus of the work we do and the campaign promises made are going to be promises kept,” she said.

State lawmakers are processing a supplemental budget that features appropriations to cover explosive Medicaid spending and any changes to that program will be watched closely for fiscal impacts on the state budget and those covered by the sweeping health insurance and safety net program. Legislators now have members of the state’s congressional delegation poised to help set national policies in 2027 and 2028, although their offerings could be vetoed by President Trump.

Clark served in the Massachusetts House from 2008 until 2010 and in the state Senate from 2011 until 2013. A Revere Democrat and current minority whip, she is favored to become the next majority leader – and the first woman to hold the role – after Democrats won back control of Congress on Tuesday.

US Rep. Richard Neal, who’s viewed as the next chair of the US House Ways and Means Committee, told the News Service that he’d like restoration of ACA credits to be one of the House’s first actions. He also believes that some Republicans, who will now be in the minority party, can feel freer to oppose tariffs that President Donald Trump proposes.

“We’re likely to have a substantial majority, and they’re likely to be able to read what happened to them at this last election,” Neal said.

Neal said he and Clark are on the same page and meet regularly.

“We convene for breakfast, the Democratic leadership team every Wednesday morning at 8:15 a.m., and Katherine and I actually sit next to Hakeem Jeffries. So it’s been a good, strong relationship that we’ve had,” he said.

Democrats flipped 31 US House seats to secure 240 spots to Republicans’ 147 with 48 races yet to be called as of about 9:45 a.m. on Thursday, according to The Associated Press. In the Senate, Democrats flipped seven seats for a majority of 54-44 with two races undecided.

And as top Democrats still need the caucus’s backing to solidify their leadership roles, they will have to focus more efforts on understanding the priorities of newly elected members that flipped seats in areas that have been dominated by Republicans, said James Messner, former deputy political director for US House Majority Leader Steve Scalise.

“They’re there because of the large majority that these members in Trump-won districts have provided them, and they haven’t been on the ground talking to voters like these new members have, so they’re going to learn a lot over the next couple weeks of what is it exactly that these voters want done from these new members, and it’ll adjust the priorities,” Messner said, adding that the cost of living will likely remain House Democrats’ top priority.

Neal is aware of this reality and said he wants to craft legislation that those members can feel good about supporting as well as include them in the legislative process.

“I think there’s a reminder there for the Democratic caucus, and I think Hakeem Jeffries has understood it quite clearly, and that is that many of these members that got elected last evening – they come from purple districts. They’re likely to have major opponents in two years,” he said.

Also, while some Democrats have called for impeaching Trump, Jeffries has been less enthusiastic about the idea.

“I haven’t had a single member of the House Democratic caucus talk to me about impeachment,” he said. “We’ve been relentlessly focused on affordability and on accountability because the House is a separate and co-equal branch of government, we recognize that we don’t work for Donald Trump, we don’t work for J.D. Vance, we don’t work for the Supreme Court.”

“House Democrats are going to lead a Congress that does serve as a check and balance on an out-of-control executive branch,” Jeffries said, adding that he has not “heard from President Trump.”

To cement the caucus’s support, Clark and Jeffries – along with others seeking leadership roles – are also expected to be spending the next several days and weeks contacting newly elected members of Congress.

“Those relationships are largely intact well before Election Day, and they’re spending today calling them directly to find out ‘how can I support you in staffing your office?’” said Messner. “…A lot of these members are going to need assistance, and Jeffries and Clark are going to be that main point of contact to help them get set up.”

The idea of Jeffries and Clark leading the caucus is not new – in 2022, former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi endorsed the pair along with California Rep. Pete Aguilar as the next trio of top Democrats. Also, experts say the reelection campaigns for those seeking leadership roles have also doubled as unofficial internal campaigns as they spent much of the election cycle fundraising and backing candidates.

“In a sense, that was their campaign. They were out there over the past two years proving to their colleagues that they deserve to have these leadership positions and they were raising resources, recruiting candidates, coaching those candidates, traveling to those districts, supporting them, so that when it comes time to take this vote in early January, that that it’ll be a no-brainer,” said former Democratic New Hampshire US Rep. Annie Kuster.

That’s largely the case for Neal, who was first elected to Washington in 1988. He was elected chair of the House Committee on Ways and Means in 2019 and held that post until 2023 when Republicans took control of Congress. Neal, the committee’s ranking member, told the News Service that he’s maintained “pretty good loyalty with Democratic members” and helped dozens of candidates throughout the election.

“I would anticipate that,” Neal said when asked if he viewed his support for other candidates as an unofficial campaign for chairmanship. “I also would point out that I had a pretty good run the last time I was chairman, and I would intend to certainly build upon what we did.”

—

title: NYT: Katherine Clark Could Be the House Majority Leader. Who Is She?
text:
Representative Katherine M. Clark of Massachusetts, the No. 2 House Democrat, is set to become the majority leader in January, after her party won control of the chamber.

Ms. Clark, 63, a quiet, progressive power player in Congress, would make history as the first woman to hold that role, though Representative Nancy Pelosi broke a higher glass ceiling in 2007 when she became the first woman to be speaker.

“I feel a weight of responsibility,” Ms. Clark said in an interview this week. “It’s the women’s voices from traveling across my district and the country that really haunt me.”

Described by friends as similar in ideology and temperament to Senator Elizabeth Warren, also of Massachusetts, Ms. Clark is set to be the most liberal member on House Democrats’ leadership team next year. The majority leader is responsible for setting the schedule, but Ms. Clark has also come to be known in her caucus as a master of member management, keeping up with the needs and issues, both personal and political, of Democratic lawmakers.

Here is what you need to know about Ms. Clark.

She built her base of power among women.

Unlike Representative Hakeem Jeffries, the New York Democrat who is poised to be speaker and who has been viewed as a rising star since he entered state politics, Ms. Clark’s path was not always obvious.

A lawyer by training, Ms. Clark first became involved in politics when she joined her school committee to advocate all-day kindergarten for her children. She served in the State Legislature before she was elected to Congress in 2013.

In Washington, she quietly built a base of support, starting with the female lawmakers who lived in her apartment building near the Capitol.

“One of the first roles in leadership was recruitment,” recalled Representative Grace Meng, Democrat of New York, a close friend who lives in the building. “I’d see her spend countless hours counseling candidates, especially women candidates, and slowly people realized what a leader she was.”

In the role of minority whip, Ms. Clark has gained the trust of members across the caucus, who said her mantra was simple: “You vote your district every time; you just let me know how you’re going to vote.”

She also brings an attentive eye and parental energy to the job.

“She takes care of us in many ways,” said Representative Lateefah Simon, a progressive Democrat from California. “I remember her telling me in the hall that my jacket was a little wrinkly. She said, ‘We’ll steam it for you.’”

And her style has engendered loyalty.

Ms. Simon, who lost her husband to leukemia in 2014, said Ms. Clark requested to visit a children’s hospital in her district in Oakland to highlight the Trump administration’s canceling clinical trials for cancer patients.

“I thought, ‘I’ll follow you anywhere,’” she said.

Ms. Warren, another close friend who said the two often catch up at the JetBlue terminal on their way to and from Washington, said of Ms. Clark: “She’s on my speed dial, and I hope I’m on hers.”

She is further to the left on Israel than Hakeem Jeffries.

Speaking at an event in her district last year hosted by a Quaker organization, Ms. Clark described Israel’s actions in Gaza as a genocide when she encouraged people to take action on political issues, including “stopping the starvation and genocide and destruction in Gaza.”

That made her the most senior Democrat in leadership to use the term, which she then abruptly retracted. Ms. Clark said in a statement that she had repeated the word “genocide” in response to a question and stated: “I am not accusing Israel of genocide.”

Still, Ms. Clark is notably further to the left on Israel than Representative Hakeem Jeffries, a longtime supporter of the Jewish state who represents one of the largest Jewish communities in the country and is in line to become speaker.

In July, when the House voted on a Republican measure to eliminate U.S. aid to Israel, Mr. Jeffries opposed it while Ms. Clark voted in favor. Ms. Clark said at the time that she supported the measure, “not because I agree with the entirety of the amendment, or the G.O.P.’s cynical motivations for its consideration, but because I believe we must change course.”

And it was notably Ms. Clark — not Mr. Jeffries — who first reached out to offer congratulations in the primary victory of Darializa Avila Chevalier, a democratic socialist from New York who attended a pro-Palestinian rally in the city the day after the Hamas attack on Israel in October 2023.

Her trans daughter has shaped her views.

Ms. Clark has been a vocal advocate of rights for transgender people, often invoking her support for her trans daughter, Riley Dowell, when opposing legislation and statements that target the group.

“I rise in honor of trans joy that deserves to be celebrated, not eradicated,” Ms. Clark said on the House floor three years ago. “I rise with unconditional love for my trans daughter, Riley, and I rise in solidarity with every trans American seeking nothing less than their inalienable right to the pursuit of happiness.”

Representative Sarah McBride, Democrat of Delaware and the first openly transgender member of Congress, said: “As the mother of a trans kid, she understands on a deeply personal level the importance of standing up for the dignity of every person, and I have felt that support firsthand.”

Ms. Clark’s personal life has shaped her policy views in other ways. She has spoken at length about being a primary caregiver to her parents and her three children, noting how that experience influenced her priorities. She has long made accessible and affordable child care one of her top issues.

“I ran for this seat originally in large part because of child care and making sure that is something that all families can access and afford,” she said in the interview. “That we’re also bringing up the wages of child care providers and early educators that are overwhelmingly women and women of color to a livable wage continues to be a high priority for me.”

Ms. Clark said she thinks constantly about the women she has met on the campaign trail who are struggling.

“There are moms who try and brush off that they are giving up one or two meals a day so their kids can eat,” she said. “They tell me, ‘Well, I could stand to lose a few pounds.’”

She is the rare No. 2 who hasn’t sought to be No. 1.

Historically, the second-ranking leader in the House is smarting (and sometimes actively seething) over the fact that he isn’t in the top job.

Representative Steny H. Hoyer, Democrat of Maryland and the former majority leader, saw his political ambitions over two decades sometimes squeezed by Ms. Pelosi, a onetime rival for power.

Representative Steve Scalise, Republican of Louisiana and the majority leader, was a longtime rival to former Speaker Kevin McCarthy. After Mr. McCarthy’s ouster, Mr. Scalise made his own, failed bid for the top job that ultimately went to a more junior congressman from his state, Mike Johnson. That relationship has also been tense underneath the veneer of southern politeness.

Ms. Clark and Mr. Jeffries are not close friends, but work well together and are in constant communication, according to people familiar with their relationship, and she has shown no interest in holding the top job. In fact, when Ms. Pelosi announced in 2022 that she would step aside from the top job, Ms. Clark cut a deal with Mr. Jeffries that he would seek the No. 1 position and she would be the No. 2, even though Ms. Clark had a more senior position on the leadership team.

For one, the job of speaker involves being the lead fund-raiser for the party, and Ms. Clark has never relished the task, though she raised $50 million this cycle.

“She is very respectful to Hakeem, and they talk all the time,” Ms. Meng said. “They are really thoughtful about strategizing and presenting a united front to the caucus.”

—

title: WCVB: Mass. Rep. Katherine Clark asks Democrats for support to become first woman House majority leader
text:
House Minority Whip Katherine Clark has sent a letter to her fellow Democrats asking for their support to become the next Majority Leader.

Clark would be the first woman to serve in that top leadership role.

Right now, Democrats are plotting their strategy for the new Congress, after overwhelming victories nationwide during the midterm elections.

They say they want to focus on lowering costs, as well as accountability and oversight.

“We’re going to lower their costs, we’re going to make healthcare affordable and available, and we’re going to hold the crooks accountable,” Clark said. “Unfortunately, there are a lot of potential subjects.”

“Obviously, everything he’s done is now on the table and the Democrats will have subpoena power, will be able to root out what Trump and his children, his cronies, his corporations have been doing. And we will just follow the evidence,” said Sen. Ed Markey.

Democrats said they want to end the war in Iran, reverse health care cuts and put a stop to tariffs.

Markey was asked if he’d support Chuck Schumer as Senate Majority Leader.

He did not say either way, but did say that Schumer called him on election night to congratulate him.

title: Whip Clark on CNN: “Affordability Democrats” Will Put People First
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Today, Democratic Whip Katherine Clark (MA-5) appeared on CNN’s News Central to discuss House Democrats’ sweeping victory and their affordability agenda for the 120th Congress. Below are excerpts of the conversation.

On the Priorities of a Democratic House Majority:

“We campaigned as Affordability Democrats. That was the message of every single candidate across this country. And that is exactly how we’re going to govern … we know this: that we are going to put the focus on a people-based agenda.

“And our first bills and acts are going to be about lowering costs, making sure healthcare is affordable for everyone. That is what we have promised the American people. It’s why they voted in this historical way. The voters have really conducted a peaceful revolution in this country, and we are going to govern with their voices as our guides.”

On Democrats’ Fight to End the War in Iran:

“What we have seen is a president who has taken us into a reckless war that had no exit strategy, had no clear goals, and has had a terrible impact on the American people — whether it’s the cost of gas and diesel skyrocketing prices even further.

“We’re going to have very clear discussions about how we have voted repeatedly to end this war, and how they continue to fund this without ever coming to Congress and having a discussion about what these goals are, and how we get out of this and make sure the American people and our troops are safe.”

On Holding Crooks Accountable and Delivering for Working Families:

“Part of our promise to the American people is that we’re going to lower their costs, we’re going to make healthcare affordable and available, and we’re going to hold the crooks accountable. Unfortunately, there are a lot of potential subjects.

“But I can tell you that it will be a continuation of making sure that taxpayers are not paying the costs for personal enrichment, for the corruption that we are seeing from this administration, and that has been tolerated by the Republican Party. It is part of what has led to this landslide victory for Democrats.

“The American people understand they are not the ones who are being enriched in this economy. The metaphors I heard throughout my travels in the campaign is that ‘my family is drowning in bills, we’re barely able to keep our head above water.’ And so our focus, whether it’s lowering costs or looking at corruption, is all going to be through the lens of the working family and making their lives easier.”

On the Diversity and Strength of the House Democratic Caucus:

“We have seen leadership across this country, and certainly in our class, that is emerging. The voices that we are going to bring forward are going to be not only our senior leadership, but those of our newest Members. And we are seeing Members coming in from across this country, coast to coast, from the heartland, from the South, and that is going to be a real strength of this caucus. We’re going to make sure that their voices are heard, because that is representational government. From different parts of our country, different parts of the ideological spectrum, we come together. We make a better product that puts the people of this country at the center of it.”

title: Kennedy Announces Nearly $150,000 in Federal Grants for Buffalo Naval Park to Tell the Stories of African American Sailors and Honor Western New York Veterans
text:
National Park Service Grant will Fund an Exhibit on African American Naval Service - Institute of Museum of Library Services Grant Supports a Virtual Wall of Honor

BUFFALO, N.Y. - Congressman Tim Kennedy (NY-26) today announced two federal grants totaling nearly $150,000 for the Buffalo and Erie County Naval & Military Park. The National Park Service (NPS) awarded $97,176 through its African American Civil Rights Preservation and History Grants program for an African American Naval Service exhibit, which will interpret the history of racial segregation aboard the park’s historic naval vessels and the experiences of the African American sailors who served during that era. The Institute of Museum and Library Services (IMLS) awarded a $51,591 matching grant through its Inspire! Grants for Small Museums program to create a Virtual Wall of Honor that preserves and shares the stories and service records of Western New York veterans.

“The Buffalo Naval Park is where Western New York comes to remember those who served, and these grants will help it tell even more of that story,” said Congressman Kennedy. “African American sailors served our country with honor and distinction while facing segregation aboard the very ships that visitors tour today, and an honest account of their experiences belongs in our understanding of that complex history. The Virtual Wall of Honor will make it easier for families to find and learn about the veterans they love. I congratulate everyone at the Naval Park on earning these highly sought after awards and I’m glad to see this support coming to Buffalo’s waterfront.”

“These federal investments will help us preserve more than history,” said Brian Luallen, President & CEO, Buffalo Naval Park. “They will help us tell the stories of the men and women who lived it. From the experiences of African American sailors aboard our historic ships to the legacies of Western New York veterans honored on our Wall of Honor, every name represents a life and every story deserves to be told. We're grateful to Congressman Kennedy, the National Park Service, and the Institute of Museum and Library Services for helping us carry these stories forward for generations to come.”

The NPS grant is one of 54 projects in 18 states funded this year through the African American Civil Rights Preservation and History program, which draws on the Historic Preservation Fund. The IMLS grant was highly competitive. The agency received 299 applications requesting more than $11 million and made 88 awards totaling $3.3 million. In 2025, Kennedy fought back against efforts to dismantle the IMLS. The Virtual Wall of Honor will give visitors a multisensory way to explore veterans’ stories and learn about family members, hometown neighbors, and others connected to them, and the project includes staff training. Located at Canalside, the park is home to the USS The Sullivans, USS Little Rock, USS Croaker, and PTF 17. The park first opened to the public in 1979.

title: Local Leaders, Caltrain, Mullin Secure $90 Million Grant for Burlingame Grade Separation Project
text:
San Mateo, CA — U.S. Rep. Kevin Mullin (CA-15) is pleased to share that the Federal Railroad Administration (FRA) has awarded $90.4 million for construction of the Caltrain Broadway Grade Separation Project in Burlingame through the Railroad Crossing Elimination Program.

Rep. Mullin advocated in support of Caltrain’s application for the capital grant in partnership with the San Mateo County Transportation Authority (SMCTA) and the city of Burlingame. The California Public Utilities Commission ranks the Broadway crossing as the top-priority grade separation in California. More than 30,000 vehicles travel through the crossing each day. By separating the rail line from the street, the project will improve safety, reduce congestion and lower emissions.

In addition to the $90 million federal grant made possible through the 2021 Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, earlier this year Rep. Mullin was able to secure an additional $3 million in federal funds for the project as part of the annual appropriations process.

“Caltrain, the City of Burlingame, and the San Mateo County Transportation Authority have been working tirelessly to make important safety upgrades at Broadway, which has been deemed the most dangerous rail crossing in all of California,” said Rep. Mullin. “I have been partnering with Caltrain, the SMCTA and the City to bring home more federal support for the Broadway Burlingame Grade Separation project and am thrilled it has rightfully earned an additional $90 million grant from the Federal Railroad Administration. In addition to the $3 million in federal Community Project Funding I brought home earlier this year, this FRA grant will go a long way to helping improve safety in our community.”

“These federal awards advance the grade separations our communities need to enhance protection for pedestrians, cyclists, drivers and our passengers, and create a safer corridor for generations to come,” said Rico E. Medina, Caltrain Board Chair.

“This federal investment marks a major milestone for the Broadway Grade Separation Project and reflects the sustained partnership among SMCTA, Caltrain, the City of Burlingame and our state and federal leaders,” said Julia Mates, chair of the San Mateo County Transportation Authority Board of Directors. “SMCTA’s local investment helped position this critical project for delivery, improving safety and regional mobility.”

“The City of Burlingame thanks its federal partners for joining our State, County and City financing team to finally make Broadway grade separation a reality,” said Burlingame Mayor Michael Brownrigg. “Hard work, sharp pencils, and leaders who focus on the long term are what helped get this critical project over the goal line, and our residents and our region will be the better and safer for it.

This FRA grant secures a critical piece of the grade separation project’s funding and keeps the project on track for construction. The partners will continue to pursue funding for additional pedestrian and bicycle circulation improvements and coordinate those improvements with project delivery. Site preparation, utility relocation and other early construction work are expected to begin in May 2027. Construction is expected to be complete in January 2032.

title: Rep. Nancy Mace Introduces Bill to Expose Microplastics Hidden in Clothing
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. (Nov. 5, 2026) – Today, Congresswoman Nancy Mace introduced the Clothing Microplastic Transparency Act of 2026, legislation requiring clothing companies to disclose microplastic content in the products they sell.

“Americans deserve to know what is in the clothing touching their skin all day long,” said Congresswoman Mace. “While current labels list fiber content, they do not disclose microplastics. Our bill puts the facts on the tag. At a time when microplastics and other components have fueled health concerns, you deserve to know what you wear.”

The Clothing Microplastic Transparency Act would:

Require any company selling or offering clothing for sale to disclose the estimated mass of microplastic in each item through a stamp, tag, label, or similar identification.

Direct the Federal Trade Commission (FTC), in consultation with the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), to issue regulations within one year of enactment, including a standardized test method companies must use to estimate microplastic content.

Treat violations as unfair or deceptive acts or practices under the Federal Trade Commission Act, enforced by the FTC.

title: Rep. Joe Neguse Announces Candidacy for Assistant Speaker
text:
Washington, D.C. — Today, Colorado Congressman Joe Neguse announced his candidacy for the position of Assistant Speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives. Neguse currently serves as Assistant Democratic Leader, and at Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries’ request, served as Chair of House Democrats’ Litigation Task Force in the 119th Congress.

If elected, Neguse will become the youngest lawmaker in the history of the Congress to assume the role of Assistant Speaker, a position previously held by leading voices in the Democratic Party, including Whip Katherine Clark and Senator Ben Ray Luján.

In a letter sent to his colleagues, Neguse cited efforts to ensure voices from across the House Democratic Caucus are uplifted, included, and heard. He pointed to the broad constituency of his own large congressional district in the Rocky Mountain West—spanning rural, suburban, and urban areas—as a demonstration of this ability. The millennial Congressman, 42, is the only non-coastal member of senior House Democratic leadership, and the youngest member of the team.

Neguse also highlighted his team’s work to expand support for Members, specifically by assisting new Members with their transition to Congress, enhancing staff assistance programs, and assessing and addressing the needs of congressional offices across the country. He also pointed to his successful efforts as Chair of the Litigation Task Force as an example of how he would continue to use his leadership skills to assist Committee leaders and fellow Members in fighting back against the Trump administration’s rampant lawlessness.

During the 119th Congress, the Litigation Task Force was responsible for taking unprecedented steps to stand up for the American people, filing dozens of legal challenges in federal courts across the country and paving the way for judges to strike down disastrous and unconstitutional directives from the Trump White House, including illegal tariffs, restrictions on voting by mail, stripping individuals born on U.S. soil of the guarantee to birthright citizenship, and unlawful impoundments of taxpayer funds.

Read Neguse’s entire letter to his colleagues HERE and below.

November 5, 2026

Dear Colleague:

It has been an honor to serve as Assistant Democratic Leader, and to work alongside each of you during the 119th Congress. I remain deeply inspired by the talent, commitment, and tenacity our caucus has consistently shown. With our decisive and overwhelming victory this week, it is more important than ever for the House Democratic Caucus to be unified in the 120th Congress, and to repay the faith that the American people have put in us to lower costs, end corruption, and deliver for working families. To that end, and as we embark on that road together, I write to respectfully request your support for Assistant Speaker.

I’m deeply grateful to have had the opportunity to serve our caucus in House Leadership, mostly recently as Assistant Democratic Leader and previously as a Co-Chair and Chairman of the DPCC, DCCC Recruitment/Red-to-Blue Co-Chair and National Finance Co-Chair. In each position, I’ve worked to engage everyone in our caucus, firmly rooted in my belief that every member has much to offer to the House and to the country. As someone who represents a large rural, suburban, and urban district (with agricultural communities extending all the way to the Wyoming border), I’ve long worked hard to effectively serve a broad constituency — and I’ve adopted that same approach as a member of the leadership team, ensuring voices from across our caucus and the ideological spectrum are elevated, included, and heard.

As Assistant Leader, my focus has been on serving our caucus — by expanding opportunities for members, enhancing staff assistance programs, and ensuring our office is addressing your technical needs. With your help, we launched the successful New-Member ADL Mentorship Program to assist new members with their transition to the Congress. We also worked to uplift each and every member of the broader caucus, including through monthly ADL press conferences and corresponding special order programming — elevating your talents and expertise for the benefit of the country. And through our office’s management of House Democrats’ District Director Services Program, our team has worked to assist your District staff with their everyday needs, including via our weekly roundtables, technical assistance programs, annual Conference & Fly-In, and the new District Director Mentoring program we launched earlier this year.

Finally, at the request of Leader Jeffries, I was proud to serve as Chair of the Litigation Task Force for House Democrats, and in so doing, provide Members with opportunities to weigh-in on over twenty lawsuits against the Trump Administration's lawlessness. From our successful amicus briefs in multiple cases, our groundbreaking lawsuit against ICE, and regular programming opportunities for member engagement with legal experts, I’m deeply grateful to the many members of our caucus who made the Task Force’s work so consequential and impactful. And with your support, I would be honored to continue that work with each of you and our talented Committee leaders in the 120th Congress.

If elected Assistant Speaker, my goals would be straight-forward — to prioritize direct member services for every member of our diverse and talented caucus, and to assist Speaker Jeffries and our incredible Democratic Leadership team. In addition to continuing the existing programming of the Assistant Leader’s Office, I’d relish the opportunity to launch multiple new programs, including expanding training programs for our District Directors, launching a new technical assistance program for subcommittee chairs, and enhancing the mentorship and transition programming for new members. All in all, I believe such efforts will ensure that every member and their office has the resources they need to succeed.

In sum, it has been such a privilege to work alongside each of you over the past several years, and it would truly be an honor to serve our caucus, the Congress and the country as Assistant Speaker. I look forward to continuing the conversation with you about my candidacy and ideas, and thank you so much for your consideration.

Sincerely,

###

title: Pelosi Statement on the Sentencing of Joshua Wong
text:
San Francisco — Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi issued this statement on the Hong Kong court’s decision to sentence pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong to 10 years in prison.

“A Hong Kong court’s decision to sentence Joshua Wong to a new 10-year prison term under Beijing’s so-called national security law is an appalling abuse of power. After nearly six years behind bars, Joshua was just two months from going home. Now he faces imprisonment until 2036.

“Joshua has stood with the people of Hong Kong in their struggle for freedom since he was a teenager. While the judge said the sentence was meant to deter others, it’s clear the example Joshua has set will outlast any prison sentence.

“The United States and the international community must demand Joshua’s immediate and unconditional release. Beijing is counting on Joshua and others imprisoned for defending Hong Kong’s freedoms to believe no one cares enough to speak out for them. We will never forget Joshua Wong, Jimmy Lai or their fellow political prisoners, and we will keep speaking out until they are free.”

title: Pressley, Warren, 31 Colleagues Press Dept. of Education Secretary on Federal Student Loan Servicing Failures
text:
Lawmakers amplify concerns raised by state student loan ombudspersons in 7 states and D.C.

“Failures in federal student loan servicing have repeatedly posed severe and costly problems for American families.”

Text of Letter (PDF)

BOSTON – Today, Congresswoman Ayanna Pressley (MA-07) and Senator Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) led 31 colleagues on a letter to Department of Education (ED) Secretary Linda McMahon highlighting serious concerns regarding the federal student loan servicing system that were recently raised by a coalition of eight state Student Loan Ombudspersons.

“Failures in federal student loan servicing have repeatedly posed severe and costly problems for American families. . . .Rather than tackle these servicing failures, the Trump administration has enabled more to occur,” wrote the lawmakers.

In September 2026, the Student Loan Ombudspersons in Massachusetts, Washington, California, Oregon, Nevada, Connecticut, the District of Columbia, and Illinois sent a letter to Secretary McMahon highlighting “recurring systemic problems involving income-driven repayment (IDR) plans and Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF) that materially affect borrowers’ payment obligations, loan balances, and access to forgiveness.” The Ombudspersons raised a host of specific issues, including inaccurate calculations of monthly payments, loan balances, and IDR payment counts, and severe delays in the processing of IDR applications.

“The scale and severity of the errors documented by the Student Loan Ombudspersons—and their recommended solutions—demand immediate consideration and a meaningful response,” concluded the lawmakers.

Text of the letter is accessible here.

Federal representatives from all eight jurisdictions represented by the Ombudspersons signed the letter.

In addition to Senator Warren and Representative Pressley, the letter was signed by U.S. Senators Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), Dick Durbin (D-Ill.), Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.), Ed Markey (D-Mass.), Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.), Patty Murray (D-Wash.), and Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), along with U.S. Representatives Julia Brownley (D-Calif.), Judy Chu (D-Calif.), Lou Correa (D-Calif.), Jim Costa (D-Calif.), John Garamendi (D-Calif.), Lateefah Simon (D-Calif.), Mark Takano (D-Calif.), Maxine Waters (D-Calif.), Joe Courtney (D-Conn.), Rosa DeLauro (D-Conn.), Eleanor Holmes Norton (D-D.C.), Danny Davis (D-Ill.), Jonathan Jackson (D-Ill.), Bill Keating (D-Mass.), Stephen Lynch (D-Mass.), Jim McGovern (D-Mass.), Seth Moulton (D-Mass.), Lori Trahan (D-Mass.), Dina Titus (D-Nev.), Suzanne Bonamici (D-Ore.), Val Hoyle (D-Ore.), Emily Randall (D-Wash.), and Kim Schrier (D-Wash).

title: Reps. Salinas, Mackenzie Introduce Bill to Protect Patients When Insurance Companies Drop Their Providers
text:
Washington, D.C. — Today, Congresswoman Andrea Salinas (OR-06) and Rep. Ryan Mackenzie (PA-07) introduced the Right to Re-Enroll Act. The bipartisan bill would protect patients from unexpected changes to their health insurance coverage. It would allow Americans enrolled in Affordable Care Act (ACA) marketplace plans to switch insurance plans outside of the annual open enrollment period if their provider or health system is dropped from their insurance network.

When providers and insurance companies fail to reach agreements on contracts, patients can suddenly lose access to the clinicians and hospitals they rely on. These disputes are becoming increasingly common. Between 2021 and 2025, nearly one in five non-federal hospitals experienced a public contract dispute with an insurance company, and nearly 10 percent temporarily fell out of network with an insurer.

“Families are already paying too much for health care. They shouldn't have to worry about losing their provider on top of it,” said Rep. Salinas. “Right now, patients can find themselves stuck paying for a plan that no longer covers their provider or hospital. That's especially concerning for people living in rural areas who are far from other providers, or for people undergoing treatment who can't afford an interruption in care. No one should lose access to their provider because their insurance company and health system can't agree on a contract. This bill gives patients the freedom to find a plan that meets their needs and protects them from unexpectedly losing access to care.”

“Patients and families across the Lehigh Valley and the Poconos should not have to worry about losing access to their trusted doctors or facing unexpected disruptions in care because of changes to their insurance network,” said Congressman Ryan Mackenzie. “The bipartisan Right to Re-Enroll Act would give patients more options when unexpected changes to their insurance coverage disrupt their access to care. By working across the aisle, we can put patients first and help ensure greater access to quality, affordable health care.”

Currently, Medicare Advantage enrollees have the ability to change plans when significant changes are made to their provider networks. However, Americans who purchase health insurance through ACA marketplaces do not have the same protections when their insurance company drops a provider from its network.

The Right to Re-Enroll Act would:

Give patients the right to switch plans: Create a 60-day special enrollment period for individuals enrolled in ACA marketplace plans when a provider leaves their insurance network, outside of the annual enrollment period.

Protect patients from unexpected costs: Require insurers to maintain existing coverage terms and in-network cost-sharing for qualifying patients who continue receiving care from an affected provider for 90 days.

Require insurers to notify patients: Ensure patients receive notice within seven days of a network change, including information about their right to switch plans and how changing plans could affect their deductible and out-of-pocket costs.

The legislation would apply to ACA marketplace plans beginning in 2027.

“When changes happen in insurance networks or coverage, continuity of care keeps treatment for patients safe and consistent,” said Becky Hultberg, president and CEO of the Hospital Association of Oregon. “Reducing avoidable disruption is the right thing to do for patients, safeguarding their care and easing their burden during treatment. Rep. Salinas’ Right to Re-Enroll Act puts patients first, giving them the peace of mind of knowing they can choose a different health plan during a special re-enrollment period so they can continue getting the care they need without interruption.”

This legislation is endorsed by Families USA, American Psychological Association, Young Invincibles, and the Hospital Association of Oregon.
