title: Quigley's Bill Reauthorizing ALS Research Funding Signed into Law
text:
On November 3, 2026, Chicago Congressman Mike Quigley’s bill—the Access to Critical Therapies for ALS Reauthorization Act (ACT for ALS Reauthorization Act) of 2026—was signed into law. Led by Representatives Quigley (IL-05) and Ken Calvert (CA-41) in the House and Senators Lisa Murkowski (R-AK) and Chris Coons (D-DE) in the Senate, the law renews programs from the 2021 ACT for ALS Law.

“For the past five years, the ACT for ALS has advanced scientific research and helped people with ALS access the promising treatments they need. This reauthorization of the bill continues that work and lends hope to a future where there is a cure for ALS,” said Congressman Quigley. “I'm glad this important bill was signed into law, and I’m thankful to my colleagues in both the House and the Senate for getting this done.”

“I'm thrilled that the ACT for ALS Reauthorization Act has been signed into law, renewing our commitment to finding cures and treatments for ALS,” said Rep. Calvert. “As a Co-Chair of the bipartisan ALS Caucus, I know just how hard those impacted by ALS have worked to get this bill enacted and I applaud their tireless advocacy. With the ACT for ALS Reauthorization Act officially signed into law, we celebrate this victory while remaining focused on the work ahead to end this terrible disease.”

The ACT for ALS Reauthorization Law will codify the Department of Health and Human Services’ (HHS) interpretation of Expanded Access Program eligibility guidelines and require the FDA to create a new 5-year Action Plan for rare neurodegenerative diseases. It will also continue to advance scientific understanding of neurodegenerative diseases and help Americans living with ALS access promising new treatments.

This legislation has been endorsed by I AM ALS, the Muscular Dystrophy Association, the ALS Association, and the ALS Network.

“Over the past 7+ years, this community has changed what's possible in ALS,” said I AM ALS co-founder Brian Wallach. “The I AM ALS community's leadership has brought us closer than ever to a cure by unlocking over $2 billion for federal ALS research, expanding and protecting access to life-changing therapies, and accelerating scientific breakthroughs. We thank our ALS congressional champions—including sponsors Senators Coons (D-DE) and Murkowski (R-AK) and Representatives Quigley (D-IL-05) and Calvert (R-CA-41)—and all the tireless advocates who helped renew this historic legislation for five more years.”

“These past months didn't just get a critical bill passed; they inspired a community that continually renews itself, welcomes new advocates, develops new leaders, and ensures that every generation is ready to fight for the next breakthrough,” said Troy Fields, volunteer co-chair of the I AM ALS legislative affairs team, and person living with ALS. “ALS is relentless, but we continue to prove so are we.”

“We must accelerate research and technology to help make ALS livable and cure it. To every advocate who walked into a congressional office and wouldn't leave without a commitment: you did this. To the families who shared their hardest moments, so other families might have more time: you did this,” said Calaneet Balas, president and CEO of the ALS Association. “We're grateful to our champions on both sides of the aisle who helped make this legislation possible. People living with ALS cannot wait, and neither will we.”

“Today's signing is a defining moment for the ALS community and for everyone working toward a future without this devastating disease,” said Sharon Hesterlee, Ph.D., President and CEO of the Muscular Dystrophy Association. “The Muscular Dystrophy Association was proud to help lead the effort to reauthorize the ACT for ALS because we know that every day matters for people living with ALS. This law preserves the momentum that is driving scientific breakthroughs, expands opportunities for people to participate in research and access promising therapies, and strengthens the partnerships that will lead to the next generation of treatments. Together, we are creating a future where ALS is no longer a fatal diagnosis but a disease that can be effectively treated and ultimately cured.”

“Final passage is a major win for people living with ALS and their families, and a testament to what sustained, collective advocacy can accomplish,” said Sheri Strahl, MPH, MBA, president and CEO of ALS Network. “ALS Network has been deeply engaged throughout this process, working directly with congressional leaders, shaping policy recommendations, bringing the lived experience of people with ALS to Capitol Hill, and mobilizing advocates across the country. We are proud of the role we played alongside partners throughout the ALS community, and are deeply grateful to Representatives Calvert and Quigley, Senators Murkowski and Coons, and every advocate whose persistence helped carry this legislation across the finish line.”

title: Amata Honors the Life of Congresswoman and Educator Pat Saiki
text:
Washington, D.C. – Congresswoman Uifa’atali Amata is honoring the life of Congresswoman Pat Saiki, and her years of public service and lifelong dedication to educational opportunities. At the invitation of her family, Amata was humbled to speak Saturday at the Celebration of Life at Central Union Church in Honolulu.

Honoring the life of history-making Congresswoman Pat Saiki

Remarks in celebration of Pat Saiki’s life:

Talofa lava,

I join you in honoring the precious life of a beloved friend, Patricia Saiki. Most of us knew her as Pat. She lived a remarkable life of service, much of it right here in beautiful Hawaii, first as an educator, as state legislator, as Hawaii’s first Republican Member of the U.S. House since statehood, and just the second Congresswoman in Hawaii history, then as SBA Administrator under President George H.W. Bush. She was a history-maker, a difference-maker, and a champion for opportunities in education.

Pat was an example to me in both public life and private, since I knew the person and the public figure. For instance, she was bipartisan when possible, bridging divides, bringing people together. Washington could use more of that, but she exemplified that approach to putting people first and recognizing that politics, while important, had to be kept in perspective. She could balance being direct and a truth-teller with being diplomatic and tactful. In other words, she was skilled at her public roles. What counts more, is that she put that to use for people. Her energy and drive went for the public good, always a cause or project that would help people, often in the field of education.

I knew her for decades. Through her generous spirit, she had a key role in an eventful part of my life. She was the person behind my opportunity to serve as Secretary of a National Convention. You have to understand how unheard of that was at the time for someone from American Samoa, and this was years before I was elected to Congress. It simply would not have happened without her, but to her it was just being a friend and putting in a good word, and these attributes were a way of life for her. She was a friend to her friends, and she had a lot of friends. We will hold our memories of her friendship close to our hearts.

She was a wife and mother and grandmother. To her children and her grandchildren, I know you brought her joy, and that she was more proud of you than her titles and accolades, though she deserved every accolade.

Speaking at the Celebration of Life

She left us for a better place at the age of 96, and I think a long life can be something of Heaven’s reward on earth, before the true Heavenly rewards to come.

Today, may you all feel the strong support of others around you, and feel the many prayers and thoughts for you, her closest loved ones.

May those of us here resolve to live our lives well, as she did. Her presence was a joy and help to others, and a life to be celebrated. She was a blessing to us, and may we live like her, to bless others. May God’s comfort be near to each one today as we say goodbye to our friend and loved one, in joyful hope of the resurrection, enriched by having known her.

Thank you. Soifua ma ia manuia.

###

title: Amata Pushes to Save ASG Expiring ARPA Dollars in Final Funding Bill
text:
Washington, D.C. – Congresswoman Uifa’atali Amata is pushing to use the last remaining legislative path to save ASG’s expiring ARPA funds, through possible inclusion in a year-end Continuing Resolution (C.R.), often called stopgap funding, that will be necessary to extend funding into 2027 for the U.S. government.

At the same time, Congresswoman Amata is sending a letter to U.S. Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent making the same case and once again highlighting the additional challenges of an island economy that relies heavily on shipping for necessary construction materials and equipment, and the need for additional leeway to complete projects.

“We’re fighting for more time for ASG while facing a firm deadline for ARPA use,” Amata said. “The fact that there are states that also are coming up against the deadline and facing loss of funds with unfinished projects means we’re not alone in urging this extension. In addition to calling for inclusion in the funding legislation, I’m making the same case again to Secretary Bessent, urgently asking for his support in providing more time for ASG.”

The current stopgap funding measure expires on December 11, 2026. With government funding set to expire, lawmakers must act to pass either full-year appropriations bills, another stopgap, or a hybrid package to avoid a partial government shutdown.

“I’m calling for Congress to avoid a shutdown, extend federal funding across the board, and include an ARPA extension in any funding legislation,” concluded Congresswoman Amata. “This would give time for the new Congress to work together on the funding priorities the American people want and expect.”

title: RILEY ANNOUNCES TOOL TO HELP UPSTATE NEW YORKERS SAVE ON UTILITY BILLS
text:
In one minute or less, new site lets NY-19 residents check eligibility for federal and state programs to lower bills, weatherize homes

WASHINGTON D.C. — Today, Congressman Josh Riley (NY-19) announced a new online tool to help Upstate New Yorkers lower their utility bills. With utility costs squeezing family budgets, many residents may qualify for assistance they don’t even know is available. By answering a few short questions at riley.house.gov/save, residents can easily see which federal and state programs they may qualify for and exactly where to apply.

“Heating bills are too high, and winter is just getting started. There’s help out there, but like most things in government, it couldn’t be more confusing, and a lot of people who qualify never even apply,” said Riley. “So my office built a tool to cut through the red tape. In about a minute, you’ll know what you’re eligible for and how to get it, so you can keep more of your hard-earned money in your pocket where it belongs.”

The tool checks eligibility for a range of energy assistance and efficiency programs, including the Home Energy Assistance Program (HEAP), Emergency HEAP, EAP, EEAP, EmPower+, HEAP Clean & Tune, and the Weatherization Assistance Program (WAP). Together, these programs can help with heating costs, emergency assistance when households face a shutoff or run out of fuel, furnace and heating equipment maintenance, and home energy upgrades that lower bills over the long term.

The tool is open to all residents of New York’s 19th Congressional District and comes as the 2026–2027 HEAP season begins. Residents can access the tool at riley.house.gov/save, and constituents who need additional help or have questions about an application can contact Congressman Riley’s office at (607) 242-0200.

The new tool is the latest step in Riley’s fight to take on the utility monopolies and lower costs for Upstate families. Since taking office, Riley has:

Joined the NYSEG and Central Hudson rate cases to fight their rate hikes directly, going head-to-head with the companies on behalf of Upstate ratepayers.

Introduced the Weatherization Enhancement and Readiness Act (H.R. 1355) to help families weatherize their homes, use less energy, and lower their monthly bills.

Introduced the Keep the Lights Local Act (H.R. 5487) to end foreign ownership of American utilities.

Introduced the No Bonuses for Utility Executives Act (H.R. 6590) to ban utility executives from cashing in on bonuses while they jack up rates faster than inflation.

Introduced the No Taxes on Utility Bills Act (H.R. 8350) so families can deduct the taxes and state surcharges tacked onto their gas and electric bills.

Introduced the Lowering Utility Bills Act (H.R. 8568) to stop utility companies from overcharging customers.

Introduced the FAIR Data Act (H.R. 9655) to make sure Big Tech’s data centers pay their own way instead of sticking Upstate families and small businesses with higher energy bills.

Introduced the Smart Meter Data Privacy Protection Act (H.R. 10284) to stop utility companies from selling your personal data collected through smart meters.

title: Schakowsky and Blumenthal Lead Call for Trump Administration to Halt Program Expanding Surveillance of Americans' ED Visits, Raise Privacy Concerns About Use of AI to Analyze Patient Data
text:
Full Text of Letter (PDF)

WASHINGTON – Today, U.S. Representative Jan Schakowsky (IL-09) and U.S. Senator Richard Blumenthal (D-CT) led a letter to U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) Acting Chair Peter Feldman demanding answers about the Trump Administration’s proposed changes to a program used to inform product safety recalls that would expand surveillance of Americans’ emergency department records and risk patients’ privacy. In their letter to Feldman, Schakowsky, Blumenthal, U.S. Representative Kevin Mullin (CA-15), and U.S. Senator Adam Schiff (D-CA), raised concerns that the CPSC’s proposed changes to the National Electronic Injury Surveillance System (NEISS) unnecessarily expands the scope of the program’s surveillance efforts and exposes patient data to security risks due to the implementation of artificial intelligence (AI) in the program.

“The NEISS is an important tool that allows the CPSC to monitor product safety trends and issue product recalls or warnings to protect consumers. However, a review of the proposed NEISS-Remodel (NEISS-R) raises serious concerns about potential violations of agency process, changes to data collection that could impact agency rulemaking, and the use of AI,” the lawmakers wrote.

The lawmakers continued, “As you know, the NEISS allows hospitals across the country to voluntarily submit information on emergency department visits involving consumer products. With this information, the CPSC is able to produce estimates of product-related injuries, monitor safety trends, and determine if a product recall or warning is necessary. On July 22, 2026, the CPSC announced an update to the system that will dramatically increase the scope of its surveillance and the use of AI.

The lawmakers continued, “Based on the novel nature of AI and the plethora of concerns that have been raised by experts, including AI industry leaders, it is essential that the CPSC seek appropriate input from relevant stakeholders – as required by law – before exposing patient data to undue risk. Therefore, we continue to strongly urge the CPSC to hold off on further action until the proper procedures are followed.”

The lawmakers also raised concerns about the CPSC’s intention to expand data collection under the NEISS-R program, “Historically, hospitals have been instructed to exclude reports on emergency department visits outside of the CPSC’s jurisdiction. Based on public reporting, the NEISS-R appears to be effectively eliminating that guidance and dramatically expanding data collection efforts to include more than 10,000 injury codes. This includes incidents with no relation to consumer products governed by the CPSC, including both suicide attempts and vaccines.”

The lawmakers continued, “Given President Donald Trump’s recent claims that widely used vaccines could be ‘quite lethal’, these actions raise concerns that yet another formerly nonpartisan arm of government has been conscripted into Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy’s relentless search for data to bolster his unsupported theories about the dangers of approved vaccines.”

The lawmakers called on CPSC to halt the implementation of NIESS-R in light of privacy concerns and a lack of transparency involving its implementation process “The use of AI has the potential to expose patient data to unnecessary security risks, including unintended data breaches and the improper use of individuals’ data to train current or future AI systems. Some of these concerns have already been echoed by former CPSC officials who explained the liability associated with collecting and storing massive amounts of data…Americans deserve the certainty that their personal health information is safe and that the CPSC is adequately managing the roll out of NEISS-R.”

title: Rep. Scholten Introduces the Counsel for Kids Act to Ensure Pro Bono Legal Services for Unaccompanied Children
text:
WASHINGTON, DC – This week, U.S. Representative Hillary Scholten (D-MI-03) introduced the Counsel for Kids Act. The legislation would guarantee pro bono, in-person, independent legal counsel to unaccompanied children as they navigate immigration proceedings.

“Kids don’t belong in immigration court, period. Full stop. But when they are forced into that situation, they should not be alone. I know firsthand from working with migrants at a community legal aid organization the difference independent, quality legal support makes,” said Congresswoman Scholten. “The Counsel for Kids Act would guarantee free access to counsel for unaccompanied minors, which will help ensure children show up to their hearings, complete the required paperwork, and move through the process in a way that reduces backlogs and keeps the system functioning. For so many of these kids, having an attorney is the difference between finding protection and being deported, and we can do better than forcing them to face that alone.”

Under current law, the Office of Refugee Resettlement within the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) is responsible for providing pro bono legal counsel for unaccompanied children “to the greatest extent practicable.” This has historically been accomplished through contracting with third party providers who are trained in representing unaccompanied children in court. However, the Trump administration has recently announced that unaccompanied children will be represented by lawyers directly employed by HHS, rather than independent, third-party providers, threatening the right to independent legal representation and opening the door to violations of attorney-client privilege. The Counsel for Kids Act provides clear directives, stating that children are to receive in-person, independent counsel without charge – leaving no room for HHS to interpret the law in a way that infringes on their legal rights.

The Trump administration has also attempted to move legal consultations for children from in-person to online platforms, which would hinder attorneys’ ability to build a relationship with the child and prepare them properly for court proceedings. This bill strengthens current law to ensure the Trump administration cannot erode the quality of legal services to unaccompanied children under what they deem to be “the greatest extent practicable.”

The Counsel for Kids Act reflects Congresswoman Scholten's commitment to providing resources and legal representation to unaccompanied migrant children.

title: Congresswoman Schrier Introduces Bill to Protect Lunch and Recess Time for Kids
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, Congresswoman Kim Schrier, M.D. (WA-08), introduced her Healthy Meal Time Act to ensure schools schedule enough time for children to eat a balanced, nutritious meal each day. Congresswoman Schrier is joined in introducing this legislation by Congresswoman Suzanne Bonamici (OR-01).

“Kids need to have enough time to eat and play at school," said Congresswoman Schrier, M.D. "As a pediatrician and a mom, I know that students will often skip lunch and rush to recess without eating enough. I am proud to introduce this bill to make sure our kids have the time they need to eat a nutritious meal at school. Creating schedules that ensure kids have enough time to eat and exercise will help them focus in school and stay healthy.”

The Healthy Meal Time Act would direct the U.S. Department of Agriculture, with input from the U.S. Department of Education, to create a study to share successful efforts and current best practices with schools surrounding meal and recess timing. Currently, no federal guidelines surrounding adequate school lunch times exist.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends that students have a minimum of 20 minutes of seated eating time at lunch. This legislation would require best practices to take into account this CDC recommendation, the time it takes for non-eating activities, and the time it takes to eat minimally processed and unprocessed foods.

“School meal times let students refuel and refresh their growing brains, and learning is limited when kids don't have enough food or time to eat. The Healthy Meal Time Act would establish best practices for lunch timing and length, giving schools key guidance and resources to make the best decisions for their students,” said Congresswoman Bonamici.

“Providing nutritious school meals is essential, but children also need adequate time to eat and benefit from them,” said Tamara Randall, MS, RDN, LD, CDCES, FAND, president of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics. “The Academy supports the Healthy Meal Time Act because it would help schools establish evidence-based practices for lunch and recess schedules, ensuring students have the time they need to eat nutritious meals and support their health and well-being. We applaud Representatives Schrier and Bonamici for their leadership on this important issue.”

The Healthy Meal Time Act has been endorsed by the National Education Association, the Center for Science in the Public Interest, the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, and the School Nutrition Association.

title: Rep. Watson Coleman, State Senator Zwicker Call On NJ DEP to Pause Sentinel Data Center in South Brunswick
text:
Ewing, NJ (November 9, 2026) - Today, Congresswoman Bonnie Watson Coleman (NJ-12) and State Senator Andrew Zwicker (District 16 - Hillsborough) announced a letter to Commissioner Ed Potosnak of the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection demanding a pause on the permitting of the Sentinel Data Center in South Brunswick.

The letter highlights potential gaps in the environmental study of the project that could lead to adverse environmental and health impacts on the surrounding communities.

The letter reads, in part:

We respectfully request that DEP not issue the permit in its current form. Before any final decision, DEP must independently recalculate the Sentinel Data Center facility’s potential to emit and properly classify the facility to account for emergency operation and the full planned buildout; publish its health risk assessment inputs and its review of them; add enforceable limits on non-emergency use; and give the public an opportunity to review and comment on that information. We are not asking DEP to prejudge the application.

We are asking for a complete, transparent review that protects public health and gives residents confidence that the law will be enforced.

Congresswoman Watson Coleman introduced the Data Center Community Impact Act, legislation that would authorize a federal study on the environmental, economic, and public health impacts of data centers, with a focus on communities of color and low-income communities. Watson Coleman is also an original cosponsor of the AI Data Center Moratorium Act.

Senator Zwicker is a primary sponsor of NJ S4659, which would require the DEP to conduct a study and submit a report to the Governor and the Legislature concerning the environmental impacts of data center development in the State and prohibit the construction of new data centers until the study is complete.

Last month, State Senator Zwicker, along with Assemblymembers Frieman and Drulis, secured from the state an extension on the public comment period for the Sentinel Data Center project.

title: Modernizing the Electricity Grid
text:
Modernizing the Electricity Grid

HOW BIPARTISAN PERMITTING REFORM CAN BREAK TRANSMISSION BOTTLENECKS, BRING MORE POWER ONLINE, AND LOWER COSTS FOR CONSUMERS

America cannot meet rising electricity demand simply by building more power plants. New generation must connect to the grid, electricity must reach the communities and businesses that need it, and investments in transmission infrastructure must be planned and financed fairly.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) addresses these interconnected challenges, helping America build a more reliable, affordable, and efficient electricity system.

THE PROBLEM WITH THE STATUS QUO

Building transmission infrastructure is extraordinarily difficult. Major lines often cross multiple states and regulatory jurisdictions, creating opportunities for overlapping reviews, siting disputes, and litigation that can delay projects for years.

New Mexico’s SunZia transmission project took 17 years to permit and build, as Senator Martin Heinrich, one of the BAAJA’s sponsors, recently noted. Other projects, including Cardinal-Hickory Creek and New England Clean Energy Connect, have encountered similar obstacles. As Senator Armstrong explained in a June op-ed, transmission lines face many of the same permitting challenges that have delayed pipelines, regardless of the energy source they serve.

Even when new power plants are ready to move forward, connecting them to the grid presents another obstacle. According to Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, approximately 8,200 proposed generation and storage projects, representing more than 2,000 gigawatts, were awaiting interconnection at the end of 2025. Not all will be built, but the backlog illustrates how grid constraints can prevent new electricity supplies from reaching customers.

Compounding these challenges, neighboring electricity markets frequently disagree over which transmission projects are needed, who benefits, and how costs should be shared. The result is a fragmented system that makes it harder and more expensive to deliver reliable power where it is needed.

HOW THE BIPARTISAN BILL HELPS

BAAJA would address three fundamental obstacles to modernizing America’s electricity grid:

1. Making interstate transmission easier to build. Major transmission projects should not remain indefinitely stalled because they cross state boundaries. The legislation would expand federal backstop siting authority for qualifying interstate projects when state permitting processes fail to produce necessary approvals. Better coordination of federal and state reviews would also help reduce delays while preserving environmental safeguards.

2. Improving transmission planning and cost allocation. Electricity does not stop at state lines, but transmission planning often does. BAAJA would strengthen regional and interregional coordination, establish clearer approaches to allocating costs, and help utilities plan infrastructure around the broader benefits it provides. This would make it easier to advance projects serving multiple markets while promoting fairer treatment of customers.

3. Connecting new generation and making better use of existing infrastructure. The legislation would improve coordination between transmission planning and generator interconnection, helping address bottlenecks that keep new power projects waiting. It would also encourage technologies that increase the capacity of existing transmission lines, allowing more electricity to reach customers without relying exclusively on new corridors.

The potential benefits for American households and the broader economy are substantial. A Rhodium Group analysis estimates that the legislation’s modeled provisions could lower average household electricity bills by 50–78 annually by 2040, reflecting both infrastructure reforms and protections against shifting data-center costs onto other customers.

Resources for the Future projects that the modeled provisions could increase U.S. transmission capacity by approximately 30% by 2041, more than double interregional transfer capability, and reduce electricity-system costs by over $350 billion through 2050. Separately, the Center for Climate and Energy Solutions and Greenline Insights estimate that transmission and interconnection reforms could reduce the cost of electricity shortfalls by more than 76% by 2035 across four major power regions.

WHO SUPPORTS IT — AND WHY

The breadth of support for BAAJA reflects a shared recognition across the electricity sector: America needs to build and connect more power, faster.

Clean energy developers and industry associations see permitting and transmission reform as essential to bringing new generation online. Five leading organizations—SEIA, ACP, Advanced Energy United, ACORE, and CEBA—jointly expressed strong support for the agreement. SEIA President Tim Pawlenty called it “exactly the kind of bipartisan action America needs,” while Heather O’Neill of Advanced Energy United praised its potential to accelerate advanced energy development. ACP CEO Jason Grumet and ACORE President Ray Long have emphasized the importance of durable permits and investment certainty. ACP estimates the legislation could enable more than 300 gigawatts of additional clean power capacity, while Fervo Energy CEO Tim Latimer described the current permitting system as “built for the past.”

Electric utilities, power generators, and transmission developers recognize that meeting rising demand requires both greater permitting certainty and better coordination of infrastructure investment. On November 9, the Edison Electric Institute (EEI), representing America’s investor-owned electric utilities, endorsed the revised legislation, emphasizing improvements to transmission planning, regulatory certainty, and customer protections. ITC Holdings, the nation’s largest independent transmission owner and operator, similarly praised reforms that would accelerate investment in high-voltage transmission.

Their support builds on endorsements from American Electric Power CEO Bill Fehrman, AES Chairman and CEO Andrés Gluski, and Berkshire Hathaway Energy’s Mark Hewett. The Electric Power Supply Association (EPSA), representing competitive power suppliers, also strongly endorsed BAAJA and renewed its call for Senate action on November 5, linking infrastructure constraints to rising demand and electricity affordability.

Transmission experts and advocates have likewise emphasized the importance of a stronger, better-connected grid. Patrick Hughes of Americans for a Clean Energy Grid highlighted the need for stronger connections between regions. Grid Strategies’ Rob Gramlich described the transmission provisions as “very well-crafted,” while the Niskanen Center’s Liza Reed called passage essential to addressing the nation’s struggling grid.

Consumer-owned utilities see similar benefits for the communities they serve. In a joint letter, the National Rural Electric Cooperative Association (NRECA) and American Public Power Association (APPA) expressed strong support for the legislation, emphasizing the certainty utilities need to invest in reliable, affordable energy infrastructure.

Grid-equipment manufacturers and industrial companies have also joined the coalition, underscoring the broader economic importance of modernizing America’s electricity infrastructure. A November 9 letter signed by 85 organizations brought together major grid technology and equipment providers—including GE Vernova, Hitachi Energy, Schneider Electric, and Siemens USA—alongside industrial manufacturers such as Nucor, Cummins, and Volvo Group North America. Their support for the broader permitting agreement highlights the connection between infrastructure investment, American manufacturing, and economic competitiveness.

Energy developers and major electricity customers recognize that new generation has little value if it cannot reach the market. Leeward Renewable Energy endorsed the legislation, pointing to $4.5 billion in planned solar and storage investments on federal land that could deliver seven gigawatts of new generation. Greater permitting certainty and transmission capacity would help make those investments possible.

CEBA CEO Rich Powell described BAAJA as a “generational opportunity to unleash abundant American energy,” while Amazon’s Craig Sundstrom highlighted its potential to unlock investment in generation and transmission. Center for Climate and Energy Solutions President Nathaniel Keohane also called it a critical step forward in modernizing the grid, while Ceres and the Business Council for Sustainable Energy have emphasized permitting certainty and investment confidence.

National security leaders have underscored another dimension of the challenge: military readiness depends on the reliability of the civilian electric grid. Major General Paul D. Eaton, U.S. Army (Ret.), warned that decade-long transmission delays represent a strategic vulnerability.

Across these diverse stakeholders, the message is consistent: America’s ability to deliver affordable, reliable electricity depends not only on producing more power, but on building the infrastructure needed to connect it to customers.

title: Baldwin, Johnson Introduce Bipartisan Resolution Congratulating Milwaukee Brewers on Historic World Series Championship
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, U.S. Senators Tammy Baldwin (D-WI) and Ron Johnson (R-WI) introduced a bipartisan resolution congratulating the Milwaukee Brewers on winning the 2026 Major League Baseball World Series, the first championship in franchise history. The win marked the end of a historic season, including a franchise-record 103 regular-season victories and their fourth consecutive National League Central Division title.

“In a season for the history books, the Milwaukee Brewers brought so much pride to Milwaukee and the entire state of Wisconsin. Generations of Wisconsin families cheered on the Brew Crew, kids stayed up well past their bedtimes, and game after game, this team showed what it means to win the Wisconsin way – with resilience, teamwork, and grit. This was a season to remember, and it is a privilege to recognize and honor the team that made history and the fans who cheered them on every step of the way,” said Senator Baldwin.

“Congratulations to the Milwaukee Brewers’ players, coaches, and staff on their historic World Series victory. I am thrilled for this team and its loyal fans, who have waited more than 40 years for this moment,” said Senator Johnson. “Wisconsinites are proud to call the Brewers our own and to celebrate this historic achievement together. Go Brewers!”

The Brewers’ World Series victory marked the first championship in franchise history and Milwaukee’s first Major League Baseball championship since the Milwaukee Braves won the World Series in 1957. After finishing the regular season with a franchise-record 103 wins, the Brewers defeated the San Diego Padres in the National League Division Series and swept the Los Angeles Dodgers in the National League Championship Series to secure their first pennant since 1982. The Brewers finished the postseason with an 11-2 record, defeating the Tampa Bay Rays in five games to bring the Commissioner’s Trophy home to Milwaukee.

The resolution also celebrates the unwavering support of Brewers fans across Wisconsin, including the estimated 750,000 fans who attended the team's World Series championship parade, and recognizes the countless stadium workers and support staff who helped make the historic season possible.

A copy of the resolution can be found here.

title: Sens. Banks, Warren Statement on National Security Concerns Surrounding NVIDIA
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, Sen. Jim Banks (R-Ind.) joined Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) in releasing the following statement following NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang’s confirmation of a relationship with a suspected Chinese spy:

“In March, bipartisan members of Congress urged the Department of Commerce to suspend or reconsider NVIDIA’s export licenses to China and conduct a full national security review. Since then, NVIDIA has reportedly received approvals to export hundreds of thousands of advanced AI chips to China, including to companies tied to China’s military, all while attempting to influence the debate over chip controls in Washington, D.C.

“NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang’s confirmation of a relationship with a suspected spy for China’s intelligence service makes these national security concerns even more urgent and raises important questions NVIDIA must answer about the extent to which these activities were related.

“It is time for Congress to take decisive action to pass key bills like the AI Overwatch Act in the NDAA that will cut off the various pathways through which China accesses advanced chips. The Commerce Department should complement these efforts with immediate action to close export control loopholes and ensure that advanced AI chips are not going to China’s military.”

Background:

In April 2026, Senators Jim Banks (R-Ind.) and Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) introduced the AI OVERWATCH Act. This bill ensures that the chips powering the next generation of AI fuel American innovation and American national security, not the military and surveillance apparatus of the Chinese Communist Party.

The AI OVERWATCH Act codifies President Trump’s restrictions on exports of the most advanced AI Chips to foreign adversaries and was included in the Senate’s Fiscal Year 2027 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), ensuring that the chips powering the next generation of artificial intelligence strengthen American innovation and national security.

title: Bennet Draws Hard Line Against Iran War Funding, Pushes Senate to Refuse Appropriations Packages that Provide Spending for Trump’s War
text:
Washington, D.C. — Colorado U.S. Senator Michael Bennet, a member of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, sent a letter on Saturday to his Senate colleagues urging them to draw a hard line on Iran war funding and refuse to advance any funding package that includes further appropriations for President Trump’s disastrous war. Bennet will vote against any continuing resolution that includes Iran funding, and is working to rally his colleagues to join him.

“We return to the Senate with clear direction from the American people. Together, we must bring President Trump’s disastrous war with Iran to an end. His short-sighted misadventure has driven up the cost of gas, groceries, and fertilizer, while achieving none of the goals he set out. As you know, we have an important deadline before us. Government funding is set to run out on December 11. I believe we would abdicate our responsibility if we voted to provide billions of additional dollars for President Trump’s war of choice in Iran. We must refuse to invoke cloture on any package that includes another cent for his war,” wrote Bennet.

Bennet has persistently fought to rein in Trump’s reckless war of choice with Iran. In March 2026, Bennethighlighted Trump’s failures to heed the Intelligence Community’s warnings that the war would lead to a more entrenched, hardline Iranian regime with greater incentive to pursue nuclear weapons. Bennet has demandeda full accounting of the costs of Trump’s war, introduced legislation to stop the Trump Administration from obscuring the true cost of this war, and called on President Trump to provide plans on how he intends to lower energy prices. In December 2025, Bennet voted – for the first time in his career – against the National Defense Authorization Act because of his grave concerns about President Trump’s reckless foreign policy and Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth’s lawless Department of Defense.

The text of the letter is available HERE and below.

We return to the Senate with clear direction from the American people. Together, we must bring President Trump’s disastrous war with Iran to an end. His short-sighted misadventure has driven up the cost of gas, groceries, and fertilizer, while achieving none of the goals he set out. As you know, we have an important deadline before us. Government funding is set to run out on December 11. I believe we would abdicate our responsibility if we voted to provide billions of additional dollars for President Trump’s war of choice in Iran. We must refuse to invoke cloture on any package that includes another cent for his war.

Americans all across the country are paying the price for President Trump’s war, a war that he is losing. At the grocery store and at the gas pump, families are facing higher prices and fewer options. Farmers and ranchers – who were already struggling under the weight of high tariffs and an ill-conceived trade war – have been hit with increased fertilizer and farm diesel costs. Meanwhile, the radical Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps continues to control Iran, has every incentive to pursue nuclear weapons, and is threatening global shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. We have expended high-end munitions and interceptors against Iran at a far faster pace than we can replace them, undermining our ability to help Ukraine defend itself or deter China and Russia. Our children will bear the costs of this catastrophe for decades.

The stakes are too high for us to fall into our usual shutdown politics. Instead, we should act in a bipartisan manner to forcefully reject the Administration’s request for additional funding for the Iran war, a war Congress never authorized and the American people do not want. If we fail to exercise our constitutional duty, we know from Afghanistan and Iraq that these Middle Eastern wars can take decades to end – all the while the American people will bear the cost. Together, we can bring this conflict to a close. It is what the American people demand, and what they deserve.

title: Blumenthal & Schakowsky Lead Call for Trump Administration to Halt Program Expanding Surveillance of Americans' ED Visits, Raise Privacy Concerns About Use of AI to Analyze Patient Data
text:
[WASHINGTON, D.C.] – U.S. Senator Richard Blumenthal (D-CT) and U.S. Representative Jan Schakowsky (D-IL) today led a letter to U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) Acting Chair Peter Feldman demanding answers about the Trump Administration’s proposed changes to a program used to inform product safety recalls that would expand surveillance of Americans’ emergency department records and risk patients’ privacy. In their letter to Feldman, Blumenthal, Schakowsky, U.S. Senator Adam Schiff (D-CA), and U.S. Representative Kevin Mullin (D-CA) raised concerns that the CPSC’s proposed changes to the National Electronic Injury Surveillance System (NEISS) unnecessarily expand the scope of the program’s surveillance efforts and expose patient data to security risks due to the implementation of artificial intelligence (AI) in the program.

“The NEISS is an important tool that allows the CPSC to monitor product safety trends and issue product recalls or warnings to protect consumers. However, a review of the proposed NEISS-Remodel (NEISS-R) raises serious concerns about potential violations of agency process, changes to data collection that could impact agency rulemaking, and the use of AI,” the lawmakers wrote.

The lawmakers continued, “As you know, the NEISS allows hospitals across the country to voluntarily submit information on emergency department visits involving consumer products. With this information, the CPSC is able to produce estimates of product-related injuries, monitor safety trends, and determine if a product recall or warning is necessary. On July 22, 2026, the CPSC announced an update to the system that will dramatically increase the scope of its surveillance and the use of AI.”

The lawmakers continued, “Based on the novel nature of AI and the plethora of concerns that have been raised by experts, including AI industry leaders, it is essential that the CPSC seek appropriate input from relevant stakeholders – as required by law – before exposing patient data to undue risk. Therefore, we continue to strongly urge the CPSC to hold off on further action until the proper procedures are followed.”

The lawmakers also raised concerns about the CPSC’s intention to expand data collection under the NEISS-R program, “Historically, hospitals have been instructed to exclude reports on emergency department visits outside of the CPSC’s jurisdiction. Based on public reporting, the NEISS-R appears to be effectively eliminating that guidance and dramatically expanding data collection efforts to include more than 10,000 injury codes. This includes incidents with no relation to consumer products governed by the CPSC, including both suicide attempts and vaccines.”

The lawmakers continued, “Given President Donald Trump’s recent claims that widely used vaccines could be ‘quite lethal’, these actions raise concerns that yet another formerly nonpartisan arm of government has been conscripted into Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy’s relentless search for data to bolster his unsupported theories about the dangers of approved vaccines.”

The lawmakers called on CPSC to halt the implementation of NIESS-R in light of privacy concerns and a lack of transparency involving its implementation process “The use of AI has the potential to expose patient data to unnecessary security risks, including unintended data breaches and the improper use of individuals’ data to train current or future AI systems. Some of these concerns have already been echoed by former CPSC officials who explained the liability associated with collecting and storing massive amounts of data…Americans deserve the certainty that their personal health information is safe and that the CPSC is adequately managing the roll out of NEISS-R.”

The full text of today’s letter is available here and below.

Dear Acting Chair Feldman,

We are deeply troubled by the Consumer Product Safety Commission’s (CPSC) decision to continue with the expansion of the National Electronic Injury Surveillance System (NEISS) without providing detailed information about its rollout to the public or to Congress. The NEISS is an important tool that allows the CPSC to monitor product safety trends and issue product recalls or warnings to protect consumers. However, a review of the proposed NEISS-Remodel (NEISS-R) raises serious concerns about potential violations of agency process, changes to data collection that could impact agency rulemaking, and the use of artificial intelligence (AI).[1]

As you know, the NEISS allows hospitals across the country to voluntarily submit information on emergency department visits involving consumer products.[2] With this information, the CPSC is able to produce estimates of product-related injuries, monitor safety trends, and determine if a product recall or warning is necessary.[3] On July 22, 2026, the CPSC announced an update to the system that will dramatically increase the scope of its surveillance and the use of AI.[4] Under the Paperwork Reduction Act, the CPSC is obligated to submit a Federal Register notice and set up a public comment period along with publishing a System of Records notice before making this change.[5] Despite this legal requirement, the Commission has yet to initiate this process.[6] Based on the novel nature of AI and the plethora of concerns that have been raised by experts, including AI industry leaders,[7] it is essential that the CPSC seek appropriate input from relevant stakeholders – as required by law – before exposing patient data to undue risk. Therefore, we continue to strongly urge the CPSC to hold off on further action until the proper procedures are followed.

Not only is the CPSC disregarding federal law and risking patient privacy, it is also departing from established operating policies. Historically, hospitals have been instructed to exclude reports on emergency department visits outside of the CPSC’s jurisdiction.[8] Based on public reporting the NEISS-R appears to be effectively eliminating that guidance and dramatically expanding data collection efforts to include more than 10,000 injury codes. This includes incidents with no relation to consumer products governed by the CPSC, including both suicide attempts and vaccines.[9]

Recently, you told Nextgov/FCW that collecting medical records on vaccines was necessary because the CPSC regulates drug packaging under the Poison Prevention Packaging Act. This absurd justification is wrong on its face: PPPA was enacted to require the use of child-resistant packaging, primarily for household products.[10] While the law includes certain medications, such as common over the counter drugs, that could pose a hazard to children if they are not appropriately packaged, patients are not shopping for vaccines and taking them home, where they could be accidentally tampered with by a child. You also did not provide any evidence to back up your claim that there have been reported poisoning incidents involving vaccines that were not in child-resistant packaging.[11] Given President Donald Trump’s recent claims that widely used vaccines could be “quite lethal”, these actions raise concerns that yet another formerly nonpartisan arm of government has been conscripted into Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy’s relentless search for data to bolster his unsupported theories about the dangers of approved vaccines.[12]

Further, we are deeply concerned that these changes under NEISS-R could impact agency rulemaking procedures and outcomes. Major changes to the NEISS could fundamentally reshape how safety rules are prioritized, justified and litigated. NEISS is designed to represent a statistical sample of injury data from across U.S. that the CPSC has used to estimate national injuries and deaths, as well as support rulemakings. It is unclear how this new system will provide comparable nationally representative data and whether differences in methodology and data collection could hamper future rulemakings that require demonstrable risk over time. Consumer safety from hazardous products hinges on strong agency rules that hold industries accountable. It is critical that the agency provide honest and transparent information to the public regarding this matter.

The need for transparency is increasingly important given the use of AI in analyzing patients’ personal information and medical data. Konza Health, the CPSC’s contractor for this project, has claimed it will use “advanced analytic parsing and filtering capabilities” to automatically filter and transmit the massive amount of data collected from hospitals to the CPSC.”[13] Additionally, a spokesperson from the CPSC shared that after receiving the information from Konza Health, the CPSC would use AI to conduct data analysis and identify trends. Given the role that AI will play in the NEISS-R and the fact that Konza Health could be responsible for storing and securing large swaths of user medical data, it is imperative that the public receive a full account of what technologies and software they will use to comply with this initiative.[14] This is especially important because neither Konza Health nor the CPSC have confirmed if patients will be asked to consent to having their information shared. The use of AI has the potential to expose patient data to unnecessary security risks, including unintended data breaches and the improper use of individuals’ data to train current or future AI systems. Some of these concerns have already been echoed by former CPSC officials who explained the liability associated with collecting and storing massive amounts of data.[15]

Americans deserve the certainty that their personal health information is safe and that the CPSC is adequately managing the roll out of NEISS-R, including strong oversight of Konza Health. The CPSC has claimed that the final architecture of the NEISS-R has not yet been determined since the CPSC does not expect to finalize the NEISS-R until 2027. If that is indeed true, this means that hospitals have been solicited for participation and asked to consent to data sharing requirements before the CPSC can even answer basic questions about the new system. If the CPSC is committed to honesty and transparency, implementation of the NIESS-R must be publicly halted until the CPSC, Congress, and the public have an understanding of the full scope and impact of these updates. To achieve this, we request answers to the following questions by November 19th, 2026:

Will the CPSC require consent from patients prior to the use of their medical data for the NEISS-R system?

How will the CPSC use AI to analyze and sort the data collected from hospitals?

Konza Health has claimed that they are not using AI. Please describe how Konza Health will perform its obligations under its contract and whether it includes the use of AI.

Will any Personally Identifiable Information (PII) obtained through NEISS-R be used to train AI software?

If using a third-party AI product not hosted by the CPSC, will PII be used as an input or otherwise exposed to the model?

What restrictions, if any, does the CPSC plan to implement on transferal of PII to any third party?

Please provide a detailed description of any current or future plans to share NEISS-R data with the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS).

Please specify what type of data analyses Konza Health will conduct that require the use of PII.

Please explain why the analyses cannot be done with data that has been anonymized and/or aggregated before Konza has access.

How will changes to data collection methodologies impact the CPSC’s ability to extrapolate trends or use the data for rulemaking?

How will the CPSC ensure the statistical validity of the system if hospitals select not to respond to the request for information?

As stated above, you recently defended the CPSC’s decision to collect vaccine information because of the CPSC’s oversight of the Poison Prevention Packaging Act. Please explain how the PPPA applies to vaccines administered in a health care setting.

Please provide a detailed list of incidents related to the “poisonings associated with… pharmaceutical packaging that doesn't meet specific child-resistant special packaging requirements” that you alluded to in your statement.

Please provide a detailed explanation of any staffing changes planned to accommodate NEISS-R and the expanded use of AI.

What support is the CPSC providing to hospitals to meet its request for information?

Does the CPSC plan to issue a System of Records Notice or to publish the proposal for public comment as required by the Paperwork Reduction Act? If so, when and if not, please explain why?

-30-

title: Blumenthal Releases Damning New Report Showing How Trafficking Survivors Suffer as Trump Administration Withholds Over $130 Million in Funding
text:
[WASHINGTON, D.C.] – U.S. Senator Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), a member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, released a damning new report revealing that the Trump Administration has failed to award approximately $133.5 million in anti-human trafficking grant funding – about 75 percent of what Congress has appropriated for the last two years – forcing programs that support trafficking victims to shut down or dramatically reduce their services.

This shocking withholding of funding follows the Administration allowing about $190 million in anti-human trafficking grants to lapse, including approximately $140 million that was previously dedicated to direct services for survivors of human trafficking and $16 million that was previously dedicated to supporting law enforcement’s ability to investigate and prosecute trafficking crimes.

“This report is sickening— and it should shock the conscience of every Administration official and lawmaker who claims to support trafficking survivors,” Blumenthal said. “From the botched release of the Epstein Files to withholding funding to support survivors and prosecute sex crimes, the Trump Administration has shown exactly how little it cares about victims of trafficking. Whether the Trump Administration has withheld these funds out of malice or pure incompetence is immaterial. What matters are the tens of thousands of victims and survivors who are suffering without it. I am demanding that this funding be released immediately and the Trump Administration provide me – and survivors – with a clear commitment that these services will not be allowed to lapse again.”

“Please consider what losing this program’s funding would mean for the people whose lives depend on it. I have worked hard to build this life, but I could not have done it alone. This program helped me become a mother who could bring her son home, a person with a career, and someone who could believe in herself again,” said an anonymous survivor who is quoted in the report. “Without it, I would not be where I am today. Losing it could put everything I have built at risk, including my life. I am only one of many survivors with something to lose—and there are others still waiting for the chance to heal.”

The Department of Justice (DOJ) Office for Victims of Crime (OVC) is the primary entity overseeing grant programs that provide funding to organizations fighting human trafficking and supporting survivors. Providers who receive funding through OVC grant programs serve more than 10,000 human trafficking survivors quarterly, including children. As a result of the Trump Administration’s mismanagement and withholding of grant funding, service providers have been forced to close or drastically downsize their programming, with dire consequences for survivors:

A wraparound program helping youth who have been trafficked for sex could not accommodate all of the children referred for services and was forced to put them on a waitlist. In disclosing that they do not have the resources to work with all the children who approach them for help, this provider said that it resulted in children “being further exploited.”

A transitional housing program that provided no-cost housing and services to support survivors in healing, securing permanent housing, and finding employment was shuttered because the provider could not pay the rent or the staff after funding lapsed. The program served over a dozen survivors annually with housing and full therapeutic support. It had a proven history of success—almost every survivor graduated from the program successfully, building a stable life and avoiding a return to trafficking.

A program providing no-cost counseling, behavioral healthcare services, and vocational training will close in January 2027 without federal funding. While the service provider has managed to fill the gaps following the lapse of federal grants, it will no longer be able to do so in less than two months. Unless funding is released, the program will close its doors to the 100 human trafficking survivors it serves each year and lay off its staff—including peer support personnel who themselves are survivors of trafficking.

A transitional housing program will likely face closure if funding is not released. It provides 24/7 support and no-cost housing to at least five human trafficking survivors annually. Most are survivors of sex trafficking, and many were sold for sex while still minors. Many survivors enter the program with substance use disorders, PTSD, and other severe mental illness, and therefore rely not only on the program’s housing but also on its addiction recovery and mental health support services. The program is incredibly successful—90 percent of the participants successfully graduate into permanent housing of their own.

Blumenthal wrote Brecht Donoghue, Director of the OVC Human Trafficking Division at DOJ, demanding that the Administration release the funding immediately and provide an explanation for its lapse.

“President Trump purports to care about survivors of human trafficking—he claims his Administration is committed “to end[ing] the evil of human trafficking” and that he is “working tirelessly” to “end the scourge of human trafficking once and for all.” It is shocking that an Administration that has claimed to prioritize stopping the “scourge of human trafficking” has instead caused a two-thirds reduction in the OVC funding available to the anti-trafficking field,” Blumenthal wrote.

“But perhaps this total disregard for human trafficking survivors should not come as a surprise from the Administration that not only fought the enactment of and then failed to fully comply with the Epstein Files Transparency Act but also repeatedly retraumatized survivors through its botched file release. Put simply, human trafficking survivors deserve so much better from their government.”

The text of Blumenthal’s letter to Donoghue is available here and copied below.

Dear Director Donoghue,

I write with concern about the delay in awarding Office for Victims of Crime (OVC) human trafficking grant awards for Fiscal Year (FY) 2025 and 2026. By failing to issue these awards on a timely basis, the Administration has left hundreds of human trafficking victim services providers without OVC funding—and without the means to serve the thousands of survivors who rely on their support. On Tuesday, the American people sent a clear message to the Administration and the Republican Party—they will not stand for corruption in the halls of power, mismanagement of our public institutions, and neglect of the most vulnerable among us. As such, and pursuant to my congressional oversight responsibilities, I seek information about the delay in OVC’s human trafficking funding.

As of October 1, 2026, the three-year award terms for both OVC’s FY22 and FY23 human trafficking grants have lapsed. And, as of today, the Trump Administration has failed to award about 75 percent of the money that Congress appropriated to replace them—resulting in a funding shortfall of over $130 million and creating a crisis in the anti-trafficking field. Until late last week, these figures were even higher—as of November 5, 2026, over 90 percent of the funding, totaling over $160 million, had not been awarded. When the FY22 grants lapsed in October 2025, human trafficking services providers were faced with a roughly one-third reduction in OVC funding supporting their work. Following the lapse of the FY23 grants in October 2026, the field faced an approximately two-thirds cut in OVC funding in just the two years this Administration has been in office. The money is available—it was appropriated by Congress in both FY25 and FY26. The Trump Administration has simply failed to award over 75 percent of it to service providers, law enforcement, and other experts.

The harm caused by the delayed grants is not hypothetical. It has real, dire consequences for survivors of human trafficking. In the words of 29 service providers who wrote to you about the grant delays, “[s]urvivors bear the brunt of this delay.” Services organizations have been forced to close their doors or dramatically reduce their victim services offerings. As more time passes without this Administration simply awarding the funding Congress has appropriated, survivors have fewer and fewer services available as they attempt to escape trafficking and rebuild their lives.

President Trump purports to care about survivors of human trafficking—he claims his Administration is committed “to end[ing] the evil of human trafficking”[2] and that he is “working tirelessly” to “end the scourge of human trafficking once and for all.”[3] It is shocking that an Administration that has claimed to prioritize stopping the “scourge of human trafficking” has instead caused a two-thirds reduction in the OVC funding available to the anti-trafficking field. But perhaps this total disregard for human trafficking survivors should not come as a surprise from the Administration that not only fought the enactment of and then failed to fully comply with the Epstein Files Transparency Act but also repeatedly retraumatized survivors through its botched file release. Put simply, human trafficking survivors deserve so much better from their government.

I call on the Trump Administration to immediately issue the human trafficking OVC grant awards for both FY25 and FY26. Pursuant to my congressional oversight responsibilities, I also request answers to the following questions by November 20, 2026:

When do you anticipate issuing all remaining FY25 OVC human trafficking grant awards?

When do you anticipate issuing all remaining FY26 OVC human trafficking grant awards?

For both FY25 and FY26 OVC human trafficking grants:

Why have the award notices been delayed?

Who was involved within the Office of Justice Programs (OJP) and at which steps in the grantmaking process?

Who was involved from outside of OJP and at which steps in the grantmaking process?

Who made the final decisions about grant recipients?

Please provide all documents regarding the evaluation of FY25 and FY26 human trafficking grant applications to my office, including copies of the criteria used for decision making, peer reviews, OJP staff comments, and other documents and guidance used in making award decisions.

Public reporting has alleged that OJP will stop using peer reviewers to help review applications and select awardees for its competitive grants.[4]

Has OJP stopped using peer review as part of its competitive grant evaluation process?

If so:

When did that change occur?

Why was this change made?

Who was responsible for the decision to cease using peer review?

If not, does OJP plan to stop using peer review as part of its competitive grant evaluation process and, if so, when?

On January 20, 2025, how many people were employed by OVC?

How many employees worked in the OVC Human Trafficking Division?

How many employees were primarily responsible for evaluating grant applications and issuing grant awards?

How many employees were involved with human trafficking grant applications and awards?

How many employees outside of the OVC Human Trafficking Division were involved with human trafficking grant applications and awards?

In which divisions did they primarily work?

Today, how many people are employed by OVC?

How many employees are in the OVC Human Trafficking Division?

How many employees are primarily responsible for evaluating grant applications and issuing grant awards?

How many employees are involved with human trafficking grant applications and awards?

How many employees outside of the OVC Human Trafficking Division are involved with human trafficking grant applications and awards?

In which divisions do they primarily work?

If there has been a reduction in the number of employees, please explain why.

I appreciate your attention to this important issue. Trafficking survivors deserve our support—and they deserve an explanation from the Trump Administration about why that support has been so delayed.

title: STATEMENT: Senator Blunt Rochester Opposes Senate Permitting Reform Bill
text:
U.S. Senator Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-Del.) today released a statement in opposition to the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA):

“My goals for this bill were to create a strong economy with clean energy, lower costs, and protect our health and environment. While I commend the work Senators Heinrich and Whitehouse put into the negotiations of this updated permitting reform package, and I’m grateful two of my bills were included, this bill still falls short. I concur with 17 Attorneys General across the country, including Delaware’s, that more time is needed to strengthen this bill. I’m especially concerned about provisions in this package that will actively weaken environmental protections. For these reasons, I can’t support this iteration of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. I’m hopeful that we’ll be able to negotiate a more comprehensive, far-reaching package in the new Congress.”

title: Capito Applauds Announcement of $202 Million for West Virginia Through the Rural Health Transformation Program
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, U.S. Senator Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), a leader on the Senate Appropriations Committee, applauded the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services’ announcement awarding an additional $202 million to West Virginia through the Rural Health Transformation Program. The program, made possible by the Working Families Tax Cuts Act, also known as the One Big Beautiful Bill, delivers on Republicans’ promise to increase affordability and the standard of living for Americans across the country. Senator Capito voted for the legislation that made this award possible.

Senator Capito, through her position in Senate Republican leadership and as Chairman of the Senate Labor, Health and Human Services, Education, and Related Agencies (Labor-HHS) Appropriations Subcommittee, played a central role in the creation of the Rural Health Transformation Program.

“I am pleased to see an additional $202 million in funding for West Virginia awarded through the Rural Health Transformation Program. I was proud to help shape this program from the start and to support the Working Families Tax Cuts Act that made this funding possible. I am grateful for President Trump’s continued leadership and commitment to ensuring our rural communities have access to the resources they deserve,” Senator Capito said.

BACKGROUND:

The $50 billion, five-year Rural Health Transformation Program was authorized by the Working Families Tax Cuts Act and empowers states to strengthen rural communities across America by improving healthcare access, quality, and outcomes by transforming the healthcare delivery ecosystem.

The program provides $10 billion annually among all states that apply. Half is distributed equally, while the other half is determined based on several factors, including progress and successful policy implementation. This additional funding brings West Virginia’s two-year total to more than $401 million in investments through the Rural Health Transformation Program.

Senator Capito played a significant role in the creation of the Rural Health Transformation Program and has long been a leading voice in Congress for strengthening rural health care systems. She also voted in favor of the Working Families Tax Cuts Act, which established this landmark investment.

title: Senator Coons statement on permitting reform bill
text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. Senator Chris Coons (D-Del.) released the following statement on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026:

“This legislation is an important step forward to substantially lower the cost of electricity for Americans and it will have my support. I am grateful to Senators Heinrich, Whitehouse, Capito, and Lee for their leadership in crafting a bipartisan bill that will reduce emissions, deploy clean energy, upgrade old transmission lines, and fast-track urgently needed projects across the country while preserving important environmental and community safeguards. It does all of this while ensuring data centers pay their fair share and pay for upgrades to our electricity systems to benefit all communities.

“I have heard important and clear concerns from all sides about this bill and its potential. That robust engagement shows that this bill is worthy of debate, and I’m expecting an amendment process that will make further improvements. Americans told us on Tuesday that they want us to take action. I hear you. We don’t have time to waste in addressing the affordability crisis facing American families.”

title: Cortez Masto Statement on Permitting Reform Bill
text:
Washington, D.C. – Today, U.S. Senator Catherine Cortez Masto (D-Nev.) released the following statement calling to strike the Tribal provisions from the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA). The Senator will vote to proceed to debate on the bill but is demanding the changes to the National Historic Preservation Act (Title III of the BAAJA) are eliminated before final passage.

“I’ve been calling for permitting reform for years. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act will lower energy costs, make much-needed upgrades to our electrical grid, and hold data centers accountable. It also includes language I drafted to support our critical mineral and clean energy industries. Clean, reliable electricity in this country should be cheap and accessible – and permitting reform is the best way to deliver for the American people.

“But I cannot ignore the concerns that Tribes in Nevada have with this bill text. The changes to the National Historic Preservation Act were made without their input, and these changes violate the federal government’s responsibility to engage in government-to-government Tribal consultation. That’s why I’m demanding to strike this section from the bill.

“If Title III stays in this bill, I will not vote for final passage.”

###

title: North Dakota Receives $206 Million in Second Year of Rural Health Transformation Program
text:
Delegation Advancing Efforts to Transform Health Care Delivery in Rural North Dakota

BISMARCK, N.D. – U.S. Senators Kevin Cramer (R-ND) and John Hoeven (R-ND) and U.S. Representative Julie Fedorchak (R-ND) today announced North Dakota will receive $206 million for the second year of the Rural Health Transformation Program (RHTP). The announcement supports ongoing efforts to build a continuum of care across the entire state and follows a roundtable the delegation held with U.S. Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. in North Dakota last week, with the goal of ensuring an effective partnership between HHS, the North Dakota Department of Health and Human Services (NDHHS) and the state’s healthcare providers. Today’s award keeps the state on track to receive up to $1 billion over the five years of the RHTP.

“Rural hospitals are essential to our communities, and the Rural Health Transformation Program is an investment in their future,” said Cramer. “This second-year award provides an opportunity to build on the progress already being made. After a positive discussion with Secretary Kennedy last week, I look forward to working with our state leaders and CMS to deliver lasting improvements to transform healthcare delivery across our state.”

“This $206 million award builds on the progress North Dakota has made so far under the Rural Health Transformation Program and will unlock more opportunities to build a continuum of care across our state,” said Hoeven. “This award is timely, as we just had a productive conversation last week with HHS Secretary Kennedy, officials from the NDHHS and health care providers from across our state, part of our efforts to ensure this program works for our hospitals, clinics and other providers. We will continue working to support our state in implementing these funds, building effective partnerships and advancing solutions to truly transform rural health care services in North Dakota.”

“This additional $206 million in funding, on top of the $200 million we already received, represents an extraordinary opportunity to transform how we deliver health care in North Dakota, especially in our rural areas,” said Fedorchak. “I urge state leaders to think big and use these one time resources to fundamentally rethink and retool how we deliver healthcare in a way that maximizes access and quality at a cost that is sustainable.”

The delegation worked to establish the RHTP through the passage of the Working Families Tax Cut Act and supported Governor Armstrong and his team in putting forward a strong application. The state was awarded nearly $200 million for the program’s first year, which is twice the program’s baseline and comes as a result of the state:

Investing in statewide fiber optic infrastructure.

Building a network of new, state-of-the-art critical access hospitals (CAHs).

Leveraging both telehealth and CAHs to recruit and retain healthcare professionals and provide access to a comprehensive continuum of care.

NDHHS recently obligated the full year-one award, with the bulk of the funding going to the North Dakota Center for Rural Health, which will manage awards to sub-grantees. The state also advanced programs to make clinical equipment upgrades, improve healthcare workforce retention and support mobile mammography services.

title: Duckworth to Vote Against Permitting Reform Bill
text:
[WASHINGTON, D.C.] – U.S. Senator Tammy Duckworth (D-IL) issued the following statement announcing she will vote against advancing the permitting reform bill:

“It couldn’t be clearer that Americans are sick of abuses of power, sick of the sky-high cost of living and sick of business as usual. While I appreciate some of the changes in the latest version put forward by committee leadership, the bill still isn’t good enough. Not for Illinois, not for the communities who won’t have a say in data centers and development coming into their neighborhoods and not for the entire nation.”

“After Americans issued a complete and total rejection of Donald Trump, Congress should not be rushing to pass a bill that would hand that same man even more power to put Big Oil and Big Tech over ratepayers. I cannot support a bill that depends on the empty promises of Trump, who violates the law every day and continues to hold up billions in energy funding from blue states like mine simply because we did not support him in the last election. I’m also skeptical that we’ll be successful in lowering costs for the American people by passing a bill that is supported by data centers and utility corporations who are jacking up their costs.

“Americans empowered Democrats to fight for them. We must use that power to fight for a better deal that prioritizes people over profits, establishes stronger guardrails and protects states like Illinois against any future retaliation by the President.”
