title: Barrasso Secures Commitments From Trump Admin Nominees on Wyoming Soda Ash, Uranium, and Community Banks
text:
“Last week, one of the largest [soda ash] producers announced that it’s going to cut hundreds of jobs, which is a devastating blow to the workers and the families across the region, a number of whom I talked with this past weekend. And the cause is clear: It’s Communist China. They’re rigging the market against our producers. They’re flooding global markets with their subsidized soda ash.”

WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, U.S. Senator John Barrasso (R-Wyo.) secured commitments from Trump administration nominees to defend Wyoming soda ash producers and hold China accountable for dumping soda ash into global markets, support Wyoming uranium producers, and help Wyoming’s community banks by cutting burdensome regulations.

Christopher Abbott, nominee for Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Enforcement and Compliance, and Francis Browne, nominee for Under Secretary of the Treasury for Domestic Finance, testified during today’s Senate Finance Committee hearing.

On Wyoming Soda Ash Exports:

“Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Mr. Abbott, Wyoming’s Green River Basin is home of the world’s largest deposits of natural trona. It’s the mineral that is refined into soda ash.

“It’s our state’s top international export. I was with many of the folks who worked there, I was with them this past weekend.

“For generations, the industry has supported families and built strong communities across Southwest Wyoming.

“Last week, one of the largest producers announced that it’s going to cut hundreds of jobs, which is a devastating blow to the workers and the families across the region, a number of whom I talked with this past weekend.

“And the cause is clear: It’s Communist China. They’re rigging the market against our producers. They’re flooding global markets with their subsidized soda ash.

“And our miners can beat anyone on a level playing field. But Communist China has no interest in fair competition.

“Will you commit to working with our trade partners to hold China accountable for dumping soda ash into global markets?”

Follow-up:

“I’m very grateful to hear that. At the same time, some countries are moving to restrict U.S. soda ash.

“The office that you’ve been nominated to lead helps American producers fight back when other countries take unfair trade actions against us.

“So, will you help continue to defend soda ash and other American exports against unfair restrictions in the international market?”

On Russian Uranium:

“Could I also ask about uranium? Russian uranium, specifically. Because Wyoming has the largest uranium reserves in our nation.

“Our miners are ready to power America’s nuclear renaissance.

“To get there, we must end our dependence on hostile nations for nuclear fuel.

“And in 2024, this Congress banned imports of Russian uranium.

“Since then, Russia has been expanding its influence over the global uranium market, opening new paths around the ban that we have in place.

“The 2024 law gave Commerce the authority to stop that circumvention that they’ve been engaged in.

“The office that you’ve been nominated to lead is responsible for that enforcement.

“So, what steps is Commerce taking to stop uranium from Russia’s global network from entering the United States through various routes?”

Follow-up:

“Are there better things that we could be doing in Congress in terms of giving you some additional tools that can strengthen your enforcement of the ban?”

On Community Banks:

“Mr. Browne, a question for you about community banks. Because in Wyoming, we have a lot of local banks. They are the lifeblood of our rural communities.

“Twenty-six community banks are currently headquartered in the state of Wyoming. And they serve farmers, ranchers, and small businesses in places that often are really too small for a Wall Street bank to even notice.

“They know their customers. They understand the people in their communities. They understand the needs of the people that live there and work there.

“And for years, regulations written for the biggest banks have buried these small banks under mountains of paperwork.

“When one of these local banks closes, rural Wyoming loses access to credit. And it’s a real problem in our small communities.

“How will you make sure that financial regulations are better scaled to the size and the risk of community banks?”

###

title: Bennet Statement on Permitting Reform Vote
text:
Washington, D.C. — Today, Colorado U.S. Senator Michael Bennet released the following statement after voting against advancing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026:

“Our electric grid is under significant strain and faces growing demand. We need to build new transmission, bring more energy, especially clean energy, onto the grid, and keep electricity affordable. We should make it easier to build new infrastructure, and I strongly support efforts to make this a reality.

“However, permitting reform is complex, and the details matter. I am concerned that not all perspectives were sufficiently heard during the drafting of this far-reaching piece of legislation.

“As drafted, the bill does not do enough to ensure sovereign Tribal governments can protect their cultural resources and ancestral homelands, which they have stewarded since time immemorial. The bill also fundamentally overhauls how the federal government engages with the public and local communities as projects move through the permitting process. These changes must be vetted more thoroughly before passing into law. Given these concerns, I cannot support advancing this bill at this time.

“There is no doubt that we must act on these issues. That means working toward meaningful, bipartisan permitting reforms that provide certainty and reduce unnecessary delays – while also protecting our environment, respecting Tribal sovereignty and self-determination, and preserving meaningful public input. I stand ready to work with my colleagues on a path forward that achieves these goals and supports Colorado’s communities, workers, and energy priorities.”

###

title: Ahead of Veterans Day, Blackburn, Rosen Announce Introduction of Bipartisan Bills to Support Veteran Education Programs
text:
WASHINGTON, DC – Ahead of Veterans Day, U.S. Senators Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.) and Jacky Rosen (D-Nev.) announced the introduction of two bipartisan bills to support and improve veterans' education and career programs. The first bill, the Veteran Education Empowerment Act, would reauthorize and improve a grant program that helps establish and fund student veteran centers at colleges and universities. These centers serve as a critical resource for nearly one million veterans attending college each year, ensuring they have the support they need as they transition to the classroom and workforce.

The Senators also introduced the Veteran Technology Employment Success Act, a bill to improve the VET TEC High Technology program, which funds short-term, high-tech training for veterans and servicemembers to start careers in the tech industry. Specifically, this bill would require the VA to collect data on the success of the program and update implementation to ensure the training veterans receive is in line with industry demands.

title: Video: Blumenthal Secures Commitment from Trump Department of Justice Nominee to Release Millions in Withheld Funding to Help Trafficking Survivors
text:
[WASHINGTON, D.C.] – U.S. Senator Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), a member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, today pressed Arthur Kleinschmidt, nominee to be Assistant Attorney General for the Office of Justice Programs, on the approximately $190 million in anti-human trafficking grant funding that has lapsed under the Trump Administration and the over $130 million that the Trump Administration has failed to award to replace it. If confirmed, Kleinschmidt would head the Department of Justice’s principal grantmaking office, the Office of Justice Programs, which oversees these funds.

Blumenthal yesterday released a report revealing that the Trump Administration has failed to award approximately $133.5 million in anti-human trafficking grant funding—about 75 percent of what Congress has appropriated for the last two years—forcing programs that support trafficking victims to shut down or dramatically reduce their services. During their exchange, Blumenthal secured a commitment from Kleinschmidt that, if confirmed, he will release all the currently withheld funds to combat the scourge of human trafficking.

“You must be aware that the Trump Administration has allowed about $190 million in anti-human trafficking grants to lapse, and it has withheld about 75% of money appropriated by the United States Congress for groups that aid victims of human trafficking. It is about $130 million that should be going to support human trafficking survivors and strengthen law enforcement's ability to fight trafficking crime,” said Blumenthal. “Will you commit, if confirmed, to release all of the anti-trafficking funds currently withheld by the Trump Administration?”

“I am going work diligently to get these resources from the Office of Justice Programs,” answered Kleinschmidt.

“Is that a yes, you will release the money?” pressed Blumenthal.

“I'm going to be committed to addressing and getting the funds to those Americans who need them the most, yes sir. I’m going to work and do and follow all the stipulations and guidelines to get our taxpayer dollars—be a good shepherd of the taxpayer dollars—to get those resources, human trafficking victims and other victims of crime, to ensure that Americans stay safe.” said Kleinschmidt.

“I'm going to take that as a yes, that you will release the money. I'm going to hold you to it. I think our United States Congress should hold you to it because human trafficking is a scourge, and the victims deserve all of the money and more that Congress has appropriated for this purpose,” said Blumenthal.

A video of Blumenthal’s round of questioning can be found here, and a transcript can be found below.

U.S. Senator Richard Blumenthal (D-CT): Let's see if we can get maybe some original answers. Mr. Adkisson, who won the 2020 election?

Samuel Adkisson: Senator Blumenthal, Joe Biden was certified as the winner of the 2020 election.

Blumenthal: Let’s go right down the panel. If you're going to answer the same way, just say ditto.

Phil Axt: I’d agree with that answer, Senator.

Brad Kelley: Ditto, Senator.

Arthur Kleinschmidt: Yes, sir. Ditto.

Blumenthal: And was the Capitol attacked on January 6, 2021?

Adkisson: Senator, there were acts of violence, lawlessness, trespass, and destruction of property that day.

Blumenthal: But you are not willing to say the Capitol was attacked?

Adkisson: Senator, again, I condemn the acts of violence, lawlessness, trespass and destruction of property that day.

Blumenthal: Mr. Axt, ditto?

Axt: Senator, I would just add that whether the events that day are characterized as an attack could have legal ramifications.

Blumenthal: So that is a ditto, correct?

Axt: Senator, I condemn the acts of violence on that day.

Blumenthal: Mr. Kelley?

Kelley: Ditto, Senator.

Blumenthal: Dr. Kleinschmidt?

Kleinschmidt: Yes, sir. Ditto.

Blumenthal: Ditto, ditto, ditto, ditto. That is where we are on the United States District Court. Dr. Kleinschmidt, do you agree with President Trump that human trafficking is a “scourge?”

Kleinschmidt: Senator, I have had human trafficking victims on my caseload over my career, so I'm very much in favor of whatever we can do to eradicate human trafficking.

Blumenthal: And do you agree with President Trump that it is a scourge? That’s the word he used. Do you agree or not?

Kleinschmidt: I'm unsure, to be honest.

Blumenthal: You’re unsure whether it’s a scourge?

Kleinschmidt: I'm not sure what the parameters of the word scourge is.

Blumenthal: Is it a bad thing? Is it an evil?

Kleinschmidt: Yes, sir.

Blumenthal: Okay. So, let me ask you, you must be aware that the Trump Administration has allowed about $190 million in anti-human trafficking grants to lapse, and it has withheld about 75% of money appropriated by the United States Congress for groups that aid victims of human trafficking. It is about $130 million that should be going to support human trafficking survivors and strengthen law enforcement's ability to fight trafficking crime, which President Trump has called a “scourge,” and you agree that it’s a bad thing.

Kleinschmidt: Well, Senator, if I'm confirmed, I am going to follow all federal laws regarding grant implementation. I very much take serious the victims of human trafficking.

Blumenthal: Well let me ask the question, if you don't mind, before you provide an answer. The question is, will you commit, if confirmed, to release all of the anti-trafficking funds currently withheld by the Trump Administration? Yes or no?

Kleinschmidt: Senator, I'm sorry, I didn't mean to interrupt you a second ago. I am going work diligently to get these resources from the Office of Justice Programs.

Blumenthal: Is that a yes, you will release the money?

Kleinschmidt: I'm going to be committed to addressing and getting the funds to those Americans who need them the most, yes sir.

Blumenthal: You know, you’ll “work diligently,” so the answer is yes. Would you agree with me, yes?

Kleinschmidt: Yes, I’m going to work and do and follow all the stipulations and guidelines to get our taxpayer dollars—be a good shepherd of the taxpayer dollars—to get those resources, human trafficking victims and other victims of crime, to ensure that Americans stay safe.

Blumenthal: I'm going to take that as a yes, that you will release the money. I'm going to hold you to it. I think our United States Congress should hold you to it because human trafficking is a scourge, and the victims deserve all of the money and more that Congress has appropriated for this purpose. You know, in your answers to Senator Kennedy talking about homelessness, you mentioned the criminal process. Do you think that homeless people should be arrested?

Kleinschmidt: No, sir, but I do believe that we as an institution, local authorities, could be a benefit in helping and assisting individuals out of their pain and suffering. I'm not saying they need to be arrested, but I do believe that we do—as human-to-human—do better at providing intervention to get them from Point A, suffering in the street, to Point B, in treatment and into self-sufficiency.

Blumenthal: So just to clarify, you would not favor arresting or prosecuting people?

Kleinschmidt: I do not favor that, but I do believe we could marshal resources in a fashion that will help people get the services that they need.

Blumenthal: You might not favor it, but local authorities should be permitted to arrest homeless people?

Kleinschmidt: I feel like I wasn’t even referring to arrest. What I'm trying to say is, if you have resources in the community, we should use them to help Americans. Allowing somebody to suffer in blight isn’t something that I favor.

Blumenthal: Noncriminal resources?

Kleinschmidt: Well, noncriminal resources. And I don’t even mean—and I'm a person in long-term recovery, too. I’ve been around, I’ve been in my own addiction, I have been out there, so I know exactly, sort of, what I'm saying. I wouldn’t want to remove resources from individuals who are in need. If they are suffering in the street, I would like to help them.

Blumenthal: So, if they are suffering in the street maybe they should be in jail, that’s a good place for them to be?

Kleinschmidt: No, sir.

Blumenthal: Okay, I just want to clarify in fairness to you.

Kleinschmidt: So, what I'm saying is that they are suffering in the street, should we just let them be there? What I'm looking at is, who would actually be the resources? First responders on some level could be there as well. What I'm trying to say is, I believe these individuals need services, and they need Americans to, human-to-human, assist them, getting from Point A, the suffering in the streets to—

Blumenthal: I’m out of time Mr. Chairman. Thank you.

title: Ahead of Veterans Day, Cantwell & Colleagues Introduce Bill to Ensure Iran War Veterans Are Covered Under PACT Act
text:
Ahead of Veterans Day, Cantwell & Colleagues Introduce Bill to Ensure Iran War Veterans Are Covered Under PACT Act

WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, U.S. Senator Maria Cantwell (D-WA) joined 12 of her Senate colleagues in introducing new legislation that would ensure Iran veterans are covered under the PACT Act, cutting unnecessary red tape and making it easier for our warfighters who are being exposed to toxic substances to access the unique treatment they need when they return home.

“Since we first championed the PACT Act four years ago, an estimated 90,000 Washington veterans have already filed claims to secure treatment for exposure to toxic substances,” said Sen. Cantwell. “The New PACT for Iran Veterans Act is a critical next step in this work, eliminating barriers to healthcare and disability compensation for veterans of the war with Iran and beyond.”

In 2022, the PACT Act helped generations of veterans—from Vietnam to Iraq—more easily receive care from the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) by establishing a list of locations where it is presumed by law that troops who served there were exposed to toxic hazards, like burn pits. However, Iran is currently not included on this presumed-exposure list, despite troops serving in the Iran War being exposed to many of the same hazards and President Donald Trump’s refusal to rule out inserting ground forces into Iran. The New PACT for Iran Veterans Act would require the VA to add Iran to the list of covered locations and take more proactive action to ensure Iran War veterans—and all veterans who serve in future conflicts—don’t have to jump through bureaucratic hoops in order to access the care they’ve earned through their service.

Specifically, the New PACT for Iran Veterans Act would:

Cut red tape for Iran War veterans by statutorily presuming toxic substance exposure for Iran War veterans, helping streamline their access to health care and benefits at VA. The bill would ensure that federal law protects all veterans who fought in Iran, including those who operated in Iranian airspace and territorial waters.

Leave no veteran behind by requiring, for the first time, that the VA’s Military Environmental Exposure Sub-Council (MEESC) conducts studies at least every five years to review all overseas assignments for toxic substance exposures. Additionally, when the military begins a contingency operation, the VA must commence a similar review of the locations from which servicemembers support this operation within 180 days. This would ensure the VA proactively looks into whether servicemembers are being exposed to toxic hazards, for current and future assignments.

Enhance transparency at the VA by requiring the VA Secretary to publicly explain their justification for any denial of a country that’s recommended for presumed toxic-exposures in these reviews, or any removal of existing presumptions.

The bill introduction was led by U.S. Senator Tammy Duckworth (D-IL). In addition to Sen. Cantwell, the legislation is cosponsored by U.S. Senators Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), Angus King (I-ME), Bernie Sanders (I-VT), Mark Kelly (D-AZ), Peter Welch (D-VT), Michael Bennet (D-CO), Patty Murray (D-WA), John Fetterman (D-PA), Ron Wyden (D-OR), Angela Alsobrooks (D-MD), and Chris Van Hollen (D-MD).

The legislation is endorsed by Disabled American Veterans (DAV), Iraq and Afghanistan Veterans of America (IAVA), Paralyzed Veterans of America (PVA), VoteVets, Veterans of Foreign Wars (VFW), and the American Legion.

“The PACT Act was a historic victory for veterans, but there is still much work to be done to ensure no veteran is left behind,” said Dr. Kyleanne Hunter, CEO of IAVA. “We have repeatedly raised concerns about how changes to the classification of military operations and service members can have unintended consequences for veterans’ access to earned benefits. Senator Duckworth’s legislation takes an important step toward closing these gaps by expanding recognition of toxic exposure, requiring proactive reviews of overseas military locations, and strengthening transparency and accountability at VA. IAVA is proud to support this effort to ensure veterans’ service and potential exposures are not overlooked simply because of how or where they served.”

“After Iraq and Afghanistan, veterans who came home sick from toxic exposure had to spend years fighting for their care,” said VoteVets senior advisor, Major General (Ret.) Paul Eaton. “Iran war veterans shouldn’t have to. The New PACT for Iran Veterans Act gets them covered now, not decades from now. Congress should pass it without delay.”

title: Chairman Capito Asks EPA Nominee About Energy Affordability, Cooperative Federalism in Nomination Hearing
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, U.S. Senator Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), Chairman of the Senate Environment and Public Works (EPW) Committee, held a hearing to consider the nomination of Justin Schwab to be Assistant Administrator for the Office of Air and Radiation (OAR) at the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). During the hearing, Chairman Capito asked Mr. Schwab how he would consider energy affordability and cooperative federalism in OAR responsibilities, and gained his commitment to work with her on Small Refinery Exemption program issues.

HIGHLIGHTS:

ENERGY RELIABILITY AND AFFORDABILITY:

Chairman Capito:

“The Biden EPA power sector strategy imposed costly requirements on coal-fired and natural gas power plants, raising serious legal questions and threatening the continued operation of reliable and affordable electricity generation units. At the same time, grid experts have warned us about the consequences of shutting down dependable power plants…and now electricity prices have increased as power supply hasn't kept up. The Trump administration, including EPA's Office of Air and Radiation, has taken steps to repeal these regulations in line with existing law, with the added benefit of bringing down electricity costs in the future. Mr. Schwab, how will you ensure that your office would consider electric reliability and energy affordability while carrying out the responsibilities of clean air?”

Justin Schwab, nominee to be Assistant Administrator for the Office of Air and Radiation of the Environmental Protection Agency:

“If confirmed to this position, I would ensure that energy requirements are properly taken into account. It's important to note that multiple provisions of the Clean Air Act, including Section 111, which is the chief one under which these regulations have happened in the past, specifically requires EPA to take energy requirements into account when determining what the best system of emission reduction is, and I would pledge to take that congressional direction very seriously.”

SMALL REFINERY EXEMPTION PROGRAM:

Chairman Capito:

“Congress established small refinery exemptions, and we talked about this already, to provide relief to small refiners that experienced disproportionate economic hardships under the Renewable Fuel Standard. I've raised concerns about how the EPA has administered this program, including the need for timely decisions and fair consideration. Mr. Schwab, if you're confirmed, will you commit to working with me and my staff on outstanding issues with the small refinery exemption program, to ensure that it is providing timely decisions and fair decisions for the petitioning entities?”

Justin Schwab, nominee to be Assistant Administrator for the Office of Air and Radiation of the Environmental Protection Agency:

“Yes, Senator, if confirmed to this position, I do commit to work with you and your staff, and to work inside the agency towards those ends.”

COOPERATIVE FEDERALISM:

Chairman Capito:

“This interplay between federal and state, who's got responsibilities, are lines clearly drawn where they are, and what kind of responsibilities are better off at the state level, these are really, really important issues. I would ask you, how will you work with state environmental agencies to ensure that the OAR carries out its responsibilities consistent with cooperative federalism?”

Justin Schwab, nominee to be Assistant Administrator for the Office of Air and Radiation of the Environmental Protection Agency:

“The Clean Air Act, in its design, is a design of cooperative federalism. States, generally speaking, in the first instance, design plans to attain and maintain air quality standards. If confirmed to this position, I would work respectfully and collaboratively with the states to try to get to yes wherever legally possible and supported by evidence in the record.”

title:
Senate Advances Bipartisan
American Affordability and Jobs Act
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, U.S. Senator Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), Chairman of the Senate Environment and Public Works (EPW) Committee, spoke on the Senate floor to highlight the urgency of passing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), legislation to reform our nation’s permitting and environmental review processes and make life more affordable for American families. Following Chairman Capito’s remarks, the Senate advanced BAAJA by a vote of 73-25.

Below are the floor remarks of Chairman Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.) as prepared for delivery.

“Madam President, for far too long, critical investments in our nation’s infrastructure, energy production, and economy have been forced to sit on the sidelines due to endless red tape, duplicative reviews, and regulatory uncertainty.

“Businesses large and small, looking to invest meaningfully in our country, lack the certainty they need to make decisions. Communities nationwide have waited in regulatory limbo for roads, bridges, energy infrastructure, manufacturing facilities, and other investments that create jobs and strengthen local economies. All this has led to lost jobs, missed economic opportunities, and higher prices across America.

“Data from the National Association of Manufacturers shows that permitting delays are costing America’s manufacturers $12.1 billion every year, including $87 million in additional costs in West Virginia alone. According to new data from McKinsey, $1.8 trillion of investments are locked up in the federal permitting system right now, including $22.3 billion of sidelined investments in my home state of West Virginia.

“These are projects that could provide good-paying jobs, improve mobility, increase access to clean drinking water, deploy broadband in rural areas, and so much more. The environmental permitting and review processes should be tools for informed decision-making, not reasons that decisions can’t be made. This is not a sustainable way for the United States to compete with the rest of the world, and it is certainly not a sustainable way to address the energy and affordability issues we are facing today.

“It’s no secret that America’s energy demand is growing rapidly to meet the needs of a modern economy. To meet these needs, we must modernize our grid, increase our energy production, and build the infrastructure that will keep America competitive and secure for decades to come.

“It is time for Congress to act. It is, actually, well past time.

“As Chairman of the Environment and Public Works Committee, I worked with my Ranking Member, Senator Whitehouse, as well as Chairman Lee of the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, and Ranking Member Heinrich, to introduce a comprehensive permitting reform solution: the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, or BAAJA. This bill will unlock economic opportunity, infrastructure development, and energy production across the United States.

“The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act consists of two parts. The first part of the bill is in the EPW Committee’s jurisdiction, and it consists of reforms to the laws that set the framework for our environmental review and permitting processes, including the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), the Clean Water Act, and the Endangered Species Act. The EPWsection also provides certainty that permitted projects will retain their permits if they remain in compliance with the law.

“The second part of the bill captures reforms to statutes in the ENR Committee’s jurisdiction, including the National Historic Preservation Act and the Federal Power Act. This section also includes the Ratepayer Protection Act, legislation that will make potential data centers pay their own way instead of American consumers facing increased costs through rising utility bills.

“Together, the package that our committees put together fulfills key policy priorities from members of both sides of the aisle and a diverse set of stakeholders. I believe these comprehensive permitting reforms will generate benefits for our country for years to come for three reasons.

“First, this bill is bipartisan. Senators Lee, Whitehouse, Heinrich, and I have worked together throughout this Congress to craft a solution that both Republicans and Democrats can support. That is the only way we can achieve durable and implementable reforms to our environmental review and permitting processes. There is something in this bill for everyone, because it is fair to everyone, and we owe it to the American people to come together as a body and pass this legislation in the weeks ahead.

“Second, this bill will help all types of projects. We cannot adjust the processes for some types of projects, but not others. Projects like coal mines, windmills, gas pipelines, solar farms, and steel mills will all benefit from this legislation.

“Third, the package addresses critical stages of the permitting process. This will create predictability, consistency, and finality in securing a permit. It will allow our laws to balance public health, the environment, and the needs of our economy. Finally, our legislation will prevent unnecessary delays and endless litigation that blocks growth.

“In West Virginia, investments have collapsed under the weight of legal challenges, denying potential benefits to areas that need support the most. When a project sits in the environmental review and permitting processes for years, jobs are not created, critical infrastructure is not built, energy is not brought onto the grid, and ultimately, American families and businesses face higher costs and fewer opportunities.

“The White House Council of Economic Advisers (CEA) released a report analyzing the ways that the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would benefit families and businesses, and the results are clear. According to their analysis, the reforms made under BAAJA would result in $82 billion to $164 billion in additional economic output every year. Families would feel these economic benefits directly, as CEA estimates that for the average American household, real wages will increase, electricity bills will fall, and everyday expenses will be reduced. We cannot continue to let the costs of permitting delays fall onto American families.

“I am no stranger to the challenge of addressing permitting reform in Congress. Throughout my career, I have introduced multiple bills to improve this process. While Congress has passed some very limited reforms through various legislative packages, we have not passed significant reforms to NEPA in several decades.

Republicans and Democrats alike recognize the need for reforms to unlock investment to build projects that are important to our states. On both sides of the aisle, we understand that our constituents need lower costs and good jobs, communities need economic investment, businesses need certainty, and America needs to build. These are not partisan ideals. They are American principles.

“The Trump administration has also rallied behind this deal, supporting our efforts in the Senate to pass durable reforms so we can unleash our nation’s full potential. Additionally, we have made it a priority to have a robust manager’s amendment to this legislation that makes targeted changes based on feedback from our members and stakeholders to further build support.

“I am thankful for my colleagues’ efforts to strengthen BAAJA, and the contributions from members of the House of Representatives as well. This legislation reflects a vast amount of perspectives and priorities, and I’m proud of the product we are voting on today.

“We have received letters of support from over one thousand stakeholder organizations, representing a broad swath of groups across our country, including oil and gas producers and solar energy groups, labor unions, and business associations. They all recognize the urgent need for permitting reform, and the benefits that BAAJA would have on affordability, energy reliability, and economic growth across our country.

“In a statement from the American Petroleum Institute, President and CEO Mike Sommers said, 'Washington has a generational opportunity to fundamentally transform a broken permitting system and help address the affordability challenges facing American consumers. Congress should seize this moment and finish the job.'

“In another statement from the Solar Energy Industries Association, CEO Tim Pawlenty said, 'This is the kind of bipartisan action America needs to meet growing energy demand, put downward pressure on energy prices, and deploy more affordable, exactly reliable solar and storage for American families and businesses.'

“Xan Fishman, Executive Vice President of the Energy Program at the Bipartisan Policy Center, said, '[The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act] would fix our permitting processes so that we can review and build efficiently, reducing costs, improving quality of life, growing our economy, and improving economic outcomes.'

“From my home state, the Gas and Oil Association of West Virginia’s President, Rebecca McPhail, said the following, 'GO-WV supports the [Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act]’s stated goals of modernizing federal environmental review, providing certainty for holders of federal permits and authorizations, and supporting an all-of-the-above energy strategy.'

“From the business community, Rodney Davis, Senior Vice President and Head of Government Affairs at the U.S. Chamber, said, 'The Senate's progress toward a comprehensive, bipartisan permitting reform deal brings us one step closer to streamlining the outdated process that is holding up critical projects of all kinds, from energy and water infrastructure to roads, broadband, and manufacturing.’

“Demonstrating the breadth of support this bill has received, the Laborers’ International Union of North America General President, Brent Booker, gave the following statement of support, 'For more than a decade LIUNA has testified before Congress, submitted comments, participated in roundtables, and endorsed numerous iterations of permitting bills…We urge lawmakers in both parties to seize this moment, pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, and finally deliver meaningful permitting reform.'

“And finally, representing a broad coalition of labor groups, in a letter from Sean McGarvey, President of North America’s Building Trades Unions, he said, 'This legislation represents a significant step toward a more efficient permitting system that supports job creation, strengthens America’s energy and infrastructure capabilities, and helps reduce costs for working families.'

“I could not agree more. This is an unprecedented opportunity, and a legislative breakthrough we can accomplish in this unique moment. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is a win for America, and we cannot let this moment pass us by.

“The reality is this: over the next several years, we will have no choice but to increase our national energy production and manufacturing capacity to meet increasing demand, and that means making sure our infrastructure projects can be built quickly, efficiently, and responsibly.

“The House has already passed several key pieces of legislation on this matter, including the SPEED Act and the PERMIT Act. Now, it’s our turn in the Senate to act on the opportunity in front of us. I encourage my colleagues to rise to the importance of this moment, and to vote in favor of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act.

“American growth, competitiveness, and security are at stake. With that, I yield the floor.”

title: Cassidy Recommends Bradford “Brad” J. Kelley for U.S. District Judgeship in Eastern District of Louisiana
text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. Senator Bill Cassidy, M.D. (R-LA) today recommended Brad Kelley to the Senate Judiciary Committee for consideration as a United States District Judge for the Eastern District of Louisiana. Cassidy highlighted Kelley’s distinguished military service, extensive legal experience, and record of public service.

Remarks as prepared below:

Mr. Chairman and Ranking Member,

It is my privilege to recommend Brad Kelley to the Committee to be a United States District Judge for the Eastern District of Louisiana.

Brad’s record reflects academic excellence, distinguished military service, significant public service, and sophisticated legal practice. Brad is a proud double-graduate of LSU, where he graduated, summa cum laude, with degrees in Political Science, History, and International Studies. In recognition of his academic achievement, he was inducted into Phi Beta Kappa.

Brad later attended LSU’s Paul M. Hebert Law Center, where he was an editor of both the Louisiana Law Review and the Journal of Civil Law Studies. Brad received his law degree, magna cum laude, and was inducted into the Order of the Coif.

Following law school, Brad clerked for the Honorable Donald E. Walter of the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Louisiana, where he gained a rare view into the inner workings of a federal court.

If confirmed, Brad will take an Oath to uphold the Constitution. He knows something about that firsthand. Between college and law school, he served our country honorably as a captain in the United States Army. Brad served as an infantry platoon leader and as a lead intelligence officer for a unit of nearly one thousand soldiers. During the Iraq War, he also advised senior command leadership on combat missions.

Brad’s commitment to those who serve did not end when he left the Army. As an attorney, he provides regular legal assistance and counsel to Gold Star Families––those special Americans who have suffered the grievous loss of immediate family killed in the line of duty. In addition to helping the families of those who have fallen, Brad has aided those who live on with the wounds of their service. In recognition of his extensive pro bono work on behalf of our veterans, Brad received a commendation.

Brad also brings substantial experience in public service. After a stint in private practice, Brad returned to government service, where he served as a senior official during both Republican and Democrat administrations, including as a Senior Policy Advisor at the U.S. Department of Labor and as Chief Counsel to a Commissioner of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC). Those positions gave him firsthand experience with federal law, administrative agencies, and the practical consequences of government decision-making.

Brad then returned to private practice, where he became an equity partner at one of the world’s largest labor and employment law firms. He now co-chairs the firm’s artificial intelligence and technology practice group and has served as lead counsel in complex litigation across the country.

That breadth of experience matters. Our federal district courts benefit from exposure to how difficult legal issues have been settled in other circuits, in addition to their own. Brad’s cross-jurisdictional experience makes him apt for this task. He is admitted to the practice of law in Louisiana, Virginia, and the District of Columbia. He is also admitted to the U.S. Courts of Appeals for the Third, Fourth, Fifth, and D.C. Circuits.

And Brad is no stranger to the court on which he has been nominated to serve. He has litigated several matters in the Eastern District of Louisiana, including matters as recently as this year.

Mr. Chairman and Ranking Member, I am confident that Brad Kelley has the credentials, experience, rigor, and patriotism that mark exceptional nominees to the federal bench. I support his nomination without question.

With that, I yield.

title: Senator Collins Announces More than $190 Million in Second-Year Rural Health Transformation Program Funding
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — U.S. Senator Susan Collins, Chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, today announced that Maine will receive $190,358,993 in second-year funding through the Rural Health Transformation Program (RHTP), a $50 billion initiative she proposed to support rural health care systems across the country over five years. Maine has the oldest population in the nation by median age and is among the most rural states, placing unique strains on its rural health care system. This award is nearly $360,000 larger than last year’s award, reflecting Maine’s progress toward implementation of program goals.

“I am pleased that Maine will once again receive $190 million from the Rural Health Transformation Program, plus additional funds to reflect the progress the State has made in implementing the program,” said Senator Collins. “Funding from this program has already been used to protect the Penobscot Community Health Center from bankruptcy and will be crucial to helping rural health care providers in Maine innovate to lower costs and improve health outcomes for Mainers no matter where they live.”

The Rural Health Transformation Program represents the largest single federal investment in rural health care in more than two decades. Senator Collins proposed the funding during negotiations over amendments to the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. She successfully pushed to expand the RHTP to $50 billion and ensure that a broader range of rural providers would be eligible for support, despite voting against the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The first awards from this program were announced last December. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services will continue to distribute the remaining funding in tranches of $10 billion over each of the next three years.

The State of Maine’s plan for RHTP funding, developed with the support of the entire congressional delegation, focuses on five core priorities: empowering rural Mainers to achieve their own healthy living goals; strengthening the rural health care workforce; adopting technologies such as telehealth and electronic medical records; reducing financial and transportation-related barriers to care; and ensuring the long-term viability of Maine’s rural health care system.

title: Daines Commemorates Native American Heritage Month on Senate Floor, Celebrates Rich Legacy of Montana’s Tribes
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Senator Steve Daines today spoke on the floor of the U.S. Senate to commemorate Native American Heritage Month and his memories from working with Montana’s tribes.

Watch the full speech HERE.

Daines’ remarks as prepared for delivery:

This month is Native American Heritage Month.

It’s been a meaningful tradition of mine for the last 14 years to celebrate the rich legacy of Montana’s tribes, and this month is particularly meaningful as I close out my time in the U.S. Senate.

My interest in Montana’s tribes began at a young age. I grew up in the Gallatin Valley- I’m a graduate of Longfellow Elementary & a proud Bozeman Hawk.

And as a child, I lived two doors down from a member of the Crow Tribe, who was a Code Talker during World War 2.

His name was Barney Old Coyote, and he was an American hero. Barney served our country during World War 2 by speaking the Crow language in a national “code talk” program. The beautiful complexity of the Crow language allowed it to be used to transmit and receive military intelligence without fear of being intercepted.

Because of Barney and his fellow “Code Talkers,” countless communications were securely sent overseas, and many American lives saved.

In 2015, Barney Old Coyote was awarded Congress’ most prestigious honor, the Congressional Gold Medal, along with fellow Crow Code Talkers Samson Birdinground, Cyril Not Afraid, and Henry Old Coyote.

And fun fact, I attended grade school with Rachel Old Coyote, the cousin of Darrin Old Coyote, who was Chairman of the Crow Tribe.

So you see, my roots here run deep.

Today, I’d like to reflect on memories from working with Montana’s tribes, from the wins we’ve had over the years to priorities I hope my successors will continue after my departure.

Montana is home to many tribes, including Crow, Cheyenne, Blackfeet, Assiniboine, Gros Ventres, Salish, Kootenai, Pend d’Oreille, Little Shell, Sioux, Chippewa, and Cree.

When I was elected to the U.S. House of Representatives, there were only 11 federally recognized tribes. I made it a priority to introduce the “Little Shell of the Chippewa Indians Restoration Act,” which granted federal recognition to the Little Shell Tribe.

In 2019, after years of work, my bill passed and the Little Shell were finally granted the recognition they deserved.

Today we are the home of 12 federally recognized tribes, spread across seven reservations, from Fort Peck in the East to the Flathead in the west.

It’s been my honor to visit each reservation and my priority to meet regularly with tribal leaders and members, both in Montana and D.C., and work closely together to improve the quality of life in Indian Country- from health care and education to resource development and increasing law and order.

Each one of these communities has helped weave together a rich tapestry of culture that shaped Montana into the place it is today.

The Battle of Little Bighorn, one of the most significant battles in Montana history, is one such example. This year we commemorated its 150th anniversary.

The battle marked a pivotal moment in the Great Sioux War and the American Indian Wars. It was my honor to pass a resolution commemorating and honoring all those who fought, so that future generations understand and appreciate the enduring spirit of our tribes.

Another example is the legacy of Blackie Wetzel, who was a fierce champion of his people, a former President of the National Congress of American Indians, who advocated for tribes, including in the oval office with JFK.

In 1971, Blackie worked with Coach George Allen to create the iconic logo that became a powerful symbol of leadership and excellence during Washington’s three Super Bowl victories.

Reflecting back in 2002, Blackie Wetzel proclaimed, “It made us all so proud to have an Indian on a big-time team.”

After the franchise lost its popular brand in 2020, Blackie’s son, Don Wetzel, met with me to share how important the logo remained to him, his family, and many in Indian Country. He wanted to use the logo for the good of Native Americans, especially to raise awareness of Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women.

But instead the logo was censored by even the NFL and on official merchandise.

Since then, I’m proud to say that the League and Team have taken steps to restore the logo to a place of honor and prominence.

This same Warrior-like spirit is demonstrated through a compelling fact that many don’t know: Native Americans serve in the military at the highest rate of any group. They are patriotic, courageous Americans who serve our country in uniform with distinction and pride.

As an example of that heritage, in 2020 I was honored to join a special ceremony renaming the Billings VA Outpatient Clinic in memory of Dr. Joseph Medicine Crow, a proud War World 2 veteran and Crow Nation Tribal Chief who earned a Bronze Star and was awarded the President Medal of Freedom.

During my tenure, I also fought to restore tribal rights and promote our tribal nations.

I’ve been a member of the Senate Committee on Indian Affairs since the beginning of my time as a Senator. And so from the very start, I made communication and consultation with our tribes one of my top priorities.

The “Northern Cheyenne Lands Act” was one of our earliest victories and the second bill I ever got signed into law while serving in the U.S. House.

This bill corrected a 114-year-old survey error by the federal government, when they expanded the Northern Cheyenne reservation but failed to give them control over natural resources on the land.

Tribal sovereignty has always been a core issue. And while there’s still work to be done, lots of progress has been made.

Our team has worked with tribal leaders from every corner of the state to address priorities, from water rights and infrastructure to investing in education and rural health care.

I prioritized settling longstanding water rights issues and bringing clean water to tribes. We were able to resolve all claims to water rights on the Blackfeet reservation and permanently settle the CSKT water dispute.

And most recently, my bills to reauthorize funding for water infrastructure in Fort Peck and modernize the Crow Tribe water settlement were signed into law by President Trump.

I also championed and signed into law the “Protecting Indian Tribes from Scams Act” to give tribes and the FTC tools to fight against scams targeting tribes.

We worked on countless bills to address the Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women crisis and scourge of drug trafficking and crime on our reservations.

From the “Savanna’s Act” and the “Not Invisible Act” to my Mitigating METH Act, we made significant progress in tribal public safety.

I was also honored to lead the annual resolution bringing awareness for Montana’s Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women.

There is still work to be done.

Before I leave office, I urge my colleagues to support Montana’s final Indian Water Rights Settlement and pass my bill, the “Northern Montana Water Security Act”. Closing the chapter on Montana water settlements remains a top priority for my remaining weeks.

I also urge my colleagues to pass my bill, the “Crow Revenue Act,” which would fix long-standing inholdings on the Crow reservation while providing certainty for the Bull Mountains Mine.

I’d like to thank all those who played a role in protecting and preserving our tribal legacy. It’s been an honor to collaborate so closely with leaders of Indian nation throughout the years. I am incredibly grateful to have been able to experience the traditions and cultures of our tribes, and I’ll leave office with a deep appreciation for the enduring Indian spirit.

Thank you.

###

title: Daines, Merkley Announce Sweeping Bipartisan Proposal to “Save the Senate”
text:
End the Senate’s Dysfunction and Deliver Results for the American People

WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Senators Steve Daines (R-Mont.) and Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) announced the rollout of a sweeping bipartisan proposal that would enact major changes to the Senate’s governing rules. These changes would help restore the Senate’s purpose of robust debate and bipartisan policymaking so that the Senate can legislate effectively and tackle pressing challenges facing the country.

These major reforms will “Save the Senate.”

“For much of our history the American people could rely on the Senate to tackle our hardest challenges. But over the past 50 years, deliberation in the U.S. Senate has all but ground to a halt due to toxic, partisan political culture. As a result, the Senate has become unnecessarily— and unacceptably— diminished as the world’s greatest deliberative body.

“Both parties had a role in creating the Senate’s dysfunction, and both parties have a responsibility to fix it. That’s why we’re working together— a Democrat and a Republican— to put forward this proposal to Save the Senate.

“Our proposal will incentivize bipartisan cooperation, strengthen committees, empower members of both parties to bring and amend bills on the Senate floor, help prevent government shutdowns, and reduce needless procedural delays. These reforms will help the Senate solve our nation’s problems and deliver results for the American people,” said Daines and Merkley.

Specifically, the proposal would:

Increase time for debate on more legislation by eliminating cloture votes on nominations, motions to proceed, and amendments. Retains cloture vote prior to final passage under regular order.

Create a Senate version of the House “suspension” calendar. Bipartisan bills that have cleared committee would be eligible for swift Senate passage at a two-thirds threshold.

Create a fast-track tool that would allow bipartisan bills that have cleared committee to be processed, amended and passed at a simple majority threshold.

Create another fast-track tool that would allow bipartisan spending bills to be brought to the Senate floor, amended, and passed in two days.

title: Ahead of Veterans Day, Duckworth Leads Colleagues in Introducing Bill to Ensure Iran War Veterans Are Covered Under PACT Act
text:
[WASHINGTON, D.C.] – U.S. Senator Tammy Duckworth (D-IL) today led twelve of her Senate colleagues in introducing new legislation that would ensure Iran Veterans are covered under the PACT Act, cutting unnecessary red tape and making it easier for our warfighters who are being exposed to toxic substances to access the unique treatment they need when they return home. In 2022, the PACT Act helped generations of Veterans—from Vietnam to Iraq—more easily receive care from the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) by establishing a list of locations where it is presumed by law that troops who served there were exposed to toxic hazards. However, Iran is currently not included on this presumed-exposure list, despite troops serving in the Iran War being exposed to many of the same hazards and President Trump’s refusal to rule out inserting ground forces into Iran. The New PACT for Iran Veterans Act would require the VA to add Iran to the list of covered locations and take more proactive action to ensure Iran War Veterans—and all Veterans who serve in future conflicts—don’t have to jump through bureaucratic hoops in order to access the care they’ve earned through their service.

“By establishing the landmark PACT Act, our nation finally helped generations of Veterans who suffered from toxic exposure in Vietnam, Iraq and Afghanistan more easily access the care they needed after being stonewalled by bureaucratic tape for years,” said Duckworth. “With a new generation of troops being thrown into another war in the Middle East, our nation must learn the lessons from previous conflicts and proactively ensure Iran Veterans don’t suffer from those same mistakes. Our New PACT for Iran Veterans Act would ensure no servicemember fights a war overseas only to come home and be faced with another battle to get the care they’ve rightfully earned through their service. Congress must act to care for these heroes now—not later.”

Specifically, Senator Duckworth’s New PACT for Iran Veterans Act would:

Cut Red Tape for Iran War Veterans by statutorily presuming toxic substance exposure for Iran War Veterans, helping streamline their access to health care and benefits at VA. The bill would ensure that federal law protects all Veterans who fought in Iran, including those who operated in Iranian airspace and territorial waters.

Leave No Veteran Behind by requiring, for the first time, that the VA’s Military Environmental Exposure Sub-Council (MEESC) conducts studies at least every five years to review all overseas assignments for toxic substance exposures. Additionally, when the military begins a contingency operation, the VA must commence a similar review of the locations from which servicemembers support this operation within 180 days. This would ensure the VA proactively looks into whether servicemembers are being exposed to toxic hazards, for current and future assignments.

Enhance Transparency at the VA by requiring the VA Secretary to publicly explain their justification for any denial of a country that’s recommended for presumed toxic-exposures in these reviews, or any removal of existing presumptions.

In addition to Duckworth, the legislation is cosponsored by U.S. Senators Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), Angus King (I-ME), Bernie Sanders (I-VT), Mark Kelly (D-AZ), Peter Welch (D-VT), Michael Bennet (D-CO), Patty Murray (D-WA), John Fetterman (D-PA), Ron Wyden (D-OR), Maria Cantwell (D-WA), Angela Alsobrooks (D-MD) and Chris Van Hollen (D-MD).

“The cost of war includes providing health care and benefits to veterans exposed to toxins during their military service,” said Blumenthal. “This legislation would build on the PACT Act to ensure all servicemembers sent into harm’s way, including recent veterans of the war with Iran, are able to receive the benefits they deserve.”

“Our veterans deserve access to prompt, timely healthcare – regardless of the conflict and country where they serve for our country,” said King. “Just as the PACT Act represented a historical milestone for Vietnam, Iraq, and Afghanistan veterans, our New PACT for Iran Veterans Act will ensure that the VA recognizes the unique current toxic exposure risks of our service members sacrifice and guarantee they receive the support they have earned, without delay.”

“The bipartisan PACT Act marked a historic step in ensuring that veterans and servicemembers exposed to toxic substances can get the care they need and deserve,” said Welch. “But President Trump’s reckless decision to throw our country into war in the Middle East means there’s a new generation of veterans facing conditions that could be hazardous to their health. We need to update our pact to servicemembers to ensure that Iran War Servicemembers and Veterans aren’t faced with red tape to get proper benefits and care once they come home.”

“For too long, veterans exposed to toxic substances during their service have had to fight for the care and benefits they earned. The PACT Act was a historic step toward correcting that failure,” said Bennet. “We have a responsibility to ensure the men and women serving today in President Trump’s reckless Iran war do not face those same barriers when they come home. Congress must act now to ensure all future veterans can access their hard-earned health care and benefits without having to fight the VA.”

“Donald Trump might not care, but the cost of war includes supporting our veterans when they come back home,” said Murray. “This legislation is a commonsense next step to expand the PACT Act to make sure our servicemembers who served in Iran continue to receive the care they need after their service is over. As I continue fighting to end the war—I want to be crystal clear that I won’t let this President leave American veterans in the dust.”

“As federal law, the historic PACT Act resulted in over 115,000 claims filed in Pennsylvania so veterans exposed to toxins could rightfully get the care they need. Servicemembers currently in the Middle East supporting our mission in Iran will not be eligible to file claims,” said Fetterman. “We need to change that through this bill, uphold our end of the sacred promise to those who answered the call to serve, and ensure future veterans are not subjected to the same delays as those before them.”

“American soldiers suffering after toxic exposure overseas should never have to second guess if they'll get the support they need when they come home,” said Wyden. “Our country has a duty to care for veterans of all wars, and I'm proud to stand with Senator Duckworth to help make this commonsense legislation the law of the land.”

“Since we first championed the PACT Act four years ago, an estimated 90,000 Washington veterans have already filed claims to secure treatment for exposure to toxic substances,” said Cantwell. “The New PACT for Iran Veterans Act is a critical next step in this work, eliminating barriers to healthcare and disability compensation for veterans of the war with Iran and beyond.”

The legislation is endorsed by Disabled American Veterans (DAV), Iraq and Afghanistan Veterans of America (IAVA), Paralyzed Veterans of America (PVA), VoteVets, Veterans of Foreign Wars (VFW) and the American Legion.

“The PACT Act was a historic victory for veterans, but there is still much work to be done to ensure no veteran is left behind,” said Dr. Kyleanne Hunter, CEO of IAVA. “We have repeatedly raised concerns about how changes to the classification of military operations and service members can have unintended consequences for veterans’ access to earned benefits. Senator Duckworth’s legislation takes an important step toward closing these gaps by expanding recognition of toxic exposure, requiring proactive reviews of overseas military locations, and strengthening transparency and accountability at VA. IAVA is proud to support this effort to ensure veterans’ service and potential exposures are not overlooked simply because of how or where they served.”

“After Iraq and Afghanistan, veterans who came home sick from toxic exposure had to spend years fighting for their care,” said VoteVets senior advisor, Major General (Ret.) Paul Eaton. “Iran war veterans shouldn’t have to. The New PACT for Iran Veterans Act gets them covered now, not decades from now. Congress should pass it without delay.”

A copy of the bill text is available on Senator Duckworth’s website.

title: Durbin Calls Out Trump Judicial Nominees For Their Inexperience In The Courtroom
text:
Durbin Calls Out Trump Judicial Nominees For Their Inexperience In The Courtroom

WASHINGTON – U.S. Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin (D-IL), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, today questioned judicial nominees during a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing with two panels beginning with Todd Butler, nominated to be a judge on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit. The second panel included Samuel D. Adkisson, nominated to be U.S. District Judge for the Eastern District of Tennessee; Philip Axt, nominated to be U.S. District Judge for the District of North Dakota; Bradford Kelley, nominated to be U.S. District Judge for the Eastern District of Louisiana; and Arthur Kleinschmidt, nominated to be Assistant Attorney General for the Office of Justice Programs.

Durbin first questioned Mr. Butler about his views on qualified immunity after Mr. Butler defended police officers for arresting a 10-year-old child in Eason v. City of Senatobia.

“You have defended a number of police officers who have been arrested for misuse of their authority. One case comes to mind. An officer arrested a 10-year-old child. You argued that the officer had probable cause that this child violated the Mississippi indecent exposure statute for urinating in public. Thankfully, the court rejected your argument because the 10-year-old cannot have the requisite state of mind to violate a statute. Would you like to comment on that defense?” Durbin asked Mr. Butler.

Mr. Butler asserted that while he has defended police officers in court, he also trains public officials and law enforcement to understand and abide by Americans’ civil rights. Notably, however, he has trained correctional institutions on how to avoid consent decrees, court-enforced legally binding performance improvement plans which are often put in place to compel such institutions to reform their correctional facilities and care of inmates.

Durbin then pressed Mr. Adkisson, Mr. Axt, and Mr. Kelley about their concerning lack of experience to serve in lifetime federal appointment.

“Mr. Adkisson, Mr. Axt, you each graduated from law school only eight years ago. You have been lawyers for less time than any judicial nominee considered by this Committee in the last 10 years. Mr. Adkisson, you have fewer than five years of litigation experience. Mr. Axt and Mr. Kelley, neither of you have ever tried a case,” Durbin said. “Most of you have little or no experience with trials.”

“How many civil juries have each of you participated in as lead or co-counsel?” Durbin asked.

Mr. Adkisson noted that he has tried only one case to judgment, a bankruptcy dispute before a judge, as a junior attorney. Neither Mr. Axt nor Mr. Kelley has participated in a civil jury trial as lead or co-counsel.

“How many criminal jury trials have each of you participated in?” Durbin followed up.

Again, Mr. Adkisson, Mr. Axt, and Mr. Kelley replied that none of them have experience with criminal jury trials as a lead or co-counsel.

“Have you ever picked a jury or conducted voir dire?” Durbin continued.

Both Mr. Adkisson and Mr. Axt confirmed that they have never conducted voir dire while Mr. Kelley could only point to the assistance he provided to the judge for whom he had clerked.

Durbin condemned the three judicial nominees’ lack of experience, saying: “To take a lifetime appointment for a federal district court, which is primarily a trial driven court, or at least preparation for trial, and not have any experience with the things I have asked you here, really raises the question of why were you on the list? Why did this Administration think you needed a lifetime appointment with so little personal experience? Fewer years of practice for two of you than any nominee in the last 10 years—10 years before this Committee…A lifetime appointment for a federal district trial judge, I just don’t see how you put it together.”

Durbin then questioned Mr. Kleinschmidt about his view on cutting federal grants aimed at improving public safety and providing services to victims. Last year, the Trump Administration terminated 373 Office of Justice Programs (OJP) grants that would have gone toward public safety funding. Mr. Kleinschmidt, despite previously advocating for more funding and accessibility for effective treatment programs, defended the Trump Administration’s cuts.

“Do you think that is key to good law enforcement, cutting back on these grants and mental health counseling?” Durbin asked Mr. Kleinschmidt.

Mr. Kleinschmidt claimed that he was not involved in any cuts to grants at the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) during his tenure there as Principal Deputy Assistant Secretary. Shortly after Mr. Kleinschmidt left SAMHSA, the Trump Administration announced that it would terminate an estimated $2 billion in grant funding from SAMHSA to treat addiction, mental health, and provide homelessness services. A day later, the Administration reversed course and reinstated those grants.

title: Durbin Casts 17,000th Vote In Congress
text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin (D-IL) today cast his 17,000th vote as a member of the United States Congress. Those votes include his service in the U.S. House of Representatives (1983-1997) and the U.S. Senate (1997-2027). Of the more than 12,500 members who have ever served in Congress, Durbin’s vote tally puts him in the top 100 of all-time vote casters. And of Members of Congress who have served in the Senate, only six have ever cast more yea or nay votes in their congressional careers than Durbin.

“As a kid from East St. Louis, I never imagined that I would be lucky enough to cast 17,000 votes in the United States Congress. To everyone who gave that kid a chance to serve: thank you. It has been an honor,” said Durbin.

title: Durbin Reflects On Last Codel Trip To The Balkans
text:
The Senator also called on Congress & President Trump to stand firm with Ukraine and against Russian threats to NATO and Europe

WASHINGTON – U.S. Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin (D-IL), Co-Chair of the Senate Ukraine Caucus, today delivered a speech on the Senate floor reflecting on his recent congressional delegation trip to Bosnia and Herzegovina, Albania, Montenegro, Croatia, and Kosovo in October with U.S. Senator Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH), Ranking Member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee. The trip was Durbin’s final congressional delegation trip as a United States Senator. Durbin previously traveled to the Balkans in 1999 and 2009 and has visited 40 countries in the last 20 years.

“Many of the places I visited were not resort spots. They were countries struggling to become more democratic, overcome war, or lift their populations out of abject poverty. They were countries like Belarus, Haiti, Venezuela, Cuba, Ukraine, and the Democratic Republic of Congo... When it comes to travel, I just completed my final official trip as the Senator from Illinois, when I visited the Western Balkans, including Bosnia and Herzegovina, Albania, Montenegro, Croatia, and Kosovo. It was [at least] my third time traveling to the Balkans as a member of Congress,” said Durbin.

“Many here may have forgotten the horrific war that engulfed the region in the early 1990s after the breakup of the former Yugoslavia. Bosnia, in particular, suffered a devastating conflict with the siege of Sarajevo, ethnic cleansing, and massacres in places such as Srebrenica, which we visited. Few could have imagined the cosmopolitan city of Sarajevo, that had hosted the winter Olympics just 10 years before, could be turned into such a deadly war zone. During this horrific conflict, I supported President Clinton’s decision to launch airstrikes to bring the war in Bosnia and later in Kosovo to a close. These airstrikes led to the Dayton Accords, which finally ended the war in Bosnia in 1995. And while several nations that emerged from the former Yugoslavia have prospered—joining the European Union and or NATO—others have struggled and still merit U.S. and European attention,” Durbin continued.

During the trip, the Senators met with government officials, U.S. diplomatic personnel, civil society representatives, and young leaders to discuss regional security, democratic institutions, economic opportunity, and relations with the United States. Meetings addressed the European Union accession processes, NATO cooperation, energy diversification, troubling efforts at Srpska secession and related lobbying of the Trump Administration, and implementation of the Western Balkans Democracy and Prosperity Act, enacted as part of the Fiscal Year 2026 National Defense Authorization Act. The delegation visited the Srebrenica Memorial Center and Cemetery at Potocari and attended a nearby performance by area youth at the House of Good Tones.

Durbin continued, “My visit reaffirmed my belief that we must continue to support efforts to draw these new nations into the EU and NATO and encourage the accompanying governance and economic reforms. It is our duty to continue to defend the larger peace, prosperity, and democracy that emerged from so much conflict in Europe—a peace that is now threatened again by none other than Vladimir Putin.”

Durbin then provided an update on Ukraine and urged President Trump and Congress to provide our Ukrainian allies with the support they need.

“This leads me to the ongoing war in Ukraine, a war President Trump said he would end on his first day re-elected to the White House. Of course, that didn’t happen. I don’t begrudge President Trump’s attempt to seek a diplomatic solution to this conflict, but it is long overdue that he realizes that you can’t coddle Vladimir Putin and compel him to reach an accord. In fact, what is left of American dignity for Trump to give away in this regard? The President has rolled out the red carpet for Putin on American soil [and] he held endless phone calls that led to nowhere. Trump publicly scolded Ukraine for fighting for its life, and most recently, President Trump eased Russian oil sanctions and waived other sanctions overwhelmingly passed in the Congress,” said Durbin.

Durbin said, “While President Trump belittles our ally and befriends our enemy, he is also trying to entice Putin with business deals as if this is some kind of real estate scheme… This effort is doomed to fail. Vladimir Putin is a former KGB official motivated not by money, but by warped historical grievances and perceived slights. He is the same Russian leader who provided targeting information to Iran to destroy American assets and kill American troops in the Middle East—the same leader empowering a nuclear armed North Korean regime that also threatens the United States. Attempts to pacify Putin are both fantasy and folly by an American president who seems forever enamored by this autocratic Russian leader, who is endlessly playing President Trump for a fool.”

Durbin concluded his remarks by urging the incoming Congress and President Trump to help our Ukrainian allies.

Durbin concluded, “So, as I wind down my time in Congress, let me implore upon President Trump and this new Congress: don’t give up on Ukraine. We must help it restock its air defenses, make sure bipartisan appropriated funds are delivered without any further delay, sanctions waivers are ended, and that the Ukrainians have what they need to force Putin to a real negotiating table… My recent visit to the Balkans—and my many trips to the Baltics—reminded me, we must remain steadfast [with our] NATO [allies]. That historic alliance has kept the world at peace for decades, so we can’t walk away from it. Anything else threatens to undermine American and allied security for decades to come—a potentially devastating Trump legacy that no ballroom or arch will ever erase.”

title: Durbin Slams Judiciary Committee Republicans For Violating Committee Norms To Fast-Track Judicial Nominations
text:
To fast-track unqualified MAGA extremist nominees, the Chairman is violating multiple Committee norms, all without the consent of the minority

WASHINGTON – U.S. Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin (D-IL), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, slammed Senate Judiciary Committee Republicans for violating numerous longstanding Committee standards to fast-track unqualified MAGA extremists, all without the consent of the minority. These actions include holding nominations hearings less than two weeks apart on November 10 and 18; slating nominees for the November 18 hearing despite receiving Senate Judiciary Questionnaires (SJQ) less than 28 days in advance; slating nominees for hearings even if their FBI background investigations have not been cleared by staff in advance; and slating as many as seven nominees for a single hearing.

During his opening, Durbin criticized Republicans for fast-tracking Elliot Gaiser, reportedly nominated to be a judge on the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas, for a hearing on November 18. Mr. Gaiser is one of President Trump’s former campaign lawyers who advanced baseless legal arguments to try to overturn the 2020 election. In his current role as head of the Justice Department’s Office of Legal Counsel, Mr. Gaiser issued an opinion claiming that the Presidential Records Act is unconstitutional and signed off on the creation of the infamous January 6 slush fund. Durbin also spoke out against a Texas Supreme Court Justice, James Sullivan, whose paperwork to be considered for a federal district judgeship was submitted to the Committee a day after he lost his re-election bid last Tuesday. Sullivan will also be slated for the November 18 hearing to be considered for a judicial vacancy in the Western District of Texas.

Durbin also criticized Republicans for continuing to withhold from Democrats committee records that Republican Senators used to question Special Counsel Jack Smith, including texts regarding Mr. Smith’s attendance at a basketball game. These records, which were used to justify unfounded accusations of perjury and personal attacks on Mr. Smith, are being withheld from the minority in violation of Senate rules and longstanding Committee practice. By departing from the Committee’s longstanding oversight and nominations practices, Republicans are setting precedents allowing future Democratic chairs to withhold committee records from Republicans and fast-track judicial nominees.

Key Quotes:

“Last week, on Election Day, the American people rejected this Administration’s corruption and cruelty overwhelmingly. President Trump responded to this stunning rebuke of his leadership by doubling down. He made baseless claims that the Democratic landslide was a result of fraud with no evidence forthcoming; he promoted Stephen Miller, the architect of the mass deportation campaign that led to the deaths of [Renée Good and Alex Pretti]. He is now chief of staff for the President of the United States. [Trump] ordered the Justice Department to criminally investigate members of Congress simply for conducting oversight hearings. Thanks to Republicans, President Trump has a loyalist as his Senate-confirmed Attorney General to carry out his [illegal] orders.”

“Unfortunately, it appears our Republican colleagues, who I thought learned a lesson from last Tuesday’s election, did not get the message… The Republican majority on this Committee continues to withhold Committee records that Republican Senators used to question Special Counsel Jack Smith. He appeared before this Committee under oath and testified. Now, the information that was used to attack him in the hearing, which we have requested and is routinely turned over, has been withheld in violation of Senate rules and longstanding Committee practice.”

“The majority is also violating numerous longstanding [Committee] standards in a desperate attempt to confirm the [un]qualified loyalists to lifetime appointments before Democrats take the majority. By departing from these practices, Republicans are further undermining the Committee’s ability [to carry out its constitutional oversight and advice and consent roles]… We cannot have one set of rules for Republicans and another for Democrats.”

“It’s not too late to change course. If [Republicans] are listening to the American people, I would suggest that you abandon these efforts [and instead] hold our regular DOJ oversight hearings; that we hold a hearing finally with Big Tech CEOs… and we need respond to Senator Curtis’s request for a bipartisan investigation of the Trump family’s famous wedding reception paid for by a Russian oligarch.”

“Mr. Chairman, there are many things we still can do… One of them is not to expedite nominees who have not been carefully vetted. I hope we don’t accept that as a standard in this Committee.”
