title: Durbin Slams Senate Judiciary Republicans For Attempting To Jam Through Extreme Judicial Nominees Before Democrats Take Senate Majority
text:
During today’s Senate Judiciary Committee nominations hearing, Durbin called out Committee Republicans for abandoning longstanding bipartisan Committee practices to push through extreme and unqualified nominees during the lame-duck session

WASHINGTON – During today’s Senate Judiciary Committee nominations hearing, U.S. Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin (D-IL), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, delivered an opening statement highlighting the longstanding bipartisan Committee norms that Republicans are violating to jam through the Trump Administration’s extreme and unqualified nominees during the lame-duck session. As Durbin made clear in his remarks, Committee Republicans missed multiple opportunities to slate nominees for earlier hearings, and now that Democrats are poised to lead the Senate come January, Committee Republicans are attempting to fast-track nominees.

Further, Durbin specifically called out Committee Republicans’ attempt to jam through two nominees, James Sullivan and Elliot Gaiser, for lifetime appointments to federal district courts in Texas before the new Congress in hopes of circumventing any consultation with Senator-elect James Talarico (D-TX). In a clearly premeditated move, the Department of Justice submitted Mr. Sullivan’s Senate Judiciary Questionnaire the day after he lost his election to the Texas Supreme Court. Similarly, Mr. Gaiser’s Questionnaire discloses that he was contacted by U.S. Senator Ted Cruz’s (R-TX) office about being nominated just one day after the election.

Key Quotes:

“In the waning days of this Congress, in light of the last [week’s] election, the Chairman is violating numerous longstanding Committee norms that Republicans and Democratic Chairs alike have followed for years, without consent from the minority—a key phrase when it comes to the rules of this Committee. The majority is planning to hold nominations hearings today and next week, contrary to our practice of holding nominations hearings no closer than two weeks apart. They’re slating two nominees for next week’s hearing whose Questionnaires were received 10 and 14 days before the hearing, respectively, contrary to the 28 days-[rule], which has been required by both political parties up until now. They’re calling nominees for hearings even if their FBI background investigations have not yet been cleared by staff, and they’re slating as many as seven nominees for a single hearing.”

“Why? Because the Republicans are losing the majority and they’re afraid that unqualified MAGA loyalists won’t withstand close scrutiny when Democrats are in the majority.”

“Consider two Texas nominees who are slated for next week’s hearing: James Sullivan and Elliot Gaiser. On Tuesday, November 3, James Sullivan lost his election for the Texas Supreme Court. The very next day, the Administration submitted his Senate Judiciary Questionnaire, which had obviously been prepared in advance.”

“[Gaiser’s] Questionnaire was submitted to this Committee two days ago…It says that Senator Cruz’s office contacted him the day after the election about the nomination.”

“Under the Committee’s precedents, these two nominees can’t be confirmed before the end of this Congress…So, Republicans are breaking the rules to jam through these nominees and avoid on obvious thing—on January 3, there will be a new Senator from Texas. Senator Talarico (D-TX) has the right, as all Senators do, to approve or disapprove district court nominees in a process known as the blue slip.”

“What we are seeing here is an effort to scramble quickly to resurrect defeated candidates in Texas and others to fill positions on the federal district court before Senator Talarico is sworn in on January 3. It’s pretty obvious. There’s such a scramble to do this that they are ignoring the rules of the Committee.”

“Before appointing a person to a lifetime appointment to the federal bench, shouldn’t we take a close look at their background? We have in the past, but clearly we are not any longer. I think that is a serious mistake, Mr. Chairman. When you have to live with it under a new Chairman, I’m sorry to tell you, but you asked for it.”

Duckworth. “Our heroes deserve our full support when they transition back into civilian life, including if they decide to become entrepreneurs. title: Fetterman Celebrates $15 Million in Funding for Pennsylvania School Districts
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Today, U.S. Senator John Fetterman (D-PA) announced $15 million in funding to two Allegheny County school districts through the Department of Energy’s (DOE) Renew America’s Schools program. This federal funding, which has been frozen by the administration since last year, will now go to Pittsburgh Public Schools (PPS) and Wilkinsburg School District (WSD) over the next five years.

“Bringing money back to our public schools ensures every child not only receives the education they deserve but in a place that’s safe and comfortable,” said Senator Fetterman. “I applaud DOE for taking necessary action to provide funding for crucial upgrades to ensure students in Pittsburgh and Wilkinsburg are able to learn in proper conditions.”

The Renew America’s Schools program will provide technical assistance to support critically needed infrastructure and HVAC upgrades to 20 outdated school buildings along with the necessary trained workforce to perform the upgrades, and education for regional school districts to create efficient and cost-effective schools. PPS, the second largest school system in Pennsylvania, provides educational services to 18,380 kindergarten through 12th grade students. WSD serves 535 kindergarten through 6th grade students.

title: Gallego, Colleagues Press Trump Administration to Expedite Delivery of Ukraine Aid
text:
WASHINGTON — Senator Ruben Gallego (D-AZ) joined Congressman Jim Costa (D-CA) and a bipartisan, bicameral group of lawmakers in demanding an explanation for the Trump administration’s delay in executing the $400 million Congress provided for Ukraine security assistance in Fiscal Year 2026. The letter, sent to Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought, also urged that delivery of the funds be accelerated.

“Ukraine’s armed forces need and deserve continued American support, and Congress has provided the resources to deliver it,” the lawmakers wrote. “We remain committed to supporting Ukraine’s defense and will continue to hold the Administration accountable for delivering these funds as Congress intended.”

Congress appropriated $400 million for the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative in the Fiscal Year 2026 government funding bill, supported by bipartisan majorities. The Trump Administration waited until the final days of the fiscal year to obligate the funds and have a slow delivery schedule that runs through FY2029, according to the Pentagon’s own spend plan.

In the letter, the lawmakers warned that slow delivery of support, as Ukraine enters another winter of Russian attacks on civilians and infrastructure, undermines the credibility of American commitments and the ability to deter Russian aggression.

The lawmakers urged the administration to:

Provide a written explanation of why the funds were not obligated until the final days of the fiscal year, including any conditions or holds the Office of Management and Budget placed on their apportionment.

Share a detailed delivery schedule, with the reasons delivery is projected to extend into FY2029 and the steps the Administration will take to accelerate it.

Explain why Patriot interceptors were reportedly excluded from the package and whether future Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative funding can address Ukraine’s air defense needs.

Ensure OMB apportions and executes any FY2027 Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative funding Congress provides promptly and without similar delay.

title: Ahead Of Veterans Day, Gillibrand, Goodlander Introduce Bill To Bolster Research On Gender-Specific Burn Pit Health Effects
text:
Today, U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY), member of the Senate Armed Services Committee and the Senate Appropriations Military Construction, Veterans Affairs, and Related Agencies Subcommittee, and Congresswoman Maggie Goodlander (D-NH-02), member of the House Armed Services Committee and the House Veterans’ Affairs Committee, introduced the Toxic Exposure and Women Veterans’ Health Outcomes Act to improve research on burn pits’ effects on women veterans’ health.

The bill would require the Departments of Veterans Affairs (VA) and Defense (DoD) to examine the understudied linkages between military service near burn pits and gender-specific health outcomes for women veterans, such as impacts on fertility and the prevalence of birth defects in babies born to affected women. The ultimate goal of the bill would be to justify the addition of more women-specific health conditions to the PACT Act and to provide women veterans with insight into the conditions their children may have as a result of their toxic exposure.

“I was proud to pass the PACT Act in 2022 to deliver on our country’s promise to take care of our toxic-exposed veterans. But our work is not over,” said Senator Gillibrand. “The VA must conduct more research into the effects of burn pits on our brave women veterans so we can make sure their conditions are adequately covered. It is absolutely imperative that we fill in these gaps in our data and give women veterans access to the full spectrum of care and benefits they deserve.”

“The women of America’s Armed Forces breathed the same toxic burn pit smoke as their brothers in arms. They deserve the same answers,” said Congresswoman Goodlander, a member of both the House Armed Services and Veterans’ Affairs Committees who served for more than a decade as an intelligence officer in the United States Navy Reserve.

“Instead, too many women who served our country in uniform are still left wondering whether their service cost them their health, their fertility, or the health of their children. That’s dead wrong, and Congress can fix it now. I’m proud to join Senator Gillibrand in leading this bill to close these research gaps and make sure no woman who served our country is left behind. Our veterans have always had our backs. We have a sacred obligation to have theirs.”

The Toxic Exposure and Women Veterans’ Health Outcomes Act would direct the VA, in collaboration with DoD, to conduct a comprehensive study on burn-pit related health effects experienced by women veterans. This would include:

Effects on female reproductive capacity and reproductive organs;

Effects on reproductive outcomes, including birth defects, adverse reproductive outcomes, and fertility;

Effects on developmental disabilities of the children of covered individuals;

Effects on female-specific organs and tissues; and

Other effects unique to the physiology of women.

More than two decades ago, a landmark study found that women veterans from the Vietnam War faced a significantly elevated risk of having children with moderate to severe birth defects. As a result of the study, in 2000, Congress mandated that children of female Vietnam-era veterans receive presumptive VA benefits if they are born with certain birth defects. However, despite this evidence and numerous other studies documenting the harmful effects of toxic exposures in post-9/11 veterans, research on reproductive health and birth outcomes for the over 300,000 women who served in post-9/11 conflicts remains severely limited.

“We know through our members’ stories and our own personal experiences that female service members are at extreme risk of developing toxic exposure-related health conditions, including those related to reproductive healthcare. Because these conditions are often unique to or manifest differently in women, and can remain undetected for years or even decades, DoD and the VA have struggled to fully understand the scope of these health impacts and ensure women veterans receive the recognition, care, and treatment they deserve,” said Dr. Kyleanne Hunter, CEO of IAVA. “We are thrilled with Senator Gillibrand’s introduction of the Toxic Exposure and Reproductive Health Outcomes Act, which would finally require a holistic look at the impacts of toxic exposure on women to close longstanding gaps in research, improve health outcomes, and ensure women veterans are no longer overlooked.”

“The Tragedy Assistance Program for Survivors (TAPS) is grateful to Senator Gillibrand for introducing the Toxic Exposure and Women Veterans’ Health Outcomes Act,” said Bonnie Carroll, TAPS President and Founder. “This important legislation will address long overdue gaps in care and research for women veterans exposed to burn pits and toxic substances during military service. TAPS is proud to support this legislation and looks forward to its passage.”

“Reproductive health problems after deployment are under-studied and too easily overlooked,” said Julie Tomaska, PhD, retired Air Force, Chief Scientific Officer Burn Pits 360. “For a woman veteran exposed to burn pit smoke, facing infertility, pregnancy loss, or a child’s birth defect is hard enough without wondering whether her service played a role. After Congress required VA to study women who served in Vietnam, researchers found a significantly higher risk of birth defects in their children, and those conditions are now covered. Yet for the nearly 300,000 women who served after 9/11, only two studies have examined birth outcomes. Senator Gillibrand’s bill closes that gap, building the evidence needed to recognize these conditions under the PACT Act.”

“Women veterans deserve the same recognition, research, and care for service-connected toxic exposures as their male counterparts,” said Jessica Jordan, Executive Director of Military Veterans Advocacy Inc. “This legislation represents an important step toward understanding the long-term health effects of toxic exposure on women veterans and their families. MVA strongly supports this initiative and urges Congress to advance this important legislation.”

Gillibrand was a leading champion of the PACT Act, which was signed by President Biden in 2022. The PACT Act expanded healthcare and benefits for veterans suffering from illnesses caused by exposure to burn pits and other toxic substances while serving abroad in post-9/11 conflicts. These burn pit-related medical conditions are now presumptively service-connected, meaning that veterans who were deployed overseas near burn pits no longer have to provide direct proof that their disease is service-related in order to receive benefits.

The Toxic Exposure and Women Veterans’ Health Outcomes Act is endorsed by Iraq and Afghanistan Veterans of America (IAVA), the Tragedy Assistance Program for Survivors (TAPS), the National Military Family Association (NMFA), Burn Pits 360, Military Veterans Advocacy Inc. (MVA), the Wounded Warrior Project, League of United Latin American Citizens (LULAC), and Tri-State Women Warriors.

The full text of the Toxic Exposure and Women Veterans’ Health Outcomes Act can be found here.

A video of Senator Gillibrand discussing the bill can be found here.

title: Gillibrand Holds Press Conference On Her Priorities For A Democratic Senate Majority
text:
Today, U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY) held a press conference to lay out her legislative priorities for a Democratic Senate majority.

The press conference follows historic Democratic gains she fought for as chair of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) in the midterm elections, during which both the House and the Senate flipped from Republican to Democratic control. With this new majority, Senator Gillibrand is focused on lowering costs and bringing relief to working Americans who have struggled to make ends meet under the Republican trifecta.

“Last week, voters across the country made clear that they are ready for change. But the real work is just beginning,” said Senator Gillibrand. “With a Democratic Senate majority, I am laser-focused on lowering costs to bring much-needed relief to working Americans who have struggled to make ends meet under the Republican trifecta. That starts with ending the war with Iran, halting President Trump’s tariffs, making healthcare more affordable, protecting Social Security, developing commonsense guardrails for artificial intelligence, and combating Trump administration corruption.”

Gillibrand’s top priorities for the Democratic majority include:

Ending the war with Iran: Gas prices in New York are over 40 percent higher today than they were at the start of the war more than eight months ago. Ending the war with Iran is critical to get these prices under control. Gillibrand has voted 14 times on War Powers Resolutions to end the war with Iran.

Halting President Trump’s tariffs: Gillibrand’s Banning Antiquated Duties and Delivering Equitable American Levies (BAD DEAL) Act would repeal all tariffs levied under Section 338 of the Tariff Act and refund Americans for all duties paid under this authority. This includes President Trump’s 50% tariffs on Canada, which are driving up costs in New York.

Restoring access to healthcare and bringing down healthcare costs: Gillibrand cosponsors myriad legislation to restore access to healthcare and lower healthcare costs, including the Health Care Affordability Act, which would restore and permanently extend the enhanced premium tax credits offered for Affordable Care Act marketplace plans. She also supports legislation to reverse Republicans’ Medicaid cuts made through President Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, restore coverage under New York’s Essential Plan, expand Medicare eligibility to individuals under 65, and cap prescription drug costs.

Developing commonsense guardrails for artificial intelligence: Gillibrand introduced the Secure and Accountable Military AI Act, which would impose strong restrictions on certain uses of AI by the Department of Defense, including by banning the use of AI to launch nuclear weapons.

Protecting Social Security: If Congress does not act, seniors could see their Social Security benefits cut by about 20% in just six years. Gillibrand’s Social Security Expansion Act would extend the solvency of Social Security for 75 years by requiring the wealthiest American households to pay their fair share of payroll taxes.

Combating Trump administration corruption: Gillibrand’s No Stock Act would ban senior government officials, including members of Congress, the president, the vice president, Supreme Court justices, and their spouses and dependents, from holding or trading covered financial assets.

title: Ahead of New Senate Majority, Senator Hassan Renews Call for Corey Lewandowski’s Documents, Records After Corruption Allegations, DOJ Investigation
text:
After Previously Refusing, Lewandowski Said Following Election That He Knew Hassan Would Lead Homeland Security Committee, Was “Happy to Have Any Conversations With Anybody”

WASHINGTON — U.S. Senator Maggie Hassan (D-NH), the incoming Chair of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee (HSGAC), today called on former Department of Homeland Security (DHS) official Corey Lewandowski to provide all contracting-related records from his time at DHS following widespread reports of corruption and abuse of taxpayer dollars. Lewandowski is now reportedly under investigation by the Department of Justice.

Earlier this year, Senator Hassan opened an investigation into Lewandowski, requesting records and reminding him of his legal obligation to preserve records from his time at DHS. At the time, Lewandowski’s lawyer responded, saying that Senator Hassan lacked the authority to compel the production of any documents. Following last week’s election and the new Democratic Senate majority, Senator Hassan is now expected to chair HSGAC, which comes with the legal authority to compel the production of documents and testimony to help achieve its constitutional legislative and oversight goals. On Thursday, Lewandowski went on talk radio and said that he knew Hassan would soon chair HSGAC and was “happy to have any conversations with anybody” because he had “nothing to hide.”

“I was pleased to hear you say on talk radio this week that you knew that I was going to be chair of the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs (HSGAC), that I would want to hear from you about your actions, and that you were ‘happy to have any conversations with anybody’ because you ‘have nothing to hide.’ I look forward to having those conversations, on the record, under oath,”wrote incoming Chair Hassan in a letter to Lewandowski. “In the interim, I request that you produce the records as set forth in my June 11 letter and ensure that all relevant records are preserved.”

“As incoming HSGAC Chair, I intend to use the Committee’s full authorities—including where necessary compulsory process—to expose corruption and waste. I therefore renew my request that you preserve all relevant records,” continued incoming Chair Hassan. “Should any such records prove unavailable when the Committee requests them, the Committee will want to understand how, and when, that came to be. I strongly encourage you to use the remainder of the year to begin working voluntarily with my office to answer outstanding requests. It is, after all, what you have said you are happy to do.”

Click here to read Incoming Chair Hassan’s letter today to Corey Lewandowski or see below:

Dear Mr. Lewandowski:

Five months ago, I asked you to preserve and produce records from your time at the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). Your attorneys acknowledged your receipt of my letter and responded that you had “no legal obligation” to comply with it, that my concerns were “insinuations,” and that only the Committee majority could pursue such matters. Since then, the DHS Office of Inspector General has referred allegations concerning your conduct to the Department of Justice. Federal prosecutors have reportedly opened a criminal investigation, and DHS has declined to represent that your official records were preserved as the law requires. So, I was pleased to hear you say on talk radio this week that you knew that I was going to be Chair of the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs (HSGAC), that I would want to hear from you about your actions, and that you were “happy to have any conversations with anybody” because you “have nothing to hide.” I look forward to having those conversations, on the record, under oath. In the interim, I request that you produce the records as set forth in my June 11 letter and ensure that all relevant records are preserved.

The allegations of misconduct remain serious. Reports that you demanded personal financial compensation from government contractors in exchange for favorable contract decisions, if true, would constitute corruption and abuse of taxpayer dollars. Allegations that you sought to fire military service members and law enforcement professionals for trivial reasons—in one instance, a U.S. Coast Guard pilot over a misplaced blanket—raise serious questions about your judgment and your conduct while entrusted with a sensitive national security role.

Examining these allegations requires a complete record of your tenure, and there is reason to doubt one exists. Administration sources have reportedly said that you did not always use your government email or phone for official business, thereby “avoiding digital paper trails on government systems.” While DHS has assured my office that former Secretary Noem’s attestation of compliance with federal records requirements “does not indicate any gaps or irregularities,” it has offered no such assurance about you. The Committee will want to understand why.

As incoming HSGAC Chair, I intend to use the Committee’s full authorities—including where necessary compulsory process—to expose corruption and waste. I therefore renew my request that you preserve all relevant records. Should any such records prove unavailable when the Committee requests them, the Committee will want to understand how, and when, that came to be. I strongly encourage you to use the remainder of the year to begin working voluntarily with my office to answer outstanding requests. It is, after all, what you have said you are happy to do.

The Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs is authorized by Rule XXV (k)(2)(B) of the Standing Rules of the Senate to investigate matters that aid the Committee in “studying the efficiency, economy, and effectiveness of all agencies and departments of the Government.” As a member of the Committee, I am conducting oversight into the activities of a senior DHS official, and I intend to continue investigating this matter in the new Congress. A copy of my June 11, 2026, letter is enclosed. Given that your attorney acknowledged your receipt of my June 11, 2026 letter, please confirm that you have preserved all relevant records and provide the requested documents and information no later than November 23, 2026.

title: Hoeven Introduces Phil Axt at Senate Judiciary Hearing
text:
WASHINGTON – Senator John Hoeven today introduced North Dakotan Phil Axt at a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing to consider Axt’s nomination to serve as U.S. District Court Judge for North Dakota. Hoeven recommended Axt for the position, citing among other things, his work as Solicitor General in the North Dakota Attorney General’s Office and his service in the U.S. Army.

“Phil has the right experience and legal temperament to serve on the U.S. District Court. He has dedicated his life to public service, starting with his service in the U.S. Army as an intelligence officer. Following his military service, he completed legal internships, clerkships and served as a legal fellow in the U.S. Senate. I first met Phil when he joined my office as a legal fellow, where he demonstrated a solid legal mind, along with good common sense and strong work ethic. Most recently, Phil has served as Solicitor General for the North Dakota Attorney General’s Office, overseeing our state’s litigation and representing North Dakota before federal and state courts. I encourage the committee to approve Phil’s nomination and advance his confirmation to the full Senate,” said Hoeven.

As Solicitor General in the North Dakota Attorney General’s Office, Axt oversees the state’s litigation against the federal government and other states, defends state laws from constitutional challenges and represents North Dakota before federal and state courts. Prior to this, he worked as a litigation associate representing clients in federal and state courts. He served as law clerk for the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit, a legal intern in a U.S. Attorney’s office and a legal fellow for Senator Hoeven. Axt received his law degree from Yale Law School and graduated from the U.S. Military Academy at West Point. He is a fifth generation North Dakotan, attended Bismarck High School and was raised in part on the family farm in Sheridan County.

Axt is being nominated to fill the vacancy created when Judge Daniel Traynor was confirmed to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit.

title: Hoeven: Trump Administration Advances Proposal to Expand Grazing Access on USFS Lands, National Grasslands
text:
WASHINGTON – Senator John Hoeven today issued the following statement after the Trump administration announced a proposal to expand access for grazing on U.S. Forest Service (USFS) lands, including the national grasslands in North Dakota. Today’s announcement aligns with Hoeven’s ongoing efforts as chairman of the Senate Agriculture Appropriations Committee and a senior member of the Senate Agriculture Committee to ensure the USFS is a good partner to livestock producers who rely on access to federal lands for grazing their herds. To this end, the proposal released today would:

Clarify and streamline permit eligibility and rules across USFS and the Bureau of Land Management.

Establish targeted and outcome-based grazing authorizations to help address grass buildup and reduce wildfire risk.

Help ensure vacant allotments are put to productive use.

Expand opportunities for beginning ranchers to access grazing permits.

Extend livestock use permits for up to 5 years and provide flexibility for temporary livestock use.

At the same time, Hoeven continues working with the USFS to revise the Travel Management Rule for the Little Missouri Grasslands to make section line rights-of-way available so ranchers can better access their cattle on federal lands. Hoeven has repeatedly raised this priority to administration officials, including USFS Chief Tom Schultz, and has been working to move a revised rule forward. The senator also secured a commitment from Schultz to work with North Dakota Agriculture Commissioner Doug Goehring and local grazing associations as the new rule is developed.

“The new Rangeland Management Rule is a good step by the U.S. Forest Service to be a better partner to our livestock producers and improve access to the national grasslands and other Forest Service lands,” said Hoeven. “Grazing not only benefits local economies, but it supports healthier grasslands and helps reduce wildfire risk. We appreciate Secretary Rollins and Forest Service Chief Schultz for their efforts, both on today’s proposal and as we continue working to revise the Travel Management Rule for the Little Missouri Grasslands and rightfully restore access to section lines in our state.”

title: Senator Kim Joins Baldwin and Colleagues in Introducing Bill to Lower Age of Medicare Eligibility to 50 and Lower Healthcare Costs
text:
Senator Kim builds on his Care Agenda by supporting Senator Baldwin’s Medicare at 50 Act to give more than 58 million Americans ages 50 to 64 another option for affordable healthcare.

WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, Senator Andy Kim (D-N.J.) joined Senator Tammy Baldwin (D-WI) and a group of colleagues in introducing the Medicare at 50 Act to lower the Medicare eligibility age to 50 and allow Americans ages 50 to 64 to buy into Medicare. As Americans list the cost of health care as a top concern, the legislation would expand access to affordable health care and give more than 58 million Americans more coverage options.

“Like millions of Americans, I’m raising a family while caring for my father with Alzheimer’s, and I know how crushing healthcare costs are. Voters sent a clear message in these midterms: lower costs now. Lowering the Medicare eligibility age is a bold step we can take right away,” said Senator Kim.

“Wisconsin families sent an unmistakable message last Tuesday: they are struggling to make ends meet and afford the skyrocketing cost of health care. So, I am taking this head-on,” said Senator Baldwin. “For too many folks in their 50s and early 60s, finding affordable health insurance means paying through the nose or going without the coverage they need altogether. That’s just not right. We can and must be bold and meet the moment to lower the cost of health care. I’m fighting to give more Americans the option to buy into Medicare at 50, so they can have more choices, more affordable coverage, and some much-needed breathing room in their budgets.”

More than 60 million Americans are between the ages of 50 and 64, a population that faces significant challenges accessing affordable, comprehensive health insurance. While the Affordable Care Act (ACA) expanded access to coverage, millions of older Americans continue to face high premiums, out-of-pocket costs, and limited coverage options. Today, 11.5 percent of Americans between the ages of 55 and 64 remain uninsured.

President Trump and Republicans have made matters worse with sweeping healthcare cuts in their Big Ugly Bill and their refusal to extend the ACA’s enhanced premium tax credits, driving up costs for older Americans who purchase insurance through the ACA Marketplace. In 2026, premiums for Americans ages 50 to 64 purchasing insurance through the ACA Marketplace doubled, while enrollment among this population fell by 6%.

The Medicare at 50 Act would help close this gap and give Americans between the ages of 50 and 64 the option to buy into Medicare before reaching the traditional eligibility age of 65. Individuals who choose to enroll would receive the same benefits and protections available under Medicare Parts A, B, and D, including the option to enroll in a Medicare Advantage plan. The legislation would also allow eligible individuals to receive the same premium tax credits and cost-sharing subsidies they would qualify for through the ACA Marketplace, helping make coverage more affordable.

The bill is co-sponsored by Senators Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), Jeff Merkley (D-OR), Chris Van Hollen (D-MD), Jack Reed (D-RI), Tammy Duckworth (D-IL), Cory Booker (D-NJ), Ed Markey (D-MA) and Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY).

title: Luján, Warnock Lead Broad Coalition of Senators to Push Senate Leadership to Delay Republican Medicaid Cuts Over Concerns About Coverage Loss
text:
Nearly $1 trillion in Medicaid cuts championed by Congressional Republicans and signed into law by President Trump will begin taking effect in January 2027;

Three to seven million Americans are estimated to lose their health care coverage from work reporting requirements alone;

Luján and Warnock: “The midterm results reveal a clear message: the American people are hurting, and we must do what we can to alleviate and prevent further harm”

Washington, D.C. – Today, Senate Finance Committee members U.S. Senators Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.) and Reverend Raphael Warnock (D-GA), along with 14 of their colleagues representing a broad swath of the Democratic coalition, are calling on Senate leadership to delay new Medicaid work reporting requirements enacted in Congressional Republicans’ One Big Beautiful Bill Act, warning that the work reporting requirements could cause millions of Americans to lose their health care coverage. Nearly $1 trillion in Medicaid cuts championed by Congressional Republicans and signed into law by President Trump will begin taking effect in January 2027 unless Congress moves to blunt their impact.

“The midterm results reveal a clear message: the American people are hurting, and we must do what we can to alleviate and prevent further harm,” said the senators. “While we remain committed to a full repeal of all Medicaid cuts, we urge you to include, in the next legislative vehicle, policies that can mitigate the imminent coverage loss from the work reporting requirements set to take effect on January 1, 2027.”

Medicaid is a cornerstone of the U.S. health care system, providing health insurance coverage to more than one in five Americans. The program covers 40% of U.S. births, provides 20% of all hospital funding, and is the single largest payer of long-term services and supports, including nursing home care. President Trump and Congressional Republicans have made cuts to Americans’ health care coverage a central part of their legislative agenda since President Trump returned to office. A July report found that two million fewer children were enrolled in Medicaid in April, compared to January 2025 when President Trump took office.

Alongside Senators Luján and Warnock, the letter is cosigned by Senators Michael Bennet (D-CO), Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-DE), Tammy Duckworth (D-IL), Mazie Hirono (D-HI), Tim Kaine (D-VA), Mark Kelly (D-AZ), Andy Kim (D-NJ), Alex Padilla (D-CA), Brian Schatz (D-HI), Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH), Chris Van Hollen (D-MD), Angela Alsobrooks (D-MD), Tina Smith (D-MN), and Tammy Baldwin (D-WI).

A copy of the letter can be found HERE and text is below:

Dear Chairman Crapo, Ranking Member Wyden, Majority Leader Thune, and Minority Leader Schumer,

As we approach 2027, we ask that Congressional leaders consider policies that will lessen impending harm to families, communities, and states across the country due to the Medicaid cuts from H.R. 1 in the next moving legislative vehicle. The midterm results reveal a clear message: the American people are hurting and we must do what we can to alleviate and prevent further harm. Absent the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) using its statutory authority and enforcement discretion to protect people from losing their health care due to states clearly not being ready to implement bureaucratic red tape, Congress must step in. While we remain committed to a full repeal of all Medicaid cuts, we urge you to include, in the next legislative vehicle, policies that can mitigate the imminent coverage loss from the work reporting requirements set to take effect on January 1, 2027.

No state that has attempted work reporting requirements in Medicaid has ever meaningfully increased workforce participation. Instead, every state that has done so has either seen or predicted significant coverage loss for people who continue to be eligible for Medicaid but lose coverage because they can’t navigate all the red tape. That is because affordable and reliable access to health care improves workforce participation, not the other way around: healthy people make a healthy economy.

Even disregarding the decades of empirical evidence demonstrating that work reporting requirements fail to achieve their intended effects, the reality is that states have had neither the time nor resources to set up complex work reporting systems by 2027. Under H.R. 1, states had fewer than 18 months to make complex eligibility and enrollment systems changes, conduct readiness reviews, train staff, and educate enrollees, during a time when many states are already budget-constrained and experiencing staff shortages at the agencies responsible. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) released its Interim Final Rule (IFR) on the work reporting requirements on June 1, 2026, just six months before states must have their programs up and running, and with less than one month for states to meet the required notification timeframes. The IFR also adds restrictions and requirements beyond the law to the medical frailty definition, adding unexpected complexity.

According to the non-partisan Congressional Budget Office, more than 5 million Americans are estimated to lose their coverage from the work reporting requirements alone. This represents up to one-third of adults in Medicaid expansion states losing their coverage. Most of the individuals at risk of losing coverage would likely continue to qualify for Medicaid: 92 percent of Medicaid enrollees are already working, caregiving, in school, or have an illness. But they will likely lose coverage nonetheless because of the bureaucratic red tape that Americans will be forced to navigate, a complex system made more chaotic by the rushed timeline that states have been forced to meet.

In light of these concerns, we urge Senate Leadership to consider a two-year delay in the implementation of the work reporting requirements.

Sincerely,

###

title: SENATOR MCCORMICK CELEBRATES ANNOUNCEMENT OF NEW NDIA CHAPTER IN WESTERN PENNSYLVANIA
text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. Senator Dave McCormick (R-PA) today celebrated the launch of the National Defense Industrial Association’s (NDIA) new Erie-Allegheny Chapter, a product of conversations and partnerships cultivated at Senator McCormick’s 2026 Pennsylvania Defense and Innovation Summit. NDIA President and CEO the Honorable David Norquist participated in the Summit, helping lay the groundwork for a permanent NDIA presence in Western Pennsylvania and new opportunities for regional defense businesses.

“The 2026 Pennsylvania Defense and Innovation Summit showcased the enormous opportunity we have to reinvigorate America’s defense industrial base,” said Senator McCormick. “This new NDIA chapter builds on that momentum by accelerating Western Pennsylvania’s defense industrial ecosystem, creating new business opportunities, attracting investment, and strengthening our Commonwealth’s role in our national defense.”

“It’s my honor and privilege to launch the new NDIA Erie-Allegheny Chapter alongside

exceptional business leaders in Western Pennsylvania. Western PA and the surrounding tri-state region have tremendous capabilities across defense manufacturing, robotics, energy, aerospace, and maritime,” said AJ Lewis, inaugural President of the Erie-Allegheny NDIA Chapter. “By connecting existing resources, identifying opportunities for collaboration, and giving our region a stronger voice in national defense priorities, we can help ensure that Western PA remains an important contributor to our nation’s security and defense readiness.”

Through NDIA conferences, industry events, and strategic partnerships, the chapter will connect Pennsylvania businesses with new customers and expand opportunities to support the U.S. defense industrial base. It will also help develop a skilled workforce across defense, robotics, energy, aerospace, and maritime (DREAM) industries.

Senator McCormick convened the 2026 Pennsylvania Defense and Innovation Summit in Carlisle in July, bringing together leaders from the defense industry, technology, finance, government, and academia. The Summit generated nearly $10 billion in announced investment supporting more than 5,000 Pennsylvania jobs and cultivated the relationships that contributed to the creation of the Erie-Allegheny Chapter.

The Erie-Allegheny Chapter will serve Western Pennsylvania from the State College region to the state’s western border and will also build relationships with neighboring defense and manufacturing communities in Ohio and New York.

title: Merkley, Wyden Announce $1.8 Million in Federal Funding to Support Public Safety Services in Tribal Communities
text:
Portland, OR – Oregon’s U.S. Senators Jeff Merkley and Ron Wyden today announced that four Oregon Tribes have secured a combined $1,804,643 from the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) to develop, expand, and enhance culturally appropriate services for crime victims in Tribal communities.

“We should do all we can to keep our communities safe and support victims of crime,” said Merkley. “This investment from the federal government will allow Tribal communities across Oregon to provide critical services for survivors and their families to begin the process of recovery and healing.”

“Tribal members in Oregon should feel safe in their communities and have appropriate services available if they become victims of crime,” Wyden said. “I’m glad these federal resources are available to achieve those goals, and I’ll keep battling to secure similar funds for tribal communities throughout our state.”

Four of the awards, which come from the DOJ’s Tribal Victim Set-Aside Services and the Services for the Victims of Crime programs, support Tribes implementing trauma-informed, victim-centered services, including direct services like counseling and crisis intervention, culturally specific traditional healing, and infrastructure projects like building shelters or modular homes. Funding also supports Missing or Murdered Indigenous Persons (MMIP) search efforts and family support, alongside strategic planning, community outreach, and provider training.

The four recipients for this latest Tribal Victim Services Set-Aside program funding are as follows:

$494,092 for the Columbia River Inter-Tribal Fish Commission

$284,130 for the Confederated Tribes of Grand Ronde

$264,918 for the Cow Creek Band of Umpqua Tribe of Indians

$284,130 for the Klamath Tribes

Additionally, the Confederated Tribes of Grand Ronde received $477,343 from the Services for the Victims of Crime program. With this funding, the Confederated Tribes of Grand Ronde will expand its Domestic Violence Department by funding one full-time peer support specialist to provide peer support, case management, safety planning, court accompaniment, and victim support group facilitation. The project will also offer contracted civil legal services and support transportation needs of victims. The project addresses critical victim services gaps in this rural area, which is more than 20 miles from courts and social services.

“We thank Senator Merkley and Senator Wyden for standing with the tribal communities of the Columbia River and fighting to secure this funding. Our people have always cared for one another, and this investment strengthens that care. With these resources, we can expand crisis response, legal advocacy, and culturally grounded healing, so that no Native survivor of violence or abuse along the river has to face it alone,” said Aja DeCoteau, Executive Director, Columbia River Inter-Tribal Fish Commission.

“As a tribal people, we carry with us the historical traumas of violence and racism. These fuel the domestic violence cycles that too many of our people experience in their lifetime,” said Grand Ronde Tribal Chairwoman Cheryle A. Kennedy. “Those who suffer at the hands of a loved one are looking for safety. A safe place to live, to rest, and a path to physical and emotional freedom. With these grant dollars the Tribe can further our resources to give them that. Grants like these save lives and we’re grateful that the Department of Justice recognizes that.”

“I extend our appreciation and offer our many thanks to the Oregon Congressional Delegation, Senators Jeff Merkley and Ron Wyden and Congressman Cliff Bentz, for much needed U.S. Department of Justice Tribal Victim Services Grant Award,” said Klamath Tribes Tribal Council Chairman William Ray, Jr.

“The Cow Creek Band of Umpqua Tribe of Indians is grateful for this funding and the opportunity it provides to strengthen services for victims of crime in our community,” said Cow Creek Band of Umpqua Tribe of Indians Chair Carla Keene. “Supporting individuals and families who have experienced trauma is an important responsibility, and we are committed to ensuring they have access to the resources, advocacy, and culturally responsive care they need to heal and move forward. This investment will help us continue this important work, not only for our Tribal citizens, but for the broader community we serve. We appreciate the Senators’ support and their recognition of the importance of these services.”

title: Merkley, Wyden, Bentz, Hoyle Push VA to Prioritize Oregon Veterans’ Homes
text:
Washington, D.C. – Marking Veterans Day this week, Oregon’s U.S. Senators Jeff Merkley and Ron Wyden, alongside U.S. Representatives Cliff Bentz (OR-02) and Val Hoyle (OR-04), are calling on the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) to prioritize funding for the construction of Oregon Department of Veterans’ Affairs’ (ODVA) proposed Roseburg State Veterans’ Home project and renovation of the Edward C. Allworth Veterans’ Home, a 154-bed assisted living facility in Lebanon.

“Continued investment in Oregon’s veterans’ care infrastructure is essential to meet the needs of our state’s geographically diverse veteran population, particularly in rural Oregon,” wrote the bipartisan group of lawmakers to VA Secretary Doug Collins.

Currently, ODVA operates two high-quality, award-winning veterans’ homes. These facilities provide skilled and long-term nursing, memory, and rehabilitative care to veterans, their spouses, and Gold Star parents, which allows veterans to live in a culture of community with fellow veterans and those with shared military experiences. To build on the success of the state’s veterans’ homes, the lawmakers are urging the VA to prioritize fully funding the agency’s Priority 1 State Home Construction List, including the Roseburg Veterans’ Home and Edward C. Allworth Veterans’ Home projects.

“We support efforts to fully fund the Priority 1 list and urge the VA to work quickly in coordination with Congress to make that funding a reality. By working together, the VA, Congress and the State of Oregon can help ensure that veterans and their families have access to the care, dignity and support they have earned,” the lawmakers concluded.

Roseburg has a sizable veteran population, with current estimates suggesting that Douglas County is home to over 10,000 veterans, many of whom served in the Vietnam War era or earlier. A new facility in the community would provide an affordable, high-quality, long-term care option for the estimated 68,000 veterans across the VA Southern Oregon Healthcare System service area, which includes Jackson, Josephine, Klamath, and Lake counties in Oregon as well as Siskiyou and Del Norte counties in California.

Previously, Merkley, Wyden, and Hoyle sent a letter in support of the Roseburg State Veterans’ Home project, which remains in the preliminary stages of preconstruction. With Oregon doing its part to make it a reality, the bipartisan group of lawmakers is now urging the VA to work with Congress and fully fund this long-awaited project.

title: Warren, Merkley Press White House for Answers on Insider Trading Scandal Involving Trump Teleprompter Aide
text:
Senators seek answers on alleged misuse of nonpublic information, the seemingly lack of effective White House ethics safeguards, and potential conflicts of interest involving the President’s family

“Since President Trump took office, the White House appears to have become consumed by a culture of corruption and greed that has placed personal financial interests ahead of the public interest.”

Text of Letter (PDF)

Washington, D.C. — U.S. Senators Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) and Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) pressed the White House Counsel for answers following the allegations that a former Trump aide and teleprompter operator used advance knowledge of President Donald Trump’s speeches to profit from bets on prediction markets. The senators criticized the administration’s seeming failure to take meaningful action to address ethics concerns. The letter demands information on steps the White House is taking to prevent White House employees from abusing their positions for personal financial gain.

“Since President Trump took office, the White House appears to have become consumed by a culture of corruption and greed that has placed personal financial interests ahead of the public interest,” wrote the senators.

The senators highlighted the White House’s failure to take any publicly known, meaningful steps to strengthen its practices and policies in response to the allegations against the Trump aide, despite the potential for abuse of nonpublic government information by others. In July 2026, reports revealed that Trump’s longtime teleprompter operator and a former deputy assistant to the president allegedly used advance knowledge of Trump’s speeches to place bets on Kalshi. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission reached a settlement with Perez requiring him to pay $173,539 in monetary penalties and barring him from trading for three years.

“More action is required—from the President, from you, and from other White House officials—to provide the public with confidence in the integrity of the federal government under President Trump,” continued the senators.

The senators also raised concerns about potential conflicts of interest between the President’s family and prediction-market companies. Donald Trump Jr. has held advisory roles and financial interests connected to prediction-market platforms, raising questions about the need for strong ethics safeguards and confidence in impartial federal oversight.

The senators requested answers by November 23, 2026, to determine what additional safeguards are needed to prevent abuses of power, strengthen ethics enforcement, and protect the public’s trust in government.

title: VIDEO: Sen. Moran Speaks on the Senate Floor to Honor Kansan & Aviation Leader Ed Bolen
text:
Sen. Moran’s full remarks as delivered:

“Over the weekend, there was an announcement, Madame President, and I rise as a result of that announcement. I rise tonight, this evening, to recognize Ed Bolen, a native of Salina, Kansas, who has been a leading voice for the aviation industry for decades.

“After 22 years as president and CEO of the National Business Aviation Association (NBAA), Ed announced his retirement.

“Ed’s passion for flying began early when he was introduced to aviation by his father, who served on the board of the Salina Regional Airport Authority.

“Ed went on to earn his pilot’s license, and he turned a love of flying into a career as a champion of general aviation and the men and women who support that industry.

“Early in his career, Ed served as a legislative aid for U.S. Senator Nancy Kassebaum of Kansas, where he played a key role in the passage of the historic General Aviation Revitalization Act of 1994. This legislation helped revitalize aircraft manufacturing, preserve thousands of jobs and strengthen the general aviation industry, which remains a critical component of the Kansas economy.

“Throughout his career, Ed has worked across the aisle to achieve results for aviation. His career included time as a member and chair of the Management Advisory Council at the Federal Aviation Administration, and he also served on the Commission on the Future of U.S. Aerospace Industry. In each of these roles, he helped shape our national aviation policies to further national security, economic growth and technological advances.

“Since joining NBAA in 2004, Ed has continued to be a champion for the aviation industry that he loves so much. He’s been a trusted advisor to Members of Congress, policy makers and aviation stakeholder, building consensus around issues that matter most to the future of aviation.

“Whether advocating for safer and more efficient aviation system, protecting access to our nation’s airports and airspace, supporting workforce development or championing air traffic control modernization, Ed has met every challenge with determination, thoughtful leadership and unwavering commitment to the community he represents.

“In true Kansas fashion, Ed has always focused on people, on relationships, on bringing others together to accomplish positive outcomes. The mindset has made him not only an effective advocate, but also a valued friend, advisor and respected voice throughout the aviation community. It is fitting that Ed first discovered his love for flying at a regional airport in Kansas, the Air Capital of the World.

“On behalf of the United States Senate, I want to thank Ed for his years of service and his steadfast commitment to the men and women who make up the aviation community. I express my appreciation to him and his family for his commitment, and I wish them the very best now and in the future. His leadership will clearly be missed.”
