title: Cantwell-Led Bipartisan Legislation to Modernize Weather Forecasting & Research Unanimously Passes Senate
text:
Cantwell-Led Bipartisan Legislation to Modernize Weather Forecasting & Research Unanimously Passes Senate

Act would improve wildfire forecasts and deploy new tools to fight fires, establish an atmospheric river forecast improvement program, strengthen landslide preparedness, and deploy new tech and tools to forecast droughts and heat waves that harm crops; Extreme weather is driving local impacts: August’s wind-fueled fires burned hundreds of thousands of acres and destroyed hundreds of Spokane homes, December’s atmospheric rivers dumped 5 trillion gallons of rain on WA, and 73 landslides were recor

WASHINGTON, D.C. – The U.S. Senate passed the bipartisan Weather Research and Forecasting Innovation Reauthorization Act of 2026 (the Weather Act) which authorizes programs at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) that will strengthen weather research and forecasting to save lives and better prepare our nation against dangerous weather disasters. The legislation is led by U.S. Senator Maria Cantwell (D-WA), ranking member of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation and senior member of the Senate Finance Committee.

“Americans are facing increasingly dangerous and costly weather disasters, and better forecasts give communities more time to prepare and get out of harm’s way,” said Sen. Cantwell. “The Weather Act will advance next-generation weather radar, modernize lifesaving warning systems, and improve forecasts for atmospheric rivers and wildfires, like the devastating fires that forced thousands to evacuate in Spokane last month. Senate passage brings us one step closer to giving forecasters, emergency managers, and communities the tools they need to save lives and protect property.”

Improves Fire Weather Forecasting:

The bill would establish an official Fire Weather Services Program within NOAA and fund the research and acquisition of new technology to improve forecasts of wildfire conditions. It would also create a Fire Weather Testbed to deploy new tools to fight fires, including a pilot program for unmanned aircraft to gather data such as chemical information and survey damage. It would ensure that meteorologists in the field receive fair compensation for longer-term deployments.

Wildfires burn thousands of acres in the state of Washington every year. More than 900,000 acres have burned during the 2026 fire season. Wind-fueled fires destroyed more than 800 homes in Spokane, forced tens of thousands of residents to evacuate, and is estimated to cost over $1 billion to rebuild.

The bill would also establish a NOAA program to coordinate agencies’ activities and ensure a united Federal approach to reducing risks to human health from heat and improve the delivery of data, forecasts, and warnings, related to extreme heat to help protect communities.

READ MORE: The Spokesman-Review: Spokane fire damages will exceed $1 billion

Improves Atmospheric River Forecasting:

The Weather Act would establish an atmospheric river forecast improvement program to advance accurate, effective, and actionable forecasts and warnings for atmospheric rivers. It also enables NOAA to improve atmospheric river hazard communication.

The bill would require NOAA to maintain and improve how the National Weather Service and other federal partners like the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) support emergency managers and communicate potential hazardous weather or water events to the public. It also directs NOAA to upgrade outdated weather radio technology to provide reliable and continuous weather and emergency alerts, expanding coverage to 98-99% of the United States. Despite the State of Washington having 17 National Weather Radio transmitters, large gaps in coverage remain.

December’s atmospheric rivers dumped five trillion gallons of rain across the state and caused devastating floods. In the western United States, atmospheric rivers account for 84% of flood damages costing approximately $1.1 billion a year, and in King County, atmospheric rivers are responsible for 97% of flood damages.

READ MORE: The Cascadia Daily News: Flooded Whatcom businesses face ‘long road’ to recovery

Improves Landslide Preparedness:

The bill would require the United States Geological Survey (USGS) and NOAA to incorporate risks from atmospheric rivers into landslide preparedness and response planning. It would expand the National Landslide Hazards Database to cover areas needing additional landslide risk assessments due to factors such as hydrological changes and atmospheric river flooding. It includes funding for the purchase and deployment of landslide early warning systems in high-risk area.

In December 2025 at least 73 landslides were reported after the atmospheric river event and there were likely many more that went undocumented. Some of these blocked critical transportation corridors for days on end. A section of U.S. 2 near Leavenworth was closed for weeks due to flood damage. North Cascades Lodge at Stehekin was forced to close for the summer of 2026 due to the flood damage. This week, following soaking rains and with the National Weather Service forecasting more heavy rain starting Friday, emergency management officials have warned Washingtonians about increased landslide risks.

READ MORE: National Park Service: Services limited at Stehekin Landing following winter flood damage

Improves Drought Monitoring:

The bill directs the National Integrated Drought Information System to advance and deploy next generation drought monitoring technologies and use observations from state or regional hydrological monitoring projects. The bill reauthorizes the National Weather Service’s work to provide agricultural and silvicultural weather and climate information and directs NOAA to establish at least two pilot projects to support improved extended range precipitation forecasts for agriculture and water management.

READ MORE: Yakima Herald-Republic: Washington state facing third-worst snowpack year on record, researchers say

Large portions of the State of Washington remain in moderate to severe drought, primarily due to snowpack deficits. Low precipitation and snowpack threaten irrigation water supplies, agriculture, and summer stream flows, which depend heavily on gradual snowmelt.

“We are tremendously appreciative of Sen. Cantwell’s continued leadership in protecting our natural resources, including our ocean,” said Jan Newton, Director of the Northwest Association of Networked Ocean Observing Systems (NANOOS) and affiliate professor with the University of Washington Collee of the Environment. “NANOOS is grateful that our policymakers understand the importance of the ocean to our weather, which is created and driven by many inter-related systems. We are excited that the Integrated Ocean Observing Systems (IOOS) network, of which NANOOS is a key component, is reauthorized as a part of the larger Weather Act reauthorization legislation. We thank the bipartisan group of Senators engaged in this effort.”

"Accurate weather forecasts are among the most direct ways science serves the public, and the stakes have never been higher as extreme weather grows more frequent and costly. The Weather Act Reauthorization Act would move research breakthroughs into operational forecasts faster, strengthening the nation's ability to prepare for, respond to, and recover from severe weather. AGU applauds Congress's bipartisan commitment to science-informed decision-making that safeguards communities across the country.” – Janice Lachance, Executive Director/CEO, American Geophysical Union

“Weather impacts everyone, every day, and the ability to provide timely, accurate weather information depends on a strong weather enterprise. The bipartisan Weather Act recognizes the importance of investing in the observations, science, technology, and forecasting capabilities that help us save lives, protect property, and support our economy. Strengthening those capabilities is an investment in the nation’s future." – Alan Sealls, President, American Meteorological Society

“Passage of the Weather Act Reauthorization is a giant step forward for the Weather Enterprise and its delivery of forecasts that save lives, protect communities, support businesses, and bolster our national economy. This bill strengthens public-private partnerships by augmenting critical government systems with increased use of innovative commercial data, paving the way for needed advances in observations, modeling, and information delivery. The American people will benefit every day from this legislation – from improved aviation and agricultural operations to earlier warnings for extreme weather such as tornadoes and flash flooding.” – Douglas Hilderbrand, Executive Director, American Weather Enterprise Association

Complete Highlights of the Legislation Include:

Enhancing Federal Weather Forecasting and Innovation

Addresses NOAA’s aging radar network by directing the agency to design and deploy the next generation of weather radar technology by 2037. It also authorizes NOAA to manage existing gaps in the current radar network by supplementing weather radar coverage with data, services, and technologies from third parties.

Establishes an atmospheric river forecast improvement program to develop tools and improved forecast models to address the increasingly frequent and powerful atmospheric rivers impacting the US, especially across the West coast.

Directs the National Weather Service to include turbulence events and icing conditions in their forecasting capabilities and establishes an airborne observation program to acquire atmospheric data from commercial aircraft.

Directs NOAA to improve accuracy and timeliness of weather, water, and space weather forecasts and effective dissemination of critical information using artificial intelligence.

Creates a project to improve forecasts of coastal marine fog with the goal of enhancing vessel safety and reducing the economic impact of coastal marine fog events.

Strengthening Emergency Preparedness by Improving Communication

Requires NOAA to maintain and improve the system that communicates potential hazardous weather or water events to the public.

Requires upgrades to outdated weather radio technology to provide reliable and continuous weather and emergency alerts and expands radio coverage to rural areas that do not currently have access to the National Weather Radio alert system.

Modernizing Critical Research Programs

Updates the Tsunami Forecasting and Warning Program to evaluate tsunami alert levels, maintain fail-safe warning capabilities, and align the analytic techniques and methodologies of the two existing tsunami warning centers in Hawaii and Alaska.

Builds on the progress of the Hurricane Forecast Improvement Project by establishing it as a long-term program that will incorporate social, behavioral, risk, and communication science into modeling, forecasting, and response guidance.

Expands the goals of the Tornado Warning Improvement and Extension Program to improve the effectiveness and timeliness of tornado forecasts, predictions, and warnings by increasing lead times, improving forecasting, and updating the system to rate the severity of tornadoes in collaboration with local communities and emergency managers.

Provides funding for weather laboratories; tornado, severe storm, and next generation radar research; and transitioning the latest scientific and technological advances into operations.

Supporting Farmers and Ranchers with Better Tools for Agriculture and Water Management

Directs the National Integrated Drought Information System to advance and deploy next-generation drought monitoring technologies and transition existing drought products to probabilistic forecasts, as well as use observations from state or regional hydrological monitoring projects.

Reauthorizes the National Weather Service’s work to provide agricultural and silvicultural weather and climate information and directs NOAA to establish at least two pilot projects to support improved sub-seasonal to seasonal extended range precipitation forecasts for agriculture and water management.

Codifies and authorizes the National Mesonet Program, a network of automated weather stations that are used to monitor and observe weather events and microclimates. The program is directed to obtain observations to improve understanding of and forecast capabilities for atmospheric, drought, fire, and water events and increase the quantity and density of environmental observations.

Expanding Commercial Data Partnerships

Increases NOAA’s access to critical forecasting data by expanding its authority to contract with the private sector to acquire commercial weather data.

Codifies the Commercial Data Program to coordinate and acquire a variety of weather and environmental data and services from the private sector for operational use.

Modifies the existing commercial data pilot program to be a testing program within the Commercial Data Program, and authorizes the program to test and evaluate all sources and types of observation services, imagery, products, and data from private sector entities.

Preparing for Disasters

Establishes within NOAA an interagency committee to coordinate agencies’ activities and ensure a united federal approach to reducing health risks from heat, as well as a NOAA system to improve the delivery of data, information, forecasts, warnings, prediction, and projections related to temperature and extreme heat.

Improves the monitoring, forecasting, prevention, and mitigation of harmful algal blooms and hypoxia that threaten aquatic ecosystems, hurt local economies, and endanger public health by reauthorizing and amending the National Harmful Algal Bloom and Hypoxia Program. Establishes a national harmful algal bloom observing network and a national incubator program and increases the avenues of assistance NOAA can provide to affected communities.

Requires the national landslide strategy to include an assessment of risks from atmospheric river flooding and extreme precipitation events and expands the National Landslide Hazards Database to cover areas needing further risk assessment due to factors such as hydrological changes and atmospheric river flooding

Read the bill text HERE.

Sen. Cantwell continues to insist on deploying the best technology to help our weather forecasters. Last year, Senator Cantwell called out the Administration’s decision to cancel its plan to launch a large-scale test of a new advanced weather radar technology, called Phased Array Radar.

Senate passage of the bill is another important next step to Sen. Cantwell’s 5 Point Plan to bolster the United States’ weather readiness, which she outlined in a letter to President Donald Trump in July of last year.

title: On Veterans Day, Cotton, Shaheen Applaud Senate Passage of Resolution to Establish National Warrior Call Day
text:

Contact: Tatum Wallace or Hannah McCarthy

November 11, 2026

On Veterans Day, Cotton, Shaheen Applaud Senate Passage of Resolution to Establish National Warrior Call Day

WASHINGTON—Senator Tom Cotton (R-Arkansas) and Senator Jeanne Shaheen (D-New Hampshire) announced their resolution to designate November 15, 2026, as National Warrior Call Day passed the Senate unanimously. This bipartisan resolution emphasizes the need for all Americans to reach out and build meaningful relationships with veterans and those currently serving to help support their mental health and foster community.

“Our military members and veterans deserve the support and resources they need to lead active, healthy lives after serving. This bipartisan resolution will raise awareness on the importance of service members’ mental health, and I’m glad to see it pass the Senate unanimously,” said Senator Cotton.

“No veteran should ever feel alone while struggling with their mental health, especially after sacrificing so much to defend our freedoms abroad. Warrior Call Day is one vital way that we can help connect veterans with resources while also reducing the stigma around asking for help and mental health care,” said Senator Shaheen. “I’m proud my Senate colleagues once again recognized the importance of our bipartisan resolution to designate Warrior Call Day because the health and well-being of the men and women in the military shouldn’t be a partisan issue.”

title: In Tribute to Veterans in Belleville, Duckworth Calls on Congress to Pass Her New Bill to Expand VA Care for Toxic-Exposed Veterans
text:
[BELLEVILLE, IL] — On Veterans Day in Belleville, U.S. Senator Tammy Duckworth (D-IL) called on Congress to pass her new legislation that would expand care at the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) for all Veterans who suffer from toxic exposure. Before the landmark PACT Act became law in 2022, red tape at the VA caused generations of Veterans to go without the care they needed after being exposed to Agent Orange, burn pits and other toxic hazards during their service in Iraq, Afghanistan and Vietnam. Duckworth’s New PACT for Iran Veterans Act seeks to ensure that Iran Veterans—who are being exposed to many similar hazards—and all future Veterans don’t face similar barriers to access care when they return home due to gaps in current law. Photos from today’s ceremony are available on the Senator’s website.

“Our Veterans put their country over themselves time after time, tour after tour, for the sake of families, neighbors and total strangers who will never know their names,” said Duckworth. “They deserve more than an ovation on Veterans Day. They deserve to be honored every single day of the year by a nation that makes sure they get the health care they’ve earned. Congress must learn from past mistakes and proactively ensure all future Veterans, including those serving in the Iran War, aren’t faced with similar barriers to accessing care that hurt so many Veterans who served in Iraq, Vietnam and Afghanistan. Congress must pass the New PACT for Iran Veterans Act. Because no servicemember should fight a war overseas only to come home and be faced with another battle to get the care they’ve rightfully earned through their service.”

Specifically, Senator Duckworth’s New PACT for Iran Veterans Act would:

Cut Red Tape for Iran War Veterans by statutorily presuming toxic substance exposure for Iran War Veterans, helping streamline their access to health care and benefits at VA. The bill would ensure that federal law protects all Veterans who fought in Iran, including those who operated in Iranian airspace and territorial waters.

Leave No Veteran Behind by requiring, for the first time, that the VA’s Military Environmental Exposure Sub-Council (MEESC) conducts studies at least every five years to review all overseas assignments for toxic substance exposures. Additionally, when the military begins a contingency operation, the VA must commence a similar review of the locations from which servicemembers support this operation within 180 days. This would ensure the VA proactively looks into whether servicemembers are being exposed to toxic hazards, for current and future assignments.

Enhance Transparency at the VA by requiring the VA Secretary to publicly explain their justification for any denial of a country that’s recommended for presumed toxic-exposures in these reviews, or any removal of existing presumptions.

At today’s event, Duckworth joined Veterans and their families at the City of Belleville’s 28th Annual Veterans Day Ceremony alongside Belleville Fire Department Chief Curt Lougeay and Brigadier General Joseph Janik, Eighteenth Air Force Commander.

“May we remember the sacrifices of our veterans, support them and their families, and work together to safeguard the freedoms they defended. To every veteran in Belleville and across our nation: we salute you, and we thank you,” said Belleville Mayor Jenny Gain Meyer.

The Senator also hosted a roundtable discussion with local Veteran Service Organizations (VSOs) and Veterans Commissions (VCAs) where she highlighted her New PACT for Iran Veterans Act and heard directly from the leaders who serve our nation’s heroes every day about how she can continue fighting on the federal level to protect access to resources and care for Illinois Veterans. Photos from the roundtable are available on the Senator’s website.

Duckworth has long been fierce leader and advocate for our nation’s Veterans. Some of her efforts include:

On April 29, 2026, Duckworth helped introduced the Servicemember Civilian Transition Support Act to better support servicemembers as they transition back to civilian life.

On April 3, 2026, Duckworth introduced the bipartisan Copay Fairness for Veterans Act to eliminate unfair out-of-pocket health care costs for Veterans. Earlier this year, she helped lead a bipartisan push to make it easier for Veterans to use their GI Bill benefits in apprenticeship programs.

On March 27, 2026, Duckworth helped introduced the bipartisan Veterans Health Administration Novel Therapeutics Preparedness Act to increase Veterans’ access to innovative health care and ensure the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) is prepared to better care for Veterans with emerging mental health therapies.

On February 18, 2026, Duckworth demanded that the VA rescind a rule change that put millions of Veterans’ disability ratings and care at risk. The VA later paused enforcement of the rule.

On May 7, 2025, Duckworth introduced the Protecting Veterans in Crisis Act to help safeguard the Veterans Crisis Line (VCL) for the brave Veterans who depend on it by increasing transparency and strengthening Congress’s oversight of it. On the same day, Duckworth also introduced the VA Employee Fairness Act to empower VA health care professionals with the protections needed to speak out about disruptions and advocate for the Veterans they serve as Donald Trump and Elon Musk’s VA cuts continued to jeopardize care.

On March 10, 2025, Duckworth introduced the Protect Veteran Jobs Act to reinstate Veterans who were fired from their jobs as part of Donald Trump and Elon Musk’s indiscriminate purge of federal employees.

On January 4, 2019, Duckworth’s bipartisan Veterans Small Business Enhancement Act was signed into law, allowing Veteran small business owners to acquire surplus federal equipment and personal property by adding Veterans to the list of eligible recipients, which already includes women and minority small business owners.

title: Hawley Works to Protect Missouri Farmers & Landowners in Senate Transmission Bill
text:
WASHINGTON — Today, U.S. Senator Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) introduced four amendments to the Senate’s permitting and transmission bill to better protect farmers in Missouri and across the country. Senator Hawley’s amendments would add new rights and protections for farmers, ranchers, and landowners from eminent domain takings of their land for electric transmission projects.

For years, Senator Hawley has advocated for landowners against disruptive transmission lines on agricultural land in Missouri, including by successfully securing the cancellation of a $5 billion federal loan for the Grain Belt Express project last year.

Senator Hawley’s amendments for consideration:

Amendment #1: This amendment would create a new statutory federal floor of 150% of fair market value for “just compensation” to landowners when their land is taken through eminent domain—while allowing individual states to set even higher compensation rates.

Amendment #2: This amendment would extend the time allowed for a state’s consideration of an application for a transmission line from one year to two years before the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) may exercise its backstop siting authority to issue a permit. This would give states and landowners more time to consider and debate these projects.

Amendment #3: This amendment would provide FERC the discretion to notexercise its backstop siting authority, even if all statutory conditions are met. Under existing law, FERC is required to exercise its backstop siting authority when all conditions are met.

title: Husted-led bill to expand Dayton Aviation Heritage National Historical Park passes Senate
text:
“I’m proud to support efforts that keep Dayton Aviation Heritage National Park showcasing its accomplishments and sharing Ohio’s rich history with visitors from our state and across the world.”

WASHINGTON – The U.S. Senate passed Sens. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) and Bernie Moreno’s (R-Ohio) bill that would expand the Dayton Aviation Heritage National Historical Park. Reps. Mike Turner (R-Ohio) and Greg Landsman (D-Ohio) introduced the companion bill in the U.S. House of Representatives.

“More than 120 years ago, the Wright brothers pioneered their aviation work and built the world’s first airplane in Dayton. I’m proud to support efforts that keep Dayton Aviation Heritage National Park showcasing its accomplishments and sharing Ohio’s rich history with visitors from our state and across the world,” said Husted.

Husted and Moreno introduced the bill in July 2025.

This bill would amend the Dayton Aviation Heritage Preservation Act of 1992 to extend the boundary of the park. On average, more than 81,000 people visit the Dayton Aviation National Historical Park each year.

Background:

The Dayton Aviation Heritage Preservation Act of 1992 authorized the Dayton Aviation Heritage National Historical Park. Under the law, the park contained four non-contiguous sites.

Since the park’s establishment, Congress enacted two laws expanding the boundaries to include additional sites.

The Dayton Aviation National Historical Park has limited access to minor boundary authorities under the Land Water Conversation Fund authority. For any adjustment to the park’s boundaries, congressional action is needed.

title: Warner, Kaine & Fetterman Condemn Trump-Vance Administration’s Proposed Weakening of Silica Rule That Protects Coal Miners from Black Lung

title: ICYMI: On Veterans Day, Kelly Reflects on Military Service and Honoring Veterans
text:
“When I think about Veterans Day, I think about those people I served with, the men and women serving today, and the generations of patriotic Americans who have signed up to risk their lives for our country.”

In case you missed it, Arizona Senator and 25-year Navy combat veteran Mark Kelly penned an essay in The Ripon Forum ahead of Veterans Day reflecting on his military service, the importance of teamwork and sacrifice, and the responsibility to ensure veterans receive the care and support they have earned.

Click here to read the full essay in the Ripon Forum. See key excerpts below:

On the lessons learned during his first combat mission…

Military service isn’t usually about the medals, it’s about accomplishing a mission, together. […] That clicked for me on my first combat mission. I was flying an A-6E Intruder with my bombardier navigator Paul Fujimura. One of my primary jobs as the pilot was to fly the plane and get us safely over the target. The bombardier navigator’s job was to navigate us to the target, identify it and track it with the weapons system.

We started taking anti-aircraft fire and I saw a surface-to-air missile coming right at us. I told Paul about the missile, and his response was simple: “Roger, I’m tracking the target.” I told him again and again and got the same response each time. That’s when I realized that to accomplish the mission, Paul had to do his job, and I had to do mine.

On honoring the sacrifices of veterans and military families…

I flew 39 combat missions, but I never flew any of them alone. And supporting all of us were families back home making sacrifices of their own. When I think about Veterans Day, I think about those people I served with, the men and women serving today, and the generations of patriotic Americans who have signed up to risk their lives for our country. In return, our country makes a promise that after their service, they will receive the care and support they earned.

On keeping our promise to veterans…

As a combat veteran, I take that promise personally. I helped pass the PACT Act to expand VA health coverage for servicemembers who were exposed to toxins during their service. I worked with my Republican colleagues to pass the ACES Act to study cancer rates among military aviators and aircrew. And I’ve successfully passed a bill to help build a veteran’s center in Gila County, Arizona.

On what Veterans Day means to him…

When I was 22 years old, I swore an oath to protect and defend the Constitution. That oath stayed with me through 39 combat missions and four trips to space. This Veterans Day and every day, I’m proud to stand alongside the millions of Americans who have answered the call to serve. Like I told those students, when you talk with a veteran, know that they didn’t do it for the medals or the recognition. They did it for their country and their fellow service members.

And now serving as a U.S. Senator, swearing the same oath to the Constitution again, I remember the same lesson from that first combat mission. We all have a job to do, our piece to accomplish the larger mission for our neighbor and our country.

title: Kelly, Colleagues Introduce Bill to Expand PACT Act Coverage to Iran War Veterans Exposed to Toxic Substances
text:
Senators Mark Kelly (D-AZ), Tammy Duckworth (D-IL), and eleven of their Senate colleagues introduced the New PACT for Iran Veterans Act, legislation that would ensure Iran veterans are covered under the Kelly-backed PACT Act passed in 2022, cutting unnecessary red tape and making it easier for our warfighters who are being exposed to toxic substances to access the unique treatment they need when they return home.

The PACT Act helped generations of Veterans—from Vietnam to Iraq—more easily receive care from the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) by establishing a list of locations where it is presumed by law that troops who served there were exposed to toxic hazards. Iran is currently not included on this presumed-exposure list.

The New PACT for Iran Veterans Act would require the VA to add Iran to the list of covered locations and take more proactive action to ensure Iran War veterans and all veterans who serve in future conflicts don’t have to jump through bureaucratic hoops in order to access the care they’ve earned through their service.

“As a Navy combat veteran, I know that our responsibility to servicemembers doesn’t end when they return home,” said Kelly. “We’ve seen too many veterans exposed to toxic substances during their service have to fight for years to get the health care and benefits they’ve earned. We can’t let that happen to another generation of servicemembers.”

“By establishing the landmark PACT Act, our nation finally helped generations of Veterans who suffered from toxic exposure in Vietnam, Iraq and Afghanistan more easily access the care they needed after being stonewalled by bureaucratic tape for years,” said Duckworth. “With a new generation of troops being thrown into another war in the Middle East, our nation must learn the lessons from previous conflicts and proactively ensure Iran Veterans don’t suffer from those same mistakes. Our New PACT for Iran Veterans Act would ensure no servicemember fights a war overseas only to come home and be faced with another battle to get the care they’ve rightfully earned through their service. Congress must act to care for these heroes now—not later.”

“The cost of war includes providing health care and benefits to veterans exposed to toxins during their military service,” said Blumenthal. “This legislation would build on the PACT Act to ensure all servicemembers sent into harm’s way, including recent veterans of the war with Iran, are able to receive the benefits they deserve.”

“Our veterans deserve access to prompt, timely healthcare – regardless of the conflict and country where they serve for our country,” said King. “Just as the PACT Act represented a historical milestone for Vietnam, Iraq, and Afghanistan veterans, our New PACT for Iran Veterans Act will ensure that the VA recognizes the unique current toxic exposure risks of our service members sacrifice and guarantee they receive the support they have earned, without delay.”

“The bipartisan PACT Act marked a historic step in ensuring that veterans and servicemembers exposed to toxic substances can get the care they need and deserve,” said Welch. “But President Trump’s reckless decision to throw our country into war in the Middle East means there’s a new generation of veterans facing conditions that could be hazardous to their health. We need to update our pact to servicemembers to ensure that Iran War Servicemembers and Veterans aren’t faced with red tape to get proper benefits and care once they come home.”

“For too long, veterans exposed to toxic substances during their service have had to fight for the care and benefits they earned. The PACT Act was a historic step toward correcting that failure,” said Bennet. “We have a responsibility to ensure the men and women serving today in President Trump’s reckless Iran war do not face those same barriers when they come home. Congress must act now to ensure all future veterans can access their hard-earned health care and benefits without having to fight the VA.”

“Donald Trump might not care, but the cost of war includes supporting our veterans when they come back home,” said Murray. “This legislation is a commonsense next step to expand the PACT Act to make sure our servicemembers who served in Iran continue to receive the care they need after their service is over. As I continue fighting to end the war—I want to be crystal clear that I won’t let this President leave American veterans in the dust.”

“As federal law, the historic PACT Act resulted in over 115,000 claims filed in Pennsylvania so veterans exposed to toxins could rightfully get the care they need. Servicemembers currently in the Middle East supporting our mission in Iran will not be eligible to file claims,” said Fetterman. “We need to change that through this bill, uphold our end of the sacred promise to those who answered the call to serve, and ensure future veterans are not subjected to the same delays as those before them.”

Background:

The PACT Act was signed into law in 2022 following efforts from Kelly, a Gulf War veteran, who helped pass the legislation and spoke on the Senate floor in support of the bill. The law was one of the largest expansions of VA health care benefits in history.

The New PACT for Iran Veterans Act would:

Cut red tape for Iran war veterans by statutorily presuming toxic substance exposure for Iran War Veterans, helping streamline their access to health care and benefits at VA. The bill would ensure that federal law protects all Veterans who fought in Iran, including those who operated in Iranian airspace and territorial waters.

Leave no veteran behind by requiring for the first time, that the VA’s Military Environmental Exposure Sub-Council (MEESC) conducts studies at least every five years to review all overseas assignments for toxic substance exposures. Additionally, when the military begins a contingency operation, the VA must commence a similar review of the locations from which servicemembers support this operation within 180 days. This would ensure the VA proactively looks into whether servicemembers are being exposed to toxic hazards, for current and future assignments.

Enhance transparency at the VA by requiring the VA secretary to publicly explain their justification for any denial of a country that’s recommended for presumed toxic-exposures in these reviews, or any removal of existing presumptions.

In addition to Kelly and Duckworth, the legislation is cosponsored by Senators Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), Angus King (I-ME), Bernie Sanders (I-VT), Peter Welch (D-VT), Michael Bennet (D-CO), Patty Murray (D-WA), John Fetterman (D-PA), Ron Wyden (D-OR), Maria Cantwell (D-WA), Angela Alsobrooks (D-MD) and Chris Van Hollen (D-MD).

title: WATCH: In Senate EPW Hearing, Kelly Presses EPA Nominee on Data Center Pollution and Public Input
text:
“The thing I hear most from communities in Arizona where these proposed data centers are built is ‘how can we have our voices heard?’”

Today, during a Senate Environment and Public Works (EPW) Committee hearing, Arizona Senator Mark Kelly pressed Justin Schwab, President Trump’s nominee to lead the Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) Office of Air and Radiation, on the agency’s proposal to eliminate longstanding public comment requirements for certain air pollution permits, including for data centers building their own power plants. Kelly also secured a commitment from Schwab to prioritize final approval of a Maricopa County air quality rule aimed at reducing air pollution from off-road equipment.

Kelly raised concerns that EPA’s proposal to eliminate the 30-day public comment period for certain air pollution permits could leave communities without a say in new data center projects: “As you know, there’s a massive boom in data center development across the country. The thing I hear most from communities in Arizona where these proposed data centers are built is, ‘how can we have our voices heard?’ That’s especially true if a data center is proposing to build what’s called behind-the-meter generation. Or in other words, they’re going to build their own power plant. For decades, EPA has required at least 30 days for the public to review and comment on proposed permits. Seems rather reasonable.”

Kelly questioned who pushed for the rollback after seven major data center developers responded to an October inquiry from Kelly, and none indicated they had requested the change: “Earlier this year, EPA proposed a new rule that would allow states to eliminate the public comment opportunity for any minor source facility that emits less than 100 tons of pollution per year. I think that’s unacceptable, and what I can’t understand is who asked for this.”

Last month, Kelly and Whitehouse urged EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin to withdraw the proposal, arguing that faster permitting should not come at the expense of transparency or communities’ ability to shape decisions that affect them. During the hearing, Schwab committed to looking into the senators’ letter after Kelly pressed him to ensure EPA provides a response.

Kelly also secured a commitment from Schwab to advance Maricopa County’s efforts to improve air quality: “Just last week, EPA formally approved the county’s Rule 205, which allows businesses to generate emissions credits by replacing older, higher-polluting vehicles with cleaner ones. I appreciate that progress, but Rule 204, which would establish a similar program for off-road equipment, still needs final approval.”

When Kelly asked whether Schwab would prioritize EPA’s ongoing work with Maricopa County to move Rule 204 toward final approval as quickly as possible, Schwab responded, “Yes. If confirmed, I do commit to prioritize in that regard.”

Sen. Kelly questions EPA nominees in EPW hearing.

Click here to download a video of Kelly’s remarks. See the transcript below:

Sen. Mark Kelly: Thank you, Madam Chair and thank you, Mr. Schwab, for being here today. I’d like to first ask you about Maricopa County’s efforts to improve air quality, which has spanned multiple administrations. Just last week, EPA formally approved the county’s rule 205, which allows businesses to generate emissions credits by replacing older, higher polluting vehicles with cleaner ones.

I appreciate that progress, but rule 204, which would establish a similar program for off road equipment, still needs final approval. Mr. Schwab, if confirmed, will you commit to prioritizing EPA’s ongoing work with Maricopa County to move rule 204 toward final approval as quickly as possible?

Justin Schwab, Nominee, Assistant Administrator for the Office of Air and Radiation: Thank you for the question, Senator. Yes. If confirmed, I do commit to prioritize in that regard.

Kelly: Well, thank you. Mr. Schwab, next, I want to talk about data centers. As you know, there’s a massive boom in data center development across the country. The thing I hear most from communities in Arizona where these proposed data centers are built, is how can we have our voices heard? That’s especially true of a data center is proposing to build what’s called behind the meter generation.

Or in other words, they’re going to build their own power plant. Right now, those facilities would need to get a minor new source review permit. And for decades, EPA has required at least 30 days for the public to review and comment on proposed permits. Seems rather reasonable. 30 days. It basically says to a developer, if you want to admit up to 100 tons of nitrous oxide or soot a year, you need to give the surrounding community opportunity to understand the impacts of a project and voice their concerns before construction begins.

Mr. Schwab, let me ask you a question. So, would you be comfortable with a data center that admitted just less than the 100 tons of NOx or PPM 2.5 near your home, without a guaranteed opportunity to give your input?

Schwab: Thank you for the question, senator. Matters of permitting are in the first instance, the responsibility of state or local governments.

The Clean Air Act does provide certain minimum requirements. The Clean Air Act does expressly require state permitting programs in order to be approved by EPA to provide for public engagement when it comes to major new source, review sources, but does not contain any such requirement with respect to minor news source review sources and in that regard.

Kelly: Well, that’s what I’m asking but from your personal life, would you be comfortable with a data center that admitted just less than, the cutoff is 100 tons, just less than the 100 tons of NOx or PPM 2.5 near your home without a guaranteed opportunity to give your own input. That’s the question.

Schwab: Thank you for the question, senator. It would depend on the particular circumstances of the facility.

Kelly: The circumstance is a data center is being built, and it’s going to admit, let’s say, a just under 100 tons of night nitrous oxide of NOx. Would you be comfortable with that without having an opportunity to give your own input on the issue?

Schwab: Thank you for the question, senator. As I said, matters of permitting are appropriately where consistent with federal law, the prerogative of state and local governments. And those are the ones that know their communities best.

Kelly: Yes, so you don’t think homeowners, people in the region of where the data center is being built should get a say if it’s just less than the 100 tons or you don’t think it’s up to them at all.

Schwab: Senator, the Congress Enacting the Clean Air Act, has provided those areas in which federal law does require all state permitting process to engage, to include a public participation phase. And there are other areas in which federal law does not have that express requirement. And there is a pending proposal in that regard from.

Kelly: Well, it sounds like your answer is no. I’m trying to understand where are you on this? If it’s less than 100 tons, you don’t think people should get an input. You keep coming back to the law, but I’m just asking you your opinion.

Schwab: My opinion is that, as a general principle, state and local governments and agencies understand their communities and their concerns best.

Kelly: Well, earlier this year, EPA proposed a new rule that would allow states to eliminate the public comment opportunity for any minor source facility that emits less than 100 tons of pollution per year.

I think that’s unacceptable and what I can’t understand is who asked for this. So, I worked with Ranking Member Whitehouse to ask nine of the leading data center developers said seven of them responded, and none of them said they asked EPA to make this rule. So, Mr. Schwab, you’ve been at EPA since these rules were proposed and you’ve been in the Trump administration since the president took office.

So maybe, you know, like who asked the EPA to roll back these common-sense protections?

Schwab: Thank you for the question, senator. The proposal is not specific to data centers. The proposal addresses generally requirements for minor —

Kelly: Who asked to roll them back? Because it wasn’t the data centers. So must have been somebody, unless it was just decided internally that you don’t think the community should have an input.

Schwab: Senator, the policies of the United States is articulated by the president’s executive orders are where consistent with law, to reform permitting processes to ensure that they do not include non-statutory non legally required provisions that may hinder development.

Having said that, it is the prerogative of state and local governments in the first instance where federal law is silent on a question to determine what level of public participation may be appropriate under their own —

Kelly: It sounds like you’re saying it came from the White House. Well, what I’m going to ask you here is, will you commit to speaking with Administrator Zeldin and his team about the letter we sent to make sure we get an answer to our letter.

Schwab: Thank you for the question, senator. I’m not familiar with this letter, but, yes, I do confirm the looking into the letter.

title: Kennedy on Veterans Day: “There aren’t words in English . . . to be able to express my gratitude”

title: Kennedy urges Republicans to pass a reconciliation bill: “If we fail, we fail, but at least we will have tried”
text:
Watch Kennedy’s comments here.

WASHINGTON – Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) urged his Republican colleagues to pass another reconciliation bill before the end of the year in a speech on the U.S. Senate floor.

Key excerpts of the speech are below:

“In January, the Democrats will take over, but Republicans are in power until then. The first thing we ought to do is put down our—as Republicans still in charge—put down our juice boxes and listen to the American people. The second thing that we need to do is stop the bleeding, pick ourselves up and fight.”

. . .

“Well, we had a long meeting yesterday among ourselves as Senate Republicans. And I think, obviously, we concluded that we have a lot of nominations, presidential appointments and judicial appointments that we have to address for the remainder of this Congress. If we don’t confirm these people, my Democratic friends will not. I can assure you. So, we have to do that.”

. . .

“In my opinion, that’s not enough. That’s not enough. Whatever we propose, in terms of policy, my Democrat colleagues are not going to go along because they’re going to be in charge in January, so they can just wait this out. That means for Republicans—who are still in charge—to do something, we’ve got to approach reconciliation, which only requires a majority vote. While I concede that the confirmations should come first, I don’t concede—unlike some of my colleagues—that attempting reconciliation would be a waste of time.”

. . .

“First, I would do a reconciliation bill that provides at least $200 billion for our military. . . . Our military is running out of bullets. And they need our support, and we should give it to them. The second thing I would do—and this is one person’s opinion. I’m certainly, certainly open to other ideas. Senator [Joni] Ernst has a bill to address the rampant fraud throughout the federal government. I would take up that bill, and I would pass it and use the savings from abolishing or at least undermining that fraud and use it to pay down our debt.”

. . .

“And some of my colleagues say, ‘Well, we can’t pass it, so we shouldn’t try.’ And I think that’s how we got beat. I think the American people want us to try. So, I’m for spending the time, effort and energy to put together a reconciliation bill. I would start with extra money for the military, and then I’m open to other ideas, and I would begin the process next week. And if we fail, we fail, but at least we will have tried.”

title: On Veteran’s Day, King Speaks with County Resident about Serving Country and Community
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — U.S. Senator Angus King (I-ME), a member of the Senate Veterans’ Affairs (SVAC) and Armed Services Committees (SASC), released his latest episode of “Answering the Call: Maine’s Veteran Voices.” In the series, produced in partnership with the Library of Congress’ Veterans History Project, Senator King spoke with former Army reservist Melanie Junkins of Presque Isle, Maine.

Junkins served the country for many years with the Army Reserve. She also spent time in an Active Guard/Reserve (AGR) status.

“Melanie Junkins was one of the millions of Americans who has selflessly served our country, putting her own interests aside in pursuit of the greater American good,” said Senator King. “Most importantly, however, her commitment to service and community extends far beyond her time in the Army Reserve. Since moving to Maine, she has worked diligently at the Maine Department of Education and as a professor at the University of Maine at Presque Isle. Melanie also served as a panelist on my office’s military academy nominations board, helping to select the next generation of leaders for our national service academies. Melanie Junkins is the very best of America and I am glad we can now preserve her story in the Library of Congress for posterity.”

Melanie was born in South Korea, before being adopted and raised in Iowa. Throughout her childhood, she dreamed of becoming President of the United States. After learning she was Constitutionally-ineligible, Melanie wrote a letter to then-Senator Tom Harkin. In Harkin’s response, he commended Melanie for her desire to be a public servant. Then, in high school, an Army Recruiter visited Melanie’s class. She was intrigued by the avenue of public service, and after high school, she enlisted into the Army Reserve through the Split Training Option. She was sent to bootcamp in Fort Leonard Wood, Missouri in 1997 when she was a junior in high school. She returned to Iowa for her senior year and after graduating high school, she completed her advanced training in Columbia, South Carolina. She then began working as an administrative assistant in the Army Reserves.

In 1999, Melanie joined the Active Guard Reserve in Rochester, New York, for the 98th Division Headquarters. While there, Melanie met her husband, who was Active-Duty Coast Guard, stationed on Lake Ontario. Melanie left active status in August of 2001, returning to the Army Reserve, still under the 98th Division, but in Lewiston, Maine. Melanie and her husband had their first child in early 2002 while her husband was stationed in Portland at sector New England. After leaving the Army Reserves in 2005 at the completion of her contract, they moved to the county where they gave birth to their daughter in 2006.

Throughout her career, Melanie served in Missouri, South Carolina, New York, and Maine. In New York, she supported the budget & finance office, and the personnel office, before working in training.

After retiring, she returned to Maine with her husband. A year later, in 2006, her daughter was born. In 2017, Melanie graduated from college, receiving her bachelor's degree from University of Maine, Presque Isle. In 2018, she received her Master of Science in Education in Teaching English to Speakers of Other Languages (MSed in TESOL) from the University of Southern Maine. In recent years, Melanie worked for the Maine Department of Education, as a multilingual & bilingual education specialist and as an Assistant Professor of Education at the University of Maine, Presque Isle. She still believes in giving back to her community by advocating for educational opportunities for veterans and other servicemembers as well as English language learning for the wider northern Maine community. She has previously volunteered with Maine Children’s Home, Peer to Peer tutoring at Presque Isle High School, and Dream Factory Portland. She also served as a panelist on Senator King’s military academy nominations board from 2013-2021.

The Veterans History Project is an effort by the Library of Congress to collect, preserve and distribute the personal accounts of American war veterans so that future generations may hear directly from veterans and better understand the realities of war. The interviews and primary documents from the project are then used by researchers, historians, students, and filmmakers across the country. Senator King joins many other members of Congress who’ve participated in the project, and was honored by the then-Librarian of Congress on Veterans Day 2022 when she participated in a one-on-one interview with him to talk through his Maine conversations.

Representing one of the states with the highest rates of military families and veterans per capita, Senator King is a staunch advocate for America’s servicemembers and veterans. A member of the Senate Veterans’ Affairs Committee (SVAC), he works to ensure American veterans receive their earned benefits and that the VA is properly implementing various programs such as the PACT Act, the State Veterans Homes Domiciliary Care Flexibility Act, and the John Scott Hannon Act. Recently, Senator King introduced bipartisan legislation to help reduce suicides among veterans by providing free secure firearm storage to veterans. In addition, he helped pass the Veterans COLA Act, which increased benefits for 30,000 Maine veterans and their families. Senator King has also introduced bipartisan legislation to improve care coordination for veterans who rely on both VA health care and Medicare.

title: Klobuchar Statement on Veterans Day 2026
text:
MINNESOTA - U.S. Senator Amy Klobuchar (D-MN) released the statement below in honor of Veterans Day.

“Veterans Day is a time to honor the men and women who have worn our nation's uniform and the sacrifices they made to defend our freedoms. It’s also a time to remember the promise we make to them: that we will stand by them just as they stood by us.

Veterans Day has always been personal to me because my dad served during the Korean War. After returning home, he became a newspaperman who loved writing about the "heroes among us" — ordinary people doing extraordinary things. I can think of no better way to describe the generations of Minnesotans who have answered the call to serve our country.

And this year in Minnesota — with the new Military & Veterans Museum in Little Falls telling the story of generations of Minnesotans who served, and the new veterans memorial in Bloomington — we continue to find new ways to honor these heroes among us.

Our veterans remind us that what unites us as Americans is far bigger than what divides us. Their example reminds us of the importance of coming together in service of something greater than ourselves.

And we must honor our veterans with more than our words. When our troops signed up to serve our nation, there wasn't a waiting line. And when they come home and need a job, housing, or health care, there shouldn't be a waiting line either.

That means making sure veterans can get their disability claims processed on time, access the G.I. benefits they've earned, and access quality health care and services no matter where they live.

I’ve worked with colleagues on both sides of the aisle to deliver on these commitments, including through the bipartisan PACT Act — which expanded care for those exposed to toxic substances like Agent Orange and burn pits during their service.

And I will continue fighting to make sure we honor the promises we made to those who served, whether that is in the U.S. Senate or as your next governor.

This Veterans Day, let's take time to thank the veterans throughout our communities, listen to their stories, and remember the families who stood beside them. We can never fully repay them for what they have given our country, but we can make sure they know their service will never be forgotten.

To all of Minnesota's veterans, service members, and military families: thank you. You represent the best of America, and we are forever grateful for your service.”

title: Lankford to Seek HSGAC Ranking Member Position in 120th Congress
text:
WASHINGTON, DC — US Senator James Lankford (R-OK) today announced he intends to seek the position of Ranking Member of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee (HSGAC) in the 120th Congress:

“In the days ahead, I intend to ask my Republican colleagues on HSGAC for their support for me to be selected as Ranking Member next Congress. There is important work ahead on FEMA reform, the federal workforce, and making government operate more effectively and efficiently for the American people.

“In many areas of government operation, HSGAC can operate in a bipartisan manner. Waste and inefficiency should not be a Republican or Democratic issue. Over the last decade on the Homeland Security Committee, I have worked across the aisle to improve emergency communications in federal buildings, strengthen the United States Postal Service, increase federal cybersecurity preparedness, government transparency, and the use of artificial intelligence. This Committee has a broad responsibility to make sure the federal government does its job well.

“As the only Committee with broad oversight and subpoena authority across the federal government, we have an important responsibility to ask hard questions, get answers, and make sure government is working as it should. However, the job of any Ranking Member is to also push back on a majority that goes too far. There is important work done at the Department of Homeland Security by brave men and women and their efforts should not be hampered simply because of partisan politics. Oversight is responsible, but obstruction is unacceptable.

“I look forward to serving with Senator Maggie Hassan in our new roles. We have worked together very productively on numerous occasions, most recently on our Prevent Government Shutdowns Act. Years ago, Dr. Tom Coburn of Oklahoma and Senator Tom Carper of Delaware worked together on this same Committee to do essential oversight and non-partisan work for the American people. I plan to work together when we can agree and be a fierce opposition if there is an attempt to undercut our nation’s security.

“The Department of Homeland Security is the third-largest federal department, and its work touches the lives of Americans every day. From TSA and CISA to Border Patrol and the United States Coast Guard, the men and women of DHS work to keep America safe on our borders, at sea, and in our skies. I look forward to highlighting their work and making sure the Department is fulfilling its mission.”

Background

Lankford has served on the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee since 2015 and has spent more than a decade working on issues within its jurisdiction. He has served as Chairman of the Subcommittee on Regulatory Affairs and Federal Management and currently chairs the Subcommittee on Border Management, Federal Workforce, and Regulatory Affairs, where he has led oversight hearings on border security, federal workforce readiness, government operations, and regulatory accountability.

Lankford has worked to make the federal government more accountable to the people it serves. He authored the Taxpayers Right-to-Know Act, which became law in 2021, and has worked on issues ranging from federal hiring and regulatory reform to cybersecurity and artificial intelligence.

As Subcommittee Chairman, Lankford has also led oversight of border security and federal preparedness, including a 2025 hearing examining federal readiness ahead of the 2026 FIFA World Cup, 2028 Olympics, and America’s 250th anniversary.

Former Oklahoma Senator Tom Coburn served as Ranking Member of HSGAC from 2013 to January 2015.

title: VIDEO: Sen. Moran Honors Veterans Day on the Senate Floor
text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. Senator Jerry Moran (R-Kan.) – chairman of the Senate Committee on Veterans’ Affairs – today gave remarks on the Senate floor to honor Veterans Day and highlight the importance of passing the Take Care of America’s Veterans Act in the Senate, which would support millions of veterans, their families, their caregivers and their survivors. Earlier in the day, the House of Representatives passed the legislation.

“Today, we have a special opportunity to remind the veterans in our lives of how grateful we are for them, and to share our appreciation for all they have sacrificed in uniform and how they continue to serve our nation as veterans,” said Sen. Moran. “My father served in Italy and Africa during World War II. While his military service earned him the honor that is due to all our veterans, the life he modeled for me in the years after the war embodied character and patriotism strengthened by his time in the military.”

During his remarks, Sen. Moran addressed the importance of passing the Take Care of America’s Veterans Act, which includes dozens of bipartisan and bicameral pieces of legislation that would deliver long awaited reforms for veterans, their families, caregivers, survivors and Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) staff.

“The Take Care of America’s Veterans Act would allow combat disabled veterans to receive both their earned retirement pay and their VA disability benefits,” continued Sen. Moran. “This legislation would also allow veterans in Kansas and across the U.S. – particularly the most vulnerable veterans in need of support for mental health or addiction support – to access life-saving care more easily and closer to home…It would also deliver meaningful benefits to surviving spouses and family members of our nation’s fallen servicemembers and veterans. Millions of veterans, caregivers, survivors and families have been waiting on Congress to deliver these reforms for many years. They should not have to wait any longer.”

Watch Sen. Moran’s Full Veterans Day Remarks HERE

Sen. Moran’s Remarks as Prepared:

“As our nation comes together today to recognize Veterans Day, I want to take this time to honor and pay tribute to those who have served and sacrificed to protect our freedoms.

“There is no group I hold in higher regard than our nation’s veterans. The challenges they have faced, the courage they have shown, the patriotism they exude, and their selfless sacrifice for our freedoms is something we will never be able to repay.

“Originally called Armistice Day, this day of recognition was created to commemorate the end of World War I – on the 11th hour of the 11th day of the 11th month.

“Years later, in 1953, Alvin J. King of Emporia in my home state of Kansas, proposed changing the name to Veterans Day to recognize and honor America’s veterans from all wars and conflicts.

“In 1954, Kansas’ very own President Eisenhower made the change official – establishing Veterans Day.

“For 107 years, our nation has observed this holiday, first as Armistice Day and now as Veterans Day. Each year, we remember the men and women who have served and earned our lasting gratitude.

“Today, we have a special opportunity to remind the veterans in our lives of how grateful we are for them, and to share our appreciation for all they have sacrificed in uniform and how they continue to serve our nation as veterans.

“My father served in Italy and Africa during World War II. While his military service earned him the honor that is due to all our veterans, the life he modeled for me in the years after the war embodied character and patriotism strengthened by his time in the military.

“I will never forget the first day I visited newly constructed World War II Memorial on the National Mall. Days before the formal dedication, I walked down to see what it looked like – and I thought of my father and the many heroes like him.

“I called him then and shared a message that I have repeated many times over the years, to him and all of our nation’s heroes:

“I want you to know I thank you for your service, I respect you and I love you.”

“As Chairman of the Senate Committee on Veterans’ Affairs, I have made it my mission to make certain every American veteran receives the care and support embodied by those words.

“Veterans Day is dedicated to honoring those like my father who have given so much in service to our country.

“Today, as we honor those who have worn the uniform, we have a duty as members of Congress to make certain that they are receiving the health care, benefits and services they have earned and deserve.

“Today, the U.S. House of Representatives is voting on landmark legislation that would support tens of millions of veterans and their families, their caregivers and their survivors.

“The Take Care of America’s Veterans Act would allow combat disabled veterans to receive both their earned retirement pay and their VA disability benefits.

“This legislation would also allow veterans in Kansas and across the U.S. – particularly the most vulnerable veterans in need of support for mental health or addiction support – to access life-saving care more easily and closer to home.

“The Take Care of America’s Veterans Act would support veteran caregivers during and after their caregiving journeys, while improving support for aging veterans, veterans with spinal cord injuries and disorders, and veterans with serious conditions like ALS.

“And the Take Care of America’s Veterans Act would deliver meaningful benefits to surviving spouses and family members of our nation’s fallen servicemembers and veterans.

“Millions of veterans, caregivers, survivors and families have been waiting on Congress to deliver these reforms for many years. They should not have to wait any longer.

“I can think of no better way of honoring veterans and their families than by passing the Take Care of America’s Veterans Act.

“I appreciate the support of my colleagues in the House of Representatives to advance that bill, and I will not let up on my efforts to secure a vote in the Senate as soon as possible.

“To all of the veterans in Kansas and across the country today: thank you.

“You have earned our nation’s lasting gratitude. Today and every day, we honor you, we respect you and we rededicate ourselves to providing you with the support you need.

“Thank you for your service, your sacrifices and your devotion to our country. May God bless our servicemen and women, our veterans and the country we love.”

title: Peters, Schumer, Jeffries and Garcia Statement on Sham Nomination Process for Next GAO Leader
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Senators Gary Peters, Ranking Member of the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, and Chuck Schumer, Senate Democratic Leader, and U.S Representatives Hakeem Jeffries, House Democratic Leader, and Robert Garcia, Ranking Member of the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, issued the following statement after Chairman Rand Paul initiated a sham process to recommend nominees to serve as the next Comptroller General of the GovernmentAccountability Office (GAO) for a 15-year term:

“This afternoon, Chairman Rand Paul’s office requested submissions of candidates to serve as the next Comptroller General of GAO with a deadline of less than 24 hours. This is clearly a sham to enable President Trump to appoint a handpicked nominee to lead Congress’ watchdog. We cannot allow President Trump to install a fox in the henhouse at an agency Congress relies on to provide independent, nonpartisan oversight, and expose waste, fraud, and abuse across the Trump Administration.

“Counter to the last time a GAO Comptroller was selected in 2010 in a yearlong, bipartisan process, Republican leaders have never convened the Commission for meetings, and the Commission has not interviewed a single candidate for this critical role, despite repeated requests to begin the process over the last two years. Every Member of Congress who values independent oversight and good stewardship of taxpayer dollars should call this out for what it is – a transparent effort to ram through another Trump crony at the 11th hour, and undercut Congress’ ability to conduct effective oversight of the Trump Administration.”

GAO is Congress’ nonpartisan watchdog, conducting research, investigations and audits that support Congressional oversight of the Executive Branch. By statute, a bipartisan, bicameral commission is central to the process of selecting a new Comptroller General. The 10-member Commission recommends at least three candidates, and the President chooses a nominee from the commission’s recommendations. In the past, the commission engaged in an extensive process, seeking a wide range of applicants and reviewing and interviewing candidates in a bipartisan manner. The bipartisan Commission is made up of the Speaker of the House of Representatives, the President pro tempore of the Senate, the majority and minority leaders of the House and Senate, the Chair and Ranking Member of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, and the Chair and Ranking Member of the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform. All three times the commission process has occurred in the past, the president has selected a nominee with bipartisan support.

title: Rosen Statement Commemorating Veterans Day
text:
LAS VEGAS, NV – U.S. Senator Jacky Rosen (D-NV) released the following statement commemorating Veterans Day, honoring the men and women who have served our nation.

“We are forever indebted to veterans across this country who have protected our freedoms and security for generations,” said Senator Rosen. “This Veterans Day, we honor the brave men and women who have placed their lives on the line to defend our nation and reaffirm our strong commitment to supporting them and their families. It is an honor to fight for every one of the more than 200,000 veterans who call Nevada home.”

Senator Rosen has been a champion for Nevada’s veterans, working to ensure they have access to all the care and benefits they have earned. She recently introduced two bipartisan bills to support and improve veterans’ education and career programs. Senator Rosen is also leading the charge in Congress to require the Department of Defense (DOD) to join the Department of Energy in classifying the Nevada Test and Training Range (NTTR), and all other locations where radiation and toxic exposure occurred, as contaminated. Her bipartisan bill would require the DOD to identify all military personnel who served within the NTTR, establish a process for them to provide proof of their service at such locations, and require the DOD to work with the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) to ensure that these veterans will finally be able to access the VA health care and benefits they have earned.

title: NEWS: Sanders, Bennet, Van Hollen, Duckworth Release Joint Statement Opposing More Funding for Trump’s War on Iran
text:
WASHINGTON, Nov. 11 — Sens. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), Michael Bennet (D-Colo.), Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), and Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.) released a joint statement underscoring their opposition to year-end funding that does not restrict President Trump’s ability to continue his war on Iran:

“The American people have been clear: We must end President Trump’s illegal and disastrous war with Iran. This conflict has driven up the cost of gas, groceries, and fertilizer. More than 20 American service members have been killed and hundreds more wounded, while achieving none of President Trump’s stated goals and harming civilians across the region. As we approach the December 11 funding deadline, we should not accept a short-term spending deal that continues to provide billions of additional dollars for President Trump’s war of choice. Any short-term package must include language that restricts the Trump Administration from using appropriated funds to continue his war against Iran.

“We know from Vietnam, Afghanistan, and Iraq that these wars can take decades to end – hurting our economy, draining our military resources, and making Americans less safe. Meanwhile, Americans all across the country will continue bearing the cost, with higher grocery bills, higher gas prices, and a higher toll on our troops. The American people do not want more war in the Middle East – but that is what President Trump has given them. Congress cannot allow Trump to continue his conflict – we must force him to end it. Not doing so will only prolong the American people’s pain, and opens the door to further escalation as he has threatened.

“When we vote on appropriations, we intend to fund the government and stop funds for this war. It is what the American people demand, and what they deserve.”

title: On Veterans Day, Shaheen, Cotton Applaud Senate Passage of Resolution to Establish National Warrior Call Day
text:
(Washington, DC) – U.S. Senator Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH), a senior member of the U.S. Senate Armed Services Committee, and U.S. Senator Tom Cotton (R-AR) announced their resolution to designate November 15, 2026, as National Warrior Call Day passed the U.S. Senate unanimously on Veterans Day. Their bipartisan resolution emphasizes the need for all Americans to reach out and build meaningful relationships with both those currently serving and veterans to help fight mental illness and combat the epidemic of suicide among military members.

“No veteran should ever feel alone while struggling with their mental health, especially after sacrificing so much to defend our freedoms abroad. Warrior Call Day is one vital way that we can help connect veterans with resources while also reducing the stigma around asking for help and mental health care,” said Senator Shaheen. “I’m proud my Senate colleagues once again recognized the importance of our bipartisan resolution to designate Warrior Call Day because the health and well-being of the men and women in the military shouldn’t be a partisan issue.”

“Our military members and veterans deserve the support and resources they need to lead active, healthy lives after serving. This bipartisan resolution will raise awareness on the importance of service members’ mental health, and I’m glad to see it pass the Senate unanimously,” said Senator Cotton.

A copy of the resolution can be read HERE.

The resolution is cosponsored by U.S. Senators Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), Mazie Hirono (D-HI), John Hickenlooper (D-CO), Cory Booker (D-NJ), Catherine Cortez Masto (D-NV), Tammy Baldwin (D-WI), John Fetterman (D-PA), Jacky Rosen (D-NV), Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), Michael Bennet (D-CO), Dan Sullivan (R-AK), Ted Budd (R-NC), Tim Sheehy (R-MT), Eric Schmitt (R-MO), Rick Scott (R-FL) and John Boozman (R-AR).
