title: Thune Delivers Remarks on Veterans Day
text:
Click here to watch the video.

WASHINGTON — U.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) today delivered the following remarks on the Senate floor:

Thune’s remarks below (as delivered):

“Mr. President, before I close, I want to say a few words about Veterans Day.

“Last month, I had the opportunity to attend two deployment ceremonies back home in South Dakota.

“And in this 250th year of our country’s independence, these ceremonies held a special significance.

“Celebrating 250 years of American independence would be incomplete without acknowledging that this nation endures because Americans have answered and continue to answer the call to serve.

“For many Americans, serving our country is a family tradition they trace back through generations.

“Others are the first in their family to put on the uniform.

“All – all – are ready to give their lives and their future for this country’s future.

“I’m grateful to all the Americans who have served our country in uniform.

“To Chairman Moran and members of the Veterans’ Affairs Committee – thank you for all of your work this Congress to help improve the lives of all of America’s veterans.

“And I want to wish all those who have served a happy Veterans Day.”

title: Thune: Important Work Remains for Senate Republicans
text:
Click here to watch the video.

WASHINGTON — U.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) today delivered the following remarks on the Senate floor:

Thune’s remarks below (as delivered):

“Mr. President, yesterday the Republican Conference held its first meeting with our new members for the 120th Congress.

“And we had a robust discussion about our conference’s future and how we can best serve the American people in the next two years.

“We also held our leadership elections for the coming Congress.

“I’m grateful to my colleagues for again placing their trust in me to be the Republican leader.

“And I’m looking forward to working with the other members of our leadership team and with all of our colleagues, both old and new, over the next two years.

“Mr. President, in my first speech from this desk nearly two years ago, one of the things I talked about was restoring the Senate as a place of discussion and deliberation.

“And over these last two years, I’ve striven for that ideal.

“And I’m proud of the legislative record that we have built:

“The Working Families Tax Cuts, which delivered permanent tax relief to hardworking Americans.

“The 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, a bipartisan effort to make homeownership more affordable.

“Republicans and Democrats came together to craft the first federal legislation dealing with digital assets.

“We passed the Laken Riley Act.

“The Protect College Sports Act.

“And we demonstrated what’s possible when both parties come together for a more open appropriations process.

“On nominations, we’ve faced historic obstruction from Democrats.

“And despite that, we got President Trump’s Cabinet in place at the fastest pace in over two decades.

“We’ve confirmed 605 civilian nominees.

“And put 56 Article III judges on the federal bench – and at the fastest pace since the Reagan administration.

“And we’re not done.

“Mr. President, we could not have confirmed all of these individuals or crafted and passed these bills without the hard work of our Republican conference.

“And I want to thank them for all they have done in this Congress.

“And I have no doubt that we will continue to work just as hard through the end of this year and into the 120th Congress as well.

“Mr. President, in that first speech I gave as leader last January, I talked about my leadership style, and, specifically, some of the lessons I learned from playing sports.

“In sports, you need to learn from your losses, and then move on to the next game.

“As I said, part of our meeting yesterday was a conversation about Republicans’ future.

“I expect those conversations to continue and for all Republican senators to play a role in building up our party.

“We’ll see where we need to improve, identify our strengths, and use them to best serve the American people.

“Mr. President, whether we’re in the majority or the minority, we work for the American people.

“Last week voters sent a clear message.

“And a large part of that message has to do with the cost of living.

“Mr. President, hardworking people have faced cost-of-living challenges for more than five years now – since the early days of the Biden administration.

“And while I’m proud of accomplishments like the Working Families Tax Cuts, there’s more to do.

“In the coming months and years, we’ll see legislation like the Working Families Tax Cuts and the ROAD to Housing Act continue to bear fruit.

“And affordability will continue to be at the top of our priority list here in the Senate.

“And not just next year.

“Right now.

“Mr. President, this week the Senate has advanced bipartisan permitting reform legislation.

“A more efficient permitting system would reduce costly delays, get things built faster, and provide more affordable and accessible energy across the country.

“It would also encourage investment in America, create jobs, and boost Made-in-America manufacturing.

“Mr. President, the need is real and the opportunity is ripe for us to get this done.

“We have a bipartisan agreement that has support from the president.

“We should waste no time delivering this win for the American people.

“And the sooner we finish permitting, the more time we’ll have for additional priorities.

“Mr. President, as I said, we will also be confirming more of the president’s nominees before the end of the year.

“And I expect that we will continue to face obstruction from Democrats in our efforts.

“But we’re going to put in the work to overcome that obstruction to get qualified individuals in place.

“Mr. President, over the last 22 months, we’ve been busy.

“And I hope everyone is ready to run through the tape.

“Because there’s more work to be done in the 119th Congress.

“And we are going to leave it all on the field.”

title: Warner, Kaine, Fetterman Condemn Trump-Vance Administration’s Proposed Weakening of Silica Rule That Protects Coal Miners From Black Lung
text:
WASHINGTON — Today, U.S. Sens. Mark R. Warner (D-VA), Tim Kaine (D-VA), and John Fetterman (D-PA) released the following statement criticizing the proposed weakening by the Department of Labor (DOL) Mine Safety and Health Administration (MSHA) of a rule that better protects America’s miners from health hazards related to exposure to respirable crystalline silica, also known as silica dust:

“We’ve done so much to better support our nation’s miners, miner retirees, and their families, but the Trump-Vance Administration’s proposed changes to the silica rule threaten this progress and would result in more miners getting black lung disease. We cannot allow this Administration to turn its back on our promises to our miners. We will continue to do everything we can to make sure miners are protected from harmful silica dust and able to come home from work healthy.”

In 2025, the senators sounded the alarm about the Trump-Vance Labor Department’s decision to pause enforcement of the silica rule, warning that it would likely lead to this proposed change. In 2024, the senators applauded the Biden administration’s establishment of this long-awaited rule, after urging the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) the previous year to prioritize the creation of a new silica standard.

title: WATCH: Warnock Delivers Veterans Day Message
text:
Today, Senator Reverend Raphael Warnock delivered a Veterans Day message honoring the service and sacrifice of America’s veterans

The son of a World War II veteran, Senator Warnock is committed to ensuring America’s veterans and their families have access to the federal resources and benefits they have earned

Senator Reverend Warnock: “I’m thinking about my father today, a World War II veteran, and the generations of Americans who have answered our nation’s call. We live in the shelter of their sacrifice, and we must never take that gift for granted”

WATCH: Senator Warnock’s Veterans Day Message

Washington, D.C. – Today, U.S. Senator Reverend Raphael Warnock (D-GA) delivered a Veterans Day message thanking the brave men and women whose dedicated military service has helped keep America safe. Georgia is home to over 700,000 veterans and has the sixth-largest active-duty military population in the country.

“Behind every uniform is a person, a neighbor, a loved one, somebody’s son, somebody’s daughter, someone who took on extraordinary responsibility and risk on behalf of us all,” said Senator Warnock. “That service reminds us that we belong to something larger than ourselves, that despite our differences, we are one American family, bound together by the sacred promise ‘E pluribus unum,’ out of many, one.”

The son of a World War II veteran, Senator Warnock has long championed efforts to strengthen federal resources and support for Georgia’s veterans and their families. Senator Warnock has secured over $500,000 to assist veterans experiencing homelessness in the Atlanta area and helped pass the 21st Century Veterans Healthcare and Benefits Improvement Act, which included provisions to support the surviving spouses of fallen servicemembers. He also helped pass the PACT Act, the largest expansion of veterans’ health benefits in decades.

Read the full transcript of Senator Warnock’s Veterans Day message below and watch HERE.

“To all of those who have served in our armed forces, happy Veterans Day, and thank you so much for your service. Today we honor the brave Americans who have worn our nation’s uniform, and the families who have served alongside them.

“You know, I’m thinking about my father today, a World War II veteran, and the generations of Americans who have answered our nation’s call. We live in the shelter of their sacrifice, and we must never take that gift for granted.

“Behind every uniform is a person, a neighbor, a loved one, somebody’s son, somebody’s daughter, someone who took on extraordinary responsibility and risk on behalf of us all. That service reminds us that we belong to something larger than ourselves, that despite our differences, we are one American family, bound together by the sacred promise ‘E pluribus unum,’ out of many, one.

“So, to our veterans, you stood up for us. It is our sacred obligation to stand up for you. Those who have fought for us should not have to fight with us to get the care they deserve. So let us honor your service by renewing our commitment to providing the care and support you need and deserve.

“May God bless you, may God bless your families, and may God bless the United States of America.”

title: Welch Joins Duckworth, Colleagues in Introducing Bill to Ensure Iran War Veterans Are Covered Under PACT Act
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Senator Peter Welch (D-Vt.) joined U.S. Senator Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.) and eight Senate colleagues in introducing the New PACT for Iran Veterans Act, legislation that would ensure Iran Veterans are covered under the Sergeant First Class Heath Robinson Honoring our Promise to Address Comprehensive Toxics (PACT) Act. The Senators’ legislation would cut unnecessary red tape and make it easier for servicemembers who are being exposed to toxic substances to access the unique treatment they need when they return home. The PACT Act, which Senator Welch championed as a member of the House of Representatives, was signed into law by President Biden in 2022, To date, more than 7 million veterans have been screened for toxic exposures because of the PACT Act.

The Vermont National Guard was deployed under federal active-duty mobilization to support operations in the Middle East. Adding Iran to the list of countries with presumed toxic exposure will ensure that Vermont veterans of this war received the benefits and care they need after potential exposure to toxic substances during their service.

“The bipartisan PACT Act marked a historic step in ensuring that veterans and servicemembers exposed to toxic substances can get the care they need and deserve. But President Trump’s reckless decision to send thousands of U.S. service members into an unnecessary war in the Middle East means there’s a new generation of veterans facing conditions that could be hazardous to their health,” said Senator Welch. “We need to update our pact to servicemembers to ensure that Iran War Servicemembers and Veterans aren’t faced with red tape to get proper benefits and care once they come home.”

“By establishing the landmark PACT Act, our nation finally helped generations of Veterans who suffered from toxic exposure in Vietnam, Iraq and Afghanistan more easily access the care they needed after being stonewalled by bureaucratic tape for years,” said Senator Duckworth. “With a new generation of troops being thrown into another war in the Middle East, our nation must learn the lessons from previous conflicts and proactively ensure Iran Veterans don’tsuffer from those same mistakes. Our New PACT for Iran Veterans Act would ensure no servicemember fights a war overseas only to come home and be faced with another battle to get the care they’ve rightfully earned through their service. Congress must act to care for these heroes now—not later.”

In 2022, the PACT Act helped generations of Veterans—from Vietnam to Iraq—more easily receive care from the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) by establishing a list of locations where it is presumed by law that troops who served there were exposed to toxic hazards. However, Iran is currently not included on this presumed-exposure list, despite troops serving in the Iran War being exposed to many of the same hazards and President Trump’s refusal to rule out inserting ground forces into Iran.

The New PACT for Iran Veterans Act would require the VA to add Iran to the list of covered locations and take more proactive action to ensure Iran War Veterans—and all Veterans who serve in future conflicts—don’t have to jump through bureaucratic hoops in order to access the care they’ve earned through their service. Specifically, the legislationwould:

Cut Red Tape for Iran War Veterans by statutorily presuming toxic substance exposure for Iran War Veterans, helping streamline their access to health care and benefits at VA. The bill would ensure that federal law protects allVeterans who fought in Iran, including those who operated in Iranian airspace and territorial waters.

Leave No Veteran Behind by requiring for the first time, that the VA’s Military Environmental Exposure Sub-Council (MEESC) conducts studies at least every five years to review all overseas assignments for toxic substance exposures. Additionally, when the military begins a contingency operation, the VA must commence a similar review of the locations from which servicemembers support this operation within 180 days. This would ensure the VA proactively looks into whether servicemembers are being exposed to toxic hazards, for current and future assignments.

Enhance Transparency at the VA by requiring the VA Secretary to publicly explain their justification for any denial of a country that’s recommended for presumed toxic-exposures in these reviews, or any removal of existing presumptions.

Joining Senators Welch and Duckworth on the legislation are Sens. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), Angus King (I-Maine), Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.), Michael Bennet (D-Colo.), Patty Murray (D-Wash.), John Fetterman (D-Pa.), Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), Angela Alsobrooks (D-Md.), and Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.).

The New PACT for Iran Veterans Act is endorsed by Disabled American Veterans (DAV), Iraq and Afghanistan Veterans of America (IAVA), Paralyzed Veterans of America (PVA), VoteVets, Veterans of Foreign Wars (VFW) and the American Legion.

Read and download the full text of the legislation.

This week, Senator Welch led the introduction of the bipartisan, bicameral Waste Incineration Protection, Exposure Oversight, and Updated Tracking of (WIPE OUT) Burn Pits Act, which builds on the PACT Act by ensuring all instances of toxic exposure from burn pits are accounted for. The legislation would also establish a clear framework for identifying, tracking, and mitigating risks of open‑air burn pits located near U.S. forces and push for replacement with safer alternatives. Provisions of the legislation were included in both the Senate and House versions of the Fiscal Year 2027 (FY27) National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA).

Senator Welch has championed efforts to limit toxic substance exposure among veterans in the Senate, including the bicameral Airborne Hazards and Open Burn Pit Registry 2.0 Act, which passed as part of the FY25 NDAA, and the bipartisan Burn Pit Elimination Act, both bills that would improve protections for veterans under the PACT Act and prevent future toxic exposure cases. A bipartisan amendment led by Sens. Welch, Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), and Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) requiring the VA to conduct a review on mortality and toxic exposure data for veterans who served in Kosovo also passed with bipartisan support in the Senate.

Senator Welch also cosponsored the Burn Pit Registry Enhancement Act, Reducing Exposure to Burn Pits Act, and Toxic Exposure Education for Servicemembers Act, bills that build on the PACT Act to provide increased support for veterans exposed to burn pits, improve data collection on burn pit and toxic substance exposure, and help mitigate future toxic substance exposure for servicemembers.

Senator Welch’s experienced team of caseworkers can help Veterans, families, and survivors with casework related to the VA, as well as other federal agencies. Vermont veterans and servicemembers seeking assistance are encouraged to visit welch.senate.gov or call his Burlington office: 802-863-2525.

title: Young, Booker Introduce Legislation to Give Workers More Flexibility with Employee Benefits
text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. Senators Todd Young (R-Ind.) and Cory Booker (D-N.J.) introduced the bipartisan Optimizing Participant Tax Incentives through Optional Noncash Selections (OPTIONS) Act, legislation to give American workers greater flexibility in how they receive employer-provided benefits.

The OPTIONS Act would allow employees to choose how certain employer contributions are allocated among retirement savings, student loan repayment, health savings accounts, and other eligible benefits. The legislation would provide employers with a clear legal framework to offer these options while maintaining existing tax advantages.

“American workers have different financial circumstances, and employer benefits should reflect those differences,” said Senator Young. “Whether an employee needs to prioritize saving for retirement, paying off student loans, or managing health care expenses, our legislation would give workers greater flexibility to put their benefits toward what matters most to them.”

“You can’t build long-term financial security if you can’t afford the present,” said Senator Booker. “Today, too many Americans are struggling just to keep their heads above water, let alone build for the future. Every worker carries a different burden: student debt, rising health care costs, or concerns about having a secure retirement. The bipartisan OPTIONS Act recognizes that the pathway to financial security looks different for every family and gives workers more flexibility to direct their employer-provided benefits where they need them most. At a time when families are facing an affordability crisis, this bill puts the choice back where it belongs: in the hands of the people doing the work. That’s what dignity and economic fairness look like, and I’m proud to fight for it.”

“American workers don’t all face the same financial challenges, so their benefits shouldn’t be one-size-fits-all,” said American Retirement Association (ARA) CEO Brian Graff. “The OPTIONS Act is a smart, forward-looking solution that empowers employees to direct employer contributions where they need them most, whether that’s retirement savings, healthcare, or paying down student debt. ARA applauds Senators Young and Booker for their bipartisan leadership on this important legislation, which strengthens financial security while preserving the integrity of our employer-sponsored system.”

“Today’s workforce spans generations, income levels, and life stages, and employers want the flexibility to meet employees where they are,” said Chatrane Birbal, Senior Vice President of Public Policy and Government Relations at the CHRO Association. “The OPTIONS Act gives employers clear authority to let employees direct their benefit dollars toward what matters most to them, whether that’s saving for retirement, covering health care costs, or paying down student loans. We thank Senators Young and Booker for their bipartisan leadership on legislation that helps employers deliver more value from the benefits they already provide.”

“ERIC applauds the introduction of the OPTIONS Act by Senators Young and Booker,” said James Gelfand, President & CEO, The ERISA Industry Committee (ERIC). “Large employers are at the forefront of providing innovative employee benefits, and this bill would empower employees to make decisions improving their own financial wellbeing. Workers stand to benefit from the new flexibility that would be offered by the OPTIONS Act, and we strongly support this bipartisan bill.”

The OPTIONS Act would amend the Internal Revenue Code to establish qualified benefit options plans, allowing employees to allocate eligible contributions toward:

1. Retirement savings: Employer contributions to eligible retirement plans, including 401(k) plans.

2. Student loan repayment: Employer payments through qualified educational assistance programs.

3. Health care expenses: Contributions to health savings accounts (HSAs) and health reimbursement arrangements (HRAs)

4. Other eligible benefits: Additional employer-provided benefits that qualify for favorable treatment under federal law.

Companion legislation was introduced in the U.S. House of Representatives by Representatives Greg Steube (R-Fla.-17) and Suzan DelBene (D-Wash.-01).

title: Congressman Aderholt Introduces Bipartisan Resolution Recognizing November as National Adoption Month
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, Representatives Robert Aderholt (R-AL) and Danny K. Davis (D-IL), co-chairs of the Congressional Coalition on Adoption (CCA), introduced a bipartisan resolution recognizing November as National Adoption Month, with November 21 as National Adoption Day.

The resolution raises awareness of children awaiting adoption, celebrates children and families involved in adoption, and encourages all Americans to consider adoption in November and throughout the year.

“I am proud to co-lead this resolution recognizing National Adoption Month and National Adoption Day as an important way to keep adoption a legislative priority,” said Rep. Aderholt. “Uniting families is a cause that goes beyond party lines and Congress must continue to look for ways to strengthen foster care and adoption to help ensure the safety, permanency, and well-being of every child.”

“I am proud to co-lead this bipartisan resolution recognizing National Adoption Month and National Adoption Day as important opportunities to uplift adoption as a key pathway to permanency for children,” said Rep. Davis. “These celebrations of children and families involved in adoption recognize that all children deserve a loving, “forever family” that will surround them with the joy, love, and support needed for them to grow and reach their full potential.”

As the House co-chairs of CCA, Rep. Aderholt and Rep. Davis lead the bicameral, bipartisan caucus, which works to bring national awareness of adoption and the children awaiting families, improve the adoption process, and find homes for every child looking for a family.

The CCA was founded in 1985 and has since pioneered efforts in creating meaningful legislative change. Since the first National Adoption Day in 2000, more than 95,000 children have joined permanent families on National Adoption Day.

The resolution has 42 original cosponsors: Reps. Danny Davis (IL), Mike Rogers (AL), Julia Brownley (CA), Don Bacon (NE), Eleanor Holmes Norton (DC), Zach Nunn (IA), Terri A. Sewell (AL), Rob Wittman (VA), Shontel Brown (OH), Chris Smith (NJ), Norma J. Torres (CA), Mike Kelly (PA), Sharice Davids (KS), Michael Cloud (TX), Troy Carter (LA), Julia Letlow (LA), Jonathan L. title: Smith, Dingell Introduce Bipartisan Bill to Modernize Medicare and Expand Patient Choice
text:
Today, Congressman Adrian Smith (R-NE), a senior member of the House Ways and Means Subcommittee on Health, and Congresswoman Debbie Dingell (D-MI), a member of the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, introduced the Bringing Rehabilitation, Integrated Delivery, and Greater Extended (BRIDGE) Care at Home Act. The bipartisan bill would provide Medicare beneficiaries with greater flexibility to access skilled nursing services in the comfort of their own homes following a qualifying hospital stay.

“When it comes to healthcare, one size does not fit all, and patients deserve to have choices. Too often, options are unnecessarily restricted—especially for Medicare beneficiaries. I introduced my bipartisan BRIDGE Care at Home Act to modernize Medicare and give beneficiaries more control over their care options,”said Smith.

“Across the country there is a shortage of beds in skilled nursing facilities for patients needing post-hospital short term care, resulting in extended stays in the hospital, causing delays in available beds and unnecessarily long hospital visits. This shortage of care impacts both the wishes and care of Medicare patients, and the care of all other patients across hospitals. Most patients prefer to receive care at home, so we must do more to support access to skilled nursing care in the home for patients who prefer that option. And most importantly, it is the less expensive option for both families and the government. I am proud to support this bipartisan bill which would address those shortages and put patients first,”said Dingell.

Stakeholder Support:

“Hospital at home demonstrated that seniors can be treated at home safely and effectively. The BRIDGE Care at Home Act would test the idea of skilled nursing and intensive rehabilitation services at home, helping patients maintain their independence, supporting caregivers and giving providers an alternative to working in an institutional setting,”said Moving Health Home Founder Krista Drobac.

“SNF-level rehab in the home environment allows patients to rebuild functional independence directly in the spaces where they actually live. Patients sleep better, move more, and face lower risks of delirium and nosocomial complications when their acute recovery happens at home. Advanced recovery without the hospital walls: better rest, fewer complications, and real-life rehab in the comfort of your own home,”said Sandford Health Marshfield Clinic Home Recovery Care Medical Director Swetha Gudibanda, MD.

“Our Home Recovery Care Plus has proven that patients can safely receive skilled nursing and rehabilitation services at home, with strong outcomes and high satisfaction. By combining in-person nursing and therapy, physician oversight, remote monitoring, and coordinated care, we help patients recover in the comfort of their homes while reducing unnecessary facility stays and the costs associated with institutional care. BRIDGE Care at Home builds on what is already working-giving patients more choice in where they recover, avoiding unnecessary institutional stays, and lowering health care costs,”said Highmark Health Senior Vice President for Home and Community Services Mona Siddiqui.

BACKGROUND:

Currently, Medicare covers qualifying skilled nursing care in a facility but does not offer a comparable payment model for delivering that care at home. At the same time, limited capacities at skilled nursing facilities (SNF) forces thousands of patients to remain in hospitals longer than medically necessary, delaying discharges and creating backups for other patients awaiting admission.

Smith’s BRIDGE Care at Home Act would create a five-year Medicare SNF-at-Home pilot program, allowing beneficiaries to receive skilled nursing services at home instead of at a SNF. Polling shows 85 percent of people who have had experience with care in the home would recommend it to family and friends. The program would empower providers to develop new models of care, expand options for patients, and reduce pressure on hospitals and SNFs.

The bill also directs the Department of Health and Human Services Secretary to compare the quality, outcomes, costs, and patient characteristics of beneficiaries who receive skilled nursing care at home with those who receive it in a facility over the course of the program’s five-year period.

title: Virginia House Delegation Urges Rejection of NextEra-Dominion Merger
text:
U.S. Representatives Don Beyer, Jennifer McClellan, Suhas Subramanyam, Eugene Vindman, and James Walkinshaw, Democrats from Virginia, today urged the Virginia State Corporation Commission (SCC) to reject the proposed acquisition of Dominion Energy by Florida-based NextEra. In a letter submitted ahead of the SCC’s November 12 public comment deadline, the Members warned that the merger, as currently structured, threatens to increase electricity costs for Virginia families and small businesses for decades to come.

They wrote:

“As proposed, we do not believe the merger is in the public interest. We believe the proposed transaction fails to satisfy the statutory requirements and because the joint petition lacks the structural protections necessary to prevent material harm, the Commission should deny the merger petition in its current form.”

The Members noted that while NextEra stands to benefit from the expanded investment opportunities created by the rapid expansion of data centers across Northern Virginia, residential customers and small businesses could be left footing the bill. The Members also cautioned that the merger could consolidate market power across the regional electricity grid, stifling competition and ultimately increasing electricity costs for Virginia consumers.

They argued that the proposed merger’s temporary incentives fail to offset the merger’s potential long-term costs. They also pointed to the absence of a moratorium on base rate increases, a cap on escalating rate adjustment clauses, and a binding requirement to pass operational savings on to customers.

The letter further raises concerns about NextEra’s corporate governance, including its history of political spending and interference, warning these practices could undermine regulatory oversight, create conflicts with Virginia’s Clean Economy Act requirements, and expose ratepayers to additional financial risks.

Emphasizing the SCC’s statutory responsibility to safeguard consumers and ensure the long-term reliability and affordability of utility service, the Members stated that approving the merger without adequate, enforceable protections would undermine that responsibility.

Full text of the letter follows below, and a signed copy is available here.

***

Dear Commissioners:

We write to express our opposition to the current proposed merger whereby NextEra Energy, Inc. ("NextEra") would acquire control of Dominion Energy, Inc. ("Dominion"). Under the Utility Transfers Act, the State Corporation Commission ("Commission") may approve an acquisition of control if it finds that "adequate service to the public at just and reasonable rates will not be impaired or jeopardized. “Applicants must prove that the transaction causes no harm to captive customers. We believe the joint petition fails this statutory test.

We respectfully urge the Commission to reject the proposed NextEra Dominion merger in its current form, as recommended by Commission staff.

Rate Base Inflation and Misaligned Incentives

NextEra’s investor disclosures emphasize that Dominion's territory offers immense multi-decade capital deployment opportunities, driven in large part by the extraordinary concentration of AI data centers in Northern Virginia and future planned load. Given that this projected future energy demand in the Commonwealth will be reliant on massive bulk transmission lines, which are still socialized across residential rate classes, much of that potential infrastructure will be paid for by ratepayers. And as NextEra’s growth strategy is dependent on maximizing capital deployment, its potential acquisition of Dominion risks creating a sustained, multi-decade upward pressure on ratepayers’ bills. Captive residential and small business ratepayers will be locked into paying decades of capital carrying charges, depreciation, and an authorized Return on Equity (ROE) on this expanded rate base.

We are concerned that much of NextEra’s growth strategy is heavily dependent on data center customers. This increases vulnerabilities that exist due to overbuilding and the ramifications that could materialize for ratepayers if projected revenue from large-load customers fails to cover the full cost of the transmission buildout and necessary upgrades to the grid that increased data center presence would require. While Dominion has started work to hedge against this stranded asset risk, there is insufficient protection in the case for bankruptcy, differing time horizons for service contracts and infrastructure lifespans, as well as the burden of broader grid upgrades required by data centers (rather than just point-to-point infrastructure) where every day ratepayers foot the bill.

There have also been documented concerns about how this merger affects market competition within the broader grid that Dominion is a part of, particularly with respect to transmission and energy generation and how the new merger could create “self-preferencing” or foreclose potential competition, and how those ripple effects could then increase wholesale prices and therefore raise costs for ratepayers in Virginia.

Despite those long-term upward financial pressures, the merger sweeteners of customer bill credits and added funds for the EnergyShare program are both inadequate and only short-term. Once the sweeteners expire, the Virginia-based Dominion workforce would be at risk of significant job cuts, Virginia households and small businesses would be locked into paying those multi-decade elevated rates, with the joint petition providing for no base rate increase moratorium, no cap on escalating rate adjustment clauses (riders), and no binding mechanism to track and pass fuel or operational synergies to captive customers. Additionally, the proposed bill credit for consumers barely covers the impact that increased fuel costs are having on electric bills. Dominion already petitioned the Commission for a $10 per month increase for fuel-related costs this year.

For these reasons, the Independent Market Monitor stated, the “scale, financial strength, and operational breadth all enhance market power and any economic gains are more likely to accrue to investors rather than customers.” Thus, we must look past the near-term sweeteners and toward robust binding, structural protections that prevent long-term negative impacts on Virginia ratepayers.

We believe the primary benefits of the merger should be designed to benefit our constituents, the ratepayers, and we believe the current merger design will raise rates. To that extent, we urge the Commission to, at a bare minimum, require long-term rate protections for consumers as recommended by Commission staff and require substantially larger bill credits as recommended by the Governor’s Office before any potential merger can proceed. As energy prices have considerably increased, and this merger threatens to exacerbate market conditions that could further increase prices for ratepayers it is paramount that the Commission use its authority to protect consumers who are already struggling to afford to keep the lights on.

Corporate Governance Deficits Threaten Rate Case Prudency

A utility’s corporate culture directly governs accounting integrity, affiliate transactions, and ratemaking prudency. The Commission must ensure that any acquiring entity submits to complete regulatory transparency and that captive ratepayers do not cross-subsidize non-utility operations, political spending, or parent-company agendas.

NextEra’s operational history and recent testimony demonstrates documented resistance to transparent regulatory scrutiny. NextEra recently entered into a $150 million settlement to resolve widespread political interference and dark money schemes, which included funding “ghost candidates” against state legislators and covert surveillance of an investigative journalist. This Commission’s Hearing Examiner properly recognized the relevance of these governance practices to regulatory integrity by ordering the production of the internal "Robo memo" into the evidentiary record. We share the position that this memo should be available for review to the Commission and intervenors.

At a time when regulatory scrutiny is at an all-time high, NextEra’s top leadership has aligned itself financially with federal agendas that raise rates and undermine Virginia’s statutory obligations. NextEra’s participation in high-level, opaque federal lobbying networks heightens the risk that Virginia ratepayers could be improperly forced to subsidize national political advocacy that runs counter to their own interests. In this case, aligning with a federal agenda that rolls back renewable energy incentives, curtails offshore wind development, and props up uneconomic generation. Engaging in that advocacy, including through means designed to obscure its involvement, puts NextEra in direct conflict with Virginia’s statutory mandates under the Virginia Clean Economy Act, and introduces an acute risk of asset stranding, resource inadequacy, and costly non-compliance penalties that will inevitably fall upon Virginia consumers.

It is unacceptably risky to transfer Virginia’s premier electric utility to an acquiring entity that displays such a pattern of routine spending, through opaque affiliate channels, to influence regulatory and political outcomes. Such practices, if expanded into Virginia, would directly threaten the Commission's ability to police affiliate transactions, enforce cross-subsidization prohibitions, and verify the prudency of test-year operating expenses. Captive ratepayers bear the cost when compliance breaks down, transactions lack transparent auditing, or management priorities subordinate the public interest to unregulated political agendas.

Conclusion

The Commission’s statutory mission is to safeguard captive consumers and ensure the long-term reliability and affordability of utility service. As proposed, we do not believe the merger is in the public interest. We believe the proposed transaction fails to satisfy the statutory requirements and because the joint petition lacks the structural protections necessary to prevent material harm, the Commission should deny the merger petition in its current form.

We appreciate the Commission’s careful scrutiny of this proceeding and submit these comments on behalf of our constituents.

title: Two Bills, One Promise: Bilirakis Moves Closer to Ending Wounded Veteran Tax
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. - Congressman Gus Bilirakis, lead House sponsor of the bipartisan Major Richard Star Act, celebrated House passage of two measures advancing his effort to end the “wounded Veteran tax”: the standalone Major Richard Star Act and the Take Care of America’s Veterans Act (TCAVA), which includes major provisions of his legislation. Both measures seek to address the unfair offset that prevents certain combat-injured, medically retired Veterans from receiving their earned military retirement pay alongside VA disability compensation.

“Before Major Richard Star passed away, I made him a solemn promise that I would never stop fighting until we ended the wounded Veteran tax,” said Congressman Bilirakis. “Our combat-injured Veterans earned these benefits through their service and sacrifice. They deserve both. Advancing these two measures brings us closer to fulfilling that promise, and I will continue pursuing every viable legislative pathway to get this relief signed into law.”

Bilirakis supported the discharge petition led by House Democrats to bring his standalone legislation to the floor. He also supported TCAVA, which passed by voice vote and combines dozens of bipartisan measures to strengthen Veterans’ health care, benefits, and economic opportunities. TCAVA would increase support for severely disabled Veterans and Gold Star families, improve access to community care and mental health treatment, strengthen caregiver assistance, advance traumatic brain injury research, and expand education and career training opportunities. The package is supported by more than 30 Veterans organizations, advocates, and stakeholders. Unlike the standalone bill which does not speak to how the changes will be funded – an issue that has repeatedly blocked the bill from advancing through the Senate in the past, TCAVA includes a funding offset involving changes to VA disability rating criteria for future sleep apnea and tinnitus claims while protecting existing ratings. The VA has already announced that it will pursue these changes in future rating calculations, whether or not TCAVA becomes law.

“TCAVA’s funding mechanism is not the approach I would have chosen. I believe this obligation should be met through Department of Defense funds, and I will continue advocating for a better approach as my colleagues in the Senate evaluate these proposals,”Bilirakis said. “But I will not let the perfect become the enemy of the good while wounded Veterans continue waiting for justice. Standing alongside Major Richard Star’s brother, David, after the votes reinforced what this fight means. Our Veterans kept their promise to this country. We must keep ours to them.”

title: Boyle, Lawler Introduce Bipartisan Lung Cancer Awareness Month Resolution
text:
WASHINGTON, DC – Representatives Brendan F. Boyle (D-PA-02) and Mike Lawler (R-NY-17) introduced a bipartisan resolution to designate November 2026 as Lung Cancer Awareness Month. The resolution aims to draw attention to the importance of early detection, prevention, and research to combat lung cancer, which remains the leading cause of cancer-related deaths in the United States. Boyle also leads the bipartisan Women and Lung Cancer Research and Preventive Services Act, which would take action to study and prevent lung cancer among women.

“Every day, more than 600 Americans are diagnosed with lung cancer. We must do more to raise awareness and give Americans the tools to fight back against this devastating disease,” said Congressman Boyle. “This bipartisan resolution is an important step toward encouraging screenings and supporting the research we need to save lives.”

“I’m proud to once again serve as a co-lead of the bipartisan resolution designating November as National Lung Cancer Awareness Month. Raising awareness, encouraging early detection, and supporting lifesaving research are critical to improving outcomes for patients and families affected by this disease. We must continue working together to advance these efforts and ensure more Americans have access to the screening and care they need,” said Congressman Lawler.

“Lung Cancer Awareness Month is about more than raising awareness. It's about turning awareness into action. The Women and Lung Cancer Research and Preventive Services Act represents an important opportunity to close gaps in our understanding of lung cancer in women, strengthen early detection, and improve outcomes. We have an opportunity to make meaningful progress, and we must keep moving forward,” said David Benson, CEO of GO2 for Lung Cancer.

According to the American Cancer Society, more than 229,000 people are expected to be diagnosed with lung cancer in 2026. This resolution highlights the urgent need to increase public awareness, expand access to screening programs, and invest in lifesaving research.

The text of the resolution is available here.

title: Cammack Votes to Pay Combat-Wounded Veterans in Full, Backs 60-Bill Package for Veterans and Their Families
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Congresswoman Kat Cammack (FL-03) this week voted on legislation that would end a decades-old penalty on combat-wounded veterans and protect the benefits of Gold Star spouses.

On Veterans Day, the House passed what House Veterans’ Affairs Committee Chairman Mike Bost calls the most comprehensive veterans package in a decade: more than 60 veterans-focused measures to expand health care access for rural veterans, cut red tape at VA, and ensure surviving spouses aren’t penalized for finding love again.

Right now, a surviving spouse who remarries before age 55 forfeits survivor benefits. The Love Lives On Act ends that penalty, letting them keep those benefits and restoring TRICARE coverage if a later marriage ends.

“We owe veterans, active duty servicemembers, and their families a debt we will never be able to fully repay,” said Congresswoman Cammack. “For too long, we’ve walked back our promises to these brave men and women even after they’ve kept theirs. If you lost your husband or wife in service to our country, you shouldn’t have to choose between finding love again and keeping the benefits your family earned, and if you’re wounded in combat and medically retired, Washington shouldn’t dock your pay. It is fitting the House is acting on these important bills as we observe Veterans Day, and I will keep fighting every single day for veterans in North Central Florida and around the country.”

Beyond the Star Act and the Love Lives On Act, highlights of the package include:

Benefits for veterans and survivors

Raises monthly pay for veterans with the most severe service-connected disabilities, the first significant increase in decades

Boosts survivor payments an extra 1% a year for three years

Guarantees surviving spouses of veterans lost to ALS the full survivor benefit, no matter how long the illness lasted

Health care

Expands suicide and overdose treatment and speeds up admission to VA residential treatment programs

Extends VA’s community suicide prevention grants for three more years

Locks in community care access standards for eight years, so veterans far from a VA hospital keep their options

Puts a lactation space in every VA medical center

Claims and accountability

Stops VA from denying a claim because a veteran missed a single exam

Lets the Board of Veterans’ Appeals decide appeals that raise the same issue together, under a three-year pilot

Sends military sexual trauma claims to a specialized team

Gives veterans one VA phone number to call, with call centers in every time zone

Families and caregivers

Extends health coverage for family caregivers six months after the veteran passes away or leaves the program, with help getting back to work

Lets spouses and dependent children receive a VA headstone, whatever the date of death

Jobs and education

Raises GI Bill housing pay for student veterans studying online or training in apprenticeships

Expands VET TEC tech training to fields like artificial intelligence and semiconductors

These reforms are backed by more than 30 veterans and military family organizations, including the Military Order of the Purple Heart, the Military Officers Association of America, TAPS and Gold Star Spouses of America.

Earlier this week, the House also passed the Veterans’ Compensation Cost-of-Living Adjustment Act (H.R. 8552), which raises VA disability compensation and survivor benefits on December 1 to keep pace with the cost of living.

Cammack also voted in favor of the Major Richard Star Act (H.R. 2102).

This bill allows veterans with combat-related disabilities who were medically retired before 20 years of service to collect their military retirement pay and their VA disability compensation in full. The Congressional Budget Office counts about 58,000 retirees who would qualify. Cammack has cosponsored the bill in every Congress she has served.

North Central Florida is home to about 57,000 veterans, and Florida has about 1.4 million, the third most of any state. The district anchors the nation’s largest VA health care system, from the Malcom Randall VA Medical Center in Gainesville to the Lake City VA Medical Center.

“I wanted to serve twenty years, and I would have, except for what happened to me in the war. We have so many young veterans who served two or three years before they were blown up by an IED in Iraq or Afghanistan, and they still get their retirement cut. It’s just not fair. Every veteran wants the other veteran to be treated fairly, especially those who gave of themselves in combat, and we appreciate and support Congresswoman Cammack’s efforts to get these veterans what they earned,” said Captain Stephen Petty, U.S. Army (Ret.), a Vietnam helicopter pilot from Ocala, FL.

“We support the effort to pass the Star Act, and we appreciate Congresswoman Cammack standing up for our veterans,” said Charles Calhoun, President of the On Top of the World Veterans Club and Chairman of the Marion County Veterans Advisory Council.

title: Opening statement of Chairman Smith at Nigeria hearingOne Year Later: Assessing Nigeria’s Efforts to Protect Christians and Secure the Middle Belt
text:
The following are excerpts of Chairman Chris Smith’s (R-NJ) opening statement at the House Foreign Affairs Africa Subcommittee’s November 12th hearing—his fourteenth hearing chaired on the religious persecution of Christians by radical Islamist groups in Nigeria—entitled “One Year Later: Assessing Nigeria’s Efforts to Protect Christians and Secure the Middle Belt”:

On October 31st of last year, President Trump said: “Christianity is facing an existential threat in Nigeria. Thousands of Christians are being killed. Radical Islamists are responsible for this mass slaughter. I am hereby making Nigeria a ‘COUNTRY OF PARTICULAR CONCERN’” (pursuant to the International Religious Freedom Act of 1998 (PL 105-292) and the Frank R. Wolf International Religious Freedom Act of 2016 (PL 114-281)).

The CPC designation was a wakeup call for Nigeria and an urgent call to action to protect religious believers—mostly Christians—who have been victims of brutal attacks by ethnic Fulani militia and other terrorist groups, like Boko Haram and ISIS West Africia.

It has been just over one year since this designation, and almost exactly one year since this Subcommittee held a hearing on this topic—where I said that the designation is only the first step.

One of our witnesses today, Nina Shea, will testify:

“A year later, the atrocities continue to mount, and Nigeria maintains its ranking as the world’s deadliest place for Christians for faith-related reasons, accounting for 72 percent of such killings worldwide, according to Open Doors… The greatest threat to Nigeria’s Christians in recent years has been posed by bands of Fulani Muslim militants in the Middle Belt states particularly Benue, Plateau, Kaduna, and Taraba. In a consistent pattern evidencing a degree of organization, coordination, and funding support, Fulani militias invade rural Christian villages and farming areas and murder, maim, rape, and kidnap for ransom the defenseless residents and their church leaders. Thousands of Christians have been killed and taken hostage for ransom in these unprovoked attacks, which continue to the present. This violence has forced over a million survivors of such attacks from their lands and homes, and they are now destitute and hopeless, indefinitely consigned to camps for displaced persons. Nigeria’s government has failed to protect the Middle Belt Christians from Fulani terror.”

For years, my congressional colleagues and I warned that the violence was escalating, that Fulani perpetrators were operating with impunity, and that the Nigerian government's failure to protect its citizens demanded a sustained response, with serious encouragement from the United States.

Today, just over one year later, we confront an even more troubling reality.

The violence has not ended. Christian communities continue to face killings, abductions, attacks on churches, and the destruction of their homes and livelihoods.

The purpose of today’s hearing is not merely to revisit the benign admonishment of the United States to a friend and ally—friends don’t let friends commit human rights abuses.

It is to examine the Nigerian government’s continued failure to protect vulnerable communities and hold those responsible accountable; assess how the United States has engaged with Nigeria since its CPC redesignation; and determine what additional measures are needed to end the violence and prevent further atrocities against Christian communities in the Middle Belt and throughout Nigeria.

I have worked to bring sustained congressional attention to the persecution of Christians in Nigeria for decades and have chaired over a dozen hearings focused on Nigeria, undertaken fact-finding trips, and met face-to-face with survivors of horrific violence, including victims of Boko Haram attacks in Jos in 2013.

Fourteen years ago—in 2012—I chaired a hearing focusing on the slaughter of Christians by Boko Haram, and the Assistant Secretary of State for African Affairs Johnnie Carson testified “that the phenomena of Boko Haram is one of discrediting the Central Government in power for its failure to deliver services to people.”

Are you kidding?

I responded by asking why Boko Haram abducts and rapes Christian girls and uses force and coercion—even death—to convert Christians to Islam? Where are they getting their weapons? Are the IEDs coming from Iran? Not only should Nigeria be designated a Country of Particular Concern (CPC) for failing to protect believers, but why isn’t Boko Haram designated a Foreign Terrorist Organization (FTO)?

After three years of appealing to President Obama and the State Department to designate Boko Haram a FTO, on the day of markup on my legislation—the Boko Haram Terrorist Designation Act of 2013 (HR 3209)—to put Congress on record demanding FTO designation, the Administration designated Boko Haram a Foreign Terrorist Organization.

For too long, the Nigerian Government and the world have looked away—a culture of denial—as radical Fulani militants, Boko Haram and ISIS/West Africa have waged a relentless campaign of terror, murder, and displacement across Nigeria.

I—and many others— have consistently advocated for stronger diplomatic pressure, conditioning U.S. assistance on measurable progress, targeted sanctions against perpetrators, and direct humanitarian support for communities devastated and displaced by this violence.

I commend the State Department’s continued action, including the high-level visits to Nigeria from Undersecretary Hooker and Assistant Secretary Garcia and the recent U.S.-Nigeria Joint Working Group meetings. We look forward to hearing more about how these engagements are translating into observable action by the Nigerian government.

This Congress, the committee was tapped by the White House, in coordination with the Committee on Appropriations, to draft a report on the steps needed to capitalize on the CPC designation. We turned this report into legislation through the Nigeria Religious Freedom and Accountability Act of 2026 (HR 7457).

Our objective has remained unchanged: to end the persecution, ensure accountability, and protect the fundamental right of every Nigerian to practice their faith without violence or fear.

We cannot allow this opportunity to fall flat once more. The Nigerian government has a critical responsibility to protect its citizens, and I urge the State Department to leverage all diplomatic tools to bring action and accountability.

One year ago, we sounded the alarm. Today, we must ensure that alarm is answered with action.

Today, for our first panel, we have Assistant Secretary of State for the Bureau of African Affairs Frank Garcia and Assistant Secretary of State for the Bureau of Democracy, Human Rights, and Labor Riley Barnes.

Thank you both for being here, and I look forward to hearing about the steps your bureaus have taken over the past year, the obstacles that remain, and what more must be done to end this horrific violence.

###

title: Victory for veterans – 23 years in the makingHouse passes Major Richard Star Act to protect and expand veterans’ benefits
text:
“As an original cosponsor of the Major Richard Star Act (HR 2102), I have long believed that we must repeal the current policy that forces wounded veterans to sacrifice their duly earned retirement pay if they are determined to be eligible for VA disability benefits,” said Rep. Chris Smith (R-NJ), the former Chairman of the House Veterans Affairs Committee and a leading lawmaker for servicemembers and veterans.

“It is truly deplorable that our wounded veterans are being penalized for the injuries they incurred while courageously defending our country—paying what amounts to a ‘wounded veterans’ tax,’” continued Smith, the author of fourteen laws to assist veterans, including by bolstering and broadening VA disability benefits.

Smith noted that the legislation will complete the process he aggressively worked over 20 years ago to restore full compensation for all wounded veterans. At that time, Smith, along with then-Congressman Mike Bilirakis (R-FL), helped secure a historic compromise—which he viewed as a first step—to allow veterans with 50% or greater service-connected disabilities to receive their full disability payments, without offsets for their pensions. With this new legislation, Smith said, fairness will finally be restored for all our disabled veterans.

“I strongly urge my colleagues in the Senate to quickly pass this legislation and grant our Nation’s heroes the full benefits they deserve.”

title: EWTN News article on Smith's Nigeria hearing'Republicans demand more progress in halting Christian persecution in Nigeria'
text:
By Tyler Arnold

Published November 12, 2026 at 6:48 PM ET

As Christians continue to suffer persecution and the death toll from ethnoreligious conflicts keeps rising in Nigeria, some Republican lawmakers are urging the Department of State to demand more accountability of the Nigerian government.

“I really question, along with many others, as to whether enough has been done,” Rep. Bill Huizenga, R-Michigan, said during a Nov. 12 hearing by the U.S. House Foreign Affairs Subcommittee on Africa.

“My question is, has any work been done?” he asked. “Has any real work been done?”

The subcommittee convened to assess the ongoing crisis of terrorism, banditry, kidnappings, and mass casualty attacks rooted in ethnoreligious violence, in which Christians make up a disproportionate share of the victims. Much of the violence is perpetuated by Fulani Ethnic Militias but also includes attacks by Boko Haram and the Islamic State West Africa Province.

A resident stands among burnt debris and damaged homes following the attack in Woro, Kwara State, Nigeria, on Feb. 5, 2026. | Credit: Light Oriye Tamunotonye/AFP via Getty Images

Two Department of State assistant secretaries — Frank Garcia and Riley Barnes — along with specialists in religious freedom and international relations delivered testimony slightly more than one year after President Donald Trump designated Nigeria as a country of particular concern (CPC) for its toleration of “systematic, ongoing, and egregious violations of religious freedom.”

The CPC designation and cooperation between the U.S. and Nigeria has not reduced fatalities from this violence. According to the Nigeria Risk Index, Nigeria saw a slight decrease in security incidents from January through June 2026 when compared with the same period in 2025 but saw an increase in fatalities.

The number of security incidents decreased from 2,242 to 2,199, but the fatalities from those incidents increased by nearly 37%, from 2,242 to 4,435. The average fatality rate per incident rose from 1.45 to 2.02.

CPC designations must be reviewed annually, and the decision is left to the executive branch. Many of the Republican lawmakers expressed concern that the intended goals are far from being completed.

Both Garcia and Barnes argued there has been some progress with the Nigerian government acknowledging the crisis and working with the American government after the designation, but they warned that many problems persist and the Department of State’s work is ongoing.

“We are engaging the Nigerian government through direct, results-driven diplomacy,” Garcia told the lawmakers.

He pointed to the U.S.-Nigeria Joint Working Group, which was created to address the security issues and efforts to protect Christian communities through increased Nigerian security and law enforcement deployments, more timely responses to impending attacks, and biometric sharing with the government to help catch and prosecute those who perpetuate violence. The U.S. has also worked with the Nigerian government to target terrorist financial networks.

However, Garcia said the “pace” of the progress has been “insufficient,” acknowledging that “the violence has not stopped.” He called the crisis “an ongoing atrocity.”

Barnes said “the levels of violence and atrocities committed against Christians in Nigeria are appalling” and warned that attacks from the Fulani Ethnic Militias are often rooted in religious persecution.

“Nigerians I have spoken to on the ground have underscored the depth and breadth of suffering for many and ample witness testimonies over even the past year have stated plainly that perpetrators use religious language during their attacks, specifically identifying Christians for killing and abduction,” he said. “President Trump shined a light on these atrocities and made clear we must work to protect these vulnerable communities.”

Barnes also said the administration is pressing the Nigerian government to halt its enforcement of anti-blasphemy laws, which he warned are used to target Christians who speak about Islam.

Ongoing concerns

Republican lawmakers who questioned the assistant secretaries highlighted that significant work must still be done to address the crisis.

Rep. Riley Moore, R-West Virginia, said “there are certainly some positive signs” and cited Nigerian cooperation with the United States to target Fulani militants and detain suspected terrorist leader Mahmoud Adam.

“These steps followed sustained American engagement, and they are welcome,” he said. “But steps are not results. The … communities whose suffering prompted the designation are still waiting for protection and justice.”

“Success here means a definitive end to the genocidal murder of our brothers and sisters in Christ, and the peaceful return of [internally displaced persons] to their ancestral lands,” Moore said. “By that measure, [Nigeria] is falling short.”

Huizenga also expressed concern that the Nigerian government is “out of touch with what’s really happening,” which he called a “tragedy.”

“What needs to happen?” he said. “When are they going to take it serious and when are they going to do something about it?”

Rep. Chris Smith, R-New Jersey, who chairs the subcommittee, said during the hearing that CPC designation “is the beginning” but “not the end” of what is needed.

Speaking to EWTN News after the hearing, Smith praised the work of the Department of State in Nigeria, saying that without the CPC designation, “it would be far worse” because Nigeria “would have no incentive or pressure to try to mitigate the violence.”

“These are people, unfortunately, who are so radicalized that the only good Christian is a dead Christian,” he said. “And to me, thatʼs disgusting. All people, Christian, Jewish, Muslim should be allowed to thrive on their faith and believe as they would like freedom of religion.”

Smith also said the pace of progress has been “slow” and needs to “accelerate.”

title: Ciscomani Applauds House Passage of the Richard Star Act
text:
Washington, D.C. — The House of Representatives today passed H.R. 2102, the Major Richard Star Act, legislation that would ensure combat-injured veterans medically retired before completing 20 years of service can receive both their full military retirement pay and VA disability compensation.

“Those who sacrifice to protect our nation should never have to fight for the benefits they earned,” said Rep. Juan Ciscomani. “Veterans across Arizona’s Sixth Congressional District made it clear that passing the Major Richard Star Act was a top priority. I am proud to help advance this historic legislation, close a longstanding gap in veterans’ benefits, and ensure our nation’s heroes receive the full support they deserve.”

Under current law, some combat-injured veterans medically retired with fewer than 20 years of service are prevented from receiving both their full military retirement pay and VA disability compensation. According to the Military Officers Association of America, tens of thousands of veterans lose approximately $14,400 annually because of this policy.

The legislation addresses a longstanding inequity affecting approximately 54,000 wounded veterans nationwide. It also advances critical investments in veterans’ healthcare, suicide prevention programs, and the modernization of local VA facilities, strengthening the support available to veterans and their families.

Rep. Ciscomani heard directly from veterans, service organizations, and stakeholders across Arizona’s Sixth Congressional District about the importance of advancing the Major Richard Star Act. As one of 341 co-sponsors of the legislation, he has consistently championed efforts to strengthen veterans’ benefits and ensure those who served our country receive the care, resources, and recognition they have earned.

Passage of the Major Richard Star Act represents an important step toward fulfilling our nation’s commitment to those who have sacrificed in uniform. Rep. Ciscomani will continue working to ensure Arizona veterans have access to the benefits and support they deserve.

title: Higgins Supports Major Richard Star Act for Combat-Injured Veterans

title: President Trump Signs Cline Legislation to Support Small Businesses
text:
WASHINGTON, DC –President Trump has signed H.R. 7730, Congressman Ben Cline’s (VA-06) Bankruptcy Threshold Adjustments Act of 2026, into law, marking an important step toward helping small businesses overcome financial challenges, protect jobs, and keep their doors open to serve their communities.

“I am proud to support small businesses across our Nation by ensuring they have the tools they need to navigate financial challenges, protect jobs, and keep their doors open,” said Rep. Cline. “Small businesses are the backbone of our economy, driving growth, creating jobs, and strengthening our communities. I will continue fighting for policies that give small business owners the resources and flexibility they need to overcome challenges, succeed, and keep our economy strong.”

---

For years, small businesses across the Commonwealth of Virginia have faced significant financial challenges, making it difficult to recover, rebuild, and regain their footing. Right here in Virginia’s Sixth District, we have had multiple small businesses including restaurant and catering companies, a roofing company, a small-engine repair company, a trucking company, and a flooring contractor avail themselves of the opportunity to reorganize while keeping their operations running, employees working, and payments to suppliers intact.

H.R. 7730, the Bankruptcy Threshold Adjustments Act of 2026, raises the Subchapter V small-business debt limit to $7.5 million and the Chapter 13 consumer debt limit to $2.75 million, expanding access to critical protections that give business owners greater flexibility to restructure debt, maintain operations, retain employees, and continue serving their communities. These reforms strengthen Main Street businesses and help ensure that hardworking entrepreneurs have the opportunity to recover, rebuild, and succeed.

BACKGROUND: This legislation passed the House of Representatives on September 16, 2026, and the Senate on September 28, 2026. It builds on Rep. Ben Cline’s previous work on this issue. As a freshman in the 2019 class, he became the first Republican member of his class to have legislation signed into law with the Small Business Reorganization Act, which established the Subchapter V reorganization process.

title: Courtney Votes for Final Passage of the Major Richard Star Act, Sends Bill to the Senate
text:
WASHINGTON, DC — Today, Joe Courtney (CT-02) voted for final passage of the Major Richard Star Act (H.R. 2102). The bill passed the House by a vote of 392-18 and now heads to the Senate. The Major Richard Star Act would fix an injustice in the law that currently diminishes earned retirement benefits for veteran retirees who also collect service-connected disability benefits. Courtney and a bipartisan coalition successfully forced today’s vote via a discharge petition, which Courtney signed earlier this year.

“All of us have a duty, particularly here in Congress, to provide support for veterans – real tangible support in terms of health care and financial services,” Courtney said. “By finally passing the Major Richard Star Act, a bipartisan coalition just took a major step to follow through on that mission. This bill ends one of the greatest injustices in the Veterans Administration system that denies medically retired veterans the full scope of their earned retirement benefits. I urge the Senate to swiftly pass the Major Richard Star Act and send it to be signed into law.”

Currently, combat-injured veterans who were forced into medical retirement are only able to receive either U.S. Department of Defense retirement benefits or U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs disability compensation. The Major Richard Star Act would amend the law to allow these medically retired veterans to receive both their full retirement pay and disability compensation.

On Monday, in a speech on the House floor, Courtney called on his colleagues to pass the Major Richard Star Act. To watch and download Courtney’s full speech, click here.

title: In Letter to Navy, Courtney, Smith Express Deep Frustration Over Failure to Notify Congress of USS South Dakota Command Triad Relief
text:
WASHINGTON, DC — Today, Reps. Joe Courtney (CT-02), Ranking Member of the House Seapower and Projection Forces Subcommittee, and Adam Smith (WA-09), Ranking Member of the House Armed Services Committee, sent a letter to the Department of the Navy expressing their deep frustration over the Navy’s failure to notify Congress of the relief of the USS South Dakota (SSN 790) Commanding Officer, Executive Officer, and Chief of the Boat in October 2026. To view the letter, click here.

FULL LETTER TEXT

Dear Acting Secretary Cao and Admiral Caudle:

We write to express deep frustration over the Navy’s failure to notify the House Armed Services Committee of the relief of the Commanding Officer, Executive Officer, and Chief of the Boat of the USS South Dakota (SSN 790) on October 14, 2026.

On November 11, 2026, a reporter requested comment on the dismissal of SOUTH DAKOTA’s command triad, allegedly attributed to a grounding incident. Though nearly a month after the relief of the command triad, no notifications of the personnel actions or the underlying incident had been made to the House Armed Services Committee. On November 12, 2026, an article was published on the incident, including confirmation from the public affairs office for Commander, Submarine Force Atlantic that the commanding officer of SOUTH DAKOTA was relived from his role on October 14, 2026.

The Department of the Navy’s failure to communicate these incidents to Congress is unacceptable. The committee and Department maintain long-standing customs for information sharing, that though not expressly written in statute, have included notifications for various types of at-sea incidents, accidents, and dismissals of members of the command triad. In the wake of the collisions affecting USS Fitzgerald (DDG 62), USS John S. McCain (DDG 56), and the grounding incidents involving USS Hartford (SSN 768) and USS Connecticut (SSN 22), clear and timely communication with Congress was necessary to make informed decisions to ensure personnel safety and readiness of the fleet. Even after these events, Congress relied on continued good-faith communication with the Department, as opposed to codifying notification

requirements. Failing to provide timely notifications to Congress is counterproductive to good policymaking and undermines the Department’s stated goals of transparency and accountability and put leadership judgement into question.

To date, the Department of the Navy has not provided the committee with an official notification of the details of the CO’s dismissal. The Navy’s lack of transparency leave many outstanding questions about not only what occurred, but the impact of the events leading the triad’s dismissal on the structural health of SOUTH DAKOTA, the well-being of the crew, and whether the incident laid bare any systemic issues with training to standard procedures that must be addressed. As a result of the Navy’s failure to communicate, what should have been a standard exercise in information sharing has instead raised questions about the Navy’s commitment to transparency and its commitment to a productive working relationship with Congress.

We request the following information to be provided not later than November 20, 2026:

What events led up to the relief of the entire SOUTH DAKOTA command triad on October 14, 2026?

Was their dismissal a result of a grounding or other mishap at sea? If so, provide details of the circumstances of the grounding or other mishap at sea.

If a grounding or mishap occurred, what is the preliminary cost assessment of damages?

If a grounding occurred, what are the details on the structural damages to SOUTH DAKOTA?

If a grounding occurred, what is the expected timeline for maintenance following the grounding of SOUTH DAKOTA?

If a grounding occurred, how many injuries were incurred and what were the extent of injuries?

What is the reason for the decision not to notify Congress, in contradiction of past standard practice?

title: Davids Secures Millions to Fix Dangerous Roads, Speed Up Emergency Response Across Johnson County
text:
Today, Representative Sharice Davids announced multiple federal grants from the U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT) to fix dangerous intersections, eliminate hazardous train crossings, and make local roads safer across Johnson County. Davids was the only member of the Kansas congressional delegation to vote for the bipartisan infrastructure law that made these safety grants possible.

“Every time a parent drives their kids to school or a neighbor heads to work, they should feel confident they’ll get home safely,” said Davids. “And we’ve all seen the dangerous intersections and train delays that slow down ambulances and put lives at risk in our communities. I worked to pass the bipartisan infrastructure law so we could bring our tax dollars back home to fix these exact problems. These projects will save lives, cut down traffic, and keep Kansas families safe.”

The total $33,341,466 comes through the DOT’s Safe Streets and Roads for All (SS4A) and Railroad Crossing Elimination (RCE) grant programs. These programs, created by the bipartisan infrastructure law, focus on fixing dangerous crash zones and making sure emergency vehicles like fire trucks and ambulances can move through town without delays.

The funding will support specific projects across Johnson County:

City of Spring Hill: $29,976,080 (RCE) and $2,805,386 (SS4A)

Eliminating an at-grade rail crossing to decrease emergency response times, removing vehicle-train conflict points, and enhancing freight movement.

Implementing safety improvements along the 215th Street and South Street Corridor from Webster Road to U.S. 169 Highway, including intersection reconfiguration, new sidewalk construction, and high-visibility pedestrian crossings.

City of De Soto: $240,000 (SS4A)

Developing a comprehensive, citywide Safety Action Plan to curb serious and fatal crashes. As De Soto continues to grow, the city will analyze traffic patterns, forecast future land use, and engage with community members to build a prioritized list of road safety projects — focusing especially on high-risk areas where rural roads transition into busier, high-volume corridors.

City of Leawood: $320,000 (SS4A)

Delivering a detailed road safety audit and corridor study along 3.75 miles of Lee Boulevard. City planners will evaluate existing road conditions, analyze recent crash data, and design implementation-ready upgrades — such as targeted safety countermeasures and alternative traffic designs — to prevent future serious and fatal accidents.

title: CONGRESSMAN DOWNING HONORS AMERICA'S VETERANS IN HOUSE FLOOR SPEECH
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Yesterday, Congressman Troy Downing (MT-02) delivered remarks on the floor of the U.S. House of Representatives in recognition of Veterans Day, honoring the brave men and women who answered the call to serve our nation and recognizing the sacrifices made by military families.

Watch the full speech HERE.

Downing’s remarks as prepared for delivery:

Today, on Veterans Day, we honor the brave men and women who answered the call to serve our great nation.

Every veteran has a different story. Some joined out of a sense of patriotic duty. Others

sought an opportunity to build a better future.

But every one of them shared something in common.

They signed their name on the dotted line and made a solemn commitment to defend our Constitution and our country.

They took that oath knowing it could one day result in putting their life on the line.

That takes courage. It's a commitment that commands our nation's deepest gratitude.

We must also remember the families who stand behind our service members. The spouses who hold down the fort at home. The children who miss their parents. The loved ones who wait and pray for their safe return.

Their sacrifices deserve recognition too.

Following the attacks of September 11, I answered that same call and enlisted in the United States Air Force.

During my two deployments to Afghanistan, I served with a Combat Search and Rescue squadron.

When we crossed the wire into hostile territory, I knew the men and women beside me had my back. Every single time.

The pararescue creed is simple: "These things we do, that others may live."

Those words have stayed with me ever since.

To every veteran across Montana and our great nation, thank you for your courage, your service, and your commitment to our country.

May God bless our veterans, and may God bless the United States of America.
