title: Brown Seeks Answers from Federal Pipeline Safety Administration on Rainbow Terrace Explosion
text:
Washington, DC – Congresswoman Shontel Brown (OH-11) has written to the Department of Transportation (USDOT) demanding answers related to the explosion at the Rainbow Terrace Apartments in Cleveland.

On November 10, Brown wrote to the USDOT Secretary Sean Duffy and Paul Roberti, Administrator of the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) seeking information related to the federal investigation into the explosion. The PHMSA develops and enforces regulations for the safe, reliable, and environmentally sound operation of the nation's pipelines.

Brown’s extensive letter seeks answers to 28 specific questions and is focused on determining if the PHSMA, the Public Utilities Commission of Ohio, as well as Enbridge Gas, took proper action before and after the explosion, and if the federal regulator is recommending next steps to improve public safety. Brown’s letter gives USDOT and PHSMA thirty days to respond. The letter was also sent to the leaders of the relevant committees in the House.

“I speak with and speak for my constituents at Rainbow Terrace and across Northeast Ohio: we had a deadly explosion here in Cleveland and we still don’t know why. That’s simply unacceptable. We need answers, answers so there can be accountability and answers so we can prevent further tragedies,” said Congresswoman Shontel Brown.

Brown writes, “Because of this tragedy, people were killed, injured, and lost their homes, and many more are now worried about the safety of their own home or apartment building. Over a year later, we still don’t know why this explosion happened and my constituents need answers. This letter seeks a full accounting of the federal response to the Rainbow Terrace Explosion, clear answers on if Enbridge and PUCO fully cooperated with federal reporting requirements, if Enbridge and PUCO fully cooperated with federal and local investigations, if federal safety violations were identified, and what steps are being taken to prevent another explosion.”

For a pdf of the letter click here.

The full letter reads as follows:

Dear Secretary Duffy and Administrator Roberti:

I write regarding the June 23, 2025 explosion and fire at Rainbow Terrace Apartments in Cleveland, Ohio, which resulted in the death of one resident, injuries to others, the destruction of 44 apartment units, and the displacement of families. I respectfully request information concerning the U.S. Department of Transportation’s (“DOT”) and Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration’s (“PHMSA”) federal pipeline safety responsibilities, including the applicable regulatory requirements, the response, and coordination with the Public Utilities Commission of Ohio (“PUCO”).

On September 28, 2026, the City of Cleveland released an Executive Summary of Rainbow Terrace Investigative Efforts, together with investigative materials prepared by the Cleveland Division of Fire, PUCO, Enbridge Gas Ohio, and Enbridge’s retained investigator. The Cleveland Division of Fire concluded that natural gas accumulated in the lower levels of the affected building before encountering an unknown ignition source. However, investigators could not establish the source of the gas release or ignition, and the cause of the explosion remains classified as undetermined.[1]

Although PUCO did not identify regulatory or compliance failures by Enbridge that caused or contributed to the explosion, its investigation documented deficiencies in the company’s post-incident response. These included inaccurate geographic information system (“GIS”) mapping that failed to identify an active service line, difficulties identifying and isolating the appropriate gas infrastructure, and deficiencies in post-incident leak detection. According to the investigative materials, an uncontrolled release of natural gas continued for approximately 20 hours following the explosion.[2]

These findings raise important questions regarding the adequacy of pipeline operator emergency-response procedures, infrastructure records, incident-investigation practices, and compliance with applicable safety requirements. They also warrant clarification of the respective responsibilities of PHMSA, PUCO, and regulated pipeline operators when serious incidents occur.

Under 49 U.S.C. Chapter 601, PHMSA establishes minimum federal pipeline safety standards, including requirements governing natural gas distribution systems. Ohio administers a certified state pipeline safety program under 49 U.S.C. § 60105, through which PUCO exercises enforcement responsibilities for covered intrastate facilities, subject to federal oversight.[3]

Given the seriousness of the Rainbow Terrace explosion and the deficiencies identified in the subsequent response, I respectfully request information concerning PHMSA’s role in this matter, the applicable federal pipeline safety requirements, and any opportunities to strengthen pipeline safety and emergency preparedness. Because of this tragedy, people were killed, injured, and lost their homes, and many more are now worried about the safety of their own home or apartment building. Over a year later, we still don’t know why this explosion happened and my constituents need answers. This letter seeks a full accounting of the federal response to the Rainbow Terrace Explosion, clear answers on if Enbridge and PUCO fully cooperated with federal reporting requirements, if Enbridge and PUCO fully cooperated with federal and local investigations, if federal safety violations were identified, and what steps are being taken to prevent another explosion.

This inquiry is focused on DOT’s and PHMSA’s federal pipeline safety responsibilities.

I. PHMSA’s Investigative Role and Federal-State Coordination

Please provide information concerning PHMSA’s involvement in the Rainbow Terrace incident and its coordination with PUCO, including:

Whether PHMSA received notification of the June 23, 2025 explosion, an incident report from Enbridge, investigative findings from PUCO, or other relevant information concerning Rainbow Terrace. Please provide the dates, nature, and disposition of such notifications or submissions;

Whether PHMSA conducted, participated in, assisted with, or independently reviewed any investigation of the incident, including any technical assessments, compliance evaluations, or reviews of Enbridge’s post-incident response;

Whether PHMSA has reviewed PUCO’s investigative findings, including the deficiencies involving gas-system mapping, service-line identification and isolation, and post-incident leak detection, and whether PHMSA concurs with, disputes, or has sought clarification regarding any of those findings;

A description of PHMSA’s oversight responsibilities concerning PUCO’s certified state pipeline safety program, including the circumstances under which PHMSA may request additional information, conduct a federal review, provide technical assistance, or recommend further regulatory action following an intrastate pipeline incident;

Whether PHMSA has communicated with PUCO, Enbridge, the City of Cleveland, or other relevant entities regarding corrective actions, additional inspections, compliance concerns, or safety recommendations arising from Rainbow Terrace; and

Whether PHMSA anticipates any additional investigative, technical, regulatory, or oversight activities concerning this incident and, if so, the anticipated scope and timeline.

II. Federal Pipeline Safety Requirements

Federal pipeline safety regulations establish requirements for operator procedures, emergency preparedness, incident investigation, and the safe operation of regulated natural gas infrastructure. Among potentially relevant provisions are 49 CFR §§ 192.605, 192.615, and 192.617, governing operating procedures, emergency plans, and the investigation of failures and incidents, respectively.[4]

The applicability of particular requirements depends on the infrastructure involved, the location of the regulated service-line endpoint, and the circumstances of the incident. Accordingly, please provide:

PHMSA’s assessment of which portions of the natural gas infrastructure serving the affected Rainbow Terrace buildings were subject to federal pipeline safety requirements, including the applicable regulatory boundary between Enbridge-operated service lines and customer-owned piping;

A description of the federal statutory and regulatory requirements applicable to Enbridge’s emergency response following the explosion, including requirements concerning prompt response, coordination with emergency personnel, identification and isolation of gas infrastructure, and mitigation of continuing hazards;

Whether PHMSA has evaluated, or requested that PUCO evaluate, Enbridge’s actions following the explosion against the applicable requirements of 49 CFR Part 192, including §§ 192.605, 192.615, and 192.617;

Whether the inaccurate GIS mapping, failure to identify an active service line, difficulties isolating the appropriate gas infrastructure, and post-incident leak-detection deficiencies identified by PUCO implicate any federal pipeline safety requirements and, if so, which specific provisions;

Whether PHMSA or PUCO identified any violations of applicable federal pipeline safety requirements in connection with Enbridge’s response, investigation, or subsequent corrective actions. For each identified violation, please describe the applicable requirement, finding, enforcement or corrective action, and current status;

Whether PHMSA has reviewed the adequacy of Enbridge’s written emergency-response and incident-investigation procedures, including whether those procedures were followed during the incident and subsequent response;

Whether Enbridge has undertaken any corrective actions, modifications to operating procedures, mapping updates, employee training, additional inspections, or other safety improvements as a result of the incident, and whether PHMSA or PUCO has assessed their adequacy; and

Whether PHMSA has identified any gaps between minimum federal pipeline safety requirements and recommended industry practices that may be relevant to the circumstances documented at Rainbow Terrace.

III. Incident Investigation, Documentation, and Safety Accountability

The investigation of serious pipeline incidents is essential not only to determining their causes, where possible, but also to identifying deficiencies in operator practices and preventing similar events.

Under 49 CFR § 192.617, pipeline operators must establish and follow applicable procedures for investigating and analyzing failures and incidents, including appropriate examination of failed components and incorporation of lessons learned.[5]

To better understand the applicable federal requirements and their implementation, please provide:

Whether the Rainbow Terrace explosion met the federal incident-reporting criteria under 49 CFR Part 191 and, if so, whether Enbridge submitted the required notifications and reports, including any supplemental or amended submissions;

Whether PHMSA has reviewed the completeness, accuracy, and timeliness of any incident reports or investigative materials submitted by Enbridge;

The federal requirements applicable to Enbridge’s investigation of the incident, including the examination, documentation, testing, retention, or preservation of relevant pipeline components and other physical evidence, where required;

Whether PHMSA or PUCO assessed Enbridge’s handling of physical evidence and investigative documentation for compliance with applicable regulatory requirements and, if so, the findings of that assessment;

Whether PHMSA identified any limitations in the available investigative record that prevented a more complete assessment of the incident or Enbridge’s compliance with federal safety requirements;

Whether PHMSA considered an independent technical review, additional testing, or coordination with the National Transportation Safety Board or other appropriate investigative entities, and whether such involvement was warranted under applicable authorities; and

Whether PHMSA has identified any administrative, regulatory, or investigative practices that should be strengthened to ensure that serious natural gas incidents receive thorough, independent, and technically sound review.

IV. Coordination, Emergency Preparedness, and Lessons Learned

The Rainbow Terrace explosion underscores the importance of reliable infrastructure information, effective emergency response, and coordination among pipeline operators, first responders, and state and federal regulators.

Even where the cause of an explosion cannot be conclusively determined, documented deficiencies in the subsequent response may offer important opportunities to strengthen pipeline safety and prevent additional harm.

Accordingly, please provide:

A description of PHMSA’s coordination with PUCO, Enbridge, the City of Cleveland, local emergency responders, and other relevant entities regarding the incident and its aftermath;

Whether PHMSA has assessed the adequacy of federal requirements and operator practices concerning the accuracy, maintenance, and accessibility of natural gas distribution-system maps, particularly during emergencies;

Whether the circumstances at Rainbow Terrace have prompted PHMSA to examine the adequacy of emergency isolation procedures, leak-detection practices, coordination with first responders, or response protocols at multifamily residential properties;

Whether PHMSA has identified broader safety concerns involving older natural gas distribution infrastructure, inactive or poorly documented service lines, or the regulatory boundary between utility-operated infrastructure and customer-owned piping;

Whether PHMSA has issued, or is considering, any safety advisories, technical guidance, recommended practices, training improvements, or other measures informed by the Rainbow Terrace incident or comparable events;

Whether PHMSA has identified opportunities to strengthen the coordination of federal and state regulators, pipeline operators, local emergency responders, and property owners when serious natural gas incidents occur; and

Any additional actions DOT or PHMSA expects to undertake to strengthen operator accountability, emergency preparedness, and the investigation of serious natural gas incidents.

The families affected by the Rainbow Terrace explosion deserve answers, continued support, and confidence that the public safety systems serving their community are functioning as intended. Although the precise cause of the explosion remains undetermined, that uncertainty should not prevent a careful assessment of the documented response deficiencies or the effectiveness of applicable safety requirements.

Congress has an important responsibility to understand how federal pipeline safety standards are implemented and enforced, whether regulatory oversight is effective, and whether serious incidents reveal opportunities to strengthen public safety.

I appreciate DOT’s and PHMSA’s attention to these matters. I respectfully request a written response within 30 days of receipt of this letter and welcome a briefing from appropriate Department and/or PHMSA staff concerning the federal regulatory responsibilities and findings discussed above.

[Signature]

cc:

The Honorable Sam Graves, Chairman, House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure

The Honorable Rick Larsen, Ranking Member, House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure

The Honorable Daniel Webster, Chairman, Subcommittee on Railroads, Pipelines, and Hazardous Materials

The Honorable Dina Titus, Ranking Member, Subcommittee on Railroads, Pipelines, and Hazardous Materials

Robert Burrough, Director, Eastern Region, Office of Pipeline Safety, Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration

title: Congressman Eric Sorensen Announces New Legislation to Lower Prices for Illinois Farmers
text:
WASHINGTON, DC – Today, Congressman Eric Sorensen announced the introduction of the Fair Premiums for Farmers Act, legislation he authored to help ensure farmers in the Midwest pay crop insurance rates applicable to their actual risk of production.

“At a time when they already face record-high costs for farm inputs—including diesel, fertilizer, seed, and equipment—we need to do everything we can to lower costs for our farmers,” said Congressman Eric Sorensen. “For too long, farmers in the Midwest, especially in Illinois, have been forced to pay higher crop insurance rates as a way of subsidizing farmers in other parts of the country. My legislation is an important step forward in righting this wrong, ensuring fair crop insurance rates for all farmers, and helping to lower costs for farmers across the board.”

The Department of Agriculture’s Risk Management Agency (RMA) sets rates for insurance policies in the Federal Crop Insurance Program (FCIP). Loss ratios measure the financial performance of the program and are determined by dividing the indemnities paid to policyholders by the total amount of premiums collected for the policies sold within the year.

By law, RMA must administer the FCIP in a manner that is actuarially sound, meaning the total premiums paid by farmers over time must roughly equal the total value of indemnities paid out for confirmed losses. Additionally, RMA is also required to periodically review rating methodology.

Unfortunately, the current system can often produce wide disparities in loss ratios for certain states and commodities. Midwest soybeans produced in states like Indiana, Iowa, Ohio, Nebraska, Missouri, Wisconsin, and Illinois have experienced very low 10-year loss ratio averages—some nearly one-quarter the average. As a result, farmers in these states are overpaying for their policies in comparison to farmers in other regions where loss ratios are considerably higher.

To address this, the Fair Premiums for Farmers Act would:

Direct RMA to complete a study on loss ratios for all covered commodities under the FCIP by state and commodity to identify the policies and plans which contribute to high loss ratios.

Direct RMA to analyze extreme weather events which account for various levels of loss.

Require RMA to publish, and make available for public comment, a report of the findings, including a proposed plan to remedy disparities in loss ratios within three years.

Read the full text of the legislation here.

Addressing loss ratios for farmers in Illinois has long been a top priority for Congressman Sorensen, and he recently joined a letter with Senator Durbin, Senator Duckworth, and Congresswoman Budzinski on this issue.

To learn more about Congressman Sorensen’s work on behalf of farmers—and all of his neighbors—visit his website here.

Congressman Eric Sorensen represents Illinois’ 17th District in the United States House of Representatives. Prior to serving in Congress, Sorensen was a local meteorologist in Rockford and the Quad Cities for more than 20 years. His district includes Illinois’ Quad Cities, Rockford, Peoria, and Bloomington-Normal.

title: ICYMI: Rep. Suozzi Op Ed in Philadelphia Inquirer: Philadelphia Stood Up to Antisemitism. We Must All Remain Vigilant.
text:
Washington, D.C.—In a new opinion piece in The Philadelphia Inquirer, Congressman Tom Suozzi (NY-03) warns that we must remain vigilant in the face of antisemitism and hatred. He argues that despite the quick response from Philadelphia's lawmakers and community in speaking out against the antisemitic boycott of Jewish-owned and Israeli-affiliated businesses last weekend, we cannot mistake the failure of one hateful demonstration for the defeat of the hatred that fueled it.

As the late Congressman and Holocaust survivor Tom Lantos said, "The veneer of civilization is paper thin. We are its guardians, and we cannot rest!" Rep. Suozzi argues that we must follow his lead and ensure that never again means something.

Opinion | Philadelphia Stood Up to Antisemitism. We Must All Remain Vigilant.

By Thomas R. Suozzi, The Philadelphia Inquirer

The ugly attempt to intimidate Jewish-owned businesses in Philadelphia backfired spectacularly on Sunday. Organizers hoping to drive Jewish and Israeli-associated restaurants out of the city were met by hundreds of Philadelphians who turned out to support the very businesses being targeted. Customers lined up outside restaurants, elected officials condemned the boycott, and ordinary citizens sent an unmistakable message: Antisemitism has no place in the City of Brotherly Love.

That is something worth celebrating. But we must not mistake the failure of one hateful demonstration for the defeat of the hatred that inspired it. We must remain vigilant.

Restaurants targeted

“No business for Zionists! These Zionist establishments must go! Not in our city!” Those were the words used to promote Sunday’s demonstration targeting six Jewish-owned and Israeli-associated restaurants in Philadelphia, the birthplace of American liberty.

The timing was particularly chilling. The demonstration occurred on the eve of the anniversary of Kristallnacht, the infamous Night of Broken Glass, when Nazi mobs attacked Jewish people, businesses, homes, and synagogues across Germany and Austria on Nov. 9 and 10, 1938.

Years earlier, in 1933, the Nazis organized a nationwide boycott of Jewish businesses, seeking to isolate Jews economically and socially and mark them as outsiders in their own communities.

We should not equate Sunday’s protest with the Nazi atrocities that followed. But the disturbing resemblance between calls to boycott Jewish businesses then and demands to drive Jewish-owned establishments out of Philadelphia today cannot be ignored.

History teaches us that hatred does not begin with concentration camps. It begins when ordinary people are singled out, dehumanized, and told they do not below.

I understand something about the destructive power of prejudice because of my family’s experience.

My father, Joseph Suozzi, came to America from Italy as a young boy. He became a decorated World War II hero, serving as a B-24 bomber navigator and earning the Distinguished Flying Cross. After the war, he attended Harvard Law School on the GI Bill, graduating in 1948.

Despite his extraordinary qualifications, New York City law firms refused to hire him. Anti-Italian prejudice closed doors that his service, sacrifice, and education should have opened.

He persevered, eventually becoming a respected judge on New York’s highest trial court and later its appellate division. He taught me that America’s promise of opportunity means little if discrimination determines who belongs.

That lesson has guided my public life.

Throughout my years in Congress, I have fought antisemitism and stood firmly with Israel and the Jewish American community. In 2019, I cosponsored legislation opposing the global Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement, known as BDS, and spoke against it on the House floor.

Right to worship

More recently, I helped lead bipartisan legislation, the Right to Worship Act, to protect Americans from intimidation when attending religious services. No American should fear going to a synagogue, church, mosque, or any other house of worship.

Americans have every right to criticize the Israeli government, advocate for Palestinians, and engage in peaceful political protest. Those freedoms are fundamental to our democracy.

But there is an enormous difference between criticizing a government and targeting American business owners because they are Jewish or presumed to hold particular beliefs.

Philadelphia’s response deserves recognition. Mayor Cherelle L. Parker, Gov. Josh Shapiro, religious leaders, and countless ordinary citizens spoke out. Hundreds showed their solidarity not merely with words, but by patronizing the businesses under attack.

They demonstrated the best of America. But Sunday’s events also reminded us how easily ancient prejudices can resurface in modern political movements.

Philadelphia is where our founders proclaimed that all people are created equal. Its citizens showed that they will not stand by while their Jewish neighbors are threatened or intimidated.

That same spirit must prevail throughout America.

We cannot condemn the antisemitism of the past while tolerating its warning signs in the present.

The late U.S. Rep. Tom Lantos, the only Holocaust survivor to have served in Congress, reminded us: “The veneer of civilization is paper thin. We are its guardians, and we cannot rest!”

We cannot rest. We must recognize "never again" must mean something. And it must mean something now.

###

title: Rep. Sykes Announces $2 Million for Street Safety in Summit County
text:
AKRON, OH – Today, U.S. Representative Emilia Sykes (OH-13) announced the U.S. Department of Transportation awarded a $2 million Safe Streets for All Grant to Summit County for its Criminal Justice Fiber Ring Adaptive Signalization Project. The project will upgrade traffic signals at 36 intersections between North Revere Road and Downtown Akron to help traffic move more smoothly and make roads safer.

“Every community deserves safe, reliable infrastructure, and I’m proud to help deliver that for Summit County. This $2 million federal investment will help Summit County use innovative technology to prevent crashes, improve traffic flow, and make our roads safer for everyone. With more than 4,200 crashes along this corridor in just five years, these improvements are urgently needed,” said Rep. Sykes. “I will continue working as a member of the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee to bring federal dollars back to Ohio’s 13th Congressional District to improve our communities.”

“This project is an important investment in making our roads safer and our transportation system more efficient. By leveraging the Summit Connects fiber infrastructure, we can use technology to improve traffic flow, give emergency vehicles a clearer path through intersections, and support more reliable public transportation. It’s an example of how Summit County is putting our investments in technology and infrastructure to work for the benefit of our residents and communities,” said Summit County Executive Ilene Shapiro. “We are thankful for Congresswoman Emilia Sykes’ support of this project and her commitment to bringing federal resources to our region to improve transportation safety.”

Between 2019 and 2023, the corridor between North Revere Road and Downtown Akron saw 4,210 crashes, including 12 fatalities and 58 suspected serious injuries. New technology will allow traffic signals to adjust to changing traffic conditions, give emergency vehicles more time to get through intersections, and help buses stay on schedule. These improvements are designed to reduce crashes, improve traffic flow, and make travel safer for everyone. The project will also include safety reviews, engineering and environmental planning, and opportunities for community input to help guide the improvements.

title: Rep. Sykes Votes to Secure Benefits for Disabled Veterans
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Representative Emilia Sykes (OH-13) voted to pass the Major Richard Star Act (H.R. 2102), a bipartisan bill which will provide qualifying combat-disabled veterans full veterans' disability compensation and retirement pay.

Prior to this legislation, veterans forced into retirement before completing 20 years of service due to a disabling injury were unable to receive both U.S. Department of Defense retirement benefits and U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs disability compensation without facing a penalty. Now, this bill will allow qualified veterans to receive an estimated $1,200 in benefits every month.

“The Major Richard Star Act is long overdue. This bill recognizes the great sacrifice made by our veterans and provides financial assistance to America’s 59,000 medically retired veterans who have served our nation with honor,” said Rep. Sykes.

Congresswoman Sykes is one of 342 cosponsors on this bill, and earlier this year, she signed onto a discharge petition to force a vote on this measure on the House floor.

The legislation passed the House and now moves to the Senate for consideration.

title: Rep. Tran Leads Bipartisan Letter to Senate Demanding Action on Critical Legislation That Will Help Millions of Small Businesses
text:
Washington, D.C. – U.S. Representative Derek Tran (CA-45) led a letter urging the Senate to act on 32 House-passed bills that would help the nation's 36.2 million small businesses, including over 400,000 small businesses in Orange County.

Out of the bills listed in the letter, Rep. Tran personally shepherded the following:

Introducing H.R. 5788 - the 504 Program Risk Oversight Act, which would increase transparency and efficiency within the Small Business Administration,

Co-Leading H.R. 787 - the Plain Language in Contracting Act, which would help small businesses compete for government contracts,

and Co-Leading H.R. 1642 - the Connecting Small Businesses with Career and Technical Education Graduates Act, which would connect small businesses with a more robust workforce pipeline.

Alongside Rep. Tran, this bipartisan letter was co-led by Representatives Kimberlyn King-Hinds (R-MP-AL), Johnny Olszewski, Jr. (D-MD-02), and Tony Wied (R-WI-08), and signed by additional members of the House Small Business Committee, including Representatives Lateefah Simon (D-CA-12), Gilbert Ray Cisneros, Jr. (D-CA-31), Kelly Morrison (D-MN-03), Pete Stauber (R-MN-08), and Hillary J. Scholten (D-MI-03).

Currently, over 30 bipartisan small business bills have passed the House of Representatives and are awaiting Senate consideration. This includes legislation that would expand workforce development, address fraud, improve transparency, and enhance technology solutions for small businesses across the nation. In the letter to Chairwoman Ernst and Ranking Member Markey of the Senate Committee on Small Business and Entrepreneurship (Senate SBC), Rep. Tran and his colleagues called on their Senate counterpart committee to prioritize the passage of this legislation before the 119th Congress ends in January.

If the Senate fails to act before the end of the 119th Congress, all 32 bipartisan bills will expire. Each bill would have to be reintroduced in the 120th Congress and restart the legislative process, further delaying relief for American small businesses.

“As Members of the House Small Business Committee, we urge the Senate Committee on Small Business and Entrepreneurship (Senate SBC) to prioritize consideration of bipartisan small business legislation that has already passed the House of Representatives. Congress must take every opportunity to advance policies that strengthen small businesses’ ability to invest, innovate, create jobs, and serve their communities. With limited time remaining in the 119th Congress, we respectfully urge that the Senate SBC act on them before the end of this year,” the members wrote in the letter.

“As a second-generation small business owner, I know what it takes to operate a family-owned business. Californians need legislation that makes it easier, not harder, to successfully pursue entrepreneurship. As members of the House Small Business Committee, we have proudly passed thirty-two bipartisan, common-sense bills that will help small business owners and aspiring entrepreneurs throughout California and the country. The 119th Congress is quickly coming to a close, and the Senate must do its part and consider these bills before time is up,” said Representative Tran.

“Members of the House Small Business Committee have been hard at work this Congress passing legislation to support our small businesses and put Main Street first,” said Congressman Wied. “Legislation like H.R. 4549 and H.R. 8879, which I was proud to co-lead, are exactly the types of bills small business owners deserve, helping increase transparency and ensuring rural small businesses have access to the tools they need to succeed. It’s time for the Senate to take action and get these important bills across the finish line.”

“Small businesses are the backbone of our communities, and they need access to the resources to grow and succeed. The House has passed more than 30 bipartisan bills, including my Northern Mariana Islands Small Business Access Act, which would make CNMI small businesses eligible for SBA microloans, helping entrepreneurs access the capital they need to start and grow their businesses. Now it’s time for the Senate to act and get these bills across the finish line,” said Congresswoman Kimberlyn King-Hinds (MP-AL).

“Small business owners don't have time to wait on Washington: they need a government that works as hard as they do and policies that help them grow, hire, and compete," said Congressman Johnny Olszewski. "The House has done its work, passing more than 30 bipartisan bills that deliver practical solutions for Main Street America. Now it's time for the Senate to step up and get these bills across the finish line before this term expires.”

title: Reps. Carter, Lieu, Menendez, McCormick, Dunn Introduce First-Ever Bladder Health Awareness Month Resolution
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, Congressman Troy A. Carter, Sr. (D-LA), Congressman Dr. Rich McCormick (R-GA), Congressmen Ted Lieu (D-CA), Congressman Robert Menendez (D-NJ), and Congressman Dr. Neal Dunn (R-FL) announced the introduction of the first-ever National Bladder Health Awareness Month Resolution with Congressmembers Carol Miller (R-WV), Jonathan Jackson (D-IL), and Kevin Mullin (D-CA) cosponsoring. The Bladder Health Awareness Month Resolution would support the recognition of November as Bladder Health Awareness Month and encourage efforts to increase public education, reduce stigma, and improve access to care.

“Bladder Health Awareness Month isn’t just about improving personal outcomes — it’s about encouraging preventative care, making informed decisions, and prioritizing bladder health in a way that protects not just individuals but the Americans in their network,” said Congressman Carter. “Too many Americans skip checkups, stay silent about symptoms, and lose precious years of their lives because of stigma or lack of access to care. The Bladder Health Awareness Month Resolution certifies bladder health as an integral part of overall health and wellbeing and works to increase public education, reduce stigma, and provide millions of Americans with the care they deserve.”

“As a physician, I know firsthand that bladder health is an integral part of overall health and quality of life. Yet millions of Americans suffer in silence because of stigma, embarrassment, or a lack of awareness about available treatments. No one should have to wait years to seek care for a condition that affects their daily life. I am proud to join Congressman Carter in recognizing November as Bladder Health Awareness Month and helping ensure patients have the information, resources, and confidence to seek the care they deserve,” said Congressman Rich McCormick, M.D. (GA-07).

“Millions of Americans struggle with bladder conditions and diseases that can significantly impact their health and quality of life,” said Congressman Lieu. “It’s important that we raise awareness of these conditions to encourage individuals to recognize symptoms and have informed conversations with their health care providers. I’m pleased to support this resolution to empower people to make the best decisions for their health.”

“Breaking the silence around bladder health can help save lives,” said Congressman Rob Menendez. “Recognizing November as Bladder Health Awareness Month helps raise awareness, reduce stigma, and encourage Americans to talk with their health care providers about symptoms and concerns. By making these conversations easier, we can help more people get the care they need sooner.”

“As a physician and urologist, I have seen firsthand the importance of bladder health to an individual’s overall health and quality of life,” said Congressman Dunn. “I am proud to join my colleagues in raising awareness about this important issue and encouraging Americans to take a proactive approach to their health.”

“The Men's Health Network is deeply grateful to Representatives Carter and McCormick along with the other leaders of the Congressional Men's Health Caucus for their recognition of Bladder Health Awareness Month. While bladder concerns are most often thought of as pelvic floor issues among women, there is less awareness of the millions of men who suffer from bladder issues including overactive bladder, incontinence, bladder cancer, prostatic enlargement, and side effects of prostate cancer treatment. Bladder Health Awareness Month is a critical component of the effort to improve awareness and treatment of these conditions,” said Ronald Henry, President of the Men's Health Network.

Background

The Bladder Health Awareness Month Resolution would support the recognition of November as Bladder Health Awareness Month and encourage efforts to increase public education, reduce stigma, and improve access to care. The resolution also encourages the Department of Health and Human Services to disseminate information about bladder health, support partnerships with nonprofit organizations, consumer groups, academic institutions, and public-private initiatives, promote evidence-based education and training for health care professionals, and encourage individuals to speak openly about bladder health and seek appropriate medical care.

Millions of Americans live with bladder health conditions that can significantly affect their health, well-being and quality of life. Bladder control problems, including overactive bladder and urinary incontinence, affect an estimated 43 million, or 1 in 6, U.S. adults of all ages. These conditions can disrupt sleep, reduce work productivity, contribute to social withdrawal and mental health challenges, and increase the risk of falls, fractures, urinary tract infections, and skin breakdown.

Despite their prevalence, bladder health conditions often go untreated due to stigma, lack of awareness, and misdiagnosis. Increasing public awareness and education can help individuals recognize symptoms, understand available treatment options, and seek care earlier. Improving access to reliable information, strengthening provider education, and encouraging open conversations about bladder health can help reduce barriers to diagnosis and treatment.

The need for greater awareness is significant. Research indicates that the average time between symptom onset and initiation of treatment is approximately seven years, and only 1 in 3 patients ever seek treatment. The total national cost of overactive bladder is estimated to exceed $80 billion, including direct health care costs and lost productivity.

As millions of Americans continue to experience bladder health conditions, the Bladder Health Awareness Month Resolution offers a practical approach to increase awareness and encourage earlier access to care.

The Bladder Health Awareness Month Resolution is endorsed by: American Urological Association, American Urogynecologic Society (AUGS), National Association For Continence (NAFC), Association for Pelvic Organ Prolapse Support (APOPS), Women's Health Advocates, Interstitial Cystitis Association (ICA), Men's Health Network, Bladder Cancer Advocacy Network (BCAN), Society of Urodynamics, and Female Pelvic Medicine & Urogenital Reconstruction (SUFU).

title: Virginia House Delegation Urges Rejection of NextEra-Dominion Merger
text:
Washington D.C. – Today, Congressman James Walkinshaw (VA-11) joined Congressmen Don Beyer (VA-08), Congresswoman Jennifer McClellan (VA-04), Suhas Subramanyam (VA-10), and Eugene Vindman (VA-07), Democrats from Virginia, to urge the Virginia State Corporation Commission (SCC) to reject the proposed acquisition of Dominion Energy by Florida-based NextEra. In a letter submitted ahead of the SCC’s November 12 public comment deadline, the Members warned that the merger, as currently structured, threatens to increase electricity costs for Virginia families and small businesses for decades to come.

They wrote:

“As proposed, we do not believe the merger is in the public interest. We believe the proposed transaction fails to satisfy the statutory requirements and because the joint petition lacks the structural protections necessary to prevent material harm, the Commission should deny the merger petition in its current form.”

The Members noted that while NextEra stands to benefit from the expanded investment opportunities created by the rapid expansion of data centers across Northern Virginia, residential customers and small businesses could be left footing the bill. The Members also cautioned that the merger could consolidate market power across the regional electricity grid, stifling competition and ultimately increasing electricity costs for Virginia consumers.

They argued that the proposed merger’s temporary incentives fail to offset the merger’s potential long-term costs. They also pointed to the absence of a moratorium on base rate increases, a cap on escalating rate adjustment clauses, and a binding requirement to pass operational savings on to customers.

The letter further raises concerns about NextEra’s corporate governance, including its history of political spending and interference, warning these practices could undermine regulatory oversight, create conflicts with Virginia’s Clean Economy Act requirements, and expose ratepayers to additional financial risks.

Emphasizing the SCC’s statutory responsibility to safeguard consumers and ensure the long-term reliability and affordability of utility service, the Members stated that approving the merger without adequate, enforceable protections would undermine that responsibility.

Full text of the letter follows below, and a signed copy is available here.

***

Dear Commissioners:

We write to express our opposition to the current proposed merger whereby NextEra Energy, Inc. (“NextEra”) would acquire control of Dominion Energy, Inc. (“Dominion”). Under the Utility Transfers Act, the State Corporation Commission (“Commission”) may approve an acquisition of control if it finds that “adequate service to the public at just and reasonable rates will not be impaired or jeopardized. “Applicants must prove that the transaction causes no harm to captive customers. We believe the joint petition fails this statutory test.

We respectfully urge the Commission to reject the proposed NextEra Dominion merger in its current form, as recommended by Commission staff.

Rate Base Inflation and Misaligned Incentives

NextEra’s investor disclosures emphasize that Dominion’s territory offers immense multi-decade capital deployment opportunities, driven in large part by the extraordinary concentration of AI data centers in Northern Virginia and future planned load. Given that this projected future energy demand in the Commonwealth will be reliant on massive bulk transmission lines, which are still socialized across residential rate classes, much of that potential infrastructure will be paid for by ratepayers. And as NextEra’s growth strategy is dependent on maximizing capital deployment, its potential acquisition of Dominion risks creating a sustained, multi-decade upward pressure on ratepayers’ bills. Captive residential and small business ratepayers will be locked into paying decades of capital carrying charges, depreciation, and an authorized Return on Equity (ROE) on this expanded rate base.

We are concerned that much of NextEra’s growth strategy is heavily dependent on data center customers. This increases vulnerabilities that exist due to overbuilding and the ramifications that could materialize for ratepayers if projected revenue from large-load customers fails to cover the full cost of the transmission buildout and necessary upgrades to the grid that increased data center presence would require. While Dominion has started work to hedge against this stranded asset risk, there is insufficient protection in the case for bankruptcy, differing time horizons for service contracts and infrastructure lifespans, as well as the burden of broader grid upgrades required by data centers (rather than just point-to-point infrastructure) where every day ratepayers foot the bill.

There have also been documented concerns about how this merger affects market competition within the broader grid that Dominion is a part of, particularly with respect to transmission and energy generation and how the new merger could create “self-preferencing” or foreclose potential competition, and how those ripple effects could then increase wholesale prices and therefore raise costs for ratepayers in Virginia.

Despite those long-term upward financial pressures, the merger sweeteners of customer bill credits and added funds for the EnergyShare program are both inadequate and only short-term. Once the sweeteners expire, the Virginia-based Dominion workforce would be at risk of significant job cuts, Virginia households and small businesses would be locked into paying those multi-decade elevated rates, with the joint petition providing for no base rate increase moratorium, no cap on escalating rate adjustment clauses (riders), and no binding mechanism to track and pass fuel or operational synergies to captive customers. Additionally, the proposed bill credit for consumers barely covers the impact that increased fuel costs are having on electric bills. Dominion already petitioned the Commission for a $10 per month increase for fuel-related costs this year.

For these reasons, the Independent Market Monitor stated, the “scale, financial strength, and operational breadth all enhance market power and any economic gains are more likely to accrue to investors rather than customers.” Thus, we must look past the near-term sweeteners and toward robust binding, structural protections that prevent long-term negative impacts on Virginia ratepayers.

We believe the primary benefits of the merger should be designed to benefit our constituents, the ratepayers, and we believe the current merger design will raise rates. To that extent, we urge the Commission to, at a bare minimum, require long-term rate protections for consumers as recommended by Commission staff and require substantially larger bill credits as recommended by the Governor’s Office before any potential merger can proceed. As energy prices have considerably increased, and this merger threatens to exacerbate market conditions that could further increase prices for ratepayers it is paramount that the Commission use its authority to protect consumers who are already struggling to afford to keep the lights on.

Corporate Governance Deficits Threaten Rate Case Prudency

A utility’s corporate culture directly governs accounting integrity, affiliate transactions, and ratemaking prudency. The Commission must ensure that any acquiring entity submits to complete regulatory transparency and that captive ratepayers do not cross-subsidize non-utility operations, political spending, or parent-company agendas.

NextEra’s operational history and recent testimony demonstrates documented resistance to transparent regulatory scrutiny. NextEra recently entered into a $150 million settlement to resolve widespread political interference and dark money schemes, which included funding “ghost candidates” against state legislators and covert surveillance of an investigative journalist. This Commission’s Hearing Examiner properly recognized the relevance of these governance practices to regulatory integrity by ordering the production of the internal “Robo memo” into the evidentiary record. We share the position that this memo should be available for review to the Commission and intervenors.

At a time when regulatory scrutiny is at an all-time high, NextEra’s top leadership has aligned itself financially with federal agendas that raise rates and undermine Virginia’s statutory obligations.NextEra’s participation in high-level, opaque federal lobbying networks heightens the risk that Virginia ratepayers could be improperly forced to subsidize national political advocacy that runs counter to their own interests. In this case, aligning with a federal agenda that rolls back renewable energy incentives, curtails offshore wind development, and props up uneconomic generation. Engaging in that advocacy, including through means designed to obscure its involvement, puts NextEra in direct conflict with Virginia’s statutory mandates under the Virginia Clean Economy Act, and introduces an acute risk of asset stranding, resource inadequacy, and costly non-compliance penalties that will inevitably fall upon Virginia consumers.

It is unacceptably risky to transfer Virginia’s premier electric utility to an acquiring entity that displays such a pattern of routine spending, through opaque affiliate channels, to influence regulatory and political outcomes. Such practices, if expanded into Virginia, would directly threaten the Commission’s ability to police affiliate transactions, enforce cross-subsidization prohibitions, and verify the prudency of test-year operating expenses. Captive ratepayers bear the cost when compliance breaks down, transactions lack transparent auditing, or management priorities subordinate the public interest to unregulated political agendas.

Conclusion

The Commission’s statutory mission is to safeguard captive consumers and ensure the long-term reliability and affordability of utility service. As proposed, we do not believe the merger is in the public interest. We believe the proposed transaction fails to satisfy the statutory requirements and because the joint petition lacks the structural protections necessary to prevent material harm, the Commission should deny the merger petition in its current form.

We appreciate the Commission’s careful scrutiny of this proceeding and submit these comments on behalf of our constituents.

Sincerely,

title: Unlocking American Investment: Why Permitting Certainty Matters
text:
Unlocking American Investment: Why Permitting Certainty Matters

HOW MORE PREDICTABLE FEDERAL APPROVALS CAN UNLOCK PRIVATE INVESTMENT IN AMERICAN INFRASTRUCTURE

Capital is ready to build. Investors need to know whether the government will let their projects finish.

THE PROBLEM WITH THE STATUS QUO

Infrastructure projects depend on substantial capital commitments long before construction is complete or revenues begin flowing. Banks and investors must evaluate not only construction costs and market conditions, but also whether projects can secure approvals on a predictable schedule. When permitting timelines are uncertain, investors may demand higher returns, increase financing costs, or direct capital toward projects with more manageable risks.

Senator Alan Armstrong experienced this firsthand in the energy industry. In a Right of Way interview, he recalled that Williams required returns three or four times higher for pipeline projects crossing New York than for comparable investments in Texas, Oklahoma, or Louisiana because of regulatory risk.

Financial institutions face similar challenges. In a JPMorganChase discussion, infrastructure finance executive Fuat Savas explained how fragmented approvals complicate financing and delay viable projects. A 2026 ACORE survey likewise identified federal policy, regulatory risk, and interconnection uncertainty among the leading barriers to clean-energy investment.

The costs can be substantial. McKinsey estimates that prolonged project timelines can increase construction costs by 24% to 30%, although not all of that escalation is attributable to permitting. Delays also postpone revenue and increase exposure to changing market conditions.

The result is a financing bottleneck: America has capital ready to invest, but regulatory uncertainty can prevent projects from moving forward.

HOW THE BIPARTISAN BILL HELPS

For banks and investors, permitting certainty directly affects whether infrastructure projects can attract financing on competitive terms. BAAJA would address three risks that shape investment decisions:

Uncertain construction schedules: Firmer federal review deadlines would help developers and lenders plan financing around more predictable project timelines.

Prolonged litigation exposure: A 150-day filing window for specified legal challenges would help limit the period of uncertainty surrounding qualifying federal approvals.

Risk of losing approvals: For covered NEPA violations, the bill would generally require courts to remand deficient reviews without vacating project approvals, reducing the risk that committed capital is stranded while agencies correct review errors.

Together, these reforms could make infrastructure projects easier to finance, reduce financing costs, and improve the economics of long-term American investment. A Bipartisan Policy Center analysis explains how reducing permitting delays and litigation risk could also benefit consumers by limiting financing costs passed through to energy and infrastructure prices.

WHO SUPPORTS IT — AND WHY

Business and infrastructure finance leaders want approvals and construction schedules they can plan around. Business Roundtable CEO Joshua Bolten endorsed BAAJA, calling for faster, more durable approvals that support investment. The Global Infrastructure Investor Association and Equipment Leasing & Finance Association joined a coalition urging passage; infrastructure investment firm HASI signed a separate November 9 letter. State Business Executives highlighted how predictable reviews and durable permits give employers greater confidence to invest.

Energy developers and investors need permitted projects to move reliably from planning to construction. ACORE President and CEO Ray Long urged passage and endorsed the November 7 substitute amendment, citing the need for investment certainty. Clearway Energy Group CEO Craig Cornelius emphasized review deadlines, permit durability, and transmission, while the Nuclear Innovation Alliance backed the bill’s approach to providing certainty for capital-intensive nuclear projects.

Capital-formation advocates have described permitting uncertainty as a barrier to deploying available private capital. The American Council for Capital Formation endorsed BAAJA, with President and CEO George David Banks observing: “The constraint on American energy and infrastructure investment is no longer a shortage of capital. It is the inability to deploy that capital against a predictable schedule.” Elemental Impact founder and Earthshot Ventures partner Dawn Lippert described permitting timelines as “part of the capital stack” and joined 47 clean-technology executives and investors in a letter urging passage.

ClearPath has explained why permitting risk can be more difficult to finance than ordinary project risk. CEO Jeremy Harrell argued that investors can price construction, technology, and market risks, but unpredictable permitting delays are harder to assess. In a separate analysis of BAAJA, he argued that clear, technology-neutral rules and durable approvals could support investment across energy technologies.

Capital doesn’t build on uncertainty. It builds on predictable timelines and the confidence that approved projects can move forward.

title: Baldwin, Colleagues Fight to Overturn Trump Admin Abortion Ban at the VA
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Senator Tammy Baldwin (D-WI) joined more than 200 Senate and House Democrats in filing an amicus brief to Minority Veterans of America v. Secretary of Veterans Affairs, a lawsuit challenging the Trump Administration’s abortion ban at the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA). The ban restricts veterans’ right to reproductive health care across the country, including in Wisconsin, even in cases of rape, incest, or when their health is endangered. Wisconsin is home to over 25,000 female veterans.

The lawsuit, pending before the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit, seeks to overturn VA’s ban on abortion care and counseling. In the brief, the lawmakers argue the Trump Administration’s 2025 policy banning abortion counseling and abortion care in almost all cases rests on a flawed legal premise.

“VA’s Final Rule rests on a faulty interpretation of federal law that has significant negative consequences for our nation’s veterans. The issues presented in this case potentially reach roughly 462,000 women veterans of reproductive age who are enrolled in VA health care, along with an estimated 112,000 women of reproductive age enrolled in the Civilian Health and Medical Program of the Department of Veterans Affairs (CHAMPVA),” wrote Baldwin and the lawmakers.

“For them, the Final Rule means a VA physician is prohibited from discussing the full range of a patient’s options during a pregnancy, prohibited from providing the full range of health care available to pregnant women, and is prohibited from intervening when a pregnancy threatens the patient’s health or is the result of rape or incest,” Baldwin and the lawmakers continued.

The lawmakers argue in the brief that VA’s erroneous interpretation of federal law means these women now cannot receive abortion care or counseling even in the most harrowing circumstances. They also argue the Veterans’ Health Care Eligibility Reform Act of 1996 allows VA to provide any medical services the Secretary “determines to be needed” and that the Veterans Health Care Act of 1992, which VA used to justify its abortion ban, does not restrict the Secretary’s authority to add abortion care to its medical benefits package.

In September 2022, VA began to offer abortion counseling to all pregnant veterans and CHAMPVA beneficiaries, and abortion care in cases of rape, incest, or life or health endangerment of the veteran or CHAMPVA beneficiary. This was in response to the Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization ruling, which created urgent risks to the lives and health of pregnant veterans and CHAMPVA beneficiaries in states that banned or otherwise severely restricted access to abortion. VA’s dangerous abortion ban means that veterans nationwide now face those same risks.

More than 462,000 veterans of reproductive age are enrolled in VA health care, and more than 112,000 women of reproductive age are enrolled in CHAMPVA. More than half of these women live in states that have enacted abortion bans or restrictions.

Senator Baldwin has long led the charge to restore abortion access nationwide, including leading the entire Senate Democratic caucus in introducing the Women’s Health Protection Act, legislation to guarantee access to abortion everywhere across the country and restore the right to comprehensive reproductive health care for millions of Americans.

In the Senate, the amicus brief was signed by all 47 Democratic U.S. Senators. In the House, the brief was signed by 165 Democratic U.S. Representatives.

Full text of the amicus brief can be found here.

title: ICYMI: Fighting for Hoosier Veterans
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Yesterday, Senator Jim Banks marked Veterans Day with an op-ed highlighting his work on the Senate Veterans’ Affairs Committee to improve healthcare, benefits, and support services for Indiana’s 400,000 veterans. Earlier this year, Senator Banks led the entire Indiana delegation urging the Senate Appropriations Committee to preserve full funding, as requested in President Trump’s fiscal year 2027 VA budget, for the construction of a new Roudebush Medical Center in Indianapolis. This week, the Appropriations Committee released its proposed fiscal year 2027 Military Construction, Veterans Affairs, and Related Agencies appropriations bill prioritizing the project and allocating the full $1.64 billion requested by the president.

Read the op-ed below:

This Veterans Day is a special one. 250 years after the founding of the greatest country in the history of the world, we remember and honor the men and women in uniform who continue to keep the spirit of 1776 alive. It was the greatest privilege of my life to wear the American flag on my uniform, and I join Hoosiers and all Americans in saying to our veterans: thank you for your service. We pay tribute to you for your sacrifices and hope that your service inspires the next generation of Americans to serve.

Fighting for Indiana’s veterans is some of the most important work I do in the Senate. Indiana is home to over 400,000 veterans. Since the Indian Wars and the Civil War, there have been 99 Hoosier Medal of Honor recipients. Hoosiers are proud of our veterans’ legacy of service, and you can see that pride in our war memorials all around our great state. You see it from the National Memorial Shrine in Fort Wayne, to the Military Honor Park and Museum in South Bend, to the Indiana Military Museum in Vincennes, to the Ernie Pyle Museum in Dana.

Veterans choose Indiana because this is a patriotic state that values service, honors sacrifice, and takes care of its own.

I am incredibly proud of what I have been able to accomplish for Hoosier veterans on the Senate Veterans’ Affairs Committee. I worked with my colleagues to move legislation through the committee that improves the benefits claims process, makes sure veterans can be buried with their spouses in national cemeteries if they choose, reforms how the VA builds health care facilities, and guarantees that service-disabled veterans can access the prosthetics they need to exercise and play sports.

I’m also working to upgrade our VA medical facilities around the state. Last year, I made the case for a new Roudebush medical center repeatedly to Secretary Doug Collins and other VA leaders, and President Trump ranked it the VA’s top construction priority in this year’s budget. Roudebush is more than 75 years old, and veterans deserve a state-of-the-art, flagship hospital. In June, I organized a letter from the whole Indiana congressional delegation to the Appropriations Committee supporting full funding for the project. I’m looking forward to securing the dollars to build it in the next few months.

A new, major VA outpatient clinic in Fishers is also moving forward. I’m pushing the Senate to authorize the project before the end of the year. It will allow veterans north of Indy to get all their outpatient care closer to where they live, without going into the city. I’m also working with the VA to plan a new clinic in Northwest Indiana, and I expect the plans for that new clinic to be announced next year. Last week, I worked with DAV to establish a vet center community access point in Kokomo. Veterans, servicemembers, and their family members can now get counseling at DAV Chapter 28 in Kokomo. I’m grateful to Commander Ross Havrick for this great idea, and we made it happen in record time. I will keep pushing for a full-scale vet center in North Central Indiana.

Getting these projects approved is just the beginning. I will be working with our veteran service organizations, the VA, and community leaders to break ground on these facilities and build them as efficiently as possible. Indiana can set the example for the rest of the country in how to develop modern medical facilities for veterans faster, more affordably, and more innovatively.

Our veterans risked life and limb for this country, and I will not stop fighting to make sure that they have all the resources they need to thrive.

title: Barrasso Details Aggressive Year-End Agenda for Senate Republicans
text:
“In 52 days, the 119th Congress ends. Senate Republicans will make every second count.”

WASHINGTON, D.C. – Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso (R-Wyo.) today outlined the Senate Republican agenda for the next 52 days, including confirming judges to lifetime appointments, confirming President Donald J. Trump’s qualified nominees, passing permitting reform, and funding the government.

Click HERE to watch Senator Barrasso’s remarks.

Sen. Barrasso’s remarks:

“In 52 days, the 119th Congress ends. Senate Republicans will make every second count. The American people sent a clear message last Tuesday. Republicans heard them. We know we have work to do to regain their trust. We will do this by delivering results. That work has already begun. Republicans are still in the majority. President Trump is still in the White House.

“In the next 52 days, we have important work to complete. We will waste no time. We will confirm dozens of conservative federal judges to the courts. We will confirm many qualified nominees to positions across the federal government. We will pass historic permitting reform. We will fund the government. Some of this work will be bipartisan. Some of it will require long hours. Senate Republicans are ready for both.

“We welcome bipartisanship when it serves the national interest. Bipartisanship can never come at the expense of conservative values. We will never apologize for our conservative convictions.

“Let me begin with judges. In the coming days, we will have two dozen federal judges to confirm. Federal judges serve for life. Their decisions will shape our laws for generations. These will be judges who will uphold the Constitution and apply the law as written.

“Under Chairman Grassley, the Senate Judiciary Committee has advanced judges at the fastest pace since Ronald Reagan. Now, we must finish the work. If that means long days, we are here to work. If that means late nights, we are here to work. We will leave no vacancy behind.

“The same commitment applies to nominees across the federal government. Our committees are working to approve nominees under their jurisdiction. We will complete a final nominations package before the end of the year. President Trump deserves to have his team in place. Senate Republicans will deliver.

“Next, Republicans will continue to work to lower costs. American families are feeling the pain of high prices. They need relief. Fixing our country’s broken permitting system is one of the best ways to provide relief.

“America is ready to build. We have the ability to build. We need to get Washington, D.C., out of the way. Many energy projects that would help lower prices remain frozen for years waiting for approval from the federal government. Even after being approved, lengthy lawsuits can drive up costs and create uncertainty.

“Senator Capito of West Virginia and Senator Lee of Utah have worked with their Democrat counterparts to write a bipartisan bill that makes it easier to build. Their legislation streamlines environmental reviews. It also reins in out-of-control judicial review and abusive lawsuits.

“These reforms are common sense. Building better, faster, cheaper, and smarter is the right path to lower energy costs for families. It is the responsible path both

to respond to our nation’s energy needs and to respect the environment. That is why, this week, 73 Senators voted in favor of cutting through the government red tape that slows down our progress. Republicans support it. Democrats support it. President Trump will sign it. Congress needs to pass it.

“What I hear is that Democrats in the House and Democrats who will be coming to the House in January are not so sure. Let me remind the Democrats – specifically the current Minority Leader in the Democrat House – of what even The New York Times had to say in an Editorial, November 12, posted today on their website. It said, ‘The Senate this week is debating a bill on the subject that is more important than it sounds.’ Even The New York Times admits what we’re doing here is more important than it sounds – it is permitting reform. They go on to say, ‘This bill would make it easier to build solar energy farms, battery storage, power lines, and more.’ As a result, they say, ‘It will reduce energy prices.’ That’s what Republicans and Democrats on this Floor have been saying for the last several weeks. ‘The status quo is expensive, dirty, and unstable. The country needs to build a lot of big new things to make its future cheaper and cleaner.’

“There is a lot to this Editorial that the House of Representatives and the incoming Democrats ought to pay attention to. Which is why it’s important for Democrats, not just in this body but across the hall in the House, to get in line and get this done and get those prices down. It’s critical, and I’m happy to see such bipartisan work being done right here in the United States Senate.

“With regard to government funding, Republicans will keep the government open. Government funding runs out in less than a month. It is the responsibility of Congress to fund the government. Republicans want to keep the government open, pay our troops, and protect essential services.

“Some Democrats are threatening to once again shut down the government. They intend to do this right before Christmas. The last thing this country needs is another painful, chaotic Democrat government shutdown. For families who live paycheck to paycheck – including military families – a Democrat shutdown means more strain, more stress, and more suffering.

“I’ve heard Senator Schumer come to this Floor and talk endlessly about chaos. Nothing would be more chaotic than a decision by Senator Schumer and Democrats to once again shut down the government.

“The American people sent a clear message last Tuesday. Republicans are listening. We are committed to regaining their trust. We will do this by delivering results. The Senate has important work to do in the next 52 days. Republicans will stand strong, united, and energized on behalf of the American people.”

title: Bennet, Costa, Colleagues Press Administration to Expedite Delivery of Ukraine Aid
text:
Washington, D.C. — Colorado U.S. Senator Michael Bennet, a member of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, joined U.S. Congressman Jim Costa (D-Calif.) and a bipartisan, bicameral group of colleagues on a letter demanding that Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought explain the Trump administration’s delay in executing the $400 million Congress appropriated for Ukraine security assistance in Fiscal Year 2026 (FY26). The letter also urged the immediate acceleration of that delivery.

“Ukraine’s armed forces need and deserve continued American support, and Congress has provided the resources to deliver it,” the lawmakers wrote. “We remain committed to supporting Ukraine’s defense and will continue to hold the Administration accountable for delivering these funds as Congress intended.”

Congress appropriated $400 million for the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative (USAI) in the FY26 government funding bill, supported by bipartisan majorities. The Trump administration waited until the final days of FY26 to obligate the funds and have a slow delivery schedule that runs through FY29, according to the Pentagon’s own spend plan.

In the letter, the lawmakers warned that slow delivery of support will undermine Ukraine’s self-defense heading into winter, as well as the credibility of American commitments and our collective ability to deter Russian aggression. The lawmakers urged the administration to:

Provide a written explanation of why the funds were not obligated until the final days of the fiscal year, including any conditions or holds the Office of Management and Budget placed on their apportionment;

Share a detailed delivery schedule, with the reasons delivery is projected to extend into FY29 and the steps the administration will take to accelerate it;

Explain why PATRIOT interceptors were reportedly excluded from the package and whether future USAI funding can address Ukraine’s air defense needs; and

Ensure OMB apportions and executes any FY27 USAI funding Congress provides promptly and without similar delay.

Bennet has long supported the Ukrainian people’s fight against Putin aggression. Bennet leads legislation in the Senate intelligence and defense bills, both of which have passed their respective committees, to bolster intelligence and drone cooperation with Ukraine. Upon recent news of the Starshield and Starlink disruptions to Ukraine, Bennet demanded SpaceX restore full service and called for answers from SpaceX CEO Elon Musk.

Earlier this year, Bennet joined bipartisan colleagues to introduce and pass the Sanctioning Russia Act. He also sponsors legislation to impose sanctions on entities trading in Russian oil, to punish Russia’s systematic persecution of religious communities in Ukraine, and to repurpose frozen Russian sovereign assets held in the United States to support Ukraine, building on legislation he co-sponsored that former President Joe Biden signed into law in April 2024. Earlier this year, Bennet led a letter to Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent urging the Trump administration to crack down on a Russian state-backed cryptocurrency sanctions evasion network funding Putin’s war.

In addition to Bennet and Costa, Senators Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), Dick Durbin (D-Ill.), Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), Adam Schiff (D-Calif.), Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.), Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.), Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa), Joni Ernst (R-Iowa), and John Cornyn (R-Texas); and by Representatives Eugene Vindman (D-Va.), Salud Carbajal (D-Calif.), Mike Quigley (D-Ill.), Don Bacon (R-Neb.), Wesley Bell (D-Mo.), Marcy Kaptur (D-Ohio), Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.), Rick Larsen (D-Wash.), Jimmy Panetta (D-Calif.), Sylvia Garcia (D-Texas), Val Hoyle (D-Ore.), Bradley Schneider (D-Ill.), Ed Case (D-Hawaii), Johnny Olszewski, Jr (D-Md.), Ted Lieu (D-Calif.), Raja Krishnamoorthi (D-Ill.), Chrissy Houlahan (D-Pa.), Julia Brownley (D-Calif.), Madeleine Dean (D-Pa.), William Keating (D-Mass.), and Mary Scanlon (D-Pa.) signed the letter.

The text of the letter is available HERE and below.

Dear Secretary Hegseth and Director Vought:

As Ukraine prepares for its fifth winter campaign since Russia’s full-scale invasion, timely American security assistance is critical to the survival and livelihood of the resilient Ukrainian people. We write regarding the $400 million Congress provided for Ukraine security assistance in Fiscal Year (FY) 2026. The Administration’s delay in executing these funds requires an explanation, and we urge that their delivery to Ukraine be accelerated.

The FY2026 National Defense Authorization Act, which the President signed on December 18, 2025, authorized $400 million for the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative. The Department of Defense Appropriations Act, 2026, with its accompanying explanatory statement, provided that $400 million in full and was allocated for Ukraine. These funds have strong bipartisan support, a clear intent, and an established deadline for obligation.

The Department of Defense has now obligated these funds, but only after months of unnecessary delay and without an acceptable delivery timeline. Despite Secretary Hegseth’s public claims in April that the funds had been released, and despite repeated congressional correspondence, the Department waited until the final weeks of the fiscal year to obligate most of these funds. Worse, the Department’s spend plan does not project final delivery of assistance until FY2029, following the end this Administration’s term in office. The package also reportedly does not include Patriot interceptors, the only system in Ukraine’s arsenal that can reliably defend against Russian ballistic missiles. That need will only grow as Russia intensifies its strikes on Ukraine’s cities and energy infrastructure this winter.

Accordingly, we request a written explanation, no later than November 30, 2026, of why these funds were not obligated until the final days of the fiscal year. The explanation should identify any conditions or holds the Office of Management and Budget placed on their apportionment. We also request a detailed delivery schedule for the assistance, with the reasons delivery is projected to extend into FY2029 and the steps the Administration will take to accelerate it. We also request an explanation as to why Patriot interceptors were excluded and whether future USAI funding can address Ukraine’s air defense needs. Finally, OMB must ensure that any FY2027 Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative funding Congress provides is apportioned promptly and executed without similar delay.

Ukraine’s armed forces need and deserve continued American support, and Congress has provided the resources to deliver it. Accordingly, we urge you to ensure the $400 million in FY2026 security assistance reaches Ukraine without further delay. Such a gap, particularly as Ukraine enters another winter of Russian attacks on Ukrainian civilians and infrastructure, undermines the credibility of American commitments and our ability to adequately deter Russian aggression. We remain committed to supporting Ukraine’s defense and will continue to hold the Administration accountable for delivering these funds as Congress intended. We expect your prompt response to this urgent matter.

###

title: Bennet, Sanders, Van Hollen, Duckworth Release Joint Statement Opposing Spending Package that Funds Trump’s War on Iran
text:
Washington, D.C. — Colorado U.S. Senator Michael Bennet and Senators Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), and Tammy Duckworth (D-IlI.) released a joint statement underscoring their opposition to year-end funding that does not restrict President Trump’s ability to continue his war on Iran:

“The American people have been clear: We must end President Trump’s illegal and disastrous war with Iran. This conflict has driven up the cost of gas, groceries, and fertilizer. More than 20 American service members have been killed and hundreds more wounded, while achieving none of President Trump’s stated goals and harming civilians across the region. As we approach the December 11 funding deadline, we should not accept a short-term spending deal that continues to provide billions of additional dollars for President Trump’s war of choice. Any short-term package must include language that restricts the Trump Administration from using appropriated funds to continue his war against Iran.

“We know from Vietnam, Afghanistan, and Iraq that these wars can take decades to end – hurting our economy, draining our military resources, and making Americans less safe. Meanwhile, Americans all across the country will continue bearing the cost, with higher grocery bills, higher gas prices, and a higher toll on our troops. The American people do not want more war in the Middle East – but that is what President Trump has given them. Congress cannot allow Trump to continue his conflict – we must force him to end it. “When we vote on appropriations, we intend to fund the government and stop funds for this war. It is what the American people demand, and what they deserve.”

This statement follows Bennet’s letter urging Senate colleagues to block any funding package that includes additional appropriations for Trump’s war.
