title: NEWS: Casar, Mayor Watson, Judge Brown, Austin Electeds Urge Austin Parking Lot Owners to Prohibit ICE Stagings
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, Congressman Greg Casar (D-TX), along with Austin Mayor Kirk Watson, Travis County Judge Andy Brown, Congressman Lloyd Doggett (D-TX), and local Austin elected officials sent a letter urging owners and operators of parking lots in Austin to prohibit ICE from using their properties as staging areas for enforcement operations.

Last month, Congressman Casar’s office was notified that ICE used Austin parking lots as staging areas for the transportation of immigrants to deportation centers in at least two instances. At the time, Congressman Casar issued a statement in response to the stagings, stating: “ICE is making Austin less safe. Kids are scared to go to school, parents are scared to go to work, and crime victims are even scared to talk to police. I am urging owners and operators of parking lots in Austin to not rent or lend your property to ICE for these operations.”

The elected officials write: “We have seen in cities like New York how using lots for staging can directly lead to horrific violence.”

In the letter, the elected officials ask property owners to commit to prohibiting ICE from using their lots as a staging ground for operations and make the prohibition clear to ICE.

The letter is led by Congressman Casar, and is signed by Congressman Lloyd Doggett (TX-37), Austin Mayor Kirk Watson, Travis County Judge Andy Brown, Austin City Council Members Vanessa Fuentes (District 2), José Velásquez (District 3), José “Chito” Vela (District 4), Ryan Alter (District 5), Krista Lane (District 6), Mike Siegel (District 7), Paige Ellis (District 8) & Zohaib “Zo” Qadri (District 9), Travis County Commissioners Brigid Shea (Precinct 2), Ann Howard (Precinct 3), & George Morales (Precinct 4), and Texas State Representative Lulu Flores.

Read the full letter here.

###

Congressman Greg Casar represents Texas’s 35th Congressional District in the U.S. House of Representatives, which runs down I-35 from East Austin to Hays County to the West Side of San Antonio. A labor organizer and son of Mexican immigrants, Casar serves as the Chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus for the 119th Congress. He also serves on the Committee on Education and Labor and the Committee on Oversight and Accountability.

title: Castor, Obernolte, Matsui Introduce Bipartisan Bill to Lower Electric Bills and Strengthen Grid Reliability
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, U.S. Rep. Kathy Castor (FL-14), Jay Obernolte (CA-23) and Doris Matsui (CA-07) introduced the Optimizing Networks for Distributed Energy Management and New Demand (ON-DEMAND) Act to help lower electric bills and meet growing energy demand. The legislation supports wider adoption of virtual power plants by directing the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) to adopt standards, strengthen consumer protections and provide technical assistance to utilities, regulators and grid operators.

“My neighbors need relief from sky-high electric bills, and we should be putting every practical solution to work to lower their costs,” said Rep. Castor. “Our ON-DEMAND Act would help communities use rooftop solar, batteries, and smart appliances more safely and effectively, with strong protections for consumers. As demand for electricity grows, we must make our grid more reliable and ensure the benefits of innovation reach the people paying the bills.”

“As electricity demand continues to grow, innovative solutions like virtual power plants can help strengthen our electric grid and lower energy costs for American families,” said Congressman Obernolte. “The ON-DEMAND Act will help remove barriers to the adoption of this technology, allowing consumers to make better use of existing energy resources while improving grid reliability and reducing costs.”

“Families in Sacramento and across the country are paying too much for electricity, and we need to do more to bring those costs down,” said Congresswoman Matsui. “The ON-DEMAND Act will help lower utility bills by making smarter use of the energy resources we already have, including home batteries and smart appliances, to meet growing electricity demand without driving up costs. This is a practical solution that puts money back in Americans’ pockets while building a cleaner, more reliable energy grid.”

Virtual power plants coordinate devices across homes and businesses, such as batteries, smart thermostats, water heaters and rooftop solar systems, to help balance electricity supply and demand. For example, water heating could be shifted to a less busy time or battery power can be deployed during peak demand.

View the full bill text HERE and section-by-section HERE.

“Amid an unprecedented rise in energy demand, some of the most promising solutions are the distributed resources already in our homes and communities — rooftop solar, smart thermostats, and EV chargers — and the Virtual Power Plants (VPPs) that help them work together. From lowering bills for families to keeping the lights on, VPPs support a more flexible, affordable, and resilient electric grid. Advanced Energy United is proud to support the ON-DEMAND Act. We applaud the work of Representatives Castor, Matsui, and Obernolte to bring this bill to fruition and believe it will help unlock the benefits of VPPs for all Americans." – Dylan Reed, Managing Director at Advanced Energy United.

“Energy security and economic growth depend on a resilient and efficient electric power system. Virtual power plants provide a proven, scalable way to deliver reliable, affordable power amid growing grid constraints,” said NEMA Senior Vice President of Government Affairs, Will Hupman. “By directing the Department of Energy to pursue open, stakeholder-driven processes for VPP standards development and other objectives, the ON-DEMAND Act promises to eliminate hurdles to VPP deployment and scaling, ushering in a new era of grid flexibility.”

“The ON-DEMAND Act represents an important step toward modernizing America's electric grid and ensuring we can meet growing electricity demand affordably and reliably,” said John Pappas, Government Affairs Director for Siemens USA. “By addressing barriers to the deployment of virtual power plants, this legislation will help utilities unlock the full potential of distributed energy resources, improve grid flexibility, and make more efficient use of existing infrastructure. Establishing consistent standards and expanding technical assistance will help accelerate the adoption of innovative grid technologies and build a smarter, more resilient, and more affordable energy system.”

"Leveraging customer-focused energy independent solutions like distributed power plants is essential to creating a more cost-effective, resilient and clean grid for all, particularly amidst the surging demand for electricity. The ON-DEMAND Act will help accelerate the customer-led revolution that's tackling these challenges head-on." – Mary Powell, CEO, Sunrun

"Schneider Electric applauds the introduction of the ON-DEMAND Act and its support for the flexible energy resources needed to build a more resilient, reliable, and affordable grid. As electricity demand grows, flexibility will be essential to balancing supply and demand, improving grid performance, and empowering consumers. Virtual power plants are one important way to unlock that flexibility at scale, and we welcome policies that help accelerate their adoption." – Ruben Llanes, CEO, Digital Grid, Schneider Electric

Endorsing organizations include Advanced Energy United, Deploy Action, Electricity Consumers Resource Council, Environmental Defense Fund, GoodLeap, GridWise Alliance, Information Technology Industry Council, National Association of State Energy Officials, National Electrical Manufacturers Association, Rewiring America, Schneider Electric, Siemens USA, Sierra Club, Sunrun, and Utilize Coalition.

title: Wed., Nov. 18: Rep. Chris Smith to chair hearing on Christian persecution“Worldwide Persecution of Christians: Responding to New Challenges”
text:
On Wednesday, November 18th, Rep. Chris Smith (R-NJ), Co-Chair of the Tom Lantos Human Rights Commission (TLHRC), will chair a congressional hearing entitled “Worldwide Persecution of Christians: Responding to New Challenges.”

In many countries, governments impose restrictions on religious practice, discriminate against Christians and other religious minorities, and subject religious leaders and believers to surveillance, imprisonment, and other forms of repression. In other places, Christians face violence and intimidation from non-state actors, including extremist movements, militias, and criminal organizations. Armed conflict, political instability, religious nationalism, and weak rule of law can further expose Christian communities to attack and displacement.

Witnesses will examine where persecution is increasing, which state and non-state actors are responsible, and what political, ideological, and social factors are driving these developments; assess how churches, civil society organizations, and foreign governments are responding, including efforts to assist victims, protect vulnerable communities, and promote accountability; and consider how the U.S. government can be more effective in defending the universal right of Christians and other religious communities to practice their faith freely and safely.

WHAT: Congressional hearing examining the persecution of Christians around the world, particularly emerging threats and efforts by governments and civil society to protect vulnerable Christian communities.

title: Rep. Crane Supports Flood Recovery Efforts and Advances Priorities for Rural Arizona
text:
As the 119th Congress draws to a close, Rep. Eli Crane (R-AZ) remains focused on serving the people of Arizona’s Second Congressional District. Over the past few months, he has introduced and supported legislation to advance the priorities of rural communities.

In the aftermath of the recent floods, Rep. Crane and his staff have been on the ground throughout the region. From Prescott to Kayenta, they have connected with law enforcement, first responders, and community leaders to survey damage and assess immediate needs. This morning, he visited Camp Verde, one of the hardest-hit areas in the state, to meet with key personnel.

Earlier this week, Rep. Crane also sat down with Flagstaff Mayor Becky Daggett and City Manager Joanne Keene. Their discussion covered storm recovery, plans for Big Fill Lake, and ongoing work to prioritize the Rio de Flag project with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (Corps). The long-planned initiative would reduce flood risk in downtown Flagstaff and around Northern Arizona University.

Much of the disaster assistance provided by the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) requires a major disaster declaration under the Stafford Act. Securing one begins with damage assessments conducted by local, state, and Tribal officials alongside FEMA. If the losses exceed what the state or Tribe can handle, its Governor or Tribal Chief Executive may request a declaration. The President then decides whether to grant it.

Although Members of Congress cannot initiate the process, Rep. Crane is using the tools at his disposal to support those affected. He is in active communication with FEMA Administrator Cameron Hamilton, and his team remains in close contact with the office of Governor Katie Hobbs, Tribal leadership, and local partners. Assessments are still in their early stages. Should a request move forward, he will press for its swift approval.

Constituents in need of help can find official updates and safety guidance on the Arizona Emergency Information Network’s November 2026 Storms page. County-specific resources are listed in Rep. Crane’s previous release. For questions about next steps, residents can reach the Prescott District Office at (928) 286-5338 or the D.C. Office at (202) 225-3361.

Click on the images below to see more:

Given how much of the West is federally owned, many rural counties have a harder time meeting FEMA’s criteria for a major disaster declaration. In October, Rep. Crane introduced the Rural Disaster Fairness Act of 2026 to address this issue. His bill would make it easier for counties with limited taxable land to secure federal aid.

Because federal property is exempt from local taxes, these counties often have smaller budgets for maintaining infrastructure, responding to emergencies, and rebuilding. FEMA’s county per capita indicator does not reflect this reality. The benchmark compares estimated public assistance damages to population, but it ignores how much revenue a jurisdiction can raise. A county can therefore face serious financial strain and still fail to qualify.

Under Rep. Crane’s bill, FEMA would cut the indicator’s threshold in half for any county that can levy property taxes on less than 15 percent of its land. This change would apply nationwide and more accurately capture the true toll a disaster takes on these counties. In turn, they would have a fairer shot at relief.

Click on the image below to see more:

While that reform centers on recovery, Rep. Crane is working just as hard to strengthen flood protection before the next storm hits. He supported the Water Resources Development Act (WRDA) of 2026, which cleared the House in September by an overwhelmingly bipartisan 415-9 vote. The legislation would authorize Corps projects across the country, from ports and harbors to inland waterways.

Arizona secured several wins in this year’s version. Rep. Crane backed a new flood-control authorization for Dudleyville in Pinal County. He also helped make three more sites eligible for Corps funding, including McCormick Wash in Globe. Together, they would better protect homes, businesses, and emergency access from high water.

Local water and wastewater systems stand to benefit too, with $54 million in environmental infrastructure authorizations for Cottonwood, Gila County, the Gila River Indian Community, and the City of Maricopa. WRDA would raise the investment cap for existing programs in Flagstaff and Winslow. Beyond these provisions, Rep. Crane pushed for language directing the Corps to move faster on four Arizona projects already on the books.

Click on the image below to see more:

Reliable electricity is another pressing need in rural Arizona, where the federal government has operated a utility for decades. Congress created the San Carlos Irrigation Project (SCIP) in 1924 to irrigate land on the Gila River Indian Reservation and nearby areas. The project later added a hydroelectric plant at Coolidge Dam, and the Bureau of Indian Affairs extended service across roughly 2,400 square miles.

Today, about 10,000 residential customers depend on SCIP, and many have endured frequent outages and rising bills. With generation at the dam halted since a 1983 flood, the system now relies on short-term deals and the day-ahead market for power. Bureaucratic procedures make long-term contracts difficult to obtain. Some facilities are also more than 80 years old, and SCIP cannot issue bonds to upgrade them. Ratepayers ultimately bear these costs.

After hearing from constituents whose livelihoods have suffered, Rep. Crane asked the Department of the Interior’s Office of Inspector General to investigate SCIP in September 2025. The inquiry had yet to produce meaningful findings, so he partnered with affected families, Tribal leaders, and utility providers to draft the San Carlos Irrigation Project Divestiture Act of 2026.

Introduced last month, the bill would transfer SCIP’s transmission and distribution lines, excluding Coolidge Dam and its generating facilities, to operators better positioned to invest in them. A plan developed with federal, state, Tribal, local, and private stakeholders would guide the handoff. The legislation would also waive a provision from a 1991 law that has kept the system in government hands since an earlier divestiture deadline passed in 1992.

Click on the image below to see more:

Throughout his tenure, Rep. Crane has worked to close gaps in the care available to Native veterans, who experience some of the highest homelessness rates in the nation. The Tribal HUD-Veterans Affairs Supportive Housing (HUD-VASH) demonstration program aims to reduce these numbers. It provides rental assistance and case management to veterans who are homeless or at risk.

Although the program has helped many find stable housing, it lacks a clear way for Tribes to return vouchers they cannot use or secure additional ones. Resources can sit unused in one community while veterans in another go without. To correct this, Rep. Crane teamed up with Rep. Sharice Davids (D-KS) on the bipartisan Tribal Veterans Voucher Flexibility Act.

The bill would require the Department of Housing and Urban Development to create a voluntary process for reallocating surplus vouchers. Tribes could give back any they do not expect to need, while others facing a shortage could request more. Releasing vouchers would not count against a Tribe in future allocations. Rep. Crane believes this approach makes the most of existing support and avoids growing the size of government.

Click on the image below to see more:

Alongside his legislative work, Rep. Crane’s office helps cut through federal red tape. Since January 2023, his team has resolved 4,017 cases and recovered more than $12 million for constituents. These funds are not new spending. Rather, they reflect delayed or stalled payments Arizonans were already owed, such as tax refunds, retirement and disability benefits, and veterans’ compensation.

Rep. Crane can contact agencies, including the IRS, Social Security Administration, and Department of Veterans Affairs, on behalf of those he serves. His caseworkers check on claims, catch paperwork errors, and follow up until there is an answer. They cannot override an agency’s decision, but they push for a fair and timely review.

Because the district covers a large portion of Arizona, staff have held 232 mobile office hours to bring these services closer to home. Anyone seeking assistance can start a case online or call the Prescott District Office at (928) 286-5338. Privacy law generally requires written consent before records can be shared, so a signed release form is needed.

title: Dingell, Smith Introduce Bipartisan Bill to Modernize Medicare and Expand Patient Choice
text:
U.S. Representatives Debbie Dingell (D-MI-06) and Adrian Smith (R-NE-03) introduced the Bringing Rehabilitation, Integrated Delivery, and Greater Extended (BRIDGE) Care at Home Act. The bipartisan bill would provide Medicare beneficiaries with greater flexibility to access skilled nursing services in the comfort of their own homes following a qualifying hospital stay.

“Across the country there is a shortage of beds in skilled nursing facilities for patients needing post-hospital short term care, resulting in extended stays in the hospital, causing delays in available beds and unnecessarily long hospital visits. This shortage of care impacts both the wishes and care of Medicare patients, and the care of all other patients across hospitals. Most patients prefer to receive care at home, so we must do more to support access to skilled nursing care in the home for patients who prefer that option. And most importantly, it is the less expensive option for both families and the government. I am proud to support this bipartisan bill which would address those shortages and put patients first,” said Congresswoman Dingell.

“When it comes to healthcare, one size does not fit all, and patients deserve to have choices. Too often, options are unnecessarily restricted—especially for Medicare beneficiaries. I introduced my bipartisan BRIDGE Care at Home Act to modernize Medicare and give beneficiaries more control over their care options,” said Congressman Smith.

“Hospital at home demonstrated that seniors can be treated at home safely and effectively. The BRIDGE Care at Home Act would test the idea of skilled nursing and intensive rehabilitation services at home, helping patients maintain their independence, supporting caregivers and giving providers an alternative to working in an institutional setting,” said Moving Health Home Founder Krista Drobac.

Currently, Medicare covers qualifying skilled nursing care in a facility but does not offer a comparable payment model for delivering that care at home. At the same time, limited capacities at skilled nursing facilities (SNF) forces thousands of patients to remain in hospitals longer than medically necessary, delaying discharges and creating backups for other patients awaiting admission. The BRIDGE Care at Home Act would create a five-year Medicare SNF-at-Home pilot program, allowing beneficiaries to receive skilled nursing services at home instead of at a SNF. Polling shows 85 percent of people who have had experience with care in the home would recommend it to family and friends. The program would empower providers to develop new models of care, expand options for patients, and reduce pressure on hospitals and SNFs.

The bipartisan bill also directs the Department of Health and Human Services Secretary to compare the quality, outcomes, costs, and patient characteristics of beneficiaries who receive skilled nursing care at home with those who receive it in a facility over the course of the program’s five-year period.

title: Dingell Leads Over 170 Colleagues in Bipartisan Push Urging Senate to Pass Legislation Supporting Domestic Violence Survivors
text:
U.S. Representative Debbie Dingell (D-MI-06) and colleagues sent a letter to U.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, Judiciary Committee Chair Chuck Grassley, and Ranking Member Dick Durbin urging the immediate passage of the Crime Victims Fund (CVF) Stabilization Act.

In January 2026, the House of Representatives unanimously passed the bipartisan CVF Stabilization Act, which redirects unobligated funds collected through the False Claims Act to the CVF through Fiscal Year 2029 to stabilize the fund.

“As the co-chairs of the Bipartisan Working Group to End Domestic Violence, House co-leads of the CVF Stabilization Act, and members of Congress who voted to pass this bill in the House of Representatives, we urge you to prioritize the passage of the CVF Stabilization Act before the conclusion of the 119th Congress,” the lawmakers said. “Enactment of this bill would help stabilize this critical source of non-taxpayer funding for victim services, giving service providers the support they need to keep their doors open and support the needs of both survivors and their families.”

The CVF is the largest source of federal, non-taxpayer grant funding for victim service organizations. These organizations rely on this funding to provide essential, lifesaving services, including counseling, emergency shelters, and victims’ advocates.

The lawmakers continued, “Without federal funds, victim service providers would be significantly limited in their ability, and in many cases unable, to carry out programs that support survivors, their families, and communities to both prevent and respond to violence. Any funding interruption may also embolden perpetrators of domestic and sexual violence, as the legal system will be unable to respond to crises – making our communities less safe.”

The CVF has seen a drastic decline in recent years. According to DOJ, the CVF balance dropped by 82.94% from $13.08 billion in FY2017 to $2.23 billion by the end of FY2024. As a result of this shortfall, Congress dropped the statutory obligation cap from $1.9 billion in FY2023 to $1.35 billion in FY2024. This $550 million cut in obligations resulted in each state seeing a 40% decrease in funding for victim assistance programs.

Dear Majority Leader Thune, Minority Leader Schumer, Chairman Grassley, Ranking Member Durbin:

This letter is regarding the urgent need for the Senate to pass H.R. 909, the Crime Victims Fund (CVF) Stabilization Act. In January 2026, the House of Representatives unanimously passed the bipartisan CVF Stabilization Act, which redirects unobligated funds collected through the False Claims Act to the CVF through Fiscal Year 2029 to stabilize the fund. This bill passed with 327 bipartisan cosponsors and now awaits passage in the Senate. As you know, the CVF – created in the 1984 Victims of Crime Act (VOCA) – is the largest source of federal, non-taxpayer, grant funding for victim service organizations. These organizations rely on this funding to provide essential, life-saving services including counseling, emergency shelters, and victims’ advocates. The current financial challenges facing victim service organizations demand immediate action from the United States Senate.

VOCA grants from the CVF are funded by monetary penalties associated with federal criminal convictions and deferred- and non-prosecution agreements. These penalties are deposited into the CVF, and appropriators decide how much to release from the CVF every year. These deposits fluctuate based on the cases the DOJ successfully prosecutes and settles. After years of historically low deposits, the CVF has been depleted. According to the National Association of VOCA Assistance Administrators, after accounting for settlement funds being held in reserve and funds remaining for Fiscal Year (FY) 2026 obligations, there is only $140 million in the fund for FY2027.

Without federal funds, victim service providers would be significantly limited in their ability, and in many cases unable, to carry out programs that support survivors, their families, and communities to both prevent and respond to violence. Any funding interruption may also embolden perpetrators of domestic and sexual violence, as the legal system will be unable to respond to crises – making our communities less safe. These vital, often life-saving programs need adequate staffing and capacity to serve those who depend on them to heal and move forward. Domestic and sexual violence can happen to anyone, anywhere, at any time and it is critical we have programs in place to serve survivors in the short- and long-term.

As the co-chairs of the Bipartisan Working Group to End Domestic Violence, House co-leads of the CVF Stabilization Act, and members of Congress who voted to pass this bill in the House of Representatives, we urge you to prioritize the passage of the CVF Stabilization Act before the conclusion of the 119th Congress. Enactment of this bill would help stabilize this critical source of non-taxpayer funding for victim services, giving service providers the support they need to keep their doors open and support the needs of both survivors and their families.

title: Dingell, Tlaib Introduce Bill to Secure Temporary Protected Status for Lebanon
text:
U.S. Representatives Debbie Dingell (D-MI-06) and Rashida Tlaib (D-MI-12) introduced the Lebanon TPS Act, a bill to secure and extend temporary protected status (TPS) for Lebanon, which is currently set to expire later this month. Those who qualify for TPS are allowed to remain in the U.S. temporarily while conditions in their country of origin remain too dangerous for a safe return.

“Michigan is home to tens of thousands of Lebanese Americans who have lived here for generations. Today, they live in fear for their families as conditions in Lebanon are too dangerous for them to return. We have a responsibility to provide refuge to those seeking shelter from catastrophe and conflict, and I have long fought for temporary protected status to provide safety and security to those who need it most,” said Congresswoman Dingell. “We must extend temporary protected status until we can ensure that families can safely return home.”

Conditions in Lebanon have drastically deteriorated since the country was first designated for TPS in November 2024. Over the past 25 months, 9,000 Lebanese have been killed and over 30,000 have been injured. Over 1.2 million people, 20% of the entire Lebanese population, have been displaced from their homes. Those displaced have faced acute shortages of shelter, food, water, healthcare, and education.

“We must stand up for our Lebanese neighbors,” said Congresswoman Tlaib. “The Israeli government continues to illegally occupy and ethnically cleanse entire towns in Lebanon, bulldozing homes that have housed our constituents’ families for generations. Israeli airstrikes continue to kill Lebanese civilians, armed and funded with our tax dollars. To tear Lebanese TPS holders from our communities and send them back to suffer from these war crimes is unacceptable. Our neighbors deserve safety and stability. They belong here, and I will always fight for them.”

Hundreds of thousands of people remain displaced and entire towns and villages have been demolished. The United States must extend TPS for Lebanon and continue providing refuge to our neighbors escaping this crisis. Representative Dingell and Tlaib's bill would designate TPS for Lebanon until April 2029.

title: Congresswoman Maxine Dexter, M.D. and 17 Other U.S. Lawmakers Arrive at COP 31 to Signal America’s Return to Sensible Climate Policy
text:
ANTALYA, TÜRKİYE — Congresswoman Maxine Dexter, M.D. (OR-03) and a delegation of 17 other Members of the U.S. House of Representatives led by the Sustainable Energy and Environment Coalition Institute (SEEC Institute) has arrived in Antalya for the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31).

“American voters just went to the polls to demand a Congress that helps families get ahead and takes climate change seriously,” said Max Frankel, Executive Director of SEEC Institute. “That’s a mandate, and our Thriving Economy Project offers a blueprint for meeting it. We’re bringing 18 Members of Congress to COP31 ready to get to work, because the challenges we face don’t stop at our borders.”

From November 14–16, the delegation will meet with international policymakers, civil society organizations, advocates and activists, community and business leaders, and experts to strengthen partnerships and explore opportunities for renewed U.S. engagement on climate, energy, and economic policy.

SEEC Institute arrives with a policy blueprint for action at home already in place. Released in September with chapters authored by 9 Members of Congress alongside policy experts, the Thriving Economy Project outlines more than 800 policy recommendations grounded in the belief that a healthy economy and environment go hand in hand. At COP31, Members of Congress will build on that work.

The delegation's programming is organized around eight issue areas:

Food Security, Agricultural Innovation, and Trade

Clean Electrification, Climate Finance, and Private-Sector Competitiveness

Oceans, Science, and Coastal Resilience

Adaptation, Disaster Resilience, and Community Preparedness

Forests, Nature, and Natural-Capital Resilience

Transatlantic Industrial, Trade, and Energy Policy

Climate Equity, Mobility, and Community Leadership

Climate, Energy, and National Security

title: Finstad Applauds House Passage of the SBIC Reporting Modernization Act of 2026
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Congressman Brad Finstad (MN-01) applauded the passage of the SBIC Reporting Modernization Act of 2026 in the U.S. House of Representatives. Introduced by Congressman Finstad and Congresswoman Kelly Morrison (MN-03) earlier this year, this bipartisan legislation requires the Small Business Administration (SBA) to publish quarterly, rather than annually, reports regarding the performance of the Small Business Investment Company (SBIC) program, ultimately enhancing reporting metrics and improving Congressional oversight.

Congressman Finstad spoke on the House Floor in support of the bill’s passage. His remarks are here and below, as prepared for delivery:

Thank you, Mr. Speaker, and thank you Chairman Williams for yielding.

I rise today in strong support of H.R. 10353, the SBIC Reporting Modernization Act of 2026.

This bipartisan legislation requires the Small Business Administration to publish quarterly reports regarding the performance of the Small Business Investment Company program, ultimately enhancing Congressional oversight.

The SBIC program is one of the highest performing programs within the SBA and plays a vital role in helping our entrepreneurs and small business owners across the country access the capital they need to start and grow their businesses.

Requiring the SBA to publish quarterly, rather than annually, reports on the performance of this program will not only ensure Congress and the American people have clear information and reporting measures, but it will also ensure our small businesses are succeeding.

This is a commonsense, bipartisan effort that will deliver for Main Street.

I urge a YES vote and I yield back.

title: Congresswoman Lizzie Fletcher Introduces Bipartisan Legislation to Strengthen and Support Coastal Communities
text:
Today, Congresswoman Lizzie Fletcher (TX-07) introduced the Coastal Resilience Investment Act along with Congressman Randy Weber (TX-14). This legislation supports coastal communities and resources by creating the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation Coastal State Fund, which the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation (NFWF) will establish and manage. This fund will provide $50 million per year from Fiscal Years (FY) 2028 to 2032 for grants to coastal states to support and promote coastal resources, infrastructure, and ecosystems.

“Along the Texas Gulf Coast, we have seen the devastating impact of coastal flooding and disasters, and understand the importance of investing in our coastal communities,” said Congresswoman Fletcher. “The investment provided in the Coastal Resilience Investment Act will help us understand and utilize Texas’ vital coastal resources, natural infrastructure, and ecosystem. I am glad to partner with Congressman Weber in introducing this legislation.”

“On the Texas Gulf Coast, we know what a storm can do to a community, and we know recovery is a lot harder than preparation,” said Congressman Weber. “The Coastal Resilience Investment Act puts resources in the hands of coastal states to prepare their communities before disaster strikes. I’m glad to partner with Congresswoman Fletcher on this bipartisan bill to protect Southeast Texas and keep America moving."

The Coastal Resilience Investment Act allocates funding to coastal states as follows:

70 percent is divided equally to coastal states;

15 percent is dispersed according to the ratio of tidal shoreline of each of the coastal states; and

15 percent is dispersed according to the population density in coastal areas to that of other coastal states.

Additionally, under the legislation no coastal state may receive more than five percent of the total funding per fiscal year, and any additional funding a state would receive based on the criteria listed will be divided equally among the other coastal states.

In the 117th and 118th Congress, Congresswoman Fletcher introduced similar legislation, the Reinvesting in Shoreline Economies and Ecosystems (RISEE) Act to help protect coastal communities by creating a new stream of funding for coastal infrastructure and flood resiliency projects and helped incentivize new clean energy projects.

title: Congresswoman Lizzie Fletcher Leads  Texas Democrats in Demanding the Release of  Miguel Parra Hernández from ICE Custody
text:
Effort details Trump administration failure to uphold ICE’s own detention standards

Today, Congresswoman Lizzie Fletcher (TX-07) led members of the Texas Democratic Delegation in demanding the United States Secretary of Homeland Security (DHS) Markwayne Mullin and Acting Director of United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) David Venturella take immediate steps toward the release of Miguel Parra Hernández from ICE custody.

“On October 10, 2026, an ICE agent struck Mr. Parra Hernández, a 48-year-old construction worker, with an unmarked vehicle while chasing him through a West Houston parking lot—severely injuring Mr. Parra Hernández and leaving him hospitalized with a broken leg with injuries to his hip and ankle,” the members wrote. “For more than 30 years, Parra Hernández has called Houston home. He has no criminal record and was not the intended target of ICE’s operation, yet was severely injured and has remained under ICE custody during his recovery.

“During this past month, ICE has repeatedly hindered and restricted Mr. Parra Hernández's access to his family members and lawyer,” the members continued. “ICE personnel have restricted Mr. Parra Hernández’s lawyer when trying to consult with Mr. Parra Hernández about the legal options available to him or to present legal documents to him, and have remained by his side since the incident—and even throughout his surgical procedure—raising concerns about the lack of confidentiality and patient privacy. ICE has hindered similar attempts from Mr. Parra Hernández’s family members to see or speak with him, as well. Even food brought for him by his family has reportedly been rejected and discarded by ICE personnel. ICE has not allowed Mr. Parra Hernández to shower or shave during the duration of his recovery, contradictory to the agency’s national detention standards, and ICE agents standing beside him react defensively whenever Mr. Parra Hernández tries to move or adjust himself in bed.

“We demand that the DHS give all due consideration of Mr. Parra Hernández’s situation and take immediate steps to release Mr. Parra Hernández from ICE custody,” the members concluded. “We also demand that you restore rightful access to his lawyer and family members as the Constitution requires. We urge the Department’s immediate attention to this matter and await your response.”

A Harris County grand jury recently indicted the ICE agent who struck Mr. Parra Hernández on second-degree felony charges of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon. The ICE agent responsible was hired during ICE’s hiring surge last year and released on bond, while Mr. Parra Hernández remains under constant surveillance by ICE personnel.

In February, Congresswoman Fletcher introduced the Freeze ICE Act, H.R. 7392, to stop the rapid recruitment of unvetted individuals at ICE. In March, she introduced an amendment to a previous DHS funding proposal to institute a hiring freeze at ICE.

Congressmembers Greg Casar (TX-35), Joaquin Castro (TX-20), Jasmine Crockett (TX-30), Lloyd Doggett (TX-37), Veronica Escobar (TX-16), Sylvia Garcia (TX-29), Al Green (TX-09), Julie Johnson (TX-32), Christian Menefee (TX-18), and Marc Veasey (TX-33) joined Congresswoman Fletcher in the letter request.

title: Fong, Valadao, Calvert Release Statement on Bay-Delta Water Plan
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, Congressmen Vince Fong (CA-20), David Valadao (CA-22), and Ken Calvert (CA-41) released the following statement after the California State Water Resources Control Board voted 4-1 to adopt its update to the Bay-Delta Water Quality Control Plan over the objections of Central Valley water agencies and nearly every party to the 2022 agreement the plan was supposed to benefit:

"In a bait and switch, the State Water Board and Governor Newsom have gone back on their word and adopted a plan that nearly every state, local, and federal partner vehemently opposes. By pushing this deeply flawed proposal, Sacramento is undermining years of negotiated agreements with California’s public water agencies, ignoring science, and threatening vital water resources for communities across California. What should have been a comprehensive, collaborative deal will instead invite years of litigation.

"This updated Bay-Delta plan guts water supply for Central Valley farms, businesses and families. For too long, we have persevered through constant uncertainty of reduced water supplies. Now more than ever, ensuring Californians have reliable, stable, and abundant supplies demands urgent action with real input from our communities.

“Politicians in Sacramento have repeatedly proven they are unwilling to operate in good faith. The Department of Interior, Bureau of Reclamation, and local water agencies need to reject this unworkable plan and put forward a viable solution that secures California’s water future."

Background

On October 29, 2026, the State Water Resources Control Board voted 4-1 to adopt amendments to the Bay-Delta Water Quality Control Plan, the first major change to the plan's Sacramento River and Delta provisions since 1995. The vote followed two days of hearings in which more than 200 speakers testified, the large majority in opposition.

The plan was supposed to implement the 2022 Memorandum of Understanding, in which California's public water agencies, the California Natural Resources Agency, the California Environmental Protection Agency, and the Bureau of Reclamation agreed to a science-based program of flow contributions, habitat restoration, dedicated funding, and adaptive management. That agreement included a robust science program and a governance structure designed to resolve disputes among the parties and avoid a decade of litigation.

The State Water Board instead adopted a plan that changes how water contributions are counted, reduces the credit water users receive for commitments already made, removes limits on future demands, and concentrates key decisions in the Board's Executive Director without clear standards.

The plan also reaches into federal jurisdiction. The Bureau of Reclamation, which operates the Central Valley Project, formally objected to the plan in comments to the Board.

The Central Valley is the food production capital of the nation, growing nearly a quarter of the food on Americans' tables. Without reliable water resources, the foundation of our region's economy and the entire nation's food supply is at risk.

title: RELEASE: In Honor of Veterans Day, Gottheimer Hosts Roundtable with Local Veterans, Announces New Bipartisan Legislation to Expand VA Disability Benefits
text:
Above: Gottheimer Announces Federal Actions to Expand VA Disability Benefits.

BOGOTA, N.J. — Today, Friday, November 13, 2026, Congressman Josh Gottheimer (NJ-5) hosted a roundtable with North Jersey veterans and representatives from veteran service organizations at the Bogota VFW Post 5561 in honor of Veterans Day. Gottheimer also introduced three new pieces of bipartisan legislation to expand disability benefits for veterans with his colleague Congressman Mike Lawler (NY-17).

“Nothing is more important in this job than my responsibility to always have the backs of those who have stepped forward to protect us — to bravely get our backs. That’s why I’m proud to have worked across the aisle to improve veterans’ benefits and care, and to continue that work to find common ground to ensure you receive the benefits you deserve,” said Congressman Josh Gottheimer (NJ-5).

Watch Gottheimer’s full remarks here.

New Jersey is home to nearly 300,000 veterans, including about 38,400 across Bergen, Passaic, and Sussex counties: 22,085 in Bergen, 10,616 in Passaic, and 5,683 in Sussex. More than 65,000 New Jersey veterans receive VA disability compensation. More than 65,000 New Jersey residents receive VA disability compensation, and nearly 74,000 turned to the VA for care in 2023.

Following the roundtable, Gottheimer announced new bipartisan federal legislation to make it easier for veterans to qualify for VA disability benefits:

The SARC Act (Sarcoidosis After Service Recognition and Coverage Act) will allow veterans who develop sarcoidosis more than a year after leaving the military to qualify for VA disability benefits. Under current VA rules, sarcoidosis is presumed to be service-connected only if it becomes at least 10 percent disabling within one year of separation or if the veteran qualifies under the PACT Act. The SARC Act would remove the one-year cutoff so eligible veterans whose sarcoidosis becomes at least 10 percent disabling at any point after service could qualify for disability benefits..

The LINK Act (Linking Identified Neurological Conditions to Known PTSD Act) will allow eligible veterans with service-connected PTSD who later develop dementia or Parkinson’s disease to qualify for VA disability benefits by presuming the condition is linked to their PTSD.

The Protecting Vets From Chronic Illness Act will require the VA to review its list of 41 chronic diseases presumed to be connected to military service, which hasn’t been updated since 1988. The bill would require the VA to recommend updates to its chronic disease list, including diseases to add and deadlines to extend for conditions that become disabling after veterans leave the military.

“We are immensely grateful to Representative Josh Gottheimer for introducing this bill on behalf of the as many as 32,000 veterans who have been diagnosed with sarcoidosis or are still navigating their path to their sarcoidosis diagnosis. The Foundation for Sarcoidosis Research (FSR) enthusiastically endorses this bill,” said FSR’s President and CEO, Mary McGowan. “For far too long veterans with sarcoidosis have struggled to be seen, understood, and treated – the introduction of this bill ushers in a new era that acknowledges these veterans’ sacrifice and provides them hope for the future.”

“Sarcoidosis is one of the most difficult diseases to diagnose. Patients often visit four or more physicians and wait three to five years from their first symptoms to a diagnosis, long after the VA’s one-year window has closed. Veterans who served our country should never lose the benefits they earned because their disease took longer to diagnose. The Life & Breath Foundation for Sarcoidosis proudly endorses Congressman Gottheimer’s bill and thanks him for standing up for veterans living with sarcoidosis,” said Saul Kuciauskas, Vice President of the Life & Breath Foundation.

Gottheimer also highlighted that the House overwhelmingly passed the bipartisan Major Richard Star Act this week. This bill will ensure that combat-injured veterans who were medically retired can receive both their retirement pay and their VA disability compensation, so that about 59,000 veterans can receive both payments in full.

Gottheimer’s new legislation builds on his record to improve care and expand access to benefits for veterans. Gottheimer’s first piece of legislation signed into law helps the VA hire post-9/11 veterans. Gottheimer also helped author and secure provisions in the PACT Act to address the mental health impacts of toxic exposure for veterans. In July, the House passed Gottheimer’s bipartisan bill to rename the Newton VA clinic in Sussex County to the Anthony “Tony” J. Gallopo VA Clinic, honoring the local veteran who fought to open it. He has also introduced bipartisan legislation, including the Data-Driven Suicide Prevention and Outreach Act to use AI to identify suicide risk factors among veterans, the Veterans STAND Act to expand access to assistive technology for veterans with spinal cord injuries, the VETS Act to make sure VA residential facilities and state veterans’ homes have resident advocates, among others.

Gottheimer was joined by Senator Gordon Johnson; Mayor Danielle Fede of Bogota; Councilwoman Diana Vergara of Bogota; Councilman John Mitchell of Bogota; Mayor John Glidden, Closter; Howard Burrell, Former Mayor of Vernon Township; Mary McGowan, Foundation for Sarcoidosis Research; Marsha Henderson, Sarcoidosis Veteran; Bradley Christensen, VSO from the NJ Department of Veterans Affairs; Shaun Hutchinson, Director of the Bergen County Department of Human Services Division of Veterans Services; Gloria Derteano, Deputy Director of Veterans Services at the Bergen County Administrative Departments; Alexander Hernandez, Bogota VFW Commander; Members of VFW Post 5561, Bogota; Members of Service Academy Board 2026; Jeremy Baratta, Benefits Protection Team Leader, DAV – Department of New Jersey; Joseph Fricker, First Vice Commander for American Legion of NJ.

title: Congressman Pat Harrigan Votes to Deliver Long-Overdue Benefits to Combat-Injured Veterans
text:
Contact: Lexi Kranich (814) 380-4408

WASHINGTON, D.C.—Today, Congressman Pat Harrigan (NC-10) voted to passthe Major Richard Star Act, legislation that would allow combat-injured veterans who were medically retired from the military to receive both their military retirement pay and VA disability compensation in full. The legislation addresses a long-standing gap in federal law that has prevented certain veterans whose military careers were cut short by combat-related injuries from receiving both benefits without a reduction.

“Military retirement and VA disability compensation exist for two different reasons. One recognizes your service, and the other compensates you for the injuries you sustained because of it,” said Congressman Harrigan. “I've never understood why a veteran who was wounded in combat and forced to retire early should have to give up part of one to receive the other. As a Green Beret, I served with men whose careers ended because of injuries sustained downrange, and I know what they've given for this country. I'm proud to support finally fixing this, and I hope the Senate gets it across the finish line.”

Under current law, certain combat-injured veterans who were medically retired before completing 20 years of service have their military retirement pay reduced when they receive disability compensation from the Department of Veterans Affairs. The Major Richard Star Act would eliminate that offset for eligible veterans, allowing them to receive both benefits without a reduction.

With House passage, the Major Richard Star Act now moves to the Senate for consideration. Congressman Harrigan is urging the Senate to advance the legislation and deliver long-overdue relief to veterans who were forced to end their military careers because of injuries sustained in service to the country.

title: Jayapal Statement on Jim McDermott’s Passing
text:
SEATTLE, W.A. — U.S. Representative Pramila Jayapal (WA-07) released the following statement on the passing of Jim McDermott, the Representative for Washington’s 7th Congressional District from 1989-2017.

“Congressman Jim McDermott served the 7th Congressional District of Washington for 28 years with incredible commitment, passion and skill. As a psychiatrist and a global health champion, he understood how critical universal healthcare was here at home and our responsibility to those around the world. As a staunch advocate against forever wars and for peace, he led this district and the country in speaking out against the war in Iraq. As a committed champion for the rights and dignity of workers, he always led on ensuring collective bargaining rights, living wages and dignity on the job. Congressman McDermott was a true champion for justice and left behind a long legacy of accomplishment on critical pieces of legislation in Congress that encompassed AIDS, housing, social security, mental health and so much more.

“For me, his commitment to immigrant justice was unparalleled. He was an inspiration and mentor to me personally after September 11, 2001, when I met with him as a constituent who was deeply concerned about the hate crimes and violations of civil liberties against Arabs, Muslims and South Asians by the then-Bush Administration. He immediately jumped into action and before I knew it, he had worked with me to organize a massive press conference at the Seattle Center to declare Washington State a hate-free state, and to work with me over the next decade to fight alongside the immigrant rights movement here at home for the rights and dignity of immigrants from all over the world. Soon after, he was one of the first Members of Congress to commit to our national Immigrant Workers Freedom Ride across the country, and he was always willing to stand up with us—even before it was popular—for immigrant justice. I will never forget his dedication to the immigrant rights movement and the legacy of his courage on this and many other issues.

“I am grateful to have called him a mentor and friend and will truly miss him. On behalf of the constituents of the 7th Congressional District who were so incredibly well served by his leadership, his courage and his heart, I express our deepest condolences to his family, his loved ones, and all our constituents who are mourning his loss and celebrating his legacy.”

title: MassLive: Mass. women are about to run Capitol Hill. Here’s what they have planned
text:
U.S. Sen. Elizabeth Warren has big plans when she and her fellow Democrats fully retake control of Capitol Hill next year.

Mostly, that means delivering on the populist economic agenda that Democrats pitched on the campaign trail and that voters chose when they propelled a historic blue wave on Election Day.

“Some people have said it is wasted energy to send strong policy changes to the Trump White House. I disagree,” Warren, D-Mass., said in a post-election video posted to YouTube.

“(President Donald Trump) says he welcomes the nickname ‘Mr. Veto.’ Well, let’s test him out on that. That means passing legislation to make life more affordable for Americans and to make our government less corrupt,” the Cambridge lawmaker said.

First, Warren says she wants to end the administration’s war in Iran, which she has denounced as illegal. Second, she wants to cut costs. She’s spent months castigating Trump for failing to do that during the first two years of his second term.

“Trump may still be president, but Democrats have the power on spending bills. And we should use it,” she said.

If all goes to plan, Warren could be uniquely positioned to put those plans into action next year. She’d also have plenty of company.

Three more Massachusetts women lawmakers — U.S. Reps. Katherine Clark, D-5th District, Lori Trahan, D-3rd District, and Ayanna Pressley, D-7th District — will see their clout and prestige increase in the new Congress.

“It reflects the great bench that Massachusetts has in the House of Representatives,” Tatishe Nteta, a pollster and political science professor at UMass Amherst, said. “The number of capable women who have distinguished records and will continue to build (them) up.”

They are part of a larger contingent of women lawmakers who will change the way the next Congress will operate.

At least 116 Democratic women will serve in Congress next year, up from the previous record of 111 set in 2025, according to the Center for American Women and Politics at Rutgers University’s Eagleton Institute of Politics.

Of them, 100 Democratic women are expected to serve in the 435-member House, according to the center’s research. That’s up from the 2025 record of 95 Democratic women.

Democratic women were responsible for flipping at least 10 formerly Republican seats nationwide.

Meanwhile, the number of Republican women in Congress — both the U.S. House and Senate — as well as statewide elected executive offices will drop as a result of the midterms, the center’s research found.

“This was an impressive result for women in American politics, with women setting records and breaking significant barriers around the nation,” the center’s executive director, Debbie Walsh, said.

“But it also shows how closely women’s fortunes are bound to the fortunes of the Democratic Party. The Republican Party consistently runs fewer women candidates than Democrats. Women are nearing parity across levels of office among Democrats,” Walsh said. “Political parity in America can’t be achieved if only one party is intentionally recruiting and supporting women candidates.”

In Massachusetts, Warren is poised to take the reins of the Senate Banking Committee, which would give her a big say over financial policy. She’s currently its ranking Democrat.

She’s also believed to be eyeing the No. 3 leadership position in the Senate Democratic Conference.

That’s Steering and Policy chair, a post U.S. Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., is vacating after winning her home state’s gubernatorial race on Election Day.

The job would put Warren in charge of shaping the Democrats’ strategic and legislative priorities. On a more mechanical level, she’d also be in charge of doling out committee assignments.

One of the upper chamber’s most high-profile and vocal progressives, Warren also will serve as a “bridge” to the party’s moderates, Nteta said.

Warren donated hundreds of thousands of dollars to Democratic candidates during the midterms. And she crisscrossed the country to campaign for the party’s candidates.

That work matters. And her voice could speak loudly if, as expected, current Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., faces a bumpy road in his quest to become majority leader.

Warren “understands how to wield influence and clout,” Nteta said.

Clark, of Melrose, is set to become the first woman to serve as U.S. House majority leader when, as expected, current Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., steps into the role of House speaker.

In a Nov. 5 speech before the left-leaning Center for American Progress, Clark reflected on the election and the message voters had sent by electing Democrats.

“And in every corner of this country, people who feel angry, exhausted, cheated by their own government summoned what hope they had left and turned out to vote,” she said.

“And these are people who are voting to survive, whether it’s under the brutality and terror or the crushing weight of a broken and rigged economy, cuts to their health care, hikes in their bills, whether they live in the cities or the suburbs or across rural America, whether the media deem them red or blue voters, people fighting to survive the uncertainty of tomorrow and what that may bring to their families,” Clark said. “They found faith in this 250-year-old promise and experiment that they made it work and they forced it to work by voting for something better.”

She’s positioned to become the highest-ranking lawmaker from the Bay State since the late Democratic U.S. House Speaker Thomas P. “Tip” O’Neill of Cambridge.

In her years on Capitol Hill, Clark has been an “invisible powerhouse,” rising steadily through the ranks, Nteta said. He’ll be watching to see if the suburban Boston lawmaker emerges as a “household name” like Jeffries and other prominent Democrats next year.

Pressley, of Boston, will serve on an energized U.S. House Oversight Committee, which is expected to launch investigations of Trump and the Republican White House. A fellow Bostonian, U.S. Rep. Stephen Lynch, D-8th District, also serves on the panel.

“We fully intend … to use the full weight of our subpoena power. And let me just say this, Jacob,” Pressley told MS Now in a recent interview. “We might not win every fight, but we have a responsibility to the electorate, to the communities and the people that we serve, at least to go after it. We may not win every fight, but we have to fight. And that’s exactly what I expect this committee to do.”

The media-savvy Pressley is likely to become a public face as House Democrats launch their White House probes, Nteta said.

“She definitely knows how to speak in quotable phrases, which will be a benefit as the committee makes its case.” he said. “This is something the American people wanted — for Congress to root out possible corruption.”

Trahan, of Westford, has emerged as the Democrats’ point-person on artificial intelligence policy.

She’s reportedly revamping an AI safety bill she introduced in August with U.S. Rep. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., to reduce efforts to preempt state laws that seek to regulate the industry, Politico reported.

In October, she also unveiled legislation that would hold AI developers liable for the rogue actions of their agents.

“When someone breaks the law and hurts you, you can take them to court. That shouldn’t change just because the wrongdoer is an AI agent,” Trahan said in a statement.

“Developers have already built systems capable of acting on their own and causing real damage. The CLAIM Act makes sure they answer for what their systems do.”

Two more Bay Staters, U.S. Reps. Richard Neal, D-1st District, and Jim McGovern, also are set to occupy important leadership perches.

McGovern, of Worcester, will take the gavel on the powerful House Rules Committee, the chamber’s “traffic cop” controlling the flow of legislation to the House floor.

Neal, of Springfield, will chair the budget-writing House Ways and Means Committee, putting him in a position to bring home federal money to Massachusetts.

“We’re in line for a lot of influence,” Nteta said.

—

title: Larsen Votes to Give Combat-Wounded Veterans Full Benefits

title: Larsen Reintroduces Bill to Expand Lifesaving Opioid Harm Reduction
text:
Today, U.S. Representative Rick Larsen (WA-02) reintroduced the Closing the Substance Use Care Gap Act to expand access to lifesaving, community-based harm reduction programs and services, and to strengthen the federal response to the opioid and fentanyl epidemic.

“The opioid crisis has devastated families and communities in Northwest Washington, and while we have made progress reducing deaths and disrupting trafficking, there is more to be done. Congress must stay focused on solutions that meet people where they are, prevent overdoses and save lives,” said Rep. Larsen. “Too many people struggling with addiction want treatment but do not receive it. This bill helps to close that gap by giving local organizations the resources they need to help people who want to recover from substance use.”

According to the 2024 National Drug Control Strategy, the vast majority of people who want substance use care do not receive it. The main reasons preventing people from getting the care they want are being unable to stop using and not knowing where to find programs that offer services they need. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) identifies harm reduction as an approach that provides care that meets people where they are, is free of stigma and mitigates he harms of drug use. Lifesaving harm reduction options, such as naloxone (an overdose reversal medication) and fentanyl test strips, are vital resources for people at the highest risk of overdose or poor health outcomes. Despite the demand and effectiveness of harm reduction services, these resources remain substantially underfunded at the state and federal level.

The Closing the Substance Use Care Gap Act would provide community-based organizations with more resources to administer life-saving harm reduction programs and services to people struggling with substance use. The legislation would expand access to substance use care and help connect individuals to recovery support services. It would also provide funding to organizations to establish procedures and mechanisms for connecting individuals with evidence-based treatment and recovery support services.

The full text of the Closing the Substance Use Care Gap Act is available here.

A one-pager on the Closing the Substance Use Care Gap Act is available here.

Broad Support from the Medical Community for Larsen’s Bill

The Closing the Substance Use Care Gap Act is supported by the American College of Physicians (ACP), American Nurses Association (ANA), National Alliance on Mental Illness (NAMI), Washington State Medical Association (WSMA), Washington State Hospital Association, University of Washington Harm Reduction Research and Treatment (HaRRT) Center, American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM), Overdose Prevention Initiative at GHAI, Association of American Medical Colleges (AAMC), and Washington State Association of Counties (WSAC).

“Substance use disorders are treatable chronic medical conditions that should be addressed through the expansion of evidence-based public and individual health initiatives to prevent, treat, and promote recovery, rather than relying on criminalization and incarceration,” said Jan K. Carney, MD, MPH, FRCP, president, American College of Physicians (ACP). “That is why the American College of Physicians supports legislation like the Closing the Substance Use Care Gap Act, that would increase patient access to evidence-based treatment and supports. As physicians, we see patients every day experiencing significant health challenges due to substance use disorder. Expanded federal funding for harm reduction strategies, could greatly help to improve the health and safety of those patients.”

“Nurses care for patients impacted by substance use disorders every day and see firsthand how essential harm reduction programs are—not only saving lives but creating pathways to treatment and recovery for those not yet ready to stop using,” said President Jennifer Mensik Kennedy, PhD, MBA, RN, NEA-BC, FAAN. “The American Nurses Association (ANA) stands in support of the Closing the Substance Use Care Gap Act. This legislation supports and expands access to critical programs and services—ensuring nurses specializing in substance use disorder treatment can bridge the treatment gap and connect individuals battling substance use disorders to needed care, especially for those in rural and underserved communities. ANA commends Representatives Larsen for introducing this important bill and urges Congress to pass it swiftly.”

“As we continue our work toward overcoming the opioid epidemic in our country, we must ensure communities have all the resources they need to support people who are impacted.” said Hannah Wesolowski, Chief Advocacy Officer of the National Alliance on Mental Illness (NAMI). “It's vital that communities have the resources to address behavioral health needs and turn the tide on our nation's opioid crisis. NAMI thanks Rep. Larsen for introducing the Closing the Substance Use Care Gap Act, and we are proud to support this bill to help ensure communities have vital lifesaving harm reduction resources.”

“The Washington State Medical Association (WSMA), representing physicians practicing in every specialty and corner of the state, applauds Congressman Rick Larsen’s introduction of the Closing the Substance Use Care Gap Act,” said Matthew Hollon, MD, MPH, MACP, President, Washington State Medical Association. “The WSMA supports policies that facilitate and improve access to evidence-based harm reduction efforts. This measure will save lives by directly engaging with people who use drugs to prevent overdoses and infectious disease transmission while establishing connections for ongoing care and treatment.”

“The Closing the Substance Use Care Gap Act is a critical step towards ensuring that people struggling with substance use have access to the care and support they need,” said Cassie Sauer, CEO, Washington State Hospital Association (WSHA). “Harm reduction is a proven strategy to prevent overdoses and life-threatening infections from unclean needles. This bill will help patients across Washington access evidence-based treatment and recovery support services. The Washington State Hospital Association applauds Congressman Larsen’s leadership on this issue.”

“The Closing the Substance Use Care Gap Act will ensure the availability of federal funding for evidence-based and life-saving harm-reduction services and treatment programs. It is critical that this reauthorization will support community-led and grassroots harm-reduction agencies and organizations, who work on the frontlines of the overdose epidemic,” said Susan Collins, PhD, and Seema Clifasefi, PhD, LICSW, Co-Directors of the University of Washington Harm Reduction Research and Treatment (HaRRT) Center. “Funds will bolster services provided by state, Tribal, local and territorial governments to reduce substance-related harm and improve health and well-being for their citizens, families and communities. By investing in these essential harm-reduction services and more inclusive treatment approaches, this bill will better meet the needs of individuals and lift them up in their recovery journeys.”

The Association of American Medical Colleges wrote a letter in support of the bill, which is available here.

Larsen Focused on Combating Opioid and Fentanyl Crisis

Rep. Larsen continues to focus on supporting local efforts to combat the opioid crisis and save lives. In 2024, he released a districtwide opioid report that outlines a four-pillar framework to combat the crisis. Rep. Larsen leads three additional bills aimed at combating the crisis:

This September, Rep. Larsen reintroduced his Workforce Opportunities for Communities in Recovery Act with Rep. Pramila Jayapal (WA-07) and Sen. Edward J. Markey (D-MA) to create employment opportunities for people in recovery and support communities impacted by widespread opioid use.

This May, Rep. Larsen reintroduced the bipartisan End Fentanyl Trafficking with Local Task Forces Act with Reps. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (WA-03) and Dan Newhouse (WA-04) to establish a dedicated federal funding stream to help multi-jurisdictional drug task forces combat opioid trafficking in Washington state and across the country.

Last July, Rep. Larsen reintroduced the bipartisan Protection for Reservation Occupants against Trafficking and Evasive Communications Today (PROTECT) Act with Rep. Ryan Zinke (R-MT) and Sens. Steve Daines (R-MT) and Tina Smith (D-MN) to give Tribal courts and law enforcement more tools and resources to combat the opioid epidemic.

title: Larson Votes for Major Richard Star Act to Ensure Fair Pay for Disabled Veterans
text:
Washington, D.C. - Today, Rep. John B. Larson (CT-01) released the following statement after voting for the Major Richard Star Act, a bipartisan bill that allows veterans who were medically retired as a result of combat or training injuries to receive both retired pay and disability compensation, regardless of time served. After Republican leadership blocked the bill from advancing to the floor, Larson signed a discharge petition to force a House vote on the Major Richard Star Act.

“Congress has a sacred duty to do right by our brave veterans, who put their lives on the line to defend our freedoms,” said Larson. “As we recognized Veterans Day this week, I was honored to cast my vote in favor of the Major Richard Star Act, so we can finally ensure all disabled veterans receive the pay and benefits they have earned and deserve. It was disappointing to see Speaker Johnson play politics with this critical bill over the last few months, refusing to hold a vote and instead weaponizing a procedural gimmick to force through a bill that would reduce disability compensation for nearly two million Americans and triple VA home loan fees—on Veterans Day no less. After yesterday’s shameful attack on veterans benefits by the outgoing Republican majority, I am glad that common sense and the duty every Member of Congress has to support our veterans prevailed yesterday. I urge the Senate to send the Major Richard Star Act to the President’s desk and vote down the benefit cuts that should have never passed the House of Representatives.”

title: Ranking Member Lofgren Notifies Agencies, Companies, and Individuals Tied to Committee Oversight to Preserve All Records
text:
(Washington, DC) — Yesterday, Ranking Member Zoe Lofgren (D-CA), sent letters to over 30 companies, individuals, and federal agencies informing them to preserve their records. Letter recipients include companies and individuals with ties to ongoing Science Committee Democratic investigations and agencies over which the Committee has jurisdiction.

In her letters to individuals and private companies, the Ranking Member writes:

“This letter serves to formally notify you of your obligation to identify, retain, and preserve all information and materials in your possession or control, including personal property if applicable, that could potentially be relevant to the Committee’s oversight. You must preserve all information and materials subject to this obligation until further notice. … Failure to act as instructed may be interpreted as the deliberate obstruction of Congress’s power of inquiry. The Committee reserves the right to respond accordingly.”

In her letters to agency leaders, the Ranking Member sites the Federal Records Act:

“The Federal Records Act and the regulations promulgated to implement it require the head of each federal agency to safeguard against the removal or loss of agency records. Records and documentation regarding policies, decisions, procedures, transactions, and deliberations are subject to these statutory preservation requirements. The requirement to preserve records extends to applicable government documents and communications on personal property and in encrypted electronic messaging applications. Additionally, other records of interest may be covered by The Presidential Records Act.”
