title: Womack Votes to Support Combat Veterans and Improve Veteran Access to Telemedicine Services
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — November 13, 2026…This week, Congressman Steve Womack (AR-3) voted in support of two pieces of legislation aimed at providing American veterans and their families with the proper access to benefits, programs, and services administered by the Department of War (DoW) and the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA):

H.R. 2102, the Major Richard Star Act, would allow military retirees with combat-related disabilities who served less than 20 years to concurrently receive full retirement pay and disability benefits

H.R. 9237, the Take Care of America’s Veterans Act, is a comprehensive package of more than 60 bipartisan bills to modernize, enhance, and reform benefits and services administered by the DoW and VA—including provisions championed by Congressman Womack to improve veteran access to telemedicine services and service dogs. The bill also includes a version of the Major Richard Star Act.

Congressman Womack said, “While we can never fully repay the debt of gratitude we owe our nation’s veterans for their service, Congress has a responsibility to strengthen the systems and resources that contribute to their well-being. The Major Richard Star Act and the Take Care of America’s Veterans Act both help ensure our veterans receive the support they have earned.”

Congressman Womack continued, “I am proud that the core tenets of my proposal to preserve veteran access to telemedicine services are included in the Take Care of America’s Veterans Act, ensuring veterans continue receiving the vital healthcare they require. For our combat veterans, the Major Richard Star Act ensures they are not unfairly penalized for their sacrifice and can receive their full benefits when their military careers are cut short. I look forward to the Senate’s swift consideration of these pieces of legislation so we can support those whose lives have been forever impacted by their service in defense of our nation.”

Background on the Major Richard Star Act

Under current law, the retirement pay of combat-wounded, medically retired veterans with under 20 years of service is reduced by the amount of VA disability received.

The Major Richard Star Act would allow this specific class of veterans to receive both their VA disability compensation and their full retirement pay without offsets.

The Take Care of America’s Veterans Act includes a similar version of the Major Richard Star Act, with differences in how benefits are calculated. This version ensures combat-related, medically retired veterans can receive the retirement pay they have earned for their years of service and the VA disability pay that provides for the loss of future opportunities and income due to service-connected injury. The Take Care of America’s Veterans Act is fully offset to be able to provide these additional benefits while protecting our nation’s fiscal future.

Background on veteran access to telemedicine services in the Take Care of America’s Veterans Act:

The Ryan Haight Online Pharmacy Consumer Protection Act of 2008 was enacted on April 13, 2009. This bill was designed to combat the rogue internet pharmacies that proliferated in the late 90s, selling controlled substances online.

Under this Act, a practitioner is required to conduct at least one in-person medical evaluation of the patient before issuing a prescription for a controlled substance.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, requirements under the Ryan Haight Act for a patient to meet with a practitioner in-person for the prescription of a controlled substance were temporarily waived.

On November 19, 2024, the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) and Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) announced the continuation of a temporary extension of flexibilities around telemedicine prescribing of controlled substances from the COVID-19 public health emergency through December 31, 2025.

Congressman Womack introduced the Protecting Veteran Access to Telemedicine Services Act of 2025 to make this extension permanent. The House passed the legislation in September 2025. Read more HERE.

On December 31, 2025, the DEA and HHS announced a further extension of telemedicine flexibilities through December 31, 2026.

The Take Care of America’s Veterans Act would extend many of the core tenets of Congressman Womack’s legislation, including allowing for the prescription, delivery, distribution, and dispensation of controlled substance medication through telemedicine.

Background on veteran access to service dogs in the Take Care of America’s Veterans Act:

The Puppies Assisting Wounded Servicemembers (PAWS) for Veteran Therapy Act, or PAWS Act, was enacted on August 25, 2021. This bill created a pilot program on dog-based therapy to provide dog-training skills and service dogs to veterans with PTSD.

This bipartisan legislation aims to reduce veteran suicide connected to mental health conditions.

On April 2, 2025, the Service Dogs Assisting Veterans Act, or SAVES Act, was introduced to assist nonprofit organizations in carrying out programs to provide service dogs to eligible veterans.

Congressman Womack cosponsored the SAVES Act—included in the Take Care of America’s Veterans Act—which builds on the PAWS Act to broaden access to the life-saving assistance service dogs can provide.

In addition to these important programs, the Take Care of America’s Veterans Act would:

Expand and refine VA health programs, grants, research initiatives, and pilots, and strengthen access to specialized care.

Protect employees from government overreach by improving policies and transparency in the hiring, development, retention, and accountability of the VA workforce.

Require the VA to conduct preventative health evaluations of veterans with spinal cord injuries and assess them for eligibility for modern assistive mobility devices.

The Take Care of America’s Veterans Act bill text is available HERE.

Congressman Steve Womack (AR-3) has represented Arkansas’s Third Congressional District since 2011. He is a member of the House Appropriations Committee.

title: Consensus Grows for Permitting Reform
text:
Consensus Grows for Permitting Reform

WHY LEADING EDITORIAL BOARDS AND POLICY VOICES ARE FINDING COMMON GROUND ON PERMITTING REFORM

When the New York Times and Wall Street Journal find common ground on energy legislation, Washington should pay attention.

NATIONAL EDITORIAL BOARDS FIND COMMON GROUND

The New York Times editorial board endorsed BAAJA, urging Democrats to advance their affordability agenda and warning that they “should not pass up a chance to start delivering immediately.” The Washington Post editorial board called the agreement “a major step toward historic permitting reform,” emphasizing the opportunity to build energy infrastructure faster.

The Wall Street Journal editorial board warned that permitting delays “may be America’s biggest economic Achilles’ heel,” while Bloomberg Opinion described Congress as being “on the cusp of a major bipartisan victory” and urged lawmakers to complete the agreement.

BEYOND THE EDITORIAL PAGES: POLICY LEADERS MAKE THE CASE

Policy commentators have also examined the deal through the lenses of affordability, investment, and governing consistency. Wall Street Journal chief economics commentator Greg Ip examined the economic costs of delayed approvals. Jane Flegal and Pavan Venkatakrishnan of the Searchlight Institute explicitly argued for passage to accelerate clean-energy construction. Republican strategists Chris Johnson and Liam Donovan argued that predictable permitting rules must apply consistently, regardless of which projects political leaders favor.

Climate and center-left voices have made different arguments for accepting the compromise. Writing in the New York Times, Ezra Klein assessed the tradeoffs of accepting an imperfect deal, while former Energy Secretary Jennifer Granholm called for passage. Climate investor Tom Steyer appealed to fellow progressives: “this is a bill we should support, and I’m asking you to join me.” Third Way’s Josh Freed criticized groups “more interested in obstructing imperfect solutions than working to improve them,” while Columbia University’s Jason Bordoff argued against rejecting the clean-energy and affordability opportunities solely because the agreement also benefits fossil fuels. Arnab Datta and Skanda Amarnath examined the relationship between affordable, reliable electricity and climate goals, while Colin Mortimer of the Progressive Policy Institute linked the agreement to a broader center-left permitting-reform agenda.

Former economic and national security officials offered a direct bipartisan endorsement. In an October 20 letter organized by the Institute for Progress, 19 former officials—including Treasury Secretaries Janet Yellen, Steven Mnuchin, Timothy Geithner, Henry Paulson, and Robert Rubin; former Secretary of State Mike Pompeo; and former National Security Advisor Jake Sullivan—urged Congress to pass BAAJA, citing the importance of infrastructure development to U.S. competitiveness in semiconductors, critical minerals, artificial intelligence, and energy.

Policy institutions have contributed both explicit endorsements and analysis of the agreement’s practical effects. Sarah Ladislaw of the New Energy Industrial Strategy Center argued that permitting reform is essential to delivering semiconductor, energy, and defense projects. Alex Mechanick and Baillee Brown of Inclusive Abundance examined how the bill could improve government capacity and remove infrastructure supply constraints. Thomas Hochman examined transmission reform, enforceable timelines, and durable approvals, while Rachel Levine of the Niskanen Center stressed the urgency of transmission development in western states. The Institute for Progress, led by co-CEO Alec Stapp, endorsed BAAJA as “the most ambitious bipartisan permitting bill in decades.” Timothy Male of the Environmental Policy Innovation Center discussed ways to accelerate infrastructure and environmental projects while maintaining safeguards.

Consensus this broad is rare. Congress needs to meet this moment.

title: Baldwin, Colleagues Urge FTC to Crack Down on Corporations Pocketing Consumers’ Tariff Refunds
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — U.S. Senator Tammy Baldwin (D-WI) joined her colleagues in urging the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) to investigate giant corporations that are pocketing tariff refunds after raising prices on consumers. The senators pressed FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson to investigate whether these companies violated federal law by pocketing refunds instead of paying their customers back when President Trump’s tariffs were found to be illegal.

“Not a single one of these corporations provided any assurance that they will actually pass along refunds directly to their consumers,” wrote Baldwin and the Senators.

Giant retailers raised prices after President Trump imposed sweeping tariffs in April 2025. The letter cites estimates that consumers will pay 95 percent of Trump’s tariff costs, and that the tariffs will add an average of $2,500 to families’ expenses. After the Supreme Court struck down President Trump’s initial set of across-the-board tariffs in February 2026, the Trump administration began issuing refunds to corporations and importers. The government has paid out more than $100 billion in refunds — but the consumers that bore the brunt of cost increases have received no direct refunds.

The senators highlighted responses from Walmart, Nike, Apple, Target, and Energizer. Walmart touted efforts to lower prices but refused to specify how much of its refund would go toward those cuts. Nike offered no explanation for how it would use the money. Apple cited investments in the United States, while Target pointed to holiday promotions and domestic investments. Energizer acknowledged it had identified no specific use for the funds beyond supporting its business operations and investments. Not one of the five companies committed to directly paying back customers who covered the cost of the tariffs.

This “appears to be a massive theft from the middle class, facilitated by the Trump Administration and giant corporations that raised prices for middle class consumers in response to Trump tariffs and are now pocketing their refunds,” the Senators continued.

The FTC Act bans unfair or deceptive practices and unfair methods of competition. The senators urged the agency to investigate whether these companies violated those protections. They warned that keeping tariff refunds could give companies an unfair advantage over their competitors. Meanwhile, the Trump administration has failed to provide guidance to companies on returning refunds to consumers.

“The agency should act quickly to hold accountable any corporation that is ripping off consumers,” concluded Baldwin and the Senators.

The letter also warns that Trump’s later tariffs could extend the ripoff for families. Several of those tariffs face legal challenges. If courts strike them down, corporations could collect another round of refunds while consumers get nothing back. The Trump administration has not provided a plan to get those potential refunds back to families.

The letter comes as last month a brand-new report found that, from the ongoing trade war, war in Iran, and chaos, Congressional Republicans and President Trump are costing Wisconsin families more than $4,500 for everyday essentials like housing, gas, and groceries.

The letter was led by Senator Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) and also signed by Senators Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Elissa Slotkin (D-MI), Cory Booker (D-NJ), Ed Markey (D-MA), and Mark Kelly (D-AZ).

Full text of the letter is available here and below.

Dear Chair Ferguson:

We write to urge you to open an investigation to determine whether giant corporations that have received massive tariff refunds from the United States government have engaged in unfair or deceptive practices or unfair methods of competition, or have otherwise violated federal competition or consumer protection laws, by refusing to provide tariff refunds to their customers.

In April 2025, President Trump imposed sweeping, across-the-board tariffs on U.S. trading partners under the authority of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA). These tariffs were passed on to consumers by giant retailers that increased prices, with many companies sharing messages with their customers explaining the need to raise prices in light of the new tariffs. Corporate executives admitted that they were passing on tariff costs to consumers — a Walmart executive acknowledged that “the magnitude of these increases is more than any retailer can absorb.” American consumers will end up paying for 95 percent of Trump’s tariffs, with the tariffs costing families an average of $2,500 in added expenses. But in February of this year, the Supreme Court declared that these tariffs from President Trump were illegal, and the government began the process of providing refunds — not to consumers, but to corporations and importers. In fact, the Administration’s refund program — set up through the Homeland Security Department’s Customs and Border Protection agency (CBP)—has paid out more than $100 billion in tariff refunds thus far, including to some of the world's biggest and most profitable corporations.

But the American consumer—who paid almost the full cost of the IEEPA tariffs—have received no direct refunds or restitution. The Trump Administration has repeatedly sidestepped Congressional inquiries about how American consumers will get their money back. The Administration has also failed to even provide any guidance to corporations regarding passing along tariff refunds to their consumers, allowing firms to simply pocket these large sums. Indeed, almost none of the corporations that have received tariff refunds have indicated that they have any coherent plan to return these refunds quickly and directly to consumers. Indeed, others have explicitly referred to these refunds as a boon to their bottom line–the CEO of multi-billion dollar furniture company Wayfair called the tariff refunds “sort of a one-time working capital benefit companies will get.” The CEO of Lowe’s told the press that the company didn’t plan to invest tariff refunds in lower consumer prices, instead preferring to boost shareholder earnings. Apparel company Levi Strauss said they would use most of their multi-million dollar tariff refund on holiday season marketing. Eyewear company Warby Parker described the company’s forays into artificial intelligence as “fully funded by the tariff benefits.”

Senator Warren wrote to six large, profitable corporations who had received multi-million dollar (or even billion-dollar) refunds and who had also increased their consumer prices after the imposition of tariffs. Not a single one of these corporations provided any assurance that they will actually pass along refunds directly to their consumers. Some companies provided evidence of their investment in their company’s U.S.-based development, and some provided vague assurances of lower prices in the future, but none indicated any plans to provide direct restitution to consumers who paid inflated prices due to IEEPA tariffs.

Walmart said they are “already putting [tariff refunds] to work for customers,” by “investing tariff refunds back into price leadership.” They did not quantify their pricing efforts or share figures indicating how much of their refund has been dedicated to lowering prices. Nike did not substantively respond to questions about how their tariff refund would be deployed. Apple pointed to their ambitious investment plans in the U.S. and indicated that tariff refund cash would be invested in those ventures, though they didn’t provide specific projects or numbers. Target pointed to a lack of price increases and upcoming holiday promotional prices rather than any plan to refund consumers, as well as planned investments in the U.S. Energizer admitted that “Beyond our disclosed expectation that the remaining refund balance will contribute to cash generation needed for the operation of and investment in our business, we have not identified any specific allocation” for tariff refunds.

These answers - or the silences in lieu of answers - are alarming. They indicate what appears to be a massive theft from the middle class, facilitated by the Trump Administration and giant corporations that raised prices for middle class consumers in response to Trump tariffs and now are now pocketing their refunds.

The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) has “a broad mandate to protect consumers from fraud and deception in the marketplace.” The Federal Trade Commission Act (FTC Act) outlaws “[u]nfair methods of competition in or affecting commerce, and unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce,” and the FTC is responsible for enforcing this statute on behalf of Americans. The FTC has found that conduct that is “exploitative,… abusive, deceptive, [or] predatory” may be investigated as an unfair method of competition. By increasing consumer prices, ostensibly due to tariff costs, and then refusing to provide refunds to consumers when they are later reimbursed for those tariff costs, corporations may be in violation of the FTC Act. This practice allows companies to increase prices, using tariffs as an excuse, with no accountability to consumers when those tariffs are struck down and refunded, and nothing consumers can do to right this wrong. Keeping the windfall from the tariff refunds could also give companies an unfair advantage over their competitors.

It is important that the FTC establish a precedent here that will prevent giant corporations from trying to rip off consumers on tariff-related matters. On the same day the Supreme Court struck down his IEEPA tariffs, President Trump imposed a blanket 10 percent tariff on nearly all imports under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974. In May, the Court of International Trade ruled that those tariffs were illegal, and the case currently sits pending before an appeals court. On July 20, 2026, President Trump invoked Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930—or the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act, most commonly known for its role in exacerbating the Great Depression—to impose 50 percent tariffs on a broad range of Canadian imports. Experts have called the President’s rationale for the tariffs “spurious,” “untested,” and “misapplied.” Just days later, on July 24, 2026, President Trump imposed yet another set of broad new tariffs, this time claiming authority under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. These tariffs have already drawn legal challenges from multiple groups of small businesses. And on August 23, the President announced a new set of tariffs on billions of dollars of imports from Canada, employing once again the Section 338 tariff authority that legal experts have called “untested” and “vague.”

Like the illegal IEEPA tariffs before them, the costs of these new but similarly chaotic tariffs will be borne by American consumers and small businesses. Despite the legal doubt surrounding the fate of these new tariffs, the Administration has refused to provide a plan as to how it would get refunds back to the American people in the event they are struck down. This means that consumers could once again be left with nothing as giant corporations pocket tariff refunds.

Given the magnitude of the costs of President Trump’s tariff chaos to consumers, we urge you to take action. The FTC should investigate whether companies that increased their prices due to IEEPA tariffs and then received tariff refunds which were not refunded to consumers violated federal law, including engaging in an unfair method of competition or an unfair or deceptive practice. The agency should act quickly to hold accountable any corporation that is ripping off consumers.

Thank you for your attention to this important matter.

Sincerely,

###

title: Sen. Banks Asks Navy to Award USS Indianapolis Battle Star
text:
Letter seeks to recognize the ship and its eligible crew for their final combat engagement

WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Senator Jim Banks (R-Ind.) called on the Navy to formally review whether USS Indianapolis (CA-35) and its eligible crew should receive a Battle Star, also known as an engagement star, for the ship’s final combat engagement.

In a letter to Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao, Banks said the ship’s sinking after a Japanese submarine attack on July 30, 1945, meets the Navy’s criteria for an engagement star. He asked the Department of the Navy to complete its review as promptly as possible, as Harold Bay, the last living survivor of the USS Indianapolis, is 99 years old.

Read the exclusive here:

Read the full letter here or below:

Dear Secretary Cao:

I write to request a formal review to award USS Indianapolis (CA-35) and her eligible crew a Battle Star, also known as an engagement star, for the ship’s final combat engagement on July 30, 1945.

After delivering components of the atomic bomb Little Boy to Tinian, later used on Hiroshima, USSIndianapolis was ordered from Guam to Leyte to join Task Group 95.7 for training. While transiting unescorted in the Philippine Sea, she was attacked by Japanese submarine I-58 and struck by two torpedoes. The ship sank in approximately 12 minutes. Of the 1,195 Sailors and Marines aboard, 879 died and only 316 survived.

The 1953 Navy and Marine Corps Awards Manual provides the relevant standard. It states that stars authorized for actual combat in operations and engagements, as authorized by the Chief of Naval Operations, “will be known as engagement stars.” The manual defines an “engagement” as “an action with the enemy taking place within a restricted time and area, and of sufficient intensity and significance to justify recognition.”

Based on that standard, USS Indianapolis meets the criteria for an engagement star. The sinking was an action with the enemy: Japanese submarine I-58 attacked and sank the ship. It occurred within a restricted time and area: the early morning of July 30, 1945, while USS Indianapolis was transiting from Guam to Leyte under Navy orders. It was of undeniable intensity and significance: two torpedoes sank the ship in minutes, and the sinking remains the deadliest single loss of life at sea in U.S. Navy history.

USS Arizona (BB-39) provides relevant precedent. She received Battle Star credit after being destroyed during the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor while moored in port, showing that enemy destruction of a ship can qualify for Battle Star recognition. USS Indianapolis was likewise destroyed by enemy action, after completing an essential national mission and while still operating under follow-on Navy orders.

Harold Bray, the last living survivor of USS Indianapolis, is 99 years old. Given Mr. Bray’s age and his status as the last living survivor, I respectfully request that the Department complete this review as promptly as possible. For these reasons, I believe USS Indianapolis and her eligible crew should be credited with a Battle Star/engagement star for the ship’s final combat engagement.

Thank you for your continued leadership and I look forward to working with you to ensure that the USS Indianapolis is properly recognized for its sacrifice.

###

title: Barrasso Applauds $207 Million in Funding for Wyoming Rural Healthcare
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Senator John Barrasso (R-Wyo.) released the following statement after the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) announced over $207 million in funding for Wyoming under year two of the Rural Health Transformation Program (RHTP):

“Wyoming is a rural state. We deserve access to local care that is affordable, reliable, and high-quality. That’s why I fought last year to create the Rural Health Transformation Program. In year one, Wyoming is using its $205 million award to give rural hospitals and rural providers tools to launch new initiatives, purchase equipment, and invest in upgraded technology. Those dollars are making an immediate impact to create regional partnerships, alleviate health professional shortages, improve chronic disease management, and upgrade aging infrastructure.

“Wyoming’s over $207 million year-two award gives the state financial freedom to invest in long-term rural health delivery system improvements. More funding will come to Wyoming over the next three years. Wyoming has proven it will use these dollars wisely to strengthen and expand access to medical care in every corner of our state.”

Senator Barrasso joined Wyoming Governor Mark Gordon and healthcare leaders from across the state last month to announce Wyoming’s year-one RHTP awardees. Supported projects will help fund critical access hospitals, EMS services, and other rural healthcare services across Wyoming.

Background:

Congressional Republicans delivered the largest federal investment in rural health care in American history. The Working Families Tax Cut Act created the Rural Health Transformation Program (RHTP). RHTP provides a total of $50 billion to be allocated to the States over five fiscal years. Each year CMS awards $10 billion, beginning in fiscal year 2026 and ending in fiscal year 2030. Annual reporting and quarterly state data submissions help CMS monitor state plan implementation progress against the approved application goals.

As of October 2026, funding allocations, competitive applications, and awards have been completed for year one of Wyoming’s $205 million Rural Health Transformation Program (RHTP).

In year two of the RHTP, Wyoming will advance rural health initiatives from its state-developed transformation plan. Wyoming’s federally approved RHTP plan consists of four major initiatives.

title: Bennet, Duckworth, Colleagues Introduce Bill to Ensure Iran War Veterans Are Covered Under PACT Act
text:
Denver — Colorado U.S. Senator Michael Bennet, a member of the Senate Intelligence Committee, joined Senator Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.) and 11 of their Senate colleagues in introducing new legislation to ensure veterans of President Trump’s illegal and reckless Iran war can be covered under the PACT Act, which Bennet helped pass in August 2022. The New PACT for Iran Veterans Act will cut unnecessary red tape and make it easier for our servicemembers who have been exposed to toxic substances to access critical treatment when they return home.

Passage of the PACT Act helped generations of veterans — from Vietnam to Iraq — more easily receive care from the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) by establishing a list of locations where it is presumed by law that troops who served there were exposed to toxic hazards. Iran is not, however, currently included on this presumed-exposure list, despite troops serving in the Iran war being exposed to many of the same hazards. The New PACT for Iran Veterans Act would require the VA to add Iran to the list of covered locations and take more proactive action to ensure Iran veterans — and all veterans who serve in future conflicts — do not have to jump through bureaucratic hoops in order to access the care they’ve earned through their service.

“For too long, veterans exposed to toxic substances during their service have had to fight for the care and benefits they earned. The PACT Act was a historic step toward correcting that failure,” said Bennet. “We have a responsibility to ensure the men and women serving today in President Trump’s reckless Iran war do not face those same barriers when they come home. Congress must act now to ensure all future veterans can access their hard-earned health care and benefits without having to fight the VA.”

“By establishing the landmark PACT Act, our nation finally helped generations of Veterans who suffered from toxic exposure in Vietnam, Iraq and Afghanistan more easily access the care they needed after being stonewalled by bureaucratic tape for years,” said Duckworth. “With a new generation of troops being thrown into another war in the Middle East, our nation must learn the lessons from previous conflicts and proactively ensure Iran Veterans don’t suffer from those same mistakes. Our New PACT for Iran Veterans Act would ensure no servicemember fights a war overseas only to come home and be faced with another battle to get the care they’ve rightfully earned through their service. Congress must act to care for these heroes now—not later.”

“The cost of war includes providing health care and benefits to veterans exposed to toxins during their military service,” said Blumenthal. “This legislation would build on the PACT Act to ensure all servicemembers sent into harm’s way, including recent veterans of the war with Iran, are able to receive the benefits they deserve.”

“Our veterans deserve access to prompt, timely healthcare – regardless of the conflict and country where they serve for our country,” said King. “Just as the PACT Act represented a historical milestone for Vietnam, Iraq, and Afghanistan veterans, our New PACT for Iran Veterans Act will ensure that the VA recognizes the unique current toxic exposure risks of our service members sacrifice and guarantee they receive the support they have earned, without delay.”

“The bipartisan PACT Act marked a historic step in ensuring that veterans and servicemembers exposed to toxic substances can get the care they need and deserve,” said Welch. “But President Trump’s reckless decision to throw our country into war in the Middle East means there’s a new generation of veterans facing conditions that could be hazardous to their health. We need to update our pact to servicemembers to ensure that Iran War Servicemembers and Veterans aren’t faced with red tape to get proper benefits and care once they come home.”

“Donald Trump might not care, but the cost of war includes supporting our veterans when they come back home,” said Murray. “This legislation is a commonsense next step to expand the PACT Act to make sure our servicemembers who served in Iran continue to receive the care they need after their service is over. As I continue fighting to end the war—I want to be crystal clear that I won’t let this President leave American veterans in the dust.”

“As federal law, the historic PACT Act resulted in over 115,000 claims filed in Pennsylvania so veterans exposed to toxins could rightfully get the care they need. Servicemembers currently in the Middle East supporting our mission in Iran will not be eligible to file claims,” said Fetterman. “We need to change that through this bill, uphold our end of the sacred promise to those who answered the call to serve, and ensure future veterans are not subjected to the same delays as those before them.”

“American soldiers suffering after toxic exposure overseas should never have to second guess if they’ll get the support they need when they come home,” said Wyden. “Our country has a duty to care for veterans of all wars, and I’m proud to stand with Senator Duckworth to help make this commonsense legislation the law of the land.”

“Since we first championed the PACT Act four years ago, an estimated 90,000 Washington veterans have already filed claims to secure treatment for exposure to toxic substances,” said Cantwell. “The New PACT for Iran Veterans Act is a critical next step in this work, eliminating barriers to healthcare and disability compensation for veterans of the war with Iran and beyond.”

Specifically, the New PACT for Iran Veterans Act would:

Cut red tape for Iran war veterans by statutorily presuming toxic substance exposure for Iran veterans, helping streamline their access to health care and benefits at the VA. The bill would ensure that federal law protects all veterans who fought in Iran, including those who operated in Iranian airspace and territorial waters.

Leave no veteran behind by requiring, for the first time, that the VA’s Military Environmental Exposure Sub-Council (MEESC) conducts studies at least every five years to review all overseas assignments for toxic substance exposures. Additionally, when the military begins a contingency operation, the VA must commence a similar review of the locations from which servicemembers support this operation within 180 days. This would ensure the VA proactively looks into whether servicemembers are being exposed to toxic hazards, for current and future assignments.

Enhance transparency at the VA by requiring the VA Secretary publicly explain their justification for any denial of a country that’s recommended for presumed toxic-exposures in these reviews, or any removal of existing presumptions.

The legislation is endorsed by Disabled American Veterans, Iraq and Afghanistan Veterans of America (IAVA), Paralyzed Veterans of America, VoteVets, Veterans of Foreign Wars, and the American Legion.

“The PACT Act was a historic victory for veterans, but there is still much work to be done to ensure no veteran is left behind,” said Dr. Kyleanne Hunter, CEO of IAVA. “We have repeatedly raised concerns about how changes to the classification of military operations and service members can have unintended consequences for veterans’ access to earned benefits. Senator Duckworth’s legislation takes an important step toward closing these gaps by expanding recognition of toxic exposure, requiring proactive reviews of overseas military locations, and strengthening transparency and accountability at VA. IAVA is proud to support this effort to ensure veterans’ service and potential exposures are not overlooked simply because of how or where they served.”

“After Iraq and Afghanistan, veterans who came home sick from toxic exposure had to spend years fighting for their care,” said VoteVets senior advisor, Major General (Ret.) Paul Eaton. “Iran war veterans shouldn’t have to. The New PACT for Iran Veterans Act gets them covered now, not decades from now. Congress should pass it without delay.”

Bennet has worked tirelessly with Colorado’s military community to ensure veterans can access the benefits and care they earned for themselves and their families. Bennet helped pass the first PACT Act, expanding VA health care eligibility to over 3.5 million toxic-exposed veterans. In June, Bennet introduced legislation holding claims sharks and other predatory actors accountable for exploiting veterans’ and survivors’ earned benefits from the VA. In April, Bennet celebrated the Senate Veterans Affairs Committee’s passage of legislation to expand research on birth defects among descendants of toxic-exposed veterans. Bennet is also a co-sponsor of the Major Richard Star Act to provide combat-injured veteran retirees their full benefits and continues to fight for its passage.

In addition to Bennet and Duckworth, U.S. Senators Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), Angus King (I-Maine), Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.), Peter Welch (D-Vt.), Patty Murray (D-Wash.), John Fetterman (D-Penn.), Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), Maria Cantwell (D-Was.), Angela Alsobrooks (D-Md.) and Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) cosponsored this legislation.

title: Bennet Leads Senate Agriculture Democrats to Demand USDA Withdraw Proposed Rule Restricting Food Assistance
text:
Denver— Colorado U.S. Senator Michael Bennet, a senior member of the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry, along with Senators John Fetterman (D-Pa.) and Ben Ray Lujan (D-N.M.), led Senators Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.), Tina Smith (D-Minn.), Dick Durbin (D-IlI.), Cory Booker (D-N.J.), Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.), Peter Welch (D-Vt.), Adam Schiff (D-Calif.), and Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) in urging the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) to withdraw its proposed rule restricting Broad-Based Categorical Eligibility (BBCE) under the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) that will severely narrow eligibility requirements for the nation’s largest anti-hunger program.

“We write to strongly urge the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) to withdraw its proposed rule restricting Broad-Based Categorical Eligibility (BBCE) under the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP). Should this rule take effect, an estimated 6.3 million Americans, including many seniors and nearly 1.8 million children, would lose SNAP benefits according to the USDA’s own analysis. At a time when everyday Americans are already struggling to afford groceries, USDA should not be making changes to SNAP that leave families with fewer resources to meet their basic needs,” began the senators.

Broad-Based Categorical Eligibility helps working families and seniors afford groceries at a time when the rising costs of housing, child care, health care, and other necessities are stretching household budgets. It gives states flexibility to help low-income households access food assistance while supporting work and financial stability. Without BBCE, families could lose SNAP benefits even when they are still struggling to make ends meet. It also allows families and seniors to build and maintain modest savings without jeopardizing their access to food assistance. Protections like these are critical not only to ensure struggling Americans meet their basic needs, but also to help these individuals build toward greater financial mobility.

This proposed rule would also make SNAP more challenging and costly for states to administer, increasing paperwork, the risk of payment errors, and demands on state workers. These added burdens come as states are already absorbing a larger share of SNAP administrative expenses under The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, leaving states with fewer resources to manage these additional requirements.

The consequences would extend beyond SNAP. Children in households that lose SNAP eligibility could also lose automatic certification for free school meals, requiring families to submit additional applications to establish eligibility and creating more administrative work for schools. This added red tape could prevent eligible children from receiving meals and reduce federal reimbursements for schools, threatening efforts to provide free school meals to all students. The proposal could also create additional red tape for families seeking assistance through the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC), potentially leaving some families unable to access benefits and others ineligible for assistance altogether.

“In the proposed rule, USDA repeatedly claims that it is aligning SNAP rules with congressional intent, but the legislative history clearly demonstrates otherwise. Congress established categorical eligibility to simplify access to food assistance and preserved this framework when it created Temporary Assistance for Needy Families in 1996. States have relied on this flexibility for decades to serve low-income households and administer SNAP more efficiently. Congress subsequently considered proposals to eliminate or restrict BBCE during the 2005 reconciliation debate and the 2014 and 2018 Farm Bill negotiations, but these restrictions were ultimately rejected on a bipartisan basis and excluded from the final legislation. While maintaining SNAP eligibility for 6.3 million Americans who need it should be reason enough, the fact that this proposed rule is contrary to congressional intent and the law is another reason it should be withdrawn,” continued the senators.

“Children should not go hungry, seniors should not have to spend down their savings to afford groceries, and working families should not lose assistance while they are still struggling to make ends meet. USDA’s proposal would put these families at greater risk while adding costs and complications for states. We urge USDA to withdraw the proposed rule in its entirety,” concluded the senators.

Bennet is a vocal advocate for SNAP and has tirelessly fought the Trump Administration’s numerous efforts to use hunger as a political weapon. Last month, Bennet visited the Food Bank of the Rockies to hear how the Trump Administration’s historic SNAP cuts are pushing Colorado families to rely on food pantries. In August 2026, Bennet fought to protect vital Colorado SNAP funding in the 2026 Farm Bill during a Senate Agriculture Committee business meeting. In April 2026, he also joined U.S. Senators Jim Justice (R-W.V.), John Fetterman (D-Pa.), and Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.V.) to introduce the Hot Rotisserie Chicken Act, which would allow SNAP participants to purchase hot rotisserie chicken with their benefits.

In October 2025, Bennet and Senator John Hickenlooper (D-Colo.) called on USDA Secretary Brooke Rollins to release billions of dollars in funding to ensure SNAP benefits continued during the shutdown. Despite this, the Trump Administration illegally withheld funding for SNAP, leaving millions of Americans unsure whether they would receive the benefits they need to put food on the table. In November 2025, Bennet and Hickenlooper joined the entire Senate Democratic Caucus to introduce the Restoring Food Security for American Families and Farmers Act, which would repeal all the devastating Republican cuts to SNAP made in the Republican One Big Beautiful Bill Act. That same month, Bennet and Hickenlooper joined the Senate Democratic Caucus to introduce the Keep SNAP and WIC Funded Act, legislation to protect Americans’ food access while the Trump Administration illegally withheld available funds. Bennet and Hickenlooper also introduced a resolution in November 2025 calling on Senate Republicans to force President Trump to immediately use all congressionally approved funding to keep families from going hungry.

The text of the letter is available HERE and below.

Dear Secretary Rollins:

We write to strongly urge the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) to withdraw its proposed rule restricting Broad-Based Categorical Eligibility (BBCE) under the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP). Should this rule take effect, an estimated 6.3 million Americans, including many seniors and nearly 1.8 million children, would lose SNAP benefits according to the USDA’s own analysis. At a time when everyday Americans are already struggling to afford groceries, USDA should not be making changes to SNAP that leave families with fewer resources to meet their basic needs.

The costs of housing, utilities, child care, health care, and other necessities are leaving working families and seniors on fixed incomes with little money left for food. BBCE helps these households access food while supporting work and financial stability. Without it, a working family could lose SNAP benefits entirely after a modest raise, even when the additional earnings are not enough to replace the assistance it loses. BBCE allows states to prevent this abrupt cutoff so that families can continue receiving assistance as their earnings increase and their SNAP benefits gradually decline. It also allows low-income families and seniors to maintain modest emergency savings without losing assistance. These protections help people meet their basic needs while building assets and working toward greater financial security and economic mobility. This flexibility has been embraced by leaders of both parties and is now used in 43 states, the District of Columbia, Guam, and the U.S. Virgin Islands.

Beyond the direct harm to families, the proposal would make SNAP more difficult and expensive for states to administer. Most states use BBCE to raise or eliminate SNAP’s restrictive and complex federal asset test, reducing paperwork and the potential for payment errors. Reinstating these tests would require households to provide additional financial verification and place significant new demands on state workers. According to an analysis by the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, asset-related errors added approximately one percentage point, on average, to SNAP payment error rates in states that retained asset tests in fiscal year 2023. Under H.R. 1, which ties states’ share of SNAP benefit costs to their payment error rates, even a small increase could push states into higher cost-sharing tiers. With states already absorbing a larger share of SNAP administrative expenses, this proposal would impose new burdens while leaving them with fewer resources to manage those demands.

The effects would also reach well beyond SNAP. Children in households that lose SNAP eligibility would lose their SNAP-based automatic certification for free school meals, requiring families without another automatic eligibility pathway to submit additional applications and schools to verify eligibility. This would add unnecessary red tape for families and schools and increase the risk that eligible children miss out on meals. Fewer children directly certified through SNAP would also put federal school meal reimbursements at risk, particularly for schools participating in the Community Eligibility Provision. USDA’s own analysis warns that declining federal reimbursements could threaten the financial viability of state efforts to provide free school meals, such as universal breakfast and lunch programs in Colorado and New Mexico and universal free breakfast in Pennsylvania. The proposal would also complicate access to the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC), requiring some families to provide additional income documentation and leaving others ineligible for assistance altogether.

In the proposed rule, USDA repeatedly claims that it is aligning SNAP rules with congressional intent, but the legislative history clearly demonstrates otherwise. Congress established categorical eligibility to simplify access to food assistance and preserved this framework when it created Temporary Assistance for Needy Families in 1996. States have relied on this flexibility for decades to serve low-income households and administer SNAP more efficiently. Congress subsequently considered proposals to eliminate or restrict BBCE during the 2005 reconciliation debate and the 2014 and 2018 Farm Bill negotiations, but these restrictions were ultimately rejected on a bipartisan basis and excluded from the final legislation. While maintaining SNAP eligibility for 6.3 million Americans who need it should be reason enough, the fact that this proposed rule is contrary to congressional intent and the law is another reason it should be withdrawn.

Children should not go hungry, seniors should not have to spend down their savings to afford groceries, and working families should not lose assistance while they are still struggling to make ends meet. USDA’s proposal would put these families at greater risk while adding costs and complications for states. We urge USDA to withdraw the proposed rule in its entirety.

title: Senator Blumenthal: Week in Review 11/6/2026-11/13/2026
text:
Honoring Veterans Day

[WASHINGTON, D.C.] – U.S. Senator Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), incoming Chairman of the Senate Veterans’ Affairs Committee, released the follow statement to commemorate Veterans Day:

“We should be forever grateful—and proudly express it—to the brave veterans who served and sacrificed to defend our nation. On Veterans Day, we say thank you and reflect on the promises made to these men and women. Today and every day, I will fight to make sure we keep these promises and provide veterans and their families the support, care, and benefits they earned and deserve.”

Blumenthal attended ceremonies honoring veterans and their sacrifice in service of our country across the state of Connecticut—including Derby, New Haven, Stamford, and Middletown.

“Derby marked Veterans Day on its historic Green—with enduring gratitude to all who’ve served. A beautiful sunfilled day,” wrote Blumenthal on Twitter/X.

“New Haven’s Veterans Day Ceremony featured music & memorials—tributes to all who have served & sacrificed. We’re the land of the free because we’re the home of the brave,” wrote Blumenthal on Twitter/X.

“Stamford’s Vets Day Parade Sunday brought out dedicated marchers—& great crowds. Thank you all!” wrote Blumenthal on Twitter/X.

“Hauntingly beautiful & serene, the Middletown Veterans Cemetery was the site of CT’s statewide Veterans Day ceremony. Taps played, as shadows lengthened over the headstones,” wrote Blumenthal on Twitter/X.

Demanding Accountability from Trump Administration in Face of Baseless Intimidation Attempt

Blumenthal, incoming Chair of the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, released the following statement in response to a letter he received from the U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Texas:

“The Trump Administration is so afraid of transparency and oversight that they are weaponizing the Department of Justice to baselessly target Congress in direct violation of the Constitution. As incoming Chair of the Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, I will not be intimidated, and I will work on behalf of the American people to vigorously pursue investigations into this Administration's persistent misuse of taxpayer dollars and any corporate entity that has enabled their boundless corruption.”

In response to this baseless threat from the Department of Justice, Blumenthal demanded the Trump-appointed U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Texas preserve all records and correspondence, including with the White House or senior Department of Justice officials, related to the Administration’s efforts to protect corporate donors and Administration officials from legitimate oversight.

“I am aware of your letter, posted to X today, which purports to initiate an investigation into me for conducting a congressional inquiry. This is just the latest in a series of unlawful actions on the part of the Trump Administration attempting to intimidate Members of Congress for engaging in constitutionally protected activity. Your implied threat of an investigation is baseless,” wrote Blumenthal.

Blumenthal continued, “The public deserves to know the terms under which dozens of American companies were persuaded to donate millions of dollars to the President’s vanity projects, and whether lawsuits were dismissed, contracts were awarded, or regulations went unenforced in exchange for that money. The public deserves transparency about whether the White House and the corporations it cajoled extracted favors at the expense of American taxpayers. Not only are these appropriate subjects for congressional oversight, but such inquiries are among the constitutional duties that Members of Congress must undertake to become informed about matters on which legislation may be necessary.”

“Since you appear to have evidence of the Trump Administration’s efforts to protect corporate donors and Administration officials from legitimate oversight, I accordingly direct you to preserve all records and correspondence, including all communications with the White House or senior officials at the Department of Justice, related to the decision to draft and post your letter,” Blumenthal concluded.

Blumenthal has led an inquiry into the waste, fraud, and abuse associated with the White House ballroom and other projects throughout the nation’s capital. Blumenthal recently wrote to Big Tech companies and others who may be seeking pay-to-play government favors from their donations to President Trump’s White House ballroom and other projects, reminding recipients of the Subcommittee’s expectation for their prompt cooperation.

The full text of the letter is available here.

Blumenthal further highlighted his letter on Twitter/X.

“This investigation into me for conducting a congressional inquiry is just the latest in a series of unlawful actions on the part of the Trump Admin attempting to intimidate Members of Congress for engaging in constitutionally protected activity. The implied threat of an investigation is baseless. As incoming Chair of the Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, I will not be intimidated. The public deserves transparency about whether the White House & the corporations it cajoled extracted favors at the expense of American taxpayers. Not only are these appropriate subjects for congressional oversight, but such inquiries are among the constitutional duties that Members of Congress must undertake to become informed about matters on which legislation may be necessary,” wrote Blumenthal on Twitter/X.

Blumenthal also joined MS NOW and CNN to discuss his letter to the U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Texas and to highlight the need for proper oversight into Trump’s vanity projects.

“Americans deserve the truth about potential misuse of taxpayer dollars & corporate corruption involved in Trump's vanity projects. Instead of targeting corruption, Trump's DOJ is trying to intimidate investigators attempting to carry out oversight—I joined MS NOW to discuss,” wrote Blumenthal on Twitter/X.

The full MS NOW interview can be found here. The full CNN interview can be found here.

Blumenthal further emphasized his efforts to carry out oversight over the Trump Administration’s brazen corruption on Twitter/X.

“I’m taking action to uncover Trump admin corruption. DOJ is threatening to investigate me because of it. I won’t be intimidated or stop working to uncover the pay-to-play schemes, dropped regulation, or misuse of taxpayer dollars,” wrote Blumenthal with an accompanying video on Twitter/X.

Slamming the Trump Administration for Withholding Funding for Trafficking Survivors

Blumenthal, a member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, released a damning new report revealing that the Trump Administration has failed to award approximately $133.5 million in anti-human trafficking grant funding – about 75 percent of what Congress has appropriated for the last two years – forcing programs that support trafficking victims to shut down or dramatically reduce their services.

This shocking withholding of funding follows the Administration allowing about $190 million in anti-human trafficking grants to lapse, including approximately $140 million that was previously dedicated to direct services for survivors of human trafficking and $16 million that was previously dedicated to supporting law enforcement’s ability to investigate and prosecute trafficking crimes.

“This report is sickening— and it should shock the conscience of every Administration official and lawmaker who claims to support trafficking survivors,” Blumenthal said. “From the botched release of the Epstein Files to withholding funding to support survivors and prosecute sex crimes, the Trump Administration has shown exactly how little it cares about victims of trafficking. Whether the Trump Administration has withheld these funds out of malice or pure incompetence is immaterial. What matters are the tens of thousands of victims and survivors who are suffering without it. I am demanding that this funding be released immediately and the Trump Administration provide me – and survivors – with a clear commitment that these services will not be allowed to lapse again.”

“Please consider what losing this program’s funding would mean for the people whose lives depend on it. I have worked hard to build this life, but I could not have done it alone. This program helped me become a mother who could bring her son home, a person with a career, and someone who could believe in herself again,” said an anonymous survivor who is quoted in the report. “Without it, I would not be where I am today. Losing it could put everything I have built at risk, including my life. I am only one of many survivors with something to lose—and there are others still waiting for the chance to heal.”

The Department of Justice (DOJ) Office for Victims of Crime (OVC) is the primary entity overseeing grant programs that provide funding to organizations fighting human trafficking and supporting survivors. Providers who receive funding through OVC grant programs serve more than 10,000 human trafficking survivors quarterly, including children. As a result of the Trump Administration’s mismanagement and withholding of grant funding, service providers have been forced to close or drastically downsize their programming, with dire consequences for survivors:

A wraparound program helping youth who have been trafficked for sex could not accommodate all of the children referred for services and was forced to put them on a waitlist. In disclosing that they do not have the resources to work with all the children who approach them for help, this provider said that it resulted in children “being further exploited.”

A transitional housing program that provided no-cost housing and services to support survivors in healing, securing permanent housing, and finding employment was shuttered because the provider could not pay the rent or the staff after funding lapsed. The program served over a dozen survivors annually with housing and full therapeutic support. It had a proven history of success—almost every survivor graduated from the program successfully, building a stable life and avoiding a return to trafficking.

A program providing no-cost counseling, behavioral healthcare services, and vocational training will close in January 2027 without federal funding. While the service provider has managed to fill the gaps following the lapse of federal grants, it will no longer be able to do so in less than two months. Unless funding is released, the program will close its doors to the 100 human trafficking survivors it serves each year and lay off its staff—including peer support personnel who themselves are survivors of trafficking.

A transitional housing program will likely face closure if funding is not released. It provides 24/7 support and no-cost housing to at least five human trafficking survivors annually. Most are survivors of sex trafficking, and many were sold for sex while still minors. Many survivors enter the program with substance use disorders, PTSD, and other severe mental illness, and therefore rely not only on the program’s housing but also on its addiction recovery and mental health support services. The program is incredibly successful—90 percent of the participants successfully graduate into permanent housing of their own.

Blumenthal wrote Brecht Donoghue, Director of the OVC Human Trafficking Division at DOJ, demanding that the Administration release the funding immediately and provide an explanation for its lapse.

“President Trump purports to care about survivors of human trafficking—he claims his Administration is committed “to end[ing] the evil of human trafficking” and that he is “working tirelessly” to “end the scourge of human trafficking once and for all.” It is shocking that an Administration that has claimed to prioritize stopping the “scourge of human trafficking” has instead caused a two-thirds reduction in the OVC funding available to the anti-trafficking field,” Blumenthal wrote.

“But perhaps this total disregard for human trafficking survivors should not come as a surprise from the Administration that not only fought the enactment of and then failed to fully comply with the Epstein Files Transparency Act but also repeatedly retraumatized survivors through its botched file release. Put simply, human trafficking survivors deserve so much better from their government.”

The text of Blumenthal’s letter to Donoghue is available here.

Blumenthal further highlighted his report and letter to Donoghue on Twitter/X.

“My damning new report reveals that the Trump admin has failed to award approximately $133.5 million in anti-human trafficking grant funding—about 75% of what Congress appropriated for the last 2 years—forcing programs to shut down or reduce services. Whether the Trump admin has withheld these funds out of malice or pure incompetence is immaterial. What matters are the tens of thousands of victims & survivors who are suffering without it.I am demanding this funding be released immediately & the Trump admin provide me—& survivors—with a clear commitment that this funding will not be allowed to lapse again,” wrote Blumenthal on Twitter/X.

Blumenthal pressed Arthur Kleinschmidt, nominee to be Assistant Attorney General for the Office of Justice Programs, on the approximately $190 million in anti-human trafficking grant funding that has lapsed under the Trump Administration and the over $130 million that the Trump Administration has failed to award to replace it. If confirmed, Kleinschmidt would head the Department of Justice’s principal grantmaking office, the Office of Justice Programs, which oversees these funds.

During their exchange, Blumenthal secured a commitment from Kleinschmidt that, if confirmed, he will release all the currently withheld funds to combat the scourge of human trafficking.

“You must be aware that the Trump Administration has allowed about $190 million in anti-human trafficking grants to lapse, and it has withheld about 75% of money appropriated by the United States Congress for groups that aid victims of human trafficking. It is about $130 million that should be going to support human trafficking survivors and strengthen law enforcement's ability to fight trafficking crime,” said Blumenthal. “Will you commit, if confirmed, to release all of the anti-trafficking funds currently withheld by the Trump Administration?”

“I am going work diligently to get these resources from the Office of Justice Programs,” answered Kleinschmidt.

“Is that a yes, you will release the money?” pressed Blumenthal.

“I'm going to be committed to addressing and getting the funds to those Americans who need them the most, yes sir. I’m going to work and do and follow all the stipulations and guidelines to get our taxpayer dollars—be a good shepherd of the taxpayer dollars—to get those resources, human trafficking victims and other victims of crime, to ensure that Americans stay safe.” said Kleinschmidt.

“I'm going to take that as a yes, that you will release the money. I'm going to hold you to it. I think our United States Congress should hold you to it because human trafficking is a scourge, and the victims deserve all of the money and more that Congress has appropriated for this purpose,” said Blumenthal.

A video of Blumenthal’s round of questioning can be found here.

On the Senate Veterans’ Affairs Committee

Blumenthal released the following statement after House Republicans abused House procedure to pass the Take Care of America’s Veterans Act by voice vote on Veterans Day. This controversial veterans’ legislation would cut nearly $57 billion in veterans’ benefits for veterans with sleep apnea and tinnitus.

“House Republicans resorted to a blatant abuse of established procedure—bypassing a fair vote—to sneak the biggest cut to veterans’ benefits in American history. This disrespect and deduction to well-deserved disability compensation is totally unacceptable, most especially on Veterans Day. Such secretive and shameful tactics are condemnable. Make no mistake—their disgusting slash to veterans’ benefits will be defeated in the Senate.”

In July, House Republicans cancelled a planned vote on the Take Care of America’s Veterans Act, following a bipartisan House vote to replace the Republican benefit cuts with a proposal to utilize unobligated Department of Defense funds. Congressional Democrats and Veterans Service Organizations have publicly opposed the Republican funding proposal included in the Take Care of America’s Veterans Act.

Blumenthal along with U.S. Senator Patty Murray (D-WA), Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY), and House Veterans’ Affairs Committee Ranking Member Mark Takano (D-CA) led more than 200 Senate and House Democrats in filing an amicus brief to Minority Veterans of America v. Secretary of Veterans Affairs, a lawsuit challenging the Trump Administration’s abortion ban at the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA).

The lawsuit, pending before the US Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit, seeks to overturn VA’s ban on abortion care and counseling. In the brief, the lawmakers argue the Trump Administration’s 2025 policy banning abortion counseling and abortion care in almost all cases rests on a flawed legal premise.

“VA’s Final Rule rests on a faulty interpretation of federal law that has significant negative consequences for our nation’s veterans. The issues presented in this case potentially reach roughly 462,000 women veterans of reproductive age who are enrolled in VA health care, along with an estimated 112,000 women of reproductive age enrolled in the Civilian Health and Medical Program of the Department of Veterans Affairs (CHAMPVA),” the members wrote.

The members continued, “For them, the Final Rule means a VA physician is prohibited from discussing the full range of a patient’s options during a pregnancy, prohibited from providing the full range of health care available to pregnant women, and is prohibited from intervening when a pregnancy threatens the patient’s health or is the result of rape or incest.”

VA’s abortion ban, implemented by the Trump Administration in 2025, prohibits abortion counseling and care for veterans and CHAMPVA beneficiaries—even in cases of rape, incest, or if a veteran’s health is endangered. The lawmakers argue in the brief that VA’s erroneous interpretation of federal law means these women now cannot receive abortion care or counseling even in the most harrowing circumstances. They also argue the Veterans’ Health Care Eligibility Reform Act of 1996 allows VA to provide any medical services the Secretary “determines to be needed” and that the Veterans Health Care Act of 1992, which VA used to justify its abortion ban, does not restrict the Secretary’s authority to add abortion care to its medical benefits package.

In the Senate, the amicus brief was signed by all 47 Democratic U.S. Senators. In the House, the brief was signed by 165 Democratic U.S. Representatives.

In March, all present Democratic Senators voted in support of Senator Blumenthal’s Congressional Review Act (CRA) resolution to overturn the Trump Administration’s policy ending abortion counseling entirely and abortion care for veterans in cases of rape, incest, or health endangerment. A CRA resolution is an oversight tool Congress can use to overturn final rules issued by federal agencies with a simple majority vote. The vote failed 48-50 due to lack of adequate Republican support, leaving VA’s abortion ban in place. While the CRA resolution did not receive a vote in the House, it garnered the support of 155 Democratic cosponsors.

In September 2022, VA began to offer abortion counseling to all pregnant veterans and CHAMPVA beneficiaries, and abortion care in cases of rape, incest, or life or health endangerment of the veteran or CHAMPVA beneficiary. This was in response to the Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization ruling, which created urgent risks to the lives and health of pregnant veterans and CHAMPVA beneficiaries in states that banned or otherwise severely restricted access to abortion. VA’s dangerous abortion ban means that veterans nationwide now face those same risks.

More than 462,000 veterans of reproductive age are enrolled in VA health care, and more than 112,000 women of reproductive age are enrolled in CHAMPVA. More than half of these women live in states that have enacted abortion bans or restrictions.

The amicus brief can be read in full here.
