title: Release: Representative Ro Khanna’s Free Child Care for America Act Endorsed by Over 50 Childcare Groups Across the Country
text:
Washington, DC — Representative Ro Khanna (CA-17), introduced the Free Child Care for America Actto begin building a universal child care system that works for families no matter how they choose to care for their children.

The Act creates three pathways for families. Families with children under age 6 and not yet in kindergarten can access free care at participating licensed child care providers if their income is at or below the greater of 200 percent of their State median income or $250,000. Parents with children under 3 and household incomes at or below 100 percent of State median income can instead receive $1,000 per month per child to stay home and provide care themselves. And families at or below 100 percent of State median income can have a family member, friend, or neighbor they trust paid to provide care, with payment rates designed to support a living wage.

Critically, the legislation does not simply give families more purchasing power it also builds the child care supply families need but cannot find today. Title I invests $78 billion annually to help meet the operating costs necessary for providers to operate sustainably, provide free care to eligible families, and raise child care worker pay to a local living wage. Dedicated Facilities, Home-Based Child Care, and Innovation Funds invest in new and existing facilities, help home-based providers grow, and develop and scale new models of care.

The Act also invests in the people who make child care possible. It establishes wage and benefit ladders, requires wage supplements sufficient to bring child care worker pay to an area living wage, invests in education and professional development so workers can build careers in child care, protects organizing rights, and gives States a pathway to establish collective bargaining rights for self-employed family child care providers and Family, Friend, and Neighbor caregivers.

Taken together, the Free Child Care for America Act addresses affordability, supply, and the child care workforce at the same time while giving families the freedom to choose the care arrangement that works for them.

The Free Child Care for America Act has been endorsed by over 50 groups across the country. To view the full list, click here.

“This legislation addresses the real needs of families in three ways: childcare is defined broadly to include family, neighbors, parents, and centers; childcare providers—who are often parents themselves—will be better paid, valuing care work as the essential career path it is; and all forms of childcare will be more affordable. The result is that, for all who qualify, providers make more money, parents keep more money because care is affordable, and parents get a real choice about who, how, and where their children are cared for. We’re thrilled to see a policy that pulls two critical levers at once—making care affordable, and building up care work in flexible ways that support families’ varying needs and stages. This is the kind of legislation America needs to solve its childcare crisis, and we throw our full support behind it as an organization,” said Erin Erenberg, Chief Executive Officer, Chamber of Mothers.

“For too long, the millions of grandparents, aunts, uncles, and trusted neighbors who form the invisible backbone of our nation’s child care system have been left completely out of the child care policy conversation. The Free Child Care for America Act is a historic step forward because it finally recognizes and invests in Family, Friend, and Neighbor (FFN) care. By building a dedicated $5 billion annual program to support these essential caregivers with fair compensation, free training, and safety resources, this bill doesn't just lower costs for parents—it builds a child care system that meets families exactly where they are,” said Natalie Renew, Home Grown Executive Director.

“The Childcare for America Act recognizes that America’s child care crisis is both a cost crisis and an access crisis, and gives families the flexibility and a pathway to choose the solution that works best for them. For small businesses, these options can mean fewer employees forced to cut hours, leave the workforce, or turn down jobs because they cannot find or afford reliable care. By making child care more affordable and available while supporting the care economy, this bill would strengthen the workforce that small businesses depend on and help keep dollars circulating in local communities. Main Street Alliance is proud to support the Childcare for America Act as an important down payment on a child care system that works for families, workers, and small businesses alike,” said Lauren Bealore, National Director of Policy & Programs, Main Street Alliance.

“Congressman Ro Khanna's Free Child Care for America Act recognizes that care giving is the foundation of a strong family. Strong families make strong communities. Expanding access to childcare gives every family the freedom to pursue opportunities knowing their children are supported and safe. And helps all of us thrive. Danny Mercer,” said Vice President The National At-Home Dad Network."

“Child care is an affordability issue, a workforce issue, and an economic security issue. Here in Pennsylvania, child care shortages alone are costing our Commonwealth an estimated $6.65 billion every year in lost earnings, productivity, and revenue, while families struggle to find and afford care and providers struggle to keep classrooms open and pay the workers who care for our children what they deserve. The Pennsylvania Policy Center is proud to support the Free Child Care for America Act because families should not have to choose between earning a living and finding safe, quality care for their children. By lowering costs, investing in the child care workforce, expanding the supply of care, and recognizing that families need different options, from child care centers to trusted family caregivers to parents caring for their own young children, this legislation treats child care as the essential economic infrastructure it is,” said Felicity A. Williams, Esq., Executive Director, Pennsylvania Policy Center.

"Rep. Khanna's Free Child Care For America Act sets a new standard for child care legislation. By offering parents a real choice to move between free high-quality licensed programs, trusted care provided by family members or close friends, and care from parents themselves, this bill supports parents with the freedom to raise their kids as they prefer while providing for their households. Doing so strengthens local communities and the national economy; all Americans benefit when our families and children have a strong start,” said Elliot Haspel, child care policy expert and author of Raising a Nation: 10 Reasons Every American Has a Stake in Child Care for All.

“Too often, D.C. politicians offer little but the same tired answers to family policy questions. Rep. Khanna deserves immense credit for expanding the policy conversation to meet parents where they are and rethink how we might support families with young kids. There will always be disagreement on specifics, but the Child Care for America Act brings welcome energy and new thinking to the question of meaningfully expanding child care choices for parents from all walks of life,” said Patrick T. Brown, Fellow, Ethics and Public Policy Center.

“The Free Child Care for America Act recognizes that high-quality child care facilities are the cornerstone of a strong child care ecosystem. By investing in the spaces where children learn, grow, and thrive, we can expand access, strengthen communities, and support families for generations to come,” said the Executive Committee, The National Children's Facilities Network.

“The Child Care for America Act is an example of exactly the kind of real policy solutions we need to address the affordability crisis for working families. The impacts of the high cost of childcare and the low wages paid childcare providers affects all of our communities but has an even larger impact on Black and brown women and families,” said Glenn Harris, President Race Forward Action.

“When asked which issues the President and Congress should address regarding child well-being, almost half of the respondents in our 2026 National Latino Family Report rated access to quality, affordable childcare as the most pressing issue. The Free Child Care for America Act addresses challenges on both sides of our child care system: Helping families afford childcare while also building and strengthening the supply of child care across communities. AP-OD is proud to endorse legislation that recognizes the investment in children, families, educators, and our collective future,” said Diana Dominguez Abriendo Puertas, Opening Doors.

title: Larsen Releases Statement on the Passing of Congressman Jim McDermott
text:
Today, Representative Rick Larsen (WA-02) released the following statement:

“I am saddened by the passing of my friend and former colleague, Congressman Jim McDermott. My thoughts are with his family, friends, former staff and the people of Seattle he represented for so many years.

“Jim was in his 7th term when I was elected to Congress. He gave me an early lesson in hard work that was straight to the point, hard to hear and has stuck with me to this day.

“When I asked Jim for an endorsement for my first race, Jim looked at me straight in the eye and said simply, “Rick, you are not the golden boy. You need to make yourself the golden boy.” Great advice in politics: work hard on the campaign, on your issues, on your goals, and eventually people will come to your side.

“Jim devoted his life to public service as a physician, a Navy psychiatrist, a member of the Washington legislature and, for 14 terms, a representative in the House.

“Washington has lost a dedicated public servant and tireless voice for people who often go unheard. We could all use a Jim McDermott in our corner.”

###

title: Bennet Calls for CDC Director to Resign Amid Loss of Measles Elimination Status, Mounting Measles-Related Deaths
text:
Washington, D.C. — Colorado U.S. Senator Michael Bennet today called on U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) Director Dr. Erica Schwartz to resign immediately following the Pan American Health Organization stripping the United States of its measles elimination status it has held since 2000.

In just the last week alone, health officials reported two more measles-related deaths, including the death of a child. This escalating outbreak has now resulted in 10 deaths and over 5,400 confirmed cases this year. Despite these mounting failures, Dr. Schwartz said this week that the CDC would not change its measles response even if the United States lost its elimination status, saying: “Let’s say we did lose our measles elimination status. We’re going to be doing the same exact thing that we’ve been doing today, which is working with the states.” She also claimed that “these decisions and the focus of where we’re going with the CDC rests on my shoulders.”

“As Dr. Schwartz said, the direction of the CDC rests on her shoulders – and her comments this week prove why she should not be in charge. Ten Americans have died from a preventable disease this year, including another child, and the U.S. is losing an elimination status we protected for 26 years. Those failures are egregious enough on their own, yet Dr. Schwartz looked at this public health crisis and declared the CDC will keep doing ‘the exact same thing’. This will be her legacy. I have no confidence that she will do what it takes to course-correct at the CDC, and she should resign immediately.

“Instead of sounding the alarm and mounting an urgent response to protect our kids, Dr. Schwartz is offering excuses and complacency while the Trump Administration, spearheaded by Secretary Robert Kennedy Jr., dismantles childhood vaccine policy. The American people deserve a CDC Director who will stand up to this reckless, anti-science agenda and fight for public health – not continue business as usual.”

Bennet has consistently fought against the Trump Administration’s anti-science agenda. In October 2026, Bennet and U.S. Representative Kim Schrier, M.D. (D-Wash.), led 29 colleagues in a letter to Dr. Erica Schwartz, the Director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), to call out efforts to reject settled vaccine science and demand answers about the CDC’s efforts to implement President Trump’s childhood vaccine Executive Order (EO), underreport measles-associated deaths, and delay access to childhood immunizations. In September 2026, Bennet reiterated his call on the Senate floor for Trump to rescind the unscientific childhood vaccine EO and fire Kennedy. In August 2026, Bennet led 90 of his Congressional colleagues to demand Trump rescind his EO that directs federal health agencies to overhaul longstanding childhood vaccine recommendations and encourages states to reconsider school immunization requirements. In April 2026, Bennet questioned Kennedy during a Senate Finance Committee hearing on the Secretary’s skepticism of childhood vaccines amidst the largest measles outbreak in the U.S. in over thirty years.

###

title: Heinrich Successfully Includes $338 Million for New Mexico in Appropriations Bills for 2027
text:
WASHINGTON — U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), a member of the U.S. Senate Appropriations Committee and Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Appropriations Subcommittee on the Legislative Branch, announced that he was able to get $338 million for New Mexico included in the newly released Fiscal Year 2027 (FY27) Military Construction and Veterans Affairs (VA); Commerce, Justice, Science, and Related Agencies (CJS); Agriculture, Rural Development, and Food and Drug Administration (FDA); Interior and Environment; Homeland Security; Energy and Water Development; and Legislative Branch Appropriations Bills, including Congressionally Directed Spending for 42 local projects.

“I’ve spent months fighting to secure federal funding to help New Mexico families put food on the table and afford housing, give local law enforcement the tools they need to keep our communities safe, support our veterans and military installations, and invest in critical water infrastructure, including $63 million for the Navajo-Gallup Water Supply Project. I’m proud to have secured $338 million for New Mexico in the released bills. But I remain frustrated by Senate Republicans refusal to include the critical funding needed for rural communities, necessary reforms to rein in an out-of-control ICE, and oversight tools to hold this administration accountable,” said Heinrich, a member of the U.S. Senate Appropriations Committee.

Heinrich continued, “Together, we got a lot into these bills. But New Mexicans deserve better than the totality of what Senate Republicans included, and my vote will reflect that. In this and future appropriations cycles, I will continue working to bring home investments that lower costs for working families, create more good-paying jobs, strengthen our communities, and honor the service of those who keep us safe.”

FY27 Military Construction, Veterans Affairs, and Related Agencies Key Points and Highlights

Military Construction

Heinrich successfully included $206 million for the following two projects:

$185,000,000 for a new operational facility that will support the intelligence needs of the Defense Intelligence Enterprise and the U.S. Space Force.

$21,000,000, combined with the $90,000,000 Heinrich secured in FY26, to build a new 192-bed dorm for the Air Force Special Operations Command at Cannon Air Force Base.

Heinrich and U.S. Senator Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.) also successfully included $32.75 million for the following two projects:

$25,000,000 for the construction of a Deployment Processing Center at Cannon Air Force Base.

$7,750,000 for the construction of an Explosive Operations Building at Kirtland Air Force Base.

Veteran Healthcare

Toxic Exposure: This bill includes $54.6 billion to implement the PACT Act, which expands and extends eligibility for VA healthcare for veterans of the Vietnam War, Gulf Wars, and post-9/11 era who were exposed to dangerous toxins while serving our country. Heinrich championed the PACT Act into law in 2022.

Home Healthcare: Heinrich secured language that requires the VA to study the impacts of the 19% cut to reimbursement rates for home health aides serving veterans in New Mexico. If the VA finds that these cuts negatively affected veterans’ access to care, the VA is required to issue waivers to allow home healthcare providers to receive higher reimbursement, reversing the cuts and protecting veteran access to home healthcare.

Earlier this year, Heinrich led New Mexico and Texas congressional Democrats in introducing the Protecting Home-Based Care for Rural Veterans Act, legislation to reverse the Trump administration’s cuts to reimbursement rates for essential homecare services for veterans in New Mexico and Texas.

Rural Health: This bill provides $349 million to help veterans living in rural communities access health care, including the Highly Rural Transportation Grant, which provides free transportation services to help veterans in rural areas travel to VA health appointments at no cost.

An estimated 2.7 million rural and highly rural veterans are enrolled in the Veterans Health Administration (VHA). Many rural veterans enrolled in the VA healthcare system are at an advanced age, with approximately 54 percent aged 65 or older. With the aging veteran population growing increasingly medically complex and more likely to be diagnosed with chronic conditions like diabetes, obesity, high blood pressure, and heart disease, each requiring more frequent, ongoing, and costly care, these funds would help close the gap and get highly rural veterans the care they need.

Telehealth: The bill includes $6.7 billion to sustain and expand telehealth services at the VA, helping more veterans access care.

Mental Health: The bill includes nearly $3.7 billion for suicide prevention efforts at the VA. This includes a program to identify at-risk veterans established under the Commander John Scott Hannon Veterans Mental Health Care Improvement Act of 2019, which Heinrich helped pass into law.

Education

GI Bill: The bill asks the VA to study and report how much it would cost to adjust for inflation the books and supplies stipend GI Bill recipients receive. The current stipend has not been adjusted since 2008. This builds on Heinrich’s Veteran Education Assistance Adjustment Act, bipartisan legislation that will increase veterans’ yearly books and supply stipend to $1,500 to keep up with inflation. The bill also increases the supply stipend for veterans enrolled in apprenticeships and pursuing careers in the trades.

Housing

Reducing Veteran Homelessness: The bill includes $3.8 billion to help connect veterans with stable, secure housing with the goal of putting 45,000 veterans experiencing homelessness into long term housing by 2027.

FY27 Commerce, Justice, Science, and Related Agencies Key Points and Highlights

Congressionally Directed Spending

Heinrich successfully included $5 million for the following seven local projects:

$1,082,000 for Navajo United Methodist Center to expand support services for their Helping Hand Program, which helps domestic violence survivors secure housing and employment.

$931,000 for the Domestic Violence Resource Center to expand survivor access and response capacity.

$751,000 for Catholic Charities of Albuquerque to expand community-based legal navigation and accredited services for underserved individuals facing legal barriers.

$750,000 for Families and Youth, Inc. to expand their youth mental health intervention services across Doña Ana County communities.

$750,000 for the City of Portales to acquire a regional mobile command center.

$533,000 for Central New Mexico Community College to add campus lighting and security cameras to improve campus safety.

$350,000 for the Children’s Safehouse at All Faiths Children’s Advocacy Center to expand their capacity to conduct forensic interviews.

Heinrich and Luján also successfully included $6.5 million for the following seven projects:

$1,605,000 for Albuquerque Police Department to purchase forensic and investigative technology.

$1,320,000 for the Bernalillo County Sheriff’s Office to purchase four Crime Scene Investigation vans and ten patrol vehicles.

$1,000,000 for Chaves County Court Appointed Special Advocates Program to provide services and resources to child crime survivors, foster families, and trauma-response teams.

$1,000,000 for Albuquerque Police Department to replace their law enforcement training range and equipment.

$720,000 for the University of New Mexico to create trustworthy AI research, education, and infrastructure.

$500,000 for the Second Judicial District Attorney’s Office to expand its cold case investigation.

$368,000 for Albuquerque Community Safety to expand their youth violence intervention services.

Keeping New Mexico Communities Safe and Combating Crime

Combatting Crimes on Tribal Lands: Heinrich successfully included language directing the Department of Justice (DOJ) to continue allocating additional resources to address the crisis of Missing and Murdered Indigenous Persons, including providing sufficient funding to investigate, respond to, and prevent crimes in Tribal communities.

Fentanyl Tracking System: Heinrich successfully included language directing the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) to develop a comprehensive fentanyl tracking system. That tracking system would include documentation of seizure location, chemical composition, probable or known manufacturing location, and probable or known point of entry into the United States. Currently, fentanyl interdiction is compiled at land ports of entry by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), but the DEA does not have readily accessible tracking data on the movement of illicit drugs within the U.S. or their point of origin. Requiring the compilation and organization of that data will complement DHS’ work and improve our country’s work to effectively combat the fentanyl crisis.

Firearm Straw Purchases Prevention: Heinrich successfully included language calling on the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) to continue its public awareness campaign to reduce firearm straw purchases at the retail level and to educate would-be straw purchasers of the penalties associated with knowingly participating in an illegal firearm purchase. This language builds on Heinrich’s work to negotiate and author the provision in the Bipartisan Safer Communities Act that increased criminal penalties for straw purchases and made it illegal to traffic firearms out of the United States. To date, more than 1,000 defendants have been charged by the Department of Justice because of those provisions, removing hundreds of firearms from the streets.

Removing Barriers to Lifesaving Medication: Heinrich successfully included language directing the DEA to take further action to remove barriers to access for opioid use disorder medications such as buprenorphine. The data clearly shows that prescriptions of medications for opioid use disorder significantly reduce the risk of overdose death, but despite their demonstrated effectiveness, approximately 87% of those suffering from opioid use disorder do not have a prescription for these lifesaving medications. The inclusion of this language will assist local medical and mental health providers and make medications, including buprenorphine, more accessible to New Mexicans.

FY27 Agriculture, Rural Development, Food and Drug Administration (FDA), and Related Agencies Key Points and Highlights

Congressionally Directed Spending

Heinrich successfully included $6 million for the following seven local projects:

$2,000,000 for New Mexico State University to rehabilitate and update the Farmington Agricultural Science Center Site.

$1,650,000 for Pueblo of Zuni Fire Department to purchase a ladder truck and equipment for the ladder truck.

$750,000 for Pueblo of Zia to purchase heavy equipment to maintain roads.

$550,000 for BEN Initiative to equip and expand the CHIYAAN Community Food and Nutrition hub to help support the aggregation and distribution of locally grown and culturally appropriate foods.

$500,000 for the City of Belén to update the Old City Hall building.

$500,000 for San Cristobal Mutual Domestic Water Consumers Association to upgrade the San Cristobal Community Center.

$75,000 for Guadalupe County Clerk’s Office to purchase a new election vehicle to ensure secure, reliable, and timely transportation of election equipment and staff to polling locations.

Heinrich and Luján successfully included $1.4 million for the following two projects:

$938,000 for Sandoval County to purchase and equip a wildland fire truck.

$500,000 for the Village of Mosquero to construct a new fire station.

Nutrition Assistance

WIC: The bill fully funds the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC), which serves nearly 7 million women and children nationwide, including over 45,000 in New Mexico — by providing $8.5 billion for the program, a $300 million increase over FY26. This increase will ensure that all eligible participants can continue to rely on the essential nutrition assistance and support provided by WIC.

SNAP: The bill fully funds the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), which serves an estimated 36 million people each month, including roughly 440,000 New Mexicans, without imposing new restrictive policy riders. While fully funding SNAP is critically important, it does not undo the cuts enacted through Trump and Republicans’ Big, Bad Bill. Those cuts have saddled New Mexico with hundreds of millions of dollars in new, unfunded mandates and contributed to a sharp decline in SNAP enrollment nationwide, including more than 20,000 New Mexicans who have lost their benefits.

Child Nutrition: The bill fully funds Child Nutrition Programs — like the School Lunch program, school breakfast program, and Summer EBT program — to ensure schools can continue to serve healthy meals to all eligible children. In 2027, this funding will help serve an estimated 5.3 billion lunches and 2.7 billion breakfasts to kids across the country.

Commodity Supplemental Food Program: The bill rejects the Trump administration's budget proposal to eliminate this program’s funding and provides $495 million, a $70 million increase over FY26, so that the program can continue to provide supplemental food to low-income Senior citizens.

Supporting New Mexico Rural Communities, Agriculture, and Food Security

Rental Assistance: The bill provides $1.7 billion for rental assistance to help ensure Americans living in rural communities have access to safe and affordable housing. The bill also includes $1 billion in Single Family Direct Loans to help more low-income families and first-time home buyers get mortgages.

Tribal Communities: The bill provides $271 million for the Food Distribution on Indian Reservation Program (FDPIR), a $36 million increase over FY26. The bill also provides $700,000 for processing and federal inspection of Tribal bison, which will help support Tribal food sovereignty by enabling Tribes to include bison raised on their own lands to be included in federal nutrition programs like school meals.

Additionally, the bill provides $5.1 million for the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s (USDA) Office of Tribal Relations, which is responsible for government-to-government relations between USDA and Tribal governments.

Economic Development: The bill includes a $3 million investment in the Southwest Border Commission (SBRC), a $500,000 increase over FY26, which supports economic and community development in southern New Mexico. Previously, Heinrich successfully secured the first-ever congressional investments to finally allow the SBRC to jump-start and expand its operations. The SBRC is one of eight authorized federal regional commissions and authorities.

Conservation and Wildlife: The bill rejects the administration’s proposal to eliminate all discretionary funding for the Natural Resources Conservation Service’s Conservation Technical Assistance program, which helps farmers and ranchers protect their land, improve soil health, and conserve water. Instead, the bill provides $748 million for conservation programs, $50 million more than FY26. This includes $51.6 million to help communities prevent flooding and protect watersheds and $10 million to help ranchers maintain healthy grazing lands.

The bill further provides $5.5 million to support non-lethal strategies to reduce wildlife-livestock conflict and includes direction to expand the Migratory Big Game and Working Lands for Wildlife Initiatives, a long-time Heinrich priority. Finally, the bill includes $22.5 million in funding for research and management of Chronic Wasting Disease, which funds the program created by Heinrich’s Chronic Wasting Disease Research and Management Act, passed into law in 2023.

Agriculture Research: The bill fully funds agricultural research, including a $39 million increase over FY26 for the Agricultural Research Service (ARS), which conducts research to help farmers and ranchers improve their operations and protect their land. The bill also continues funding for Climate Hubs, which help farmers and ranchers prepare for drought and extreme weather, and the Long-term Agroecosystems Research (LTAR) Network, which studies how to keep farmland and grazing lands healthy and productive for years to come. This includes research conducted jointly by New Mexico State University (NMSU) and ARS Experimental Station in Las Cruces. The bill also provides $1.5 million for agrivoltaics research by ARS and NMSU, which explores how farmers can use the same land to grow crops and produce solar energy.

Small Farms and Local Food Systems: The bill provides $5 million for the Office of Urban Agriculture, which helps people grow food in urban communities by providing training, resources, and tools to manage risks. Albuquerque is home to one of the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s (USDA) Urban Service Centers, which helps local farmers and growers access these resources. The bill also provides $16.3 million for the Local Agriculture Market Program (LAMP), which helps farmers and ranchers sell their products directly to customers, expand local food markets, and create new products from the crops and livestock they raise.

Food Safety: The bill provides $1.226 billion for the Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS), an increase of $11 million over FY26. This funding will help ensure FSIS can perform its vital work protecting America’s food supply without being forced to reduce its staffing levels, which would jeopardize food safety and exacerbate supply chain delays. The bill also includes $1.176 billion for the Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, including $10 million, in additional funding for efforts to address the New World Screwworm infestation, a $5 million increase over FY26. This funding is in addition to over $1 billion the USDA has already spent using Commodity Credit Corporation funding and emergency funding.

Promoting Competition: The bill provides nearly $33 million for enforcement of the Packers and Stockyards Act to promote competition and prevent unfair or deceptive practices and monopolies.

International Food Aid: The bill provides $1.38 billion for the Food for Peace Program and $240 million for the McGovern-Dole International Food for Education and Child Nutrition Program. This funding is necessary to save lives around the world and reduce conflict.

Food and Drug Administration (FDA): The bill provides $7.265 billion for the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), including $3.5 billion in annual funding, a $196 million increase over FY26. This includes $2.6 billion for the Center for Drug Evaluation and Research, which helps ensure prescription drugs are safe and effective; $627 million for the Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research, which oversees vaccines, blood products, and other medical treatments; and $71 million for the National Center for Toxicological Research, which studies the safety of drugs, chemicals, and other products. The bill also provides $19 million for the Orphan Products Grants Program, which supports research into treatments for rare diseases, including $5 million for the FDA Rare Neurodegenerative Disease Grants Program, which funds research into rare diseases that damage the brain and nervous system.

The bill also provides at least $200 million for FDA enforcement efforts, including working with other federal agencies to crack down on illegal e-cigarettes and nicotine pouches, remove these products from the market, and hold companies that illegally import or sell them accountable.

FY27 Interior and Environment Key Points and Highlights

Congressionally Directed Spending

Heinrich successfully included $5.65 million for the following 10 projects:

$1,000,000 for the New Mexico Environment Department to address hexavalent chromium water contamination at San Ildefonso Pueblo.

$900,000 for the Pueblo of Cochiti to plan, design, and construct a new solid waste transfer station.

$750,000 for the Indian Pueblo Cultural Center to purchase climate-controlled equipment for the preservation and public display of their collection of cultural artifacts.

$700,000 for the University of New Mexico to conduct aerial waterfowl surveys.

$550,000 for Santa Fe County to purchase and install reverse-osmosis water filters.

$530,000 for the New Mexico Institute of Mining and Technology to conduct magnetotelluric geothermal resource screening activities.

$500,000 for Taos Pueblo to conduct rehabilitation and renovation projects for the historic village.

$500,000 for the Bureau of Land Management to conduct trail maintenance within the Rio Grande del Norte National Monument.

$125,000 for the Forest Stewards Guild to conduct statewide home hazard risk assessment training.

$70,000 for the Pueblo of Zia to install new advanced water meter technology.

Heinrich and Luján included $1.87 million for the following 2 projects:

$1,200,000 for the New Mexico Department of Forestry to conduct forest and watershed health activities in the Rio Chama watershed.

$675,000 for the Village of Jemez Springs to rehabilitate its wastewater treatment and collection system.

Supporting Tribes, Investing in Education, and Conserving New Mexico’s Lands and Wildlife

Safeguard Tribal Objects of Patrimony (STOP) Act Implementation: Heinrich successfully included $500,000 to implement the Safeguard Tribal Objects of Patrimony (STOP) Act, a bipartisan law that Heinrich championed and passed in 2022 to prohibit the exporting of sacred Native American items and increase penalties for stealing and illegally trafficking Tribal cultural patrimony. Representing only the second year that this program has received dedicated funding, it will be used to halt the trade of culturally significant items and repatriate stolen pieces to the Tribal communities where they belong. Heinrich first introduced the STOP Act in 2016 after he helped halt the auction of a shield, stolen from the Pueblo of Acoma. Heinrich played a role in the effort to bring the shield home to Acoma by working with Governors Kurt Riley and Brian Vallo to call for its return.

Tribal Education: Heinrich fought for and successfully included $13,482,000 for the Institute of American Indian and Alaska Native Culture and Arts Development (IAIA). After the administration threatened to withhold FY25 funding from the IAIA, Heinrich secured the release of the funds and secured FY26 funding for the IAIA. This appropriations bill will ensure continued investment for the IAIA through FY27, supporting its mission to advance Indigenous arts, culture, and education for future generations. Heinrich also included language directing the U.S. Department of the Interior to continue to address the deferred maintenance backlog at Bureau of Indian Education (BIE) schools.

Historic Preservation: Heinrich successfully secured level funding for the Tribal Historic Preservation Offices, totaling $23,750,000 after the Trump Administration proposed zeroing out the program.

Abandoned Hardrock Mine Reclamation Program: Heinrich successfully included continued funding for the Abandoned Hardrock Mine Reclamation Program, after championing the creation of the program in the 2022 Infrastructure Law. Hardrock mines and mining features are related to the extraction of metals like copper, gold, silver, and uranium. When not reclaimed, many hardrock mines pose a hazard to public health and the environment. This funding will be used to clean up federal, state, Tribal, and private land and water resources affected by abandoned hardrock mines.

Southwest Ecological Research Institutes: Heinrich fought for and successfully maintained funding for the Southwest Ecological Research Institutes (SWERIs) after the Trump Administration proposed cutting the funding. SWERIs offer unique opportunities for dedicated research in forest science and watershed health and represent the future of science in forest management. New Mexico Highlands University houses one center along with Colorado State University and Northern Arizona University. This funding would ensure the continuation of valuable research in southwestern forest and fire management.

Conservation: Heinrich successfully protected funding for the North American Wetlands Conservation Fund, which leverages private dollars to restore waterfowl habitat across the country. Heinrich led the reauthorization of this fund last Congress. He also protected core wildlife management and science capabilities at the Fish and Wildlife Service and the U.S. Geological Survey from the steep cuts proposed by the Trump administration.

FY27 Homeland Security Key Points and Highlights

Heinrich successfully included $1.7 million for the following two projects:

$1,150,000 for the New Mexico Environment Department to complete two large-scale river and floodplain restoration projects in watersheds severely affected by the Hermit’s Peak/Calf Canyon Fire.

$550,000 for the City of Roswell to conduct a city-wide study of its drainage system and guide future investment in order to mitigate against future disasters.

Strengthening Public Safety, Election Security, and Emergency Preparedness

Election Security: Heinrich helped secure $39,610,000 for the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s (CISA) Election Security Program, which the Trump administration proposed eliminating in its FY27 budget request. The Election Security Program provides state and local election officers with intelligence, resources, and tools to help secure critical election infrastructure.

Fentanyl Analogues: Heinrich helped secure language directing U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) to identify the specific types of fentanyl analogues and fentanyl-related substances that it encounters at ports of entry, rapidly deploy technology to detect, interdict, and deter the flow of illicit drugs, and provide a briefing on how the agency tracks fentanyl with the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA). Currently, interdiction data is compiled at ports of entry by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), and the DEA does not have readily accessible tracking data on the movement of illicit drugs within the U.S. or their point of origin when it is seized within the U.S.

E-Cigarettes: Heinrich fought for and secured a $5,000,000 allocation from CBP to improve the Office of Field Operations (OFO) and the Food and Drug Administration’s (FDA) work on stopping the flow of illegal e-cigarettes into the U.S. The allocation will fund increased random inspections at ports of entry, increase the number of field examinations at ports of entry with high import volumes, and improve screening systems for field staff to better detect illegal e-cigarette imports.

Next Generation Warning System: Heinrich helped secure $56,000,00o for the Next Generation Warning System (NGWS). The NGWS supports the continuity, reliability, and resiliency of public broadcasting infrastructure, which is used across the country to provide alerts, warnings, and interoperable communications during emergencies.

FY27 Energy and Water Development Key Points and Highlights

Heinrich successfully included $2 million for the following two projects:

$1,782,000 for the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers to monitor water operations in the Upper Rio Grande.

$500,000 for the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers to perform construction activities to support wildfire prevention and restoration in the Middle Rio Grande Bosque in and around the City of Albuquerque.

Additionally, Heinrich and Luján successfully included $63,333,000 for the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation to design and construct the Navajo-Gallup Water Supply Project.

Heinrich and Luján have long supported efforts to fund and complete the Navajo-Gallup Water Supply Project. For more information, click here.

Investing in New Mexico Water Infrastructure, Sandia and Los Alamos National Laboratories, and the Southwest Border Regional Commission

Oversight of Federal Water Infrastructure: Heinrich successfully included report language that provides key oversight on federal water infrastructure throughout New Mexico, including the El Vado Dam and the San Juan-Chama Project.

Water Conservation and Natural Infrastructure: Heinrich secured level funding and significant increases for key Bureau of Reclamation WaterSMART programs that provide water savings and ecosystem benefits for New Mexico and across the West.

Southwest Border Regional Commission: Heinrich successfully included $5.5 million for the Southwest Border Regional Commission (SBRC). Since joining the Senate Appropriations Committee, Heinrich successfully secured the first-ever congressional investments to finally allow the SBRC to start its operations.

National Labs: Heinrich helped include $8.4 billion for the U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE) Office of Science, which supports both Sandia National Laboratories (Sandia) and Los Alamos National Laboratory (LANL). Over the course of his tenure in Congress, Heinrich has helped double the total budgets for Sandia and LANL, significantly increasing the total employees and local economic impact of both labs.

Hexavalent Chromium Plume: Heinrich secured $20 million for addressing groundwater contamination by hexavalent chromium in the area surrounding LANL. Heinrich has consistently pushed the DOE’s Office of Environmental Management to clean up its legacy waste. Within that funding, $2 million would support the San Ildefonso Pueblo to remediate its drinking water, and $5 million would be provided to Los Alamos County to build a new water well in another location away from the chromium plume.

FY27 Legislative Branch Key Points and Highlights

At a time when maintaining checks and balances is more important than ever, this bill falls short of ensuring Congress can effectively serve the American people and hold the executive branch accountable. As Ranking Member of the Legislative Branch Subcommittee, Senator Heinrich does not support this bill, which fails to provide robust funding for the Government Accountability Office (GAO) and the Congressional Research Service (CRS), both of which are crucial to Congress’s oversight functions.

Safety and Security: The bill includes $965 million to support security operations for members, staff, and visitors to the Capitol campus. This funding allows continued recruitment and retention of sworn and civilian personnel.

The bill also provides authority to continue mutual aid reimbursements for state and local law enforcement, which helps cover costs incurred by state and local police departments when protecting lawmakers and congressionally sponsored events. And the bill responds to increasing safety threats by providing $75 million for enhanced member security for both the Senate and the House.

Government Accountability Office (GAO): The bill rejects House Republicans’ efforts to cut the GAO by over $200 million but falls short of providing adequate resources to support aggressive oversight of the executive branch. Funding for the GAO is crucial for protecting taxpayer dollars, promoting government efficiency, and providing rigorous, nonpartisan oversight that builds public trust. Additional funding is necessary to support audits of federal programs, review of expenditures, and analysis of federal resource utilization.

Library of Congress: This bill includes $878.5 million for the Library of Congress, including $19.8 million for programs including Teaching with Primary Sources, the Surplus Books Program, Veteran History Project, and the Lewis Houghton Civics and Democracy Initiative. This is a rejection of House Republicans’ efforts to rewrite American history and hide the truth.

title: Reed Calls for Independent Probe of FAA Ground Stop & Public Hearings to Ensure Air Safety & Accountability
text:
PROVIDENCE, RI -- After the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ended an incredibly rare and chaotic nationwide grounding of airplanes that led to a stoppage of air traffic and stranded thousands of passengers at airports across the country, U.S. Senator Jack Reed is demanding answers, independent investigations, and public hearings.

Reed says that he was disappointed by unconvincing explanations from Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin yesterday, who initially suggested the ground stop occurred because newly installed technology overloaded the agency's aging air traffic control systems. Then today, Secretary Duffy Reed pointed the finger at possible incompetence by FAA contractor L3Harris. Reed says the public deserves more information and he will work on a bipartisan basis to help get them the truth.

Reed also said he is unconvinced by Duffy’s demand for an immediate infusion of $50 billion to fix the issue, a seemingly arbitrary figure that is $19.9 billion higher than the $30.1 billion that Duffy formally requested just a day earlier, especially when the FAA seems to be prioritizing speed over safety and air traffic disruptions.

Reed stated:

“This was a national fiasco and the American people deserve answers. It wreaked havoc on our economy, people’s travel, and airline schedules that will take days to untangle. The American people are owed an explanation and what we’ve heard so far from the Trump Administration is insufficient.

“Every passenger who boards a plane deserves to have full confidence in the safety of our air travel system.

“Americans deserve a more complete explanation. Even today, it’s still not clear what happened or if it was correctly addressed. If it was routine maintenance, then why were the system updates being conducted during the busiest time of air travel instead of off-peak overnight hours when air traffic is at lower levels? Let’s get people the facts and ensure this problem is solved.

“We need an independent investigation into this incident, and we need timely public testimony from non-partisan experts to ensure air safety. Congress must follow the facts, truth, and evidence, wherever it leads.

“Shoveling money at the problem isn’t the same as fixing it. Legitimate questions have already raised about whether the FAA’s implementation strategy was moving faster than its safety evaluations, workforce training, and independent oversight actually support. So let’s get the facts and solve the problem, not try to mislead people or give incomplete impressions.”

title: Boston Herald: Rep. Katherine Clark speaks to new Majority Leader position, items on top of Dems agenda
text:
As the prospective second-in-command for the incoming U.S. House Democrats, Rep. Katherine Clark spoke on the issues at the top of their agenda and the controversial online push for her Massachusetts colleague Rep. Ayanna Pressley to take over as Speaker of the House.

“With a 260-person Democratic majority, we are going to have the ability to really focus on the American people, put them back in the agenda,” said Clark on a WCVB segment aired Sunday. “And they sent a clear message to Donald Trump and the Republicans in Congress: you have betrayed us and forgotten about us, and put the interests of corporations and the very wealthy over ours, and we are not going to stand for it. So we want all the voices of our broad coalition to be involved in setting this agenda.”

Clark, who currently serves as House Minority Whip, is in position to become the first female House Majority leader in the country’s history when the new Congress is sworn in in January. The title would position her as second ranking Democrat in the House.

The Massachusetts congresswoman laid out her party’s priorities as the new sweeping Democrat majority is sworn in, citing intent to put back in “Medicaid, Medicare, veterans’ benefits, food programs” cuts in January.

“We are going to work with every tool we have to make sure that we are lowering costs,” Clark said in the “On the Record” segment. “That means going after the tariffs that this president has put in. That means ending this war in Iran so we can get relief, not only at the at the gas pump, but also in diesel costs that are going to drive up our cost of food even further. All of this is is working together against the middle class.”

Clark went on to list an effort to raise the $7 an hour federal minimum wage.

The representative said she “takes responsibility” for the failed attempt to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, which fell short, 211 to 204 votes with 11 House Democrats recorded as absent. Clark said they would “not have had a different outcome, but it’s a terrible look,” adding “we have to do better.”

If he’s still employed in January, Clark said Hegseth’s “day of reckoning is coming.”

Likewise in January, Clark said Democrats intend to investigate former NVIDIA president Jensen Huang’s affair and the potential security breach, as well as how much and when Commerce Secretary Howard Lutwick knew.

“We said we’re going to lower your costs, we’re going to make your healthcare affordable, and we are going to hold the crooks accountable, because corruption has a cost back to the American people, and they know it,” said Clark. “And so we’re going to do all of these things.”

On the subject of the next Speaker of the House, Clark expressed support for current Minority Leader Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, calling him a “steady leader” who delivered a “huge victory” in the midterms.

Asked about some progressives’ pushback on Jeffries for the position and an online petition with tens of thousands calling for Rep. Ayanna Pressley to take the top spot, Clark said “to my knowledge, she is not running for Speaker.”

“What we’re really focused on with our new caucus members is what do you want to see? What are your priorities as we move forward?” Clark said. “And what I’m hearing is what the importance to them is, not so much the individual, but what will the priorities be, and so that has been the focus of our conversations. They want to hear that we understand the desire for change and the message the American people sent that they want the people to be back in the people’s house.”

title: WCVB: Rep. Katherine Clark On The Record about Democratic leadership in Congress, investigating Jensen Huang, impeaching Pete Hegseth
text:
Rep. Katherine Clark, the House Minority Whip who has represented Massachusetts’s fifth district since 2013, is poised to become the first woman to serve as House Majority Leader after the blue wave election propelled Democrats to control of the chamber in the next Congress.

“It is beyond exciting,” she told WCVB’s On The Record. “It is historic in that, as you said, the first woman in the 250 years of our country to hold this position, which is the second in seniority in the House of Representatives.”

Clark pointed out that the 120th Congress will also have a record-breaking 120 women in the House Democratic Caucus.

Leadership questions

The current House Minority Leader, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York’s 8th district, is also expected to make history as the first Black Speaker of the House when Democrats take control. While Democrats in the U.S. Senate are not sure about their future majority leader, Clark said the decision in the House is clear.

“Hakeem has been a steady leader for us through the four years of minority, not afraid to take on this administration or anybody who is cheating the American people, and he has delivered a huge victory,” Clark said. “Hakeem played a huge role in making sure that Democrats were poised to win this House by what is a landslide.”

When asked if Clark was aware of a groundswell of support pushing Massachusetts Rep. Ayanna Pressley to run for Speaker of the House, she praised the Boston Congresswoman’s work and said she will likely be an influential voice in the caucus.

“To my knowledge, she is not running for Speaker. But listen, I think Ayana is an incredible voice, and I think that, you know, we want to have robust debates about all of the agenda and how we can best meet this moment,” she said.

Clark told OTR that she, Jeffries and the party are working to set priorities for the next two years. She said that effort includes considering priorities from the progressive wing of the party.

“With a 260-person Democratic majority, we are going to have the ability to really focus on the American people, put them back on the agenda,” Clark said.

Clark said the American people can expect “quick action” from the Democrats to reverse cuts to programs that were made during the first two years of President Donald Trump’s term.

“That is what this election was about, making sure that they are not paying the price for corruption,” she said.

Impeaching Hegseth?

OTR also asked Clark about the 11 Democrats who missed a recent vote on articles of impeachment for Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth. Republicans were able to shift the issue to committee, effectively blocking the effort.

“Did Democrats screw this up?” OTR’s Sharman Scachetti asked.

“Yes. You know, we have to take accountability for that,” Clark responded.

Clark went on to say that if he’s not “long gone by January,” the Democrats could try again.

“We have a huge job to do, and part of it is holding Pete Hegseth and the President responsible for this reckless war, and that is the work we are going to do in January,” she said.

Investigating former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang

Clark said that her party will “absolutely” lead an investigation into former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s reported affairs, including a relationship with an alleged Chinese spy.

Huang resigned from the company he co-founded this week.

“AI is on the minds of Americans and to have this kind of potential national security breach, where the Chinese are able to access these chips, is very, very serious,” Clark said. “So we will be bringing in Jensen Huang. We will be investigating this fully.”

Clark said the investigation would also extend to what Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick may have known about the case.

“Did they know about this, and did they try to cover it up?” Clark said.

Assessing the next Congress

Political analysts Mary Anne Marsh and Ginny Buckingham assess the path forward for Democrats in Congress and Clark’s expected new roles.

Marsh, a Democratic strategist, said she expects Clark and Jeffries to make history.

“It is very clear from the interview you guys did with her that affordability and accountability are No. 1 issues right there, and they’re prepared to go after it,” Marsh said.

While offering “kudos” for Clark’s accomplishments, Buckingham offered some words of caution from the Republican perspective.

“I also think this verbal gymnastics of saying, ‘Accountability and affordability are the same thing,’ People aren’t going to be fooled by that,” Buckingham said. “Voters aren’t stupid. Go for accountability, but own it.”

Marsh and Buckingham also discussed the political fallout following the conviction of former police officer Matthew Farwell in connection with the death of Sandra Birchmore.

This week’s political wins

Buckingham and Marsh shared their nominees for the most impactful political wins of the week.

title: Following Whistleblower Disclosure On Deadly Iran War Drone Attack, Blumenthal Demands Hegseth Answer For Failure To Protect Servicemembers
text:
[WASHINGTON, DC] – After receiving information from a whistleblower who survived the Iranian drone strike on Port Shuaiba, Kuwait that killed six U.S. servicemembers, U.S. Senator Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), Ranking Member of the Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations (PSI), wrote Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth demanding a briefing and documents that would show “whether senior civilian leaders in the Department ignored known threats and failed to take necessary precautions to protect American servicemembers.”

The whistleblower, U.S. Army Reserve Maj. Stephen Ramsbottom, was wounded in the drone attack on Port Shuaiba, Kuwait and shared his experience exclusively with 60 Minutes.

“Bolstered by this courageous whistleblower revelation, I am again demanding full disclosure about the Port Shuaiba attack – an accounting of misjudgments by political appointees that likely led to increased vulnerability and greater casualties,” Blumenthal said. “The nation should be grateful, as I am, for their fortitude coming forward. The whistleblower’s firsthand experience shows exactly how President Trump and his inept Secretary of Defense pushed our nation into a senseless, lawless war and put our servicemembers at heightened risk. The families of the six fallen servicemembers, the wounded survivors, and the American people deserve full transparency and accountability. It is time for a reckoning.”

“Soldiers were killed and wounded at the Port of Shuaiba, and their families deserve a full and honest accounting of why,” said Andrew P. Bakaj, counsel for Maj. Ramsbottom. “Our client came forward through lawful, protected channels because these questions have not been answered. The Army cannot be expected to investigate decisions made by its own senior leaders. An independent investigation is the only way to get to the truth. Our client does not seek to assign blame. He wants the lessons of March 1 identified now, while the records and witnesses are still available, so that no command post moved out of harm’s way is ever again left as exposed as the Port of Shuaiba.”

The whistleblower disclosure provided to Blumenthal includes information about Port Shuaiba’s vulnerability against Iranian drones and alleges that these concerns were raised directly to senior leaders within the Department of Defense at least three times in the week prior to the attack. The installation experienced an Iranian drone strike near Port Shuaiba the day before the deadly attack on March 1, and the whistleblower describes how this warning did not appear to prompt any action, with servicemembers directed to resume operations outside protective bunkers almost immediately. The whistleblower also describes a lack of adequate medical personnel, ambulances, and established casualty evacuation and collection capabilities at Port Shuaiba and raises the possibility that at least one of the six servicemembers killed could have survived had adequate medical support been available.

Blumenthal’s letter to Hegseth, which includes the whistleblower’s disclosure, is available here and copied below.

Dear Secretary Hegseth,

I write regarding reports of failures within the Department of Defense regarding force protection, command and control, and medical preparedness in connection with the March 1, 2026, Iranian drone strike on U.S. forces at Port Shuaiba, Kuwait, which killed six American servicemembers and injured more than 30 others. My office has received information from a whistleblower who survived the attack, and their statement raises serious questions about whether senior civilian leaders in the Department ignored known threats and failed to take necessary precautions to protect American servicemembers.

According to the Whistleblower, U.S. forces at Port Shuaiba lacked adequate defenses against Iranian drones despite repeated warnings about the vulnerability of the installation. Public reporting indicates that Port Shuaiba had been identified as a potential Iranian target, and military officials had raised concerns prior to the attack about the vulnerability of the tactical operations center (TOC), which concentrated U.S. personnel in a facility lacking adequate protection against Iranian strikes.[1] The Whistleblower alleges that these concerns were raised directly to senior leaders within the Department at least three times in the week before the hostilities.[2] Additional reporting indicates that alternative plans to relocate personnel to more defensible locations were rejected.[3]

Even more alarming, the Whistleblower described how an Iranian drone struck near Port Shuaiba the day before the deadly March 1 attack.[4] This stark warning of the imminent threat to U.S. personnel does not appear to have prompted any action.[5] Servicemembers were directed to resume operations outside protective bunkers on March 1, despite the absence of overhead protection and concerns that the available radar systems could not reliably detect low-flying drones.[6] The fatal strike occurred shortly thereafter.

The failures further extend to the immediate medical response. The Whistleblower has described a lack of adequate medical personnel, ambulances, and established casualty evacuation and collection capabilities at Port Shuaiba.[7] Survivors reportedly relied on improvised transportation to evacuate wounded personnel, despite earlier requests for additional medical resources.[8] The Whistleblower has informed my office that they believe one of the six servicemembers killed could have survived had adequate medical support been available. The possibility that inadequate medical preparedness cost American servicemembers their lives demands immediate answers and accountability.

Congress has repeatedly sought answers regarding this attack, yet your Department has failed to provide a complete accounting of the decisions that preceded it or the findings of the Army’s investigation. The families of the six fallen servicemembers, the wounded survivors, and the American people deserve transparency and accountability. Accordingly, I am demanding answers to the following questions:

What force-protection measures, including counter-unmanned aircraft systems, overhead protection, hardened shelters, and early warning capabilities, were available at Port Shuaiba on March 1, 2026? What additional capabilities were requested between March 1, 2025 and March 1, 2026, by whom, and were any requests denied or left unfulfilled?

Were proposals developed to retrograde or relocate personnel from Port Shuaiba to more defensible locations, including facilities in Saudi Arabia? Who reviewed or rejected these proposals, what was the rationale, and were the force-protection risks formally documented and accepted?

Were Iranian drones detected or confirmed to have struck Port Shuaiba or its immediate vicinity before the fatal strike on March 1? For each incident, what warning was provided to personnel, and what changes, if any, were made to protective measures or operating procedures?

What medical personnel, supplies, ambulances, and casualty evacuation capabilities were available at Port Shuaiba on March 1? Were requests for additional medical support submitted before the attack, and if so, why were those capabilities not provided?

Was there an approved mass-casualty response and evacuation plan for Port Shuaiba, and had personnel rehearsed it before March 1? What were the timelines for providing initial medical treatment and evacuating each wounded servicemember, and has the Army assessed whether additional medical resources could have prevented any deaths?

The Army reportedly completed its investigation of the attack in June but has yet to release the report.[9] Has the Army indeed completed its investigation into the Port Shuaiba attack? Did it specifically examine the decisions of senior commanders regarding threat warnings, force protection, alternative basing, bunker evacuation, medical preparedness, and command-and-control responsibilities? Please provide the complete investigation, including findings, recommendations, and any supporting documents, as well as the status of any related Inspector General or CENTCOM investigations.

Additionally, I request that you provide the Subcommittee a classified briefing on this topic and provide the following documents:

The complete AR 15-6 investigation with all classified annexes.

All relevant Army Central (ARCENT) operations orders and annexes.

Task Force Spartan daily update products from February 15, 2026 to March 10, 2026.

All force protection assessments for the Port of Shuaiba.

Thank you for your attention to this urgent matter. I request a written response within 14 days of receipt of this letter.

-30-

[2] Whistleblower Disclosure, pp. 4, 6.

[4] Whistleblower Disclosure, p.4.

title: Aderholt Welcomes Hudson Hill as New Field Representative for Marshall, DeKalb and Blount Counties

title: Congressman Bentz Votes YES to Supporting Veterans’ Benefits
text:
Washington, D.C. — On the day after Veterans Day, Congressman Cliff Bentz (R-OR) voted YES for H.R. 2102, the Major Richard Star Act, a bill that would allow veterans to receive disability compensation without reduction to retirement pay.

As it stands now, veterans with fewer than 20 years of creditable service who sustained combat-related disabilities cannot receive disability compensation without a sizeable reduction to their retirement pay. This bill, if passed by the Senate and signed by the president, would allow these veterans to receive their disability compensation without this reduction, starting on the first of the month that follows its enactment.

Congressman Bentz said: “We must support those who sustain lifelong injuries in the defense of our people and our nation. This bill does exactly that.”

title: Bera, Democratic Doctors Caucus Demand Accountability After U.S. Measles Elimination Status Is Dropped
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. –– Today, Representative Ami Bera, M.D. (CA-06) issued the following statement alongside his colleagues in the Democratic Doctors Caucus after the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) removed measles elimination status from the United States after decades of sustained containment of the deadly virus:

“For the first time since 2000, our nation can no longer say measles has been eliminated. Experts at the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) have officially determined what we already knew: Measles is now rampant in our country.

“As members of the Democratic Doctors Caucus, we are acutely aware and deeply alarmed that this decision is directly linked to the doubt and misinformation that HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has spread surrounding vaccines.

“Under his leadership, deadly, preventable diseases like measles are back. Our Caucus will do everything we can with our new Democratic majorities in Congress to hold RFK Jr. accountable, rebuild our public health infrastructure, and save lives.”

title: Bergman Leads Veterans Day Push for a Veterans Cemetery in the Upper Peninsula
text:
On Veterans Day, Rep. Jack Bergman announced two coordinated efforts to bring a Veterans cemetery to Michigan’s Upper Peninsula and address the longstanding lack of accessible burial options for Veterans and their families.

Rep. Bergman introduced the Veterans Cemetery Access Modernization Act to reform the way the National Cemetery Administration (NCA) of the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) funds the construction of Veterans cemeteries, and he led his Michigan Delegation colleagues in a letter asking NCA to give the Upper Peninsula a fair shot under the rules as they stand today. Together, these efforts are aimed at ending the longstanding gap in burial access for Veterans and their families living in the Upper Peninsula.

Michigan currently has no VA grant-funded Veterans cemetery, and the Upper Peninsula has no active Veterans cemetery of any kind. For Veterans living in Marquette, the nearest option is Northwoods National Cemetery near Rhinelander, Wisconsin - approximately 160 miles away and across state lines. The closest in-state option, Great Lakes National Cemetery in Holly, requires a roughly 400-mile drive across the Mackinac Bridge.

NCA has long operated with the goal of ensuring Veterans have access to an open Veterans cemetery within 75 miles of their homes. While the agency establishes new national cemeteries in underserved areas with more than 80,000 Veterans and provides grants to states and counties to serve less populated regions, its criteria continue to prioritize population over geography. This puts rural and geographically isolated communities like the Upper Peninsula at a significant disadvantage. Further complicating the issue, NCA measures the 75-mile distance in a straight line rather than by actual driving distance, failing to account for the real-world transportation challenges facing Veterans and their families.

Rep. Bergman stated, “Our Veterans earned the right to be laid to rest with dignity, and their families should not have to travel hundreds of miles to honor them. For far too long, Veterans in Michigan’s Upper Peninsula have been overlooked by a system that puts population numbers ahead of common sense and geographic reality. A 75-mile radius on a map means very little when the actual drive is several hours. This legislation is about making sure rural Veterans and their families are no longer left behind.”

Bergman’s Veterans Cemetery Access Modernization Act would provide a long-term solution by requiring NCA to evaluate cemetery accessibility based on actual driving distances rather than straight-line measurements. The legislation would also ensure geographic challenges, not just population totals, are considered when determining where new Veterans cemeteries are built and funded.

Specifically, the legislation would:

Prioritize VA cemetery grants for underserved areas. NCA would give priority to state and county cemetery applications that serve areas where more than 10,000 Veterans live more than 75 miles’ driving distance from an open national, state, or county Veterans cemetery in-state, or more than 35 miles’ driving distance from such a cemetery located across state lines.

Map who is being left out. Every two years, NCA would report to Congress, and publish online, every area of the country where Veterans lack reasonable burial access, including how many Veterans live there, the nearest cemetery, and the average drive to reach it.

Require plans for new national cemeteries. Each year, NCA would propose at least three new national cemeteries in those underserved areas, ranked first by the longest average drive and then by the number of Veterans affected. At least one proposal must serve a smaller, rural area with fewer than 25,000 unserved Veterans, where one exists.

Because Upper Peninsula Veterans and their families should not have to wait for changes in law, Rep. Bergman also led a letter to VA Under Secretary for Memorial Affairs Sam Brown, signed by Reps. Moolenaar, Scholten, Dingell, Walberg, McClain, Huizenga, Barrett, James, and Tlaib urging NCA to exercise flexibility to give an Upper Peninsula site for a state or county Veterans cemetery a fair shot at federal funding.

The Members asked Under Secretary Brown to make an exception for Michigan’s unique geography so that an Upper Peninsula site could be considered now. They pointed to NCA’s own Rural Initiative, which built Northwoods National Cemetery to serve rural Wisconsin, as proof that geographic isolation can justify a different approach than population counts alone. Should Michigan bring forward an Upper Peninsula site, the delegation asked NCA to lend its full support.

title: Wyden, Merkley, Bonamici Announce $440,000 to Support Coastal Victims of Trafficking
text:
Washington, D.C. – U.S. Senators Ron Wyden and Jeff Merkley, along with U.S. Representative Suzanne Bonamici, today announced $440,000 in federal awards to support victims of trafficking in Clatsop County.

“Survivors of human trafficking carry unimaginable trauma, and they deserve strong, coordinated support systems rooted in their own communities,” Wyden said. “I’m glad to see these federal dollars heading to Astoria so The Harbor can broaden its outreach, strengthen local emergency response networks and ensure no victim in Clatsop County has to navigate recovery alone.”

“We must continue to do everything in our power to protect people from the horrors of human trafficking and support its survivors,” Merkley said. “This essential funding will help The Harbor continue its critical work of raising awareness, supporting victims, and providing hope to survivors in Clatsop County.”

“We must empower and support survivors of the despicable crime of human trafficking. The Harbor in Clatsop County has been doing this important work and has earned the community's trust and support,” Bonamici said. “This grant will help to deliver more services and outreach where they are needed throughout Clatsop County, increase awareness of trafficking, and help develop a coordinated response. I’m grateful to my colleagues in the Senate for helping secure this funding and to The Harbor’s staff for their important work.”

The $440,000 in federal awards from the Department of Justice’s Office of Justice Program will be distributed to The Harbor in Astoria. The Harbor is a nonprofit that provides advocacy, prevention and support for survivors of domestic violence, sexual assault and stalking in Clatsop County. The federal award will be used to expand services to victims including crisis intervention, case management, safety planning, shelter, emergency financial assistance and referrals. The Harbor will also conduct outreach to increase awareness of trafficking and available services for victims and will develop partnerships with local agencies and organizations to develop a coordinated human trafficking response.

title: Ranking Members Larsen, Carson Statement on Last Night’s Nationwide Ground Stop
text:
Washington, D.C.—Today, Ranking Member of the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure Rick Larsen (D-WA) and Ranking Member of the Subcommittee on Aviation André Carson (D-IN) released the follow statement regarding last night’s nationwide ground stop and this morning’s press conference with U.S. Department of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Federal Aviation Administration Administrator Bryan Bedford.

“Thank you to our air traffic controllers, safety technicians and all transportation workers who sprang into action to protect travelers during yesterday’s nationwide ground stop,” Ranking Members Larsen and Carson said. “This ground stop left the flying public and aviation workforce in disarray and seeking answers that the Trump administration waited hours to share. The safe travel of the flying public must always be our top priority. Our committee, on behalf of the flying public, will hold the administration accountable for what happened to make sure this chaos does not happen again.

“Let’s look at the facts. Congress approved $12.5 billion for the Department of Transportation to make necessary safety upgrades to our air traffic control system. Fifteen months later, the administration’s obligated $4.3 billion but only spent $1 billion, leaving $8 billion unobligated and $11 billion unspent. Explain to Congress, again, why they need more money?

“FAA and DOT staff will brief our staff on Monday about the additional $30 billion originally requested by the administration. We also expect to receive clear answers from FAA Administrator Bedford at our early December hearing—unless that can happen sooner.

"Heading into the next Congress, T&I Democrats are reconstituting the Oversight and Investigations staff of the Committee, and the rollout of ‘BNATCS’ will be a top priority of this new team. With holiday travel around the corner, we must avoid chaos that leads to mass, unexpected travel delays.”
