title: Rep. Obernolte Applauds House Passage of Major Richard Star Act to Support Combat-Injured Veterans
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Congressman Jay Obernolte (CA-23) applauded the House passage of the Major Richard Star Act, bipartisan legislation he cosponsored to help ensure combat-injured Veterans receive the full retirement and disability benefits they have earned through their military service. Congressman Obernolte has been a passionate advocate for this legislation for years. It passed the House with overwhelming bipartisan support.

“Our nation has a responsibility to honor the service and sacrifices of the men and women who have defended our freedoms,” said Congressman Obernolte. “Veterans who sustained injuries in combat should not be denied the retirement benefits they have earned simply because those injuries prevented them from completing their military careers. The Major Richard Star Act is an important step toward fulfilling our commitment to those who have served, and I am pleased to support this bipartisan effort to ensure our combat-injured Veterans receive the benefits they have earned.”

Under current law, some combat-injured Veterans who are medically retired before completing twenty years of service must forfeit a portion of their military retirement pay when they receive VA disability benefits. The Major Richard Star Act eliminates this reduction for eligible veterans, allowing them to receive both benefits in full.

Named in honor of Major Richard Star, a U.S. Army Reserve Veteran who advocated for this reform after being medically retired due to a combat-related illness, the legislation seeks to ensure that veterans are not financially disadvantaged because of injuries sustained in service to our country.

Following its bipartisan passage in the House, the Major Richard Star Act now awaits consideration in the Senate.

title: Amid FCC’s Moves to Discontinue Landline Service for Hundreds of Thousands of Californians, Panetta, Schiff, Matsui, and Thompson Call on FCC to Abandon Proposed Order
text:
Monterey, CA – As the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) moves to clear the way for AT&T to discontinue landline services essential to Californians, United States Representatives Jimmy Panetta (CA-19), Doris Matsui (CA-07), and Mike Thompson (CA-04), along with U.S. Senator Adam Schiff (D-CA), pushed the FCC to drop this effort that would prevent California from ensuring vulnerable and rural communities have reliable landline phone service.

This new inquiry follows a July 2026 letter the lawmakers sent to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr urging him to stop AT&T from shutting down landline services; however, rather than address the lawmakers’ concerns, the FCC approved AT&T’s application to decommission approximately 360 wire centers in California. On October 30, the FCC issued a draft order to preempt California’s carrier of last resort (COLR) rules — the exact issue the lawmakers warned about.

If the FCC adopts this order, it will eliminate California’s ability to require proof that wireless or fiber replacements actually work before copper wires are discontinued. It will also allow AT&T to discontinue landline service at several hundred wire centers in the state, affecting roughly 184,000 residential customers and 15,000 business customers in rural areas in California.

“These rules require telecommunications companies to provide basic phone service to anyone within their service area who requests it, ensuring that no Californian is left without access to essential communications services, including 911,” wrote the lawmakers.

While the transition from copper to fiber-optic systems and other technologies will modernize communications systems, the lawmakers emphasized the need to ensure service reliability and accessibility for communities.

“We urge you to provide the public with sufficient time and a fair opportunity to review and weigh in on the full text of the order, rather than rush through a final decision that undermines public trust. … We share the Commission’s goal in modernizing our nation’s communications networks and expanding fiber-optic infrastructure to underserved communities. However, these efforts must be executed carefully, in a manner that protects vulnerable communities during emergencies and outages and preserves universal telephone service for all Americans,” concluded the lawmakers.

Full text of the letter is available here and below:

Dear Chairman Carr:

We write again to raise concern over the Federal Communications Commission’s (FCC) efforts to eliminate California’s legal authority to require carriers to verify that wireless or fiber replacements function properly before retiring copper telephone networks. The draft order you circulated to the Commission on October 30, 2026, purports to preempt the California Public Utilities Commission’s (CPUC) Carrier of Last Resort (COLR) rules. These rules require telecommunications companies to provide basic phone service to anyone within their service area who requests it, ensuring that no Californian is left without access to essential communications services, including 911.

On July 22, 2026, twenty-eight members of the California Congressional delegation asked the Commission to deny AT&T’s petitions, and that request still stands. Following that letter, the Commission approved AT&T’s application to decommission approximately 360 wire centers in California covering about 184,000 residential locations in California.

If the FCC issues this purported blanket preemption, it will take away any oversight ability of California and other states to make sure sufficient alternative service exists without putting any system in place at the federal level to make that determination. In March, the Commission replaced its adequate replacement test with a carrier certification that a replacement service is available. The FCC relies on coverage reported by carriers and does not independently verify that there is alternative functioning service in the areas where copper will be retired. Without verification or oversight, California residents, including those in High Fire Threat Districts, will continue to lose basic service without access to an adequate replacement.

It should be noted that California’s rules do not stand in the way of modernization and are not meant to relegate Californians to outdated technology. The CPUC has told the FCC that its rules require reliable minimum service but do not require that service to be delivered over copper. If carriers can provide a replacement that meets California’s reliability standards, nothing prevents them from retiring copper systems. Congress preserved this protection in Section 253(b) of the Communications Act to allow states to create any necessary requirements to protect public safety, safeguard consumers’ rights, and ensure the continued quality of telecommunications services.

This month, the Commission is allowing copper retirement to begin in eighteen states – Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Michigan, Mississippi, Missouri, North Carolina, Ohio, Oklahoma, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas, and Wisconsin. Those customers’ experiences over time may be helpful in determining the adequacy of wireless replacements. However, there is no dedicated mechanism for consumers to report problems with replacement service after discontinuance. These problems could range from thousands of blocked calls to 911 to problems with TTY devices, medical alert systems, or home alarms. Rural communities and elderly populations will be most at risk.

We urge you to provide the public with sufficient time and a fair opportunity to review and weigh in on the full text of the order, rather than rush through a final decision that undermines public trust. As carriers migrate their networks from copper to fiber optic systems and other technologies, this transition brings new opportunities to modernize our communications systems. At the same time, it raises serious questions about service reliability and accessibility, especially in areas prone to natural disasters, which increasingly extends well beyond California. The Commission recognized these concerns in September when it pulled another discontinuance application from automatic approval for further review, and it should apply the same level of scrutiny in this circumstance. At the very least, any order should carve out areas at high risk for fires and other natural disasters and areas without verified indoor cellular coverage.

We also request that you respond in writing to the following questions by December 15, 2026, and before any vote on the draft order:

1. Should a carrier have to show, with independently verified data, that its replacement service provides reliable indoor coverage before retiring copper in high-fire-threat areas? If not, what showing should be required?

2. Of the more than 184,000 California locations approved for discontinuance, how many are in High Fire Threat Districts, and how many lack indoor wireless coverage?

3. Do you agree that demonstrating wireless coverage under normal operating conditions does not necessarily establish that a network will remain reliable during a wildfire, extended power outage, or other natural disaster?

4. If testing identifies locations where the replacement service is unreliable or unavailable, will the FCC require the carrier to maintain existing service until an adequate alternative is available?

5. Many wireless services stop working when the power goes out. Will the FCC require backup power for replacement services in disaster-prone areas so customers can still call 911 during outages?

6. For customers in states approved for copper retirement, what mechanisms will be available to those individuals to report service failures, and how will the FCC use those reports?

7. Should a state be permitted to require a carrier to demonstrate that its replacement service is reliable before landline service is discontinued? Should a federal discontinuance authorization automatically override state public safety requirements that address risks the FCC did not evaluate rigorously?

8. Why should the Commission act before the courts rule on the challenges to the Network Modernization Order?

9. Will the FCC share outage reporting data with state commissions, local governments, and first responders, with any necessary confidentiality safeguards applied to the data?

We share the Commission’s goal in modernizing our nation’s communications networks and expanding fiber-optic infrastructure to underserved communities. However, these efforts must be executed carefully, in a manner that protects vulnerable communities during emergencies and outages and preserves universal telephone service for all Americans.

###

title: Congresswoman Pettersen Announces Her Bipartisan Legislation Creating a Federal Program Mirroring Colorado’s FMLA Program for Parents With an Infant in NICU
text:
ARVADA – Congresswoman Brittany Pettersen (CO-07) today joined with advocates, stakeholders, and community members to announce her latest legislation that would allow NICU parents to take up to an additional 12 weeks of dedicated FMLA leave to be with their newborn. FMLA leave can be essential to ensuring that parents have time to recover, bond with their infant during a pivotal stage, and adjust to their family’s “new normal” while protecting their employment. Pettersen was joined at the event today by two NICU parents who shared their stories, as well as advocates from Women’s Foundation of Colorado, A Better Balance, Love for Lily, Mother Forward Colorado, Children’s Hospital Colorado, and Illuminate Colorado.

Pettersen introduced the bipartisan legislation alongside Reps. Ryan Mackenzie (PA-07) Morgan McGarvey (KY-03), and Mike Lawyler (NY-17).

“Childbirth is an incredibly stressful time for any family, much less when their baby is admitted to the NICU. No parent should have to spend that time worrying about whether they will have their job once their baby comes home,” said Congresswoman Pettersen. “Giving an employee that basic decency shouldn’t be dependent on the whims of individual employers. I’m proud to introduce the Stand By NICU Babies and Families Act, which will ensure every parent is afforded the ability to support their baby and family during their most vulnerable time.”

"For parents with a newborn in the NICU, the last thing they should have to worry about is whether they'll have enough time off work to be there for their child,” said Congressman Mackenzie.“Having seen firsthand the difference that exceptional NICU care can make for a family, I know how important it is for parents to have the time and support they need during such a difficult period. The Stand By NICU Babies Act would give working parents greater peace of mind by ensuring they have additional job-protected leave to be by their baby's side when it matters most.”

“When your baby’s in the NICU, all you can focus on is getting them home,” said Congressman McGarvey. "My wife and I waited 99 days to bring our twins home. During those difficult days, no parent should be worried about their parental leave running out. I’m grateful for Rep. Pettersen’s leadership, and I’m proud to co-lead this bill to give NICU parents the same precious days at home with their newborns as every other parent.”

"Every working parent deserves the chance to be there for their child, especially when that child is facing a serious medical challenge. Parents of newborns in the NICU are often forced to use their leave before they even get to bring their baby home. That’s not how it should be. The Stand By NICU Babies and Families Act would give these families more time to care for their newborn and be together once they’re home. I’m proud to support this effort,” said Congressman Lawler.

NICU parents face unique challenges, and working parents with a NICU newborn can easily exhaust most or all of their allotted FMLA leave during their infant’s hospitalization, which leaves little time for bonding. Establishing this dedicated time provides additional protections to ensure NICU parents and infants are adequately supported during these complex health situations.

Specifically, this legislation:

Provides eligible employees with up to 12 additional workweeks of FMLA leave that can be used while they have a son or daughter admitted to the NICU

Ensures NICU leave does not count against the existing 12 weeks of FMLA leave available to eligible employees

Allows parents to take NICU leave flexibly, on an as-needed basis, for the first year of their child’s life

Colorado has been a national leader in expanding paid family leave. In November 2020, Coloradans voted to establish the statewide Family and Medical Leave Insurance (FAMLI) program to provide up to 12 weeks of paid family and medical leave for eligible employees. In January 2026, Colorado expanded this program to establish up to 12 weeks of paid NICU leave for qualifying employees that had an infant admitted to a neonatal intensive care unit. Colorado became the first state to adopt dedicated neonatal care in the United States. Since this program took effect at the beginning of the year, over 2,300 claims for NICU leave have been submitted across the state.

For more information, see a one-pager on the legislation here.

Organizations supporting this legislation include: National Partnership for Women & Families, A Better Balance, NICU Parent Network, American Academy of Pediatrics, Third Way, Zero to Three, Perigee Fund, March of Dimes, Chamber of Mothers, Paid Leave for All, MomsRising, Main Street Alliance, Bobbie, Center for Law and Social Policy (CLASP), Caring Across Generations, National Perinatal Association, Institute for Women’s Policy Research, Children’s Hospital Colorado, Illuminate Colorado, Colorado Children’s Campaign, Mother Forward Colorado, The PPROM Foundation, PreemieWorld Foundation, Tiny Transitions Therapy Consulting PLLC, NICU Alumni, Konnected Thru 22, Inc., The Tiny Miracles Foundation, Lambie’s Love, Boost Therapeutics Innovations, The Skylar Project, Silvie Bells, Forever Jewelz Foundation, Project Sweet Peas, Lily’s Hope Foundation, National Collaborative for Infants & Toddlers, NICU Parent Club, Family-Centered Care Taskforce, Family Values @ Work, Engage: Promoting Women’s Economic Security.

“Newborn babies in the NICU need their parents by their side, especially when they are fighting for their young lives,” said Jocelyn Frye, president of the National Partnership for Women & Families. “The 12 weeks of job-protected leave provided under the FMLA can be insufficient for parents when their newborn is experiencing an extended health crisis. NICU parents shouldn’t have to choose between rushing back to work so they can save their leave for when they bring their baby home from the hospital or using their leave to support their baby in the hospital and then having no time to bond at home. The Stand By NICU Babies and Families Act would provide up to12 additional weeks of job-protected leave for parents who need to be at the hospital fighting alongside their child. This bipartisan bill builds on the FMLA and helps to solve a problem that far too many families face. We’re grateful to the bill’s champion, Rep. Brittany Pettersen, for bringing this important issue to the forefront.”

“No parent should have to worry about losing their job while their newborn is in critical condition. But far too many NICU parents in this country are forced to either return to work while their baby is still in the hospital, exhaust their leave before they can even bring their baby home, or risk losing their job,” said Inimai Chettiar, President of A Better Balance. “When a baby needs intensive care, having their parents in the hospital as part of their care team gives them the best possible chance to thrive. And as families across the country face a crisis of affordability, updating our laws to better support NICU parents’ job security is just common sense—it’s encouraging to see lawmakers on both sides of the aisle recognizing that. We applaud Rep. Pettersen for leading the effort to build on momentum in states like Colorado and introduce the bipartisan Stand By NICU Babies and Families Act. We thank Rep. McGarvey, Rep. Mackenzie, and Rep. Lawler for their leadership in cosponsoring this bill.”

title: Pou Announces $493,000 Federal Award for North Jersey Sustainability
text:
WASHINGTON, DC – Congresswoman Nellie Pou (D-NJ-09) and City Green in Clifton, New Jersey, today announced a $493,998 federal grant from the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) Farmers Market Promotion Program.

This federal funding will train farmers and local producers on innovative mobile marketing practices and improve their technical skills. Additionally, a statewide agritourism promotional platform – modeled after the Virginia Farmers Market Association’s Farmers Market University platform – will be created to connect New Jersey farms, local food retailers, and consumers.

“New Jersey has an incredibly diverse economy, and oftentimes people can overlook the contributions from our agricultural industry,” said Congresswoman Nellie Pou. “Our farmers need our support and investment. This federal funding will enable City Green to empower producers and further solidify their role in our communities and in our statewide economy.”

City Green is a nonprofit farming and gardening organization. Since 2004, City Green has enhanced the statewide food system by connecting farms and markets with nutrition assistance programs like SNAP and WIC. Additionally, through providing practical, technical and financial resources to farmers, City Green is increasing food access and creating sustainable, healthy communities throughout New Jersey.

“City Green’s is grateful to the USDA for selecting this project for the Farmers Market Promotion Program grant,” says Jennifer Papa, City Green’s Founder and Executive Director. “Our vision is to strengthen a local food culture in New Jersey that places farmers markets as core cultural assets in the Garden State. Through this award, we plan to develop new and innovative marketing techniques for farmers markets, provide much-needed technical assistance to market operators, increase the customer base for markets and farmers by amplifying agritourism statewide. City Green is excited to launch this initiative in support of a resilient local food system in New Jersey with strong direct-to-consumer markets and deeply invested consumers.”

The USDA Farmers Market Promotion Program works to expand direct producer-to-consumer channels and support the domestic consumption of regionally produced agricultural products. building a statewide agritourism promotional platform that connects farms, local food retailers, and consumers.

title: THE DIGNITY ACT SURPASSES 50 CO-SPONSORS, EXPANDING BIPARTISAN SUPPORT IN CONGRESS
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Today, Congresswoman María Elvira Salazar (R-FL-27) announced that 16 additional Members of Congress have joined the bipartisan DIGNITY Act (H.R. 4393), bringing total congressional support to 56 lawmakers. The latest additions mark another significant milestone for the legislation, which has continued to expand its congressional support and build a broad national coalition throughout 2026.

The announcement comes amid renewed national debate over immigration enforcement, the future of millions of long-term undocumented immigrants, and the economic impact of immigration policy on American workers, businesses, and families.

“Sixteen more Members of Congress are joining an effort that has been growing all year, both on Capitol Hill and across the country. This proves that Republicans and Democrats can still come together to find a solution to America's immigration crisis,” said Congresswoman María Elvira Salazar. “We are building a coalition around a simple principle: America can have law and order, economic prosperity, and human dignity. We do not have to choose. The legislation is written, the support is growing, and now Congress has an opportunity to turn that progress into law.”

The 16 new co-sponsors include Rep. Carlos Gimenez (R-FL-28), Rep. Steven Horsford (D-NV-04), Rep. Angie Craig (D-MN-02), Rep. Greg Landsman (D-OH-01), Rep. Chris Deluzio (D-PA-17), Rep. Frank Mrvan (D-IN-01), Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet (D-MI-08), Rep. Seth Moulton (D-MA-06), Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi (D-IL-08), Rep. Julie Johnson (D-TX-32), Rep. Josh Gottheimer (D-NJ-05), Rep. Sharice Davids (D-KS-03), Rep. Sarah Elfreth (D-MD-03), Rep. Chris Pappas (D-NH-01), Rep. Josh Riley (D-NY-19), and Rep. Val Hoyle (D-OR-04).

Click here to view the full list of DIGNITY Act co-sponsors.

The DIGNITY Act

Introduced by Representatives María Elvira Salazar (R-FL) and Veronica Escobar (D-TX), the DIGNITY Act offers a bipartisan solution to America's broken immigration system. The legislation strengthens and codifies border security, provides an earned path to legal status for eligible long-term undocumented immigrants, protects Dreamers, and modernizes America's legal immigration system. It also protects American workers and supports businesses by addressing critical workforce needs and strengthening the U.S. economy.

A GROWING NATIONAL COALITION

The addition of 16 new co-sponsors marks another milestone in a year of significant progress for the DIGNITY Act, reflecting growing support both on Capitol Hill and across the country.

Congressional support has grown from 35 lawmakers at the beginning of 2026 to 56 today. Beyond Congress, the legislation has secured endorsements from more than 100 national organizations, representing a broad coalition of businesses, manufacturers, farmers, builders, hospitality leaders, faith organizations, veterans, and immigration reform advocates.

The DIGNITY Act has also earned the formal endorsement of the bipartisan Problem Solvers Caucus, while the National DIGNITY Coalition and nationwide DIGNITY Tour have brought together lawmakers, employers, workers, faith leaders, Dreamers, and families to engage communities across the country on immigration reform.

Together, these developments reflect the continued expansion of a coalition that crosses party lines, industries, and communities, strengthening congressional support and bringing a broad range of stakeholders into the discussion over America's immigration future.

As Washington considers the next steps on immigration reform, the DIGNITY Act provides an established bipartisan legislative framework addressing law and order, economic prosperity, and human dignity.

For more information about the DIGNITY Act, visit https://salazar.house.gov/dignity-act

title: Congresswoman Scholten Introduces Legislation to Level the Playing Field for Small Businesses
text:
WASHINGTON, DC – U.S. Congresswoman Hillary Scholten (D-MI-03), member of the House Small Business Committee, reintroduced the Enhancing Competition in Contracting Orders Act, which would expand contracting opportunities for small businesses participating in the HUBZone program. Specifically, this bill would amend the Small Business Act to allow Historically Underutilized Business Zone (HUBZone) price preferences in certain contracts, including full and open competition contracts, multiple award contracts, and partial set aside contracts.

“The HUBzone program is a unique opportunity created to give small businesses in economically disadvantaged communities a fair shot at government contracts,” said Congresswoman Scholten. “The program’s 10% price preference levels the playing field against larger companies and clarifies its benefits. I'm proud to introduce this commonsense piece of legislation that will help small businesses in Michigan and across the country grow and compete.”

The HUBZone program is one of four small business federal contracting programs. Small businesses that are HUBZone-certified are located in economically distressed communities, as determined by the U.S. Census data. Congress has established a 3 percent goal for contract dollars to go to HUBZone businesses, but most federal agencies unfortunately fall short of this goal. By clarifying when the price preference tool can be used, the Enhancing Competition in Contracting Orders Act enables HUBZone-certified businesses to bid for contracts they otherwise would struggle to win. As a result, qualified HUBZone businesses will be able to compete for a wider range of government contracts, providing more opportunities for those businesses who are economic anchors of their communities.

Congresswoman Scholten also secured a critical provision for small businesses in the Fiscal Year (FY) 2027 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA). This provision ensures that certain Department of Defense (DoD) contracts reach small defense contractors, which will strengthen both America’s national security and small business economy.

title: Congresswoman Schrier’s Bills to Lower Energy Costs, Expand Clean Energy Pass the House
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Congresswoman Kim Schrier’s two bipartisan bills, the Efficient Nuclear Licensing Hearings Act and the American Enrichment Deployment Act, passed the U.S. House of Representatives. These bills aim to eliminate red tape and bolster the domestic production of nuclear fuel, ultimately lowering energy costs, curbing reliance on carbon emissions, and safeguarding the reliability of the electric grid.

“We need to expand and accelerate our nation’s buildout of clean energy to lower prices, curb carbon emissions, and protect our environment,” said Congresswoman Schrier in a speech on the House floor prior to passage. “Nuclear power is essential to this energy mix … It is time to lower costs and build out more energy resources while lowering emissions. Our constituents are demanding it, and our country needs it. I urge my colleagues to pass these bills.”

View Congresswoman Schrier’s floor remarks HERE.

BACKGROUND:

Efficient Nuclear Licensing Hearings Act:

Congresswoman Schrier, Congressman Morgan Griffith (VA-09), and Congressman Marc Veasey (TX-33), members of the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, introduced the Efficient Nuclear Licensing Hearings Act in September 2025. This bipartisan bill aims to reform federal nuclear licensing processes and improve the overall effectiveness of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC).

This legislation drops the requirement for the NRC to hold a public hearing at the end of the licensing process if the license is not contested by an affected party. Uncontested licensing hearings result in hours of preparation for the NRC staff, greatly inflate application fees, and unnecessarily delay the approval of applications. Both Democratic and Republican commissioners of the NRC expressed support in this modernization effort at an E&C hearing, and experts, such as Columbia University’s Center on Global Energy Policy, recommend the action.

American Enrichment Deployment Act:

Congresswoman Schrier and Congressman Russell Fry (SC-07) introduced the American Enrichment Deployment Act in July 2026. Currently, the U.S. operates just one uranium enrichment facility while Russia represents nearly half of the world’s enrichment capacity. With a ban on Russian enriched uranium imports taking effect in 2028 and without enough facilities to enrich uranium for commercial nuclear fuel, the U.S. risks not having enough available fuel for the expanded nuclear fleet coming online in the coming years.

This legislation aims to bolster domestic production of nuclear fuel by modernizing the regulatory process for new facilities while maintaining safety and environmental safeguards. Specifically, the bill brings the licensing process of enrichment facilities in line with other front-end fuel cycle facilities while maintaining environmental review under the National Environmental Policy Act. Importantly, this allows applicants to begin construction once NRC dockets an application at the applicant’s own risk and subject to all applicable laws, reducing unnecessary delays and lowering costs.

title: Spartz: Jeffries’ First Act - Bankrupt Medicare, Bankroll Insurers, and Bury Our Kids in Debt
text:

title: Congresswoman Lee Leads Delegation in Support of Nevada’s Bid to Host New U.S. Space Academy
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Congresswoman Susie Lee (NV-03) led the Nevada delegation in sending a letter to NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman in support of the state’s bid to host the new U.S. Space Academy. Senators Catherine Cortez Masto (D-NV) and Jacky Rosen (D-NV), and Representatives Steven Horsford (NV-04), Mark Amodei (NV-02), and Dina Titus (NV-01) joined Congresswoman Lee in sending the letter.

“Nevada offers a distinctive combination of federal training and test infrastructure, active NASA lunar training capabilities, nationally recognized research universities, a growing aerospace and defense workforce, and an interior location, which, combined, make Nevada an ideal location to host the envisioned United States Space Academy,” wrote the Members.

On August 28, 2026, President Trump signed an Executive Order to create a Presidential Commission to establish a new federal academy to prepare the next generation of Americans to advance the United States’ interests in space. The proposed United States Space Academy (USSA) will be a federal academy dedicated to combining technical education with leadership development, discipline, and a durable commitment to public service, with the goal of preparing graduates for careers supporting America’s military, civil, and broader space enterprise.

As the Members highlighted in their letter, Nevada is well-positioned to serve as the home for the U.S. Space Academy for several reasons:

Nevada already supports the nation’s lunar exploration enterprise.

The Nevada Space Proving Grounds at the Nevada National Security Site (NNSS) provides mission-scale lunar and Martian testing and training.

NASA astronauts preparing for Artemis IV are training there today, and every Apollo astronaut who walked on the Moon trained at the NNSS before flying to the lunar surface.

Nevada also offers substantial federal range and airspace capacity.

The Nevada Test and Training Range (NTTR) spans approximately 2.9 million acres and 12,000 square miles of military airspace.

Together with NNSS and the missions centered at Nellis and Creech Air Force Bases, Nevada provides an established federal ecosystem for national security training, research, testing, and operations.

Roughly 80% of the state is federal land, much with low population density and clear, predictable weather, making it ideal for a future partnership of this scale.

Nevada also has a robust academic and industrial base to support USSA’s mission.

The University of Nevada, Las Vegas (UNLV) and the University of Nevada, Reno (UNR) are both Carnegie R1 research institutions.

Nevada’s aerospace and defense sector supported more than 21,000 jobs in 2025, a roughly 56% increase over the prior decade.

As southern Nevada’s sole representative on the House Appropriations Defense Subcommittee, Congresswoman Lee is fighting to boost and diversify southern Nevada’s economy through local defense contractors, which create good-paying jobs.

title: Tokuda, Moylan Urge USPS to Reverse Service Delivery Cuts for Island Communities
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Today, U.S. Representatives Jill N. Tokuda (HI-02) and James Moylan (GU-At Large) led a bipartisan, bicameral group of lawmakers, including members of the Hawaiʻi and Alaska congressional delegation and U.S. territories, in urging Postmaster General David Steiner to reverse changes to USPS Ground Advantage service that threatens to extend delivery times for lightweight packages in noncontiguous states and U.S. territories.

Starting October 1, 2026, USPS began transporting Ground Advantage packages weighing less than one pound primarily by boat rather than air between the contiguous United States and noncontiguous states and U.S. territories. As a result, communities in the Pacific and Caribbean could face delivery times of 10 days or more—nearly double the standard five-day domestic delivery window. This policy change compounds longstanding concerns about packages taking weeks or even months to arrive, while residents continue to face rising postal rates and additional holiday surcharges.

“For our rural and island communities, reliable mail service is more than a convenience. It’s a lifeline for obtaining medications, household goods, and other necessities that simply aren’t available on local store shelves. At a time when families across Hawaiʻi and the country are already struggling with rising costs, the last thing they need is to pay more for slower mail service,” said Rep. Tokuda. “Yet, USPS is once again raising shipping rates while extending delivery times for the communities that depend on mail service the most. USPS must reverse this decision and uphold its responsibility to provide timely, reliable service to every community it serves.”

“Reliable and affordable postal service is essential for Guam’s families and small businesses," said Rep. Moylan. "While we recognize the need for safe and efficient operations, USPS must also consider the unique shipping challenges facing noncontiguous communities. We should be improving delivery standards, not creating further delays. I thank my colleagues for their partnership on this effort and join them in urging USPS to reconsider this policy."

The lawmakers urged USPS to restore air transportation for eligible lightweight Ground Advantage packages and reconsider the policy's disproportionate impact on noncontiguous states and U.S. territories. They requested a response by November 25, 2026.

Full text of the letter may be found here.

title: Walberg Honors Jackson County Veteran
text:
Today, Congressman Tim Walberg (MI-05) recognized Walter Reed of Clarklake as the Veteran of the Month for November. The Congressman presented Walter with the Congressional Record containing his remarks honoring Walter's service to our nation and local community.

Walter graduated from Michigan State University’s ROTC program in 1962 and went on to serve as an Armor Officer in the United States Army, attaining the rank of Major. During his career, he served in Germany and later in Vietnam, where he completed two tours of duty and coordinated logistics for peace talks. Walter was awarded the Purple Heart and 5 Bronze Star medals for his service.

Following his time in active duty, Walter continued his commitment to our nation through his service in the Army Reserves and his work with General Dynamics Land Systems, where he led the development and delivery of programs throughout the United States and Europe.

Walter's dedication to serving others extends to the local Jackson County community, where he is an active member of the Lions Club and supports annual fundraising efforts to ensure the organization has the resources necessary to support those in need. He is also involved with Vietnam Veterans of Jackson, where he regularly visits local high schools to share his experience, helping students better understand the sacrifices of those who have served.

"It is a privilege to recognize Walter Reed of Clarklake as the Veteran of the Month for November," said Rep. Walberg. "Walter dutifully served our country throughout the Vietnam War and continues to serve our local community today as an active member of multiple service organizations. His continued commitment to others and his devotion to our nation inspires us all. I commend his contributions and extend my deepest gratitude for his enduring service."

You can view pictures of the presentation here.

Background

Congressman Walberg's office is accepting submissions for the Veteran of the Month program, an initiative to honor the exemplary contributions of veterans in Michigan's 5th Congressional District. Each month, Congressman Walberg will recognize one outstanding veteran, celebrating their commitment to serving our community and their exceptional service in the military.

title: ALSOBROOKS LEADS COLLEAGUES IN PUSHING SEC FOR ANSWERS, TRANSPARENCY ON TOKENIZED STOCK CHANGE
text:
November 16, 2026

WASHINGTON, DC – As reported in POLITICO’s Morning Money, Senators Angela Alsobrooks (D-Md.), Catherine Cortez Masto (D-Nev.), Mark Warner (D-Va.), and Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.) are demanding answers after the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) published its September 17, 2026 Order exempting tokenized stocks from securities laws without public input. The SEC’s Innovation Exemption invites confusion for investors and corporations alike, evidenced by over sixty public companies declining to participate in the Order’s framework. The Innovation Exemption as drafted lacks clarity in the application of the illicit finance, market integrity, and investor protection rules that make America’s capital markets the envy of the world. In a letter to SEC Chairman Paul Atkins, the Senators request answers to and more public engagement involving these questions.

“We share the goal of ensuring U.S. capital markets and investors benefit from new technology—including through faster settlement, modernized recordkeeping, and broader access—and consider the Exemption with the most important shared principle: a tokenized security is a security. We are concerned the Exemption lacks clarity in three crucial areas that, if unaddressed, could undermine the integrity of our capital markets and threaten public companies and investors alike,” wrote the lawmakers.

“As of this writing, over sixty public companies (“issuers”) have objected to their shares being tokenized. Issuers may object within 30 days of notification by a [Tokenized Securities Venues (TSV)] of an intent to tokenize and list their stock. There is no apparent way for issuers to lodge a standing objection against their stock being tokenized; to object after the 30-day window closes; or to ever rescind consent. There is also no apparent consideration of how an opt-out, rather than opt-in, regime could burden small public companies lacking the compliance and legal resources to monitor and respond to every third-party’s attempt to tokenize their stocks,” continued the lawmakers.

Read the full text of the letter here or below:

Dear Chairman Atkins:

We write regarding the Commission’s September 17, 2026 order (“the Exemption”) granting temporary exemptive relief to Tokenized Securities Venues (“TSVs”) to trade tokenized stocks. We share the goal of ensuring U.S. capital markets and investors benefit from new technology—including through faster settlement, modernized recordkeeping, and broader access—and consider the Exemption with the most important shared principle: a tokenized security is a security. We are concerned the Exemption lacks clarity in three crucial areas that, if unaddressed, could undermine the integrity of our capital markets and threaten public companies and investors alike.

Most significant, the Exemption leaves vague how illicit finance protections, including Anti-Money Laundering (AML), Know-Your-Customer (KYC) and Counter-Terrorism Financing (CFT) protections, apply to tokenized equity trading. Beyond requiring a TSV to be a U.S. person subject to OFAC sanctions, the Exemption sets no identity-verification standard and does not require an AML program. The Exemption requires a TSV to disclose “applicable AML/CFT requirements” but leaves unknown which requirements are applicable and whether compliance is mandatory. The Exemption does not make TSVs a financial institution under the Bank Secrecy Act or impose an actual AML program. Finally, the Exemption requires TSVs to permission access to trading but does not require transfer restrictions in smart contracts at the token level. As a result, a tokenized equity purchased by a verified individual could be transferred to an unverified wallet, including one held by a foreign person or illicit actor, beyond the reach of the U.S. regulatory perimeter.

As of this writing, over sixty public companies (“issuers”) have objected to their shares being tokenized. Issuers may object within 30 days of notification by a TSV of an intent to tokenize and list their stock. There is no apparent way for issuers to lodge a standing objection against their stock being tokenized; to object after the 30-day window closes; or to ever rescind consent. There is also no apparent consideration of how an opt-out, rather than opt-in, regime could burden small public companies lacking the compliance and legal resources to monitor and respond to every third-party’s attempt to tokenize their stocks. Further, neither the public nor issuers can readily identify in a consolidated, searchable way, all of the potential venues where TSVs have filed notices of intentions to tokenize stocks, and all of the venues where the stock tokens for an issuer may be traded.

Finally, we consider the effects on investors. Retail investors may seek to purchase tokenized equities directly from a TSV, without any broker-dealer intermediary. Though a tokenized equity under the Exemption would be “deemed to provide the same rights and privileges” as a holder of the underlying stock, the Exemption leaves vague which core investor protections could apply to the accounts or trading activities in this scenario, including regulations related to advertising, a requirement for best execution of trades, Securities Investor Protection Corporation insurance coverage, and other consumer protection rules. For example, platforms can operate without complying with Regulation NMS, which means TSVs are not required to display their best prices to traders and are not required to report trades to the rest of the market in real time. These protections help ensure that investors receive competitive prices and can be confident that they are getting a fair deal.

Given the Exemption took effect immediately—with public and stakeholder comment invited afterward—companies and investors have a right to greater transparency about the Commission’s next steps as they decide how to respond. Though tokenization may well improve efficiencies in the market and broaden access, long-term success relies on investors and issuers trusting that this new regulatory regime upholds the safeguards that make the U.S.’s capital markets the envy of the world. We respectfully request that you pursue any changes to the regulatory treatment of tokenized securities through a transparent rulemaking process and that you consider and respond to the following questions within thirty days.

Which AML/KYC/CFT requirements does the Commission consider “applicable” to a TSV that is not a registered broker-dealer or bank? How will the SEC enforce compliance of the applicable AML/CFT requirements?

Why does the Exemption not require transfer restrictions at the token level to ensure that tokenized equities remain with verified holders after leaving the TSV?

Once a tokenized equity moves from a verified participant to an unverified or offshore wallet, which regulated entity is responsible for it? Does the Commission have the tools and legal authority to trace, freeze, or recover such tokens, and if not, should it require that tokenized NMS stock traded on a TSV be capable of being frozen or recovered?

Given that the exemption relies on TSV’s own disclosures and self-verification, how does the SEC plan to verify the accuracy of those disclosures and enforce the conditions attached to the exemption?

Can an issuer withdraw an objection to its stock being tokenized by a TSV? Conversely, can an issuer withdraw its consent to its stock being tokenized by a TSV?

Will the Commission consider the burdens and compliance costs for small public issuers to respond to numerous TSV requests? Will the SEC reduce the burden on public companies by retaining a central public repository to track TSV requests?

Will the Commission allow an issuer to file a single standing objection that applies across all TSVs, or requiring an issuer’s affirmative consent before third-party tokens of its stock may trade?

When an investor trades directly on a TSV, who owes that investor a duty of best execution?

What does the holder of a tokenized equity legally own? What happens to holders if a third-party tokenizer becomes insolvent?

How is the SEC ensuring the tokenized securities are appropriately backed and investors are getting what they pay for?

How do entities tokenizing the securities have to custody the underlying asset?

Before making the Exemption permanent, will the Commission commit to proceeding through notice-and-comment rulemaking?

What data will the Commission collect and publish to evaluate the market’s response to the Exemption?

Sincerely,

Angela D. Alsobrooks

United States Senator

Mark R. Warner

United States Senator

Ruben Gallego

United States Senator

Catherine Cortez Masto

United States Senator

title: Sen. Banks Celebrates Opening of IU Applied Research Center

BLOOMINGTON, Ind. – U.S. Senator Jim Banks (R-Ind.) joined Indiana University President Pamela Whitten and leaders from IU and Crane on Friday, November 13, to celebrate the opening of IU’s new Applied Research Center.

title: Blumenthal Applauds Sweeping House Passage of the Major Richard Star Act, Calls for Immediate Senate Vote
text:
[WASHINGTON, D.C.] – U.S. Senator Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), incoming Chairman of the Senate Veterans’ Affairs Committee, today called for immediate passage of the Major Richard Star Act—bipartisan legislation to deliver nearly 59,000 combat-injured veterans their full military benefits. This legislation passed in the House last week by a vote of 392-18 and does not include a funding offset proposed by Republican leadership to cut veterans’ disability benefits.

“Combat-injured veterans deserve justice— long overdue—ending the disgraceful Wounded Veteran Tax. Last week’s sweeping bipartisan passage of the Richard Star Act in the House of Representatives shows this legislation has the votes to pass without cutting benefits to other deserving disabled veterans. The Senate must act immediately and decisively. I am eager to lead this fight.”

The Major Richard Star Act is bipartisan legislation to fix an injustice preventing combat-injured veterans from receiving their full military benefits. Currently, only veterans with disability ratings above 50 percent and more than 20 years of service are eligible to receive the full amount of their Department of Defense retirement and Department of Veterans Affairs disability payments—leaving behind nearly 59,000 combat-injured military retirees.

Blumenthal has led the effort on the Senate side to pass the Major Richard Star Act and oppose attempts to fund the legislation by cutting nearly $57 billion in veterans’ benefits for veterans with sleep apnea and tinnitus. Senate Republican leadership has blocked eight attempts from Blumenthal, including in October, March, May, and June, to advance or vote on the bill.

This legislation has overwhelming support from the majority of both chambers of Congress, with 80 bipartisan cosponsors in the Senate and 342 bipartisan cosponsors in the House.

title: Blumenthal, Britt, & Booker Introduce Legislation To Hold Big Tech Accountable For Failing To Keep Kids Safe, End Forced Arbitration That Silences Victims Of Online Harms
text:
[WASHINGTON, D.C.] – U.S. Senators Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), Katie Britt (R-AL), and Cory Booker (D-NJ) today introduced legislation to ensure families whose children have been killed, sexually assaulted or exploited, or otherwise hurt by Big Tech’s online platforms can seek public accountability through the civil justice system. The Ending Forced Arbitration of Children Online Act would re-establish Americans’ Seventh Amendment right to seek justice and stop Big Tech companies from strong-arming families out of court and into closed-door forced arbitration proceedings.

“Our initiative addresses a monstrous failure in current law: Big Tech companies routinely force grief-stricken families into closed-door contests where they write the rules and evade responsibility for endangering kids online,” said Blumenthal. “Our measure ensures that parents and survivors seeking Big Tech accountability can go to court and seek justice.”

“When a child is harmed online, that family deserves their day in court should they choose, not a closed-door process dictated by an online platform and private arbitrators,” said Britt. “For too long, Big Tech has weaponized forced arbitration to shield themselves from accountability and keep the harm done to children out of public view. The results of this bipartisan bill will shine a much-needed light on the predatory practices of Big Tech and take meaningful steps to protect America’s next generation by ensuring that when a platform fails our children, families get to decide how they seek justice.”

“I’m proud to partner with Senators Blumenthal and Britt to introduce this legislation which would ensure that the families of children harmed online can hold mega platforms accountable in court,” said Booker. “Our children are vulnerable to serious harms online, from sexual exploitation, unsafe content, and manipulation by AI chatbots. Their families should not lose the right to seek justice in a courtroom just because companies inserted fine print in their terms of service forcing them into arbitration. We must hold companies that harm children online accountable.”

There are currently upwards of 180 lawsuits from across the country pending in federal court, and over 30 in state court, against gaming platform Roblox alleging harms that children have suffered including self-harm, abduction, sexual exploitation, rape, sextortion, grooming, and physical abuse. Roblox is systematically trying to force these children and their families into forced arbitration in an effort to evade legal accountability, arguing that a child who clicks “I Agree” to the terms and conditions on the gaming platform means that that child and their family should be forced out of court and into arbitration.

Another company, Character.AI (C.AI), tried to argue that the mother of a 15-year-old boy, who alleges her son died by suicide after C.AI bots repeatedly encouraged him to take his own life, was bound to the platform’s terms which required forced arbitration and included a maximum liability of $100, because her son “agreed” to the terms and conditions. The Ending Forced Arbitration of Children Online Act would render forced arbitration agreements like those used by Roblox and C.AI unenforceable.

The Ending Forced Arbitration of Children Online Act is endorsed by the National Center on Sexual Exploitation (NCOSE) and ParentsTogether Action.

“Digital platforms try to avoid legal responsibility by incorporating forced arbitration language into the terms and conditions that users – even children – agree to when they create accounts. Roblox and Discord are prime examples, and both of those platforms are being sued for causing harm to children. Families should be able to sue a digital platform for causing harm, not be forced into arbitration,” said Richie Hamm, President of NCOSE.

“Parents are already up against the most powerful tech companies in the world as they try to keep their kids safe online. When a child gets hurt, families should not also have to face those companies’ lawyers in a forced arbitration process. The bipartisan Ending Forced Arbitration of Children Online Act from Senators Blumenthal and Britt would protect families in this unfair fight by ensuring their access to the courts, which is a necessary step in holding these companies accountable,” said Alien Arreaza, Executive Director of ParentsTogether Action.

Bill text is available here.

title: Boozman Joins Bipartisan Effort to Honor Women Veterans
text:
WASHINGTON—U.S. Senators John Boozman (R-AR), Marsha Blackburn (R-TN), Cory Booker (D-NJ), Thom Tillis (R-NC), Jacky Rosen (D-NV) and Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH) to honor the contributions of women veterans with the introduction of a bipartisan resolution recognizing their service and sacrifice.

“Women veterans have made tremendous sacrifices in service to our nation, and their contributions deserve our gratitude and recognition. I am proud to help lead this resolution reaffirming our commitment to honoring women veterans and supporting them and their families. Their service in every branch of our Armed Forces has helped defend our freedoms and strengthen our nation, so this Veterans Day, we recognize that sacrifice and reaffirm that their contributions will never be forgotten,” Boozman said.

“From the women who disguised themselves to fight in the American Revolution and Civil War to the Hello Girls of World War I to today’s brave female service members, women have always answered the call to defend our nation. Generations of women have served our country, and this resolution would honor their courage, sacrifice, and vital contributions to our military,” said Blackburn.

“Women have served our country with courage in every generation often without the recognition they deserve. This resolution acknowledges all the brave women who have worn our nation’s uniform, and we must do more to provide them with the benefits and support they have earned,” Booker said.

“Countless women in Nevada and across this country have bravely and selflessly served our nation in uniform, and we owe them a debt of gratitude that can never be repaid. I’m proud to help introduce this bipartisan resolution honoring the contributions of women veterans, and I’ll continue working to recognize and support all of Nevada’s veterans,” said Rosen.

“Throughout our nation’s history, women have played a critical role in defending our freedoms and protecting our national security, often overcoming significant barriers to serve our country with courage and distinction. I’m proud to join my colleagues on this bipartisan effort to recognize the invaluable contributions that women veterans have made and ensure that their service and sacrifices are never forgotten,” Shaheen said.

“Today, we recognize and honor the women who have worn our nation’s uniform and answered the call to serve with courage and dedication. Their sacrifices, strength, and commitment to defending the freedoms we hold dear deserve our utmost gratitude and lasting recognition. We must ensure that every woman who has served our country, across all branches of the Armed Forces, receives the respect, recognition, and support she has rightfully earned,” said Tillis.

The Women Veterans Recognition Resolution also acknowledges the unique challenges women veterans face in accessing health care and benefits we well as reaffirms our nation’s support for women veterans and their families.

Click here to read the resolution.

Background

Boozman is a member of the Senate Veterans’ Affairs Committee and has consistently championed enhanced support for women veterans. In the 119th Congress, he led introduction of the Veterans’ Outcomes, Inclusion, Care, and Experience (VOICE) for Women Veterans Act that would modernize an annual report from the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) so legislators, the VA and veteran advocates have a comprehensive reference to drive change and resolve issues affecting the care and benefits women veterans have earned and deserve.

title: U.S. Senators Katie Britt, Richard Blumenthal, Cory Booker Introduce Bipartisan Bill to Let Families Hold Online Platforms Accountable in Court for Harms to Children
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — U.S. Senators Katie Britt (R-Ala.), Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), and Cory Booker (D-N.J.) today introduced the Ending Forced Arbitration of Children Online Act, bipartisan legislation that would give families the right to take online platforms to court when a child is harmed, rather than being forced into private arbitration by terms of service agreements.

“When a child is harmed online, that family deserves their day in court should they choose, not a closed-door process dictated by an online platform and private arbitrators,” said Senator Britt. “For too long, Big Tech has weaponized forced arbitration to shield themselves from accountability and keep the harm done to children out of public view. The results of this bipartisan bill will shine a much-needed light on the predatory practices of Big Tech and take meaningful steps to protect America’s next generation by ensuring that when a platform fails our children, families get to decide how they seek justice.”

“Our initiative addresses a monstrous failure in current law: Big Tech companies routinely force grief-stricken families into closed-door contests where they write the rules and evade responsibility for endangering kids online,” said Senator Blumenthal. “Our measure ensures that parents and survivors seeking Big Tech accountability can go to court and seek justice.”

“I’m proud to partner with Senators Blumenthal and Britt to introduce this legislation which would ensure that the families of children harmed online can hold mega platforms accountable in court,” said Senator Booker. “Our children are vulnerable to serious harms online, from sexual exploitation, unsafe content, and manipulation by AI chatbots. Their families should not lose the right to seek justice in a courtroom just because companies inserted fine print in their terms of service forcing them into arbitration. We must hold companies that harm children online accountable.”

Many online platforms require users to accept arbitration clauses and class-action waivers as a condition of signing up. Those provisions can force families into private arbitration, even when the user is a child, and the claim involves serious harm.

The Ending Forced Arbitration of Children Online Act would give families the choice to go to court. At the election of the person bringing the claim, no pre-dispute arbitration agreement or pre-dispute joint-action waiver would be valid or enforceable in a case where the alleged harm relates to a minor’s use of a covered platform. The bill applies to cases alleging physical injury, mental or psychological harm, or a violation of privacy or misuse of personal data, whether brought individually or on behalf of a class.

The legislation applies broadly to the platforms children use. Covered platforms include any online platform, video game, messaging application, video streaming service, or artificial intelligence system that connects to the internet and is used, or is reasonably likely to be used, by a minor. This includes popular gaming platforms, such as Roblox.

Under the bill, whether the law applies to a dispute would be determined under federal law. A court, rather than an arbitrator, would decide whether the law applies to an arbitration agreement and whether that agreement is valid and enforceable. The bill would take effect on the date of enactment.

The Ending Forced Arbitration of Children Online Act is endorsed by the National Center on Sexual Exploitation (NCOSE).

“Digital platforms try to avoid legal responsibility by incorporating forced arbitration language into the terms and conditions that users – even children – agree to when they create accounts. Roblox and Discord are prime examples, and both of those platforms are being sued for causing harm to children. Families should be able to sue a digital platform for causing harm, not be forced into arbitration,” said Richie Hamm, President of NCOSE.

Senator Britt has made protecting children online a top priority since taking office. She leads the Stop the Scroll Act with Senator John Fetterman (D-Pa.), which would require a mental health warning label on social media platforms, and joined Senators Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) and Blumenthal in introducing the GUARD Act. She is also a cosponsor of the Children and Teens’ Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA 2.0), which passed the Senate unanimously in March, and the Kids Off Social Media Act.

The full text of the bill can be found here.

title: Senate Appropriations Committee Releases Capito FY2027 Labor-HHS Bill
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – The Senate Appropriations Committee today released proposed legislation, authored by U.S. Senator Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), Chairman of the Senate Labor, Health and Human Services, Education, and Related Agencies (Labor-HHS) Appropriations Subcommittee, to fund the U.S. Departments of Health and Human Services (HHS), Education, and Labor for Fiscal Year (FY) 2027.

The Labor-HHS bill would provide investments in biomedical research, rural health, child care, and increased support for mental health care and substance use disorder prevention and treatment, as well as resources for research at institutions of higher learning in West Virginia and improved facilities at numerous West Virginia medical facilities. The release of this bill is an important part of completing the FY 2027 annual appropriations process, which unfortunately has been delayed by partisan maneuvers by the Democrats in the Senate.

“As Chair of the Labor-HHS Appropriations Subcommittee, I am proud to put forward a strong bill that supports the critical missions of the agencies under our subcommittee’s jurisdiction while reflecting priorities that have long enjoyed bipartisan support. This legislation makes meaningful investments in biomedical research, child care, education, mental health care, and rural health care, while continuing our efforts to combat the opioid epidemic. Importantly, this bill advances priorities that will make a real difference in the lives of West Virginians and communities across our state,” Senator Capito said.

WEST VIRGINIA PRIORITIES:

Chairman Capito was able to ensure many items important to West Virginia were in the package, including resources for opioid and Alzheimer’s research and care, rural health programs, and the Childhood Cancer STAR Act.

CONGRESSIONALLY DIRECTED SPENDING (CDS) PROJECTS:

If this bill were to become law, it would include $110,419,000 in direct spending measures for 22 initiatives and projects across West Virginia. These CDS awards were authored by Senator Capito after having consulted with entities and organizations across West Virginia.

BILL HIGHLIGHTS:

Biomedical Research: $49 billion for the National Institutes of Health (NIH) to support American leadership in biomedical research, including:

Alzheimer’s: $4 billion for Alzheimer’s disease and related research.

Cancer: $7.5 billion for the National Cancer Institute, including $35 million for the Childhood Cancer STAR Act.

Diabetes: $2.4 billion for the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases.

Rare Disease Research: $20 million increase for rare disease research.

Women’s Health Research: $116.5 million for the Office of Research on Women’s Health and $88.4 million for the Implementing a Maternal Health and Pregnancy Outcomes Vision for Everyone (IMPROVE Initiative).

21st Century Cures Act Innovation Programs: $20 million for the BRAIN Initiative and $50 million for the All of Us Program.

Biodefense and Emergency Preparedness: $3.7 billion for the Administration for Strategic Preparedness and Response (ASPR) to support advanced research and development of life-saving medical products and U.S. manufacturing.

Opioid Epidemic: Funding to support research and programs to combat the opioid crisis and other substance abuse disorders, including:

$1.6 billion for the State Opioid Response grants.

$2 billion for the Substance Use Prevention, Treatment, and Recovery Services Block Grant.

$510.6 million for CDC’s opioid overdose prevention and surveillance work.

$650.6 million for NIH’s Helping to End Addiction Long-term (HEAL) Initiative.

$147 million for the Rural Communities Opioid Response Program.

Rural Health: Funding to address health care challenges in rural America, including:

$455.5 million for HRSA’s rural health programs.

$471 million for NIH's Institutional Development Awards (IDeA) Program to build biomedical research capacity in states that have historically received relatively low levels of NIH funding.

$10 million for a new pilot program at NIH to improve cancer outcomes in rural America.

$8 million for CDC’s Office of Rural Health.

Mental Health: Funding to support mental health research, treatment, and prevention, including:

$549.6 million for the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline.

$385.5 million for Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinics.

$2.2 billion for NIH’s National Institute of Mental Health.

$1 billion for the Mental Health Block Grant.

$164 million for school-based mental health grants at the Department of Education.

K-12 Formula Grants: $18.4 billion to support Title I Grants to Local Educational Agencies, $1.3 billion for the 21st Century Community Learning Centers program, and $15.2 billion for Individuals with Disabilities Education Act State Grants.

School Choice: $500 million for Charter School Program grants for the startup, replication, and expansion of high-quality charter schools to increase families’ educational choice.

Career and Technical Education: $1.5 billion for Career and Technical Education programs.

Pell Grants: Funding to address the long-term stability of the Pell Grant program and maintain the maximum Pell Grant award at $7,395 for the 2027-2028 school year.

Child Care: Funding to support early education and affordable child care options for working families, including:

$8.9 billion for the Child Care and Development Block Grant.

$12.4 billion for Head Start.

Energy Assistance: $4.1 billion for the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program to help low-income families and older adults afford home heating and cooling costs.

Apprenticeship Funding: $305 million to support the apprenticeship grant program.

Caregiving: $237 million for the Administration for Community Living’s family caregiving and respite care programs.

Senior Nutrition Program: $1.1 billion for the Senior Nutrition Program to support access to nutritious meals for older adults.

Maintains Legacy Riders: The bill maintains all long-standing riders, including the Hyde Amendment and Weldon conscience protections, needle exchange prohibition, NLRB electronic voting prohibition, and the Dickey Amendment. The bill includes no new funding for Title X and continues protections against the use of Title X funds for abortions.

title: Cortez Masto, Schumer, Murray, Blumenthal, Colleagues Fight to Overturn the Trump Administration’s Abortion Ban At VA
text:
More Than 200 Senate and House Democrats Filed an Amicus Brief Challenging the Trump VA’s Ban on Abortion Care for Veterans in Cases of Rape, Incest, or Health Endangerment

Washington, D.C. – U.S. Senators Catherine Cortez Masto (D-Nev.), Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), Patty Murray (D-Wash.), and Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.); Congressman Mark Takano (D-Calif.-39); and more than additional 200 Senate and House Democrats urged the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit to strike down the Department of Veterans Affairs’ (VA) abortion ban.

The lawmakers filed an amicus brief in Minority Veterans of America v. Secretary of Veterans Affairs, which seeks to overturn VA’s ban on abortion care and counseling. In the brief, they argue the Trump Administration’s 2025 policy banning abortion counseling and abortion care in almost all cases rests on a flawed legal premise.

“VA’s Final Rule rests on a faulty interpretation of federal law that has significant negative consequences for our nation’s veterans. The issues presented in this case potentially reach roughly 462,000 women veterans of reproductive age who are enrolled in VA health care, along with an estimated 112,000 women of reproductive age enrolled in the Civilian Health and Medical Program of the Department of Veterans Affairs (CHAMPVA),” wrote the lawmakers.

“For them, the Final Rule means a VA physician is prohibited from discussing the full range of a patient’s options during a pregnancy, prohibited from providing the full range of health care available to pregnant women, and is prohibited from intervening when a pregnancy threatens the patient’s health or is the result of rape or incest,” they continued.

VA’s abortion ban prohibits abortion counseling and care for veterans and CHAMPVA beneficiaries – even in cases of rape, incest, or if a veteran’s health is endangered. The lawmakers argue in the brief that VA’s erroneous interpretation of federal law means these women now cannot receive abortion care or counseling even in the most harrowing circumstances.

In the Senate, the amicus brief was signed by all 47 Democratic U.S. Senators. In the House, the brief was signed by 165 Democratic U.S. Representatives. The full text of the brief can be found here.

Senator Cortez Masto is a fierce advocate for women’s reproductive rights. Last November, she sent a letter to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and former FDA Commissioner Marty Makary expressing alarm over the Trump Administration’s plans to conduct “its own review of the evidence” on the safety and effectiveness of mifepristone. Cortez Masto is leading legislation to protect the right of women to cross state lines to seek abortion care, to repeal the Comstock Act, and to expand health insurance coverage of birth control throughout the country. She voted against the confirmation of Secretary Kennedy in part because of his inability to answer questions regarding women’s health care rights.

title: Crapo, Welch Introduce Bipartisan WIPE OUT Burn Pits Act to Protect Servicemembers from Toxic Exposure
text:
Washington, D.C.--U.S. Senators Mike Crapo (R-Idaho) and Peter Welch (D-Vermont) introduced the bipartisan Waste Incineration Protection, Exposure Oversight and Updated Tracking of (WIPE OUT) Burn Pits Act to protect U.S. servicemembers from toxic exposure to open-air burn pits near military installations overseas. The legislation would strengthen monitoring and reporting requirements for burn pits, including those operated by foreign partners, and improve documentation of potential exposure in servicemembers' health records. Companion legislation was also introduced in the U.S. House of Representatives by Raul Ruiz (D-California), Gus Bilirakis (R-Florida) and Claudia Tenney (R-New York).

“While the Pentagon has largely phased out the use of burn pits, many foreign partners and entities continue to operate them near installations where U.S. personnel live and work,” said Crapo. “We must take proactive steps to reduce the risk of toxic exposure by providing safer waste disposal alternatives, working with foreign partners to eliminate hazardous burn pits and ensuring servicemembers’ health records accurately document potential exposure so veterans can access appropriate benefits and care in the future.”

“When we passed the PACT Act four years ago, we took a major step toward ensuring that the cost of war always includes the cost of caring for the warrior. But there’s always more we can do to improve servicemember safety, including finding better ways to track and mitigate the risks of burn pits,” said Welch. “I’m proud to partner with Senator Crapo on this bill which builds on our bipartisan work to expand benefits and open doors to care for veterans exposed to toxic chemicals.”

A July 2024 U.S. Department of Defense (DOD) Office of Inspector General report found that the U.S. military does not track or require commanders to monitor foreign-controlled burn pits near U.S. installations. As a result, servicemembers' health records may not accurately reflect potential exposure to toxic substances, creating challenges for veterans seeking health care and benefits related to their military service.

Specifically, the WIPE Out Burn Pits Act would:

Strengthen monitoring and reporting by requiring DOD to identify and report to Congress on burn pits near U.S. installations, including those operated by foreign partners and local entities;

Improve exposure documentation by requiring air-quality testing, adding identified sites to the DOD’s burn pit watch list and incorporating relevant exposure information into potentially affected servicemembers' health records;

Promote safer waste disposal by requiring alternative solid waste disposal systems at locations where the DOD continues to operate burn pits; and

Encourage international cooperation by directing the administration to engage with host nations to eliminate hazardous burn pits that pose exposure risks to U.S. personnel.

Background

Crapo has consistently supported legislative efforts to address toxic exposure among servicemembers and improve access to health care and benefits for impacted veterans. In 2021, Crapo joined Senator Amy Klobuchar (D-Minnesota) to introduce the bipartisan Toxic Exposure Training Act to improve training for U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) personnel to identify and treat illnesses associated with burn pits and other toxic substances. Crapo also co-sponsored the Veterans Burn Pits Exposure Recognition Act to reduce barriers for veterans seeking VA health care and benefits related to toxic exposure, as well as the Toxic Exposure in the American Military (TEAM) Act to expand VA health care eligibility and improve the process for veterans to receive benefits for illnesses caused by toxic exposure. Provisions from all three bills were incorporated into broader veterans' health care legislation signed into law in 2022.

title: Fetterman Celebrates $640,000 in Funding for Venango Wastewater Treatment Facility Project
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Today, U.S. Senator John Fetterman (D-PA) announced nearly $640,000 in Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) funding to Venango County to kickstart the Wastewater Treatment Facility Project at the Two Mile Run county park, an outdoor recreation space and water access.
