title: Grassley Leads Colleagues in Seeking Explanation, Urging Reconsideration of Changes to Kratom-Derived Scheduling
text:
WASHINGTON – Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) and seven of his Republican colleagues are urging the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) and the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to explain and reconsider changes to the emergency scheduling order for semi-synthetic, kratom-derived substances, including deadly 7-hydroxymitragynine (7-OH) and mitragynine pseudoindoxyl (MP).

Following a revised recommendation from FDA, the DEA in October issued an updated proposal that doubled the threshold originally established for 7-OH and removed MP from Schedule I of the Controlled Substances Act. DEA’s October decision would allow both chemicals to be present in over-the-counter kratom products at levels higher than those found naturally in the kratom plant. Prior to DEA’s updated proposal, Grassley, along with Sens. Susan Collins (R-Maine) and Mike Lee (R-Utah), had urged DEA and FDA to implement the agencies’ original scheduling order and permanently place all harmful kratom-derived substances into Schedule I.

“Kratom is a drug in any form with addictive properties, and we believe this combined threshold level for 7-OH and MP set by DEA is inappropriately high and unsound… If the administration’s goal is to remove all unsafe products from the shelves, particularly synthetic or enhanced kratom products, this order misses the mark,” the senators wrote.

“The psychoactive alkaloids of the kratom plant are potentially dangerous substances that should be treated with caution, particularly given the lack of adequate regulation on its products… The American people deserve peace of mind about what is sold on marketplace shelves and a public health system that makes sound regulatory decisions,” the senators continued.

Specifically, the senators are requesting DEA and FDA:

Provide Congress the scientific and medical evaluations the agencies relied on to set a higher threshold limit for 7-OH.

Explain how a higher threshold for 7-OH better protects American families than the original, lower threshold.

Reconsider the updated threshold level for 7-OH and place kratom substances containing any amount of MP in Schedule I.

Grassley is joined by Sens. Susan Collins (R-Maine), Rick Scott (R-Fla.), Mike Crapo (R-Idaho), Bill Cassidy (R-La.), Jerry Moran (R-Kan.), Shelley Capito (R-W.Va.) and Jim Risch (R-Idaho).

Read the full letter HERE. A fact sheet on kratom and the timeline for DEA’s proposed scheduling order is available HERE.

Background:

Kratom leaves contain two major psychoactive ingredients: mitragynine and 7-hydroxymitragynine (7-OH). These substances can be concentrated and chemically modified to produce extremely potent, semi-synthetic compounds – MP, MGM-15 and MGM-16. Kratom and kratom-derived substances are sold over the counter across the country, available to all age groups as “natural” energy boosters, mood lifters and pain relievers.

According to the FDA, known side effects of kratom include liver toxicity, seizures, substance use disorder and, in rare cases, death. According to the DEA, state health authorities have linked the use of 7-OH products and concentrated extracts to dependence, addiction, acute psychosis, slowed breathing, cardiac arrest and death.

Kratom-derived 7-OH has been identified as having a similar abuse potential to heroin or fentanyl and is known to be 13-times more potent than morphine. Other kratom-derived compounds, like MP, are known to be 20-times more potent than morphine.

title: ICYMI: “Public Safety is a Rare Bipartisan Win Congress Shouldn’t Let Slip Away”
text:
Public safety is a rare bipartisan win Congress shouldn’t let slip away

By Rachel Wright, National Policy Director for Right on Crime

November 13, 2026

The Hill

...It isn’t a new feeling, but [partisan tension] is increasingly a roadblock to good policy that improves Americans’ lives. However, Congress now has a real opportunity to set that tension aside and deliver meaningful public safety solutions through a package of bipartisan bills.

Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) and Ranking Member Dick Durbin (D-Ill.) have offered a set of public safety bills as amendments to the National Defense Authorization Act. Together, they show what a thoughtful, targeted approach to crime looks like, tackling online child sexual exploitation, organized retail crime and contraband in federal prisons.

Their approach? Address each problem narrowly and specifically, so the policy actually moves the needle on community safety. Rather than piling on punishment for its own sake, the bills aim for consequences that fit the threat and are serious enough to hold offenders accountable for reprehensible conduct.

Government’s first duty is to protect the most vulnerable among us, especially children. That responsibility does not disappear when crime moves online. Sextortion, which means coercing someone into sending sexually explicit images, often by threatening to expose them, can reach any child with an internet connection. In 2024 alone, the FBI received nearly 55,000 sextortion complaints, a 59 percent jump from the year before.

Federal law has not kept pace. The proposed James T. Woods Act, named for a victim of online sextortion, would update federal sentencing laws for child sexual abuse material. It would also create two new crimes targeting sextortion and violent online networks like 764, which coerce children into harming themselves or others. The goal is simple — hold predators accountable and ensure fewer children become victims.

Additionally, law-abiding citizens and businesses also should not bear the cost of organized crime. Organized retail theft is not petty shoplifting. It is driven by sophisticated networks that operate across state lines, raising prices and putting workers at risk. Because these schemes cross jurisdictions, the federal government has a role to play. The Combating Organized Retail Crime Act would strengthen the federal response by creating a multi-agency task force, improving coordination between retailers and law enforcement, and giving authorities new tools to recover stolen goods.

Public safety also extends behind prison walls. Incarceration should protect the public and prevent further crime, not give offenders a way to keep operating from their cells. Contraband cell phones let inmates continue directing criminal activity on the outside. The Lieutenant Osvaldo Albarati Stopping Prison Contraband Act would make possessing a contraband phone in federal prison a felony rather than a misdemeanor. What happens inside prisons can feel out of sight, out of mind. But safe, secure prisons are essential to public safety, officer safety, and the integrity of the justice system...

Online exploitation, interstate theft rings, and federal prisons are inherently federal challenges. And the National Defense Authorization Act, which has passed every year for more than six decades, is one of the few reliable vehicles in what feels like a gridlocked Congress.

The real question is not whether a policy sounds tough, but whether it offers a targeted, effective response to serious criminal conduct. Today, sizable gaps in federal law leave children exposed, let criminal networks profit, and allow offenders to keep operating behind bars. These bills close those gaps.

In a climate in which distrust of the political process seems to be at an all-time high, lawmakers should seize every chance to show that protecting the public is a shared priority. This is one of those chances. Congress should keep this package in the final National Defense Authorization Act and not let the moment slip away.

title: Senator Hassan Presses Education Department to Resume Oversight of Student Loan Servicers
text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. Senator Maggie Hassan (D-NH) is pressing the U.S. Department of Education to resume assessing student loan servicers for accuracy and call quality to help protect borrowers from costly errors and ensure that they have the information that they need to repay their loans. A Government Accountability Office (GAO) report found that the Department stopped evaluating servicers on these key performance metrics in February 2025. In a letter to Education Secretary Linda McMahon, Senator Hassan raised concerns that the Department's failure to properly oversee student loan servicers could financially harm borrowers and allow servicing problems to go unnoticed.

“Families with federal student loan debt rely on loan service companies to correctly process their loan payments, accurately convey important financial information, and respond promptly when they encounter difficulties with loan payment systems,” Senator Hassan wrote. “Unfortunately, the U.S. Department of Education has decided to stop important assessments of whether loan service companies are accurately processing payments and appropriately responding to calls from families with student loan debt.”

The federal government manages more than $1.6 trillion in student loan debt for more than 40 million borrowers. In April 2024, the Department of Education began new contracts with five student loan servicers that established performance standards for accuracy and call quality. Between July and December 2024, four of the five servicers failed to meet these standards, resulting in approximately $850,000 in financial penalties.

Despite these failures, the Department stopped assessing servicers for accuracy and call quality in February 2025. A March 2026 GAO report found that cuts to Federal Student Aid staff under the Trump Administration contributed to the Department's decision to stop evaluating these performance metrics. GAO recommended that the Department resume these assessments, but the Department disagreed with the recommendation.

“American taxpayers deserve optimal service from the federal government, and contractors must be held accountable for meeting contractually obligated performance standards,” Senator Hassan continued. “I urge you to immediately resume assessments of whether student loan servicers are meeting all required performance standards and to ensure that the Department has the expert staff to provide this proper oversight.”

Read the full text of Senator Hassan’s request to Secretary McMahon here or below.

Dear Secretary McMahon:

Families with federal student loan debt rely on loan service companies to correctly process their loan payments, accurately convey important financial information, and respond promptly when they encounter difficulties with loan payment systems. Unfortunately, the U.S. Department of Education has decided to stop important assessments of whether loan service companies are accurately processing payments and appropriately responding to calls from families with student loan debt. I urge the Department to immediately resume the work of measuring loan servicers’ accuracy and call quality and to ensure that the Department has the capacity to properly oversee these services that are provided to families with federal student loan debt.

The federal government manages more than $1.6 trillion in student loan debt and relies heavily on loan servicer companies to service this debt. Service accuracy and quality are essential to ensuring that our nation’s more than 40 million student loan borrowers have a well-functioning system to interact with. This is especially critical at a time when more than 10 percent of borrowers are in delinquency.

In April 2024, the Department began new five-year contracts with five student loan servicers, with potential extensions of up to 10 years. These contracts set servicer performance standards on specific metrics, including accuracy and call quality. Between July 2024 and December 2024, the Department found that four of five servicers failed to meet accuracy and call quality performance standards. As a result, the Biden Administration enforced financial penalties of approximately $850,000 on the loan servicers that failed to meet the performance standards.

In February 2025, the Department stopped assessing student loan servicers on contractually obligated performance standards despite evidence that some servicers had previously failed to adequately meet standards. In a March 2026 U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO) analysis, the GAO stated that these gaps in oversight may “negatively affect borrowers and enable systemic servicing problems to go unnoticed, which is contrary to Education’s strategic objective to support borrowers in successfully repaying their loans and to hold contractors accountable.” GAO also found that the Trump Administration’s cuts to Federal Student Aid staff played a role in the Department’s decision to stop evaluating servicer accuracy and call quality. Federal Student Aid staff play an essential oversight and accountability role in providing necessary customer service to borrowers who are working hard to repay their debt.

The GAO recommended that the Department resume measuring student loan servicer accuracy and call quality, which are essential in holding servicers accountable for their performance. The Department disagreed with this recommendation, in an apparent abandonment of its responsibility to deliver quality service to the American people. American taxpayers deserve optimal service from the federal government, and contractors must be held accountable for meeting contractually obligated performance standards.

I urge you to immediately resume assessments of whether student loan servicers are meeting all required performance standards and to ensure that the Department has the expert staff to provide this proper oversight.

Thank you for your attention to this important matter.

###

title: Hawley, Durbin Introduce Bill Empowering Survivors of Online Exploitation Ahead of Groundbreaking Hearing on Roblox
text:
WASHINGTON — Today, U.S. Senators Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) and Dick Durbin (D-Ill.) introduced new bipartisan legislation to empower families of children harmed by tech products and by child sexual exploitation online. This bill allows the families of minor children who are exploited online to take their claims to court, even if they agreed to a company’s terms of service requiring private arbitration.

“I am investigating allegations that Roblox, a popular online gaming platform for kids, has become a breeding ground for sexual predators,” said Senator Hawley. “This week, as my Subcommittee holds the first-ever congressional hearing on Roblox’s practices, Senator Durbin and I will introduce new bipartisan legislation to give survivors justice. We must hold these platforms accountable and ensure no child is left vulnerable to exploitation online.”

“In the digital age, predators can target our kids from anywhere—including online gaming platforms like Roblox. And sadly, the numbers show that they have. Therefore, an ‘agreement’ buried in the terms of service shouldn’t limit a child’s or family’s rights to bring their claim before a judge or jury. I’m proud to partner with Senator Hawley on this bipartisan issue, and I won’t stop until this bill—and other key measures to protect children online—are signed into law,” Senator Durbin said.

In August, Senators Hawley and Durbin launched a joint investigation into Roblox in the Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism.

Tomorrow, Senator Hawley will convene the first-ever hearing into this massive gaming platform entitled: Roblox and Online Gaming: Digital Playgrounds Endangering America’s Children. The hearing will occur at 2:30 PM ET in Dirksen Senate Office Building Room G50. Watch the hearing LIVE here.

The No Forced Arbitration for Child Sexual Exploitation and Cyber Injuries Act would:

Open courthouse doors to families of children harmed by tech products or sexual exploitation, allowing them to file lawsuits even if they signed terms of service requiring private arbitration.

Closes loopholes to ensure that a click-through agreement can’t limit a child’s rights, and provides that a judge, rather than an arbitrator, decides whether the law applies to a child’s claim.

Allows class-action lawsuits, permitting claims either individually or collectively in class or collective action.

Preserves choice for survivors and their families, allowing them to choose whether to bring their claim in public court or confidential arbitration.

title: Heinrich Op-Ed: A Plan to End America’s Most Expensive Bottleneck
text:
WASHINGTON – In an op-ed published by The Economist, U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, highlighted the need for the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), explaining how the legislation will speed up the federal approval process for energy projects to get more power onto the grid, lowering electricity bills for Americans and creating more jobs – while codifying into law Tribal consultation, maintaining key environmental protections, and holding data centers accountable for their costs.

“In June, the largest clean-energy-infrastructure project in the western hemisphere came online in New Mexico. “The[SunZia] project took 17 years to permit and build—and SunZia isn’t alone. Across America, energy-infrastructure projects take far too long to permit… Indeed, permitting might be the economy’s most expensive bottleneck,” began Heinrich.

“America’s ability to meet the energy demands of the 21st century depends on its ability to build a modern, clean energy economy… That process is now standing in the way of getting new clean energy online and unlocking important economic investment,” continued Heinrich. “The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act—which the Senate voted to advance on November 9th and which I co-sponsor with another Democrat and two Republicans—does not remove environmental considerations, the ability to litigate projects or the ability for local communities to comment… But it does make these reviews a standardized part of a predictable process.”

“Modelling by Resources For the Future suggests that BAAJA could cause a decline in cumulative CO2 of about 1.8 gigatons—more than if the entire light-duty vehicle fleet was taken off America’s roads for a year—between now and 2041. Similarly, the Solar Energy Industries Association, a trade body, estimates that BAAJA’s adoption would mean solar and wind would provide 37.4% of America’s electricity generation in 2035, against 19.6% if the current permitting regime remains in place. These forecasts starkly illustrate the heavy drag America’s permitting regime places on the economy. For the nation’s future prosperity and security, it must be reformed,” concluded Heinrich.

Heinrich’s full op-ed is here and below:

A plan to end America’s most expensive bottleneck

By: U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee

In June, the largest clean-energy-infrastructure project in the western hemisphere came online in New Mexico. The SunZia Wind and Transmission Project’s 916 wind turbines now power over 1m homes. It’s a momentous accomplishment I was proud to help deliver, but it’s one that should have come a dozen years sooner. The project took 17 years to permit and build—and SunZia isn’t alone. Across America, energy-infrastructure projects take far too long to permit. The approval process can stretch on a decade or more, before a single digger has moved in. Indeed, permitting might be the economy’s most expensive bottleneck.

America’s ability to meet the energy demands of the 21st century depends on its ability to build a modern, clean energy economy. Its permitting regime tells companies what they can build and how: projects like transmission lines, pipelines, energy-generation facilities, manufacturing plants and transport infrastructure require multiple approvals from multiple federal agencies across several environmental and permitting statutes. That process is now standing in theway of getting new clean energy online and unlocking important economic investment. McKinsey estimates that more than $3trn in American economic activity is tied to infrastructure projects awaiting federal permits.

At the same time, America’s electricity needs are expected to grow dramatically over the next decade, threatening grid reliability, energy affordability and economic competitiveness. I see the effects of this growing strain on my constituents every day.

Fortunately, there is a plan for tackling these problems head-on, and it goes by the acronym BAAJA. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act—which the Senate voted to advance on November 9th and which I co-sponsor with another Democrat and two Republicans—does not remove environmental considerations, the ability to litigate projects or the ability for local communities to comment. Those are necessary. But it does make these reviews a standardized part of a predictable process.

First, BAAJA creates standardized timelines for these processes, from authorization decisions to public comment periods to litigation windows. BAAJA takes reviews that drag on and on—because there is no legally mandated timeline—and creates a predictable workflow. Legitimate environmental considerations, legal challenges and community input are protected, but those processes would be efficient. For both project developers and consumers, this means getting electrons on the grid faster, more cheaply and more predictably. A study by Columbia University estimates that BAAJA would save eight years for transmission projects, three years for solar projects, two and a half years for geothermal projects and about two years for offshore and onshore wind projects.

BAAJA also creates new policies that would benefit energy production. It codifies federal transmission planning so that different regions all plan together instead of separately. It bans right-of-refusal rules, which currently give incumbent utilities the first chance to build new regional lines—creating a more competitive marketplace. It opens wholesale markets and requires grid operators to allow aggregators to energize the grid, which would allow small-scale power sources like solar panels to connect to the grid in times of high usage. And BAAJA would make it financially costly and virtually impossible for an administration to block or undo permits on a whim, so worthwhile renewables projects couldn’t be shut down by a president overnight simply because he is skeptical of clean energy.

BAAJA is also the first federal legislation to meaningfully hold data centers accountable for their costs. The bill requires them to pay the costs of connecting to the grid, a burden American citizens are currently shouldering. By requiring electric utilities to charge data centers for transmission services, we can drive down transmission charges to other customers. Grid Strategies, an energy consultancy, estimates that $55bn in transmission costs could be collected from data centers over ten years under BAAJA.

Now, this is a bipartisan bill that demanded compromise. While there are strict timelines under BAAJA, deadlines should not be mistaken for lack of review. The requirement that infrastructure projects consider the environments and communities they affect remains. Environmental Impact Statements—detailed documents on a project’s potential environmental consequences— are given two years with BAAJA, still substantial time for consideration. The bill mandates consultation with Native American tribes and other communities that may worry about the impact of cutting “red tape” for a clean-energy transition; the current administration, by contrast, has threatened to eliminate those requirements.

And although it is true that BAAJA will make it easier to permit any kind of project, clean or not, the reality is that a huge share of the energy waiting to connect to the grid is renewable energy and storage. Modelling by Resources For theFuture suggests that BAAJA could cause a decline in cumulative CO2 of about 1.8 gigatons—more than if the entire light-duty vehicle fleet was taken off America’s roads for a year—between now and 2041. Similarly, the Solar Energy Industries Association, a trade body, estimates that BAAJA’s adoption would mean solar and wind would provide 37.4% of America’s electricity generation in 2035, against 19.6% if the current permitting regime remains in place.

These forecasts starkly illustrate the heavy drag America’s permitting regime places on the economy. For the nation’s future prosperity and security, it must be reformed.

title: Heinrich Statement on Interior’s Plans to Sell Public Lands
text:
WASHINGTON — U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, released the following statement in response to the Department of the Interior’s (DOI) new plan to sell off public lands:

“The Interior Department says it’s going to sell off lands that aren’t of ‘national interest.’ But anyone who lives in the West knows that some of our most beloved public lands don’t meet that definition. They’re the places where our kids have their favorite picnic spot, where we go fishing on the weekends, or where we hike with our dogs.

“There is nothing in our public lands laws that says a place needs to be of ‘national interest’ to remain in public hands. These lands belong to the American people — not private interests or corporations looking to cash in.

“I’ve fought before to stop efforts to sell off millions of acres of public lands, and I’ll do it again. I will keep fighting to protect all of our public lands — from Yosemite to the Organ Mountains to all the places with no line around them on a map that mean so much to the communities who know and love them.”

Background:

The Federal Land Policy and Management Act (FLPMA) authorizes the sale of BLM-managed public land only if the land is difficult or uneconomic to manage as public land and can’t be used be another Federal agency; if the land was acquired for a specific purpose and is no longer needed for that or any other Federal purpose; or if the sale will serve important public objectives that can’t be achieved “prudently or feasibly” on other land, and which outweigh other public objectives like recreation or scenic values. There is no authority to sell land based on whether they are “nationally significant.”

In addition, the proceeds from the sale of BLM land cannot be transferred back to the purchasing entities, as proposed in DOI’s strategic plan. The Federal Land Transaction Facilitation Act requires proceeds from BLM land sales to be used to acquire new public land for conservation and recreation.

The Department of the Interior does not have the authority to sell land managed by agencies other than the Bureau of Land Management without explicit Congressional direction.

As Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, Heinrich is leading the fight in Congress to protect our public lands, expand access to national parks, and hold the Trump administration accountable for its attacks on our treasured places — from efforts to erase history in our national parks to diverting funding to Trump’s vanity projects.

This month, Heinrich demanded answers from Bureau of Land Management Director Steve Pearce about the Trump administration’s push to develop AI data centers on public lands. Heinrich raised concerns about the administration’s consideration of at least 15 proposals spanning more than 17,000 acres across six Western states, emphasizing that public lands must be managed in the best interests of the American people and the communities directly impacted by development. Heinrich called on BLM to provide transparency about the authorities it is using to approve data center development, the projects under consideration, and the public lands identified as eligible for development.

In October, Heinrich successfully pressured Major League Baseball to abandon its proposal to host a professional baseball game in Grand Teton National Park. After Heinrich sent a letter to MLB Commissioner Robert Manfred urging the league to withdraw its proposal, MLB confirmed it would no longer consider Grand Teton as a potential site. Heinrich emphasized that national parks are no place for commercial sporting events and warned that allowing such development would set a dangerous precedent for future uses of public lands.

In September, Heinrich joined a bipartisan group of 153 lawmakers in urging the DOI to abandon a proposed transfer of federally managed public land within Yosemite National Park that would facilitate private access to and development of an 83-acre parcel adjacent to the park known as Hazel Green Ranch. During a U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee hearing, Heinrich criticized the Trump administration for its plan to exchange public land in Yosemite National Park for private development.

In September, Heinrich led his Senate colleagues in sending a letter to DOI Secretary Doug Burgum demanding that the Trump administration stop work on President Trump’s commemorative arch on federal property, which federal officials have admitted will harm historic sites on public lands, including Arlington National Cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial.

In September, Heinrich spoke in support of the Roadless Rule at a New Mexico Wild community event, encouraging New Mexicans to submit public comment in support of preserving the Roadless Rule. The public had until October 6, 2026 to submit comments on the Trump administration’s repeal of the Roadless Rule. You can read more about Heinrich’s actions to protect the Roadless Rule here.

In August, Heinrich led his colleagues in opposing the Bureau of Land Management’s (BLM) proposal to overturn the 2024 Waste Prevention, Production Subject to Royalties, and Resource Conservation rule (the 2024 Waste Prevention Rule). The move will increase pollution on public lands, reduce domestic energy supply, expose nearby communities to avoidable health risks, and waste publicly owned natural gas, costing Americans tens of millions in foregone revenue.

In August, Heinrich joined top Senate Democrats in sending a letter to the Government Accountability Office (GAO) Acting Comptroller General Orice Williams Brown to audit and assess the full scope and cost of the White House ballroom project.

In August, Heinrich sent a letter requesting that the DOI Deputy Inspector General Caryl Brzymialkiewicz investigate what Department officials knew – and when they knew it – about engineering failures at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and whether Department employees withheld evidence from federal prosecutors.

In July, Heinrich criticized legislation that removes protections for public lands, emphasizing the need for bipartisan collaboration within the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee. Heinrich additionally fact-checked Trump administration actions that undo protections for the Chaco Canyon Cultural Protection Zone. You can read about Heinrich’s actions to protect Chaco Canyon here and here.

In July, Heinrich sent a letter to DOI Secretary Doug Burgum and U.S Park Chief of Police Scott Brecht demanding answers and transparency about the U.S. Park Police’s new vehicle pursuit policy following news reports that an innocent bystander, Nolberto Armando Sanabria Meza, a 46-year-old food delivery driver, was hit and tragically killed in D.C. by a driver being chased by U.S. Park Police.

In June, Heinrich helped advance the America the Beautiful Act, bipartisan legislation introduced by U.S. Senators Steve Daines (R-Mont.) and Angus King (I-Maine) to reauthorize the National Parks and Public Land Legacy Restoration Fund, out of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee.

In June, Heinrich sent a letter demanding answers from DOI Secretary Doug Burgum about the Trump administration redirecting tens of millions of dollars from fees paid to the NPS to fund President Trump’s vanity projects in Washington, D.C. – including redirecting funds collected at New Mexico sites such as Carlsbad Caverns National Park and Bandelier National Monument.

In April, during a U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee hearing to examine the Trump administration’s Budget Request for the DOI Fiscal Year 2027 (FY27), Heinrich grilled DOI Secretary Doug Burgum about the Department’s draconian staff cuts at the NPS.

In March, Heinrich joined lawmakers in filing an amicus brief that would put a stop to President Trump’s plan to construct a commemorative arch on federal property. The amicus brief argues that the President’s plan is illegal unless Congress authorizes it.

In March, Heinrich led his colleagues in delivering remarks on the Senate floor in condemning and drawing attention to the Trump administration’s efforts to erase American history from public lands.

In March, Heinrich sent a letter to DOI demanding answers from the NPS following reports that NPS staff across the country are removing signage from national parks about slavery, Tribal history, and climate change.

In February, Heinrich led his colleagues in calling on DOI Secretary Doug Burgum to halt efforts to create the Department’s new U.S. Wildland Fire Service (USWFS), citing potential life-or-death consequences that could come as a result of decoupling wildfire management from land management agencies, and emphasizing concerns related to recent reductions in staffing, combined with improperly severing wildfire management from land stewardship.

Last December, during a U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Subcommittee on National Parks hearing to consider 26 pending bills, Heinrich criticized the Trump administration for removing fee-free admission on Juneteenth and Martin Luther King, Jr. Day.

Last October, Heinrich delivered remarks on the Senate floor, criticizing Republicans for pushing forward Congressional Review Act (CRA) resolutions of disapproval targeting BLM Resource Management Plans (RMPs) that would undo protections for national parks, including the Gates of the Arctic National Park and Preserve.

Last October, during the government shutdown, Heinrich urged the DOI Secretary Doug Burgum to classify the Department’s staff as essential during the Republican government shutdown to maintain the health and safety of Americans who visit public lands, wildlife refuges, and national park sites.

In June of 2025, Heinrich successfully fought Senate Republican provisions to sell off public lands in the Big Bad Bill, lead an amendment to prevent the privatization of our public lands, hosted a roundtable and sounded the alarm about New Mexico public lands that were at risk of being sold off by Republicans, continuously uplifted New Mexicans’ voices who called his office to raise their concern with Republicans’ plan to sell off these lands, and released a statement immediately criticizing Senate Republicans’ plan to sell off public lands following the release of the reconciliation text.

In June 2025, Heinrich blasted the Trump administration for its plans to transfer national park units to state control, criticizing the administration for “cutting off our access to public lands and devastating state economies in the process, overwhelming state budgets and dismantling the systems that keep public lands running.”

In June 2025, Heinrich grilled the DOI Secretary Doug Burgum over the Trump administration’s Fiscal Year 2026 (FY26) budget request for the Department, which slashes funding for national parks and guts staffing for the agency.

In May of 2025, Heinrich sent a letter to DOI Secretary Doug Burgum, demanding answers from the Trump administration regarding its plans to transfer National Park System units from federal management. The letter followed Heinrich’s questioning of Secretary Burgum during a Senate Interior, Environment, and Related Agencies Appropriations Subcommittee hearing, where Burgum failed to provide sufficient answers on the Trump administration’s plan to transfer hundreds of sites managed by the NPS to the states.

In January 2025, Heinrich’s Simplifying Outdoor Access for Recreation (SOAR) Act and Every Kid Outdoors Extension Act, which extends free access to national parks and other public lands to all American fourth grade students and their families through 2031, were signed into law as part of the Expanding Public Lands Outdoor Recreation Experiences (EXPLORE) Act. The broader bipartisan package bolsters outdoor recreation and promotes public lands in New Mexico and across the United States.

title: Hirono, Booker, Durbin Reintroduce Legislation to Improve Maternal Healthcare for Incarcerated Moms
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. –U.S. Senators Mazie K. Hirono (D-HI), Cory Booker (D-NJ), and Dick Durbin (D-IL) reintroduced the Justice for Incarcerated Moms Act, legislation to improve care for pregnant and postpartum women who are incarcerated. The bill would fund high-quality maternal healthcare and support programs in prisons and jails, commission research on the maternal health crisis behind bars, and incentivize states and localities to end the shackling of pregnant people.

“Far too many women in prison and jail are forced to give birth in shackles—a practice that is both cruel and needlessly dangerous to mother and child,” said Senator Hirono. “This commonsense legislation protects maternal health in prisons by banning shackling a woman during childbirth and by funding comprehensive healthcare and wellness support before, during, and after childbirth.”

According to the Prison Policy Initiative, nearly 200,000 women and girls are incarcerated in the United States on any given day. Incarcerated women face a heightened risk of maternal mortality and severe maternal morbidity, and these poor outcomes disproportionately affect Black women, who are imprisoned at 1.6 times the rate of white women.

“Every person, including those who are incarcerated, deserve dignity and support at all stages of motherhood,” said Senator Booker. “A woman’s incarceration does not diminish her humanity or her worth, and it should never mean she is denied the basic care every mother deserves. We have a moral obligation to protect these mothers and their babies.”

“No mother should have to deliver their child while shackled. Our correctional system should have standard practices and programs to ensure that moms who are incarcerated get the care they need to have healthy and safe pregnancies and deliveries,” said Senator Durbin. “I’m proud to join Senators Booker and Hirono to introduce the Justice for Incarcerated Moms Act to improve maternal and child health outcomes for incarcerated individuals.”

Specifically, the Justice for Incarcerated Moms Act would:

Incentivize state and local prisons and jails to end the practice of shackling pregnant people.

Provide funding for federal, state, and local prisons and jails to establish programs for pregnant and postpartum people in their facilities, including access to doulas and other perinatal health workers, counseling, reentry assistance, and maternal-infant bonding opportunities, as well as diversion programs that keep pregnant and postpartum people out of incarceration.

Commission a comprehensive study on maternal mortality and severe maternal morbidity among incarcerated people, with a particular focus on racial and ethnic disparities in maternal health outcomes.

Senator Hirono has long championed maternal and reproductive health, co-sponsoring the Justice for Incarcerated Moms Act in each Congress since its introduction in 2021, when it was introduced as part of the Black Maternal Health Momnibus Act that addressed the maternal health crisis and racial and ethnic disparities in health access and outcomes. In September, Senator Hirono reintroduced the Affordability is Access Act, which would ensure the FDA-approved over-the-counter birth control pill is accessible and affordable for women nationwide. In March 2026, Senator Hirono pressed U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to immediately release Title X funding, which was set to lapse and jeopardizing reproductive care for hundreds of thousands nationwide. She also led the Convenient Contraception Act in 2025, aimed at creating a statutory right to obtain and use contraceptives and ensure healthcare providers have a right to provide contraceptives and share information about essential care.

Senator Hirono has also pushed for commonsense policy to protect the rights of incarcerated people. In 2025, she led 14 colleagues in a bicameral letter to President Trump condemning his unlawful invocation of the Alien Enemies Act, which allowed rapid deportations to foreign prisons without judicial review or remedy. In 2024, Senator Hirono directed 11 colleagues in introducing the Next Step Home Act, legislation aimed at restoring voting rights for individuals with felony convictions who have been released and successfully reentered society.

The Justice for Incarcerated Moms Act is endorsed by The Sentencing Project; Campaign Legal Center; Chicago Votes; Civil Survival; Community Spring; Dream.Org; Empowering Descendant Communities to Unlock Democracy; Equity and Transformation; EXPO of Wisconsin; FirstFollowers; Gift of Voice; Healing Our Land Inc; Illinois Alliance for Reentry and Justice; Illinois Coalition to End Permanent Punishments; Just Future Project; Live Free Illinois; More Than Our Crimes; National Association of Criminal Defense Attorneys; National Coalition for Prisoner Voting Rights; NCJW Chicago North Shore; Raise The Floor Alliance; SACRED Acts (South Asian American Coalition to Renew Democracy Acts); Unlock Civics Coalition; Unlock Civics NM; Urban Community Unity Solutions LLC; Vermont Citizens and United for the Rehabilitation of Errants.

title: Husted, Booker, Collins introduce bipartisan bill to ensure federal law enforcement officers receive fair retirement benefits
text:
“Federal law enforcement officers who put their lives on the line shouldn’t be shortchanged on retirement because of a technicality in the law.”

WASHINGTON – Sens. Jon Husted (R-Ohio), Cory Booker (D-N.J.) and Susan Collins (R-Maine) introduced the Law Enforcement Officers Equity Act, bipartisan legislation to make sure all federal law enforcement officers receive the same retirement benefits.

“Federal law enforcement officers who put their lives on the line shouldn’t be shortchanged in retirement because of a technicality in the law. These men and women risk everything for our safety and face the same dangers as the officers next to them. This bill fixes that oversight so every one of them gets the benefits they’ve earned,” said Husted.

“Federal police officers at VA hospitals, military installations, and federal facilities across the country protect veterans, servicemembers, and federal workers, and face the same dangers as their fellow law enforcement officers. It is unfair that the federal government denies them the same retirement benefits because of a job classification. This bipartisan bill fixes that language to ensure every federal law enforcement officer who keeps us safe receives the full benefits they have earned through their service and sacrifice,” said Booker.

“In Maine, we are fortunate to have so many terrific and professional law enforcement officers devoted to their duty and to doing what is right. This legislation would expand retirement and pension benefits to thousands of federal law enforcement officers who are currently excluded from them under the outdated federal definition of a law enforcement officer,” said Collins.

“All Federal law enforcement officers put their lives on the line every day, no matter which Federal agency they work for. This bill will ensure that all Federal law enforcement officers receive the same benefits when they retire. The FOP is grateful to Senators Booker, Husted, and Collins for introducing this legislation, which would expand the definition of ‘law enforcement officer’ for retirement benefits to include all Federal law enforcement officers,” said Patrick Yoes, President, National Fraternal Order of Police.

Thousands of federal law enforcement officers are locked out of the retirement benefits their colleagues receive. They have the same training, do the same job and face the same dangers. But because of an outdated gap in federal law, they aren’t officially classified as law enforcement officers.

The Law Enforcement Officers Equity Act closes that loophole. It extends the same enhanced retirement benefits to every federal law enforcement officer, so no one is left behind because of how their position happens to be labeled.

This bill was previously introduced in the Senate in 2023 by Booker and J.D. Vance.

Background:

Congress decided long ago that federal law enforcement officers should receive enhanced pay and retirement benefits, known as “6(c)” benefits, because of their training and the danger of their work. But many officers don’t qualify because of how their positions are classified, even though their duties are the same as those of officers who do. This includes certain officers at the Department of Defense, Department of Veterans Affairs, the U.S. Postal Service and the Federal Protective Service, among other agencies.

The Law Enforcement Officers Equity Act would:

Provide all federal law enforcement officers with 6(c) retirement benefits. That means they could retire after 20 years of service at age 50, or after 25 years of service at any age.

Expand the definition of “law enforcement officer” for retirement purposes to cover all federal law enforcement officers. This ends the situation where two officers doing the same work are treated differently depending on how their job is classified.

Count officers past federal law enforcement service toward their retirement. This way, officers don’t lose credit for years they’ve already served.

The Law Enforcement Equity Act is supported by the Fraternal Order of Police, the Federal Law Enforcement Officers Association, the National Association of Police Organizations and the American Federation of Government employees.

title: Following Luján’s Push, Trump Administration Delays New Medicaid Requirements by Six Months
text:
Days After Luján Called for a Delay of Medicaid Cuts, the Trump Administration Announced it Would Give States Who Opt-In an Additional Six Months to Prepare for the New Requirements

Washington, D.C. – Just days after U.S. Senators Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.) and Reverend Raphael Warnock (D-GA), both members of the Senate Finance Committee, led a coalition of Democratic Senators in calling for a delay of new Medicaid cuts enacted in Congressional Republicans’ One Big Beautiful Bill Act, the Trump administration announced it would give states that opt-in an additional six months to prepare for the new requirements. The move will allow states to delay denying or terminating Medicaid coverage for individuals who do not meet work reporting requirements until July 2027.

“After calling for a delay of the new Medicaid cuts enacted by Republicans, this administration has finally acknowledged the need to delay these harmful requirements,” said Senator Luján. “Millions of Americans, including New Mexicans, are at risk of losing their health care because of President Trump and Congressional Republicans’ Medicaid cuts. While this delay is necessary, six months is not enough. I will continue fighting to protect Medicaid and ensure New Mexicans can access the health care they need.”

Medicaid is a cornerstone of the U.S. health care system, providing health insurance coverage to more than one in five Americans. The program covers 40% of U.S. births, provides 20% of all hospital funding, and is the single largest payer of long-term services and supports, including nursing home care. President Trump and Congressional Republicans have made cuts to Americans’ health care coverage a central part of their legislative agenda since President Trump returned to office. A July report found that two million fewer children were enrolled in Medicaid in April, compared to January 2025 when President Trump took office.

title: Luján, Bennet, Senate Agriculture Democrats Demand USDA Withdraw Proposed Rule Restricting Food Assistance
text:
Washington, D.C. – U.S. Senators Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the Senate Agriculture Committee’s Subcommittee on Food and Nutrition, Michael Bennet (D-Colo.), and John Fetterman (D-Pa.) led U.S. Senators Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.), Tina Smith (D-Minn.), Dick Durbin (D-IlI.), Cory Booker (D-N.J.), Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.), Peter Welch (D-Vt.), Adam Schiff (D-Calif.), and Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) in urging the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) to withdraw its proposed rule restricting Broad-Based Categorical Eligibility (BBCE) under the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) that will severely narrow eligibility requirements for the nation’s largest anti-hunger program.

“We write to strongly urge the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) to withdraw its proposed rule restricting Broad-Based Categorical Eligibility (BBCE) under the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP). Should this rule take effect, an estimated 6.3 million Americans, including many seniors and nearly 1.8 million children, would lose SNAP benefits according to the USDA’s own analysis. At a time when everyday Americans are already struggling to afford groceries, USDA should not be making changes to SNAP that leave families with fewer resources to meet their basic needs,” began the senators.

Broad-Based Categorical Eligibility helps working families and seniors afford groceries at a time when the rising costs of housing, child care, health care, and other necessities are stretching household budgets. It gives states flexibility to help low-income households access food assistance while supporting work and financial stability. Without BBCE, families could lose SNAP benefits even when they are still struggling to make ends meet. It also allows families and seniors to build and maintain modest savings without jeopardizing their access to food assistance. Protections like these are critical not only to ensure struggling Americans meet their basic needs, but also to help these individuals build toward greater financial mobility.

This proposed rule would also make SNAP more challenging and costly for states to administer, increasing paperwork, the risk of payment errors, and demands on state workers. These added burdens come as states are already absorbing a larger share of SNAP administrative expenses under The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, leaving states with fewer resources to manage these additional requirements.

The consequences would extend beyond SNAP. Children in households that lose SNAP eligibility could also lose automatic certification for free school meals, requiring families to submit additional applications to establish eligibility and creating more administrative work for schools. This added red tape could prevent eligible children from receiving meals and reduce federal reimbursements for schools, threatening efforts to provide free school meals to all students. The proposal could also create additional red tape for families seeking assistance through the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC), potentially leaving some families unable to access benefits and others ineligible for assistance altogether.

“In the proposed rule, USDA repeatedly claims that it is aligning SNAP rules with congressional intent, but the legislative history clearly demonstrates otherwise. Congress established categorical eligibility to simplify access to food assistance and preserved this framework when it created Temporary Assistance for Needy Families in 1996. States have relied on this flexibility for decades to serve low-income households and administer SNAP more efficiently. Congress subsequently considered proposals to eliminate or restrict BBCE during the 2005 reconciliation debate and the 2014 and 2018 Farm Bill negotiations, but these restrictions were ultimately rejected on a bipartisan basis and excluded from the final legislation. While maintaining SNAP eligibility for 6.3 million Americans who need it should be reason enough, the fact that this proposed rule is contrary to congressional intent and the law is another reason it should be withdrawn,” continued the senators.

“Children should not go hungry, seniors should not have to spend down their savings to afford groceries, and working families should not lose assistance while they are still struggling to make ends meet. USDA’s proposal would put these families at greater risk while adding costs and complications for states. We urge USDA to withdraw the proposed rule in its entirety,” concluded the senators.

As Ranking Member of the Subcommittee on Food and Nutrition, Specialty Crops, Organics, and Research, Senator Luján has led the charge to protect and restore access to Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) in New Mexico and across the country. In November, Senator Luján led the entire Senate Democratic Caucus in introducing legislation to repeal all the devastating Republican cuts to SNAP made in the Republican Budget Betrayal.

The text of the letter is available HERE and below.

Dear Secretary Rollins:

We write to strongly urge the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) to withdraw its proposed rule restricting Broad-Based Categorical Eligibility (BBCE) under the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP). Should this rule take effect, an estimated 6.3 million Americans, including many seniors and nearly 1.8 million children, would lose SNAP benefits according to the USDA’s own analysis. At a time when everyday Americans are already struggling to afford groceries, USDA should not be making changes to SNAP that leave families with fewer resources to meet their basic needs.

The costs of housing, utilities, child care, health care, and other necessities are leaving working families and seniors on fixed incomes with little money left for food. BBCE helps these households access food while supporting work and financial stability. Without it, a working family could lose SNAP benefits entirely after a modest raise, even when the additional earnings are not enough to replace the assistance it loses. BBCE allows states to prevent this abrupt cutoff so that families can continue receiving assistance as their earnings increase and their SNAP benefits gradually decline. It also allows low-income families and seniors to maintain modest emergency savings without losing assistance. These protections help people meet their basic needs while building assets and working toward greater financial security and economic mobility. This flexibility has been embraced by leaders of both parties and is now used in 43 states, the District of Columbia, Guam, and the U.S. Virgin Islands.

Beyond the direct harm to families, the proposal would make SNAP more difficult and expensive for states to administer. Most states use BBCE to raise or eliminate SNAP’s restrictive and complex federal asset test, reducing paperwork and the potential for payment errors. Reinstating these tests would require households to provide additional financial verification and place significant new demands on state workers. According to an analysis by the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, asset-related errors added approximately one percentage point, on average, to SNAP payment error rates in states that retained asset tests in fiscal year 2023. Under H.R. 1, which ties states’ share of SNAP benefit costs to their payment error rates, even a small increase could push states into higher cost-sharing tiers. With states already absorbing a larger share of SNAP administrative expenses, this proposal would impose new burdens while leaving them with fewer resources to manage those demands.

The effects would also reach well beyond SNAP. Children in households that lose SNAP eligibility would lose their SNAP-based automatic certification for free school meals, requiring families without another automatic eligibility pathway to submit additional applications and schools to verify eligibility. This would add unnecessary red tape for families and schools and increase the risk that eligible children miss out on meals. Fewer children directly certified through SNAP would also put federal school meal reimbursements at risk, particularly for schools participating in the Community Eligibility Provision. USDA’s own analysis warns that declining federal reimbursements could threaten the financial viability of state efforts to provide free school meals, such as universal breakfast and lunch programs in Colorado and New Mexico and universal free breakfast in Pennsylvania. The proposal would also complicate access to the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC), requiring some families to provide additional income documentation and leaving others ineligible for assistance altogether.

In the proposed rule, USDA repeatedly claims that it is aligning SNAP rules with congressional intent, but the legislative history clearly demonstrates otherwise. Congress established categorical eligibility to simplify access to food assistance and preserved this framework when it created Temporary Assistance for Needy Families in 1996. States have relied on this flexibility for decades to serve low-income households and administer SNAP more efficiently. Congress subsequently considered proposals to eliminate or restrict BBCE during the 2005 reconciliation debate and the 2014 and 2018 Farm Bill negotiations, but these restrictions were ultimately rejected on a bipartisan basis and excluded from the final legislation. While maintaining SNAP eligibility for 6.3 million Americans who need it should be reason enough, the fact that this proposed rule is contrary to congressional intent and the law is another reason it should be withdrawn.

Children should not go hungry, seniors should not have to spend down their savings to afford groceries, and working families should not lose assistance while they are still struggling to make ends meet. USDA’s proposal would put these families at greater risk while adding costs and complications for states. We urge USDA to withdraw the proposed rule in its entirety.

title: SENATOR MCCORMICK JOINS BIPARTISAN PUSH TO BRING U.S. SPACE ACADEMY TO PITTSBURGH
text:
PITTSBURGH — U.S. Senators Dave McCormick (R-PA) and John Fetterman (D-PA) joined Governor Josh Shapiro, Penn State University, and regional partners in announcing Pennsylvania’s formal proposal to establish the United States Space Academy (USSA) near Pittsburgh International Airport (PIT). The proposed academy would prepare the next generation of American scientists, engineers, and space leaders while building on Pennsylvania’s growing aerospace industry and advanced manufacturing capabilities.

“Pennsylvania has the talent, technology, and industrial strength to help America win the race for space dominance,” said U.S. Senator Dave McCormick. “Bringing the U.S. Space Academy to Pittsburgh would build on those strengths, create new opportunities for Pennsylvanians, and train the next generation of leaders who will ensure America remains the world’s leader in space.”

“As a proud member of the Senate Commerce Committee, I’m deeply committed to investing in NASA and its workforce, our national security, and making sure Pennsylvania is part of those important conversations,” said U.S. Senator John Fetterman. “Our Commonwealth has contributed significantly to the nation’s military readiness, space exploration, and preparing the next generation of leaders in those areas and more. I join my colleagues in supporting the continuation of that legacy as we push for Pennsylvania to host the U.S. Space Academy.”

“The Commonwealth of Pennsylvania powered the first industrial revolution nearly 200 years ago and made the arsenal of democracy the most powerful manufacturing base in the world. Pennsylvania is now uniquely positioned to welcome the United States Space Academy – building off our robust space industry and world-class research universities – to launch the next generation of America’s scientists, engineers, astronauts, and servicemembers and ensure America remains the global leader in space,” said Governor Josh Shapiro. “Pennsylvania’s application provides the federal government with an opportunity to strengthen and diversify America’s space industry. My Administration is all in and we’ve assembled a bipartisan team of Pennsylvania leaders who are committed to the Space Academy’s success here in our Commonwealth.”

The proposal calls for a new campus on 300 acres near Pittsburgh International Airport, with construction beginning in 2027 and the academy opening to 1,200 students by fall 2031. The campus could eventually accommodate up to 4,000 students, attract billions of dollars in public and private investment, and support thousands of jobs across the region.

Pennsylvania is already a major contributor to America’s space industry, with more than 550 businesses generating approximately $8.6 billion in economic impact over the past four fiscal years. The proposed academy would build on this foundation, drawing on the Commonwealth’s strengths in robotics, artificial intelligence, advanced manufacturing, and aerospace technology.

Under the proposal, Penn State University and six other Pennsylvania research universities would help develop the academy’s curriculum. An interim campus at the former Pittsburgh Technical College would welcome the first 300 students in 2028, ahead of the permanent campus opening.

The bipartisan proposal was submitted in response to President Trump’s August 2026 executive order and a NASA request for information. If selected, Pennsylvania would become home to the nation’s first new federal service academy since 1955.

title: Wyden, Merkley, Bonamici Announce $440,000 to Support Coastal Victims of Trafficking
text:
The Harbor in Clatsop County to benefit.

Washington, D.C. – U.S. Senators Ron Wyden and Jeff Merkley, along with U.S. Representative Suzanne Bonamici, today announced $440,000 in federal awards to support victims of trafficking in Clatsop County.

“Survivors of human trafficking carry unimaginable trauma, and they deserve strong, coordinated support systems rooted in their own communities,” Wyden said. “I’m glad to see these federal dollars heading to Astoria so The Harbor can broaden its outreach, strengthen local emergency response networks and ensure no victim in Clatsop County has to navigate recovery alone.”

“We must continue to do everything in our power to protect people from the horrors of human trafficking and support its survivors,” Merkley said. “This essential funding will help The Harbor continue its critical work of raising awareness, supporting victims, and providing hope to survivors in Clatsop County.”

“We must empower and support survivors of the despicable crime of human trafficking. The Harbor in Clatsop County has been doing this important work and has earned the community’s trust and support,” Bonamici said. “This grant will help to deliver more services and outreach where they are needed throughout Clatsop County, increase awareness of trafficking, and help develop a coordinated response. I’m grateful to my colleagues in the Senate for helping secure this funding and to The Harbor’s staff for their important work.”

The $440,000 in federal awards from the Department of Justice’s Office of Justice Program will be distributed to The Harbor in Astoria. The Harbor is a nonprofit that provides advocacy, prevention and support for survivors of domestic violence, sexual assault and stalking in Clatsop County. The federal award will be used to expand services to victims including crisis intervention, case management, safety planning, shelter, emergency financial assistance and referrals. The Harbor will also conduct outreach to increase awareness of trafficking and available services for victims and will develop partnerships with local agencies and organizations to develop a coordinated human trafficking response.

“Every survivor deserves to feel safe, supported, and empowered to move forward,” said Terri Steenbergen, Executive Director of The Harbor. “At The Harbor, we know how important it is to meet people where they are, especially in rural and coastal communities where accessing services can be challenging. This investment will help us reach more survivors, build stronger community partnerships, and ensure that those experiencing trafficking know there is a place to turn. We are incredibly grateful for this funding and for the continued commitment to the safety and well-being of our coastal communities.”

title: Wyden, Merkley, Colleagues Push for Senate, House Leadership to Strip Provisions in Defense Bill that Mandate Concerning U.S.-Israel Defense, Intelligence Cooperation
text:
Washington D.C.—U.S. Senators Ron Wyden and Jeff Merkley said today they have joined Senate colleagues in pressing congressional leadership to exclude provisions in the FY2027 National Defense Authorization Act that would require the president to expand and enhance concerning aspects of defense cooperation and intelligence sharing with the Israeli government.

The provisions would undermine the United States’ ability to act independently and in line with U.S. national security interests at a time when the government of Israel’s actions are increasingly not aligned with those interests, the Oregon senators said.

“These provisions would constrain the Administration’s ability to independently determine how best to protect U.S. national security and would lock in long-term commitments despite our serious concerns with the Israeli government’s actions in Gaza, the West Bank, and other parts of the region,” the lawmakers wrote to Senate and House leadership.

“The agreements and projects these provisions envision threaten U.S. national security interests by handing Israel leverage over American weapons systems and military technology. This is not hypothetical. The Netanyahu government has already leveraged its existing coproduction agreement with the United States on missile defense to block American Iron Dome batteries from reaching Ukraine, in direct opposition to U.S. national security interests,” the lawmakers continued. “Should these provisions be enacted, it would further increase Israel’s leverage over the United States through some of the most sensitive technologies in warfare. That is not in the U.S. interest. If enacted, these agreements would create long-term dependencies by embedding Israeli technology into the U.S. defense industrial base that could make future policy changes costly or difficult to implement. President Trump, at his own discretion, could choose to enter new agreements with Israel under existing law. The executive branch does not need a congressional mandate to more deeply entrench U.S.-Israel defense cooperation.”

“Moreover, we do not share, let alone co-produce, many of these sensitive technologies even with our closest partners, including NATO or other treaty allies. To do so in this instance would be unwise, especially as the Government of Israel continues to pursue policies in Gaza, the West Bank and other parts of the region that are inconsistent with U.S. interests and values,” the lawmakers wrote.

“Prime Minister Netanyahu has openly stated that such an initiative was his idea. In a letter to Representative Stutzman, who led a resolution calling for an effort similar to these provisions, Prime Minister Netanyahu states, ‘I was glad to receive your proposed Congressional resolution endorsing my plan to shift the framework of the US-Israel defense cooperation from aid to partnership.’ The intention behind this is clear: to move U.S. security assistance governed through more traditional pathways, like Foreign Military Financing and arm sales, to more opaque, less discernible avenues through defense acquisitions and programs of record that reduce transparency, as well as increase Israel’s leverage over the United States and our dependency on Israeli technology. This is particularly problematic after Prime Minister Netanyahu boasted that he has been trying to start a war with Iran for 40 years. That war has proven to be a strategic disaster for the United States and against U.S. interests,” the senators wrote.

The letter was led by U.S. Senator Chris Van Hollen, D-Md. In addition to Wyden and Merkley, the letter was signed by U.S. Senators Patty Murray, D-Wash., Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii, Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., Edward J. Markey, D-Mass., Tammy Duckworth, D-Ill., Tina Smith, D-Minn., Peter Welch, D-Vt., and Andy Kim, D-N.J. The letter was sent to Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., Senate Armed Services Committee (SASC) Chair Roger Wicker, R-Miss., Ranking Member Jack Reed, D-R.I., House Armed Services Committee Chair Mike Rogers, R-Ala., and Ranking Member Adam Smith, D-Wash.

title: Senator Moody Makes Case for U.S. Space Academy to Be Located in Florida as Deadline for Applications Closes
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C.—As the deadline for state applications for the newly announced U.S. Space Academy closes, Senator Moody is making the case for Florida to host the new institution. From the first Mercury astronauts to this year’s Artemis II launch from Kennedy Space Center, Florida has been the launchpad for American space exploration and innovation. Since the announcement of the new academy earlier this year, Senator Moody has been calling for the institution to be built in Florida.

“Placing the new U.S. Space Academy in Florida simply makes sense. Our Space Coast has been the nation’s gateway to the stars since the beginning of the U.S. space program—placing the academy here means its students have a front-row seat to the new innovations coming out of both NASA and the private sector, giving them connections and experience they can’t get anywhere else. Why spend years and millions of dollars replicating what we’ve already built here? The U.S. Space Academy belongs in Florida,” said Senator Ashley Moody.

BACKGROUND:

The newly announced U.S. Space Academy will train future U.S. Space Force officers, and it will also serve NASA and the commercial spaceflight industry.

Launches on Florida’s Space Coast have increased by more than 500% since 2016.

Senator Moody introduced the STARS Act to bring the U.S. Space Academy to Florida. Rep. Mike Haridopolos and Governor-Elect Byron Donalds introduced a House companion to Senator Moody’s legislation.

In addition to filing this legislation, Senator Moody has been working with state partners to respond to the NASA’s request for information (RFI) and position Florida as the academy’s home.

In September, Senator Moody rallied space industry leaders to make the pitch for Florida to house the new academy.

Senator Moody has a strong record of supporting Florida’s Space Coast.

Senator Moody passed the Secure U.S. Leadership in Space Act to ensure the U.S. remains competitive and at the forefront of space innovation and exploration.

The legislation bolsters public-private partnerships by allowing spaceports to use tax-exempt bonds, as airports and seaports already can.

Senator Moody recently introduced the Space Ready 2.0 Act, which would establish a NASA-wide pilot program allowing the agency to accept voluntary private contributions for infrastructure improvement projects at NASA centers. The proposal requires no new federal spending; it lets private partners voluntarily invest in NASA infrastructure that supports their missions.

The proposal builds upon NASA’s existing authority and allows private-sector partners to voluntarily invest in infrastructure improvements that directly support the missions they rely upon.

Senator Moody also introduced the CAPE Canaveral Act to relocate NASA headquarters to Florida’s Space Coast—where it belongs.

In July, Senator Moody met with the crew of Artemis II at Kennedy Space Center where the crew thanked the hundreds of NASA engineers, mathematicians, and scientists who built the rocket that launched them farther into space than any human has ever traveled.
