title: Pressley Joins Senators Markey, Warren, Massachusetts Delegation in Urging Trump Admin. to Ensure Benefits for Salvadoran TPS Holders
text:
Pressley Has Urged Extension of El Salvador TPS, Led Efforts in Congress to Extend TPS for Haiti, Other Countries Enduring Humanitarian Crises

Text of Letter (PDF)

WASHINGTON – Congresswoman Ayanna Pressley (MA-07) joined Senators Edward J. Markey (D-Mass.) and Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) and the entire Massachusetts delegation—Representatives Richard Neal (MA-01), Jim McGovern (MA-02), Lori Trahan (MA-03), Jake Auchincloss (MA-04), Katherine Clark (MA-05), Seth Moulton (MA-06), Stephen Lynch (MA-08), and Bill Keating (MA-09)—in sending a letter to Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) Director Joseph Edlow urging the Trump administration to ensure that essential benefits for Salvadoran Temporary Protected Status (TPS) holders remain available, and to restore any benefits wrongfully terminated.

Reports indicate that, after the Trump administration failed to publish a formal notice of the extension of TPS benefits, Salvadorans have been unable to access Social Security Administration (SSA) benefits, renew drivers’ licenses, and verify employment authorization, owing in part to the failure of USCIS’s Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) and E-Verify programs to recognize their status as TPS holders. In the letter, the lawmakers demand that the Administration uphold the lawful immigration status of Salvadoran TPS holders.

In the letter, the lawmakers wrote, “The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) formally announces TPS decisions in the Federal Register, the government’s official publication for agency actions. These notices explain who is covered, how long protections last, and how employers and agencies should recognize extended work permits. Yet the Trump administration let September 9, 2026, pass without publishing a new notice for El Salvador. U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) has nevertheless announced that Salvadoran TPS holders retain their protections, including work authorization, pending a further announcement. But a website assurance is no substitute for clear instructions and systems that recognize those protections.”

The lawmakers continued, “One Massachusetts resident received an October 2, 2026, Social Security Administration (SSA) notice stating: ‘We cannot pay you benefits because you are not lawfully present in the U.S.’ SSA said benefits were no longer payable beginning in September, demanded repayment of more than $1,200 within 30 days, and gave the recipient just 10 days to submit proof of lawful presence to prevent an interruption. That is not an abstract paperwork problem. It is a sudden loss of income, a bill for more than $1,200, and a scramble to prove eligibility.”

The lawmakers requested answers by Friday, November 27, 2026, to questions including:

What information are SAVE and E-Verify returning for Salvadoran TPS holders whose documents show expired dates?

When did DHS and USCIS first learn of these verification problems, and what caused them?

How many Salvadoran TPS holders have been affected since September 9, 2026?

What is DHS doing with SSA to determine why Salvadoran TPS holders have been found not lawfully present?

What written guidance have you provided to employers and benefit and licensing agencies to prevent further harm?

How will you prevent these failures from recurring?

Text of the letter is accessible here.

Congresswoman Pressley has consistently worked to protect TPS holders from Trump administration attacks.

In September 2026, Rep. Pressley urged the Trump Administration to extend Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for El Salvador.

In April 2026, Rep. Pressley secured a major victory in the House of Representatives, passing critical legislation to extend Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Haiti by a vote of 224-204. The effort, which Congresswoman Pressley championed through a bipartisan discharge petition, is a watershed moment in her years-long advocacy for Haitian communities and immigrant families and marks an essential step forward in the fight to defend Haitian nationals from deportation.

In August 2026, Congresswomen Pressley and Clarke, Co-Chairs of the House Haiti Caucus, issued a statement condemning the deportation and dehumanizationv of Haitian nationals.

In August 2026, Rep. Pressley issued a statement denouncing the termination of TPS for Haiti and Syria and standing in vigorous support of TPS holders and their families.

In July 2026, Rep. Pressley alongside Congresswoman Laura Gillen, urged Senators to support legislation to extend Haiti TPS and protect the lives and livelihoods of Haitians and Americans alike.

In June 2026, Rep. Pressley commended Senators Edward J. Markey (D-Mass.) and Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-Del.), along with Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) and 16 other Senate colleagues, for introducing legislation to designate Haiti for Temporary Protected Status (TPS) in the Senate.

In June 2026, Rep. Pressley denounced the Supreme Court’s devastating ruling to allow Trump’s attempt to terminate Temporary Protected Status for Haitians and Syrians.

In June 2026, Rep. Pressley held a press conference outside of the Supreme Court with Senator Markey, other lawmakers, advocates, and impacted community members to highlight the catastrophic impact the termination of TPS would have on our communities, businesses, schools, care economy, and more.

In May 2026, Rep. Pressley, Senator Warren, and Senator Markey released a new investigative report revealing how President Trump’s attempts to end Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Haiti would devastate the health care, elder care, and disability care workforce, harm patients, and hurt communities.

In April 2026, Rep. Pressley held a press conference alongside colleagues and a coalition of seniors, care workers, advocates, and allies to demand the Supreme Court defend Temporary Protected Status (TPS).

In April 2026, Rep. Pressley, alongside Rep. Wasserman Schultz and Senators Ed Markey and Chris Van Hollen, led 26 Senators and 157 Representatives in filing an amicus brief in the U.S. Supreme Court in Miot v. Trump, a consolidated case challenging the Trump administration’s unlawful termination of Haiti and Syria Temporary Protected Status (TPS).

On March 28, 2026, Rep. Pressley’s discharge petition to force a House vote on extending Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Haiti successfully met the 218-signature threshold to move forward with bipartisan support.

In March 2026, Rep. Pressley joined Haitian faith leaders and advocates to urge the Supreme Court to affirm the lower courts’ rulings that deemed Trump’s push to terminate Haiti TPS unlawful.

In February 2026, Rep. Pressley applauded a federal judge’s ruling to temporarily block Trump’s move to terminate Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Haitians. Ending TPS for Haitians would leave over 350,000 Haitian nationals at risk of deportation, many of whom reside in the Massachusetts 7th congressional district.

In January 2026, Congresswoman Pressley, alongside Senator Markey, held a field hearing on the importance of extending Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Haiti. She documented this testimony in the legislative record. Footage from the hearing is available here and photos here.

In January 2026, Rep. Pressley also organized a press conference in D.C. in January to sound the alarm on the harm of terminating TPS for Haiti on seniors and the U.S. care economy.

On June 28, 2025, Congresswoman Ayanna Pressley (MA-07) issued the following statement condemning the Trump Administration’s abominable termination of Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Haiti effective September 2nd, 2025.

On June 5, 2025, Congresswoman Ayanna Pressley (MA-07) and Yvette D. Clarke (NY-09) issued the following statement on Donald Trump’s executive order that bans citizens of 12 countries, including Haiti, from traveling to the United States, and places partial restrictions on citizens of seven more nations.

On March 18, 2025, Congresswoman Ayanna Pressley (MA-07), Congresswoman Yvette Clarke (NY-09), and Senator Chris Van Hollen (D-MD) led 62 of their colleagues in the House and 23 of their colleagues in the Senate in a letter to Department of Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem demanding the Trump Administration redesignate and extend Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Haiti, which the administration recently canceled on questionable legal authority.

On February 20, 2025, Congresswomen Ayanna Pressley (MA-07), Yvette Clarke (NY-12), and Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick (FL-20) issued the following statement condemning the Trump Administration’s decision to end Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Haiti.

On April 23, 2024, Rep. Pressley, alongside Co-Chairs Congresswoman Yvette D. Clarke (NY-09) and Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick (FL-20), led a group of 50 lawmakers urging the Biden Administration to redesignate Haiti for Temporary Protected Status (TPS), pause on deportations back to Haiti, extend humanitarian parole to any Haitians currently detained in Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s detention centers, end detention of Haitian migrants intercepted at sea, and provide additional humanitarian assistance for Haiti.

On April 18, 2024, Rep. Pressley and Haiti Caucus Co-Chairs led a letter to House Ways and Means Committee leadership emphasizing support for the early renewal of the Haitian Hemispheric Opportunity through Partnership Encouragement (HOPE) and the Haiti Economic Lift Program (HELP) Acts, commonly known as HOPE/HELP.

On April 12, 2024, Rep. Pressley joined Haitian-led activists, organizations, and a directly impacted person in Haiti for a press call urging federal action to address the worsening humanitarian crisis in Haiti.

On March 27, 2024, Rep. Pressley joined Senator Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) and her colleagues on the Massachusetts congressional delegation in urging the Biden Administration to expedite visa processing for Haitians, particularly for relatives of U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents.

On March 12, 2024, Rep. Pressley and Haiti Caucus Co-Chairs Reps. Cherfilus McCormick and Yvette Clarke issued a statement on the resignation of Haitian Prime Minister Ariel Henry.

On March 6, 2024, Rep. Pressley issued a statement on the recent jailbreak and State of Emergency in Haiti.

On December 8, 2023, Rep. Pressley and Congresswoman Yvette Clarke urged the U.S. Department of State to withdraw U.S. support for an armed foreign intervention in Haiti and encourage negotiations for a Haitian-led democratic political transition.

On December 6, 2022, Rep. Pressley issued a statement applauding the Biden Administration’s extension and re-designation of Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Haiti.

On December 1, 2022, Rep. Pressley, Rep. Cori Bush, and Rep. Mondaire Jones led 14 of their colleagues on a letter to Department of Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas urging the Department to extend and redesignate Haiti for Temporary Protected Status (TPS).

On August 17, 2022, Rep. Pressley, along with Haiti Caucus Co-Chairs Reps. Val Demings, Yvette Clarke, and Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick (FL-20), called on President Biden to appoint a new Special Envoy to Haiti, a position that has remained unfilled since September 2021.

On May 31, 2022, Rep. Pressley and Reverend Dieufort Fleurissaint, chair of Haitian Americans United, published an op-ed in the Bay State Banner in which they called on the Biden administration to withdraw support for de facto ruler of Haiti, Ariel Henry, and instead support an inclusive, civil society-led process to restore stability and democracy on the island.

On May 26, 2022, Rep. Pressley, along with Representatives Jan Schakowsky (IL-09), Andy Levin (MI-09), Jim McGovern (MA-02), and Frederica Wilson (FL-24), led a letter to United States Agency for International Development (USAID) Administrator Power urging her to act to ensure food security in Haiti.

In February 2022, Reps. Pressley, Judy Chu (CA-27), and Nydia Velázquez (NY-07) led 33 other House Democrats on a letter to CDC Director Walensky demanding answers about the agency’s justification for treating asylum seekers as a unique public health threat, how these expulsions are being coordinated, how asylum seekers being returned to dangerous situations are being cared for, and more. Days later, Rep. Pressley once again called on the Biden Administration to reverse the Title 42 Order and other anti-Black immigration policies.

On March 16, 2022, Rep. Pressley and Rep. Mondaire Jones called on Department of Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Director Rochelle Walensky to fully end Title 42, cease deportations of people to Haiti and affirm their legal and fundamental human right to seek asylum.

On February 16, 2022, Rep. Pressley joined Congresswoman Cori Bush (MO-01), Senator Cory Booker (D-NJ), and 100 House and Senate colleagues in urging President Biden to reverse inhumane immigration policies – such as Title 42, originally introduced under the Trump Administration – that continue to disproportionately harm Black migrants.

On February 14, 2022, Congresswoman Ayanna Pressley (MA-07), alongside Representatives Judy Chu (CA-27) and Nydia Velázquez (NY-07), led 33 other House Democrats on a letter to Rochelle Walensky, Director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, demanding answers about the agency’s justification for treating asylum seekers as a unique public health threat, how these expulsions are being coordinated, how asylum seekers being returned to dangerous situations are being cared for, and more.

In April 2022, she joined her colleagues at a press conference reaffirming her support for President Biden’s decision to end Title 42. Full video of her remarks at the press conference is available here. Rep. Pressley applauded the Biden Administration’s end of Title 42 in a statement in April 2022.

In September 2022, Rep. Pressley and Rep. Velázquez led 54 of their colleagues on a letter calling on the Biden Administration to immediately halt deportations to Haiti and provide humanitarian parole protections for those seeking asylum. The lawmakers’ letter followed the Administration’s resumption of deportation flights to Haiti as thousands of Haitian migrants continue to await an opportunity to make an asylum claim at the border.

In September 2022, Rep. Pressley joined her colleagues on the House Oversight Committee in demanding answers regarding the inhumane treatment of migrants in Del Rio, Texas, by Border Patrol agents on horseback and pushing to Biden Administration to end the ongoing use and weaponization of Title 42.

On July 7, 2022, Rep. Pressley and Haiti Caucus Co-Chairs Reps. Andy Levin (MI-09), Val Demings (FL-10) and Yvette D. Clarke (NY-09) released a statement marking the one-year anniversary of the assassination of Haitian President Jovenel Moïse.

On November 21, 2021, Rep. Pressley and Senator Elizabeth Warren led the Massachusetts congressional delegation on a letter to the Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR) calling on them to coordinate with the government agencies of the Commonwealth of Massachusetts to assist newly arrived families from Haiti.

On October 18, 2021, Rep. Pressley, and Haiti Caucus Co-Chairs Reps. Val Demings (FL-10), Yvette Clarke (NY-09), and Andy Levin (MI-09) issued a statement following the kidnapping of American and Canadian missionaries in Haiti.

On October 18, 2021, Rep. Pressley issued a statement on the civil rights complaint filed by Haitian families demanding a federal investigation into the heinous actions perpetrated by federal officials at the border.

On October 22, 2021, Rep. Pressley, along with Oversight Chairwoman Carolyn B. Maloney, Subcommittee on Civil Rights and Civil Liberties Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-MD), and Reps. Rashida Tlaib (MI-13), Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (NY-14), and Debbie Wasserman Schultz (D-FL), sent a letter to Troy A. Miller, the Acting Administrator of U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), demanding a briefing and answers regarding press reports of the inhumane treatment of migrants in Del Rio, Texas, by Border Patrol agents on horseback.

On September 17, 2021, Rep. Pressley and Congresswoman Nydia M. Velázquez (NY-07) led 52 of their colleagues calling on the Biden Administration to immediately halt deportations to Haiti and take urgent action to address the concerns of the Haitian Diaspora after a 7.2 magnitude earthquake devastated Haiti.

On August 14, 2021, Rep. Pressley Yvette Clarke (NY-09), Andy Levin (MI-09) and Val Demings (FL-10) and Mondaire Jones (NY-17) released a statement regarding the recent earthquake in Haiti.

On July 14, 2021, Rep. Pressley and Haiti Caucus Co-Chairs Reps. Yvette Clarke (NY-09), Andy Levin (MI-09) and Val Demings (FL-10) sent a letter to U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas calling on him to take a series of steps to support the Haitian diaspora amid ongoing political turmoil in Haiti.

In July 2021, the Reps. Pressley, Clarke, Demings and Levin issued a statement condemning the assassination of President Moïse and calling for swift and decisive action to bring political stability and peace to Haiti and the Haitian people.

In May 2021, on Haitian Flag Day, Reps. Pressley, Levin, Clarke and Demings announced the formation of the House Haiti Caucus, a Congressional caucus dedicated to pursuing a just foreign policy that puts the needs and aspirations of the Haitian people first.

title: WATCH: Pressley Lays Out Vision for Democratic Majority, Solicits Community Feedback on “People’s Agenda”
text:
At East Boston Town Hall, Congresswoman Calls for Medicare for All, Abolishing ICE, Reparations, Reproductive Freedom, Housing Affordability, and More

Pressley Has Called on Democrats to Meet the Moment by Delivering Bold, Transformative Policy in 120th Congress

Video (YouTube)

BOSTON –At a town hall in East Boston, Congresswoman Ayanna Pressley (MA-07) laid out her vision and priorities for the Democratic majority in the 120th Congress and solicited feedback from constituents about what policies she should fight for in a “People’s Agenda.” Congresswoman Pressley, who has always sought to model “cooperative governing,” was joined at the town hall by State Senator Lydia Edwards.

Congresswoman Pressley has consistently called on Democrats to meet the moment and use their new majority to pursue bold, transformative policies and aggressively pursue accountability for the corruption, cruelty, and harm inflicted by the Trump administration over the past two years.

In her remarks at the town hall, the Congresswoman outlined several policy fights Democrats should take on in the 120th Congress, including but not limited to:

Medicare for All and Healthcare Justice: Passing Medicare for All so no person or family goes bankrupt because they get sick, restoring funding for Medicaid, and renewing the Affordable Care Act tax credits Republicans let expire.

Housing Affordability: Building on the success of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act by further expanding affordable housing and investing in homeownership to ensure working families can afford to remain in the communities they call home.

Abolishing ICE and Immigrant Justice: Abolishing ICE, ending qualified immunity for ICE agents, and extending Temporary Protected Status for Haitian, Venezuelan, Salvadoran, and other immigrant communities.

Reproductive Freedom: Overturning the horrific Dobbs decision, passing the EACH Act to end the discriminatory Hyde Amendment, and expanding access to the full suite of reproductive healthcare, including IVF and contraception.

Racial and Economic Justice: Advancing reparations for Black America by passing H.R. 40 to address the harmful legacy of slavery and establish a federal commission to develop reparations proposals.

Affordability and Economic Justice: Passing universal childcare and paid leave, raising wages, investing in workforce development, and addressing the crisis of Black unemployment.

Peace and Human Rights: Ending Trump’s illegal war with Iran and passing the Block the Bombs Act to stop U.S. tax dollars from funding the Israeli government’s genocide in Gaza.

AI Regulation and Stopping Data Centers: Enacting a federal moratorium on data centers until comprehensive federal AI legislation and stringent environmental protections are in place, including the AI Civil Rights Act.

Rooting Out Corruption and Pursuing Accountability: Conducting aggressive oversight and pursuing accountability for the cruelty, callousness, and corruption of the past two years, including the economic harm done to families across our country.

A transcript of excerpts from the Congresswoman’s opening remarks at the town hall is available below and the video is available here.

Transcript: Pressley Lays Out Vision for Democratic Majority, Solicits Community Feedback on “People’s Agenda”

November 16, 202

East Boston, MA

…

Look, I believe that the election outcome was truly a cease-and-desist letter sent at the ballot. It was a condemnation. It was a condemnation and rejection of an anti-freedom agenda, a fascist administration that wants to control your body, that wants to control the books you read, that wants to attack the free press, that wants to criminalize free speech, that wants to disenfranchise you at the ballot box–that is an anti-freedom agenda.

So what happened on Election Day was a condemnation and a rejection of that anti-freedom agenda. It was not an affirmation of the Democratic Party, in my opinion.

And so the job is not finished because it was never a compelling enough argument for Democrats to simply say “we are not them.” We now have a responsibility to affirm who are we, and we have to move with boldness and with urgency because it is about keeping not only the trust of the people, it is about, again, advancing a people’s mandate and agenda in the People’s House.

And moreover, in my opinion, we’ve got to move quickly because I want us to get to the work of a trifecta in getting that executive. I’m excited about what we have, having that gavel back in the House and the Senate, but we have so much work to do.

And East Boston is not afraid of hard work. You know, I just want to say thank you, East Boston, for how you stand up every day for your neighbors. Everybody deserves places of safety and belonging and joy. And thank you for how you show up for one another. You have one of the most inspiring blueprints for what radical mutual aid really looks like. The infrastructure that you have stood up as a community and as a people, and so let’s just you know clap for the nonprofit and community-based organizations, the everyday people taking care of one another.

And so again as I think about this mandate for justice, a mandate for compassion, a mandate for progress, as I consider this powerful rejection of cruelty, callousness, and corruption by the people, as I think about the subpoenas will issue from the oversight committee on which I serve.

You know my priorities and what is top of mind for me in this moment is that we not operate from a place of incrementalism. I think the first thing we have to focus on is repair. So when you think about Medicaid cuts and SNAP and vouchers and all those things, so we have to do the work of repair and restoration.

And true enough, the Big Betrayal of a Bill, the Big Ugly Bill, the impacts of that will not really be felt until January 1, and they’ve done that on purpose because they knew the Democrats would likely be the governing majority, and they wanted us to wear that bill. We have to continue to remind people who are the architects of that bill, and we have to actively do the work of mitigating those acute harms, and that means working with boldness and urgency to do repair and restoration.

But in my opinion, yes, we can address affordability and accountability, and we can ensure, and we can ensure that we do not default to an unjust status quo.

…

Now, before I turn it over to Senator Edwards and your questions, again, I’m just going to take a few minutes to outline my priorities for this majority, so in no particular order:

Medicare for All. So we’ve already spoken a bit about healthcare and the cuts to Medicaid and Obamacare subsidies [that] have made coverage simply unaffordable for too many people. This is a top priority for me. As I said, I represent a district that’s deeply unequal, that has disparate outcomes across all issues, but including and especially when it comes to health. You know, people are tired of me saying the statistic, but I’ll keep saying it until it changes. From Cambridge to Roxbury, life expectancy drops by 23 years.

Okay, and because of the nefarious work that is private equity, I’ve lost Carney Hospital, St. Elizabeth’s, and other healthcare assets in my district, and so this is quite literally a matter of people’s lives. So the goal is Medicare for All, so that no person and no family has to go bankrupt because they get sick in the richest country in the world.

…

No one should be rationing, in the richest country in the world, rationing asthma inhalers and insulin, but that is exactly what is happening.

So, in this majority, my message is: don’t tell me what a majority is. Show me what a majority is. So don’t just talk about healthcare justice. Pass Medicare for All. Healthcare is a human right, and our policies should reflect that.

Secondly, housing. Housing is our most important infrastructure. It is a determinant for health. It is social and economic mobility. I serve on the Financial Services Committee. We have got to make housing more affordable. You all know people should not be spending more than 30 percent of their income on rents, and home ownership is farther, increasingly so, farther and farther out of reach. People are spending upwards of 80 percent of their income on rents. So housing costs remain one of the most urgent burdens facing working families. I know that is true in East Boston, certainly throughout the Massachusetts 7th. Rent is too high. Homeownership is out of reach. Too many families, quite literally, are one emergency away from eviction or homelessness, one illness, one death, one divorce, one layoff, one disruptive life event away. The majority of people in this country do not even have $400 saved for an emergency.

So this crisis impacts everyone: young people who dream of home ownership and seniors who want to remain in the community that they help build. It affects working families who are doing everything right and still finding that the cost of housing is becoming impossible to manage.

…

[W]e have to be exhaustive in our efforts to ensure that families can afford to live in the communities they call home. And Washington should be acting with urgency, and I will continue to advocate.

Okay, so Medicare for All, housing. Third, abolish ICE.

Now, as the kids would say, I’m not new to this, I’m true to this. While in 2026, it has taken the harm and the injury and the murder for many to understand that this racist, rogue, lawless agency cannot be reformed. I have been calling for ICE to be abolished since I ran for Congress in 2018. It is beyond reform, and you have experienced it here on the front lines. They terrorize our communities, kidnap our neighbors, kill people on the street with impunity. There is no reforming this lawless agency and Congress should not be funding their campaign of cruelty.

They are quite literally profiting off of people’s pain, and I have to say that this is two sides of the same evil for-profit coin. If you give a damn about mass incarceration locking up low-income and Black and Brown folks, the same corporations like GEO and CoreCivic that are incentivized to lock folks up in that way, are the same people financially profiting and incentivized to lawlessly disappear people, our neighbors from community to detain and to deport them. So those issues are closely connected.

So we must abolish ICE, and we have to end qualified immunity for ICE agents.

Okay, Medicare for All, housing, abolish ICE, and abortion access.

I will be co-chairing the Reproductive Freedom Caucus in the 120th Congress. We have to both restore, protect, and expand abortion access. Fight for full rights and freedoms is not completed, that does not include the fundamental right to reproductive freedom and bodily autonomy. Abortion care is healthcare, a fundamental human right. So we need to restore abortion protections and we need to expand them.

And this is what I mean about a reimagining, because even when Roe was the law of the land, because of racist and discriminatory policies like the Hyde Amendment, there were still many people that could not access health care. It prevented folks on Medicaid and other government-sponsored health plans from having abortion coverage. And so, not only do we need to restore Roe, we also need to repeal the Hyde Amendment. We also need to enshrine the right to contraception, IVF treatment, and ensure folks have access to the full suite of reproductive health care.

So I have a north star bill, which I think is actually very attainable if we have the political will and courage. And I have a mandate of the people behind me to get it done to advance my Abortion Justice Act, which would speak to all of these tenets. So again, very proud to serve as co-chair of the Reproductive Freedom Caucus.

Okay, making sure y’all are keeping up. We’re rounding out here, I promise. Okay, the good senator here already spoke about my commitment to extending Temporary Protected Status.

For those of you unaware, I do represent the third largest Haitian diaspora in the country. That is certainly a source of pride for me. In Congress, I do chair the House Haiti Caucus, and as was shared, because I love to do the work of consensus building, we built a broad coalition and used a rare procedural maneuver. And the House ultimately did pass my bill with bipartisan support: 10 Republicans and one independent. Because I will appeal to any person of conscience that is serious about doing this work, and that is how we were able to get that bill done.

So I will continue to champion this priority. Hundreds of thousands of lives are at stake here, including not just our Haitian neighbors, but our Salvadorian neighbors, right, Senator, Venezuelan, Syrian, Honduran, and also our Nepalese families. TPS holders are essential. They’ve built their lives here, strengthened our economy, and deepened the fabric of our communities. So let me say this clearly: the fight is not over. We will not abandon our friends to be sent back to countries that are quite literally a death sentence.

Okay, and then the last two tenets. Before turning it over to you, I’m just going to name them and just list them off.

Okay, child care and paid leave. The care economy is not a nice to have; it is a must have.

We have to end the war in Iran. The American people spoke loud and clear. They do not want this war to continue, so we have to heed their calls and end it once and for all.

Also, we need to block the bombs. Okay? Now look, the headlines have faded, but the Israeli government is still carrying out a genocide in Gaza. Starvation, targeting, the murdering of Palestinians is still happening in broad daylight, despite the so-called ceasefire in the region. So we have to continue to push to save lives, and for a true, just, and lasting peace, we can start by passing the Block the Bombs Act to stop our tax dollars from funding this genocide.

All right, y’all. I promise you, I’m rounding out, Senator. It’s just a robust agenda. It’s a robust agenda.

Okay, reparations. HR 40. It is one of the honors of my life. You may be unaware of this history, but an ancestor, may he rest in peace and power, the first black state senator in the state legislature, Bill Owens, was the first member of a state legislature to introduce a bill for reparations. That bill became foundational for legislation authored by the great John Conyers, a congressman from Detroit, who carried that mantle. He’s an ancestor. That mantle was then passed on to Congresswoman Sheila Jackson Lee of Texas. She is an ancestor, and when the congresswoman transitioned, they asked if I would pick that mantle up as a part of this broad coalition. It has been 40 years since that legislation, HR 40, was introduced, and it is high time we have a floor vote on that. There is momentum around the country for reparations to begin the process of reparative justice for Black America, and this bill would create a pathway toward truth, reconciliation, and accountability. It is even more important after two years of anti-Blackness on steroids by this administration, attacks on DEI, rising Black unemployment, especially among our federal workforce.

So black folks, especially black women, delivered this historic Democratic majority, and it’s time Democrats deliver for Black America reparations now.

Okay, and the last edict, I promise, is we have to stop the data centers. The groundswell has been loud and clear. It’s been incredible as I’ve traveled the country in places like Tennessee to see rural and urban folks coming together, coalescing around this issue. Now, look, I just have the honor of presenting on the main stage at Afro Tech. I am very clear that AI is here, but we need to create sensible guardrails and stringent environmental protections in place.

A community like East Boston knows what it looks like when that doesn’t happen. So, in my opinion, we should push for a moratorium on data centers until we can pass comprehensive federal and human-first AI legislation to regulate them and ensure that no town or city is bearing the environmental, economic, or health burden for the billionaire CEOs.

So I know that was a long list, but these are the fights that I’m prepared, the righteous fights, I’m prepared to take on, that have been informed and shaped by my being, you know, daily in conversation and in community, actively listening to all of you. And I’m eager to hear what else is on your mind.

Thank you.

title: Raskin, Spartz Legislation Finalizing Details for National Memorial Honoring Indispensable American Patriot Thomas Paine Passes House
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C.—Today, the U.S. House of Representatives passed bipartisan legislation led by Representatives Jamie Raskin (MD-08) and Victoria Spartz (IN-05) directing U.S. Department of the Interior (DOI) Secretary Doug Burgum to place a forthcoming memorial honoring American hero Thomas Paine in “Area 1” of the National Mall. Area 1 is reserved for monuments and memorials of the highest national significance.

The Common Sense 250 Actinstructs Secretary Burgum to place this already-approved memorial in the central section of the National Mall between the U.S. Capitol and the Lincoln Memorial. The memorial honors Paine, who wrote the 1776 pamphletCommon Sensewhich galvanized passionate support for the American Revolution.

“With his undaunted quill, Tom Paine fought back against King George and the tyrants of his time, sparking the American Revolution for freedom and democracy and a land where the King would no longer be the law, but the law would be King,”said Rep. Raskin.“Today the House overwhelmingly passed our bipartisan legislation to properly honor this hero of democracy and freedom and advance our plans to erect a memorial so his legacy and writings will be forever captured in our national memory and dialogue.”

“Thomas Paine’s Common Sense lit the spark of the American Revolution and laid the foundation of our Republic,”said Rep. Spartz. “As America marks its 250th anniversary, I’m proud to join Rep. Jamie Raskin in honoring a patriot whose words still call us to courage. May his legacy inspire future generations to defend the freedoms he helped secure—and bring some common sense back to Washington.”

"Today’s House passage of the Common Sense 250 Act is an extraordinary milestone for the Thomas Paine Memorial Association and for everyone who has worked to see this long-held vision become reality,”said Margaret Downey, President of the Thomas Paine Memorial Association. “We are one major step closer to giving Thomas Paine the national recognition he has long deserved. We are deeply grateful to Representatives Jamie Raskin and Victoria Spartz for their bipartisan leadership in introducing this legislation, and to the members of the House who supported it. We also thank the National Capital Memorial Advisory Commission, our supporters, donors and everyone who has helped advance this effort.”

“We’re so grateful to Rep. Raskin and Rep. Spartz for their leadership, and to the House for approving a permanent memorial to our nation’s forgotten founder in this historic semiquincentennial year,”said Annie Laurie Gaylor, Co-President of the Freedom from Religion Foundation. “We look forward to its passage by Congress this session.”

The Paine memorial is already completely funded by private donations. The Thomas Paine Memorial Association plans to commission the renowned sculptor Zenos Frudakis to build the memorial.

title: RILEY INTRODUCES BILL TO MAKE UTILITY MONOPOLIES PAY CUSTOMERS BACK WHEN THEY FAIL ON SERVICE AND RELIABILITY
text:
Demands action as NYSEG, Central Hudson, and National Grid fail state audits four years in a row.

WASHINGTON, DC — Representative Josh Riley (NY-19) introduced the Utility Accountability Actto hold utility monopolies accountable for safety failures, frequent, prolonged outages, and poor customer service. Under Riley’s bill, an investor-owned utility that fails a state audit of its performance, reliability, or safety standards would owe each of its residential customers a $100 credit towards their bill.

The legislation follows the New York State Public Service Commission’s latest audit, which found that NYSEG, Central Hudson, and National Grid failed to meet minimum customer service standards for the fourth consecutive year, resulting in nearly $35 million in penalties for 2025 alone.

Those findings are consistent with what Upstate New Yorkers reported in a survey conducted as part of Riley’s investigation into local utilities. Of the more than 5,000 NY-19 residents who responded, 38% reported unexpected increases in their utility bills, 16% reported poor customer service, and 7% reported problems with their smart meters. And when residents turned to their utilities for help, two-thirds of those who reported a problem said the company never fixed it.

“Upstate New Yorkers are being forced to pay through the nose for electricity each month – but instead of using our money to improve service and upgrade the grid, the utility monopolies are sending record profits overseas. I’ve heard from folks struggling with blackouts, broken smart meters, bills that make no sense, and hours on hold. And more often than not, when they report a problem, it never gets fixed,” said Riley. “Enough is enough. If these monopolies can’t meet basic standards of service, they should pay Upstate New Yorkers back out of their own pockets.”

Under the Utility Accountability Act, state utility regulators would conduct annual audits certifying whether investor-owned electric utilities meet state performance, reliability, and safety standards. If a utility fails, it would be required to issue direct bill credits to residential customers starting at $100 in the first year and increasing by $100 for each consecutive year of failure ($100 in year one, $200 in year two, $300 in year three…).

To protect taxpayers and ratepayers, the bill explicitly prohibits utilities from passing the cost of the credits back onto residential customers — forcing corporate investors to absorb the full cost — and authorizes the Secretary of Energy to withhold federal assistance from state regulatory authorities that fail to enforce the bill credit orders.

You can read the text of the billHERE.

The Utility Accountability Act builds on Riley’s ongoing work to take on utility monopolies and lower energy costs for Upstate New York families. Riley has:

Joined the NYSEG and Central Hudson rate cases to fight their rate hikes directly, going head-to-head with the companies on behalf of Upstate ratepayers.

Introduced the Weatherization Enhancement and Readiness Act (H.R. 1355) to help families weatherize their homes, use less energy, and lower their monthly bills.

Introduced the Keep the Lights Local Act (H.R. 5487) to end foreign ownership of American utilities.

Introduced the No Bonuses for Utility Executives Act (H.R. 6590) to ban utility executives from cashing in on bonuses while they jack up rates faster than inflation.

Introduced the No Taxes on Utility Bills Act (H.R. 8350) so families can deduct the taxes and state surcharges tacked onto their gas and electric bills.

Introduced the Lowering Utility Bills Act (H.R. 8568) to stop utility companies from overcharging customers.

Introduced the FAIR Data Act (H.R. 9655) to make sure Big Tech’s data centers pay their own way instead of sticking Upstate families and small businesses with higher energy bills.

Introduced the Smart Meter Data Privacy Protection Act (H.R. 10284) to stop utility companies from selling your personal data collected through smart meters.

title: Reps. Kelly and McClellan Introduce Resolution to Designate November as Prematurity Awareness Month
text:
WASHINGTON — On Prematurity Awareness Day, Congresswoman Robin Kelly (IL-02), Chair of the Congressional Black Caucus Health Braintrust, and Congresswoman Jennifer McClellan (VA-04) introduced H.Res. 1664, a resolution to federally recognize November as Prematurity Awareness Month.

Preterm birth remains a serious threat to the health and lives of mothers and their children. Prematurity is a leading cause of infant death, can result in lifelong health complications and is often preventable. Yet preterm birth rates remain stubbornly high amid persistent racial disparities and gaps in access to maternity care, earning the United States a D+ preterm birth grade in the 2026 March of Dimes Report Card. For the fourth year in a row, the United States had a preterm birthrate of 10.4%, with nearly 380,000 babies born prematurely in 2025, and babies born to Black, American Indian and Alaska Native mothers experience preterm birth rates significantly higher than those born to white mothers. Thousands of families face the devastating consequences of preterm birth, underscoring the urgent need to raise awareness, expand resources and strengthen prevention efforts.

“Too many families have to face the life-threatening impacts of preterm birth. A healthy start to life begins with a healthy mom, and every mother deserves adequate care before, during, and after delivery,” said Congresswoman Robin Kelly. “In particular, Black and Indigenous moms continue to face disproportionate barriers to maternal care, resulting in significantly higher rates of preterm birth and maternal mortality rates. I’ve sounded the alarm on maternal mortality since I first came to Congress, and I am committed to continuing the fight for the wellbeing of moms and infants.”

“My daughter and I both nearly died when my placenta ruptured nine weeks before her due date. Her six weeks in the NICU were the most stressful of my life,” said Congresswoman McClellan. “While preterm birth can affect any family, communities of color bear a disproportionate burden in tackling this public health crisis. Behind every statistic lies a family whose life has been changed because of a premature birth. We cannot begin to address our maternal and infant health crisis without first raising awareness and ensuring families have access to the resources and support they need. During my tenure in the Virginia legislature, I fought to designate November as Prematurity Awareness Month. Now, I’m committed to carrying on these efforts at the federal level.”

“For the fifth consecutive year, the U.S. has received a preterm birth grade of D+, meaning nearly 380,000 babies were born too soon last year,” said Stacey Brayboy, Senior Vice President of Public Policy and Government Affairs at March of Dimes. “Persistent racial inequities also remain with Black babies facing a higher preterm birth rate than white and Asian babies. We must keep working together to raise awareness, advance policies that support healthier pregnancies and births, and address the systemic barriers that put too many families at risk. March of Dimes is grateful for the leadership of Representatives Jennifer McClellan and Robin Kelly in recognizing Prematurity Awareness Month and remains committed to fighting for the health of all moms and babies, so that every family has the best possible start.”

The resolution is cosponsored by Reps. Eleanor Homes Norton (DC), Nikema Williams (GA-05), Nanette Barragan (CA-44), Yvette Clarke (NY-09), Jonathan Jackson (IL-01), Paul Tonko (NY-20), Debbie Dingell (MI-06) and Morgan McGarvey (KY-03).

Read the full text of H.Res. 1664 here. Read the 2026 March of Dimes Report Card here.

title: Congresswoman Scanlon Leads PA Democratic Colleagues in Investigation Concerning ICE Uniforms and Militarized Equipment
text:
Washington, D.C. — Congresswoman Mary Gay Scanlon (PA-05) last week led her Pennsylvania Democratic colleagues in pressing Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Acting Director of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) David Venturella for answers about uniforms and equipment issued to ICE officers across the country, including the Philadelphia Field Office. The inquiry comes amid reports that ICE and DHS have failed to train or equip its agents with body cameras and is purchasing and deploying military armor, shock gloves, and other dangerous equipment to agents on American streets.

“Under this administration, there has been a noted increase in the militarization of federal law enforcement officials, rising concerns about the identities of ICE officers being obscured during enforcement activity, and numerous incidents of excessive force by the officers employed by your department,” the members wrote. “As Members of Congress who wield appropriations power, we need to understand how taxpayer dollars are being spent by your agency and to ensure that equipment being purchased by ICE is not becoming a threat to public safety and the American people.”

On July 22, 2026, Congresswoman Scanlon sent a standard inquiry to ICE Congressional Relations and the Philadelphia Field Office requesting “any available details about the uniforms and equipment issued to ICE officers detailed to the Philadelphia Regional Office,” including whether there are standard items issued to every officer.

On August 31, 2026, ICE issued a generic response about labeling on ICE-issued field equipment and identification of non-uniformed officers, such as displaying badges and wearing vests, jackets, or other clothing with markings such as “POLICE,” “ICE,” or both. ICE-issued field equipment typically displays “ICE Enforcement Removal Operations,” “ICE Homeland Security Investigations,” and/or “POLICE ICE” to indicate the specific law enforcement agency being represented, but ICE officers are also authorized to conduct immigration enforcement in plain clothes.

The inquiry is part of a broader push for oversight of ICE as the Trump administration continues aggressive—and at times unlawful—immigration enforcement operations in communities across the country. This year, Congresswoman Scanlon has visited the Philadelphia Federal Detention Center and the Moshannon Valley Processing Center, and joined her Pennsylvania Democratic colleagues on the Oversight Access Act of 2026 to expand congressional oversight access at ICE facilities.

In the letter, the members are requesting answers to questions about ICE’s uniforms and equipment by Friday, November 27, 2026.

title: Congresswoman Scholten Backs Legislation to Extend Temporary Protected Status for Lebanese Nationals
text:
WASHINGTON, DC – Today, U.S. Congresswoman Hillary Scholten (D-MI-03) announced her strong support and advocacy for the Lebanon Temporary Protected Status (TPS) Act, which would extend temporary protections for Lebanese nationals living in the United States while conditions in Lebanon remain too dangerous for them to safely return home. Fellow Michigan lawmakers Congresswomen Rashida Tlaib (D-MI-12) and Debbie Dingell (D-MI-06) lead the legislation.

“Temporary Protected Status provides a literal lifeline to people whose home countries are measurably unsafe, and extending this status for Lebanese nationals is the right thing to do,” said Congresswoman Hillary Scholten. “Tens of thousands of Lebanese-Americans call Michigan home, and their families should not have to live in fear that loved ones could be sent back to a country where their safety is at great risk. As long as conditions in Lebanon remain this dangerous, we have a responsibility to give people the opportunity to remain here safely with their families and communities.”

TPS is a federal designation that allows eligible individuals from countries experiencing armed conflict, natural disasters, or other extraordinary circumstances to remain in the United States temporarily and receive protection from deportation while conditions in their home countries make return unsafe. The current TPS designation for Lebanon is set to expire later this month, and this legislation would extend it through April 2029.

title: Congresswoman Scholten's Statement on Trump Administration’s Cancellation of Pay Increase for Head Start Teachers
text:
WASHINGTON, DC – Today, Congresswoman Scholten released a statement on the Trump Administration’s decision to cancel cost-of-living pay increases for Head Start teachers, a result of the “Restoring Flexibility to Support Head Start Program Access” rulemaking, which rolls back a $10,000 pay raise for most Head Start teachers and basic benefits for full-time staff. Congresswoman Scholten joined a June letter opposing the rule.

The Congresswoman released the below statement:

“The Trump Administration’s decision to cancel cost-of-living adjustments for Head Start teachers sends a clear message about its priorities: penny-pinching educators’ salaries while covering the White House in gold. This is unacceptable.

“For more than 60 years, Head Start has supported early education, health and dental care, and healthy meals while connecting families to job training and housing support. Now, the program is asking for the bare minimum: funding to maintain its operations and to help absorb higher costs amid the affordability crisis.

“The decision to withhold the requested funding will force programs to choose between a livable wage for educators, spaces for more children, and healthy meals on the table. I have heard directly from my constituents who run these programs about how this will negatively impact our community. This is unacceptable, and I will keep fighting to protect Head Start, because the educators and families who depend on it deserve better than this.”

Head Start leaders have requested a 4.97 percent cost-of-living adjustment, which would let programs pay staff more competitively, keep experienced educators in their classrooms, and give families the consistency they count on. The rule also removes requirements that programs provide full-time staff with health care coverage, paid leave, and behavioral health services, and that they help part-time staff access health coverage and other eligible benefits. Together, these changes will affect more than 250,000 Head Start educators and staff and put services at risk for nearly 716,000 children and their families nationwide.

title: Reps. Sewell and Dingell Introduce Legislation to Cap Out-of-Pocket Medicare Costs, Lower Healthcare Costs for Seniors
text:
Legislation would cap annual out-of-pocket costs for traditional Medicare and expand financial assistance for low-income beneficiaries

Washington, D.C. – Today, U.S. Rep. Terri Sewell (AL-07) joined Rep. Debbie Dingell (MI-06) in introducing the Medicare Cost Cap Act, legislation to establish an annual $5,000 out-of-pocket cap for services covered under traditional Medicare and expand programs that help low-income seniors and people with disabilities afford their healthcare.

"In Alabama and across the country, Medicare beneficiaries who have worked hard their entire lives are still vulnerable to overwhelming out-of-pocket costs when they get sick," said Rep. Sewell. "While Medicare Advantage plans already provide an annual limit on out-of-pocket spending, traditional Medicare offers no such protection, leaving millions of seniors exposed to potentially devastating medical bills. By establishing a $5,000 annual cap on out-of-pocket costs in traditional Medicare, this bill will provide meaningful relief and greater financial certainty for seniors and their families. At a time when too many Americans are struggling with the rising cost of health care and everyday necessities, this legislation represents a commonsense step toward making health care more affordable and strengthening the Medicare program for generations to come."

“People work their entire lives and pay into Medicare expecting it will be there when they need it. But a serious illness can still leave them facing medical bills they cannot afford,” said Rep. Dingell. “I hear from seniors who are stretching every dollar and worrying about whether getting the care they need will cost them their savings. This legislation would put a limit on what people pay out of pocket for care under traditional Medicare and help more people with limited incomes get financial assistance. No one should have to put off seeing a doctor or getting the care or medicine they need because they are afraid of the bill.”

The Medicare Cost Cap Act would:

Establish a $5,000 annual out-of-pocket cap for deductibles, copayments, coinsurance, and other cost-sharing for services covered under traditional Medicare Parts A and B. Once beneficiaries reach the limit, they would owe no additional cost-sharing for covered services for the remainder of the year. The cap would be adjusted annually based on growth in Medicare spending.

Expand financial assistance to more low-income beneficiaries by raising the income eligibility thresholds for the Qualified Medicare Beneficiary program and the Medicare Part D Low-Income Subsidy, also known as Extra Help, to 200 percent of the federal poverty level beginning in 2028.

Eliminate asset tests for these assistance programs, allowing otherwise eligible beneficiaries to qualify without being disqualified because of their savings.

Simplify access to assistance by aligning eligibility rules and requiring qualifying Extra Help recipients to be treated as Qualified Medicare Beneficiaries, helping people receive assistance with both medical and prescription drug costs.

The legislation is endorsed by SEIU, Protect Our Care, National Council on Aging (NCOA), Social Security Works, the National Academy of Elder Law Attorneys (NAELA), No Patient Left Behind, Center for Health and Democracy, Community Catalyst, Justice in Aging, Village to Village Network, United States of Care, Just Care USA, LeadingAge, the Center for Medicare Advocacy, National Association of Nutrition and Aging Services Programs, the Elder Justice Coalition, and Michigan Health & Hospital Association.

“After their historic victory last week, Democrats are ready to hit the ground running on delivering lower costs for working families and fighting back against Donald Trump and Republicans’ senseless war on health care to fund tax breaks for billionaires,” said Protect Our Care President Brad Woodhouse. “The Medicare Cost Cap Act will provide much-needed relief to millions of families struggling with the soaring costs of health care, especially seniors, who primarily rely on their Social Security benefits to pay their premiums. Alongside the Medicare Cost Cap Act, Democrats will fight tooth and nail to strengthen Medicare by containing costs system-wide, adding dental, vision, and hearing benefits, and expanding Medicare drug price negotiations. Democrats are determined to fix what Trump broke, and they’re just getting started.”

“Most people in the United States are just one serious illness or injury away from financial ruin. It is well past time for Congress to level the playing field for Medicare beneficiaries and add an out-of-pocket cap in Traditional Medicare. After all, the best healthcare in the world is useless unless people can afford it. Social Security Works is proud to endorse the Medicare Cost Cap Act,” said Alex Lawson, Executive Director, Social Security Works.

“Medicare can be expensive for older adults living on fixed incomes, and getting help with those costs is too complicated. The Medicare Cost Cap Act would bring much needed relief by expanding and simplifying enrollment in premium and cost-sharing assistance for Medicare enrollees with low incomes and limiting out-of-pocket costs for everyone with Medicare. Justice in Aging is pleased to see this bill introduced in the House and proud to endorse this legislation, which will make it possible for more older adults to afford their health care and other basic needs,” said Natalie Kean, Managing Director of Health Advocacy, Justice in Aging.

“While people covered by Medicare are largely satisfied with the program, we know through our listening work that people with Medicare still have trouble affording their care. This is especially true in Traditional Medicare, where people are not protected by an annual cap on their out-of-pocket costs like those in Medicare Advantage plans,” said Natalie Davis, CEO and co-founder of United States of Care. “The Medicare Cost Cap Act will go a long way in helping to improve affordability for people covered by Medicare. It will also level the playing field between Traditional Medicare and Medicare Advantage and streamline the eligibility and enrollment process for Medicare Savings Programs. United States of Care is proud to endorse this legislation and we thank Representatives Dingell and Sewell for their leadership on this issue.”

"With the Medicare Cost Cap Act, Reps. Dingell and Sewell are giving every older adult and person with a disability a real choice of traditional Medicare. For too long, traditional Medicare has been an option only for those wealthy enough to afford supplemental coverage against catastrophic costs, while everyone else was locked into Medicare Advantage, even when they were inappropriately denied the care they needed,” said Diane Archer, Founder, Just Care USA.

Bill text is available here.

title: House Passes Common Sense 250 Act, Bringing Thomas Paine to the National Mall
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — The U.S. House of Representatives has passed H.R. 9600, the Common Sense 250 Act of 2026. The bipartisan legislation authorizes the placement of the Thomas Paine Memorial in Area I of the National Mall, an area reserved for memorials of exceptional national significance.

The vote comes 250 years after Common Sense helped transform colonial discontent into a revolution for American independence. Yet the nation’s capital still has no national memorial honoring Paine’s extraordinary contribution to the founding of our Republic.

“Thomas Paine’s Common Sense lit the spark of the American Revolution and laid the foundation of our Republic. As America marks its 250th anniversary, I’m proud to join Rep. Jamie Raskin in honoring a patriot whose words still call us to courage. May his legacy inspire future generations to defend the freedoms he helped secure—and bring some common sense back to Washington,” said Rep. Victoria Spartz (R-IN).

“With his undaunted quill, Tom Paine fought back against King George and the tyrants of his time, sparking the American Revolution for freedom and democracy and a land where the King would no longer be the law, but the law would be King,” said Rep. Raskin (D-MD). “Today the House overwhelmingly passed our bipartisan legislation to properly honor this hero of democracy and freedom and advance our plans to erect a memorial so his legacy and writings will be forever captured in our national memory and dialogue.”

“Today’s House passage of the Common Sense 250 Act is an extraordinary milestone for the Thomas Paine Memorial Association and for everyone who has worked to see this long-held vision become reality. We are one major step closer to giving Thomas Paine the national recognition he has long deserved,” said Margaret Downey, President of the Thomas Paine Memorial Association. “Paine’s words helped inspire a revolution, but his contribution did not end with independence. He challenged Americans to think beyond monarchy, to embrace representative government, and to recognize that human rights do not come from kings or governments, but belong to people by virtue of being human. His writings helped shape the ideals upon which this nation was founded.”

Earlier bipartisan legislation sponsored by Reps. Raskin and Spartz authorized the Thomas Paine Memorial Association to establish the memorial. In 2024, the National Capital Memorial Advisory Commission recommended Area I as its location.

The Common Sense 250 Act now moves to the U.S. Senate.

The memorial will be funded entirely through private donations, without taxpayer funding. The Association plans to commission sculptor Zenos Frudakis.

Published in January 1776, Common Sense is estimated to have sold 500,000 copies, helping rally colonial support for independence. Paine allowed his work to be widely reproduced and later served the revolutionary cause. His writings helped shape the ideals of liberty, self-government, and individual rights that continue to define the American Republic.

title: Rep. Subramanyam Introduces Bipartisan Bill to Bolster American Leadership in Science and Engineering
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Representatives Suhas Subramanyam (VA-10) and Vince Fong (CA-20) have introduced the Promoting High-skilled Doctoral Talent (PHD Talent) Act, bipartisan legislation to speed up the process for students to obtain a Ph.D. in critical and emerging technology fields. This legislation will propel more American scientists and engineers into the domestic workforce, ensuring the United States remains a global technological leader that delivers life-changing breakthroughs.

The bill creates a five-year Department of Energy (DOE) pilot program that brings universities, National Laboratories, and private industry together. Students in these programs would get hands-on research experience, mentorship, and workforce training while earning an advanced degree in less time.

Congressman Subramanyam issued the following statement on the bill:

“Our country faces a critical shortage of scientists, engineers, and mathematicians. This bill shores up and strengthens our pipeline of researchers. This will in turn help the next generation of students make breakthrough discoveries in science, health, and technology, solidifying our country's leadership in these fields.”

Congressman Fong issued the following statement:

“America’s economy and national security depends on us having a deep bench of skilled, capable, and credentialed American workers. Whether it’s cybersecurity, advanced manufacturing, defense research, advanced energy systems, medical innovations, or other emerging technologies, we need more homegrown talent. The PHD Talent Act gives students in the Central Valley and across the country a faster, clearer path to the advanced degrees these fields demand.”

Specifically, the bill:

Establishes a five-year DOE pilot program, with Ph.D. fellowships, for accelerated bachelor’s-to-Ph.D. pathways in critical and emerging technology fields, including artificial intelligence, quantum science, semiconductors, cybersecurity, and advanced manufacturing, among others.

Supports partnerships among universities, National Laboratories, and industry for accelerated hands-on research and training.

Shortens the time it takes to earn a STEM Ph.D. while maintaining robust academic standards.

Directs funding to fields where DOE identifies a need for more domestic doctoral talent.

Ensures taxpayer-funded student support is reserved for U.S. citizens, U.S. nationals, and lawful permanent residents.

title: Thompson, Bonamici Recognize November as National Career Development Month
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Representatives Glenn “GT” Thompson (R-Pa.) and Suzanne Bonamici (D-Ore.), co-chairs of the bipartisan House Career and Technical Education Caucus, introduced a resolution today recognizing November as National Career Development Month.

National Career Development Month marks an important time for our students and workers of all ages to consider and explore future career opportunities. It is also a time to recognize the professionals who guide learners to become the leaders of tomorrow. Throughout the month, schools and businesses will have the chance to showcase different career paths that align with various interests and skills. These opportunities will better prepare students as they begin to enter the workforce.

“National Career Development Month is an opportunity to highlight the many careers that exist for students and adult-learners, and encourages Americans to plan for their future. A highly skilled workforce is essential for our country’s economy, and I am pleased to lead this resolution to help people find fulfilling careers,” Rep. Thompson said.

“Navigating the modern American job market is an increasingly complex endeavor, and no one should have to make these life-changing decisions alone or uninformed. I’m pleased to support this bipartisan resolution to promote career development as an essential tool for professionals and students while recognizing the effort of hardworking career development professionals,” Rep. Bonamici said.

“November is National Career Development Month, and NCDA is proud to recognize the dedicated professionals who help individuals discover their potential, explore opportunities, and build meaningful career paths. Career development professionals play an essential role in shaping a stronger workforce by providing guidance, encouragement, and resources that empower people of all ages to reach their goals. Their work not only strengthens our nation's workforce but also contributes to the economic success and overall well-being of individuals and communities. We are excited to continue championing career development and creating opportunities for all Americans to build brighter futures,” said Deneen Pennington, Executive Director, National Career Development Association.

“Career development is essential to ensuring every learner has the opportunity to explore their interests, recognize their strengths, and navigate pathways to meaningful careers. Career Technical Education (CTE) plays a vital role in this process by connecting academic learning with hands-on experiences, career exploration, and real-world skills that prepare learners for success. Advance CTE is honored to support this recognition of National Career Development Month and celebrates the role of career advisors, guidance counselors, educators, employers, and community partners in providing information to learners navigating a connected path from education to a career,” said Kate Kreamer, Executive Director, Advance CTE.

This resolution is also endorsed by the Association for Career and Technical Education (ACTE).

Read the resolution here.

title: Rep. Gabe Vasquez Announces $2.1 Million in New Head Start Funding for New Mexico’s Kids
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – On November 17, 2026, U.S. Representative Gabe Vasquez (NM-02) announced that the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) had awarded over $2.1 million Head Start funding to New Mexico State University (NMSU), the Ramah Navajo School Board, and the Alamo Navajo School Board. I’m proud to see these dollars granted to NMSU, Ramah Navajo, and Alamo Navajo to invest in the early education and health and wellbeing of New Mexico’s next generation of leaders.”

title: House Passes Walberg's Bill to Protect Health of Great Lakes Fisheries
text:
Today, the House unanimously passed H.R. 8195, the Responsible Cormorant Management and Control Act. Introduced by Congressman Tim Walberg (MI-05), the bill would ensure effective, science-based management of double-crested cormorant populations across the United States. The bill directs the Secretary of the Interior to develop regional management frameworks to guide the responsible take of double‑crested cormorants, working in coordination with the nation’s four Regional Flyway Councils.

Double‑crested cormorants have long posed challenges for fisheries and wildlife populations when their numbers become overabundant. In the Great Lakes, cormorant populations have wreaked havoc on fish stocks, inflicting millions of dollars in damage to the Great Lakes fisheries and threatening $5.1 billion in economic impact for recreational fishing.

The Responsible Cormorant Management and Control Act would establish a comprehensive, collaborative framework to ensure that population management is effective and sustainable, better protecting fisheries and other wildlife habitats.

"Our Great Lakes fisheries are among Michigan’s most valuable natural resources, supporting jobs, recreation, and communities across our state," said Rep. Walberg. "In recent years, our fisheries have faced a myriad of challenges, including the overabundance of cormorant populations that threaten healthy fish stocks. I'm proud to see the House pass my legislation to help protect our fisheries and ensure future generations of Michiganders can enjoy all they have to offer."

"Unchecked cormorant populations can devastate fisheries, harm aquaculture operations and threaten the communities that depend on them," said House Committee on Natural Resources Chairman Bruce Westerman. "H.R. 8195 establishes a regionally driven process for managing double-crested cormorants based on local conditions and sound science. I commend Rep. Walberg for giving states, tribes and other regional partners a stronger voice in sustaining fisheries and supporting responsible wildlife management."

"House passage of the Responsible Cormorant Management and Control Act is an important step toward helping fishery and wildlife managers address the localized impacts of double-crested cormorants," said Taylor Schmitz, Senior Vice President and Chief Operating Officer of the Congressional Sportsmen’s Foundation. "By directing the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to work with the Regional Flyway Councils on regional management frameworks, this bill offers a practical, science-based path to better support states and the communities that depend on healthy fisheries. CSF thanks Congressional Sportsmen’s Caucus Member Rep. Walberg for his leadership and urges the Senate to advance this important legislation."

"ASA welcomes the House’s passage of the Responsible Cormorant Management and Control Act," said Connor Bevan, Inland Fisheries Policy Director at the American Sportfishing Association (ASA). "By providing states and tribes with the tools they need to address impacts on fisheries, this bill supports responsible, science-based management while maintaining sustainable cormorant populations. The sportfishing industry thanks Representative Walberg for his leadership on this issue and encourages the Senate to take up and swiftly pass this important legislation."

You may view a video of Congressman Walberg speaking in support of his legislation on the House floor here.

title: Walkinshaw, Warner Bill Would Staff Federal IT Contracting to Match Real Workloads
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Congressman James R. Walkinshaw (VA-11) and U.S. Senator Mark R. Warner (D-VA) today introduced the IT Acquisition Readiness Act. The bill would require the largest federal agencies to find gaps in their IT contracting workforce and fix them with hiring, training, and retention plans built on real workload data.

A 2025 Government Accountability Office (GAO) report found that the Social Security Administration (SSA) lacked reliable workload data to determine its IT contracting staff needs, and did not have a training plan that would adequately close known skills gaps within that workforce. The same problem plagues other federal agencies, especially as the federal workforce has lost experienced federal IT acquisition staff in the aftermath of massive cuts to the federal workforce.

“Buying laptops and replacing a legacy system an agency relies on every day can each count as one contract, but they can require very different amounts of time and expertise,” said Congressman Walkinshaw. “Our bill requires agencies to account for the volume and complexity of that work when planning how to hire, train, and retain staff.”

“Federal employees are responsible for managing increasingly complex IT contracts, but too often agencies lack the data and planning needed to ensure that they are appropriately investing in and supporting this professional acquisition workforce,” said Senator Warner. “When agencies don’t adequately plan for their workforce needs, critical projects get delayed, costs go up, and taxpayers pay the price. This legislation would require agencies to identify IT contracting skills and staffing gaps and develop plans to recruit, train, and retain workers, all while delivering better results for the people they serve.”

“A modern federal government requires a skilled acquisition workforce equipped to manage increasingly complex technology procurements. The IT Acquisition Readiness Act takes an important step toward that goal by identifying workforce gaps, strengthening recruitment and training, and leveraging technology to reduce administrative burdens on contracting professionals. The Center for Procurement Advocacy applauds Representative Walkinshaw and Senator Warner for their leadership in ensuring federal agencies have the acquisition expertise and resources necessary to deliver better outcomes for taxpayers,” said Tim Brennan, president of the Center for Procurement Advocacy (CPA).

“A skilled, well-staffed acquisition workforce is the foundation of smart IT buying. The IT Acquisition Readiness Act gives agencies a clear picture of the contracting workforce they have and the one they need to deliver modern capabilities to the mission. PSC is proud to support Rep. Walkinshaw’s and Sen. Warner’s commitment to a stronger, better-equipped federal workforce,” said Jim Carroll, PSC CEO.

The IT Acquisition Readiness Act would:

Require agencies to assess staffing and skills gaps among federal IT acquisition professionals

Require agencies to build recruitment, training, and retention plans from those assessments and from data on the quantity and complexity of employees’ workloads

Require plans to include strategies that incorporate the use of modern tools to help reduce administrative burden

Require OPM and OMB, respectively, to support related workforce development activities and implementation of the bill’s requirements across federal agencies

Require OMB to submit to congress a report on agency plans and the progress of their implementation

title: Walkinshaw Presses OMB: Where Is the Data on $100 Billion in Federal Tech Spending?
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, Congressman James R. Walkinshaw (VA-11), a Member of the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, pressed Office of Management and Budget (OMB) Director Russell Vought to explain how OMB will maintain transparency around Federal IT investment reporting.

In April, OMB announced it would sunset the Federal IT Dashboard, the government’s central public record of federal IT investments since 2009. OMB posted a public announcement promising a “streamlined” approach and further updates. To date, none have materialized.

“More than six months later, OMB’s announcement remains active and unchanged on the IT Dashboard website,” Walkinshaw wrote to Vought. He warned that OMB has offered “limited information about how it plans to streamline reporting, when streamlining efforts would be completed, and whether any centralized reporting mechanism would be launched in place of the dashboard.”

“When federal technology fails, veterans wait longer for their benefits, families wait longer for their tax refunds, and seniors wait on hold with Social Security,” said Congressman Walkinshaw. “Taxpayers deserve to know whether their money is building systems that work or paying for expensive failures. More than six months ago, OMB announced plans to shut down the public’s window into that spending and promised answers. It has delivered silence. I’m open to a better way to report this data, but the law requires transparency, and OMB owes Congress and the American people a plan.”

The Government Accountability Office has kept federal IT management on its High-Risk List since 2015 because federal IT investments “too frequently fail to deliver capabilities in a timely, cost-effective manner,” Walkinshaw wrote. “Given that the federal government spends more than $100 billion on IT each year, clear and accessible reporting on these investments is essential to protecting taxpayer dollars and improving the services Americans rely on.”

The Dashboard also supplied key data for the FITARA Scorecard, a bipartisan oversight tool credited with saving taxpayers more than $35 billion.

“I believe Congress should revisit the Scorecard in the next Congress,” Walkinshaw wrote, “but doing so will require continued access to the information the Dashboard has historically provided.”

Walkinshaw’s request asks OMB to:

Describe its full plan to streamline reporting, with a timeline for finishing it

Answer whether a replacement for the Dashboard is coming and, if not, where exactly the public will be able to access reported information

Explain why it decided the Dashboard cost too much and what “inefficient process” it set out to eliminate

Identify which data it will keep publishing, which it will drop, and how it will preserve historical records

Report how many major IT investments agency officials rated high-risk for four straight quarters, and how many received the review federal law requires

Walkinshaw asked OMB to respond by December 13, 2026.
