title: WESTERMAN BILL TO TRANSFER CROSSETT EXPERIMENTAL FOREST TO THE STATE PASSES OUT OF THE HOUSE
text:
Today, the House of Representatives passed the Crossett Experimental Forest Act of 2026 that was introduced by Congressman Bruce Westerman (AR-04). This legislation allows the Crossett Experimental Forest, located in Ashley County, Arkansas, to continue providing opportunities for research through a transfer of ownership from the federal government to the state government. Congressman Westerman released the following statement:

“It’s impossible to discuss Arkansas forestry without recognizing the Crossett Experimental Forest. As the first field station in the Southern Forest Experiment Station, the research conducted here, combined with the leadership of Dr. Don C. Bragg and Dr. James M. Guldin, most notably contributed to the development of uneven-aged southern pine management. Its international reputation for exceptional forestry research highlights the profound global impact these studies have had for nearly a century on forest management practices,” said Congressman Westerman.

“As a forester, I understand first-hand the importance of regional, real-world data. What’s more, Arkansas’s forestry industry is a major driver of our state’s economy, and its success and longevity rely on modern, science-based practices for managing and conserving one of our most valuable natural resources. This proposed transfer of forest land from the federal government to the state government secures this great legacy, offers continued recreation use as a state wildlife management area, and keeps active, hands-on research alive for future foresters to learn from and enjoy. I am pleased to see this legislation pass out of the House and call on the Senate to pass this bill expeditiously to get it onto the President's desk to be signed into law.”

Background:

The Crossett Experimental Forest, (CEF) is an experimental forest totaling 1,680 acres in Ashley County, Arkansas, and was acquired via donation by the U.S. Forest Service in 1934. CEF has subsequently operated as a research forest as part of the broader Southern Research Station.

For the past two decades, research at CEF took place under the direction of Dr. Don Bragg. Tragically, Dr. Bragg passed away in December 2023. Since Dr. Bragg’s passing, there has been virtually no research conducted at CEF.

The state is prepared to dedicate resources across CEF and work with University of Arkansas at Monticello to ensure this remains a premier location for forestry and silviculture research. Arkansas has the expertise, the partnership and the willingness to invest in its future.

title: Armstrong Urges Senate to Pass Bipartisan Permitting Reform to Lower Energy Costs and Get America Building Again
text:
Armstrong Urges Senate to Pass Bipartisan Permitting Reform to Lower Energy Costs and Get America Building Again

SENATOR HIGHLIGHTS HISTORIC COALITION BEHIND LEGISLATION TO UNLOCK INFRASTRUCTURE INVESTMENT, PROTECT CONSUMERS, AND STRENGTHEN AMERICAN COMPETITIVENESS

WASHINGTON, D.C. — U.S. Senator Alan Armstrong (R-OK) took to the Senate floor today to urge passage of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), highlighting the legislation’s potential to lower energy costs, unlock private investment, and modernize America’s infrastructure without new taxpayer subsidies or weakening environmental protections.

Drawing on his decades of experience building energy infrastructure in the private sector, Armstrong emphasized that America’s rising utility costs are driven in part by the nation’s inability to build the infrastructure needed to connect abundant domestic energy resources to growing consumer demand.

“Everyone in Washington talks endlessly about affordability. Permitting reform is one of the very few practical solutions that delivers real cost relief to consumers and unlock investment without requiring a major new federal spending program,” Armstrong said.

Armstrong praised the bipartisan work of Senators Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV), Mike Lee (R-UT), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), and Martin Heinrich (D-NM), whose leadership helped bring together years of legislative work into a comprehensive permitting reform agreement.

The Senator emphasized three central benefits of the legislation:

Lower energy costs for American families. Streamlining infrastructure development would help connect affordable, reliable energy to consumers while requiring new data centers to bear the costs of grid upgrades associated with their facilities, protecting existing utility customers from those expenses.

More investment without new taxpayer subsidies. The legislation would reduce regulatory delays and litigation uncertainty, encouraging private capital investment in energy, manufacturing, mining, and other critical infrastructure while maintaining existing environmental protections.

A stronger, more competitive America. Modernizing the nation’s permitting system would help keep investment in artificial intelligence, critical minerals, energy production, and advanced manufacturing in the United States rather than driving those opportunities overseas.

Armstrong underscored the extraordinary breadth of the coalition supporting the legislation, bringing together traditional and renewable energy industries, labor unions, manufacturers, infrastructure developers, and other stakeholders that have historically disagreed over federal energy policy.

“We have accomplished something truly unprecedented: we’ve gotten the renewables industry, the fossil fuel industry, hydropower, and mining to all stick together and support this legislation,” Armstrong said.

“This broad alignment has held together because this bill does not pick winners and losers, it does not grant subsidies, and it does not compromise our environmental protections,” he continued.

The Senator also warned that failing to enact meaningful permitting reform would threaten American leadership in emerging technologies and push major investment opportunities to foreign competitors.

“If we fail to get this bill passed, the immediate reality is that we are going to start shipping our most critical economic opportunities overseas,” Armstrong said.

Closing his remarks, Armstrong called on his Senate colleagues to seize a rare opportunity to deliver lasting reform.

“After ten years of endless debate, we finally have industry, labor, and a broad bipartisan coalition aligned; if we don’t seize this moment now, I frankly don’t know when anyone will ever have the momentum or appetite to fix permitting in this country again.”

title: Baldwin Demands Answers from Trump Admin on Root Cause of Nov. 13th Nationwide Ground Stop
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Senator Tammy Baldwin (D-WI) and her colleagues are demanding answers from Department of Transportation (DOT) Secretary Sean Duffy and Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) Administrator Brian Bedford about the cause of the November 13 nationwide ground stop that disrupted air travel across the country. The hours-long and abrupt nationwide ground stop disrupted more than 10,000 scheduled flights and affected an estimated 1.5 million passengers.

“The Department of Transportation (DOT) and FAA must explain how this failure occurred and identify the corrective actions and oversight needed to prevent a recurrence,” Baldwin and the Senators wrote. “Identifying the device that failed does not establish why it failed. FAA must investigate further to determine the root cause and report to Congress on how it intends to prevent future issues.”

The DOT and FAA leaders have blamed a router malfunction in Arkansas and FAA contractor L3 Harris’ work converting the FAA’s communications network from copper to fiber for the disruption. According to information provided by L3 Harris, the Senators learned that the copper-to-fiber transition involves converting more than 3,600 routers to Juniper devices. To date, according to the contractor, 400 devices have been installed and 69 are operational. While a small sample of the Juniper routers were tested before installation, the Senators expressed concerns about continued deployment of the new routers until the root cause of the failure has been identified.

“We request an immediate pause on the deployment of additional Juniper devices,” the Senators continued. “Deployment should resume after the FAA demonstrates the devices’ readiness for safe deployment through improved operational testing, independent validation, verified failover capability, and rollback procedures. Congress expects a briefing on these improvements before the FAA resumes deployment of the routers.”

The letter comes as Duffy and Bedford are demanding $50 billion in funding for air traffic control modernization, up from a request for $30 billion just last week and after prior outages earlier this year in Philadelphia Terminal Radar Approach Control and Minneapolis Air Route Traffic Control Center.

“DOT, FAA and OMB must provide Congress with a complete account of what happened and how additional funding would address the vulnerabilities presented on November 13,” the Senators wrote. “Congress deserves clear answers on how the FAA is ensuring the safety of the aviation system for the traveling public while these new systems are being deployed.”

“Modernization cannot come at the expense of operational safety,” they concluded.

The letter was led by Senator Maria Cantwell and co-signed by 11 other Senate colleagues.

The text of the letter can be found below and here.

Dear Secretary Duffy and Administrator Bedford,

The November 13 nationwide ground stop disrupted air travel across the country, eroded public trust in our aviation system, and raised serious questions about the Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA) ability to ensure reliable and resilient operations. Congress expects clear, fact-based answers about the root cause of this disruption and why existing safeguards failed to prevent it. The Department of Transportation (DOT) and FAA must explain how this failure occurred and identify the corrective actions and oversight needed to prevent a recurrence.

Based on information provided to our offices from L3 Harris, the copper-to-fiber transition involves converting 3,648 routers to Juniper devices. To date, it is our understanding that 400 devices have been installed, and 69 are operational. With thousands of conversions remaining, FAA must address outstanding safety and reliability concerns before expanding installation.

Identifying the device that failed does not establish why it failed. FAA must investigate further to determine the root cause and report to Congress on how it intends to prevent future issues.

We understand the FAA Technical Center tested a sample of Juniper devices before installation. The devices passed pre-deployment testing. The November 13 failure raises serious questions about whether that testing adequately reflected operating conditions or evaluated all potential failure modes or outcomes.

We request an immediate pause on the deployment of additional Juniper devices. Deployment should resume after the FAA demonstrates the devices’ readiness for safe deployment through improved operational testing, independent validation, verified failover capability, and rollback procedures. Congress expects a briefing on these improvements before the FAA resumes deployment of the routers.

The ground stop demonstrated a breakdown in a system Americans rely on, and Congress was left to piece together critical facts. We expect accurate information as soon as it is available. Concerningly, the DOT attributed the November 13 network disruption to “old switches [and] old routers,” when in fact the deployment of the new Juniper routers seem to be the problem. This discrepancy between the FAA’s contractor and the DOT further fuels our concern that the root cause of the disruption has not yet been identified, leaving the potential for another failure.

The DOT and FAA have assigned blame to L3 Harris and used this moment to call for $50 billion in funding for Brand New Air Traffic Control System (BNATCS). This is notably $20 billion more than the request from DOT and the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) that was sent on Thursday, November 12. DOT, FAA and OMB must provide Congress with a complete account of what happened and how additional funding would address the vulnerabilities presented on November 13. DOT and FAA must also take full responsibility for managing contractors working to modernize the NAS.

Congress deserves clear answers on how the FAA is ensuring the safety of the aviation system for the traveling public while these new systems are being deployed.

Further, we request a joint technical briefing with FAA, L3Harris, and Juniper, and the following information no later than November 23, 2026:

An initial safety assessment of operational Juniper devices in the NAS, identifying shared infrastructure dependencies and common points of failures, vulnerabilities in primary and backup telecommunications paths, and the adequacy of failover, rollback, and recovery procedures.

An explanation of why the FAA’s operational systems lacked sufficient redundancy to recover immediately from the November 13 outage

An explanation of how a cut fiber-optic line or other localized telecommunications failure could result in widespread operational disruption, including actions taken to reinforce network redundancy following the Philadelphia Terminal Radar Approach Control and Minneapolis Air Route Traffic Control Center outages.

Given recent events, Congress is concerned about the FAA’s oversight of the BNATCS program. Modernization cannot come at the expense of operational safety. We expect a prompt response and look forward to working with the FAA to ensure the safety, reliability, and resilience of the NAS.

We are grateful for the air traffic controllers, pilots, flight attendants, and all aviation workers who continue to be impacted by Friday’s events.

Sincerely,

###

title: Baldwin Introduces Bill to End China’s Special Trade Treatment, Put American Workers First
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, U.S. Senator Tammy Baldwin (D-WI) introduced the Ending China’s Special Treatment Act to revoke China’s Permanent Normal Trade Relations (PNTR) status, stopping the favorable tariff treatment that we give to our trusted and close trading partners. The legislation would establish a more durable U.S. trade policy that puts American workers and manufacturers first. Since being given PNTR status, China has failed to uphold the principles of fair trade, engaged in market manipulation and intellectual property theft, sought global dominance in critical industries like shipbuilding, and undermined American workers and manufacturers. The legislation comes just days before President Trump is slated to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.

“We need a trade system that puts American workers, companies, and families first. Unfortunately, for over two decades, we've rolled out the red carpet for China while they've cheated the system and left American workers paying the price,” said Senator Baldwin. “And the President’s chaotic, on-again, off-again trade policy has only raised costs for companies and consumers and not done anything to level the playing field or bring jobs back to the U.S. To start, we need to reset our trade relationship with China, be honest that they have undercut us at every turn, and put the focus back where it matters – prioritizing American workers, manufacturers, and families.”

In 2000, Senator Baldwin voted against granting China PNTR, and more than two decades later, her fears of China’s continued unfair trade practices have come to fruition. Since then, American workers and manufacturers have paid the price for unfair trade with China. According to the Economic Policy Institute, the growing trade deficit with China cost an estimated 3.7 million American jobs, including 88,900 in Wisconsin, from 2001 to 2018.

In November 2024, for the first time, the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission unanimously recommended revoking PNTR, arguing the policy failed to produce the anticipated changes in China’s economic and political behavior.

In the wake of President Trump’s chaotic trade agenda and the Supreme Court’s decision to strike down certain presidential tariffs, the Ending China’s Special Treatment Act would establish a statutory framework for China’s tariff treatment rather than relying on executive actions that change at the President’s whim or face legal challenges. Specifically, Baldwin’s bill would revoke China’s PNTR status one year after enactment, shifting imports from China to the tariff rates established under Column 2 of the Harmonized Tariff Schedule (HTS). The HTS sets the tariff rates and import categories for all goods coming into the U.S. Column 2 rates are higher than Column 1 rates currently applicable to China, although rates vary by product.

The bill would also direct the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR), in consultation with the U.S. International Trade Commission, the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission, and the U.S. Department of Commerce, to issue a report to inform future policy decisions addressing ongoing trade and economic challenges posed by China.

Baldwin has long fought to hold China accountable for unfair trade practices and protect American manufacturing. Last year, Baldwin led her colleagues in laying out a worker-first American trade policy to prioritize American workers, re-establish the United States as a world leader in manufacturing, and strengthen national security. In 2018, she introduced the Fair Trade with China Enforcement Act with Senator Rubio, which would have made it harder for China to devalue its currency, banned the sale of sensitive national security technology and intellectual property to China, prevented Chinese firms from taking over American companies in sensitive advanced manufacturing industries, and imposed tariffs on goods targeted by Made in China 2025. She also led congressional support for the Section 301 investigation into China's unfair trade practices in the maritime, logistics, and shipbuilding sectors.

title: Sen. Banks Backs Hung Cao’s Confirmation, Highlights Crane’s Growing Role in Navy’s Mission

You have shown more interest in Crane Navy base than any other Secretary of the Navy before you, and I greatly appreciate that, not just because I represent it, but because of the important role it plays in our nation’s defense.”

Banks thanked Secretary Cao for helping establish a program management office at Crane, noting that Crane is the country’s third largest naval base, led by one-star Rear Admiral Patrick Finney, who arrived in October. Cao said the office will help accelerate the Navy’s sea-launched cruise missile nuclear program and hypersonics work, adding that there is “no better place” than Crane to advance those capabilities. The Navy plans to add at least 150 government civilian positions to the office by the end of the fiscal year 2029. All told, historic investments are transforming the landscape of Crane’s broader neighborhood. Construction throughout the Crane ecosystem will create more than 5000 jobs and add up to $15 billion in potential economic impact.

Banks concluded by stating he looks forward to working with Cao to grow Crane’s role in the defense of our nation.

title: Senator Banks and Members of Indiana Delegation Request National Estuarine Research Reserve Bordering Lake Michigan
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, Senator Jim Banks (R-Ind.) and members of the Indiana Congressional delegation, including Rep. Frank J. Mrvan (D-Ind.), Rep. Jim Baird (R-Ind.), and Senator Todd Young (R-Ind.), sent a letter to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) in support of the State of Indiana’s request to establish a National Estuarine Research Reserve (NERR) in Northwest Indiana.

Senator Jim Banks (R-Ind.): “Lake Michigan is one of Indiana’s greatest natural resources and is an important part of Northwest Indiana’s economy. Establishing a National Estuarine Research Reserve would strengthen conservation efforts, expand research opportunities, and help protect our shoreline for generations. I am proud to support this effort and urge the NOAA to move Indiana’s request forward.”

The text of the letter is below and a pdf is available here.

Dear Dr. Jacobs,

We write in support of the State of Indiana’s request to establish a National Estuarine Research Reserve (NERR) in Northwest Indiana, along the coastal region bordering Lake Michigan. In November 2024, then-Governor Eric Holcomb submitted a formal request for a designation, and, in July 2026, Governor Mike Braun sent a letter reaffirming interest in this initiative. As members of the Indiana Congressional delegation, we urge NOAA to advance the State’s request through the appropriate designation process and provide an update on its status.

Northwest Indiana’s Lake Michigan coastal region is a key environmental resource that provides unique economic, recreational, and educational opportunities in our state. We are committed to preserving and strengthening this region and believe that a NERR designation would support its long-term vitality, restoration, and resilience.

Since 2001, Indiana has partnered with NOAA in coastal management through the Indiana Lake Michigan Coastal Program, which has supported public access improvements, educational opportunities, habitat preservation and restoration, and technical assistance for local coastal communities. Establishing a NERR in Northwest Indiana would build upon these efforts and provide meaningful benefits to the state and the broader Great Lakes bioregion.

Currently, Indiana does not have a NERR, and only two reserves are designated in the Great Lakes region, neither of which is located along the southern shore of Lake Michigan. This region includes unique freshwater estuarine habitats that warrant sustained research, monitoring, and education. Establishing a NERR in Northwest Indiana would provide distinct value to the overall Reserve system by addressing research gaps, advancing scientific understanding of the region’s unique ecological processes, and enhancing management and restoration efforts for similar systems across the Great Lakes.

Additionally, Purdue University’s College of Agriculture is strongly positioned to serve as the lead organization for this initiative. As a nationally recognized land grant institution, Purdue has a proven record of partnering with state and federal agencies, including the Indiana Department of Natural Resources, to advance research, education, and outreach efforts. Purdue is also home to several NOAA-funded programs, such as the Illinois-Indiana Sea Grant College Program and the Midwestern Regional Climate Center. This demonstrated expertise in coastal management prepares the university to support the long-term success of a NERR in Indiana.

The Lake Michigan coastal region is essential to Indiana’s identity, economy, and environment. By expanding opportunities for research, education, and community engagement, establishing a NERR in Northwest Indiana would safeguard this vital environmental resource for generations to come. We appreciate NOAA’s consideration of this request and look forward to continuing to work together to strengthen the Great Lakes region.

###

title: Barrasso: Senate Republicans Will Leave No Judicial Vacancy Behind
text:
“The top priority of Senate Republicans is to elevate conservative judges to the federal courts. Today, the United States Senate will confirm another in a string of federal judges during President Trump’s second term.”

WASHINGTON, D.C. – Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso (R-Wyo.) today highlighted the commitment of Senate Republicans to confirm conservative judges to the federal courts.

Senator Barrasso praised Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley and Committee Republicans for moving judicial nominees at a record pace despite Democrat obstruction.

Click HERE to watch Senator Barrasso’s remarks.

Sen. Barrasso’s remarks as prepared:

“The top priority of Senate Republicans is to elevate conservative judges to the federal courts. Today, the United States Senate will confirm another in a string of federal judges during President Trump’s second term. We confirmed one yesterday. We confirm another today. This is a lifetime appointment. These are judges who honor the Constitution. Judges who apply the law as written. Judges who protect our God-given rights.

“Republicans are not stopping here. We will confirm four more judges this week. They are ready for a vote on the Floor of the United States Senate. Chairman Grassley and the Judiciary Committee will approve more judges in Committee this morning. They will soon be sent to the Floor of the United States Senate. By the end of this year, Republicans will have installed dozens of additional judges. Senate Republicans will leave no vacancy behind.

“I want to commend Chairman Grassley and the Senate Judiciary Committee. We are here because of their diligent work. The Senate Judiciary Committee is indispensable for vetting and advancing conservative judges. Chairman Grassley is pursuing a bold confirmation schedule. Already, we have confirmed judges faster than any time in decades. When judges reach the Senate Floor, we are proceeding with strength, unity, and energy.

“The importance of confirming federal judges is clear. Remember, federal judges serve for life. They hear cases. They apply the law. They will shape our courts and our country for generations to come. That is a solemn responsibility. The men and women we are confirming have earned our trust.

“As Chairman Grassley noted last week, these are judges who have taken different paths to the federal courts. Some defend our nation in the military. Others represented clients in private practice. Others argued cases in state and federal court. All are experienced, highly qualified, and firmly committed to upholding the Constitution and the rule of law. We will confirm them.

“Democrats have tried to torpedo qualified nominees like these. For the past two years, they have waged a campaign of obstruction. Why? It’s because of politics. Pure and simple. The priority of Democrats is to stonewall President Trump. Ultimately, their goal is to load the federal courts with left-wing activists. Activists who will rewrite the law – not follow it.

“Think about this. For the first 227 years under our Constitution, from 1789 to 2016, the Senate confirmed 94 percent of judicial nominees by unanimous consent. In this Congress, not a single judge has cleared this body by unanimous consent. Democrats have bogged down them all. When the Senate has voted on these judges, nearly every single Democrat has voted in lock-step against every single one.

“All of this is the fruit of the politics of the radical left. Democrats want to paralyze President Trump and derail anyone who challenges their liberal ideology.

“In the days and weeks ahead, Republicans will continue to burst through the Democrat blockade. This Republican Senate has already confirmed judges at the fastest pace in decades. Today, more judges who are serving on the federal courts were nominated by President Trump compared to any other recent president. Senate Republicans refuse to allow Democrats to set back or scuttle the confirmation of qualified judges.

“The Senate has much to do in the next 47 days. There will be more work and more votes. The Senate will keep working. We will keep voting. We will keep confirming conservative judges. Republicans will leave no vacancy behind.”

title: Bennet Highlights Importance of Farm Bill Passage, Agriculture Priorities on Senate Floor
text:
Video of Bennet’s Full Remarks Available HERE

Washington, D.C. — Tonight, Colorado U.S. Senator Michael Bennet, a senior member of the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry, spoke on the Senate floor to highlight the importance of passing a Farm Bill and the future of American agriculture and rural policy.

During his speech, Bennet stated his hope for passage of a bipartisan Farm Bill this year while emphasizing the need for a clean two-year delay of Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) state cost shifts, opposition to the Environmental Quality Incentives Program and the Conservation Stewardship Program cuts, and ad-hoc economic assistance for farmers.

“There is no reason we should not pass a bipartisan farm bill this year. If we can address these concerns, we can provide farmers and ranchers with much-needed certainty now and lay a foundation to build on for the future, rather than hold out for an agreement that may be no easier to reach next year,” said Bennet.

Looking beyond this year’s Farm Bill, Bennet outlined a broader vision for the future of American agriculture that improves farmers’ and ranchers’ ability to make a living, lowers the costs of production, expands markets and competition, strengthens the farm safety net and conservation programs, protects nutrition programs, and invests in the schools, hospitals, infrastructure, and services that rural communities need to thrive. Tonight, he said:

“When we return to Congress next year, we should think about the future that farmers and ranchers and rural communities want to build. A prosperous future, as they once had, not just for them, but for our entire country.

“A future where our agricultural producers have a fair shot at making a living from what they produce, where we bring down the costs of farming, increase competition, expand markets, and make sure producers have the workers that they need.

“A future where our farm policy is stronger, more reliable, and better suited to the challenges producers face today. Where our farmers and ranchers can count on a strong safety net instead of another emergency bailout, and where our programs work for different regions, communities, and farm sizes.

“A future where every American family can afford nutritious food, and our farmers and ranchers have more opportunity to feed their communities. Where we protect SNAP and strengthen child nutrition and build stronger connections between the people who grow our food and the families who depend on it.

“And a patriotic future where rural communities are places the next generation can build a satisfying and fulfilled life. That’s all anybody wants in this country. Where we reinvest in rural schools and roads and utility infrastructure that have gone for decades without repair, and build new hospitals, primary care facilities, and child care centers so that Americans in rural areas can actually access the care and services that they need and that they deserve.

“That is the future.”

###

title: Blackburn Bill to Support Organizations Assisting Law Enforcement in Investigation of Child Exploitation Heads to President Trump’s Desk
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Senators Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.) and Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) released the following statements after their Safe Cloud Storage Act unanimously passed the Senate. This legislation would provide limited liability protections to law enforcement-approved vendors to securely store and transfer child sexual abuse material (CSAM) to assist in investigations of child sexual exploitation.

“Those helping law enforcement in the fight against child sexual exploitation must be able to securely store evidence of these horrific crimes,” said Senator Blackburn. “Our bipartisan Safe Cloud Storage Act would ensure investigators can securely handle and store CSAM evidence in the cloud by providing limited liability protections, and I’m pleased it is heading to President Trump’s desk.”

“We must do everything we can to protect our children from online exploitation and abuse,” said Senator Klobuchar. “This commonsense, bipartisan bill would improve investigations and prosecutions by allowing law enforcement to safely store, transmit, and evaluate evidence using cloud systems – saving time and resources. I encourage President Trump to swiftly sign it into law.”

This legislation is co-sponsored by Senators John Cornyn (R-Texas), Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), Katie Britt (R-Ala.), Chris Coons (D-Del.), Mike Lee (R-Utah), Ashley Moody (R-Fla.), Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.), and Ron Wyden (D-Ore.). Representative Laurel Lee (R-Fla.) led the House companion bill.

BACKGROUND

In 2024, Senator Blackburn’s REPORT Act was signed into law, which—among other things—provided limited liability protections for National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC)-contracted vendors to store and transfer CSAM for investigative purposes.

These civil and criminal liability protections were incredibly important for NCMEC as it reviews horrific evidence of child pornography during investigations of reports of exploitation received from online platforms.

Other third-party law enforcement vendors similarly need the ability to store and handle this investigative material without facing criminal or civil liability.

SAFE CLOUD STORAGE ACT

The Safe Cloud Storage Act would build upon Senator Blackburn’s REPORT Act by ensuring that law enforcement-approved vendors who assist in investigations of child exploitation are permitted to securely store this evidence that is critical to holding these criminals accountable.

Specifically, this bipartisan bill would permit law enforcement-approved vendors to provide secure, cloud-based storage of CSAM evidence without facing a civil claim or criminal charge—giving law enforcement the flexibility they need as they work to investigate and target these horrific criminals.

As with the REPORT Act, this legislation would require vendors to adhere to strict cybersecurity standards to ensure that this material is securely stored. Importantly, these law enforcement-approved vendors would not be shielded from civil or criminal claims under this bill’s limited liability protections if they engage in intentional misconduct, negligent conduct, or if they act with malice.

ENDORSEMENTS

This legislation is endorsed by Raven, National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC), Thorn, International Justice Mission, Fraternal Order of Police, Child Rescue Coalition, National District Attorneys Association, Association of State Criminal Investigative Agencies, and National Center on Sexual Exploitation.

“Congress’s passage of the Safe Cloud Storage Act marks a significant step toward modernizing how law enforcement investigates child sexual exploitation. By authorizing secure, cloud-based storage for CSAM evidence, the legislation will equip investigators with modern tools to move cases faster, identify victims sooner, and hold offenders accountable, while maintaining strong cybersecurity protections. Raven is proud to have worked alongside congressional offices, law enforcement, and business stakeholders to help bring this legislation across the finish line and to ensure it reflects the practical realities investigators face in the field. We are grateful for the bipartisan leadership that made this possible and look forward to seeing this important legislation signed into law,” said Jennifer Dunton, Executive Director of Raven.

RELATED

Blackburn, Klobuchar Bill to Support Organizations Assisting Law Enforcement in Investigation of Child Exploitation Passes Judiciary Committee

title: Blumenthal Presses RFK Jr. On Suppression Of Measles Safety Warning For Pregnant Women As U.S. Loses Elimination Status
text:
[WASHINGTON, D.C.] – U.S. Senator Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), Ranking Member of the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, today demanded answers from Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr about the censorship of critical public health information related to the risks pregnant women face from the ongoing measles outbreak. Pointing to recent reporting in The Washington Post, Blumenthal raised concerns that senior HHS officials blocked a Health Alert Network (HAN) warning from Centers for Disease Control & Prevention (CDC) scientists about disturbing outcomes for pregnant women and their newborn children can face as a result of exposure to measles.

Blumenthal underscored why the HAN notification CDC scientists sought to send was so critical to alerting American clinicians about measles risks during pregnancy, writing in a letter to Kennedy, “The Trump Administration’s repeated unwillingness to confront the dangers of infectious disease, and its hostility to vaccines, are squarely to blame for the Pan American Health Organization’s recent decision to revoke the United States’s measles elimination status. For a quarter-century, the United States regularly registered only small numbers of measles cases each year. That achievement, rooted in the phenomenal success of the MMR vaccine, took decades of sustained bipartisan effort to achieve, but less than two years of your tenure to squander. Indeed, the sudden return of measles is the very reason that the HAN notification the scientists proposed is so critical. Even experienced doctors may have gone their whole careers without having treated a single measles patient—precisely because of the success of past vaccination campaigns.”

Blumenthal noted that CDC scientists were repeatedly prevented by HHS from publishing this critical information: “After CDC scientists failed to obtain approval for the HAN, they sought to get the information out through the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report (MMWR), the agency’s in-house medical journal. But multiple other vaccine-related papers have been languishing in the MMWR’s approval process and the measles article appears to have been similarly hamstrung by political considerations, causing the agency scientists to seek to publish it elsewhere.”

Blumenthal continued, “On Monday, a version of the article appeared online in the New England Journal of Medicine, reporting a number of disturbing outcomes for pregnant women and their newborn children and stressing the importance of preparing healthcare systems, ‘particularly in communities with a high proportion of unvaccinated people.’ Among the 112 pregnant women with measles in the study, almost all of whom appear to have been unvaccinated, the rate of premature birth was four times higher than the background rate for the United States—information that your department somehow failed to recognize as urgent or significant.”

Blumenthal continued, “The declining rates of vaccination against measles that you encouraged as an anti-vaccine activist and now oversee as the nation’s top health official are harming pregnant women, and also creating an unprecedented risk of congenital measles in children… At least one of the six measles deaths that Pennsylvania has reported this year—a death you quickly took to social media to suggest ‘may even have been altogether fabricated’—was a newborn baby born to a mother fighting an active case of the measles.”

“If you do not permit career scientists at HHS agencies to aid clinicians and inform researchers, tragedies like these are unlikely to be the last of the preventable deaths attributable Trump Administration health policies,” Blumenthal concluded.

The full text of Blumenthal’s letter is available here and below.

Dear Secretary Kennedy:

I write regarding yet another troubling instance of the Department of Health and Human Services censoring critical public health information, this time related to the risks pregnant women face from the country’s current measles outbreak. According to public reporting, Centers for Disease Control & Prevention (CDC) scientists sought to warn doctors of rising measles rates and provide treatment guidance through the agency’s designated system for communicating urgent information with American clinicians, the Health Alert Network (HAN), but senior agency officials blocked the warning.[1] Such actions are simply inexcusable when the United States is in the midst of its worst measles outbreak in more than three decades, one that has already claimed ten American lives this year.[2]

The Trump Administration’s repeated unwillingness to confront the dangers of infectious disease, and its hostility to vaccines, are squarely to blame for the Pan American Health Organization’s recent decision to revoke the United States’s measles elimination status.[3] For a quarter-century, the United States regularly registered only small numbers of measles cases each year. That achievement, rooted in the phenomenal success of the MMR vaccine, took decades of sustained bipartisan effort to achieve, but less than two years of your tenure to squander. Indeed, the sudden return of measles is the very reason that the HAN notification the scientists proposed is so critical. Even experienced doctors may have gone their whole careers without having treated a single measles patient—precisely because of the success of past vaccination campaigns. Physicians may struggle to recognize, let alone treat, this highly infectious and potentially fatal disease.[4]

After CDC scientists failed to obtain approval for the HAN, they sought to get the information out through the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report (MMWR), the agency’s in-house medical journal.[5] But multiple other vaccine-related papers have been languishing in the MMWR’s approval process and the measles article appears to have been similarly hamstrung by political considerations, causing the agency scientists to seek to publish it elsewhere. On Monday, a version of the article appeared online in the New England Journal of Medicine, reporting a number of disturbing outcomes for pregnant women and their newborn children and stressing the importance of preparing healthcare systems, “particularly in communities with a high proportion of unvaccinated people.”[6] Among the 112 pregnant women with measles in the study, almost all of whom appear to have been unvaccinated, the rate of premature birth was four times higher than the background rate for the United States—information that your department somehow failed to recognize as urgent or significant.[7]

This attempt to suppress agency research supporting vaccination echoes other decisions your department has made regarding measles. In March of 2025—after measles had begun spreading in Texas, but before it ultimately killed two children in the state—HHS political officials held back a risk assessment from CDC’s Center for Forecasting and Outbreak Analytics, which warned of heightened risk of transmission in areas with low vaccination rates.[8] After news of the forecast leaked, HHS officials dismissed it as “not say[ing] anything the public does not already know,” even though it relied on new data about the outbreak.[9]

Since becoming Secretary, you have consistently sought to undermine vaccination, airing bluster and distortion on social media while attempting to keep HHS employees from adding to the ample record of vaccine safety and effectiveness. For example, last October, senior officials at the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) ordered agency scientists to withdraw studies and abstracts that demonstrated the safety of the COVID-19 and shingles vaccines.[10] And earlier this year, Dr. Jay Bhattacharya, then the acting CDC director, reportedly halted the publication of a different study in the MMWR, this one demonstrating the effectiveness of the COVID-19 vaccines in preventing hospitalization, even though it had already cleared the agency’s scientific review process.[11] In both of these cases, HHS defended its acts of scientific censorship by resorting to the same unsupportable critiques that it used to justify suppressing the measles forecast last year, and that is it is now using to hold back critical information about the risks pregnant women face from measles.”[12]

The declining rates of vaccination against measles that you encouraged as an anti-vaccine activist and now oversee as the nation’s top health official are harming pregnant women, and also creating an unprecedented risk of congenital measles in children. Prior to the development of the MMR vaccine, measles was widespread. Approximately 95 percent of women were believed to have had it by the time they reached childbearing age, and were therefore unlikely to contract measles while pregnant.[13] But because of the effectiveness of the MMR immunization campaign, the unvaccinated American women who are of childbearing age today are overwhelmingly likely to have never had measles by the time they become pregnant, and are highly susceptible to contracting the disease.[14] For doctors battling the current outbreak in Pennsylvania, where more than 1,500 people have been infected, congenital measles has gone from unheard of to common.[15] At least one of the six measles deaths that Pennsylvania has reported this year—a death you quickly took to social media to suggest “may even have been altogether fabricated”—was a newborn baby born to a mother fighting an active case of the measles.[16]

If you do not permit career scientists at HHS agencies to aid clinicians and inform researchers, tragedies like these are unlikely to be the last of the preventable deaths attributable Trump Administration health policies. In order to help the Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations better understand your department’s response to the ongoing measles outbreak, including its potential suppression of scientific communications, please provide the following information and records[17] by December 2, 2026:

All versions of HAN notifications that have been circulated by agency scientists for submission or approval since January 20, 2025 but which have not been published;

All internal and external communications referring or related to the HAN notifications described in request 1;

All documents reflecting policies currently in force related to HAN notifications, including requirements for review or clearance of studies by political appointees;

A list of all MMWR submissions that, since January 20, 2025, have cleared CDC’s scientific review process but have yet to be published and are not designated for publication within the next two weeks, including:

The names of the study’s authors;

The date the study cleared pre-publication review;

A description of the study’s subject matter;

The names of the official or officials who ordered the study held back;

All internal and external communications referring or related to the MMWR submissions described in request 4;

All documents reflecting policies currently in force related to publication in MMWR, including requirements for review or clearance of studies by political appointees.

All documents reflecting policies currently in force related to communication of scientific findings with the public, including the authority of political appointees to edit or modify work product of agency scientists.

I also request today that you make available for interviews the following CDC officials no later than January 22, 2027:

Althea Grant-Lenzy, Director, Office of Science, and CDC Chief Science Officer

Dr. Rebecca Greco Koné, Acting Director, National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases (NCIRD)

Dr. David Sugerman, Acting Chief, Viral Vaccine Preventable Diseases Branch, Division of Viral Diseases, NCIRD

Dr. Leonard Jack, Acting Editor-in-Chief, MMWR

Please contact my staff as soon as possible about scheduling these interviews, or if you have questions about any of the above requests. Thank you for your attention to this matter.

Sincerely,

-30-

[1] Lena Sun, CDC scientists sought urgent alert on measles in pregnancy. It wasn’t approved., Wash. Post (Oct. 30, 2026), https://www.washingtonpost.com/health/2026/10/30/cdc-has-report-measles-pregnancy-its-unclear-when-it-will-publish/.

[2] Sara Boden, 2 more people die of measles complications top 5,400, CIDRAP (Nov. 13, 2026), https://www.nbcnews.com/health/health-news/wisconsin-measles-death-us-third-week-rcna607701.

title: ICYMI: Senator Blunt Rochester Joins Commerce Committee Democrats Demanding Clear & Fact-Based Answers From DOT, FAA on Root Cause of Nov. 13th Nationwide Ground Stop
text:
Senator Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-Del.), a Member of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, joined fellow committee Democrats in sending a letter to Department of Transportation (DOT) Secretary Sean Duffy and Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) Administrator Brian Bedford demanding clear, fact-based answers about the root cause of last Friday’s nationwide ground stop. The DOT and FAA leaders have blamed a router malfunction in Arkansas and FAA contractor L3 Harris’ work converting the FAA’s communications network from copper to fiber for the disruption.

“The Department of Transportation (DOT) and FAA must explain how this failure occurred and identify the corrective actions and oversight needed to prevent a recurrence,” the Senators wrote. “Identifying the device that failed does not establish why it failed. FAA must investigate further to determine the root cause and report to Congress on how it intends to prevent future issues.”

According to information provided by L3 Harris, the Senators learned that the copper-to-fiber transition involves converting more than 3,600 routers to Juniper devices. To date, according to the contractor, 400 devices have been installed and 69 are operational. While a small sample of the Juniper routers were tested before installation, the Senators expressed concerns about continued deployment of the new routers until the root cause of the failure has been identified.

“We request an immediate pause on the deployment of additional Juniper devices,” the Senators continued. “Deployment should resume after the FAA demonstrates the devices’ readiness for safe deployment through improved operational testing, independent validation, verified failover capability, and rollback procedures. Congress expects a briefing on these improvements before the FAA resumes deployment of the routers.”

The letter comes as Duffy and Beford are demanding $50 billion in funding for air traffic control modernization, up from a request for $30 billion just last week and after prior outages earlier this year in Philadelphia Terminal Radar Approach Control and Minneapolis Air Route Traffic Control Center.

“DOT, FAA and OMB must provide Congress with a complete account of what happened and how additional funding would address the vulnerabilities presented on November 13,” the Senators wrote. “Congress deserves clear answers on how the FAA is ensuring the safety of the aviation system for the traveling public while these new systems are being deployed.”

“Modernization cannot come at the expense of operational safety,” they concluded.

Along with Senator Blunt Rochester, the letter was signed by Ranking Member Senator Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) and Senators Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.), Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.), Brian Schatz (D-Hawai’i), Ed Markey (D-Mass.), Gary Peters (D-Mich.), Tammy Baldwin (D-Wisc.), Jacky Rosen (D-Nev.), Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.), John Hickenlooper (D-Colo.), John Fetterman (D-Pa.), and Andy Kim (D-N.J.).

The text of the letter can be found below and HERE.

November 16, 2026

Dear Secretary Duffy and Administrator Bedford,

The November 13 nationwide ground stop disrupted air travel across the country, eroded public trust in our aviation system, and raised serious questions about the Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA) ability to ensure reliable and resilient operations. Congress expects clear, fact-based answers about the root cause of this disruption and why existing safeguards failed to prevent it. The Department of Transportation (DOT) and FAA must explain how this failure occurred and identify the corrective actions and oversight needed to prevent a recurrence.

Based on information provided to our offices from L3 Harris, the copper-to-fiber transition involves converting 3,648 routers to Juniper devices. To date, it is our understanding that 400 devices have been installed, and 69 are operational. With thousands of conversions remaining, FAA must address outstanding safety and reliability concerns before expanding installation.

Identifying the device that failed does not establish why it failed. FAA must investigate further to determine the root cause and report to Congress on how it intends to prevent future issues.

We understand the FAA Technical Center tested a sample of Juniper devices before installation. The devices passed pre-deployment testing. The November 13 failure raises serious questions about whether that testing adequately reflected operating conditions or evaluated all potential failure modes or outcomes.

We request an immediate pause on the deployment of additional Juniper devices. Deployment should resume after the FAA demonstrates the devices’ readiness for safe deployment through improved operational testing, independent validation, verified failover capability, and rollback procedures. Congress expects a briefing on these improvements before the FAA resumes deployment of the routers.

The ground stop demonstrated a breakdown in a system Americans rely on, and Congress was left to piece together critical facts. We expect accurate information as soon as it is available. Concerningly, the DOT attributed the November 13 network disruption to “old switches [and] old routers,” when in fact the deployment of the new Juniper routers seem to be the problem. This discrepancy between the FAA’s contractor and the DOT further fuels our concern that the root cause of the disruption has not yet been identified, leaving the potential for another failure.

The DOT and FAA have assigned blame to L3 Harris and used this moment to call for $50 billion in funding for Brand New Air Traffic Control System (BNATCS). This is notably $20 billion more than the request from DOT and the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) that was sent on Thursday, November 12. DOT, FAA and OMB must provide Congress with a complete account of what happened and how additional funding would address the vulnerabilities presented on November 13. DOT and FAA must also take full responsibility for managing contractors working to modernize the NAS.

Congress deserves clear answers on how the FAA is ensuring the safety of the aviation system for the traveling public while these new systems are being deployed.

Further, we request a joint technical briefing with FAA, L3Harris, and Juniper, and the following information no later than November 23, 2026:

An initial safety assessment of operational Juniper devices in the NAS, identifying shared infrastructure dependencies and common points of failures, vulnerabilities in primary and backup telecommunications paths, and the adequacy of failover, rollback, and recovery procedures.

An explanation of why the FAA’s operational systems lacked sufficient redundancy to recover immediately from the November 13 outage.

An explanation of how a cut fiber-optic line or other localized telecommunications failure could result in widespread operational disruption, including actions taken to reinforce network redundancy following the Philadelphia Terminal Radar Approach Control and Minneapolis Air Route Traffic Control Center outages.

Given recent events, Congress is concerned about the FAA’s oversight of the BNATCS program. Modernization cannot come at the expense of operational safety. We expect a prompt response and look forward to working with the FAA to ensure the safety, reliability, and resilience of the NAS.

We are grateful for the air traffic controllers, pilots, flight attendants, and all aviation workers who continue to be impacted by Friday’s events.

Sincerely,

title: STATEMENT: Senator Blunt Rochester Urges Continued Action to Strengthen Chip Export Controls
text:
Senator Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-Del.), a Member of the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, today released a statement in response to the Department of Commerce’s interim final rule restricting foreign actors from accessing U.S. advanced semiconductors:

“As we continue to invest in artificial intelligence and further centralize these technologies in our economy, we need to ensure these advancements are secured and intended to keep the U.S. and our allies in the lead. The federal government has a responsibility to ensure that private industries do not imperil the public’s economic and national security. Ongoing competition with adversaries like China and recent national security reports involving NVIDIA’s former CEO, Jensen Huang, have only underscored the importance of closing gaps to maintain the nation’s competitive edge.

“The Department of Commerce, acting only at the urging of the Department of the Treasury and the National Security Council, appears to be taking steps to address these challenges. It’s crucial that the Department enforce the new rules to restrict foreign actors’ access to advanced U.S. semiconductors.

“But while I welcome this action by the Department, I firmly believe we must go further. Significant gaps remain in addressing adversaries’ ability to remotely access AI chips. We need to impose stronger licensing requirements for the procurement of large quantities of U.S. chips, expand the geographic boundaries for controls on remote access, and ensure that China cannot access advanced chips in U.S. data centers. It’s clear that now is the time to invest in our standing on the global stage, and I urge the Department of Commerce to take steps to ensure we succeed.”

title: U.S. Senator Katie Britt Fighting to Bring Down Prescription Drug Costs
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — U.S. Senator Katie Britt (R-Ala.) today participated in a Senate Judiciary Committee oversight hearing on lowering prescription drug costs. The Senator questioned witnesses Merith Basey, CEO of Patients for Affordable Drugs Now; Alex Oshmyansky, MD, PhD, Co-founder and CEO of the Mark Cuban Cost Plus Drug Company; Matthew Pitlick, CEO of the Iowa Pharmacy Association; Neeraj Sood, PhD, Professor at the USC Schaeffer Institute for Public Policy and Government Service and USC Price School of Public Policy; and Karriem Watson, DHSc, MS, MPH, CEO of the UI Health Mile Square Health Center.

Senator Britt asked each witness to share what actions have actually brought down drug prices and what challenges still persist: “I want to start by just hearing from each of you. I know we’re clearly at an inflection point. We have to do something when it comes to the prescription drug pricing. I know we have done a number of things over the last couple of years from the Consolidated Appropriations Act in 2026, you mentioned new DOL rules, we know TrumpRx, Medicare Part D price negotiations … the FTC settlement, new (pharmacy benefit managers) PBM transparency. So, there are some things out there. My question is … in the last couple of years … which ones of these things have actually helped reduce prices? And then which one of these things maybe was well intended, but didn’t have the effect that we thought that it would?”

Dr. Watson cited the need for reimbursement rates that cover acquisition costs: “So, one of the things that we’ve got to get better at is ensuring that the reimbursement rates for your academic and community and those mom-and-pop pharmacies, particularly in rural areas, that they’re able to compete with other … big pharmacies. Because if we don’t do that, our patients will be left without access to the drugs that they need, and prescriptions will go unfulfilled, which is what we’ve seen.”

Professor Sood said out of pocket caps have shifted cost to premiums: “I would say the laws that have worked in terms of reducing patients’ costs are like the insulin co-pay cap or the $2,100 or $2,000 limit on out-of-pocket costs for our Medicare Part D. So, they help patients at the pharmacy counter, but, you know, there’s a trade off there that if you just control out-of-pocket costs, premiums go up. And we’ve had to spend $10 billion in Part D to stabilize those premiums.

“What I think hasn’t worked as well as I would like it to work is biosimilar competition. So, what biosimilar competition does is it does lower overall net prices. Branded companies compete with biosimilars by giving larger rebates to health plans. But again, patients are paying based on the list price of the drug. So even if there is a biosimilar, the health plan will cover the branded drug because they’re getting a bigger rebate and patients end up paying more because they’re paying based on the list price. So having cost sharing based on the actual price of the drug, minus the rebates, helps patients because you’re ensuring that that discount goes directly to the patient and not somewhere in the middle, not an intermediary. So, to me, that would be the biggest policy win, if we can have patient cost sharing be based on the net price of the drug, not the list price.”

Dr. Pitlick warned that some state-level reforms have backfired: “One thing that is maybe a double-edged sword, intended well, is many states have passed a reimbursement floor for pharmacies plus a dispensing fee. Without proper protections, that dispensing fee is often passed on to the patient. So, say a $10 dispensing fee to cover that pharmacy for overhead, staffing, etc., to dispense that prescription, say it’s $10, that $10 ends up getting passed to the patient to pay that instead of the health plan or PBM.”

Dr. Oshmyansky encouraged breaking up large health conglomerates from their pharmacies to better environment for smaller community pharmacies: “In fact, for generic drugs, Americans get the best prices in the world behind the scenes, anything else is an additional markup … You got to break up these conglomerates … It’s nonsense that your local community pharmacist cannot provide you a better standard of care than a giant mail-order specialty pharmacy in the middle of nowhere … So, the immediate win I think would be to break up pharmacies from the PBMs…”

Ms. Basey urged for the independent review of prices set by pharmaceutical companies: “We’ve supported the legislation that has already passed that has focused on PBMs and also support tackling vertical integration. I think you mentioned what will actually have a real impact on price, and I think if we really want to tackle price seriously, we need to look at the launch price of medications that is set by pharmaceutical corporations independently.”

Senator Britt recognized the importance of Congress’s role in lowering prescription drug prices, saying, “Well, there (is) no doubt we have to take a comprehensive approach to this, and we’ve got to do something. We’ve got to make sure that our rural and independent pharmacies not only survive, but thrive. And we need to make sure that the cost savings are passed to the actual consumer. We have to do something now.”

You can watch the Senator’s full remarks here.
