title: Durbin Shares 154th Dreamer Story on the Senate Floor
text:
Durbin: “To all of my Republican colleagues, please join me… in standing up for these people who epitomize the American Dream. We have an opportunity to finally give Dreamers the justice they deserve. We can do it. We have the time to do it. Let’s get to work.”

WASHINGTON – In a speech on the Senate floor, U.S. Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin (D-IL), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, shared his 154th Dreamer story. During his time in Congress, Durbin has continuously shared stories of Dreamers—young people who have lived in America since they were children, built their lives here, and are American in every way except for their immigration status. Under current law, there is no pathway to citizenship for Dreamers. Eighty-one percent of Americans support citizenship for Dreamers, including 56 percent of Republicans.

“It has been 25 years since I first came to the Senate Floor with a simple request—for Congress to protect the Dreamers. Dreamers are immigrants who were brought to the United States as children. They grew up pledging allegiance to the same flag that we do. But because of a decision on immigration that they had no control over, they are forced to live their lives in fear of deportation,” Durbin said. “I joined forces with Republican Senator Orrin Hatch of Utah, and together, we introduced the Dream Act.”

Durbin has introduced the Dream Act every Congress since 2001. The Dream Act is bipartisan legislation that would allow noncitizens without lawful status who were brought to the United States as children and meet certain education, military service, or work requirements to earn lawful permanent residence. This Congress, Durbin introduced the bill with U.S. Senator Lisa Murkowski (R-AK).

“Since then, I have come to the floor of the Senate over 150 times to share the stories of Dreamers who are doctors, nurses, business owners, educators, parents, and members of our military,” Durbin said. “I have pushed for this legislation to be included in bipartisan measures like the 2013 ‘Gang of Eight’ immigration bill, which passed the Senate with 68 votes… Over the years, the Senate has passed the Dream Act… and the House of Representatives has passed it too, but never at the same time, so that we could send the legislation to the President’s desk to be signed into law.”

In 2010, Durbin sent a letter, joined by the late U.S. Senator Richard Lugar (R-IN), asking then-President Obama to stop the deportation of Dreamers. Fourteen years ago, President Obama responded by announcing the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) program. More than 830,000 Dreamers have since come forward and received DACA, which has allowed them to contribute more fully to their country as teachers, nurses, doctors, engineers, and small business owners.

Durbin continued, “I am not going to give up on the Dreamers. Just last week, President Trump said that he was willing to work with Democrats on a bipartisan immigration deal… I ask the President of the United States now to keep his word. Work with us to pass the Dream Act, and do it now. We have enough time left to get it done this year. As I near the end of my Senate career, I ask my colleagues to support these young people who are American in every way, except for their immigration status.”

Durbin then shared the story of Brenda Bedolla, the 154th story of a Dreamer he has shared on the Senate floor. Brenda arrived in Little Village, a lively neighborhood in Chicago, from Mexico when she was just two years old. From a young age, her parents instilled in her a deep desire to learn and to use her education as a means to become something greater.

As she began to apply to college, Brenda realized that she was ineligible for financial aid due to her immigration status. But Brenda refused to let that stop her, and she earned a full-ride scholarship to Morton College. At Morton, Brenda ran on the school’s cross-country team, reported for the college newspaper, served as student body vice president, and received the Lincoln Academy of Illinois Student Laureate for outstanding achievement.

Brenda then transferred to Northeastern Illinois University, where she served as student body president and worked in an on-campus job, as well as at a restaurant on nights and weekends to support her education and her family. These experiences exposed Brenda to what it meant to advocate, organize, and represent others. They led her on the path to becoming an organizer for the Service Employees International Union, or SEIU, representing Illinois and Indiana.

Since 2019, Brenda has served as the representative of more than 90,000 care workers in essential jobs in home care, child care, nursing homes, and hospitals. She has helped hospital workers organize and supported members who have workplace grievances. Brenda also serves as a board member of the Morton College Foundation to fundraise for scholarships for students at her alma mater, as well as Arise Chicago, a faith-based worker center educating and organizing low-wage workers about fighting injustice. Brenda says her family’s own experiences with exploitative working conditions are what led her to this rewarding job.

“Brenda is exactly the type of person we need in America. This is whom we might lose if we fail to pass the Dream Act. To my Republican colleagues, I ask you, is this a person you want to remove from the United States? An advocate for health care workers who care for the elderly, our children, and our grandchildren, and our sick? Does Brenda sound like ‘the worst of the worst’? No. She is one of the hundreds of thousands of Dreamers who serve our country every day, even as they worry about being forced to leave this nation,” Durbin said.

Durbin concluded, “We owe it to these talented young people to help. And there is still time in the final weeks of the 119th Congress to get it done. To all of my Republican colleagues, please join me and Senator Lisa Murkowski of Alaska in standing up for these people who epitomize the American Dream. We have an opportunity to finally give Dreamers the justice they deserve. We can do it. We have the time to do it. Let’s get to work.”

title: In Opening Statement During Senate Judiciary Committee Hearing, Durbin Calls For Bipartisan Action To Lower Cost Of Prescription Drugs
text:
In his opening statement, Durbin called for the passage of his bipartisan Drug-price Transparency for Consumers Act to crack down on Big Pharma’s direct-to-consumer advertising

WASHINGTON – U.S. Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin (D-IL), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, delivered an opening statement during today’s Senate Judiciary Committee hearing entitled “Prescribing Sunshine: How Competition and Transparency Lowers Prescription Drug Costs.” Today’s hearing examined competition and transparency in the prescription drug supply chain, specifically consumers’ lack of access to pharmacy services; how brand name drug companies’ patent practices can inhibit competition from generics; and the role played by pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) in drug pricing and access.

In his remarks, Durbin emphasized that Americans are paying the highest prescription drug prices in the world—on average four times more than people in similar countries for brand-name drugs. To address these sky-high prices and crack down on Big Pharma, Durbin advocated for the passage of his legislation with U.S. Senator Chuck Grassley (R-IA), the Drug-price Transparency for Consumers (DTC) Act, which would require price disclosures on advertisements for prescription drugs in order to empower patients and reduce Americans’ colossal spending on medications.

Key Quotes:

“It is no secret: People in the United States pay the highest prescription drug prices in the world—on average, four times more than people in similar countries pay for brand-name drugs. Patients are forced to choose between [prescription] drugs and food.”

“Compounding this challenge is the lack of access to brick-and-mortar pharmacies. In the last 15 years, more than 800 community pharmacies in my state of Illinois have been forced to close their doors because of increased drug costs and declining reimbursement rates.”

“Congress took a first step forward to address the high cost of [prescription] drugs by passing the Inflation Reduction Act in 2022. This law capped the price of insulin at $35 per month. It set an annual out-of-pocket expense limit for seniors—$2,100 in 2026. It also let the executive branch negotiate with Big Pharma to lower prices under Medicare—something President Biden used to reduce drug prices by up to 79 percent.”

“There’s more work to do. Where should we start? Let me suggest, direct-to-consumer drug ads. There are only two countries in the world that allow consumer television ads for drugs… Big Pharma spends billions of dollars to flood the airwaves with advertisements. Why? To get American viewers to get to the point where they can not only pronounce Xarelto but spell it.”

“In July, a citizen petition was filed with the FDA asking to ban these ads… If we cannot get rid of them, we should at least require Big Pharma to let people know how much these drugs cost. Is that an outrageous idea?”

“Chairman Grassley and I have a simple bill that we put together that would require direct-to-consumer ads to disclose the price charged by the drug company. It’s a basic transparency issue to inform patients, and it’s been supported by President Trump in the past. I hope we pass it before the end of the year.”

“We must also address Big Pharma’s anti-competitive schemes to maintain monopolies. The Senate Judiciary Committee has taken a leading role in stopping these abuses. In April 2025, this Committee unanimously reported six bipartisan bills to address this issue. This includes my bill with Republican Senator Tillis to improve information sharing between the FDA and Patent Office. Congress must pass these bills sooner rather than later.”

“This hearing is going to make clear that our work to address the high cost of prescription drugs is far from over. Let’s work together, on a bipartisan basis, to do something to help families afford their prescription drugs.”

title: Ernst Names Small Business of the Week, American State Bank
text:
RED OAK, Iowa – U.S. Senator Joni Ernst (R-Iowa), Chair of the Senate Small Business Committee, today announced American State Bank of Clarke County as her Small Business of the Week. Throughout the 119th Congress, Chair Ernst plans to recognize a small business in each of Iowa's 99 counties.

“For nearly 40 years, American State Bank has made it their mission to deposit joy throughout Iowa communities” said Chair Ernst. “From financial services to investing in the local community, American State Bank continues to make customers its highest priority and interest.”

In the spring of 1987, the town of Osceola, Iowa, lost its primary banking institution due to economic conditions in the Midwest. This left $8.6 million in assets and $7.7 million in deposits available for acquisition. To address this situation, a group of five families came together to acquire the bank, ensuring that locals would continue to have a choice in where to do their banking. On April 24, 1987, the American State Bank was officially established in Osceola.

Since then, the bank has expanded its presence by establishing a central office in downtown Osceola and additional locations in Winterset and Lamoni. Today, the bank focuses primarily on agricultural lending while providing a wide range of services including personal and business banking, investments, insurance, and financial education. Beyond its banking services, American State Bank supports the communities it serves through donations to local agriculture, education, and community initiatives.

Stay tuned as Chair Ernst continues to recognize outstanding Iowa small businesses with her Small Business of the Week award.

title: Fetterman Joins Senate Agriculture Democrats in Letter to Demand USDA Withdraw Proposed Rule Restricting Food Assistance
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Last week, U.S. Senator John Fetterman (D-PA) joined Senate Agriculture Committee Democrats to urge the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) to withdraw its proposed rule restricting Broad-Based Categorical Eligibility (BBCE) under the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) that will severely narrow eligibility requirements for the nation’s largest anti-hunger program. The letter was also signed by U.S. Senators Michael Bennet (D-CO), Ben Ray Lujan (D-NM). Amy Klobuchar (D-MN), Tina Smith (D-MN), Dick Durbin (D-IL), Cory Booker (D-NJ), Raphael Warnock (D-GA), Peter Welch (D-VT), Adam Schiff (D-CA), and Elissa Slotkin (D-MI).

“We write to strongly urge the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) to withdraw its proposed rule restricting Broad-Based Categorical Eligibility (BBCE) under the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP). Should this rule take effect, an estimated 6.3 million Americans, including many seniors and nearly 1.8 million children, would lose SNAP benefits according to the USDA’s own analysis. At a time when everyday Americans are already struggling to afford groceries, USDA should not be making changes to SNAP that leave families with fewer resources to meet their basic needs,” wrote the senators.

Broad-Based Categorical Eligibility helps working families and seniors afford groceries at a time when the rising costs of housing, child care, health care, and other necessities are stretching household budgets. It gives states flexibility to help low-income households access food assistance while supporting work and financial stability. Without BBCE, families could lose SNAP benefits even when they are still struggling to make ends meet. It also allows families and seniors to build and maintain modest savings without jeopardizing their access to food assistance. Protections like these are critical not only to ensure struggling Americans meet their basic needs, but also to help these individuals build toward greater financial mobility.

This proposed rule would also make SNAP more challenging and costly for states to administer, increasing paperwork, the risk of payment errors, and demands on state workers. These added burdens come as states are already absorbing a larger share of SNAP administrative expenses under The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, leaving states with fewer resources to manage these additional requirements. USDA argues that the proposed rule aligns SNAP with congressional intent, which is false, as the senators argue.

The consequences would extend beyond SNAP. Children in households that lose SNAP eligibility could also lose automatic certification for free school meals, requiring families to submit additional applications to establish eligibility and creating more administrative work for schools. This added red tape could prevent eligible children from receiving meals and reduce federal reimbursements for schools, threatening efforts to provide free school meals to all students. The proposal could also create additional red tape for families seeking assistance through the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC), potentially leaving some families unable to access benefits and others ineligible for assistance altogether.

“In the proposed rule, USDA repeatedly claims that it is aligning SNAP rules with congressional intent, but the legislative history clearly demonstrates otherwise. Congress established categorical eligibility to simplify access to food assistance and preserved this framework when it created Temporary Assistance for Needy Families in 1996. States have relied on this flexibility for decades to serve low-income households and administer SNAP more efficiently. Congress subsequently considered proposals to eliminate or restrict BBCE during the 2005 reconciliation debate and the 2014 and 2018 Farm Bill negotiations, but these restrictions were ultimately rejected on a bipartisan basis and excluded from the final legislation. While maintaining SNAP eligibility for 6.3 million Americans who need it should be reason enough, the fact that this proposed rule is contrary to congressional intent and the law is another reason it should be withdrawn,” continued the senators.

As a member of the U.S. Senate Committee on Agriculture, Senator Fetterman has continuously fought for several legislative efforts and policy positions to protect SNAP. He has introduced legislation like the Fairness for Victims of SNAP Skimming Act to protect and reimburse SNAP recipients who lose benefits to card skimming and fraud, the School Meal Modernization and Hunger Elimination Act to expand access to free and reduced-price school lunches and streamline the certification process for school districts, and the Food Secure Strikers Act to protect and expand SNAP access for striking workers.

Read the full text of the letter below and here.

—

Dear Secretary Rollins:

We write to strongly urge the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) to withdraw its proposed rule restricting Broad-Based Categorical Eligibility (BBCE) under the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP). Should this rule take effect, an estimated 6.3 million Americans, including many seniors and nearly 1.8 million children, would lose SNAP benefits according to the USDA’s own analysis. At a time when everyday Americans are already struggling to afford groceries, USDA should not be making changes to SNAP that leave families with fewer resources to meet their basic needs.

The costs of housing, utilities, child care, health care, and other necessities are leaving working families and seniors on fixed incomes with little money left for food. BBCE helps these households access food while supporting work and financial stability. Without it, a working family could lose SNAP benefits entirely after a modest raise, even when the additional earnings are not enough to replace the assistance it loses. BBCE allows states to prevent this abrupt cutoff so that families can continue receiving assistance as their earnings increase and their SNAP benefits gradually decline. It also allows low-income families and seniors to maintain modest emergency savings without losing assistance. These protections help people meet their basic needs while building assets and working toward greater financial security and economic mobility. This flexibility has been embraced by leaders of both parties and is now used in 43 states, the District of Columbia, Guam, and the U.S. Virgin Islands.

Beyond the direct harm to families, the proposal would make SNAP more difficult and expensive for states to administer. Most states use BBCE to raise or eliminate SNAP’s restrictive and complex federal asset test, reducing paperwork and the potential for payment errors. Reinstating these tests would require households to provide additional financial verification and place significant new demands on state workers. According to an analysis by the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, asset-related errors added approximately one percentage point, on average, to SNAP payment error rates in states that retained asset tests in fiscal year 2023. Under H.R. 1, which ties states’ share of SNAP benefit costs to their payment error rates, even a small increase could push states into higher cost-sharing tiers. With states already absorbing a larger share of SNAP administrative expenses, this proposal would impose new burdens while leaving them with fewer resources to manage those demands.

The effects would also reach well beyond SNAP. Children in households that lose SNAP eligibility would lose their SNAP-based automatic certification for free school meals, requiring families without another automatic eligibility pathway to submit additional applications and schools to verify eligibility. This would add unnecessary red tape for families and schools and increase the risk that eligible children miss out on meals. Fewer children directly certified through SNAP would also put federal school meal reimbursements at risk, particularly for schools participating in the Community Eligibility Provision. USDA’s own analysis warns that declining federal reimbursements could threaten the financial viability of state efforts to provide free school meals, such as universal breakfast and lunch programs in Colorado and New Mexico and universal free breakfast in Pennsylvania. The proposal would also complicate access to the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC), requiring some families to provide additional income documentation and leaving others ineligible for assistance altogether.

In the proposed rule, USDA repeatedly claims that it is aligning SNAP rules with congressional intent, but the legislative history clearly demonstrates otherwise. Congress established categorical eligibility to simplify access to food assistance and preserved this framework when it created Temporary Assistance for Needy Families in 1996. States have relied on this flexibility for decades to serve low-income households and administer SNAP more efficiently. Congress subsequently considered proposals to eliminate or restrict BBCE during the 2005 reconciliation debate and the 2014 and 2018 Farm Bill negotiations, but these restrictions were ultimately rejected on a bipartisan basis and excluded from the final legislation. While maintaining SNAP eligibility for 6.3 million Americans who need it should be reason enough, the fact that this proposed rule is contrary to congressional intent and the law is another reason it should be withdrawn.

Children should not go hungry, seniors should not have to spend down their savings to afford groceries, and working families should not lose assistance while they are still struggling to make ends meet. USDA’s proposal would put these families at greater risk while adding costs and complications for states. We urge USDA to withdraw the proposed rule in its entirety.

title: Senator Gallego for the Wall Street Journal: “Big-Truck Democratic Populism”
text:
Gallego: “Democrats are at our best when we rally to make people’s dreams a reality, proudly stand up for communities and fight corruption and elitism — not when we’re playing hall monitor or imposing purity tests.”

WASHINGTON — Last week, Senator Ruben Gallego (D-AZ) published an op-ed in the Wall Street Journal describing what he calls “big-ass-truck populism.” In the piece, the senator detailed how congressional Democrats can address the affordability crisis and lift-up working families by expanding on the vision he laid out in his economic policy plan, “Saving the Middle Class and Restoring the American Dream.”

Read the op-ed below:

“Every Latino man wants a big-ass truck. There’s nothing wrong with that,” I told reporters in 2025. Big-ass-truck populism reverberated across the country last week as a new generation of outsider Democrats won more races than in any election since Watergate.

I saw this populism while campaigning for Gina Hinojosa in Texas, Teresa Benitez-Thompson in Nevada and Chris Pappas in New Hampshire. North and South, rural and urban, left and right, Americans feel the system has failed them. They want leaders to fight back and make their lives better, not sell them out like President Trump and his yes men in Congress did. Try filling up a big-ass truck at $5 a gallon.

Democrats are at our best when we rally to make people’s dreams a reality, proudly stand up for communities and fight corruption and elitism—not when we’re playing hall monitor or imposing purity tests.

Real populism boils down to two things: fighting for working people and community pride. We are at our best when we identify with voters personally and take their side. And voters don’t want to be scolded.

Rejection of Woke 1.0 is a great start. We need fewer professorial talks and less wordsmithing and more work stopping health insurance companies from gouging families and landlords from taking advantage of hardworking tenants.

Human beings have an irrepressible drive to give our kids a better future. I saw that while being raised by a single mother in a working-class Latino family, and I feel it as a parent of three children. People feel isolated when no one seems to be looking out for them. Families are so stressed that leaning on relatives, usually a good way to get help, is nearly impossible. A $100,000 salary doesn’t make you feel comfortably middle class anymore. Today, families work harder than ever and are more stressed than ever.

Democrats must change that. Work needs to bring dignity to the family man. Pay needs to make a mother feel she can support her kids and their dreams and, for God’s sake, actually enjoy life. We can fight for them by raising the minimum wage to $20, increasing the child tax credit, and passing legislation for universal healthcare and a massive housing plan targeting first-time home buyers. That’s a real American plan for real American families.

This country can overcome smallness and cruelty if leaders include everyone. During the Trump years, too many leaders in my party have given voters the impression that recognizing what needs to change in America should outweigh our pride and joy in being Americans. That’s a false choice. It’s pride and love of country that motivates us to make America better.

Democrats don’t have to live in a world of contradictions. We can have a safe and secure border while demanding Immigration and Customs Enforcement respects our constitutional rights. We should deport criminals who are here illegally while legalizing the millions of immigrants who have deep roots in our communities. We can have safe streets with great cops who don’t profile black and brown communities and use force when appropriate.

We can make our case to the millions of Americans who are looking for a new political home by demonstrating cultural literacy and putting ourselves on the same side as Americans’ best traditions and against frustrations with a failed system.

title: Gillibrand, Merkley Introduce Legislation To Address Republican Cuts And Help Students Access Essential Graduate Degrees
text:
Today, U.S. Senators Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY) and Jeff Merkley (D-OR) introduced the Professional Student Degree Act to ensure financial stability for students and strengthen essential workforce pipelines. The bill would reverse harmful Republican cuts to federal student loan programs by expanding the definition of a “professional degree” to include certain critical graduate programs currently excluded by the U.S. Department of Education (ED), such as those in nursing, education, and public health.

Currently, ED’s implementation of federal student loan provisions enacted by President Trump and congressional Republicans under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act creates an immediate “loan cliff” for certain graduate degrees. By narrowing the definition of a “professional degree” to just 11 eligible programs, the current framework severely limits financial access to graduate programs in essential fields already facing critical labor shortages.

Students in these newly designated “non-professional” programs face annual student loan caps that are almost $30,000 lower, and aggregate limits $100,000 lower, than students in designated professional tracks. This limits students’ ability to secure the federal loans needed to complete their education and threatens to worsen nationwide workforce shortages, particularly in healthcare.

The Professional Student Degree Act would correct this by adding several key graduate programs to the federal list of professional degrees eligible for higher borrowing limits.

“Students who want to pursue critical fields like social work, public health, nursing, and education should not have to break the bank to serve their communities,” said Senator Gillibrand. “This bill would expand the definition of what constitutes a professional degree, giving students in high-need fields access to the financial resources they need to complete their education and serve others. This bill would help our students, our universities, and our communities, and I’m determined to get it passed.”

“Nurses, teachers, and social workers are dedicated public servants, and Congress must do everything it can to help recruit the next generation of these heroes,” said Senator Merkley. “We’re already facing a shortage of these critical workers, and new limits on federal student loans for these professions and others threaten to further jeopardize the future of our workforce. Financial freedom and flexibility are essential to aspiring students, and I’m leading the charge with my colleagues to oppose these dangerous changes and stand up for affordable student loans so folks can continue to achieve their dreams and serve the public.”

The Professional Student Degree Act would impact the following degree programs:

Maintains Professional Status for: Pharmacy, Dentistry, Veterinary Medicine, Chiropractic, Law, Medicine, Optometry, Osteopathic Medicine, Podiatric Medicine, Theology, Clinical Psychology

Restores and Codifies Professional Status for: Social Work, Audiology, Physician Assistant, Occupational Therapy, Physical Therapy, Nursing, Public Health, Business Administration and Management, Accounting, Architecture, Education, and Special Education

Flexibility to Expand: The Secretary of Education may add any other programs that meet “professional degree” requirements.

Without a statutory or legislative fix, students entering these costly but essential degree programs will be priced out of the workforce, further destabilizing already high-need professions.

The bill has been endorsed by the American Academy of Audiology, American Academy of Physician Associate, American Association of State Colleges and Universities, American Council on Education, American Institute of Architects, American Institute of Architecture Students, American Physical Therapy Association, Association of Collegiate Schools of Architecture, Association of Public and Land-grant Universities, Columbia University, Commission on Independent Colleges & Universities, Dominican University New York, National Architectural Accrediting Board, National Council of Architectural Registration Boards, National Organization of Minority Architects, New York Medical College, Oncology Nursing Society (ONS), Physician Assistant Education Association, Yale University, Binghamton University, and the University at Buffalo.

The full text of the Professional Student Degree Act can be found here.

title: Watch: Gillibrand Grills Acting Sec. Cao On Dismissal Of 8 Suicide Attempts In USS Lincoln Carrier Strike Group As ‘Mitigations’: “Your Response Is Inhumane”
text:
**Watch the exchange here**

Today, U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY), a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, grilled Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao on his dismissal of 8 suicide attempts in the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group as “suicide mitigations” – and pressed the secretary over his minimization of mental health support failures in the carrier strike group.

In response to the acting secretary’s open disrespect of the sacrifice U.S. service members made aboard the USS Lincoln, Senator Gillibrand said to Cao:

“You are minimizing what mental health strain is on these service members. If it was your son or your daughter, would you be minimizing it and saying, ‘Well, there was mitigation?’ I don’t think you would. I think your response is inhumane. I think it’s inadequate. I don’t think it understands the stress and strain that these men and women are on because of these poor conditions.”

Watch key moments of the exchange here and find a transcript below:

ON THE OPEN DISRESPECT DISPLAYED IN SEC. CAO’S MINIMIZATION OF SUICIDE ATTEMPTS IN THE USS LINCOLN CARRIER STRIKE GROUP:

SENATOR GILLIBRAND: Looking back at those eight suicide attempts and the documented conditions on board, were the president and Secretary Hegseth wrong to dismiss those concerns?

SECRETARY CAO: Well, Senator, again, these are eight mitigations we’re able to mitigate because of…

GILLIBRAND: Please don’t call attempted suicide mitigations. That is such an insult. It’s an insult to these men and women who are devoting their lives to the armed services. When you say it’s mitigation, you’re compartmentalizing something that is clearly a mental health failure. The fact that a service member, a sailor, went overboard is beyond a mitigation. It is an attempted suicide that, but for the grace of God, was unsuccessful.

CAO: Senator, that sailor was not trying to kill himself, and he admitted that. He admitted that to the commanding officers.

GILLIBRAND: What was he trying to do? Swim to Guam?

CAO: He was trying to get out. He jumped overboard with a life preserver.

GILLIBRAND: Is there a logical explanation of jumping overboard to get out of service? It will result in death.

CAO: No, it does not, Senator.

GILLIBRAND: Did he jump overboard where he could swim to shore?

CAO: He jumped overboard with a life preserver on, and again he admitted it to the commanding officer afterwards.

GILLIBRAND: Maybe to save whatever discipline he was about to undergo. But I think you are minimizing what mental health strain is on these service members. If it was your son or your daughter, would you be minimizing it and saying, “Well, there was mitigation?” I don’t think you would. I think your response is inhumane. I think it’s inadequate. I don’t think it understands the stress and strain that these men and women are on because of these poor conditions.

ON THE TRUMP ADMINISTRATION’S REPEATED DISMISSAL OF REPORTS OF POOR CONDITIONS AND MENTAL HEALTH STRAIN ABOARD THE USS LINCOLN:

GILLIBRAND: Yes or no: Did President Trump claim the USS Lincoln was, quote, “beautifully maintained” in response to public reports of poor conditions that he called “fake news”? Yes or no?

CAO: I don’t know exactly what he said.

GILLIBRAND: The answer is yes. He said that. Did Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth claim reports of poor conditions and morale on board the USS Lincoln were, quote, “completely misrepresented?”

CAO: I believe he did, Senator.

GILLIBRAND: Thank you. In August, as the USS Abraham Lincoln was nearing nine months of uninterrupted time at sea, military families raised urgent alarms about rationed supplies, sanitation failures, and severe mental health strain. Did you issue a public statement calling news reports “dishonest” and accusing the press of, quote, “trying to paint our warriors as victims”?

CAO: I did, Senator, and I spoke to our sailors on board, and they felt the same way.

GILLIBRAND: Well, I disagree with your assessment.

###

title: Grassley-Backed Infrastructure Law Delivers $177,000 to Iowa Community Colleges to Bolster Commercial Driving Programs
text:
WASHINGTON – Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) welcomed news from the Department of Transportation (DOT) that Des Moines Area Community College in Ankeny and Hawkeye Community College in Waterloo will receive a total of $177,405 to support their Commercial Driver’s License (CDL) programs and strengthen Iowa’s trucking industry. The funding will be administered through DOT’s Commercial Motor Vehicle Operator Safety Training Grant Program (CMVOST), which was reauthorized in the Grassley-backed Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA). The CMVOST Program prioritizes training for current and former members of the Armed Forces, as well as certain military family members.

“Truck drivers help keep Iowa’s economy moving, so preparing the next generation of commercial drivers is critical to our state’s long-term economic health,” Grassley said. “I’m glad to know more Iowa students will soon benefit from the bipartisan infrastructure law I supported, along with the countless consumers and producers who depend on truckers for their goods and services.”

Des Moines Area Community College will receive $89,600 and Hawkeye Community College will receive $87,805, respectively.

In January, seven Iowa community colleges received federal grants stemming from the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act.

title: Grassley Honored with Lifetime Achievement Award from Clean Fuels Alliance America
text:
WASHINGTON – Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa), a lifelong corn and soybean farmer, accepted a Lifetime Achievement Award from Clean Fuels Alliance America for his work to expand market opportunities for biodiesel. Grassley is a former chairman and current member of the Senate Finance Committee.

“It’s quite an honor to be recognized for my leadership on behalf of American agriculture and biomass-based diesel. I’m proud of the success we’ve had over decades expanding market opportunities through tax policy and EPA volume obligations to maximize the outputs per bushel and keep up with innovation,” Grassley said. “I’ve long recognized the fight for renewable fuels is a boost for family farmers and rural communities. Iowans know this senator will never back down on issues important to rural America.”

“No single individual has done more to bring about supportive policies for the biodiesel and renewable diesel industry than Senator Grassley. I’m not overstating his impact when I say his leadership is why the industry grew from less than 100 million gallons in 2004 to over 5 billion gallons today,” said Kurt Kovarik, Vice President, Federal Affairs, Clean Fuels Alliance America.

Grassley accepts a Lifetime Achievement Award from Clean Fuels Alliance America.

Download photos HERE.

Grassley delivered the following remarks upon receipt of the Lifetime Achievement Award:

I’m honored to be presented with a Lifetime Achievement Award recognizing my work expanding market opportunities for biomass-based diesel.

Farmers, of course, are independent-minded, hard workers that prefer markets over government assistance for their products.

That mindset is why I’ve championed tax and energy policies geared toward leveling the playing field between conventional fossil fuels and farm grown renewable fuels.

Since I spearheaded enactments of the first biodiesel tax credit in 2004 and the Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS) in 2005, the market for biofuels has grown by leaps and bounds.

According to Iowa State University, the production and sales of biodiesel tripled from 25 million gallons to 75 million gallons in the year following the enactment of the biodiesel tax credit. Following enactment of the RFS, production more than tripled between 2005 and 2006, reaching 250 million gallons.

This year, total biomass-based diesel production will exceed five billion gallons.

To ensure continued growth of the industry, I continue to ride herd for stable and predictable renewable fuel policies.

The Clean Fuels Production Credit, which has replaced the original biodiesel tax credit, was extended through 2029 by the Working Families Tax Cuts Act.

While I know the industry would have preferred a longer extension, many of you may recall years of fighting for a single year or two extensions - frequently on a retroactive basis.

The RFS has been a consistent market for farmers, a boon to rural communities and has fostered national energy security.

Last year’s Set 2 rule from the EPA created record renewable volume obligations under the RFS.

I look forward to protecting these levels through the ongoing reallocation rule and building on them in the Set 3 rule.

As farmers face headwinds from trade disruptions and high input costs, federal biofuels policies are growing critical markets for farmers.

title: Grassley Opens Judiciary Hearing Examining Avenues to Make Prescription Drugs More Affordable
text:
Prepared Opening Statement by Senator Chuck Grassley of Iowa

Chairman, Senate Judiciary Committee

“Prescribing Sunshine: How Competition & Transparency Lowers Prescription Drug Costs”

Tuesday, November 17, 2026

I’d like to welcome everyone to this hearing examining how competition and transparency can lower prescription drug costs.

Today, we’re examining questions that matter to every family. Why do prescription drugs cost so much? How do we make them affordable?

Needless to say, the prescription drug supply chain is complicated.

Manufacturers set list prices. Wholesalers and distributors move products. Pharmacy benefit managers set prices, build formularies, process claims and create pharmacy networks.

Insurers and employers design benefits. Pharmacies fill the prescriptions. Each one of these participants affects the final cost.

However, when the transactions are hidden behind confidential contracts, rebates, fees and payments to affiliated companies, patients and consumers have a hard time following the money.

When companies are allowed to engage in anticompetitive and abusive tactics, drug prices remain high for patients.

Last year, the Senate Judiciary Committee advanced six bipartisan bills that address the high cost of prescription drugs and the abusive practices that keep prices too high for too many American families.

They’ll help make medications more affordable for the patient.

These bills address anticompetitive tactics in the pharmaceutical supply chain, including opaque pharmacy benefit managers’ (PBMs) practices, product hopping, patent games, sham citizen petitions, pay-for-delay deals and the need to strengthen collaboration in the drug patent process between the FDA and Patent Office.

I’m glad the Senate unanimously passed the Affordable Prescriptions for Patients Act in July.

It’s time for the Senate to pass the five other bills.

Last year, the Senate Judiciary Committee held a hearing focused specifically on PBMs. We learned that these entities originally existed to process pharmacy claims. Then, they began negotiating prices and managing drug benefits.

In recent years, PBMs’ role has continued to evolve. They now exercise significant power over what medications patients can access, how much the patient will pay, how the pharmacy gets paid and much more.

My two-year bipartisan investigation into insulin price gouging, cited by the FTC, found that PBMs encourage drug makers to spike a drug’s list price in order to offer a greater rebate. This, in turn, allows manufacturers to secure priority placement on covered meds – all at the expense of patients.

For years, I’ve pressed the FTC to study PBMs, and their impact on competition and drug costs.

I’m glad that the FTC listened to me and began their study into PBMs in 2022.

While the FTC’s two interim staff reports are helpful, I’m eager to get their full report with legislative recommendations. Last month, I asked the FTC for an update on when Congress will see the report.

I also appreciate that the FTC has issued two proposed consent orders with major PBMs. The enforcement of those settlements will need to be monitored to ensure they benefit patients.

While a report on PBMs is crucial, we can address some anti-competitive behavior today. In February, Congress took some action on PBM reform in Medicare Part D and the private insurance market.

I’m glad the Department of Labor implemented its regulation last month. I look forward to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services completing its regulatory work next year. I’m watching both regulations closely to ensure they help patients and lower drug costs.

These are good first steps, but more PBM reform is needed. I’m on the record calling for more transparency and accountability of PBMs.

The PBM industry may try to argue that they’ve changed their ways and they’re more accountable, but I disagree.

PBMs are still too opaque and powerful, while patients, pharmacies and taxpayers are being hurt by these powerful drug middlemen.

The efforts to lower prescription drug costs are bipartisan.

The Senate should also consider the Drug-price Transparency for Consumers Act. This bill is a priority of Senator Durbin and mine. If a drug company can advertise a prescription drug directly to the public, it should disclose the product’s price to the public too.

Sunlight gives patients information to ask better questions about price and lower-cost alternatives before they purchase at the pharmacy counter.

I appreciate President Trump’s commitment to lowering drug costs, holding foreign countries accountable for benefiting from American medical innovation and protecting rural health care through price transparency and the $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Fund.

The Trump administration’s work to root out fraud, waste and abuse in health care programs is also ensuring resources are going to those who most need them while protecting taxpayers.

Today’s hearing is about the prescription drug supply chain as a whole. The entire prescription drug supply chain needs to be put under a magnifying glass.

Accountability must follow the decision maker.

No participant can hide behind the complexity of the system or conveniently shift responsibility.

I appreciate Senator Durbin’s partnership in holding this hearing.

Today, we’ll hear testimony from a patient advocacy organization, the co-founder of a transparent cost-plus pharmacy, the Iowa Pharmacy Association, a health economist and a CEO of Illinois health clinics.

They bring different perspectives. I thank each of the witnesses for being here, and I look forward to the discussion.

title: Judiciary Committee Witnesses Urge Congress to Pass Grassley-Backed Bills to Lower Prescription Drug Costs, Echo Grassley’s Calls for PBM Transparency & Accountability
text:
WASHINGTON – Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) today chaired a hearing to examine the high cost of prescription drugs and proposed legislative solutions. Last year, the Judiciary Committee advanced six Grassley-backed, bipartisan bills to lower prescription drug prices through competition transparency and to address anticompetitive tactics in the pharmaceutical supply chain. One of those bills, the Affordable Prescriptions for Patients Act, passed the Senate unanimously in July. The remaining bills have not received a vote on the Senate floor.

Today’s witnesses urged Congress to pass bipartisan legislation and echoed Grassley’s calls for the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) to complete its 6(b) study of pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs). The witnesses also detailed how PBMs increase the cost of prescription drugs and outlined mechanisms to hold PBMs accountable.

Grassley questioned the following witnesses:

Matthew Pitlick, PharmD, chief executive officer of the Iowa Pharmacy Association

Merith Basey, chief executive officer of Patients For Affordable Drugs Now

Alex Oshmyansky, MD, PhD, cofounder and chief executive officer of the Mark Cuban Cost Plus Drug Company

Neeraj Sood, PhD, senior scholar and professor at the University of Southern California Shaeffer Institute for Public Policy & Government Service

Video and excerpts of Grassley’s questions follow. Read Grassley’s opening statement HERE.

VIDEO

On the FTC’s Final PBM Report:

GRASSLEY: “It’s been four years since the FTC began their study of PBMs. Patients, rural pharmacies and Congress are still waiting for the study and its recommendations. Dr. Pitlick, how is the delay of the FTC’s final report on PBMs impacting patients and rural pharmacies? Why is getting this report so important?”

PITLICK: “The interim reports are non-binding, but they gave great information and great insight. Like you said in your opening statement, we are waiting for the full report with legislative action that Congress can take. I think that Congress is deserving of that, the public is deserving of that, and taxpayers deserve it as well.”

On the impact of Grassley-backed, bipartisan drug pricing bills:

GRASSLEY: “Ms. Basey, last year, this committee took a comprehensive [approach] to reducing drug costs… These bills will bring cheaper treatment faster to the market and hold drug companies and PBMs accountable. The Senate has now passed just one of these six competition bills. So, for you, what impact would these remaining five bills have on patients, and why should the Senate act now?”

BASEY: “Lower cost competition is essential for the one in three Americans who are struggling to afford their prescription drug prices. These bills, if passed together, would help close some of the loopholes in the patent and regulatory systems that the pharmaceutical industry uses to abuse the system and keep prices high at the expense of American patients…

“We need lower cost drugs sooner, so that patients can benefit and so that taxpayers can benefit too. These bills would all save money, and they would make a difference for millions of patients around the country.”

On PBMs driving up the prices of prescription drugs:

GRASSLEY: “Dr. Oshmyansky, according to a recent study, Part D Medicare could save as much as $8.6 billion dollars annually if it were using the same pricing for certain generic drugs as the Cost Plus Drug Company uses. In other words, you're getting a better deal for patients, while under the Part D program, PBMs drive up the cost for seniors and taxpayers.

“So, how does the Cost Plus Drug Company achieve these lower prices, and what barriers does a company face when entering or expanding in the prescription drug market?”

OSHMYANSKY: “We try to go back to the 1850s in terms of our pricing model. You can go to our website, and you can see what it is exactly we pay for the drugs… we add a 15% margin as our markup, a $5 fee to pay our pharmacist, a $5 shipping and handling [fee], and that's the total cost of the medication. Everything else – that entire $8.6 billion difference – that's just intermediaries in the supply chain, adding their markup...

“You might get asked to pay a $3,000 copayment for Imatinib for Chronic Myelogenous Leukemia. From us, [the] exact same drug [from the] exact same drug company [would be] about $30... The one thing we cannot do at the moment is get access to the branded, patented and specialty drug products. If we could break through that, I think we could drive down drug costs for the country much further.”

On the positive impact of establishing fiduciary responsibilities on PBMs:

GRASSLEY: “I'm glad the Department of Labor recently implemented PBM reform for some employer-sponsored health plans. Under federal rules for employer-sponsored health plans, there's a question as to whether PBMs have a fiduciary responsibility to health plan sponsors. PBMs would argue that they're getting the best deal for their clients. PBMs' opaqueness and tactics made me question that position. I'm all in for regulating PBMs, but we ultimately need a comprehensive mechanism to hold these PBMs accountable. Otherwise, we're playing whack-a-mole with PBM behavior.

“You talked about this in your 2025 testimony before this committee. So, why would establishing an explicit fiduciary duty standard, given the recent Department of Labor recommendation, help ensure PBMs have a duty to work for the benefit of the consumer?

SOOD: “What the new laws do, the Department of Labor regulations and the [Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2026], is they ask PBMs to disclose to employers how they are making money and their contracts with pharmacies. But disclosure is not enough to change their practices. As Dr. Alex said, there's only three PBMs, and if every PBM is doing the same games, switching PBMs is not going to help.

“What you need is accountability ultimately to plan members. As the [PBM] FAIR Act does, it gives fiduciary responsibility to PBMs. That fiduciary responsibility is owed to employees and plan members. So, even if employers don't act under [the Employee Retirement Income Security Act (ERISA)], the Department of Labor or employees could act and hold PBMs accountable. If PBMs say they’re doing a great job for our patients, be [held] accountable for it – that's what fiduciary responsibility does.”

title: Senate Judiciary Committee Advances 11 Judicial and Executive Nominees
text:
WASHINGTON – The Senate Judiciary Committee today advanced the following nominations:

Robert E. Long, Jr., to be United States District Judge for the Middle District of Florida, by a vote of 12-10.

Peter M. Mansfield, to be United States District Judge for the Eastern District of Louisiana, by a vote of 14-8.

Jesus A. Osete, to be United States District Judge for the Western District of Missouri, by a vote of 12-10.

Stephen Husk, to be a Commissioner of the United States Parole Commission, by a vote of 17-5.

Samuel King Lee, to be United States Attorney for the Eastern District of Tennessee, by a vote of 14-8.

Gretchen C. F. Shappert, to be United States Attorney for the District of Guam and concurrently United States Attorney for the District of the Northern Mariana Islands, by a vote of 14-8.

Robert Troester, to be United States Attorney for the Western District of Oklahoma, by a vote of 12-10.

title: Senators Hassan, Cornyn Reintroduce Bipartisan Bill to Increase Awareness of Fentanyl Danger Among Young People
text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. Senators Maggie Hassan (D-NH) and John Cornyn (R-TX) reintroduced bipartisan legislation to require a comprehensive federal strategy to help prevent fentanyl overdoses in children and teens. Fentanyl is now involved in at least 75% of adolescent overdose deaths.

“As counterfeit pills laced with fentanyl and other synthetic opioids continue to take the lives of young people in New Hampshire and across the country, we need to make sure that children and teens understand the dangers of these substances,” said Senator Hassan. “This bipartisan legislation will strengthen coordination between schools and public health officials, improve education about the dangers of fentanyl and other synthetic opioids, and help schools access lifesaving overdose reversal agents.”

“Fentanyl is the leading cause of death for young Americans between the ages of 18 and 45,” said Senator Cornyn. “I’m proud to introduce this bipartisan legislation with Sen. Hassan that would protect Texans and save lives by helping educate students on fentanyl’s perils, increasing access to overdose reversal agents, and preventing the misuse of synthetic opioids.”

The Fentanyl Awareness for Children and Teens in Schools (FACTS) Act would:

Establish education partnership programs between public schools and public health agencies to prevent the misuse of, and overdose with, fentanyl and other synthetic opioids by youth;

Develop a collaborative approach among local, state, and federal officials to identify and disseminate best practices in education and prevention regarding the misuse of, and overdose with, synthetic opioids by youth;

Increase opportunities for employees of secondary schools receiving federal funds to receive professional development on the dangers of the misuse of, and overdose with, synthetic opioids by youth;

Improve the availability and utility of data regarding the proliferation of synthetic opioids by youth; and,

Allow Naloxone to be purchased by school-based health centers.

The bipartisan bill, which was also introduced in the House, has secured endorsements from Song for Charlie, National PTA, School Superintendents Association, American Psychological Association, National Association of Elementary School Principals, National Association of Secondary School Principals, National Association of School Psychologists, National Association of Counties, National Alliance on Mental Illness, and American Federation of Teachers.

Read the full text of the legislation here.

The FACTS Act is part of Senator Hassan’s ongoing efforts to combat the opioid epidemic. Since 2017, Senator Hassan has successfully worked to secure a nine-fold increase in funding for New Hampshire to address the addiction epidemic. Senator Hassan helped introduce the Modernizing Opioid Treatment Access Act, bipartisan legislation to improve access to medication-assisted treatment by allowing more addiction specialists to prescribe methadone. In 2022, Senator Hassan successfully passed into law her bipartisan Mainstreaming Addiction Treatment (MAT) Act to increase the number of medical professionals authorized to prescribe medication-assisted treatment. Senator Hassan also fought to permanently require coverage of medication-assisted treatment for substance use disorder under Medicaid. Last year, she helped pass into law the bipartisan HALT Fentanyl Act, to permanently classify all fentanyl-related substances as Schedule I drugs under the Controlled Substances Act. Senator Hassan also helped advance the DETECT Fentanyl and Xylazine Act, which became law in 2024 and is supporting law enforcement with enhanced tools to find and eliminate illegal substances such as fentanyl and xylazine. Last year, Senator Hassan introduced three bipartisan bills to expand access to lifesaving overdose prevention tools. Also last year, Senator Hassan launched an investigation into whether patients at for-profit methadone clinics encounter unnecessary barriers when seeking lifesaving methadone treatment for opioid addiction.

title: Heinrich: BAAJA Will “Make a Big Difference in People's Energy Costs”
text:
VIDEO HERE

WASHINGTON — U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, highlighted his Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), legislation to lower energy bills, hold data centers accountable, reduce emissions, and create good-paying jobs, during an interview with The Hill’s Alex Bolton.

“We can make a big difference in people's energy costs — particularly their electric bill. And there's a real desire by the American people just for us to do our jobs and produce actual results for them, and not be, you know, pulled around by the extreme voices in, in any debate,” said Heinrich.

U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, highlights his Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act during a sit-down interview with Alex Bolton, Senate congressional reporter for The Hill, November 17, 2026.

On BAAJA Lowering Energy Costs:

Alex Bolton: “I get the sense that there's real, you know, pent up demand to actually do something to pass legislation that makes an impact, and that's what we're seeing right now with these big votes.”

Senator Heinrich: “I think [there’s] just a desire to actually do things. You know, nothing's going to be perfect, but obviously the last election was prosecuted on the necessity of giving people some relief from the inflation and the higher prices that are just driving the conversation with normal Americans everywhere in the country. And this is one of the places where we can make a difference. We can make a big difference in people's energy costs, and particularly their electric bill. And there's a real desire by the American people just for us to do our jobs and produce actual results for them, and not be, you know, pulled around by the extreme voices in, in any debate.”

Bolton: “The Rhodium Group estimates the bill will reduce household electricity bills by $50 to $70 a month by the year 2040. Are you looking at that assessment? How big of an impact do you think this will have on families' energy bills over the next five to 10 years? Can you put a number on it?”

Heinrich: “I think their estimate is as good as any [estimate] I've seen. I think the principle here is that we need to put more cheap electrons onto the grid a whole lot faster, and right now we have literally almost 2,000 gigawatts of generation sitting in interconnection queues for an average of over six years, just waiting in line. That's not the permitting side of things. That's just the waiting in line to plug into the grid side of things, so we make that much faster and easier in this legislation. We make permitting faster, and so we're going to be able to put more cheap, clean electrons onto the grid, and that is the only way we're going to reverse this trend of electricity just getting more and more and more expensive.”

On Potential Amendments to BAAJA:

Bolton: “I understand there are negotiations on amendments. You're working on a manager's amendment...What changes do you think will be included in the manager's amendment? I know this requires consensus, but what do you think is most likely to be included in that amendment, or what other amendments do you think are likely to get votes before the end of the week?”

Heinrich: “There are a number of amendments around the Tribal provisions in the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA). I think those are helpful. You know, we'll release something as soon as we can. But as you can imagine, in terms of a manager's amendment, it requires four corners agreement. And those changes will be relatively modest because it requires the chairs and ranking members of both committees.

On Heinrich's Work to Codify Tribal Consultation in BAAJA:

Heinrich: “I think one of the things that's important to recognize with the Tribal provisions in the NHPA is what our actual choices are, because this administration was moving forward on a process that would have effectively replaced Tribal consultation with a 30-day comment period. And I can't overstate how problematic that would be, because what works in consultation, having been through a lot of projects in my state that require Tribal consultation, is when an agency sits down with a Tribe, and there is an actual conversation, and that deconflicts a project away from places that are problematic, places that we want to protect historic and cultural sites and landscapes. And so, we need that to be a robust process. And one of the things I like about this legislation is that we were actually able to incorporate in the manager's package a statutory requirement for the agencies to consult at each of the steps in the NHPA, and so that's actually a big step forward. But because of where we started with the administration and the Tribes, I don't think that has fully been recognized yet. Like, what an improvement to the process that will be for Tribal governments.”

On BAAJA Expediting the Approval of Clean Energy Projects:

Bolton: “You've talked about and written about the SunZia project, the largest clean energy infrastructure project in the Western Hemisphere, in New Mexico. More than 900 wind turbines. It took 17 years to permit and build. If BAAJA becomes law, what kind of impact would it have on a project like that – in terms of how long it takes?”

Heinrich: “My guess is that project could have probably been completed in five or six years as opposed to seventeen. That's a big, big difference, and, you know, that's a project that I would argue was one of the best-designed projects because the developers actually listened. They avoided the places I warned them were, you know, were to be avoided for other values. We are a big public land state. People love their wilderness and their wilderness study areas, their refuges, and so they were very smart about how they designed the transmission route. It was a clean energy project. They came in and they actually protected a bunch of habitat in order to compensate for the impacts that building has. And yet, if you have all the boxes checked, like this is one of the best-designed projects that I've had to engage with, and it still took 17 years. You know, something's wrong. And biggest project labor agreement in the history of the Southwest, $20 billion worth of economic impact to the states of New Mexico and Arizona. We should be able to get to yes for a good project in a reasonable amount of time. We should be able to get to no for a poorly designed project. And if you're going to get to no, let's fail fast and then move on to a better project.”

On Heinrich’s Priorities as the Incoming Chairman of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee:

Bolton: “With a new Democratic majority coming in, what changes do you want to further empower committees? Because I think the lesson from this is that when you empower the committees and you empower the Chairman, there's bipartisanship and things get done. How do you take that lesson going forward into the next Congress?

Heinrich: “I think we do better work when committees are empowered, and so one of the things I want from leadership on both sides is to let their Chairman negotiate and get to actual good legislation. I think the more power that is pushed down to the committees, who have the most knowledge of how to come up with a good product, the more that benefits our ability to produce a better product.”

title: Hickenlooper, Bennet, Colleagues Call for Greater U.S.-New Zealand Space Cooperation
text:
WASHINGTON – Today, U.S. Senators John Hickenlooper and Michael Bennet joined seven Senate colleagues to urge Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink to strengthen U.S-New Zealand space cooperation and advance shared national security interests.

“We write to express our continued support for the U.S. Space Force and U.S. Space Command’s efforts to collaborate with allies and partners across the Indo-Pacific and to request your consideration of additional steps to improve such efforts with New Zealand, a key Five Eyes partner, where doing so advances U.S. national security interests and strengthens collective capability,” wrote the senators. “We believe these efforts would complement existing U.S. exchange and interoperability arrangements with Australia and other Five Eyes members to enhance regional deterrence and space-related collaboration.”

The senators highlighted the Royal New Zealand Air Force’s No. 62 Squadron, which leads the Pacific cell of U.S. Space Command’s Commercial Operations (JCO) Unit, and supports training partner nations. They also noted that further development of New Zealand’s space program, combined with the country’s strategic geography and smaller bureaucracy, would advance U.S. national security objectives. These efforts could strengthen allied and partner space superiority through expanded satellite tracking, space surveillance, missile coverage, and communications redundancies while creating new opportunities for collaboration.

“As Senators representing states with U.S. Space Force missions or other space-related equities, we share a deep appreciation of the extent and complexity of securing the space domain,” continued the senators. “For this reason, we believe in the necessity of having ready and capable allies and partners. Increased interactions, particularly through U.S. New Zealand exchanges, present an opportunity to enhance both countries’ capabilities in space. ”

Hickenlooper has led previous efforts to strengthen U.S space security and cooperation. Specifically, he has introduced legislation to protect critical space infrastructure, improve space traffic coordination, and advance military capabilities.

The full text of the letter is available HERE and below.

Dear Secretary Meink,

We write to express our continued support for the U.S. Space Force and U.S. Space Command’s efforts to collaborate with allies and partners across the Indo-Pacific and to request your consideration of additional steps to improve such efforts with New Zealand, a key Five Eyes partner, where doing so advances U.S. national security interests and strengthens collective capability. We believe these efforts would complement existing U.S. exchange and interoperability arrangements with Australia and other Five Eyes members to enhance regional deterrence and space-related collaboration.

During retired Chief of Space Operations General Chance B. Saltzman’s May 2026 visit to New Zealand, he met with officials from the Ministry of Defence and the Royal New Zealand Air Force’s No. 62 Squadron, New Zealand’s only dedicated space unit. The No. 62 Squadron plays a crucial role in the U.S. Space Command’s Joint Commercial Operations (JCO) cells, serving as the Pacific Cell Lead and supporting partner nation training around the world. The Squadron’s participation in the JCO enables New Zealand to build its own space domain awareness capabilities, particularly with regard to satellite tracking.

Additionally, the New Zealand Defence Force (NZDF) works through the U.S.-led Combined Space Operations initiative to protect shared space interests from disruption, denial, or destruction, and promote responsible behavior in the domain. The NZDF has also launched experimental payloads into orbit on U.S. satellites, while Prime Minister Christopher Luxon established a dedicated ministerial position for space in 2023.

These efforts demonstrate the seriousness with which New Zealand’s government and the NZDF approach space. Further maturation of New Zealand’s space program and additional investment in capabilities that complement U.S. and allied efforts would advance U.S. national security objectives, helping ensure allied and partner space superiority by providing opportunities for additional satellite tracking, space surveillance, missile coverage, and communications redundancies. Moreover, the relatively small scale of New Zealand’s military space bureaucracy– coupled with the country’s geographically advantageous launch and operational environments and growing commercial space sector – offers considerable avenues for mutual partnership and opportunities to innovate.

As Senators representing states with U.S. Space Force missions or other space-related equities, we share a deep appreciation of the extent and complexity of securing the space domain. For this reason, we believe in the necessity of having ready and capable allies and partners. Increased interactions, particularly through U.S.-New Zealand exchanges, present an opportunity to enhance both countries’ capabilities in space. Where such arrangements address identified operational needs and provide reciprocal benefits, expanding space-related exchanges between the NZDF and our Joint Force could strengthen interoperability and enhance collective deterrence across the Indo-Pacific.

We stand ready to support efforts, as appropriate, that strengthen U.S. capabilities and enable greater contributions from Indo-Pacific allies and partners. We look forward to engaging further.

Thank you for your attention.

title: Hickenlooper, Commerce Committee Democrats Demand Clear Answers on Nationwide Ground Stop
text:
Ground stop disrupted air travel for nearly 20,000 flights

Letter comes as Trump administration requested an additional $20 billion in federal funding following the incident

WASHINGTON – Today, U.S. Senator John Hickenlooper joined his Democratic colleagues on the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation to demand the Trump administration provide clear answers about what caused Friday’s nationwide ground stop and how they are preventing further incidents. Their letter to Department of Transportation (DOT) Secretary Sean Duffy and Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) Administrator Brian Bedford comes as they are requesting $50 billion – an additional $20 billion from their previous request – to modernize air traffic control.

“The November 13 nationwide ground stop disrupted air travel across the country, eroded public trust in our aviation system, and raised serious questions about the Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA) ability to ensure reliable and resilient operations. Congress expects clear, fact-based answers about the root cause of this disruption and why existing safeguards failed to prevent it,” wrote the senators. “The Department of Transportation (DOT) and FAA must explain how this failure occurred and identify the corrective actions and oversight needed to prevent a recurrence.”

The DOT and FAA leaders have blamed a router malfunction in Arkansas and FAA contractor L3 Harris’ work converting the FAA’s communications network from copper to fiber for the disruption. According to L3 Harris, the copper-to-fiber transition involves converting more than 3,600 routers to Juniper devices. To date, according to the contractor, 400 devices have been installed and 69 are operational.

The senators expressed concerns about the continued deployment of the new routers until the root cause of the failure has been identified.

“Identifying the device that failed does not establish why it failed. The FAA must investigate further to determine the root cause and report to Congress on how it intends to prevent future issues,” the senators continued.

Hickenlooper has consistently advocated for transportation and aviation safety as a member of the Subcommittee on Aviation, Space, and Innovation.

The full text of the letter is available HERE and below:

Dear Secretary Duffy and Administrator Bedford,

The November 13 nationwide ground stop disrupted air travel across the country, eroded public trust in our aviation system, and raised serious questions about the Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA) ability to ensure reliable and resilient operations. Congress expects clear, fact-based answers about the root cause of this disruption and why existing safeguards failed to prevent it. The Department of Transportation (DOT) and FAA must explain how this failure occurred and identify the corrective actions and oversight needed to prevent a recurrence.

Based on information provided to our offices from L3 Harris, the copper-to-fiber transition involves converting 3,648 routers to Juniper devices. To date, it is our understanding that 400 devices have been installed, and 69 are operational. With thousands of conversions remaining, the FAA must address outstanding safety and reliability concerns before expanding installation.

Identifying the device that failed does not establish why it failed. FAA must investigate further to determine the root cause and report to Congress on how it intends to prevent future issues.

We understand the FAA Technical Center tested a sample of Juniper devices before installation. The devices passed pre-deployment testing. The November 13 failure raises serious questions about whether that testing adequately reflected operating conditions or evaluated all potential failure modes or outcomes.

We request an immediate pause on the deployment of additional Juniper devices. Deployment should resume after the FAA demonstrates the devices’ readiness for safe deployment through improved operational testing, independent validation, verified failover capability, and rollback procedures. Congress expects a briefing on these improvements before the FAA resumes deployment of the routers.

The ground stop demonstrated a breakdown in a system Americans rely on, and Congress was left to piece together critical facts. We expect accurate information as soon as it is available. Concerningly, the DOT attributed the November 13 network disruption to “old switches [and] old routers,” when in fact the deployment of the new Juniper routers seem to be the problem. This discrepancy between the FAA’s contractor and the DOT further fuels our concern that the root cause of the disruption has not yet been identified, leaving the potential for another failure.

The DOT and FAA have assigned blame to L3 Harris and used this moment to call for $50 billion in funding for Brand New Air Traffic Control System (BNATCS). This is notably $20 billion more than the request from DOT and the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) that was sent on Thursday, November 12. DOT, FAA and OMB must provide Congress with a complete account of what happened and how additional funding would address the vulnerabilities presented on November 13. DOT and FAA must also take full responsibility for managing contractors working to modernize the NAS.

Congress deserves clear answers on how the FAA is ensuring the safety of the aviation system for the traveling public while these new systems are being deployed.

Further, we request a joint technical briefing with FAA, L3Harris, and Juniper, and the following information no later than November 23, 2026:

An initial safety assessment of operational Juniper devices in the NAS, identifying shared infrastructure dependencies and common points of failures, vulnerabilities in primary and backup telecommunications paths, and the adequacy of failover, rollback, and recovery procedures.

An explanation of why the FAA’s operational systems lacked sufficient redundancy to recover immediately from the November 13 outage.

An explanation of how a cut fiber-optic line or other localized telecommunications failure could result in widespread operational disruption, including actions taken to reinforce network redundancy following the Philadelphia Terminal Radar Approach Control and Minneapolis Air Route Traffic Control Center outages.

Given recent events, Congress is concerned about the FAA’s oversight of the BNATCS program. Modernization cannot come at the expense of operational safety. We expect a prompt response and look forward to working with the FAA to ensure the safety, reliability, and resilience of the NAS.

We are grateful for the air traffic controllers, pilots, flight attendants, and all aviation workers who continue to be impacted by Friday’s events.
