title: Hayes Leads Bicameral Student Food Security Act to Address Food Insecurity on College Campuses
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, Congresswoman Jahana Hayes (CT-05), Ranking Member of the House Subcommittee on Nutrition, Foreign Agriculture, and Horticulture, Congresswoman Norma Torres (CA-35), and Senators Chris Murphy (D-CT), Alex Padilla (D-CA), Bernie Sanders (I- VT), Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), and John Fetterman (D-PA) introduced the Student Food Security Act of 2026, bicameral legislation to address food insecurity faced by college students nationwide.

According to a 2024 Government Accountability Office (GAO) report, nearly 3.8 million college students may face food insecurity, risking their college completion and undermining federal and state investments in higher education. The GAO report found that almost 60% of potentially eligible students were not enrolled in SNAP, highlighting how current eligibility requirements are leaving food-insecure students behind.

The Student Food Security Act would support food-insecure students by expanding eligibility for SNAP, allowing students to use SNAP benefits at on-campus dining facilities, increasing outreach by federal and state agencies to food-insecure students, and establishing an annual grant program to aid colleges and universities in better identifying and serving students with food and housing needs.

“Every student deserves the opportunity to pursue a college education without the added burden of worrying about where their next meal will come from. Yet, food insecurity remains a reality for far too many students, creating barriers that extend beyond the dining hall and into the classroom. At a time when cuts to SNAP threaten access to critical food assistance, we must do more to ensure students are not left without the resources they need to succeed, said Congresswoman Jahana Hayes. The Student Food Security Act takes a comprehensive approach to addressing campus hunger. By expanding SNAP access, strengthening campus outreach, and providing $1 billion annually to help colleges and universities meet the basic needs of students, this legislation will strengthen the safety net for students facing food insecurity.

“As everyday costs continue to rise, too many college students are going hungry while trying to earn their degrees. No student should have to skip meals or choose between buying food and paying for school,” said Congresswoman Torres. "The Student Food Security Act will expand access to SNAP so more students can afford nutritious meals and stay focused on their education and includes the BASIC Act, legislation I lead to invest $1 billion in community colleges and four year institutions to help students with basic needs. We should be giving students every opportunity to succeed and focus on their studies, not allowing hunger to stand in the way of a college degree.”

“No college student should have to sacrifice their health or their education just to make ends meet,” said Senator Padilla. “Our bill would expand access to nutrition assistance and essential resources so that more students can meet their basic needs while balancing their studies.”

“Students shouldn't have to go hungry to make ends meet while getting their degree,” said Senator Warren. “Outdated SNAP rules shut eligible students out of critical assistance, leaving them struggling to afford groceries. The Student Food Security Act ensures no one is forced to choose between paying tuition and putting food on the table.”

“Getting an education shouldn't mean you also have to worry about where your next meal is coming from. No student should have to choose between a degree and a meal,” said Senator Fetterman. “I’m proud to join my colleagues in reintroducing legislation that expands SNAP and gives these institutions more tools to support all of their students.”

Specifically, the Student Food Security Act:

Increases the SNAP eligibility of low-income college students by expanding eligibility to students who qualify for work-study, have a $0 Student Aid Index, meet the financial eligibility criteria for a maximum Pell Grant (even if they have not filed the FAFSA), or are an independent student whose household is otherwise eligible. This would make permanent an expansion of SNAP eligibility that was first enacted in response to the COVID-19 pandemic.

Increases outreach to eligible students by directing the U.S. Department of Education to work with the U.S. Department of Agriculture, the Secretary of Housing and Urban Development, and other relevant agencies to notify students they may be eligible for benefits when they file their application for federal student aid.

Requires the Department of Education to report to Congress with data on student food and housing insecurity, broken out by race and ethnicity, income, first-generation status, Pell eligibility, disability, and student parent status. It also permanently adds validated food security, housing security, and homelessness questions to the National Postsecondary Student Aid Study (NPSAS).

Creates a SNAP student hunger demonstration program to allow students to use their SNAP benefits at on-campus dining facilities at up to ten institutions.

Establishes a $1 billion per year grant program to help institutions support the basic needs of students, which includes physiological and safety necessities that are central conditions for a student to learn. This includes, but is not limited to, nutritious food, health care, childcare, technology, transportation, personal hygiene and clothing, and more. Grants can be used for research, planning, and implementation of strategies which educate students on federal, state, local, and tribal assistance programs. Institutions with increased numbers of Pell Grant recipients will be prioritized. At least 25% of grants must go to community colleges, and at least 25% must go to Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCUs), Tribal Colleges and Universities, and other Minority-Serving Institutions.

title: Himes Statement on Recent Computer Network Outages
text:
Washington, D.C. – U.S. Representative Jim Himes (D-CT), Ranking Member of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, today released the following statement:

“Over the past week, I have heard from many concerned Americans about the series of high profile and disruptive computer network outages, including Microsoft Outlook, an Air Traffic Control system, JP Morgan Chase, and an internal National Security Agency system. I want to be clear that as Ranking Member of the House Intelligence Committee, I have seen no evidence to suggest any of these outages were the result of a malicious actor. To the contrary, the owners of these systems have acknowledged publicly that the outages were caused by internal actions, not by an outside attacker.

“Stepping back, the risk of disruptive or even damaging cyberattacks is very real, and we need to do more to harden our critical infrastructure against attack. The rapid advent of highly cyber capable AI models, including open-weight models, has accelerated the ability of both attackers and defenders to discover vulnerabilities and create exploits, necessitating even greater urgency to patch systems regularly. It is possible that the increased pace of vulnerability discovery and patching could cause more frequent outages, but the breakneck pace of patching we have seen in recent months is vital to shore up the security of all IT infrastructure. Disruptions in networks, whether through internal errors or outside attack, are a fact of life, but we can do much more to be prepared and resilient.”

title: Horsford Congratulates Jeffries: “The People Delivered a Historic House Victory. Now, We Must Deliver the Change They Demand.”
text:
Today, Congressman Steven Horsford (NV-04) released the following statement after House Democrats nominated Leader Hakeem Jeffries, without opposition, as their candidate for Speaker of the House:

“The people delivered this historic victory in the House. Now, we must deliver the change they demand. Under Speaker Jeffries’ leadership, we must get to work on day one to address the affordability crisis and take on the culture of corruption in Washington.

“Hakeem Jeffries and I entered Congress together, and I’m proud to congratulate my friend and colleague on his nomination. I’ve seen his determination and his commitment to working families across the country. He has come to Nevada’s Fourth District and listened to the people I represent. Those are the voices we need to carry into the work ahead.

“The number one priority I hear from Nevadans is making life more affordable, and families across the country are telling us the same thing. They’re doing everything they can and still struggling to pay for housing, groceries, and health care. They need relief, and they expect us to act.

“As a member of the Ways and Means Committee and co-chair of the Congressional Labor Caucus, I will fight for an agenda that rewards work, lowers costs, protects access to affordable health care, and strengthens Social Security and Medicare. People should be able to pay their bills and have something left over to build a future.

“They also deserve to know their government is working for them. With Speaker Jeffries at the helm, we will hold this administration accountable and confront abuses of power. Public office is a public trust. We have a responsibility to protect taxpayer dollars and challenge those who use their positions to enrich themselves.

“Speaker Jeffries knows what it takes to bring people together and lead in this moment. Working people and families are counting on us to lower costs, protect their health care, and make government work for them. They put their trust in us. Now, we must govern - for the people.”

title: Hoyer Statement on Nomination of Leader Jeffries for Speaker of the House
text:
WASHINGTON, DC – Today, Congressman Steny H. Hoyer (MD-05) released the following statement after the House Democratic Caucus voted to nominate Hakeem Jeffries for Speaker of the House in the 120th Congress:

“For nearly the first two centuries of our nation’s independence, African Americans were made to endure slavery, segregation, and disenfranchisement. The appointment of Justice Thurgood Marshall to the highest court in our land in 1967 and the election of President Barack Obama in 2008 to the highest executive office in our country were milestones in the march toward equality and equal representation. Today, our nation took another historic step forward with the Democratic Caucus’s election of Hakeem Jeffries as the Speaker-designate of the House of Representatives. When he is officially elected by the House in January, he will become the first African American to hold that position.

“The speakership belongs not to one party but to the Congress and to all Americans. As Speaker, Hakeem Jeffries will have an opportunity to demonstrate House Democrats’ values and our vision for America, just as he will have an obligation to safeguard this institution as a forum for building consensus and seeking agreement among the representatives of 330 million Americans. I have great confidence in his ability to lead the House and to deliver on the affordability agenda the American people overwhelmingly voted for earlier this month. Though I will no longer be a Member of Congress next year, I look forward to watching Speaker-designate Jeffries and his leadership team work hard for the American people, for this institution that he and I both cherish as the jewel in our democracy, and for the principles of equality and opportunity our Caucus continues to champion.

“Congratulations, Speaker-designate Jeffries – and congratulations to our nation for this critical step toward another historic milestone.”

title: REP. HOYLE'S STATEMENT ON LEADER JEFFRIES BEING NOMINATED SPEAKER OF THE HOUSE
text:
Washington, D.C. - Congresswoman Val Hoyle (OR-04) released the following statement today on Leader Hakeem Jeffries being nominated as Speaker of the House:

“I congratulate Speaker-elect Jeffries and all members of Democratic leadership on their election. As the first Black Speaker of the House, this is not a small thing. I look forward to working with our leadership team to ensure that we follow through in making government responsive to the American people who overwhelmingly gave us a mandate for change. It’s time to stand up for working people and focus on affordability and accountability.”

title: SEEC Members Renew U.S. Climate Leadership at COP31
text:
Washington, D.C. – This week, 18 members of the House of Representatives, including House Sustainable Energy and Environment Coalition (SEEC) Vice Chairs Reps. Don Beyer (VA-08), Suzanne Bonamici (OR-01), Sean Casten (IL-06), and Mike Levin (CA-49), as well as Reps. Jared Huffman (CA-02), Yassamin Ansari (AZ-03), Ami Bera (CA-06), Kathy Castor (FL-14), Salud Carbajal (CA-24), Adriano Espaillat (NY-13), Maxine Dexter (OR-03), Jonathan Jackson (IL-01), Teresa Leger Fernández (NM-03), Lucy McBath (GA-06), Dave Min (CA-47), Emily Randall (WA-06), Raul Ruiz (CA-25), and Nikema Williams (GA-05), joined the international climate community at the 31st Conference of Parties (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye to renew and strengthen U.S. engagement on climate leadership on the global stage. The member delegation reaffirmed partnerships and highlighted shared challenges, including topics ranging from energy affordability and clean electrification to food security and disaster resilience. Members returned to Congress with new relationships and new ideas to build a more affordable, clean, and healthy future for our nation and the world.

SEEC members participated in events across 8 themes.

Forests, Nature, and Natural-Capital Resilience

SEEC members highlighted how protecting and restoring ecosystems can preserve nature’s capacity to absorb and sequester carbon, while bolstering climate resilience for our planet.

“For millions of people around the world, forests sustain their livelihoods, provide clean water, and store the carbon we desperately need to keep out of the atmosphere,” said House Natural Resources Committee Ranking Member Jared Huffman (CA-02). “As climate change fuels more destructive wildfires and floods, protecting the forests we still have and restoring those we’ve lost is essential to protecting communities, supporting local economies, and giving people a say in the future of the lands they depend on. We’ll fight to keep public lands in public hands, restore the lands and waters our communities depend on, and cut the pollution that’s making these disasters worse.”

Adaptation, Disaster Resilience, & Community Preparedness

SEEC members joined panels and discussions on adaptation, disaster resilience, and community preparedness to highlight how adaptation must be a central pillar of climate action.

“Extreme weather threatens our critical infrastructure and makes life more expensive – something my neighbors in Tampa Bay know too well,” said Congresswoman Kathy Castor (FL-14). “At COP, we showed up to work with and learn from our international partners to address these shared challenges together. We’re ready to put SEEC Institute’s Thriving Economy Project into action – our blueprint to lower costs, strengthen American leadership, and make our communities safer.”

Clean Electrification, Climate Finance,and Private-Sector Competitiveness SEEC Members engaged with experts in the clean electrification and climate finance space, and engaged with private sector voices from around the world.

“Anyone who can access electricity, heat, and transportation without burning fossil fuels not only lowers their costs, but also cuts down on pollution and helps provide a livable planet to our children and grandchildren,” said Congressman Sean Casten (IL-06). “Clean electrification is the moral and economically smart path forward for anyone interested in helping both their pocketbooks and our future. It's an imperative next step in addressing both the cost-of-living crisis and climate crisis."

Ocean, Science, & Coastal Resilience SEEC Members participated in events related to ocean, science, and coastal resilience to highlight how the climate crisis is transforming marine ecosystems and coastal livelihoods.

“The ocean has given us time we did not earn,” said Congresswoman Suzanne Bonamici (OR-01). “It has absorbed our emissions, buffered our climate, and fed our communities. The challenge now is whether we will answer that generosity with responsibility. If we get the science right, and we get the trust right, ocean carbon removal will have a fair chance to prove itself and we will have the evidence to decide wisely. The ocean, and the communities that depend on it, deserve our best evidence and our full partnership.”

Transatlantic Industrial, Trade, and Energy Policy SEEC Members highlighted how the U.S. and Europe must work together to transition away from fossil fuel dependence.

“The United States and Europe have a shared responsibility to lead the global transition away from fossil fuels,” said Congressman Mike Levin (CA-49). “That means working together to accelerate clean energy deployment, strengthen our economies, and reduce our dependence on fossil fuel markets. Our transatlantic partnership is essential to building a cleaner, more secure, and more affordable energy future.”

Climate Equity, Mobility, and Community Leadership

SEEC Members highlighted how the climate challenge exacerbates existing social inequities and climate solutions must expand economic opportunity, while giving communities agency in shaping their futures.

“The families with the least wealth, insurance, and political voice are hit first and recover last, from Chicago to the Horn of Africa to the Caribbean. Congress’ job is to help people stay home safely where they can, and move with dignity when they can’t,” said Congressman Jonathan Jackson (IL-01). “I am proud to lead the Congressional Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion Caucus in the House of Representatives. Equity should not be a controversial topic, and I am proud to be here with you today to discuss how we can work together on equitable solutions to the climate crisis.”

Climate, Energy, and National Security SEEC Members joined discussions on how climate resilience, clean energy deployment, and international cooperation are essential to our collective security.

“Now more than ever – it’s important to show the world that Democrats in Congress are committed to engaging with the global community to ensure that we are living up to our obligations to protect our planet and our future,” said Congresswoman Emily Randall (WA-06). “I’m grateful to bring the stories and experiences of my neighbors in Washington’s 6th district who face climate threats like coastal erosion and wildfires, and hear from other leaders and organizations that are both domestically and globally situated to help our communities achieve a climate-secure future.”

Food Security, Agricultural Innovation, and Trade SEEC Members participated in events related to food security, agricultural innovation, and trade that spoke to solutions to help farmers adapt to the climate crisis, build more resilient food systems on a global level, and ensure that feeding the world and protecting the planet go hand in hand.

title: Congressman Glenn Ivey’s statement on ICE’s release of University of Maryland student Maria Flores Garcia and her mother from custody
text:
WASHINGTON — Today, Congressman Glenn Ivey, (MD-04) released the following statement following ICE’s release of University of Maryland student Maria Flores Garcia and her mother from custody:

“Maria Flores Garcia is a student, a former high school valedictorian, and a valued member of our community. She never should have been detained. Period. Her case exposes the hypocrisy of an administration that claims to target the ‘worst of the worst’ while detaining young people like Maria.

“From day one, we demanded answers and fought for Maria’s release. Our community refused to stay silent, and the groundswell of support from students, families, and elected leaders made clear that Maria was not alone.

“I am relieved that Maria and her mother are free and can return to their family. But let's be clear: this never should have happened. We will continue to hold this administration accountable and demand that our immigration laws be enforced with fairness, humanity, and common sense.”

title: Rep. Ronny Jackson’s SAFE CATTLE Act Advances in House Natural Resources Committee
text:
WASHINGTON — Today, the House Committee on Natural Resources passed Representative Ronny Jackson’s (TX-13) H.R. 7466, the Safeguarding America’s Food Economy and Controlling Agricultural Threats to Livestock and Enterprises (SAFE CATTLE) Act by voice vote out of Committee. It now awaits further consideration by the full House.

This important legislation aims to advance the coordination between the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) and the Department of the Interior (DOI) to address the threat posed by New World Screwworm in wildlife, prevent its spread, and safeguard America’s livestock industry and food supply chain.

“New World Screwworm poses a serious threat to American agriculture, our livestock industry, and the livelihoods of the hardworking ranchers of Texas’ Thirteenth Congressional District,” said Rep. Jackson. “The SAFE CATTLE Act will strengthen federal coordination and ensure we have the tools and resources necessary to protect American agriculture.”

“New World Screwworm is a plague on American livestock and wildlife, threatening food security and the livelihoods of ranchers,” said Chairman Westerman. “I commend Rep. Jackson on leading legislation to improve federal coordination to better contain the screwworm and prevent its spread.”

title: Smith Secures $580,000 for Texas County Memorial Hospital Through One, Big, Beautiful Bill’s Rural Health Transformation Program
text:
HOUSTON, Mo. – Texas County Memorial Hospital has been awarded roughly $580,000 through the Rural Health Transformation Program (RHTP), an initiative that Congressman Jason Smith (MO-08) authored and fought for as part of the One, Big, Beautiful Bill. The funding will go toward upgrades that keep the hospital running safely and efficiently for the families and patients who depend on it.

Congressman Smith said, “Rural hospitals are the backbone of communities like the one I grew up in and those I represent, and TCMH is relied on by thousands of families in southern Missouri. Earlier this year, I visited this hospital and saw firsthand the quality of care this facility provides its patients and how important it is to the community. Whether it’s surgery, emergency care, or a routine visit, this hospital is where our neighbors turn, and the staff can only do their jobs well if the building and equipment are in good shape.

“That’s exactly why I authored the Rural Health Transformation Program as part of the One, Big, Beautiful Bill. Rural communities deserve the same quality of care as anywhere else in the nation, and I knew the type of investment included in the RHTP would deliver just that. I’m glad to see Texas County Memorial receive this award, and I will keep fighting to make sure rural Missouri hospitals have the resources to keep caring for their communities for years to come.”

title: Jayapal Introduces Legislation to Turn Down the Volume on Streaming Ads
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — U.S. Representative Pramila Jayapal (WA-07) is introducing the CALM Modernization Act, legislation that updates the 2010 CALM Act, which directed the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to prevent broadcasters from playing ads at a louder volume than regular programming. The original CALM Act does not apply to modern streaming services and has allowed streaming services to turn up the volume of ads on their platforms.

“The FCC made television broadcasters end the use of blaring TV ads. There’s no reason that streaming services should have a free pass to do exactly the same thanks to a loophole,” said Jayapal. “The CALM Modernization Act will ensure that streaming platforms put consumers first and turn down the volume, so people can enjoy a show without having to hold the remote the entire time.”

The CALM Modernization Act would:

Extend the CALM Act’s prohibition of ads louder than their accompanying programming to ad-supported streaming services;

Strengthen the ability of the FCC to enforce violations;

Direct the Government Accountability Office (GAO) to report on the effectiveness of the CALM Act in moderating loudness, evaluate enforcement provisions of the law, and recommend policy solutions to better moderate commercial advertisement loudness.

The CALM Modernization Act is co-sponsored by Representative Eleanor Homes Norton (DC-AL).

title: Jayapal Statement on GEO Group’s Sale of NWDC to ICE, Cashing in on $453 million of Taxpayer Money
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — U.S. Representative Pramila Jayapal (WA-07), Ranking Member of the Subcommittee on Immigration, Integrity, Security, and Enforcement, released the following statement after GEO Group, a private, for-profit detention center operator, announced they were selling the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma, W.A. to the U.S. government for $453 million, just weeks after Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) awarded them a $1.5 billion, 10-year federal contract. The city of Tacoma assessed the value of the property at just under $72.6 million, less than 1/6th of the price ICE just paid.

“I am deeply concerned by what appears to be a gross misuse of taxpayer dollars to pad the pockets of the GEO Group, a private, for-profit company that has overseen real mistreatment and abuses of detained people across the company. In the height of this Administration’s complete disregard for the real pain that families are suffering with higher gas and grocery prices and skyrocketing healthcare costs, it is unfathomable that GEO has announced it intends to use the net proceeds from this sale for stock buybacks, in yet another move to put profits over the safety and health of the people it detains.

“Let me also be very clear: if this is a thinly-veiled attempt by GEO Group to shield themselves from answering for any of the mistreatment of detained people at the Northwest ICE Processing Center, it simply will not work. In Congress, we intend to investigate every one of these sales and to demand accountability from these private, for-profit detention centers that have engaged in pay-to-play schemes with this Administration and completely ignored basic human dignity and safety.

“Since Trump returned to office, for-profit prison corporations, including GEO Group and CoreCivic, have raked in federal funding and taxpayer money, while avoiding oversight every step of the way. Under their watch, 62 immigrants have died in detention. I have visited facilities that were completely unlivable, and have heard reports of moldy food, disgusting water, and a lack of medical care from multiple other detention centers around the country.

“Now GEO and ICE are teaming up in Washington State to avoid having to answer for any of their abuses, while also taking home more of Americans’ hard-earned money. I will be investigating this corruption, and we will hold them accountable.”

Earlier this year, ICE purchased two CoreCivic detention centers in California for $1.5 billion and facilities in Kansas and Minnesota for $734 million. Despite these facilities having been purchased by ICE, CoreCivic continues to manage operations. In October, ICE purchased three detention facilities in Adelanto, California, from GEO Group for $950 million. Similarly, GEO will continue running the facilities and says ICE is considering buying 10 facilities or more from the company.

Under the Trump administration, GEO and CoreCivic have reaped enormous financial gains. In 2025, both companies received an additional $2 billion in profit each, a 13 percent increase in revenue, and there has been a revolving door between the Trump administration and these companies — including border czar Tom Homan and Acting ICE Director David Venturella, who were previously employed by GEO.

Jayapal led Members of the W.A. delegation in demanding answers and transparency on ongoing efforts from ICE to purchase existing immigration detention centers currently owned and operated by GEO Group and CoreCivic, specifically citing the Northwest ICE Processing Center ahead of the October contract award.

title: SPEAKER-DESIGNATE JEFFRIES ON MS NOW: “WE’VE GOT TO MAKE MEANINGFUL, DRAMATIC, DECISIVE PROGRESS”
text:
Today, House Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries appeared on MS NOW’s The Briefing with Jen Psaki, where he reflected on the historic nature of his nomination for Speaker of the House and made clear that under his leadership, House Democrats will continue their fight to make life better for the American people into the 120th Congress.

JEN PSAKI: Joining me now is House Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries. It’s great to see you. This was quite a day, so thank you for taking the time to be here with me tonight.

LEADER JEFFRIES: Great to be with you.

JEN PSAKI: Let me start with this. I just played some of Congressman Jim Clyburn’s reflections on the significance of your nomination and how it is—the way he talked about it is how it’s a continuation of John Lewis’s legacy and how he feels both vindicated and redeemed by that. I know he had even more extensive things that were reported that he said during the Caucus meeting today, but I just want—I want to start by asking you about what it was like to hear those reflections from someone like Jim Clyburn.

LEADER JEFFRIES: It was incredibly moving. I think everyone in that Caucus room, when Jim Clyburn speaks, and that’s always the case, you could hear a pin drop. But as he started to reflect upon his own journey, John Lewis, what it meant, of course, his close friendship to John Lewis. I had the opportunity to serve with Congressman Lewis for eight years. Mr. Clyburn talked about the fact that he met his wife, who’s up in heaven right now, amazing woman, in a jail cell, fighting to push back against the horrors of the Jim Crow South. And to be on that kind of trajectory and now to stand on Jim Clyburn’s shoulders, John Lewis’ shoulders, Shirley Chisholm’s shoulders in representing the district now in Brooklyn that Shirley Chisholm once represented. And in fact, she was my Congresswoman during the first 12 years of my life. Never had an opportunity to meet her, but now have an opportunity to continue to build upon the incredible fight and progress that she helped to bring about for America.

JEN PSAKI: Such a part of history. I know it’s so rare for someone like you, even before the election, to have time to reflect, and today is a rare time to do that before you take over in January. Sometimes, I think reflection comes from hearing from the people you love and how they’re digesting it. Have you talked to your mom? I know you’re close to her. Have you talked to your mom today? How is it sitting with her?

LEADER JEFFRIES: Well, I called my mom before the vote. I haven’t talked to her subsequent to the vote, but whenever I’m approaching a big moment, I usually reach out to Mom and ask her to say a prayer. Just want to hear her voice. She raised me in the Cornerstone Baptist Church. In fact, we were in church every Sunday, Christmas play, Mother’s Day play, Easter play. But when I look back on growing up in the church and having that opportunity at a young age, probably starting at two years old, and Mom making sure that we always, my younger brother Hasan and I, we knew our parts, and then we would stand before an affirming audience and learn how to present publicly. All of that, I think, traces up to this point where we now have this opportunity together as House Democrats, an extraordinary group of patriotic Members who represent the broad, gorgeous mosaic of the American people, and all of us committed to making a big difference in the lives of the American people, dealing with the affordability crisis and, of course, making sure that we push back against the unprecedented corruption that the Trump Cartel has unleashed on the American people.

JEN PSAKI: And we’re going to talk about all of that. And I should note we’re also going to talk to Congressman Raskin, too, about those barnburner letters that went out today. I want to ask you, too, just another thing about today, because you organized a closed-door meeting with former President Barack Obama with the new Members. What was that like? What advice did he have for the new Members? And even for you, if you had a chance to talk to him one-on-one?

LEADER JEFFRIES: Yeah, I did have a chance to meet with the President one-on-one, and it’s always wonderful to connect with President Obama. I’ve been in close contact with him as we’ve been navigating the trials and tribulations, the turbulence of the moment that we’ve been working through since January 20 of 2025, and he always has sage wisdom and advice. And I was so appreciative that he was willing to surprise the new Members of Congress today and then to spend almost two hours with us answering questions, sharing his reflections, talking about the American journey, talking about the importance of always holding firm to our values and our ideals, but also recognizing that in a legislative body, our objectives, our job is to make progress for the American people to advance the ball. And at this moment,we’ve got to make meaningful, dramatic, decisive progress and bold change, because that’s what the country needs and deserves at this moment in time.

JEN PSAKI: There hasn’t been a lot that’s come out of that meeting, but Don Leonard, who’s a new incoming Member, did tweet, ‘Sitting in a small theater with President Obama and the new Members-elect. Someone asked him about Elon Musk. He told us now is the time to amend our constitution. Now is the time. We are the people.’ I assume the context of that is Citizens United. Is that the context of that?

LEADER JEFFRIES: Yeah, in fact, I’ve made clear over the last several months that one of the high priorities that we’ll have as House Democrats is to get unregulated big money out of politics. Enough. Now, thankfully, in this most recent cycle, notwithstanding the fact that we’ve seen MAGA billionaires spend hundreds of millions of dollars trying to steal or trying to buy a Republican majority in the House or in the Senate, that the people of this great country have made clear America is not for sale. But we still have Citizens United out there. And we still have the ability of these MAGA billionaires to flood into our election all of this unregulated money, not designed to help out everyday Americans or to bring about enlightened policy, but to maintain advantage and privilege for the wealthy, the well-off and the well-connected. And so, I think President Obama has been clear that we’ve got to aggressively tackle Citizens United. That’s certainly something that, as House Democrats, we plan to do, and plan to do very early in the new Congress.

JEN PSAKI: Listen, you’re now—you’re going to be second in line to the presidency. He’s a very popular former president, so that’s a lot of power there supporting that. It’s also, I mean, Elon Musk, obviously, just flushed $500 million down the toilet, but he’s the perfect example of this. That’s the context, it sounds like, through which it came up. And he, given his past history, there’s a lot to look into him, I think, about, or I think this is a question for you. I mean, from gutting DOGE to all of the cuts that we’re now seeing impacts of, including in our cybersecurity apparatus in the federal government. I don’t—he appeared during the DealBook Conference today. We’ve just played some of this. And he seemed to be trying to black out, memory hole, from the American public everything he did during that period of time. I mean, he suggested he’s moderate. He suggested he doesn’t even know what MAGA means. To me, it seems clear he’s trying to kind of warm himself so that people don’t look more closely at him, but do you think he should be investigated?

LEADER JEFFRIES: I think that everyone who has been part of this MAGA extremist movement that has unleashed all of this carnage and damage on the American people should be prepared to answer questions as it relates to what has happened, why it’s happened and, of course, from our view, how do we prevent this type of carnage from ever happening again. So, I’m not going to get out ahead of any specific investigation or name any specific individual because that’s going to be the job of Jamie Raskin and the House Judiciary Committee Democrats. They’re going to do an amazing job. Certainly, Robert Garcia and the House Oversight Committee Democrats. We’ve made clear that if folks out there have been stealing from the American people, shortchanging the American people or screwing over the American people, that in the new Congress, we’re going to hold the crooks accountable.

JEN PSAKI: And there’s no—my point here is there’s no attempts to rewrite his history or warm himself that is going to change who people want to investigate if they want to investigate him in Congress.

LEADER JEFFRIES: Not at all. And as a matter of fact, I think he was the individual who held up a chainsaw and began the process of trying to detonate things like Social Security and Medicare and perhaps setting in motion what occurred in that One Big Ugly Bill. So look, we got to follow the facts. We got to apply the law. We’re going to be guided by the Constitution. We’re going to let the chips fall where they may. And we’ve promised that we’re going to deliver affordability as a priority and accountability as a priority.

JEN PSAKI: Let me ask you about—you’ve laid out some of your specific priorities. I should note you’re not taking power for six weeks here, but you’ve outlined in your letter to the Caucus, when you said you were going to be running for Speaker, some of the specific things you wanted to address. You reiterated them yesterday in a press conference, including bringing down the high cost of gas and groceries, doing more about housing. Yesterday, I thought it was very interesting that you talked pretty extensively, you got quite animated talking about healthcare. You talked about specifically reversing Trump’s Medicaid cuts, extending ACA tax credits, lowering the age of Medicare eligibility, expanding coverage to include vision, hearing and dental, among other things. There’s a lot of broad agreement in the public, but I think also in Congress about this sort of thing. There’s a lot you want to do in the first 100 days, but is that the first step? Is healthcare the first step that everybody should expect come January 3?

LEADER JEFFRIES: Well, I certainly think that right out of the gate, we’re going to aggressively move to end this reckless and costly war of choice—

JEN PSAKI: That’s first?

LEADER JEFFRIES: —in Iran. Well, we’ll figure out the exact order of what takes place January 3, January 4, January 5, January 6, January 7, but certainly I would say three broad areas: ending the war, stopping the Trump Tariffs and reversing the damage that’s been done as it relates to the healthcare of the American people. And that’s got to include reversing the Medicaid cuts and also extending the Affordable Care Act tax credits. I think there’s broad consensus amongst the Caucus and amongst the American people that these things need to be done. With respect to healthcare, we also promised throughout this campaign that we’re going to fight to make healthcare affordable for every single American. And that’s a two-step process. Step one is to reverse the damage that’s been done and fix our broken healthcare system in terms of what they visited upon the American people, meaning the MAGA extremists. But step two is a recognition that the status quo is not acceptable, and we’ve got to build the best possible healthcare system for the American people. And from my standpoint, yes, that absolutely should involve lowering the age of Medicare eligibility. It should involve expanding coverage to include vision and hearing and dental, and we’ve got to make sure that we’re covering every single child in the United States of America. And I believe that on the House side, led by Frank Pallone and the Energy and Commerce Committee and Richie Neal and the Ways and Means Committee, and on the Senate side, led by soon-to-be Chairman Bernie Sanders of the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee and Ron Wyden, the Chair of the Finance Committee, that we can find common ground amongst our two chambers to take the type of decisive, bold action on healthcare and a whole host of other issues to basically put the American people in the best possible position so they can live an affordable life, a comfortable life and a good life.

JEN PSAKI: And my bet is you all are going to pass some things, and you’re going to send it to Donald Trump and dare him to veto it.

LEADER JEFFRIES: That would be correct.

JEN PSAKI: Alright, House Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries. Congratulations on a huge day. Thanks for spending some time with me tonight.

LEADER JEFFRIES: Thank you.

title: SPEAKER-DESIGNATE JEFFRIES: “WE’RE COMMITTED TO DELIVERING THE CHANGE THAT THE AMERICAN PEOPLE DESERVE”
text:

title: Joyce Reintroduces Bicameral, Bipartisan Legislation to Support First Responders Struggling with PTSD
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, Congressman Dave Joyce (OH-14) and Congresswoman Deborah Ross (NC-02) reintroduced the Fighting Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder Act of 2026. This bicameral, bipartisan legislation aims to combat the rising rates of Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) among first responders and to address the long-term mental health consequences associated with PTSD. The legislation would direct the Justice Department (DOJ) to develop treatment programs for police, fire, emergency medical, and 911 personnel who suffer from job-related PTSD or acute stress disorder. The Senate has recently passed the companion legislation led by Senators Chuck Grassley (R-IA) and Chris Coons (D-DE).

“Our first responders put their lives on the line every day to protect our families and serve our communities,” said Congressman Joyce. “Congress has a responsibility to ensure they have the resources and support necessary to manage the immense pressures of their jobs and address the realities of PTSD. I want to thank my colleagues for joining me on this bicameral, bipartisan legislation and encourage other members to join us in this cause.”

“The first responders and law enforcement officers who put their lives on the line to protect our communities experience a tremendous mental toll that often goes unseen,” said Congresswoman Ross. “Their work to keep us safe puts them at higher risk of post-traumatic stress disorder and related mental illnesses. It’s time Congress acts to ensure these brave individuals can access the care they deserve while serving communities in North Carolina and across the country.”

Background

Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder disproportionately affects first responders. According to estimates cited by the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA), up to 30% of first responders develop behavioral health conditions such as PTSD. When undiagnosed or left untreated, PTSD leads to higher rates of anxiety and depression, substance and alcohol abuse, and an increase in suicidal ideation.

To address this growing crisis, this bill directs the Attorney General to develop evidence-based programs that will be made available to public safety officers across our country to treat and address PTSD. In crafting these proposals, the Attorney General must engage and consult with local, state, and federal agencies that employ first responders and non-governmental organizations that advocate on their behalf. Once these proposals are drafted, they will be submitted to Congress for formal consideration.

This bill is endorsed by the Sergeants Benevolent Association of the NYPD, the Federal Law Enforcement Officers Association, the National Association of Police Organizations, the Major County Sheriffs of America (MCSA), the Association of State Criminal Investigative Agencies (ASCIA), and the National Narcotic Officers’ Associations’ Coalition (NNOAC).

title: Ranking Members Kamlager-Dove, Raskin, and Meeks Probe Whether Lutnick’s Family Finances Shaped His Response to the NVIDIA Spy Scandal
text:
Washington, D.C. — Today, Rep. Sydney Kamlager-Dove (CA-37), Ranking Member of the House Foreign Affairs Subcommittee on South and Central Asia with jurisdiction over export controls; Rep. Jamie Raskin (MD-8), Ranking Member of the House Judiciary Committee; and Rep. Gregory Meeks (NY-5), Ranking Member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, sent a letter to Cantor Fitzgerald Chairman Brandon Lutnick demanding records to determine whether his father, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, blocked efforts to stop the suspected smuggling of advanced NVIDIA chips to China while his family’s firm held hundreds of millions of dollars in NVIDIA stock.

The letter comes days after NVIDIA announced that its CEO, Jensen Huang, had resigned amid revelations of an alleged Chinese intelligence operation tied to the suspected smuggling of billions of dollars in restricted chips.

“[T]he American people deserve to know: Did the Secretary of Commerce seriously and perhaps irreversibly compromise U.S. national security interests to make money for his adult children and Cantor Fitzgerald?” wrote the lawmakers.

From September 2025 to March 2026, White House and U.S. intelligence officials examined whether a Chinese intelligence operation had targeted NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang to help smuggle restricted AI chips to China. China’s Ministry of State Security reportedly recruited Alice Huang, the former chief executive of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based NVIDIA customer, to compromise him. Jensen Huang resigned after admitting that he had multiple extramarital affairs, including with the alleged Chinese asset.

As U.S. officials pressed to cut off Megaspeed’s access to advanced NVIDIA chips, Secretary Lutnick reportedly resisted. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said four federal agencies had backed blacklisting Megaspeed for months while Lutnick’s Commerce Department, which controls the blacklist, held out.

Before Lutnick became Commerce Secretary, Cantor Fitzgerald had disclosed holding more than 3.5 million NVIDIA shares. After his confirmation, Lutnick agreed to transfer ownership of the firm to trusts benefiting his adult children. While U.S. officials were scrutinizing Megaspeed, Cantor Fitzgerald cut its reported NVIDIA shareholdings by nearly half. The firm still held roughly $310 million in NVIDIA shares at the end of March 2026.

Secretary Lutnick’s push to weaken proposed chip export restrictions raises another question about whether Cantor Fitzgerald’s business interests influenced his decisions. The New York Times reported that Secretary Lutnick pushed to narrow proposed restrictions on overseas data centers that use advanced NVIDIA chips to serve Chinese customers. One project that could be affected is a Malaysian data center run by a Cantor Fitzgerald client.

The lawmakers are demanding records identifying every NVIDIA trade Cantor Fitzgerald has made since January 2024, along with an accounting of the firm’s business dealings in China and Southeast Asia. They are also seeking internal and client communications about U.S. export controls and suspected chip smuggling, communications with the Commerce Department about NVIDIA, Megaspeed, and Asian data center projects, and records concerning President Trump’s reported NVIDIA investments.

The lawmakers also called on Cantor Fitzgerald to immediately preserve all relevant records, including encrypted messages and business communications on personal devices, and to confirm in writing by December 1 that it has done so.

title: CBS: Katherine Clark of Massachusetts elected as next House majority leader by Democrats in historic first
text:
Democrats made history on Wednesday by voting to make Massachusetts Congresswoman Katherine Clark the next majority leader of the U.S. House of Representatives.

The 63-year-old from Revere will be the first woman to serve as a majority leader in Congress. Currently the House minority whip, Clark ran unopposed for the majority leader position in the Democratic leadership elections.

“I’m honored to have earned the trust of my colleagues to serve as House Majority Leader,” Clark said in a social media statement. “The American people sent us to Washington to deliver. Now it’s time to lower costs and build a future where every family can thrive. Let’s get to work.”

What is the House Majority Leader?

The majority leader is the second-in-command to the Speaker of the House, a job that is widely expected to go to New York Rep. Hakeem Jeffries after he won the nomination from his Democratic colleagues by a vote of 251 to 11 on Wednesday.

As majority leader, Clark will be responsible for day-to-day management of the House floor and setting the legislative calendar once the new Congress convenes in January.

“House Democrats will succeed by working as a team. We still face a tyrant in the White House, and we must devote our full energy to pushing back and pressing forward together,” Clark wrote in a letter to her colleagues earlier this month, asking for their vote. “Our unity is our greatest strength, and I will do everything in my power to ensure we stand strong together over the next two years.”

Who is Katherine Clark?

Clark is set to be the highest-ranking House member from Massachusetts since Tip O’Neill was speaker in the 1980s. WBZ-TV political analyst Jon Keller said that could mean millions of dollars in funding for the state.

“That’s an area where during the last two years of the Trump administration we have really been hurt by cuts and federal research grants and other funding sources,” Keller said.

Clark, who previously served in the Massachusetts Legislature and on the Melrose School Committee, was sworn into Congress in 2013 after winning a special election to replace now-Sen. Ed Markey.

Childcare issues have been one of Clark’s priorities in office; she introduced the Babies Act in 2022 to support new mothers with access to birth centers and midwives. She was also an outspoken opponent of President Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill,” saying it was “incredibly cruel” for cutting Medicaid and food stamps.

title: USA Today: Katherine Clark first woman majority leader, first from MA in 50 years
text:
Rep. Katherine Clark, D-Mass., is set to become the first woman to serve as majority leader in the United States House of Representatives.

The newly-elected Democratic caucus nominated Clark, who represents Massachusetts’s 5th District, on Nov. 18. She was unopposed for the role.

Clark will be the first woman to hold the position as well as the first person from Massachusetts since Rep. Tip O’Neill, D-Mass., served in the role from 1973-1977.

“Thank you to the American people and my House Democratic colleagues. I’m honored to serve as Majority Leader for the 120th Congress — the first woman to ever do so,” Clark said on social media. “Let’s get to work!”

She was one of several “firsts” to be nominated to leadership roles Wednesday: Democrats also elected Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, D-NY, as the first Black Speaker of the House and Rep. Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., as the first Latino Majority Whip.

Clark has represented the 5th District, which stretches from Framingham in the MetroWest to Revere and Winthrop on the coast, since 2013. She has served as House Whip since 2022.

Massachusetts members expected to take top positions across the board

In addition to Clark, several members of the Massachusetts congressional delegation are expected to take top posts in congressional committees.

Rep. Jim McGovern, D-Mass., is expected to chair the House Rules Committee, which decides how bills make it to the House floor, while Rep. Richard Neal, D-Mass., will likely head Ways and Means, the chief tax-writing committee.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren is expected to become the head of the Senate Banking Committee.

title: WCVB: Mass. Rep. Katherine Clark nominated to become first woman House majority leader
text:
Rep. Katherine Clark, the House Minority Whip who has represented Massachusetts’s fifth district since 2013, has been nominated to become the first woman to serve as House Majority Leader after the blue wave election propelled Democrats to control of the chamber in the next Congress.

“It is beyond exciting,” the 63-year-old from Revere told WCVB’s “On The Record” last week about the possibility. “It is historic in that, as you said, the first woman in the 250 years of our country to hold this position, which is the second in seniority in the House of Representatives.”

Clark noted that the 120th Congress will also include a record 120 women in the House Democratic Caucus.

Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York’s 8th District also made history Wednesday when he was nominated to become the first Black speaker of the House as Democrats take control.

“Hakeem has been a steady leader for us through the four years of minority, not afraid to take on this administration or anybody who is cheating the American people, and he has delivered a huge victory,” Clark said on “On The Record.” “Hakeem played a huge role in making sure that Democrats were poised to win this House by what is a landslide.”

Rep. Ayanna Pressley also said she supports Jeffries’s nomination, saying in part:

“The people delivered a mandate for bold, transformative change, and Democrats have a responsibility to honor that mandate by pursuing an affirmative agenda that goes as far and deep as the hurt our communities are facing… Today, I supported his nomination in caucus to be our next Speaker as our negotiations continue, and I will continue working to ensure Democrats deliver and that our shared agenda is responsive and urgent.”

Clark told “On The Record” that she, Jeffries and other party leaders are working to set priorities for the next two years. She said that includes considering priorities from the party’s progressive wing.

“With a 260-person Democratic majority, we are going to have the ability to really focus on the American people, put them back on the agenda,” Clark said.

Clark said Americans can expect “quick action” from Democrats to reverse cuts to programs made during the first two years of President Donald Trump’s term.

“That is what this election was about, making sure that they are not paying the price for corruption,” she said.

Thomas Whalen, a political historian and author from Boston University, emphasized the significance of Clark’s election.

“She’s broken a ceiling here that’s been long overdue,” Whalen said.

He also noted the potential impact for Massachusetts, saying, “You could just turn on the federal money spigots here, because all that funding is going to be pouring into her, at least a good part of it into Massachusetts, since, you know, we haven’t seen that since the days of Ted Kennedy and Tip O’Neill in the state.”

Rep. Pete Aguilar of California was nominated to become the first Latino majority whip.

Massachusetts Rep. Richard Neal is set to return as chair of the House Ways and Means Committee, and Massachusetts Rep. Jim McGovern will continue as chair of the Rules Committee.

Clark, Jeffries and Aguilar all ran unopposed.

title: Whip Clark Delivers Remarks After Election as House Majority Leader
text:

“First, I want to start with saluting the leadership, the vision, the tenacity, and the sheer hard work of our next Speaker, Hakeem Jeffries, and our next Majority Whip, Pete Aguilar. title: Kennedy Demands Answers on $1.5 Billion Batavia Detention Facility Contract, Blasts Administration’s Priorities During Homeland Security Hearing
text:
Newly Uncovered Contract Raises Concerns About Use of Taxpayer Dollars Following the American People’s Resounding Rejection of Trump Administration’s Immigration Agenda

WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, during a House Committee on Homeland Security hearing, Congressman Tim Kennedy (NY-26) pressed Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on the administration’s expanding immigration detention operations, including a previously unreported $1.5 billion contract awarded by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement for construction services at the Buffalo Service Processing Center in Batavia, New York.

“At a time when Americans are struggling with rising costs, skyrocketing gas prices, and putting food on the table, this administration is prepared to spend $1.5 billion on a detention facility that does not need a billion-and-a-half-dollar facelift,” said Congressman Kennedy. “These are misplaced priorities, driven by failed policies that have left families struggling while pouring billions of taxpayer dollars into mass detention. The American people deserve better, and they've had enough.”

The contract, awarded to Rapid Deployment Inc. and publicly posted on SAM.gov, raises serious concerns about the administration’s plans for the Western New York facility and the use of taxpayer dollars to expand its detention infrastructure. This comes on top of a separate $16.7 million, two-year agreement with Akima Global Services to construct and operate an additional detention structure at Batavia, with construction already underway. Together, these expenditures show an administration continuing to invest heavily in its mass detention and deportation apparatus even as President Trump himself has acknowledged that his immigration enforcement policies have been too extreme.

Kennedy challenged the administration’s justification for expanding detention capacity at Batavia, where, according to ICE’s own reporting, approximately 70 percent of detainees have no criminal record. During an October 15th unannounced oversight visit to the facility, Kennedy observed firsthand the conditions at Batavia. Noting that the facility does not appear to require anywhere near that level of expenditure in routine repairs, Kennedy asked Mullin to provide justification for a $1.5 billion construction contract. With Western New York families facing rising costs for housing, food, energy, and other necessities, the administration owes taxpayers a clear explanation of what this enormous sum will fund. The scale of this spending, coupled with the administration’s refusal to provide complete information about its planned expansion, demands greater transparency and congressional oversight.

Background

Congressman Kennedy has repeatedly pressed DHS for answers about federal immigration enforcement and detention operations in Western New York. In November 2025, he demanded information on immigration arrests and deportations in NY-26; in February and March 2026, he sought information about federal law enforcement personnel in Western New York and the CBP holding facility in Tonawanda. Following an unannounced May visit to the Tonawanda facility, Kennedy sent a follow-up letter soliciting written answers. In July, he formally called on DHS to abandon plans to construct an additional detention structure at Batavia. After receiving a response months later from the Department containing partially redacted information, Kennedy conducted an unannounced oversight visit to Batavia on October 15th and sent Secretary Mullin a follow-up letter demanding further answers about the facility and its planned expansion. Kennedy remains committed to ensuring transparency, accountability, and responsible use of taxpayer dollars from this administration.

title: LaHood’s Route 66 National Historic Trail Designation Act Passes Natural Resources Committee
text:
Washington, D.C. – Today, the House Natural Resources Committee unanimously passed Congressman LaHood's (IL-16) bipartisan bill, H.R. 5470, the Route 66 National Historic Trail Designation Act, which is co-led by Congresswoman Teresa Leger Fernádez (NM-03). The legislation would designate Route 66 as a National Historic Trail, expanding economic and historic development opportunities across all communities and states along the iconic Route 66. “Route 66 is a vital and historic transportation artery that provides powerful economic development tools for communities throughout Illinois, creating jobs and opportunities for residents of the 16th District and beyond,” said Rep. LaHood. “Covering nearly 2,400 miles, the Mother Road connects America’s heartland to the west, supporting all communities along its route. Designating Route 66 as a National Historic Trail would preserve and promote Route 66 for future generations by providing this highway with permanent support. I thank Congresswoman Leger Fernández for her collaboration on this legislation, and I applaud the House Natural Resources Committee for unanimously passing it out of committee. I am hopeful that House we will see a floor vote in the near future to preserve this iconic piece of American history."

“Today, we move one step closer to preserving the legacy and living history of Route 66 for generations to come," said Rep. Leger Fernández. "From Tucumcari to Gallup, Route 66 runs through the heart of New Mexico, carrying with it the stories, cultures, and dreams of communities and travelers. On Route 66, people discovered what Americans look like, in all our beautiful landscapes and cultural diversity. This legislation honors the legacy of the Mother Road while creating opportunities for economic development, cultural preservation, and tourism in rural and Tribal communities.”

“For a century, Route 66 has connected communities, supported small businesses and embodied America’s enduring spirit of exploration," said House Natural Resources Chairman Bruce Westerman. "H.R. 5470 designates the 2,400-mile corridor as a National Historic Trail while respecting private property rights and energy production. I commend Rep. LaHood for celebrating Route 66’s legacy and creating new opportunities for tourism and economic growth along this iconic route.”

“Few places capture the American spirit quite like Route 66, where generations of travelers have found adventure, opportunity, and a deeper connection to the distinctive people and places that define this nation. As we celebrate the Mother Road's centennial year, today’s committee vote marks a tremendous step forward for historic preservation and for the countless people across the country who have worked to build and safeguard its many roadside treasures. We thank Congressman Darin LaHood, Congresswoman Teresa Leger Fernández, and their Congressional colleagues for ensuring that future generations can experience the history and enduring spirit of Route 66," said Rob Nieweg, Acting Chief of Preservation Advocacy and Initiatives at the National Trust for Historic Preservation.

Background:

Congressman LaHood reintroduced H.R. 5470 in September of 2025. Congresswoman Leger Fernández was the original cosponsor of the legislation.

Route 66 spans roughly 2,400 miles across eight states beginning in Chicago, crossing through Grundy, Livingston, and McLean County in Illinois’ 16th Congressional district, and ending in Santa Monica, California. Following its passage out of the Natural Resources Committee, the Route 66 National Historic Trail Designation Act can now move to the full House of Representatives for consideration.

The full text of the bill can be found HERE.

title: Connecticut Congressional Delegation Blasts Federal Bureau of Prisons' Attempts to Dismantle Union Workers' Rights and Protections
text:
Washington, D.C. – Today, Reps. John B. Larson (CT-01), Joe Courtney (CT-02), Rosa DeLauro (CT-03), Jim Himes (CT-04), and Jahana Hayes (CT-05), and Senators Richard Blumenthal and Chris Murphy wrote Director of the Federal Bureau of Prisons (BOP) William K. Marshall III voicing strong opposition to the Bureau’s attempts to terminate its legally negotiated Collective Bargaining Agreement (CBA) with the American Federation of Government Employees’ National Council of Prison Locals 33 (CPL-33).

CPL-33 represents more than 30,000 public servants in critical jobs within the federal penitentiary system, including employees at the Federal Correctional Institution in Danbury. The Collective Bargaining Agreement addresses how and where staff are assigned to work, their schedule including breaks and time off, and when workers receive overtime. Furthermore, the CBA provides a framework for negotiations with wardens and institutional managers.

In September 2025, the Bureau of Prisons (BOP) initially terminated its Collective Bargaining Agreement with CPL-33, blaming President Trump’s Executive Order 14251, before later changing its tune and calling the union “an obstacle to progress.” Since then, the Bureau has stopped at nothing to strip away workplace protections, even going so far as to circumvent a preliminary injunction earlier this year that required the Bureau to operate under the Collective Bargaining Agreement.

“The BOP’s efforts to end the CBA with CPL-33 are one more example in a litany of actions the Trump Administration is taking to dismantle workers’ rights and protections. Since President Trump took office, his administration has eliminated the collective bargaining rights of more than one million federal workers. These efforts attack not only unions but also individual civil servants across our country,” the delegation members wrote.

The full text of the delegation’s letter is available here and below.

Dear Director Marshall III,

We write with concern regarding the Federal Bureau of Prisons’ (BOP) attempts to terminate its legally negotiated Collective Bargaining Agreement (CBA) with the American Federation of Government Employees’ National Council of Prison Locals 33 (CPL-33). Union members, including the 30,000 civil servants represented by CPL-33, are the backbone of the federal penitentiary system, serving in critical jobs that protect our nation. We are aghast at BOP’s unceasing, politically motivated efforts to strip away its employees’ rights, and the blatant disregard BOP has shown for the welfare of its employees over the past two years.

In September 2025, the BOP terminated its CBA with CPL-33. Although the BOP claimed President Trump’s Executive Order 14251 as the basis for its decision, you admitted to the real reason: posting a message to the BOP website on the same day BOP terminated the contract, claiming that the “whole purpose of ending this contract” was because the “union [was] an obstacle to progress” and “the current contract has too often slowed or prevented changes.” However, the CBA played a vital role in protecting BOP employees, who serve in some of the nation’s most dangerous environments and maintain and uphold our public safety. The CBA established nationwide workplace protections and provided a framework for local unions to negotiate arrangements with wardens and other institutional managers. For example, the CBA addressed how and where staff are assigned to work, their work schedule, including lunch breaks and time off, when workers receive overtime, steps BOP must take to ensure the health and safety of its employees, and the right to union representation.

Following the decision to terminate the contract, the BOP wasted no time in stripping its workers of their rights and due process protections against arbitrary management decisions. The BOP quickly dismantled its labor relations apparatus, changed more than 70 labor-related policies, and rushed to resolve pending disciplinary actions, which now lacked the procedural safeguards of the original CBA, including union representation of the employee accused of wrongdoing by management. These changes had immediate, real-life consequences. In two egregious instances, BOP sent a sick-leave abuse letter to an employee who was in the hospital for kidney surgery and placed a different employee who was recovering from surgery on Absent Without Leave (AWOL) status, erroneously and unconscionably threatening them with termination if they did not return to work. Without the CBA, these employees had to face disciplinary proceedings without due process or union support. These unwarranted, arbitrary actions are precisely why the CBA provides for a fair review process of management accusations.

Despite the preliminary injunction issued earlier this year, BOP continues to pursue avenues to avoid operating under the CBA. In October 2026, BOP attempted to circumvent the injunction by rescinding its original termination that had been enjoined, and then immediately re-terminating the contract. Although the court voided this naked power play to evade the court’s order and BOP eventually filed a Notice of Compliance with the Judge’s orders on October 28, 2026, we are concerned that the BOP will continue to undermine the CBA as the Bureau’s actions impact its employees across the country. In fact, staff have reported that the BOP’s attempts to terminate the contract are leading to low staff morale. A union representative at the Federal Correctional Institution in Mendota, California, described the efforts as “nothing more than…giving the rule of law the middle finger.” He also voiced his concerns that the BOP is still not honoring certain workplace agreements, including providing essential safety equipment such as footwear. We find it unacceptable for the BOP to subvert the CBA and leave workers who are upholding our public safety system without critical protections.

The BOP’s efforts to end the CBA with CPL-33 are one more example in a litany of actions the Trump Administration is taking to dismantle workers’ rights and protections. Since President Trump took office, his administration has eliminated the collective bargaining rights of more than one million federal workers. These efforts attack not only unions but also individual civil servants across our country. We strongly oppose BOP’s efforts to undermine CPL-33, and we urge BOP to end its misguided effort to terminate the Collective Bargaining Agreements immediately.

title: Rep. Levin Reintroduces Bill to Improve Safe Storage of Spent Nuclear Fuel
text:
Washington, D.C.—Today, Rep. Mike Levin (CA-49) reintroduced the 100 Year Canister Life Act, legislation to strengthen federal safety standards for the storage of spent nuclear fuel. The bill would direct the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) to require newly approved spent nuclear fuel storage canisters to meet a minimum 100-year safety standard, up from the current 40-year standard.

Approximately 3.6 million pounds of spent nuclear fuel remain stored at the San Onofre Nuclear Generating Station (SONGS), just 100 feet from the Pacific Ocean. More than a decade after the plant shut down, the federal government still has no permanent repository for spent nuclear fuel, leaving nuclear waste stranded at San Onofre and dozens of other sites across the country.

“The federal government has a responsibility to get nuclear waste out of SONGS, and I’ve made that one of my top priorities since coming to Congress,” said Rep. Levin. “We’ve made real progress toward that goal, but more than 3.5 million pounds of spent nuclear fuel are still sitting on our coastline with no permanent disposal site available at this time. Until we can move that waste, we need to make sure it’s stored as safely as possible. My bill would strengthen federal safety standards to better reflect the reality that communities like ours have been forced to live with this waste for decades. We need to protect our communities today while continuing the work to get this waste off our coast for good.”

Under the 100 Year Canister Life Act, the NRC would have 18 months to establish new regulations requiring nuclear waste storage systems to meet a minimum 100-year safety standard. Before issuing or renewing approvals for covered storage systems and facilities, the NRC would have to determine that they can safely store spent nuclear fuel for at least 100 years. The legislation would not require the NRC to extend the length of any licenses.

The legislation fulfills a recommendation from the SONGS Task Force, which Rep. Levin convened in 2019 to develop solutions for the safe storage and removal of spent nuclear fuel. The Task Force’s 2020 report called for federal legislation requiring nuclear waste canisters to have a design life of at least 100 years.

Rep. Levin has also helped secure nearly $250 million for spent nuclear fuel management and removal efforts nationwide, including more than $100 million in Fiscal Year 2026. He is the founder and co-chair of the bipartisan Congressional Spent Nuclear Fuel Solutions Caucus, which works to advance solutions for spent nuclear fuel stranded at nuclear sites across the country.

Rep. Levin also launched the SONGS Task Force shortly after taking office to increase oversight and accountability over the site’s decommissioning process, address safety challenges, and develop policy recommendations with local stakeholders and experts in the region.

In October, Rep. Levin released the 2026 SONGS Report outlining progress and next steps toward safely removing waste from the site. To date, all spent nuclear fuel at SONGS has been transferred from wet pools into dry storage, 52 of the facility’s 62 structures have been demolished, and more than 700 million pounds of material have been removed. Despite that progress, more than 3.5 million pounds of spent nuclear fuel remain at the site, underscoring the need for continued federal action to safely manage and ultimately remove the waste.

title: New Bipartisan Bill Will Empower Communities Facing Data Center Development
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, Congressmembers Sam Liccardo (CA-16), Nick Begich (AK-AL), Scott Peters (CA-50), and Erin Houchin (IN-09) introduced the bipartisan Data Center Community Empowerment Act of 2026. Senators John Curtis (R-UT) and Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-DE) previously introduced companion legislation in the Senate.

As data center developers look to build data centers across the country, local communities face difficult decisions about energy costs, infrastructure demands, and potential economic benefits. Yet many local governments lack the technical expertise needed to assess these projects and negotiate on equal footing with developers. This bipartisan legislation would give communities access to independent technical expertise supported by the Department of Energy, arming local leaders with the facts they need to make informed decisions.

“Local communities should decide whether hyperscalers build in their backyards. But when we pit small towns against hyperscalers, we set them up to get steamrolled,” said Rep. Liccardo. “Every data center proposal shouldn't become a David and Goliath battle. This bill gives communities a fighting chance to make the decisions that best serve their residents.”

“When local leaders have good information about what a knowledge infrastructure project means for power bills, water supplies, and local roads and services, they can make decisions in the best interest of those they represent. This bill makes sure no community is left out of these important conversations,” said Rep. Begich.

“Data centers have left communities across the country worried about their utility bills, the quality of their neighborhoods, and the environment,” Rep. Peters said. “San Diegans already pay some of the highest utility rates in the nation, and they deserve to know what’s coming before decisions are made. We should provide communities with resources and the technical knowledge to understand the real impacts of data centers, so they can make informed decisions. I’m glad to be part of the solution and to lead this bipartisan, bicameral bill that gets Americans the answers they need and helps them advocate for their best interests.”

“Local communities deserve a meaningful say in what gets built in their own backyards. That’s why I’m proud to join Congressman Liccardo on this bill to provide the information and tools needed to make informed decisions about data center development. As our nation’s demand for critical infrastructure grows, we must respect local control and ensure that economic growth and technological innovation do not come at the expense of local priorities,” said Rep. Houchin.

“Data centers need to benefit their host communities, but local officials often lack the resources to negotiate on equal footing with hyperscalers, who have the funds and expertise to tip deals in their favor,” said Brad Carson, President of Americans for Responsible Innovation. “Giving officials the expertise and information they need will help them secure fair deals with real benefits for their constituents. We shouldn’t leave local communities outmatched at the negotiating table.”

The Data Center Community Empowerment Act of 2026 would give communities access to technical expertise to better understand the potential benefits, costs, and infrastructure impacts of proposed data center development-while leaving decisions about whether and how to accommodate that development in the hands of local communities.

The bill would establish a program at the Department of Energy (DOE) to:

Provide technical assistance to State, local, and Tribal governments on the potential energy, water, infrastructure, economic, and other community impacts associated with data center development;

Develop a Data Center Community Toolkit with easy-to-understand information and resources specifically designed for nontechnical local officials;

Provide independent project analysis at a community's request, including an assessment of information voluntarily provided by a data center developer and the reliability of its data and reasonableness of its assumptions, projections, and conclusions; and

Preserve local decision-making by requiring DOE to remain neutral on individual data center projects and prohibiting the Department from recommending whether a particular project should be approved or rejected.
