title: Cantwell & Colleagues Push CTFC To Reverse Ban on Geofencing by Prediction Markets
text:
Cantwell & Colleagues Push CTFC To Reverse Ban on Geofencing by Prediction Markets

WASHINGTON, D.C. –U.S. Senator Maria Cantwell (D-WA), ranking member of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation and senior member of the Senate Finance Committee, joined Senate colleagues in calling out Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) Chair Michael Selig for the agency’s decision to prohibit prediction markets from geofencing, effectively requiring prediction markets to offer contracts in all 50 states and tribal lands. The Senators note Selig’s action directly conflicts with active court orders in California, Michigan, Nevada, and Washington – and demand that he reverse it.

“Numerous courts have held that sports-related event contracts are not swaps and instead are indistinguishable from sports bets subject to state and tribal gaming laws…. The courts have ordered platforms to cease offering various prediction contracts in Michigan, Nevada, and Washington, and on the land of two California tribes, and imposed geofencing requirements. The Commission now appears to be encouraging prediction markets to offer prohibited contracts in contempt of these court orders during active litigation,” the Senators wrote.

“We are particularly troubled that this action came just hours after the Northern District of California issued its latest court order in Blue Lake Rancheria v. Kalshi requiring Kalshi to geofence around the plaintiff’s tribal lands. This interpretation raises concerns that the Commission may be coordinating with platforms currently engaged in litigation and encouraging them to violate state and tribal gaming laws… The Commission must withdraw the interpretation or freeze all efforts to implement until litigation is resolved,” the Senators continued.

Joining Cantwell are all Senators representing California, Michigan, Nevada, and Washington, Senators Catherine Cortez Masto (D-NV), Jacky Rosen (D-NV), Patty Murray (D-WA), Elissa Slotkin (D-MI), Gary Peters (D-MI), Adam Schiff (D-CA), and Alex Padilla (D-CA), as well as the ranking member of the Senate Agriculture Committee Amy Klobuchar (D-MN).

The full text of the letter can be found here and below:

Dear Chairman Selig:

We write to express our opposition to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission’s November 5 interpretation ordering Designated Contract Markets (DCMs) to end access criteria that restrict access to certain event contract markets based on prospective traders’ location or residence (e.g., geofencing) within 30 days. Your unilateral decision directly conflicts with active court orders, undermines state and tribal law, and must be reversed.

Numerous courts have held that sports-related event contracts are not swaps and instead are indistinguishable from sports bets subject to state and tribal gaming laws. Your novel interpretation of the impartial access requirements effectively requires DCMs to offer improperly regulated gambling products in all fifty states without regard to state and tribal gaming laws and these state and federal court decisions. There is no basis or precedent under 17 CFR 38.151(b)’s impartial access requirements for this interpretation and indeed this argument has been made in several of the active cases—and rejected.

The Sixth and Ninth Circuits have ruled that states retain the authority to apply state gaming laws to prediction markets. The Ninth Circuit has also ruled that sports event contracts on Tribal lands constitute unauthorized Class III gaming under the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act in the preliminary-injunction context. The courts have ordered platforms to cease offering various prediction contracts in Michigan, Nevada, and Washington, and on the land of two California tribes, and imposed geofencing requirements. The Commission now appears to be encouraging prediction markets to offer prohibited contracts in contempt of these court orders during active litigation.

We are particularly troubled that this action came just hours after the Northern District of California issued its latest court order in Blue Lake Rancheria v. Kalshi requiring Kalshi to geofence around the plaintiff’s tribal lands. This interpretation raises concerns that the Commission may be coordinating with platforms currently engaged in litigation and encouraging them to violate state and tribal gaming laws.

The Commission must withdraw the interpretation or freeze all efforts to implement until litigation is resolved. At minimum, the Commission must expressly state that the following do not violate Regulation 38.151(b): geographic restrictions imposed by court order, those adopted to comply with the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act or tribal-state compacts, and those an exchange adopts voluntarily.

We further request that the Commission preserve all records and communications relating to the topics addressed in this letter, from January 1, 2025, to the present and continue preserving existing and future materials on an ongoing basis. This preservation hold applies to all relevant records within the Commission’s possession and any person or entity representing or purporting to be acting on its behalf. This includes, but is not limited to, records and communications via email, whether official or personal; mobile devices; encrypted or disappearing messaging applications; social media; calendar entries; meeting notes; and voicemail and text messages. To the extent that the Commission uses any auto-delete functions, it should immediately suspend auto-delete functions and notify persons with control over potentially relevant records of similar preservation obligations.

Thank you for your attention to this matter. We look forward to your prompt response by November 23, 2026, including a written confirmation that the Commission is preserving all records related to this Congressional inquiry.

###

title: Cantwell Celebrates Hard Work of Voting Rights Coalitions and Election Workers That Protected Midterms from Trump’s Overreach
text:
Cantwell Celebrates Hard Work of Voting Rights Coalitions and Election Workers That Protected Midterms from Trump’s Overreach

“In spite of President Trump and the administration...we did have a free and fair and secure election.”

WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, U.S. Senator Maria Cantwell (D-WA) delivered a speech on the Senate floor recognizing the hard work of the states, elections officials, and voting rights coalitions that preserved the integrity of November’s midterm elections, despite the Trump Administration’s concerted attempts to intimidate voters and undermine turnout.

"Fortunately, in spite of President Trump and the administration [efforts] to disrupt the elections with lawsuits or false narratives or changes to the Postal Service, we did have a free and fair and secure election," said Sen. Cantwell. "For this, I am grateful for the efforts of bipartisan and nonpartisan state election officials across the country who once again assured this outcome."

Sen. Cantwell discussed her work with Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs, the NAACP, the League of Women Voters, and others to educate voters about a change in U.S. Postal Service postmark practices that could lead to the rejection of voters’ ballots. She noted, “And so that is why, in this election, you saw many Washingtonians … putting their ballot in a ballot box instead, close to their homes, making sure that a postmark or some process by the U.S. postal system wouldn't delay them.” According to data from the Secretary of State’s office, as of November 17, nearly 80% of Washington voters opted to return their ballot by drop box, well above the rate in elections over the past decade. Moreover, Washington state voters turned out at a higher rate – more than 63% - than the national average.

Sen. Cantwell added: "As we look ahead to our work in the next Congress, the fight may not be over. We need to restore and strengthen our laws to make sure that we are protecting voter rights of all Americans. But the goal remains the same: to ensure that Americans can freely exercise their precious, precious right to vote. We did get through this election cycle, and we have to learn the lessons of trying to undermine it and instead fight hard to strengthen it."

Video of Sen. Cantwell’s speech on the Senate floor today is available HERE. A transcript of her remarks is HERE.

Sen. Cantwell spent the entirety of 2026 standing up to the Trump administration’s overreach into free and fair elections:

On Oct. 1, she voted against advancing a bill that would have imposed new and onerous voter identification laws making it harder for students and tribal members to vote.

On Sept. 28, Sen. Cantwell joined her colleagues in introducing bicameral legislation to protect voters and election workers from intimidation and threats of violence at polling places.

On Sep. 8, Sen. Cantwell joined 260 of her colleagues – including all Senate Democrats and current and former members of the House of Representatives – in filing a bipartisan, bicameral amicus brief with the Supreme Court in a case challenging the U.S. Postal Service’s (USPS) attempt to impose new requirements that would have interfered with vote-by-mail in Washington state and nationwide. On Sep. 15, the Supreme Court agreed with the lawmakers’ position and refused to reverse a lower-court ruling that blocked the USPS from implementing the onerous new requirements. In denying the stay, the Supreme Court let stand a preliminary injunction issued by a federal district court in two related cases – one brought by Washington along with other states – against the USPS rule for the upcoming election. In a statement on the Supreme Court’s ruling, Sen. Cantwell highlighted that the district court had found “on one side, that immediate implementation of the Final Rule issued less than seventy days before the November 2026 election threatens disenfranchisement of millions of United States citizens who seek to vote by mail and, on the other side, that the record includes no evidence relating to fraudulent mail voting to support the rushed implementation of the Final Rule” and granted the preliminary injunction.”

On Sep. 2, Sen. Cantwell held a press conference in Seattle to warn Washington voters about Administration efforts to undermine their right to vote. That same day Sen. Cantwell and Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs released a snapshot report showing that late-postmark rejection rates have more than doubled in 19 counties compared to the 2024 primaries – with rural counties worst affected -- following a new Trump Administration policy that can delay postmarking of mail-in ballots by several days.

On August 5, she sent a letter to then-Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche and Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin demanding the Trump Administration adhere to the National Voter Registration Act’s (NVRA) “quiet period” that prohibits systematic voter purges within 90 days of an election, pushing back against the Administration’s ongoing voter suppression efforts.

On July 29, she wrote to Blanche, Mullin, and Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth demanding to know whether the Trump administration plans to illegally deploy armed federal law enforcement officers at polling sites during the November 2026 elections.

On July 28, Sen. Cantwell sharply criticized the Trump Administration’s request that the Supreme Court allow him to seize control of state-run elections and implement an anti-vote-by-mail executive order. Lower courts have repeatedly rejected the president’s arguments and stated that his executive order is unconstitutional.

On July 2, Sen. Cantwell sent a letter to the Postmaster General about USPS's proposed illegal rule to implement President Trump’s March 31 executive order to interfere with vote-by-mail. Sen. Cantwell’s letter specifically noted the recent decisions of multiple federal courts that found Trump’s executive order unconstitutional and enjoined the USPS from implementing the proposed rule – including in separate cases brought by the State of Washington with other states and the NAACP – and demanded the USPS comply with those court orders.

On June 29, she celebrated the Supreme Court’s ruling in Watson v. Republican National Committee against an effort to stop states from counting mail-in ballots that are received after Election Day, even if they’ve been postmarked in time. The case, brought by the Republican National Committee, threatened the election administration practices of states like Washington.

On June 24, Sen. Cantwell co-sponsored the Right To Vote Act, legislation to create the first-ever affirmative federal voting rights guarantee for all eligible citizens.

On June 24, she also denounced President Trump’s announcement that he would not sign the 21st Century Road to Housing Act – an overwhelmingly popular, bipartisan bill that passed both the House and Senate earlier in the week and would have increased housing supply and brought down housing costs – until Congress passes the SAVE America Act. That legislation, which Trump has repeatedly demanded, would eliminate vote-by-mail and impose onerous new restrictions on voting and registering to vote. It would disenfranchise millions of Americans in the name of a voter fraud “crisis” that, even by the standards of the right-wing Heritage Foundation, straightforwardly does not exist. President Trump again demanded Congress pass the restrictive bill following the Supreme Court’s ruling in Watson v. Republican National Committee. Despite President Trump’s refusal to sign the bipartisan housing bill, it became law on July 11, since he failed to act on the bill within the time period prescribed by the Constitution after Congress sent him the legislation.

On June 23, she joined the entire Democratic Caucus in sending a letter to the USPS demanding the USPS abandon attempts to restrict voting by mail called for by President Trump in an illegal and unconstitutional March 31 executive order attacking mail and absentee ballots.

On June 23, she also delivered a speech on the Senate floor calling out the Trump Administration’s war on mail-in voting as the latest frontier in a long history of voter disenfranchisement in the United States.

On June 17, she joined several of her Senate Democratic colleagues for a spotlight forum highlighting President Trump’s illegal overreach into our free and fair elections.

On June 8, she joined 23 of her Senate colleagues in demanding answers over the Trump Administration’s decision to remove the most recent version of the Federal Prosecution of Election Offenses manual from DOJ’s website without explanation.

On April 29, she was tapped by Minority Leader Schumer to join a task force of senators defending our elections from interference.

title: EPW Committee Advances Schwab Nomination, Approves Resolutions at Business Meeting
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, U.S. Senator Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), Chairman of the Senate Environment and Public Works (EPW) Committee, led a business meeting where the EPW Committee advanced the nomination of Justin Schwab to be Assistant Administrator for the Office of Air and Radiation (OAR) at the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), and voted in favor of eight resolutions to approve prospectuses from the General Services Administration.

title: Cortez Masto Demands Answers from the FAA and Department of Transportation After Nationwide Ground Stop Cancels Over 17,000 Flights
text:
Washington, D.C. – U.S. Senator Catherine Cortez Masto (D-Nev.) sent a letter to Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy and Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) Administration Bryan Bedford demanding answers about the nationwide U.S. Department of Transportation (USDOT) directed ground stop that caused the cancelation of more than 17,000 flights and impacted travelers across the U.S. this week.

“The traveling public’s safety should always be our number one priority,” wrote Senator Cortez Masto. “But the FAA and the USDOT owe travelers answers about what caused a disruption of such a massive scale, how federal agencies are addressing the immediate impacts of the ground stop, and what the Trump Administration is doing to ensure this does not happen again.”

Cortez Masto outlined how Nevada’s economy is highly dependent on travel and tourism, stating that “any transportation disruptions can have major impacts on an economic sector that has been significantly weakened by the Trump Administration.” Travel and tourism accounts for 34% of Nevada’s state and local governments’ tax revenue annually, and visitor volume to Las Vegas declined by roughly 7.5% in 2025, and the trend is continuing.

“It is critical that we get answers from USDOT and the FAA about this ground stop, while assuring the traveling public of the safety of the system and competence of its management,” she continued. Her questions to the agencies include:

Why was such critical maintenance work carried out during busy work hours? Is that normal operating procedure for these kinds of updates?

What advance risk assessment did the USDOT and FAA do before the ATC overhaul?

What specific support did the USDOT provide to airlines to help address the impact on their businesses, workers, and the traveling public?

What specific communications and support did USDOT provided to aviation workers, including through their labor unions, to outline the impacts of this ground stop on their jobs? Are you seeing reports of already strained air traffic controllers having to work longer hours to get flights back on track?

How are you working with the airlines and hospitality sectors to assure that the traveling public is not burdened with the costs associated with the immediate ground stop and subsequent flight disruptions?

What is your estimate of the economic impact of this ground stop order?

She also asked USDOT and FAA for additional specifics related to their new Congressional funding request. “These details are vital not only for informing the public, but also to provide Congress with more details on USDOT’s dramatically increased request for $50 billion in non-specific funding for air traffic updates,” she concluded.

Cortez Masto asked for answers from the Trump Administration by November 30. The full letter can be found here.

Senator Cortez Masto is a fierce advocate for Nevada’s travel and tourism economy and its workers. She has repeatedly raised concerns about the Trump Administration’s policies that are driving down tourism and demanded that the administration deliver a plan to reverse the harm they’ve caused. She has also supported legislation to reverse funding cuts to the effective Brand USA travel promotion public-private partnership program. When Spirit Airlines declared bankruptcy, Cortez Masto demanded that employees receive their earned wages and accrued benefits.

text:

WASHINGTON—Senator Tom Cotton (R-Arkansas) today introduced Associate Justice James “Cody” Hiland, nominee to be United States Circuit Judge for the Eighth Circuit, to the Senate Judiciary Committee ahead of his nomination hearing.

Senator Cotton: Senator Cruz, Senator Durbin, members of the Judiciary Committee, good morning. It’s an honor to appear with Senator Boozman on behalf of the president’s nominee to the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals and my friend, Justice Cody Hiland.

title: Cotton, Klobuchar Bill to Establish Biosecurity Requirements Passes Senate Commerce Committee
text:
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE

Contact: Tatum Wallace or Hannah McCarthy

November 18, 2026

Cotton, Klobuchar Bill to Establish Biosecurity Requirements Passes Senate Commerce Committee

WASHINGTON—Senator Tom Cotton (R-Arkansas) and Senator Amy Klobuchar (D-Minnesota) released the following statements after the U.S. Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation passed their Biosecurity Modernization and Innovation Act, which would require gene synthesis providers to screen their orders and customers to ensure bad actors aren’t ordering dangerous sequences.

“The federal government must ensure Americans are protected from biosecurity threats posed by terrorists and bad actors who seek to do us harm. I’m pleased my bipartisan Biosecurity Modernization and Innovation Act passed the Senate Commerce Committee, bringing it one step closer to becoming law,” said Senator Cotton.

“While access to genetic material allows scientists to study diseases, develop lifesaving medicine, and improve crops, without safety standards it could be misused, including to create bioweapons. Our bipartisan legislation will enhance biosecurity efforts and reduce the risk of genetic material being used to cause harm by ensuring that the companies selling these products know who their customers are and how they will use genetic material,” said Senator Klobuchar.

The Biosecurity Modernization and Innovation Act is endorsed by the National Security Commission on Emerging Biotechnology, the Engineering Biology Research Consortium, Twist Bioscience, Aclid, Integrated DNA Technologies (IDT), Ginkgo Bioworks, OpenAI, Microsoft, Google DeepMind, and Anthropic, along with broad support among biosecurity and biotechnology policy researchers.

title: ICYMI: Chairman Cotton’s Opening Remarks at Intelligence Committee Confirmation Hearing
text:
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE

Contact: Tatum Wallace or Hannah McCarthy

November 18, 2026

ICYMI: Chairman Cotton’s Opening Remarks at Intelligence Committee Confirmation Hearing

Click here to view Senator Cotton’s full remarks.

WASHINGTON—Senator Tom Cotton (R-Arkansas), Chairman of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, delivered opening remarks at today’s confirmation hearing for Mr. Gary Lawkowski, nominee for General Counsel of the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, and Mr. Joseph Weirsky, nominee for Director of the National Counterterrorism Center.

Senator Cotton’s full remarks may be found here and below.

Senator Cotton: This hearing will come to order. I’d like to welcome you all to today’s hearing to consider the nominations of Mr. Gary Lawkowski to be general counsel of the Office of the Director of National Intelligence and Mr. Joseph Weirsky to be the director of the National Counterterrorism Center.

I want to remind everyone that you are welcome to attend, but the vice chairman and I agree that we will not allow any disruptions. Audience members may not verbally or physically distract from the hearing, including by shouting, standing, raising sounds, or making gestures that block the view of other members of the audience or the cameras. The committee intends to hear from our nominees, not disruptors seeking a few minutes of social media fame. If anyone is removed from the chamber, I will take further action to have them barred from the committee’s future proceedings, or the Capitol itself. Our goal in conducting the hearing is to enable the committee to consider the nominees’ qualifications and to allow our members thoughtful deliberation. While both nominees have already provided substantive written responses to dozens of questions presented by the committee today, members can ask any additional questions they have and the nominees can share their thoughts.

Before we move on to the business hand, I’d like to repeat in public today a few things I said yesterday at our closed hearing. First off, I congratulate the vice chairman on his re-election to the Senate. I congratulate the Democrats on their [recent] victory…We obviously have occasional policy differences. Most of the agencies we oversee do not set policy, however. We occasionally have differences on budget, authorities, oversight questions, but we’ve always worked together in a bipartisan spirit. That goes not just for my tenure in this chair, but Senator Rubio and Senator Burr before us. Well, Senator Warner has been there for all three of us, and we look forward to that spirit continuing.

We will be losing two members of this committee who aren’t here, but we’ll go ahead and say nice things about them behind their backs in public. Senator Collins and Senator Cornyn will be departing us. They have been invaluable members of the Intelligence Committee and the United States Senate. We will miss them dearly. They’ve been, again, incredible contributors to this committee. They’ve been fierce advocates for our intelligence officers who are risking their lives around the world, and we will wish them all the very best.

Speaking of which, I can now say it to his face. Senator Cornyn, I was just saying that you and Senator Collins have been invaluable members of the committee, and we will regret seeing you go at the end of this Congress. But we appreciate your service here, just like we know the men and women of our intelligence agencies appreciate it as well.

Now, moving on to the business at hand. First, Mr. Lawkowski, who has been nominated to serve as the general counsel of the Office of the Director of National Intelligence currently serves as deputy assistant to the president and deputy counsel to the president. In this role, he has advised on national security-related issues and represented the White House Counsel’s Office in deputy-level National Security Council meetings. During the first Trump administration, Mr. Lawkowski also held various roles at the Department of the Interior, including counselor to the deputy secretary and counselor to the solicitor. Additionally, he is a graduate of the University of Virginia and the University of Virginia School of Law.

Next, we have Mr. Weirsky, the nominee to be the director of the National Counterterrorism Center. Before joining the NCTC and holding numerous senior-level positions there, Mr. Weirsky spent five years working in the private sector and 26 years serving in the US Marine Corps. Mr. Weirsky, let me say up front on behalf of the committee, thank you for your nearly three decades of distinguished military service.

After enlisting in the Marines in 1994, Mr. Weirsky went on to serve nearly a decade as a reconnaissance marine and 15 years with the US Special Operations Command. Mr. Weirsky served at the height of the global war on terror, completing multiple war zone deployments, graduating from the operations course, and receiving three Bronze Stars, two Combat Action Ribbons, and the Legion of Merit.

In closing, I’d like to thank both the nominees and their loved ones for being here today. I look forward to hearing more about the expertise they bring to the table, how they plan to approach these leadership roles at the Office of the Director of National Intelligence and the National Counterterrorism Center, and how they intend to keep our intelligence agencies focused on the primary mission of stealing our enemies’ secrets.

At this point, I would turn it over to the vice chairman, but we have the distinguished senator from Montana, Senator Daines, who we also regret will be departing us in January. But he is here for a brief introduction before he has to get off to other pressing business. After his remarks, I will recognize the vice chairman.

###

title: Cramer Delivers Floor Speech on Permitting Reform
text:
***Click here for audio. Click here for video.***

WASHINGTON, D.C. – In response to bipartisan frustration with excessive permitting delays, the Senate has been debating the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), which would remedy many of the problems associated with federal permitting and environmental review process.

U.S. Senator Kevin Cramer (R-ND) delivered a speech on the Senate floor this evening highlighting the importance of passing BAAJA during the final weeks of the 119th Congress and encouraging his colleagues on both sides of the aisle to pass the bill.

“One of Cramer’s Convictions is: not every transaction requires a loser. Too often in this town, however, our success is measured by how badly we defeat our competitors rather than how much we produce for our constituents. What it is we actually deliver, not defeat, should be the standard.

“For decades, the process of approving the building of the infrastructure necessary to meet the demands of a growing and dynamic economy have been mired in partisan politics, and an out-of-control bureaucracy, which limits our nation's potential, our prosperity, and stifles our global competitiveness. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is an opportunity for us to turn that corner. And it's imperative, Mr. President, that we do it now while the window is open. Whether it's transmission lines to load centers, or pipelines to refineries, steel mills, or drone factories, or family housing, we must secure durable changes to the federal permitting reform process or continue to fall behind our global competitors.

Click here to watch

“We must make it easier to build in America. China, for example, dominates global manufacturing, particularly in those industries that are indispensable to a national defense. For example, China's steel production exceeds ours by roughly, get this now, 12 to 1. In shipbuilding, China possesses capacity roughly 230 times that of the United States. […] A single major Chinese shipyard can exceed the total output of the entire U.S. commercial shipbuilding industry.

“Regarding infrastructure, a recent report put out by McKinsey and Company paints a stark, very stark picture—but full of opportunities. McKinsey’s report on the economic impact of federal permitting delays highlights the massive scale of capital and economic activity that's stalled in the United States permitting pipeline, if you’ll excuse the expression. According to McKinsey’s report, U.S. federal permitting holds $1.8 trillion in infrastructure projects. And better than that, $1.1 trillion of it is private sector money. In my state of North Dakota, $24 billion sits on the sidelines while the bureaucracy holds development hostage. These delays represent over $3 trillion dollars in cumulative, unrealized economic activity.

“This bill is an opportunity to create winners all around. Both sides of the proverbial political aisle are tired of the regulatory whiplash from one administration to the next. Another one of Cramer’s Convictions is nothing brings people together like a common adversary.

“The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act or BAAJA, hits that nail right on the head. It's the kind of bill where everyone across the political spectrum gets enough of what they want. They may not get everything they want, but they get enough to claim victory. No losers.

“A project can be built and operational, yet, as of now, a litigant can file years later and throw that road, bridge, pipeline, or transmission line into doubt. We’ve experienced that phenomenon in North Dakota. Under our bill, legal challenges can also only come from those who raised the issue during the comment period and then can actually show direct harm. Law firms cannot simply create a cottage industry, exploiting would-be victims, because their feelings were hurt. If a court finds a problem, the agency needs to fix it within 180 days rather than being forced to just vacate and start the whole project over, as is often the case when activist judges look to block projects. In other words, to try and throw a legal wrench in the process, someone must have skin in the game.

“NEPA has been weaponized for decades by extreme activists who simply want to obstruct projects. NEPA is a procedural statute, according to the Supreme Court, not substantive. It’s designed to make sure agencies consider all the options before greenlighting a project. On average, this process takes roughly four years. And often much longer that, twice as long, or more. That will stop under this bill. It gets back to the intent of NEPA – to consider informed alternatives and greenlight the best, most workable option. We’re going to get back to building, not balking.

“We often say around here that energy security is national security, and this legislation certainly helps secure North Dakota energy production and energy production in every state. I submit to you that permitting reform is also essential for our national security. As a nation, we cannot build and we cannot produce at the rates necessary to counter adversaries like China, which builds three times as fast as we do, at a fraction of the cost. Now I wouldn't trade governance with China for anything. The COVID pandemic highlighted the risks, however, within our supply chains. We need to mine our own rare earth and critical minerals. […] Our defense industrial base must be able to grow at a speed necessary to deter adversaries, and allow us, the United States, to prevail, should we end up in a major conflict. These are no-fail missions, over which we can never allow ourselves to be held hostage by outsized bureaucracy.

“This bill nearly perfectly encapsulates what it takes to negotiate a true bipartisan product. It is a balance. Take electric transmission, for example. Given my experience as a former utility regulator, I've advocated precaution, and even blocked previous attempts to overhaul electricity policy. Is the transmission section what I would have written if I were the king? It is not. But I'm not the king. But the bill is an improvement over prior versions, and it strikes enough of a balance for me to get behind it given all the other provisions of the bill. The vast majority of this body has rallied around this bill because it provides certainty for everyone. Oil producers in North Dakota and Alaska, and offshore wind projects in Rhode Island, will benefit just as much as manufacturers and roads and bridges from coast to coast.

“Achieving true balance is undeniably elusive. In fact, it’s darn rare, even in the Senate where we depend on consensus. Achieving true balance though, should be the goal. Finding balance at the right time, however, is even harder. We have an open window to pass this generational legislation to empower the people who make things in America, but the window will close soon, to likely not open again for a very long time—if ever.

“It took uncommon leadership, and I'm grateful for my colleagues who worked tirelessly, mostly cheerfully, for the last year to get us to this point. Most importantly, I thank you, Environment and Public Works Chair Shelley Moore Capito, and Ranking Member Sheldon Whitehouse. I said to both of them this morning, they might be the only two senators who tolerate each other. Because they've been through this, they're better partners than ever. And thank you, Energy and Natural Resources Chair Mike Lee and Ranking Member Martin Heinrich, for hanging in there. […] The nerdy stuff these two had to work through would cause lesser people to throw in the towel. The work of these four leaders and a host of others is what results in the law that is as durable as it is balanced.

“A special thank you also goes to the president's team at the White House. President Trump and his Energy Dominance Council are on board with a bill that frankly defers a significant amount of executive power. Presidents don't give that up easily. But their constructive engagement is greatly appreciated.

“Now, let's get the job done. Let's pass the Bipartisan American Affordability [and Jobs] Act, send it to the House with a lot of momentum, and restore certainty in the federal permitting process, and build and produce in America as though our country depends on it. Because today, our country depends on us.”

title: Crapo, Republican Senators Seek Explanation, Urge Reconsideration of Changes to Kratom-Derived Scheduling
text:
Washington, D.C.--U.S. Senator Mike Crapo (R-Idaho) joined Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) and six Republican Senators in a letter urging the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) and the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to explain and reconsider proposed changes to the emergency scheduling order for semi-synthetic, kratom-derived substances, including 7-hydroxymitragynine (7-OH) and mitragynine pseudoindoxyl (MP).

In July 2026, the DEA proposed placing 7-OH above a 0.05 percent threshold in Schedule I of the Controlled Substances Act and subsequently issued an order placing three semi-synthetic kratom-related substances, including MP, in Schedule I. However, in October, the DEA reversed course, issuing a revised proposal that doubled the original threshold established for 7-OH and removed MP from Schedule I. October’s decision would allow both chemicals to be present in over-the-counter kratom products at levels higher than those found naturally in the kratom plant.

“Kratom is a drug in any form with addictive properties, and we believe this combined threshold level for 7-OH and MP set by DEA is inappropriately high and unsound… If the administration’s goal is to remove all unsafe products from the shelves, particularly synthetic or enhanced kratom products, this order misses the mark,” the lawmakers wrote.

“The psychoactive alkaloids of the kratom plant are potentially dangerous substances that should be treated with caution, particularly given the lack of adequate regulation on its products… The American people deserve peace of mind about what is sold on marketplace shelves and a public health system that makes sound regulatory decisions,” the lawmakers continued.

Specifically, the Senators’ letter requests the DEA and FDA:

Provide Congress the scientific and medical evaluations the agencies relied on to set a higher threshold limit for 7-OH;

Explain how a higher threshold for 7-OH better protects American families than the original, lower threshold; and

Reconsider the updated threshold level for 7-OH and place kratom substances containing any amount of MP in Schedule I.

Crapo and Grassley are joined on the letter by Senators Jim Risch (R-Idaho), Susan Collins (R-Maine), Rick Scott (R-Florida), Bill Cassidy (R-Louisiana), Jerry Moran (R-Kansas) and Shelley Moore Capito (R-West Virginia).

Read the full letter HERE. A fact sheet on kratom and the timeline for DEA’s proposed scheduling order is available HERE.

Background:

Kratom leaves contain two major psychoactive ingredients: mitragynine and 7-hydroxymitragynine (7-OH). These substances can be concentrated and chemically modified to produce extremely potent, semi-synthetic compounds – MP, MGM-15 and MGM-16. Kratom and kratom-derived substances are sold over the counter across the country, available to all age groups as “natural” energy boosters, mood lifters and pain relievers.

According to the FDA, known side effects of kratom include liver toxicity, seizures, substance use disorder and, in rare cases, death. The Idaho Department of Health and Welfare reported 83 deaths from kratom-related overdoses from 2020 to 2024. In November 2025, Bonneville County reported six deaths in 18 months. According to the DEA, state health authorities have linked the use of 7-OH products and concentrated extracts to dependence, addiction, acute psychosis, slowed breathing, cardiac arrest and death.

Kratom-derived 7-OH has been identified as having a similar abuse potential to heroin or fentanyl and is known to be 13-times more potent than morphine. Other kratom-derived compounds, like MP, are known to be 20-times more potent than morphine.

title: Daines Urges Colleagues to Support Bipartisan Proposal to Save the Senate
text:
“Change Is In the Air and We Cannot Avoid It, Much Less Ignore It”

WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Senator Steve Daines today spoke on the floor of the U.S. Senate about his bipartisan Save the Senate initiative. Read highlights below.

Watch the full speech HERE.

Excerpts from Daines’ speech are below:

Mr. President, “change is in the air and we cannot avoid it, much less ignore it.” Those were the words that my fellow Montanan, then Senate Majority Leader Mike Mansfield, used in 1971 to describe the bipartisan frustration with the growing abuse of the filibuster. Senator Mansfield knew that substantial reforms to the cloture rule were desperately needed, both to prevent a revolt from senators and to protect the power and prestige of this institution. Mansfield feared the Senate could even become “an innocuous House of Lords” that would cede influence to the House of Representatives. Unfortunately, the reforms that the Senate adopted during the 1970s, and since, have failed to safeguard this institution as a deliberative and functional body. And by any fair measure, dysfunction in the Senate has only gotten worse. And this institution has only become weaker in the decades since.

………….

We must also be deeply pragmatic and recognize the realities of the modern Senate and the hyper-partisanship that saturates our political discourse. Therefore, to insist on an unattainable ideal of a bygone era would be unwise. But to hold out hope for institutional self-correction is irresponsible. I believe the most responsible course, our last, best hope to Save the Senate, is to realign incentives by rewarding bipartisan deliberation and bringing the Senate back closer to its original practices.

………….

It may come as surprise to new members and the American people that the first supermajority cloture rule, adopted in 1917, was meant to help the institution overcome such crippling talking filibusters, not become synonymous with the term filibuster itself. It provided a way to shut off debate with the support of two-thirds of voting senators. We can learn a clear lesson from the development of a cloture mechanism and by the prior efforts, sometimes successful, to limit debate and overcome filibusters. And that is, when obstruction is used to kill a bill rather than improve it, senators in the majority oftentimes get fed up and contemplate decisive action to stop the obstruction. While I believe majorities should exercise restraint in those scenarios, I also believe filibustering senators should do the same and focus on enhancing deliberation, not blatant obstruction.

………….

Our plan restores the Senate’s right to amend. For most of my twelve years in the Senate, the right to amend has been a caricature of what it was in generations’ past. In an unfortunate irony, deliberation in the era of cloture and pain-free filibustering is but a fragment of what it once was, and substantive floor amendments are but crumbs. Too often the Senate is a body in the midst of a quorum call, not deliberation…Our proposal seeks to restore the opportunity for votes for a third bucket of amendments: Those that are bipartisan and would make substantive changes to legislation that its sponsors or managers might prefer to exclude but that are germane to the bill and might pass if they can get a vote. These amendments should not be suppressed, especially if they’re bipartisan. And if they create a policy conflict that must be resolved with the House in a formal or informal conference down the road, I say: That’s okay. That’s how regular order and deliberation has worked in the past and should work again.

………….

According to Senate scholar Molly Reynolds, there are at least 161 majoritarian exceptions in law. To put it more clearly, on at least 161 occasions, the U.S. Senate has voted to prohibit filibusters on specified topics and to allow related legislation to pass with simple majority support…And you’ll notice that, in the modern Senate, most of these fast-track or privileged majoritarian exceptions are used for overwhelmingly partisan initiatives…My proposal with Senator Merkley encourages the exact opposite. It establishes a majoritarian exception in Senate rules, but only for bipartisan bills. It incentivizes and rewards bipartisan policymaking, empowers committees to go forth and conquer, and brings the Senate back closer to its original design and practice: Debate. Amend. Vote. We are hopeful that these reforms will help lower the temperature in the Senate. And for those of us who think it would be damaging for the Senate to use the nuclear option to pass even more party-line legislation, I would respectfully suggest adopting these reforms—and using them—would reduce the likelihood that either party would take that unwanted action.

………….

If this were merely an academic exercise, I would suggest that what’s broken in the Senate is not the concept that a majority of States should still be able to pass a bill, but instead that the deliberative judgment that the Framers envisioned for the Senate has deteriorated.

But as I said earlier this isn’t an academic exercise. We must be clear-eyed about the dangers of the politically charged time we live in.

And for that reason, I think there is merit to the concern that returning to outright majority rule in the Senate, especially if done through the nuclear option, would do major and lasting harm to the Senate. Worse, it could further divide our citizens and create dangerous instability across our country. Our plan seeks a healthy balance. It encourages the Senate to pass legislation at majority rule wherever bipartisan consensus exists while retaining the cloture process for strictly partisan bills. It’s even possible that bills would be processed and passed with fewer votes than 60 votes—but only if the bills are bipartisan. In short, our plan encourages senators to run toward common ground rather than their own corners. I believe this transformation is urgently needed and would be extremely healthy for this institution. And it is a set of proposals that will encourage bipartisanship in both unified government, when partisan policymaking is most tempting, and in divided government. We of course will be in divided government for at least the next two years, and Senator Merkley and I are convinced these reforms could help the Senate to function better and lead in solving our nation’s pressing challenges for the good of the American people. Bipartisan policymaking will not just be preferable; it will be mandatory.

………….

In conclusion, Mr. President, I offer no conjecture on whether Senator Mansfield or Senator Byrd or Senator Hatch would support each of the bipartisan proposals that Senator Merkley and I have put forward, though I think it is quite plausible that they would. But based on their clear misgivings about the pervasive abuse of the filibuster, I am near certain that they would recognize that the Senate is increasingly diminished and that previous reforms have failed to restore this institution as a deliberative body rather than simply an obstructionist body. And I am near certain that they would want members who are now privileged to hold this office to do everything in their power, in a bipartisan way, to get the Senate working again for the American people. That is what Senator Merkley and I are seeking to do with these bold yet reasonable proposals. I urge all of my colleagues to closely review these proposals, and I look forward to continued conversations with them over the next month. For the good of the country, I hope all senators, Republican, Democratic, and Independent alike, can come together to save the Senate, halt its decline, and restore its prestige and effectiveness. Mr. President, change is once again in the air. Now is the time to act.

###

title: Daines Urges Colleagues to Support Joe Weirsky’s Nomination for Director of the National Counterterrorism Center
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Senator Steve Daines today introduced Joe Weirsky, President Trump’s nominee to serve as Director of the National Counterterrorism Center, in a Senate Intelligence Committee hearing. Joe formerly served as Defense Fellow in the Daines office.

Watch Daines’ full remarks HERE.

Daines’ introductory remarks as prepared for delivery:

I am pleased to introduce Joe Weirsky, the President’s nominee for Director of the National Counterterrorism Center. There is nobody more qualified or more deserving to serve in this role so critical to our national security.

Retired Master Gunnery Sergeant Joe Weirsky enlisted in the Marine Corps in 1994 and joined 2nd Recon Battalion in 1996. Prior to the War on Terror, Joe served abroad in Kosovo and stateside as chief instructor at the Marines’ Amphibious Reconnaissance Course.

He was then assigned to Special Operations Command where he spent the next 15 years conducting hundreds of sensitive counterterrorism missions across the Middle East as part of the Marine Corps and the Intelligence Community in support of Operations Iraqi Freedom, Enduring Freedom, New Dawn, and Inherent Resolve.

Joe is the recipient of the Legion of Merit, the Bronze Star with two gold stars, the Defense Meritorious Service Medal with two gold stars, the Joint Service Commendation Medal, the Navy Achievement Medal, the Combat Action Ribbon with gold star, and the Joint Meritorious Unit Award with a gold star. He retired from active duty in 2020 following 26 years of service.

Following his retirement, Joe spent time in the private sector as well as a year in my office as a defense fellow where he contributed to a wide range of legislative efforts and cemented himself as a key member of my team.

Joe has been the sharp end of America’s spear for decades, standing on the front lines and taking on America’s most dangerous enemies since before 9/11. He has planned, organized, and led some of our nation’s most sensitive counterterrorism missions. His long record of selfless service hunting down terrorists, combined with his recent experience as Deputy Director and Acting Director of the National Counterterrorism Center make Joe uniquely qualified to lead this critical agency at a time of incredible unrest and danger.

It is my honor to introduce Joe to you today and I urge the members of this committee to support his nomination as Director of the National Counterterrorism Center.

title: Duckworth Introduces Bill Ensuring DoD Develops a Plan to Modernize its Air Traffic Control System Alongside the FAA
text:
The Senator’s bill aims to establish a comprehensive plan to fully update our ATC system and keep our sky safe

[WASHINGTON, D.C.] – Amid a surge in calls to modernize our nation’s air traffic control (ATC) system, today U.S. Senator Tammy Duckworth (D-IL)—Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Commerce Subcommittee on Aviation and a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee—unveiled legislation that would help bolster planning and keep our sky safe by ensuring the Department of Defense (DoD) develops a comprehensive blueprint to overhaul its side of our ATC system alongside the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). The military must keep up with the FAA’s modernization efforts to ensure the safety of our airspace for our nation’s service members and the flying public.

“It’s been no secret that we need to overhaul and modernize our air traffic control system. But as the FAA works toward this goal, the Pentagon cannot fail to keep up and widen an already-existing safety gap,” said Duckworth. “We all fly in the same sky. And we need everyone to be on the same page. This commonsense bill would help ensure that our nation’s air traffic control modernization is a comprehensive effort to keep our shared sky safe.”

Specifically, Senator Duckworth’s One Sky Act—which mirrors a provision she successfully secured in the defense authorization bill that passed through the Senate Armed Services Committee—would direct the DoD to conduct a review of every ATC system it operates and develop a modernization plan aligned with the FAA’s “Brand New Air Traffic Control System,” including costs, timelines and barriers to these efforts. This legislation would increase transparency, accountability and help provide Congress with a structured roadmap for meeting our nation’s long-overdue ATC modernization goals while improving coordination between DoD and FAA.

Since the tragic American Airlines Flight 5342 mid-air collision with an Army Blackhawk led to the loss of 67 lives, there have been several alarming near-miss events between military and civilian aircraft. Mere months after the deadly collision, and in the same airspace, a military helicopter caused two commercial flights to abort landings at Washington National Airport (DCA) when it encroached on their flight paths. The investigation into the incident revealed that a hotline between the Pentagon and DCA tower had been inoperable for years and task-saturated operators used cell phones to pass time sensitive requests. These incidents underscore the necessity for a review of DoD ATC infrastructure, policies and procedures to best prioritize investment and continued action by DoD.

For years, Duckworth has been sounding the alarm that we must modernize our air traffic control system and make critical aviation safety investments immediately to prevent all-too-frequent near-misses from becoming catastrophic tragedies. Last Congress, Duckworth chaired two Commerce Aviation Subcommittee hearings—one in December of 2024 and the other a year prior—to address our aviation industry’s chilling surge in near-deadly close calls and underscore the urgent need to improve air traffic control systems to protect the flying public.

The December 2024 hearing came after the Government Accountability Office found that more than third of all air traffic control systems were unsustainable. Yet, without a joint effort by the DoD to modernize its own ATC systems alongside the FAA, the gap between civil and military aircraft and operators will continue to expand and inject risk into the system.

A copy of the bill text can be found on the Senator’s website.

title: As Republicans Shirk Committee Norms, Durbin Grills Judicial Nominees About Their Lack Of Judicial Temperament, Involvement In Baseless Prosecution Of James Comey
text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin (D-IL), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, today questioned judicial nominees during a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing with two panels beginning with Justice James Cody Hiland, nominated to be a judge on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit. During the second panel, Durbin pressed Philip Lawrence Aubart, nominated to the Middle District of North Carolina; Judge Brian Meyers, nominated to the Eastern District of North Carolina; and Justice James Sullivan, nominated to the Western District of Texas.

Before questioning Justice Hiland about his temperament, Durbin raised the alarm about Republicans abandoning the longstanding 28-day-rule, which requires that the Committee receive a nominee’s Senate Judiciary Questionnaire at least 28 days before their hearing. Justice Hiland’s Questionnaire was transmitted just seven days ago.

“You’re asking to be given that opportunity for life, for the rest of your natural life, to serve in that capacity. To say that we take this seriously is exactly what we’re supposed to do up here,” Durbin said to Justice Hiland. “We’re asked to ask serious questions so we can understand whether you are right for that job. It is also quite possible that we are troubled by the fact that we’ve had the response to your extensive questionnaires about your background, we’ve had access to that for seven days. That’s it. You would be the shortest period of time of any nominee that we received a questionnaire in the 28 years I’ve served on this Committee. To think we’re asking tough questions, that’s the reason. We have limited opportunity to review your background, and you are seeking the second highest court in the land for a lifetime appointment.”

Durbin then pressed Justice Hiland about his lack of judicial temperament when White House staff offered him a nomination to a district court in August 2026 rather than a nomination to the Eighth Circuit, which he was expecting. Months after he rejected the nomination to the district court vacancy, Justice Hiland was nominated to the Eighth Circuit after the Trump Administration withdrew Judge Lee Rudofsky’s nomination to the seat. Durbin questioned Justice Hiland on whether he has the temperament to serve in this lifetime appointment.

“In August, you spoke to a group of law students about the selection process to the federal bench. You told them that you had expected to receive a call from President Trump informing you of his intent to nominate you to this Eighth Circuit. Instead, you received a call from staff at the White House asking if you would be interested in filling a district court vacancy. Calling yourself ‘belligerent,’ you declined the offer. When asked by White House staff if they should ‘go back into the Oval Office and tell the President of the United States that you’re rejecting an opportunity to be appointed to the federal bench?’ You responded, ‘Yes, that’s exactly what I want you to tell the President of the United States,’” Durbin said.

“Do you still consider yourself ‘belligerent?’” Durbin asked Justice Hiland. “Can you control your emotions if you’re given this opportunity?” Durbin asked.

Justice Hiland claimed that his career as a prosecuting attorney and Arkansas Supreme Court justice has shown that he is capable of separating his emotions from the facts.

Durbin then asked Justice Hiland about a recent scandal at the Office of Professional Programs, which is overseen by the Arkansas Supreme Court, where he has served since 2023. In 2026, Nancie Givens, the former executive director of the Arkansas Office of Professional Programs, was arrested and charged with 65 felony counts of tampering with a public record. Investigators allege that, between July 2020 and July 2025, Givens had been deliberately altering bar exam scores. According to a press release signed by six of the seven justices on the Arkansas Supreme Court, including Justice Hiland, the court was informed about the irregularities in test scores and recordkeeping as early as February 2026; however, the criminal investigation was not initiated until April 2026. Further, a seal order has been put in place, eliminating any transparency about where the case stands.

“Earlier this month, the former executive director of the Arkansas Supreme Court’s Office of Professional Programs was arrested and charged with 65 felony counts for allegedly tampering with bar exam scores in the state of Arkansas, including adding points to scores that allowed them to pass rather than fail. The alleged misconduct took place between 2020 and 2025. You have sat on the Supreme Court since 2023… When were you first made aware of these irregularities with the bar exams?” Durbin asked Justice Hiland.

Justice Hiland claimed he was made aware in May of this year, though months earlier he had signed the press release issued by the Arkansas Supreme Court noting that it was aware of the test score irregularities.

“When were the individuals who should have failed the bar exam but are now practicing notified of the discrepancies in their scoring?” Durbin asked.

Justice Hiland replied that because this is an ongoing criminal investigation, there has been no communication with those who were incorrectly informed that they had passed the bar exam.

“For clarity, I would like to have you state for the record, under oath, whether you played any role… in the wrongdoing that’s been alleged,” Durbin said.

Justice Hiland said he was not involved in any wrongdoing.

Video of Durbin’s questions in Committee for Panel I is available here.

Audio of Durbin’s questions in Committee for Panel I is available here.

Footage of Durbin’s questions in Committee for Panel I is available here for TV Stations.

During the second panel, Durbin grilled Justice Sullivan about his nomination to the Western District of Texas, which the Committee was notified of just one day after he lost his election to the Texas Supreme Court and only two weeks before his scheduled hearing.

“What an amazing story. I have been a candidate in a lot of elections, but I’ve never had a consolation prize like this. So here you are running for the Texas Supreme Court, and you don’t know you have lost until the night before, but yet you have a Questionnaire filled out to file the next day for this federal court position. What am I missing here?” Durbin asked Justice Sullivan.

Justice Sullivan said that he first expressed interest in federal judicial service in March 2025.

“You certainly have friends in high places if you can lose an election one night and file a Questionnaire the next morning for a different judgeship. That’s quite a rebound,” Durbin replied.

Durbin then turned to Mr. Aubart and Judge Meyers, asking them about their involvement in the Trump Administration’s efforts to prosecute former FBI Director James Comey. Durbin first asked Mr. Aubart about his time serving as the First Assistant U.S. Attorney in the Eastern District of North Carolina.

“At President Trump’s urging, the Justice Department is implausibly claiming that former FBI Director Mr. Comey threatened to kill the President because he posted a picture of seashells in the formation of ‘86 47’ on social media….You [have] served as First Assistant U.S. Attorney in the Eastern District of North Carolina since 2025…[The First Assistant] typically oversees the office’s operations and supervises a large staff of prosecutors and professional staff…yet you have taken an unusually hands-on approach to the Comey prosecution,” Durbin said.

“In April 2026, you and a case agent directed the FBI to conduct keyword searches of trial transcripts from U.S. vs. Gambino, a case Comey prosecuted more than 30 years ago. What were you looking for?” Durbin asked Mr. Aubart.

Mr. Aubart said he was searching for any reference to “86” during the Gambino trial.

“Did you find it?” Durbin followed up.

Mr. Aubart said he found no reference to “86.”

“You traveled around the country to interview multiple witnesses, including to Phoenix. What did you do in Phoenix?” Durbin continued.

“Sammy the Bull was interviewed in Phoenix,” Mr. Aubart replied, referring to Salvator Gravano, who was a witness in the Gambino trial.

“What did he have to do with seashells?” Durbin pressed.

Mr. Aubart said he spoke with Mr. Gravano about his knowledge of the term “86,” but Mr. Aubart declined to provide additional details about their conversation.

“Did this case ever come up in your interviews with the Justice Department or the White House Counsel Office for this judgeship?” Durbin asked Mr. Aubart.

Mr. Aubart said he raised it as a potential topic of questioning during his nomination hearing.

Durbin then asked Judge Meyers about his involvement in the Comey prosecution as he was the U.S. Magistrate Judge who signed off on the search warrant for the personal email accounts and search history of Director Comey and his wife. Two months after signing the search warrants, Judge Meyers was contacted by U.S. Senator Ted Budd (R-NC) about his interest in serving as a district judge.

“Did this case ever come up in your interviews with the Justice Department or the White House Counsel?” Durbin asked Judge Meyers.

Judge Meyers replied that it did not.

title: Durbin Criticizes Senate Republicans For Violating Committee Norms To Jam Through Extreme, Unqualified Judicial Nominees Before Democrats Take Senate Majority
text:
During today’s Senate Judiciary Committee nominations hearing, Durbin delivered an opening statement again calling out Senate Republicans for bypassing Committee norms in an attempt to install MAGA loyalists in lifetime appointments

WASHINGTON – During today’s Senate Judiciary Committee nominations hearing, U.S. Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin (D-IL), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, delivered an opening statement again calling out Senate Republicans for violating longstanding bipartisan Committee norms to jam through the Trump Administration’s extreme and unqualified nominees during the lame-duck session. In addition to calling out Committee Republicans for missing multiple opportunities to slate nominees for earlier hearings and bypassing standards that allowed Committee staff to review each nominee’s FBI background check, Durbin criticized the Trump Administration for nominating extreme and unqualified individuals to lifetime appointments.

Nominees considered during today’s hearing include James Cody Hiland, to be U.S. Circuit Judge for the Eighth Circuit; Philip Lawrence Aubart, to be U.S. District Judge for the Middle District of North Carolina; Brian S. Meyers, to be U.S. District Judge for the Eastern District of North Carolina; Eric James Hamilton, to be U.S. District Judge for the District of Nebraska; William Grayson Lambert, to be U.S. District Judge for the District of South Carolina; Joseph Patrick Falvey, to be U.S. District Judge for the Northern District of Indiana; and James P. Sullivan, to be U.S. District Judge for the Western District of Texas.

Key Quotes:

“Just eight days after the Committee’s last nominations hearing, we’re back again because Senate Republicans are determined to confirm as many nominees as possible before control of the Senate shifts in six weeks. We’re here because the Trump White House has been slow to send nominations to the Senate.”

“Now the majority has resorted to breaking, if not changing, longstanding bipartisan Committee norms that Committee Chairs of both parties followed for decades to ensure that every member had adequate time to evaluate the nominees before us.”

“A longstanding rule, going back to at least the George W. Bush Administration, is that the Committee does not hold a hearing on a nomination until at least 28 days after the nominee’s Senate Judiciary Questionnaire is submitted. Today, we have nominees before us whose Questionnaires were received 14 days ago, and in one case, 7 days ago. This is for a lifetime appointment. It’s understandable that we’d ask for a little time to review a person’s background before the decision is made.”

“As I said yesterday, the Chairman and majority are within their rights to slate any nominee they’d like for a hearing. But it bears repeating: my Republican colleagues will regret changing our 28-day-rule to a 7-day rule.”

“We received Justice Cody Hiland’s Questionnaire one week ago. This came after Justice Hiland publicly complained about the White House passing him over for another nominee, Judge Lee Rudofsky. The nomination of Judge Rudofsky, who already had a hearing before this Committee, was withdrawn, and Justice Hiland received the nomination he publicly asked for.”

“I have deep concerns with Justice Hiland’s record. His partisan roles as Chairman of the Arkansas Republican Party and a Senior Advisor on Governor Sarah Huckabee Sanders’s campaign led to a seat on the state’s Supreme Court. On the bench, he has made it harder for Arkansans to vote and upended 75 years of precedent to weaken voter initiatives.”

“We have another state Supreme Court Justice before us today, James Sullivan, nominated to the Western District of Texas. This is an amazing political story. Two weeks ago, Justice Sullivan lost his bid to be reelected to the Texas Supreme Court. The very next day, the Administration submitted his Questionnaire, which had obviously been prepared in advance. It appears that a federal district court appointment for life is the consolation prize if you lose an election for the Texas Supreme Court.”

“Republicans are violating Committee norms to rush through this nominee because they want to deny the incoming Senator any voice in the process.”

“Also on today’s slate is Eric Hamilton, nominated to the District of Nebraska. He is currently a senior DOJ official, defending the Trump Administration’s blatantly unconstitutional actions in court…A federal judge said, ‘the Court is left with little confidence that [he] can be trusted to tell the truth about anything.’”

“Finally, the two North Carolina nominees before us today have played leading roles in the prosecution of former FBI Director James Comey for the alleged crime of posting a picture of seashells—one of President Trump’s efforts to seek revenge against his political enemies.”

“Here’s what one Republican member of this Committee said about this prosecution, quote: ‘Some bonehead in North Carolina thinks that’s a crime…Well, they better damn sure have information to back it up, because if all it is, is a picture, that person should lose their job.’ But instead of losing their jobs, they’re getting lifetime appointments.”

title: Durbin Reintroduces Legislation To Protect Student Loan Borrowers
In Speech On The Senate Floor, Durbin Calls For Guantánamo Bay Detention Facility To Finally Be Closed
text:
For years, Durbin has been a vocal advocate for shuttering the detention center at Guantánamo Bay

WASHINGTON – U.S. Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin (D-IL), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, called on the next generation of leaders to continue to fight for the ideals that make this nation great and finally close the Guantánamo Bay detention facility. Durbin has been a vocal advocate for shuttering the detention center at Guantánamo Bay. After holding the Senate’s first hearing on the need to close Guantánamo in 2013, Durbin held another hearing in 2021 where he reiterated his frequent calls to close the detention facility. Durbin emphasized that keeping the detention center open undermines America’s moral standing and credibility around the world and wastes taxpayer dollars.

“What makes America great is our aspiration to uphold the inherent dignity, equality, and inalienable rights of all of our people. All too often though, when we are faced with threats, there are those who would cast these foundational ideals aside. Unfortunately, after the terrorist attacks on September 11th, that view prevailed, promoted by those in power who believed that the risk of another attack justified compromising our basic values,” Durbin said. “This January marks the 25th anniversary of the opening of detention camps for suspected terrorists at Guantánamo Bay.”

Durbin continued, “The express purpose of sending captured suspects to Guantánamo was to detain them in a legal black hole. Our nation’s leaders wanted a place where detainees could be held and interrogated beyond the reach of our laws, our courts, our Constitution, and our ideals of justice and dignity. Detainees were tortured and subjected to unspeakable abuse at Guantánamo, as well as at secret CIA black sites around the world. Most were held in indefinite detention without charges or trial. The few who were charged were in makeshift military commissions.”

Durbin continued, “This betrayal of our values weakened America. Rather than making us safer, we fueled terrorist recruitment, surrendered the moral high ground in the argument, wasted the good will of our allies, and damaged our standing in the world. This astronomically expensive offshore prison also cost American taxpayers—and continues to—billions of dollars more than if we had used our time-tested federal court system. Meanwhile, thousands of 9/11 families continue to suffer from the emotional and financial loss of their loved ones, loss compounded by the failure of our government to give them a modicum of justice. Twenty-five years after the attacks, the 9/11 trial still has not begun, and key confessions have been ruled too tainted by torture to be admissible in a court or hearing.”

Durbin has also spoken out against the Trump Administration’s unlawful transfer of immigrants to Guantánamo Bay, and he has led other Senators in demanding answers for the legal justification for using the base as an immigration detention center.

In October, Durbin’s office released insights from an oversight visit of immigration detention at Guantánamo Bay. The staff noted that the Trump Administration staffs the facilities whether any immigrants are being detained at Guantánamo Bay or not, including during extended periods of time when there are none present. Detaining immigrant detainees at Guantánamo Bay comes at an exorbitant cost to taxpayers, with a total of approximately 852 immigrants being held at the facility since January 2025 at the cost of more than $100 million.

“We should have learned by now that we are strongest as a nation and as a people when we uphold human dignity and the rule of law. Instead, we left the Guantánamo playbook open and available for President Trump and Stephen Miller. Trump vowed during his presidential campaign in 2016 that he would not only keep Guantánamo open, but he would also ‘load it up with some bad dudes.’ And now, in his second term, the President is making good on his threat—by sending immigrants to this grotesque facility,” Durbin said. “Most migrants come to America seeking safety from persecution and torture or simply a better life. But Trump and Miller are seeking to avoid our laws and our courts by shipping these immigrants off to legal black holes around the world faster than the courts can stop them.”

Durbin then shared the story of Victor Omar Bonilla Alvarez. Victor escaped years of torture and abuse at the hands of MS-13 and law enforcement in El Salvador. He has no criminal record. An immigration judge granted him withholding of removal to El Salvador based on his credible fear of torture if he were sent back. After months of confinement in the United States, our government sent him to Guantánamo. Then, after months of confinement there, the government transferred him to Arizona and then swiftly removed him to Mexico. They did this all without informing his counsel and without any assurances from Mexico that he would not be sent to El Salvador.

“This Administration has sent an estimated 25,000 people to third countries, denying them due process and their legal protections against persecution or torture,” Durbin said. “Many, like Victor, risk being returned to torture. Others are being indefinitely detained, in abysmal conditions, and with little to no access to the rule of law or any hope for the future.”

Durbin concluded, “Violating the law to send people away to be persecuted or tortured? Is this who we are? Is this American? Is this who we aspire to be? With a new year and a new Congress on the horizon, I hope our next generation of leaders will continue to fight for the ideals that make this nation great and finally close the Guantánamo detention facility.”
