title: Gillibrand, Schumer Pass Lithium-Ion Battery Bill To Prevent Future Deadly Fires
text:
Passed Via Unanimous Consent on the Senate Floor, the Legislation Requires the Consumer Product Safety Commission to Establish Mandatory Standards for Lithium-Ion Batteries Found in E-Bikes

**Watch Senator Gillibrand’s Remarks on the Senate Floor Here**

Today, U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY) and Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY) announced that their Setting Consumer Standards for Lithium-Ion Batteries Act passed the Senate unanimously. The bill directs the Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) to mandate standards for lithium-ion batteries in micromobility devices. It passed the House in 2025 with a strong bipartisan majority and now heads to the president’s desk for his signature.

This follows three recent deadly fires in New York with possible or confirmed linkages to faulty lithium-ion batteries: one in the Mott Haven neighborhood of the Bronx on October 28 that killed four people, one in the Sunset Park neighborhood of Brooklyn on November 5 that killed six people, and one in Colonie on November 13 that killed two people. In 2026, New York City has already been the site of 406 lithium-ion battery fires. According to the FDNY, there have been 46 deaths and 628 injuries caused by lithium-ion batteries since it began recording this statistic in 2019.

“We have lost far too many New Yorkers due to underregulated lithium-ion batteries,” said Senator Gillibrand. “Fires ignited by poorly manufactured lithium-ion batteries used in e-bikes and e-scooters are on the rise, putting New Yorkers in danger. Passing this bill is an important step in preventing future fires. I urge the president to immediately sign this bill into law and for CPSC to meet its requirements.”

“Cheap, dangerous, and under-regulated lithium-ion batteries have caused fires, injuries, and deaths across New York, and federal action is needed to protect consumers, workers, and the brave firefighters on the front lines. China has inundated our markets with cheap, rechargeable batteries, but cutting corners in production has made these batteries dangerous. Consumers deserve better than cheap, unsafe products made in bulk overseas,” said Senator Schumer. “This bill will establish mandatory safety standards for lithium-ion batteries, and its passage brings us one step closer to protecting the public and firefighters from the growing hazards of these low-quality and dangerous batteries. I urge the president to sign this critical bill into law ASAP.”

The Setting Consumer Standards for Lithium-Ion Batteries Act does the following:

Directs the CPSC to set binding federal safety standards for lithium-ion batteries and electrical systems used in micromobility devices within 180 days of enactment.

Codifies industry-leading safety benchmarks.

Establishes enforceable consumer rules by granting standards the full force of a mandatory consumer product safety rule, enabling federal regulators to halt the sale, distribution, or import of non-compliant devices.

Requires comprehensive congressional hazard reporting by mandating that the CPSC submit a 5-year report to Congress.

Last month, Senators Gillibrand and Schumer, along with Congressman Ritchie Torres, called on Acting CPSC Chair Peter Feldman to complete the rulemaking process to set a mandatory federal standard for lithium-ion batteries in micromobility products such as e-bikes and e-scooters. In their letter, the members underscored the concerning number of lithium-ion battery-related fatalities among micromobility products across the country, particularly in New York City.

title: Senate Passes Gillibrand, Tenney Legislation To Designate The Finger Lakes Region As A National Heritage Area
text:
Legislation Promotes Tourism And Helps Preserve The History And Environment Of The Finger Lakes Region

Today, the Senate passed U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand’s bipartisan Finger Lakes National Heritage Area Act, which would designate the Finger Lakes region as a National Heritage Area (NHA). NHAs are established by Congress to recognize a region’s natural, cultural, or historic significance. Securing this designation for the Finger Lakes would promote tourism and help ensure that the area’s history and natural landscape are preserved for generations to come. The bill now moves onto consideration in the House.

“Home to beautiful landscapes, rich history, and thriving small businesses, the Finger Lakes are a national treasure,” said Senator Gillibrand. “In recognition of all that this area has to offer, I’m leading the push to designate the region as a National Heritage Area. This designation will promote tourism, create jobs, conserve natural resources, and make sure local communities have what they need to thrive for years to come. I am proud to have passed this bill in the Senate, and I am committed to getting it signed into law.”

Rep. Claudia Tenney (R-NY-24) has companion legislation in the House.

“The Finger Lakes is home to generations of hardworking families, historic communities, and some of the most beautiful landscapes in New York State,” said Congresswoman Tenney. “Our region has a remarkable story to tell, and a National Heritage Area designation would help preserve that history while bringing new visitors and economic opportunities to our local communities. I introduced the House companion legislation because I believe the Finger Lakes deserves this recognition. The Senate’s passage is an encouraging step forward, and I look forward to building on this progress in the House.”

The process for designating a region as a National Heritage Area usually involves two steps. First, Congress passes a bill directing the National Park Service to conduct a feasibility study, which determines whether the area is suitable for being designated as an NHA. If the results of the feasibility study are positive, Congress then must pass a second bill to formally designate the region.

Gillibrand has been leading the push to designate the Finger Lakes as an NHA for years. In 2015, she first announced the Finger Lakes National Heritage Area Study Act, which directed the National Park Service to conduct a feasibility study for the area. This bill was signed into law in 2019, and the National Park Service completed its feasibility study and confirmed the Finger Lakes’ eligibility in 2023. Now, the Finger Lakes National Heritage Area Act would complete the second step in the process and formally create the Finger Lakes NHA.

The following 14 New York counties would comprise the Finger Lakes NHA: Cayuga, Chemung, Cortland, Livingston, Monroe, Onondaga, Ontario, Schuyler, Seneca, Steuben, Tioga, Tompkins, Wayne, and Yates.

title: Grassley Votes to Advance Bipartisan Permitting Reform to Cut Red Tape and Get America Building Again
text:
WASHINGTON – Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) today voted to advance a major piece of bipartisan legislation that would overhaul the country’s broken federal environmental review and permitting system, which is currently holding up $16.8 billion worth of projects in Iowa. By reducing project delays and giving businesses more certainty to invest and build in America, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) will help lower energy costs for American families, create good-paying jobs and accelerate economic growth. The Senate approved the legislation by a vote of 62-33. The bill now heads to the House of Representatives.

“Too many critical infrastructure projects are stuck in limbo because of red tape and endless delays. This leads to lost jobs, missed economic opportunities and higher utility costs for families. Today, I voted to fix our broken permitting system so Iowans can get building without bureaucrats standing in the way,” Grassley said. “The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act will keep our country competitive for decades to come by strengthening our infrastructure, producing affordable energy and lowering costs for Iowans.”

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act also includes the Ratepayer Protection Act, which protects Iowans from paying for the rising energy costs of large electricity users, such as data centers. Specifically, the provision creates a national standard that makes data centers pay their own way for transmission lines and other infrastructure instead of forcing American consumers to face increased costs through rising utility bills. Iowa is currently home to some of the cheapest, most predictable and cleanest energy sources in the country, in part thanks to the long standing and renewed partnership between Iowa’s utility companies and data centers.

The following are the impacts of permitting delays in Iowa:

$16.8 billion: total value of Iowa projects stuck in the federal permitting process right now.

$280 million: total cost of federal permitting delays to Iowa manufacturers annually.

$29.1 billion: total economic impact on hold due to the current federal permitting holdup in Iowa (including jobs, in-state spending, tax revenue and more).

3.6%: The total economic impact of Iowa projects entering the federal permitting process annually is equivalent to 3.6% of Iowa’s total GDP.

This week, Grassley spoke on the Senate floor in support of the legislation, highlighting how delays have impacted communities across the country. In his remarks, Grassley cited a road in Colorado that took 13 years to build, a wind project in Wyoming that waited 12 years for federal approval and a mine in Minnesota that took 12 years for its environmental review. Grassley also highlighted Iowans’ support for the legislation, including Joe Murphy of the Iowa Business Council who said, “This bipartisan legislation will bring greater certainty and predictability to the federal permitting process, establish clear timelines for reviews and decisions and make important changes to the way major energy and infrastructure projects are approved.”

Background:

Currently, it takes an average of 4.5 years for federal agencies to approve environmental impact statements. Each year, manufacturers incur $12.1 billion in costs due to permitting delays, and $1.1 to $1.5 trillion in investments are currently locked up in the federal permitting system.

Without regulatory certainty, companies delay meaningful investments in communities across America, holding up roads, bridges, energy infrastructure, manufacturing facilities and other investments that create jobs and strengthen local economies.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act overhauls the federal environmental review and permitting system by establishing deadlines for environmental reviews, providing greater certainty for projects that have already received federal permits and reducing unnecessary delays and litigation. The bill is designed to help projects of all types, not adjust processes for some types of projects but not others. Projects like coal mines, windmills, gas pipelines, solar farms, and steel mills will all benefit from this legislation.

It’s estimated that this legislation could result in an $82 billion to $164 billion increase in economic output every year. The bill is also expected to increase real wages and reduce electric bills for the average household.

title: Grassley, Wyden Introduce Crime Victims Fund Prioritization Act
text:
WASHINGTON – Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) and Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) this week introduced the Crime Victims Fund Prioritization Act to authorize the transfer of funds from the Department of Justice’s (DOJ) Working Capital Fund to the Crime Victims Fund (CVF), in the event the Crime Victims Fund’s balance drops too low. This bipartisan legislation would ensure the critical program continues to have the resources necessary to support victims and survivors of crime.

“The Crime Victims Fund is a taxpayer neutral program that supports victims and survivors of crime across the United States. By establishing new funding sources, the bipartisan Crime Victims Fund Prioritization Act will ensure the critical fund can continue assisting Americans for decades to come,” Grassley said.

“Inconsistent funding has left crime victims without the support they need for far too long,” Wyden said. “It’s past time to secure a funding fix to ensure victims of crime and their families get the help and care when they need it the most, and our bipartisan bill is the way to do it.”

Bill text is available HERE.

Background:

Congress in 1984 established the Crime Victims Fund to support victims and survivors of crime across the United States. The program was designed to be taxpayer neutral, funded entirely by fines and penalties collected through federal criminal convictions and settlements.

Despite passing the Grassley-backed VOCA Fix Act to bolster the Crime Victims Fund in 2021, Grassley’s oversight last Congress revealed that billions of dollars in fines and penalties weren’t being collected or deposited into the fund. Rather, these dollars were being directed elsewhere, including to the DOJ’s Working Capital Fund, which pays for the agency’s IT services and equipment.

title: Hagerty Announces Passage of Financial Exploitation Prevention Act
text:
WASHINGTON—Yesterday, United States Senator Bill Hagerty (R-TN) announced the passage of the Financial Exploitation Prevention Act, legislation that gives the financial industry the tools necessary to address suspected financial exploitation and abuse of seniors and those with mental and physical disabilities.

Hagerty posted a video on X denoting the bill’s passage and its importance to the nation’s financial protection system.

*Click on the photo above or click here to watch*

“1 in 5 American seniors are financially exploited by scammers each year, resulting in roughly $3 billion drained from seniors’ savings,” said Hagerty. “It’s unconscionable and should never happen. Today, the Senate has passed my bill—the Financial Exploitation Prevention Act—to protect seniors.”

Background:

Over the next 10+ years, 10,000 Americans will turn 65 each day, with seniors making up 18 percent of the nation’s population by 2030. As more investors age into retirement, their risk of exploitation increases. Currently, about one in five senior investors are victimized by financial fraud, and those investors lose an estimated $2.9 billion annually in reported cases.

The Financial Exploitation Prevention Act gives the financial industry better tools to address suspected financial exploitation and abuse of seniors and those with mental and physical disabilities.

The bill requires the Securities and Exchange Commission to report to Congress on recommendations for legislative and regulatory changes on how to combat financial exploitation of seniors and vulnerable adults.

The bill also permits a registered open-end investment company or transfer agent for that company, including mutual funds, to better protect seniors by delaying the redemption period of any redeemable security if it is reasonably believed that such redemption was requested through the financial exploitation of a security holder who is a senior or an individual who cannot protect their own interests.

title: Heinrich Questions Trump Interior Nominee on Unlawful Firings of Inspectors General by the Trump Administration and Trump Energy Nominee on Skyrocketing Gas Prices Due to Trump’s War with Iran
text:
WASHINGTON — During a U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee hearing to consider pending Trump nominees, U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, cross examined Dennis Kirk, President Trump’s nomination for Inspector General of the Department of the Interior (DOI), and Toby Deen, Trump’s nomination for Assistant Secretary of Energy for Hydrocarbons and Geothermal Energy, where he pressed each nominee on the President’s unlawful firings of Inspectors General and the administration’s war with Iran.

VIDEO: Ranking Member Heinrich (D-N.M.) questions Dennis Kirk, President Trump’s nominee for Inspector General of the Department of the Interior, and Toby Deen, President Trump’s nominee for Assistant Secretary of Energy for Hydrocarbons and Geothermal Energy, November 18, 2026.

In his opening remarks, Heinrich connected Kirk’s nomination to a pattern of partisan Inspectors General appointees from the Trump administration, “More than one year into his second term, President Trump has fired or demoted more than 20 Inspectors General (IG) across the federal government. When President Trump has opted to fill IG vacancies, he has largely appointed allies with partisan backgrounds to fill those roles. I am concerned, Mr. Kirk, that your nomination continues this trend. President Trump has opted to fill the IG vacancy at the Department of the Interior with a political appointee.”

Heinrich expressed concerns over Kirk’s partisan background and allyship to the Trump administration, due to his involvement with gutting critical federal worker protections during the first Trump administration, his connection to the Heritage Foundation as a co-author of a chapter of Project 2025, and time at the IG office in the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, which sparked concerns from intelligence community officials on whether his appointment could compromise the integrity of the IG office.

“With this context in mind, I have deep concerns Mr. Kirk will be an independent and objective IG if confirmed,” said Heinrich.

When questioned during the hearing, Heinrich asked Kirk about whether Trump’s firing of Inspectors General without Congressional notification was unlawful, “In January of 2025, the President fired more than a dozen Inspectors General. And that included Mark Greenblatt, the DOI’s Inspector General. Now, the law requires the President to notify Congress prior to the firing of an IG and also provide written reasoning for that removal. That never happened. Mr. Kirk, you’re an attorney. The facts appear to me to be pretty straightforward. Was the law violated when Mr. Greenblatt was fired without providing notice to Congress or any reasoning?”

Kirk replied, “Thank you for that question, Senator Heinrich. I don’t know, because I’m not familiar with the circumstances of what happened to him. I know that Mark Greenblatt was —”

Heinrich interjected, saying, “I’m not litigating whether there was a reason to fire him. I’m litigating whether or not the law was followed, because we were not notified, and we were also not given any written reasoning. So let me let me read the law to you. This is the 1978 IG Act as amended in 2008, and it says that ‘the President shall communicate in writing the reasons for any such removal or transfer to both houses of Congress not later than 30 days before the removal or transfer.’”

Kirk responded, “Senator Heinrich, again, I don’t know why that was done that way, and I don’t know that… because I’ve never met a living President. I don’t have a picture of a President on my wall. They don’t —”

Heinrich asked again, “Does it appear that was done in violation of the law? If it is true that there was no written reasoning nor notification?”

Kirk replied, “Well, the law is the law, Senator.”

Heinrich concluded, “That’s my point.”

Heinrich also questioned Deen on Trump’s war with Iran driving up gas and diesel prices for Americans.

Heinrich asked, “The conflict in the Middle East has had a profoundly expensive impact on the American people, and we see that everywhere from the grocery store to the gas pump, certainly in diesel prices. Do you agree that the closure of the Strait of Hormuz is the primary factor driving the currently very high and unusual prices of gasoline and diesel that the American people have had to bear?”

Deen replied, “I appreciate the question, Senator. Products like diesel, refined petroleum products, are a global commodity, and it is a complex market with multiple drivers of price. Supply demand is a fundamental driver of that, and currently across the world, we are seeing a shortage of refining capacity that is a large driver…”

Heinrich responded, “Would you agree that the conflict, the impact of the conflict actually removing refining capacity from the global market, has been one of those factors?”

Deen replied, “Global refining capacity and domestic refining capacity all play a part there, and our U.S. domestic supply acts as a buffer to global supply shocks. Global supply shocks are always going to be a risk for the United States.”

Heinrich continued, “Fair enough. Did DOE look at the potential effects of having the Strait closed on energy prices? Was there some analysis done before the decisions were made to initiate that conflict?”

Deen responded, “That’s a fair question, Senator. I was not advising the Secretary or the White House regarding that conflict. The Department of Energy Secretary Wright is the President’s principal energy advisor. I’m sure they were having those discussions.”

Heinrich’s full opening remarks as delivered are below:

Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

And thank you, Mr. Kirk and Mr. Deen, for appearing before the Committee today.

Mr. Kirk, I want to start with your nomination.

The President has nominated you to serve as the Department of the Interior’s Inspector General, one of our most important government positions.

Congress created Inspector General offices as “independent and objective units.”

IG offices are often the first line of defense against wrongdoing and misconduct in government offices.

Under the IG Act, IGs are to be appointed “without regard to political affiliation and solely on the basis of integrity and demonstrated ability.”

When at their best, IGs prevent and detect fraud, waste, and abuse and promote efficiency and effectiveness in government programs and operations.

They serve as the bedrock of a functioning government.

However, under this President, we have witnessed the deliberate dismantling of independent oversight.

In his first few days of his second term, this president fired more than a dozen Inspectors General — including Mark Greenblatt, the Department of the Interior’s Inspector General at the time.

These firings occurred without notice to Congress and in clear violation of the law.

The firings continued a trend that started during President Trump’s first term — the elimination of vital oversight checks.

More than one year into his second term, President Trump has fired or demoted more than 20 Inspectors General across the federal government.

When President Trump has opted to fill IG vacancies, he has largely appointed allies with partisan backgrounds to fill those roles.

I am concerned, Mr. Kirk, that your nomination continues this trend. President Trump has opted to fill the IG vacancy at the Department of the Interior with a political appointee.

Weeks before being formally nominated, the Trump administration deployed Mr. Kirk to the IG’s office at the Department of the Interior. This was a highly unusual decision.

Mr. Kirk arrived at DOI’s IG office as a senior advisor just as the Trump administration grappled with the deeply flawed Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool project.

A project that has faced mounting scrutiny not only from myself, but from the public and from many members of Congress.

Senator Whitehouse and I wrote to DOI’s Deputy IG requesting an inquiry days before the President formally nominated Mr. Kirk.

At the Office of Personnel Management during the President’s first term, Mr. Kirk helped push along the President’s controversial personnel policies, including Schedule F, which stripped federal employees of civil service protections.

After leaving the administration, Mr. Kirk reappeared at the Heritage Foundation where he co-authored a chapter of Project 2025.

And during President Trump’s second term, Mr. Kirk served at ODNI under Director Tulsi Gabbard. After the Signal-gate controversy, Ms. Gabbard quickly deployed him to the intelligence community’s IG office.

At the time, intelligence community officials feared that Mr. Kirk’s appointment to the IG’s office could compromise the integrity of an ongoing inquiry.

With this context in mind, I have deep concerns Mr. Kirk will be an independent and objective IG if confirmed.

But you do not have to take it from me.

Listen to Mr. Greenblatt, the person who President Trump nominated in 2019 to serve as DOI IG — a position he served honorably for more than five years until President Trump fired him for doing his job.

Following Mr. Kirk’s nomination, Mr. Greenblatt stated: “President Trump’s nomination of Dennis Kirk to serve as Inspector General of the Department of the Interior raises serious concerns about the independence and credibility of one of the federal government’s most important watchdog offices.”

Mr. Greenblatt went on to say, and I believe this is particularly salient, “Mr. Kirk is not an experienced auditor, investigator, prosecutor, or oversight professional. He is a partisan operative.”

Now to Mr. Deen.

The President has nominated Mr. Deen to be Assistant Secretary of Energy for Hydrocarbons and Geothermal Energy.

Beyond natural gas export permitting, which the president and this administration appear to be singularly focused on, the office has other important responsibilities, such as fossil energy research and development, geothermal energy research, carbon capture and sequestration deployment, hydrogen production, and methane emissions reduction.

Following President Trump’s reckless decision to enter into a war with Iran, we have seen gas and diesel prices sharply increase.

Americans from Albuquerque to Philadelphia are struggling. Diesel prices are around $6.00 nationally and gas prices are almost a dollar more nationally than they were before the war.

Mr. Deen, I will be interested in hearing your thoughts on how your office can help bring down skyrocketing energy prices, and I look forward to your testimony today.

Thank you, Mr. Chair.

title: Heinrich: Senate Passage of Landmark Bipartisan Permitting Deal Will Lower Electricity Bills, Hold Data Centers Accountable, Create Over One Hundred Thousand Jobs, Reduce Carbon Emissions
text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, released the following statement after the Senate passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), bipartisan legislation to lower energy bills, hold data centers accountable, reduce emissions, and create good-paying jobs.

“In June, SunZia — the largest clean energy infrastructure project in the Western Hemisphere — came online in New Mexico after nearly two decades. The actual construction took just two years. That's how badly our permitting system is holding America back.

“Americans sent Congress a clear message in this historic election: lower costs. They're tired of watching their electricity bills go up while some of the wealthiest corporations in the world get a free ride. We don't have to wait another year to deliver relief. We can act right now.

“The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act will get more affordable energy onto the grid faster, make data centers pay their fair share of electricity and grid costs, and create more than 100,000 good-paying American jobs — all while maintaining important environmental protections and strengthening Tribal consultation.

“This was a hard-fought bipartisan agreement, and it wasn't easy. But we proved that Democrats and Republicans can put politics aside and deliver meaningful results for the American people.

“I'm proud of what we've accomplished. Now let's get this bill across the finish line and signed into law.”

Independent analyses project that the legislation will:

Now that the legislation has passed the Senate, it must also pass the House of Representatives before heading to the President's desk to be signed into law.

Heinrich, along with U.S. Senators Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, Shelley More Capito (R-W. Va.), Chairman of the U.S. Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, and Mike Lee (R-Utah), Chairman of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, introduced the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act in September.

Since introducing the legislation, Heinrich has led an extensive effort to build bipartisan support, engage stakeholders, and make the case for why permitting reform is essential to lowering energy costs and building America's energy future. title: Hickenlooper Presses Senate Leadership Candidates to Outline AI Safety, Affordability and Accountability Agenda
text:
Hickenlooper on AI “The next Majority Leader should have a day-one plan for responsible regulation.”

WASHINGTON – U.S. Senator John Hickenlooper sent a letter to Leader Schumer and Senator Van Hollen pushing the candidates to commit to an agenda that prioritizes AI safety alongside affordability and accountability.

“With the presidential election two years away, we have a two-year audition to show Americans we can deliver on three priorities: affordability, accountability, and AI safety,” Hickenlooper wrote.

“Ensuring this technology benefits all Americans, not just those building this technology will not be easy. It will take a leadership team with the right agenda and determination. That starts with an open discussion within our caucus.”

In the letter, Hickenlooper set clear expectations for the next Majority Leader on AI:

“…The next Majority Leader should have a day-one plan for responsible regulation. That should include policies that support a robust third-party evaluation ecosystem, mitigate national security challenges like cyber and biorisk, and establish clear rules of the road to hold AI companies accountable,” he wrote.

“…Meeting this moment requires more than just legislation,” he added.“We should consider a Select Committee on AI that has the power and resources to help the Senate keep pace with this rapidly evolving technology.”

Senator Hickenlooper is the ranking member of the Senate Commerce subcommittee on Consumer Protection, Technology, and Data Privacy, and previously called on the committee to lead responsible AI regulation.

Hickenlooper has long called for responsible AI regulation and outlined a framework for it in 2024. He’s introduced bipartisan legislation to responsibly regulate AI, including the VET AI Act, which directs the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) to develop standards and guidelines for independent third-party evaluations of AI systems.

Full text of the letter is available HERE and below:

Leader Schumer and Senator Van Hollen,

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is threatening to upend every part of American life. And the U.S. Senate is acting too slowly. That’s why the race for Senate Majority Leader is so important.

Thanks to the leadership of Leader Schumer, Democrats could hold as many as 56 seats. We just won in places like Kansas, Mississippi, and Texas, where Democrats haven’t won Senate races in decades. With the presidential election two years away, we have a two-year audition to show Americans we can deliver on three priorities: affordability, accountability, and AI safety.

Following two years of unchecked chaos, Americans are desperately looking to Washington for leadership — especially on AI. Young people are wondering how they’ll ever get their footing when AI is removing the first rung of the traditional career ladder. Families are worried about their energy bills climbing. Farmers are concerned about data centers draining their already limited water resources. Meanwhile, AI experts are warning that as model capabilities grow, the risks that a catastrophic incident will occur in the short term become even greater.

AI has the potential to help us solve our greatest challenges and unlock scientific breakthroughs in medicine, agriculture, and more. But we should also be deeply worried about what AI means for our future. The potential for even more massive concentrations of wealth and extreme inequality, the risks of war, blackouts, and acts of terror should concern us all. Every day the Senate fails to act moves us closer to these potential dangers.

The next Senate Majority Leader will play an outsized role in championing the tools we need to protect against consequences that are both profound and irreversible.

The next Majority Leader should have a day-one plan for responsible regulation. That should include policies that support a robust third-party evaluation ecosystem, mitigate national security challenges like cyber and biorisk, and establish clear rules of the road to hold AI companies accountable. We also need to examine how best to promote competition and open-source innovation and consider banning Recursive Self-Improvement to prevent AI systems from autonomously advancing beyond our ability to control them.

Meeting this moment requires more than just legislation. We should consider a Select Committee on AI that has the power and resources to help the Senate keep pace with this rapidly evolving technology. This Committee could complement the work of our other relevant committees while shining an even brighter, constant spotlight on AI, positioning Democrats as the party Americans trust to act in their best interests.

Ensuring this technology benefits all Americans, not just those building this technology will not be easy. It will take a leadership team with the right agenda and determination. That starts with an open discussion within our caucus.

The next Majority Leader must be prepared to deliver on affordability, accountability, and AI safety. I look forward to hearing more about your plans and working with our next leadership team to make these issues a top priority.

Sincerely,

###

title: Hickenlooper Welcomes Senate Passage of Much Needed Permitting Reform Bill
text:
Bipartisan bill will lower costs, advance clean energy projects

WASHINGTON – Today, U.S. Senator John Hickenlooper released the following statement after voting to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act.

Hickenlooper has long supported reforms to modernize what is all too often a decades-long timeline to build new transmission lines and clean energy projects.Hickenlooper pushed for amendments to increase funding for Tribal and state historic preservation offices, and to altogether strike the title revising the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA). He has hosted a series of bipartisan permitting dinners throughout the last three years, bringing key Senate negotiators together to build consensus and help move permitting conversations forward.

“Today, the U.S. Senate passed a bill that will lower electricity bills, make data centers pay their fair share, and accelerate the clean energy projects we need to combat climate change.”

“Bipartisan bills like this are rare. Where we’ve landed isn’t perfection. But it is progress toward delivering on our promise to bring down prices, hold Big Tech accountable, and stop the Trump administration’s attacks on clean energy. Our work with Tribal Nations and environmental groups doesn’t end with today’s vote. We’ll keep pushing to address their concerns.

“Democrats and Republicans have worked toward this moment for years. Now we have a chance to finally get this bill over the finish line.”

According to independent analysis, the bill would:

Create up to 105,600 good-paying trades and manufacturing jobs through 2040

Require data centers to pay for increased grid and energy costs they create, estimated at $55 billion over the next 10 years

Save $19 billion in residential electricity bills over the next 14 years

Nearly double the amount of solar and wind that can connect to the grid

Reduce power sector emissions by approximately 20 percent

Avoid 1.5 gigatons of CO₂ emissions, the equivalent of taking 39 coal plants offline for a decade

CHECK OUT WHAT THEY’RE SAYING:

“Passing BAAJA in the Senate is a major step forward. Grateful to my colleagues and our friends in the labor movement and the clean energy industry for their hard work to make this happen,” said Senator Whitehouse. “Americans will quickly begin getting some relief on their energy bills if the House follows suit. This bill kicks off Democrats bringing down energy costs, lowering emissions, creating well-paying jobs, and ending the free ride for data centers.”

“We can’t lose sight of why permitting reform is so urgently needed: across America, thousands of proposed clean-energy projects are stuck in permitting and interconnection limbo while electricity demand and consumer bills keep climbing. We have the technologies to deliver cleaner, more affordable power. What we too often lack is the ability to build and connect them quickly enough,” said former Secretary of Energy Jennifer Granholm. “This legislation tackles those obstacles.”

“In passing this bill, lawmakers can show immediate action on their affordability promises to voters: by delivering legislation that will lower energy costs, strengthen our economy, and build a cleaner energy future. Permitting reform is vital to delivering on that promise,” said Evergreen Action Vice President of Policy Pete Wyckoff.

“Earlier this month, voters sent a clear message to Washington. They want their government to refocus on building an economy that works for working people. That means more family-sustaining union jobs, investing in the infrastructure on which we all rely, and lowering costs for households,” wrote Jody Calemine, Director of Government Affairs for AFL-CIO. “Passing BAAJA will show that our government is listening.”

“If you care about climate, you should care about permitting reform,” KC Becker, former speaker of the Colorado House and a former EPA Region 8 administrator, wrote in an op-ed in the the Loveland Reporter-Herald. “There’s a real window to get this done. The Senate just introduced the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, and there are other proposals being considered. We must ensure that legislation brings clean, affordable energy to the grid and ensures data centers pay their fair share. Congress take this opportunity to pass significant legislation that, if done right, can accelerate our transition to cleaner energy sources.”

In addition to AFL-CIO’s support, organized labor strongly backs the bill. Union support includes the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers (IBEW), International Association of Iron Workers, International Association of Sheet Metal, Air, Rail, and Transportation Workers (SMART), International Brotherhood of Boilermakers, International Brotherhood of Teamsters, International Union of Operating Engineers (IUOE), Laborers’ International Union of North America (LIUNA), North America’s Building Trades Unions (NABTU), and United Association of Plumbers and Pipefitters.

The clean energy industry also unanimously supports the bill, including American Clean Power (ACP), Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA), Corporate Energy Buyers Association, American Council on Renewable Energy, Advanced Energy United (AEU), Americans for a Clean Energy Grid, Vestas, and Apex Clean Energy.

Other notable supporters include Climate Leadership Council, the Bipartisan Policy Center, Third Way, Center for Public Enterprise, Ceres, Niskanen, and Grid Strategies.

title: Hoeven: Senate Passes Bipartisan Permitting Reform to Create Jobs, Make Energy More Affordable
text:
WASHINGTON – Senator John Hoeven, a member of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, today joined his Senate colleagues in voting to pass bipartisan legislation to reform the federal environmental review and permitting processes. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026:

Provides certainty that permitted energy and infrastructure projects will retain their permits, except for extraordinary circumstances, violations of law or court order.

Makes targeted reforms to ensure energy projects are reviewed in a fair and timely manner.

Forces data centers to pay their fair share by requiring them to pay for all of their associated transmission costs.

Hoeven successfully included two pieces of legislation he authored in the package:

The Bureau of Land Management (BLM) Mineral Spacing Act to streamline and improve the permitting process for energy development, remove duplicative regulations and better respect the rights of private mineral holders. Specifically, the BLM Mineral Spacing Act removes the BLM permitting requirement in instances when:

Less than half of the subsurface minerals within a drilling spacing unit are owned by the federal government; and

The federal government does not own or lease any surface rights within the impacted area.

The Harnessing Energy at Thermal Sources (HEATS) Act to support the expanded development of geothermal energy. The bill eliminates duplicative federal permitting and ensures majority holders of a geothermal estate located on non-federal lands can exercise their property rights in developing these resources. Hoeven’s legislation would remove the federal permitting requirement for geothermal operations in instances when:

Less than half of the subsurface geothermal estate is owned by the federal government.

Geothermal exploration and production activities are conducted on non-federal surface acres.

The operator has received a state permit.

“Across the country, there are $1.1 trillion worth of projects that are held up by regulation, and this bill will help get those projects going. For home building, up to 25 percent of the cost can be due to regulation, and this will help cut that burden to bring down prices and battle inflation,” said Hoeven. “The bill makes important reforms, including ensuring that data centers pay for their transmission costs. We also successfully included my BLM Mineral Spacing Act and HEATS Act as part of this legislation to correct overreach by the federal government, enabling us to produce more energy on non-federal lands and strengthen the property rights of mineral and land owners. This is all about reforming our permitting process to make it better and more efficient, which will create jobs and make energy more affordable for American families.”

title: Husted highlights how federal benefits cliff discourages work and economic advancement
text:
“No one should have to turn down a raise out of fear they will leave their household unable to make ends meet.”

View Husted’s remarks here.

WASHINGTON – Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) delivered remarks at a U.S. Senate Special Committee on Aging hearing examining how fragmented federal anti-poverty programs can create benefits cliffs that discourage work and economic advancement.

During the hearing, lawmakers and witnesses also discussed Husted’s Upward Mobility Act, which would give states greater flexibility to coordinate federal assistance programs, reward employment and help Americans transition from government assistance toward long-term financial independence.

A benefits cliff occurs when a person receiving public assistance earns more money through a raise, promotion or additional work hours that results in the partial or complete loss of federal benefits that normally totals significantly more than the increased wages.

A single parent with two children in Dayton, Ohio could be offered a salary increase from $33,000 to $34,000. That $1,000 raise would make the family ineligible for $4,895 in food, housing and child care benefits. The $1,000 raise thus results in a nearly $4,000 negative, financial impact.

Husted’s landmark legislation, the Upward Mobility Act, seeks to reform federal welfare programs to help ensure Americans are not penalized for pursuing higher wages, additional work and greater economic opportunity. The bill would create a pathway out of poverty for lower income earners.

The Upward Mobility Act would establish a five-state pilot project. The participating states would receive their federal contribution in a single funding stream so states can design programs to smooth out their benefits cliff. It would also allow states to keep any savings generated and reinvest it in helping others out of poverty. Ohio Governor Mike DeWine has already volunteered Ohio as one of the pilot states.

Fact sheets on how the federal benefits cliff hurts Americans in every state in the nation can be downloaded at www.Husted.Senate.gov/Upward.

Key excerpts include:

“Holding this hearing on the benefits cliff and the barriers that they create for economic security and independence, this issue is deeply personal to me.

“And addressing it as one of the reasons I accepted the appointment to the U.S. Senate.”

. . .

“During my time in economic development and state government in Ohio, I heard some of the same concerns from families, workers, small businesses and workforce development professionals that too often our public assistance systems make it harder, not easier, for people to get ahead.”

. . .

“For this committee the question is straightforward: how do we ensure that the programs intended to provide stability do not instead stand in the way of greater independence?”

. . .

“Whether we are talking about an older worker considering additional hours, a person with a disability pursuing employment or a family balancing work and caregiving, the principle should be the same.”

“Earning more should leave you better off.”

. . .

“Yet conflicting eligibility rules and abrupt benefit phase outs can produce exactly the opposite result.

“A modest raise or a few additional hours of work can trigger a loss of assistance greater than the additional earnings.

“That is the benefit cliff, and it forces people into an impossible choice.

“Accept an opportunity to advance or risk losing the support they depend on or turn it down to preserve their financial stability.”

. . .

“That is why I introduced the Upward Mobility Act.

“My legislation would establish a five-year pilot program allowing five states to receive funding for participating in anti-poverty programs through one flexible funding system.

“States would receive the same level of funding, with annual adjustments for inflation, and no reduction in resources.”

. . .

“Our goal should be a safety net that provides stability when people need it and supports advancement when opportunities arise.

“No one should have to turn down a raise out of fear they will leave their household unable to make ends meet.”

title: Kaine Introduces Resolution to Demand Answers on Trump-Vance Administration’s Decisions That Benefit Russia and Harm Our Allies
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Today, U.S. Senator Tim Kaine (D-VA), a member of the Senate Armed Services and Foreign Relations Committees, introduced a resolution to force the Trump-Vance Administration to provide answers to Congress about the human rights implications and other impacts of recent decisions that benefit Russia at the expense of our allies. Specifically, the resolution requests more information about how the purchase of Russian diesel, easing of sanctions, delays in the delivery of air defense munitions, and manipulation of early warning notifications of impending missile strikes has affected Russia’s ability to wage war in Ukraine and allowed it to worsen its campaign of horrific human rights abuses. It also requests an update on the current status of negotiations to end the war. The resolution is privileged under Section 502B(c) of the Foreign Assistance Act, meaning Kaine can call it up for a vote on the Senate floor soon.

“Instead of standing with our democratic allies, President Trump has cozied up to dictators like Vladimir Putin. The Administration’s recent decisions to delay deliveries of Patriot interceptors, waive certain Russian sanctions, and buy diesel from Russia—after launching an illegal, unnecessary, and costly war in Iran—are short-sighted. We should not be buying Russian fuel from Putin so that he can turn around and use American dollars to bomb and kill innocent Ukrainians, commit human rights violations, and prop up Iran,” said Kaine. “Sunlight is the best disinfectant, and this resolution would assess the consequences of this Administration’s recent actions. I urge my colleagues to support it.”

Kaine has introduced several privileged resolutions under the Foreign Assistance Act to challenge the Administration’s third-country deportation network. In May 2025, he forced a vote in the Senate to require the Administration to produce a human rights report regarding El Salvador after the Trump-Vance Administration deported Maryland resident Kilmar Abrego Garcia to El Salvador and President Trump threatened to imprison U.S. citizens there. Kaine also joined his colleagues in introducing a resolution requiring a report on the growing violence in the West Bank, including the deaths of nine Americans in recent years.

Full text of the legislation is available here.

title: Senator Kim Introduces Legislation to Hold ICE Accountable for Abuses at Delaney Hall and Nationwide
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, Senator Andy Kim (D-N.J.) introduced the Death in Detention Transparency Act to hold U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) accountable for deaths inside detention facilities and during other encounters with ICE and CBP agents. This legislation comes after numerous families have faced uncertainty about their loved ones detained at ICE facilities and how they died. The Trump administration has continued to provide little to no answers.

“We cannot allow ICE and CBP to skirt accountability for their abuses at detention facilities around the country. We cannot allow them to try to cover up how many people have died under their watch. People like Jean Wilson Brutus, Edwin Lopez-Cornejo, and Jose Chajon-Raxon who were detained at Delaney Hall in New Jersey and died. I have spoken to families in New Jersey grieving their loved ones without the answers they deserve. While we continue to work to shut facilities like Delaney Hall down for good, this bill demands transparency and would help make sure no family is left in the dark about what is happening to their loved ones behind closed doors,” said Senator Kim.

ICE has reported two deaths inside Delaney Hall Detention Center in New Jersey but has used loopholes to avoid reporting additional deaths and information, including the death of Jose Chajon-Raxon who died after experiencing a medical emergency at Delaney Hall. This week as a part of a civil rights investigation related to the deaths, the New Jersey attorney general sued the U.S. Department of Homeland Security seeking medical and use-of-force records at Delaney Hall. According to the ACLU, there have been at least 57 reported deaths in detention since the start of Trump’s second term, which is more than double the number of deaths from previous four years combined.

As ICE agents patrol streets and conduct arrests across the country, this legislation importantly expands the kind of deaths they are required to report to also include those during encounters outside of detention facilities. Currently, federal law only requires reporting on deaths in detention facilities. The legislation would help prevent the Trump administration from being able to cover up these incidents.

The Death in Detention Transparency Act would require ICE and CBP under law to fully and accurately report the number of deaths as well as additional details of the circumstances of each incident. Specifically, it would:

Require ICE and CBP to notify Congress of a death within 72 hours and include detailed information about the circumstances surrounding that death.

Require ICE and CBP to issue an expansive death incident report 30 days after a death has occurred and to make the report public. The report must include specific information including but not limited to whether a firearm was discharged, information about body worn camera footage, a copy of the results of an independent autopsy.

Expand the kind of deaths that ICE and CBP are required to report, including a requirement to report those deaths that occur during immigration enforcement such as arrests and encounters. Under the legislation DHS must report the death of an individual who died in the hospital in circumstances where someone has been hospitalized during detention, after an enforcement encounter, or following transport by ICE or CBP to a medical facility. This fights against the inhumane practice of ICE releasing ill detainees from their custody while they are hospitalized to avoid reporting requirements.

Include enforcement provisions such as the cancellation of a contract when reporting requirements are not met, unannounced inspections, and a five-year suspension for entities (such as private detention companies) that fail to meet reporting requirements on more than three occasions.

Require DHS detention contracts include a provision requiring all detention contractors to abide by death reporting requirements.

The legislation is endorsed by: National Immigration Law Center (NILC), ACLU, National Immigrant Justice Center (NIJC), Detention Watch Network, Immigrant Legal Resource Center, Vera Institute of Justice, ACLU-NJ, La Casa de Don Pedro (NJ), Pax Christi New Jersey, and New Jersey Citizen Action. Read the full bill text for additional information.

The legislation builds on Senator Kim’s demands for justice at Delaney Hall and work to close Delaney Hall and similar facilities for good. He has conducted oversight visits and inspections in New Jersey, including holding direct conversations with those detained, as well as put forward reforms to rein in the Trump administration’s lawless ICE. He also introduced a package of legislation to end warehouse detention nationwide and prevent taxpayer dollars from funding ICE’s lawlessness.

title: King Releases Statement on Senate Passage of Bipartisan Bill to Lower Home Utility Bills, Curb Emissions, Increase Access to Renewable Energy
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, U.S. Senator Angus King (I-ME) shared the following statement after the Senate passed bipartisan legislation to lower home utility bills and increase access to renewable energy sources. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA), which passed the Senate in a 62-33 vote, is an important step forward in unlocking the bureaucratic process for transmission lines that would bring renewable energy sources like solar and wind to homes across the country.

According to energy distribution modeling, it is likely that with a level regulatory playing field that BAAJA provides, clean energy sources will prove cheaper and improve carbon emissions nationwide. It now heads to the House of Representatives for consideration.

“Today we saw the passage of the Permitting Reform Bill, and I want to share some thoughts about it. First, and foremost, it deals with two of the most pressing challenges facing America today. One immediate, and one in the longer term. The immediate one is affordability; this bill will bring down electric prices. Not right away, not next week, or next month, but in the reasonably foreseeable future. By making the grid more efficient, and by lowering and bringing on cheaper sources, I’m going to talk about that in a minute.

“The other thing that is important about the bill, and certainly important to me, it’s a major step forward in the fight against climate change. It will allow us to electrify more of America, to bring fossil fuels down as a source of energy, and to really strengthen the role that renewables play in the electric source. Which then, as we electrify transportation and home heat through heat pumps will basically reduce the carbon footprint of this country substantially.

“Now, is it a perfect bill? No, there’s some things in it that that I don’t like. If I had written it myself, it may have said some other things. But it’s the bill that we can get right now, and there is no clear alternative to it, either now or even in the next Congress. And that’s why I ended up voting ‘yes.’

“It wasn’t an easy choice. I listened to my environmental friends in Maine, many of whom were opposed to the bill, I talked to people in the energy field, particularly in the renewable field, and decided that on balance this bill is a lot better than the status quo.

“Let me talk about electricity costs for a minute: the cheapest form of energy today is solar and wind, it’s about half the cost of natural gas. If you add storage, it’s still competitive with natural gas, and then it becomes baseload power. This bill unlocks an enormous amount of renewable energy, that is now basically unable to get to the market because of a lack of transmission.

“The other piece of the bill that I really like is it requires the transmission buildout that’s inevitable, that’s going to happen, to be done in the most economic way possible and the most efficient way possible. It also specifically shifts about $35 billion worth of grid construction costs onto data centers, by making it absolutely clear that they have to pay any costs that they’re imposing on the grid.

“The bill has a lot of very important provisions, and yes, it makes it easier to permit all kinds of energy facilities, and transportation facilities like highways and bridges. But I don’t think it really compromises environmental standards. What it focuses on is the process, how long it takes to get things done. And there’s an enormous growth in energy demand in this country, and it’s going to be met one way or the other. I want it to be met by renewables. This bill is essential to unlocking those renewables, which are often far from the markets that they need to serve.

“So those are some of the reasons I came to the conclusion, as I said, this bill is a lot better than the status quo. I think it’s a one-time opportunity, I don’t think we’re going to have this opportunity in the new Congress, and it’s an opportunity for us to make our country safer, our country more affordable, and to deal with the challenge of climate change, which is bearing down on us more seriously every day.”

###

title: Klobuchar, Colleagues Introduce Bipartisan Legislation to Support Families Facing Rare Childhood Disease
text:
WASHINGTON — U.S. Senators Amy Klobuchar (D-MN), Roger Wicker (R-MS), Chris Coons (D-DE), and Eric Schmitt (R-MO) introduced the Genomic Answers for Children’s Health Act of 2026. This bipartisan legislation would clarify that Medicaid must cover genomic sequencing for children with suspected rare diseases or genetic disorders who are enrolled in the program.

“For parents, few things are harder than knowing your child needs help and not having answers or knowing what options are available to help them. By expanding access to genomic sequencing for children with suspected rare diseases and genetic disorders, we can help parents get answers faster, doctors make more accurate diagnoses, and ensure families can get the care their children need,” said Klobuchar. “This bipartisan bill is an important step toward improving health outcomes and saving children’s lives.”

“Parents of children with rare diseases often spend years waiting for a diagnosis. Even when test results arrive, the answers can be frustratingly inconclusive,” said Wicker. “Genomic sequencing offers families faster and more reliable results. Through early detection, more patients will be able to get the care they need without endless delays and extensive testing, saving families and providers money in the long run.”

“When your child is sick, there’s nothing you wouldn’t give to make them better,” said Coons. “For millions of families across the nation whose children have a rare disease, they are left waiting and waiting for the answers and treatments they need. This bill brings an end to the waiting, giving families access to the keys that could unlock their children’s futures.”

“As the father of a child with a rare medical condition, I understand firsthand the challenges Missouri families like mine face,” said Schmitt. “Worrying about the cost of care should be the last thing on a parent’s mind. By ensuring Medicaid covers genomic sequencing for children with rare diseases, Missouri families will be able to better access the answers and care their children need.”

Approximately 30 million Americans suffer from rare diseases, and half of these patients are children. For many, the diagnosis process can take between four to eight years, still yield inaccurate results, and amount to thousands of dollars in medical costs. Genomic sequencing — a type of testing that examines an individual’s entire DNA sequence — is a more efficient way for kids to get accurate diagnoses earlier, while curative treatment still may be an option.

If signed into law, this bill would:

Require Medicaid to cover whole genome sequencing and whole exome sequencing as mandatory benefits for enrollees under the age of 21;

Direct states to expand access to genomic testing in hospital settings; and

Instruct the Secretary of Health and Human Services to raise awareness about genomic sequencing.

As Co-Chair of the Senate’s Rare Disease Caucus, Senator Klobuchar has been a leader in strengthening medical research, the Food and Drug Administration’s treatment review process, and expanding access to care for kids and adults living with rare health conditions.

The full text of the bill is available here.

###

title: Lankford Announces New State Director
text:
WASHINGTON, DC — US Senator James Lankford (R-OK) today announced former Speaker of the Oklahoma House of Representatives Jeffrey W. Hickman, from Fairview, Oklahoma, will serve as State Director, overseeing the Senator’s Oklahoma City and Tulsa field offices.

“I’m excited to have Jeff Hickman join our team as State Director,” said Lankford. “He understands this state because he has lived it from the family farm to the state Capitol. Jeff’s background will be an asset to our team and his heart to serve families will be a blessing for all Oklahomans. I’m grateful for his willingness to lead our fantastic state team.”

Hickman most recently served as president and CEO of the Oklahoma Grain and Feed Association. He also recently completed a nine-year term on the Oklahoma State Regents for Higher Education. A fifth-generation farmer, Hickman continues to help run his family’s operation near Dacoma and Cherokee in northwest Oklahoma.

“I’m grateful for the opportunity to continue serving Oklahomans in the role of State Director for Senator James Lankford,” said Hickman. “Senator Lankford’s state offices are staffed by dedicated field representatives and caseworkers who stay with a problem until it’s solved. I look forward to supporting that work and making sure every Oklahoman who calls on our offices is heard and helped.”

Background

Elected to the Oklahoma House of Representatives in 2004, Hickman served as Speaker of the House for three legislative terms, from 2014 to 2016. He spent seven years working in higher education at the University of Oklahoma, where he served as university press secretary, public affairs special projects coordinator, and as special assistant to the director of athletics.

Hickman earned his bachelor’s degree in journalism with distinction from the University of Oklahoma. He and his wife, Jana, live in Fairview, Oklahoma, and have three children.

title: IN THE NEWS: Luján Demands Accountability Over FCC Nominee Danielle Thumann’s False Statements to Congress
text:
Washington, D.C. – This week, U.S. Senator Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the Senate Commerce Subcommittee on Telecommunications and Media, led efforts to hold Federal Communications Commission (FCC) nominee Danielle Thumann accountable for false statements made in her oral and written testimony before Congress:

POLITICO: Luján criticizes FCC nominee’s candor, calls for further review

“Sen. Ben Ray Luján accused Danielle Thumann Severs, the GOP nominee for the Federal Communications Commission, of not being forthcoming in her testimony about her role in multiple media proceedings, adding pressure on Republicans to delay her confirmation. Luján (D-N.M.) urged Senate Commerce Committee Chair Ted Cruz (R-Texas) to hold another hearing with Severs so she can respond before lawmakers vote to advance her nomination out of the committee.”

Cruz to hold her nomination because it appears that Thumann Severs ‘misled the committee and offered false testimony’ during her Nov. 10 confirmation hearing. Los Angeles Times: Republicans scramble to add third Trump nominee to the FCC

“With just weeks remaining before Democrats take control of Congress, a scramble is underway to fortify the Federal Communications Commission with President Trump’s allies. Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.), who also serves on the committee, separately challenged Thumann Severs’ candor in answering senators’ questions. Luján alleged that Thumann Severs ‘misled the committee and offered false testimony’ during her confirmation hearing last week.”

Punchbowl: Tensions flare over FCC nominee

“Senate Republicans’ end-of-year scramble to confirm nominees before they lose power sparked tensions at the Commerce Committee on Wednesday and could signal further floor clashes during the lame duck. Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.) said that emails he obtained showed she had worked on at least some issues before the bureau, including the Skydance-Paramount deal.”

The Verge: Democrats skip a vote on adding Brendan Carr’s adviser to the FCC

“In a letter asking Cruz to delay her confirmation vote, Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-NM) detailed his concerns. At the November 10th hearing where Thumann answered committee members’ questions, she testified that she had ‘not worked with the Chairman on any media-related issues,’ Luján noted in the letter. But documents obtained via a Freedom of Information Act request show that Thumann was “looped in” on various media matters, and ‘helped draft Skydance’s commitments that facilitated the FCC’s approval of the Skydance-Paramount merger,’ Luján wrote. ‘She also played a role in processing informal complaints related to CBS 60 Minutes alleged news distortion and she apparently orchestrated the Commission’s response to consumers regarding the Jimmy Kimmel controversy.’”

Roll Call: FCC pick advanced by Senate Commerce after Democratic boycott

“On Tuesday, Sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., wrote his own letter to Cruz calling for the removal of the nomination from the agenda based on grounds that Thumann Severs lied to the committee. ‘While Ms. Thumann testified she did not work ‘on any media-related issues,’ documents obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests demonstrate that she worked on several media related issues, including on commitments that Skydance made to pave the way for FCC approval of its merger with Paramount,’ Luján wrote.”

Bloomberg: Senate GOP Advances Trump FCC Pick as Democrats Boycott Vote

“The Senate Commerce Committee advanced President Donald Trump’s nominee for the Federal Communications Commission despite a boycott from all of the committee’s Democrats at a markup Wednesday. Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.) ranking member of the Telecommunications and Media subcommittee spoke at a press conference before the hearing, condemning Thumann and pointing out discrepancies when she denied working on any media-related issues. Lujan said he has documents, including emails, that prove she was involved in a major merger and in the decision to pull Jimmy Kimmel from air. ‘They should also pull her from the hearing today and bring her in and ask her to tell the truth, and ask why she lied to the committee,’ Lujan said.”

Cyber Scoop: Senate Republicans advance FCC nominee, slate of cyber bills

“Republicans in the Senate Commerce Committee advanced the nomination of Danielle Thumann Severs to serve as a commissioner at the Federal Communications Commission. On Tuesday committee member Sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., accused Thumann Severs of not being forthcoming about her role in support of Carr’s media bias investigations.”

Background:

Senator Luján called on Commerce Committee Chairman Ted Cruz (R-Texas) calling on him to remove the nomination of Danielle Thumann Severs to the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) following revelations that appear to contradict her testimony during her nomination hearing.

During Ms. Thumann’s November 10th confirmation hearing, she testified in response to questioning from Senator Luján that she had not worked with FCC Chairman Brendan Carr on any media-related issues. However, documents obtained by Senator Luján reveal that Ms. Thumann worked on several media-related matters, including helping draft commitments made by Skydance that facilitated the FCC’s approval of its merger with Paramount.

The documents reveal that Ms. Thumann reviewed and edited a draft letter that Skydance later submitted to the FCC outlining its commitments to eliminate diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives at Paramount. The documents also reveal Ms. Thumann’s involvement in media issues related to CBS’ 60 Minutes and Jimmy Kimmel, directly contradicting her testimony before the Commerce Committee.

“While I find it hard to believe that Ms. Thumann simply misspoke or misunderstood the question, I hope that her inability to answer was not indicative of willful deception. Either way, if her testimony departed this far from the record on what we can see, the Committee has every reason to ask her what else she has hidden. Before moving forward with her nomination, this Committee must conduct another hearing to fully explore this new information and allow Ms. Thumann to correct the record,” Senator Luján wrote in his letter to Chairman Cruz.

title: Luján, Wicker Introduce Bipartisan Legislation to Block Exploitative Bots & Protect Intellectual Property
text:
Washington, D.C. – This week, U.S. Senators Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.) and Roger Wicker (R-Miss.) introduced the bipartisan Stealth Bot Prohibition Act to confront the illegal and deceptive use of internet bots that threaten Americans’ intellectual property.

In light of the rise of artificial intelligence (AI), automated web crawlers are now roaming across the internet. While many have legitimate uses, bad actors have exploited the technology to wreak havoc on online producers, including local newspapers and journalists. Many of these advanced bots evade paywalls, scrape information, and overwhelm websites. “Stealth bots” are a particular class of disguised web crawlers that America’s adversaries deploy to steal protected online content and use it to train their own AI models.

The Stealth Bot Prohibition Act would enact transparency standards to combat these unauthorized practices. If passed, this legislation would provide a new tool for publishers to combat deceptive operators by requiring the disclosure of identities and purposes of bots when accessing websites without banning legitimate research and other beneficial automated material. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) would be in charge of the enforcement of the bill’s provisions and would empower state attorneys general to take legal action to protect residents from violators.

“AI is advancing rapidly, creating new challenges and threats for the American people. Congress must act immediately to ensure transparency and accountability for those who misuse this technology,” said Senator Luján. “That’s why I’m joining Senator Wicker in introducing the Stealth Bot Prohibition Act to crack down on bad actors and protect creatives, small businesses, and local news. No one should profit by stealing others’ hard work, ideas, or livelihoods.”

“The Chinese Communist Party is notorious for stealing Americans’ intellectual property by any means possible. Now, it is weaponizing artificial intelligence and deploying droves of malicious bots against online publishers,” said Senator Wicker. “Our legislation recognizes these threats and offers a solution to insulate digital producers from bad actors.”

“We are immensely grateful to Senator Ben Ray Luján for his leadership in co-sponsoring the Stealth Bot Prohibition Act. By bringing critical transparency to online bot activity, this common-sense legislation takes a vital step toward protecting American businesses and securing a healthy digital marketplace for news and content. With automated internet traffic now exceeding human traffic and bot and AI scraping activity growing exponentially, this has caused increased costs and slowdowns of our websites. We must have greater transparency to give website owners the choice and ability to block stealth bots and nefarious actors while allowing proper use of their sites and content,” said Patrick Dorsey, Publisher of The Santa Fe New Mexican and Board Chair, America’s Newspapers.

“We thank Senator Luján for his commitment to New Mexico’s journalism industry, and for his commitment to protect American content creators, websites, and consumers, from a flood of bad bots. News publishers of all sizes are drowning in bot traffic, hurting their ability to provide high-quality content to the American public. The Stealth Bot Prohibition Act is a common-sense, bipartisan solution to the problem of bad bots,” said Belinda Mills, President & CEO of the New Mexico Press Association.

“News publishers of all sizes are drowning in bot traffic, hurting their ability to provide high-quality content to the American public. The Stealth Bot Prohibition Act is a common-sense, bipartisan solution to the problem of bad bots. It offers straightforward transparency requirements and enforcement mechanisms that uncover bad actors while leaving responsible uses of bots unaffected. The News/Media Alliance thanks Senators Wicker and Luján for their leadership on this issue, and their commitment to protecting American content creators, websites, and consumers, from a flood of bad bots. We look forward to working with them and their colleagues in Congress to pass this critical piece of legislation and offer American businesses and the American people the relief they deserve,” said Danielle Coffey, President and CEO of the News/Media Alliance.

“As AI bots continue to pose an increasing threat across the creative landscape, the Stealth Bot Prohibition Act will be a critical tool in ensuring that the constitutional copyright protections of creators can continue to be upheld and respected, especially across online platforms. AAP thanks Senators Roger Wicker and Ben Ray Luján and Representatives Laurel Lee, Valerie Foushee, and Gus Bilirakis for introducing this important legislation to help defend the integrity of human innovation,” said Maria A. Pallante, President and CEO, Association of American Publishers (AAP).

title: Luján, Wyden, Markey Question Tech Companies Over Proliferation of ‘Nudify’ Apps, in App Stores, Digital Ads
text:
Senators Write Meta, Google and Apple Following Reports That Nonconsensual Image Generating Apps Are Evading Bans by App Stores and Meta Ads

Washington, D.C. – U.S. Senators Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.), Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), and Edward J. Markey (D-Mass.) questioned Big Tech companies over the widespread availability of so-called ‘nudify’ apps in app stores, nearly a year after the senators raised concerns about X and Grok remaining available despite enabling mass-generation of nonconsensual sexual images of women and children.

Although Apple and Google ban nudify apps in their terms of service, researchers recently revealed that apps marketed on Meta ads as nonconsensual sexual image generators are widely available in app stores, and generated over $100 million in revenue. One common tactic is for apps to be updated after passing review to add nudification tools.

“These findings raise questions not only about individual failures of app review, but also about [Google and Apple’s] ability to identify repeat offenders, disrupt coordinated networks, and monitor apps after approval,” the senators wrote.

The senators also questioned Meta over its continued role in advertising apps marketed as generating nonconsensual intimate images of women and children.

“Despite Meta’s stated prohibition on these ads, independent investigations have documented extensive ad campaigns on Facebook and Instagram directing customers to apps capable of digitally undressing people in photographs or placing their likeness into sexually explicit content without their consent,” the senators wrote.

AI tools have supercharged the spread of nonconsensual sexual imagery online, creating real harm to women and children in particular. A 2024 survey by the Center for Democracy & Technology found that 15% of U.S. public high school students knew of AI-generated nonconsensual intimate imagery (NCII) depicting someone at their school. A separate 2025 Thorn survey found that 6% of young people reported having been targeted by AI-generated NCII.

NCII is frequently weaponized against female journalists, human rights defenders, politicians, and other prominent women – not simply to humiliate them, but to discredit, intimidate, and silence their work and advocacy. Research by the American Sunlight Project revealed that one in six female Members of Congress were targeted by sexually explicit deepfakes and a 2025 New America investigation documented 100 cases involving public officials across 14 countries, 97 of them involving women.
