title: Shaheen Introduces Donna’s Law in U.S. Senate For First Time Ever to Empower Individuals to Protect Themselves from Self-Harm with Firearms
text:
(Washington, DC) – U.S. Senator Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH) today introduced “Donna’s Law” alongside Senator Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), marking the first time the bill has been introduced in the U.S. Senate. The legislation would create a federal voluntary process for individuals to add themselves to a private “do not sell” list for firearms. Currently, most Americans cannot voluntarily restrict their own ability to purchase firearms, endangering many individuals struggling with grief or mental health challenges. Nearly 60% of gun deaths in the United States are suicide by firearm, and New Hampshire’s suicide rate is above the national average. By empowering individuals to take a voluntary, proactive step to protect themselves, Donna’s Law will save lives and work to bring down gun suicides across the country.

“Anyone struggling with loss, grief or mental health challenges should be able to protect themselves from harm,” said Senator Shaheen. “In moments of crisis, all Americans should feel they can take the steps they need to shield themselves from impulsive, and potentially deadly, decisions. By establishing a voluntary list to give Granite Staters and those across the country the choice to limit their own access to firearms in times of need, Donna’s law does just that. I know this legislation will save lives and am proud to see it introduced.”

“I have struggled with mental health my entire life, and since losing my son, Nathan, to suicide by firearm, those feelings can be overwhelming. I also know firsthand the devastating, complicated grief that suicide leaves behind. I love my husband and my daughters deeply, and I want to live,” said Donna Morin, Founder of the Nate Morin Project, Educator and Mental health advocate. “Donna’s Law would allow me to proactively place my name on a Do Not Sell list, putting critical time and distance between a moment of crisis and a lethal means. That pause is everything: it gives me and others who struggle with their mental health, time to breathe, realize that our pain is temporary, and choose life. Passing this bill will save lives by empowering people to protect themselves.”

“I lost my mother to impulsive firearm suicide, and I know firsthand how devastating it is to lose someone who might have survived if there had been one more barrier between a moment of crisis and an irreversible decision,” said Katrina Brees, daughter of Donna Nathan, who is the namesake of the legislation. “Donna’s Law offers a powerful form of self-defense against suicide: the ability to protect your future self. By allowing individuals to voluntarily and confidentially restrict their own access to firearms, we can empower people to make a deeply personal decision about their own safety. This is about autonomy, privacy, and giving people the tools and rights to protect their own lives. I am profoundly grateful to see our country move this life-saving option forward.”

“Donna's Law is not gun-control, it's self-control – giving people a new tool to protect themselves against impulsive gun suicide,” said Fredrick Vars, the Robert W. Hodgkins Chairholder of Law at the University of Alabama Law School.

Donna’s Law creates a voluntary process for people to add themselves to a do not sell list (known in the bill as the Voluntary Purchase Delay Database). When licensed importers, licensed manufacturers or licensed dealers run background checks in the National Instant Criminal Background Check System (NICS) a check will also be run against the Voluntary Purchase Delay Database. Under the bill, the Department of Justice (DOJ) must establish a secure online platform that will allow people to add themselves to the Database and prevent unauthorized disclosure of the identity or information of individuals who choose to add themselves to the list. The legislation also directs DOJ to set up processes by which individuals can remove themselves from the voluntary do not sell list.

Donna’s Law was inspired by Donna Nathan, who committed suicide with a revolver she had purchased after voluntarily hospitalizing herself three times in 2018 because of bipolar disorder and depression. Donna Nathan’s daughter, Katrina Brees, then went to work alongside University of Alabama Law School professor Frederick Vars to design the legislation. Donna Morin, a New Hampshire mother who lost her son to suicide, has been a vocal advocate of Donna’s Law, as it would protect herself and others in emotional distress.

The legislation is supported by the National Alliance on Mental Illness (NAMI), American Foundation for Suicide Prevention, American Psychiatrist Association, Brady and Giffords.

The bill text can be found HERE and a one-pager on the legislation can be found HERE.

Senator Shaheen has been an advocate for gun violence prevention efforts. Just recently, Shaheen joined an amicus brief urging the Supreme Court to uphold two assault weapon bans that are being challenged. In 2022, Shaheen was a strong supporter of the bipartisan Safer Communities Act, and has pushed to expand federal background checks and close what is commonly referred to as the ‘boyfriend loophole’ to prevent those who have abused partners from buying or owning firearms and to stop convicted stalkers from purchasing a gun. In 2023, Senator Shaheen joined a group of her Senate colleagues to reintroduce “Ethan’s Law” to require safe gun storage.

title: Thune: Giving Thanks to Those Who Defend Our Freedoms
text:
Click here to watch the video.

WASHINGTON — U.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) today delivered the following remarks on the Senate floor:

Thune’s remarks below (as delivered):

“Mr. President, one of the privileges of my job is being invited to attend welcome-home or deployment ceremonies for our military men and women.

“I attended two ceremonies this fall for the South Dakota National Guard:

“An activation ceremony for members of the 155th Engineer Company.

“And a welcome-home ceremony for the 665th Support Maintenance Company.

“I also attended the U.S. Army Reserve mobilization ceremony for the 452nd Ordnance Company, 2nd platoon.

“And earlier this year I had the privilege of meeting with the 28th Expeditionary Bomb Wing, when our Ellsworth B-1 bombers were forward-deployed.

“Mr. President, whenever I go to one of these ceremonies – or meet with our military men and women in other contexts, like at Ellsworth Air Force Base – I always leave filled with both admiration and gratitude.

“Admiration for the character and courage of these men and women.

“And gratitude for their willingness to exchange a life of convenience for one of challenge and sacrifice.

“Military life is tough, Mr. President.

“It’s challenging.

“It asks a lot of you – physically, mentally, emotionally.

“In modern life, we often place a high value on comfort and convenience.

“Military life is neither comfortable nor convenient.

“There’s nothing convenient for a Guard member about having to step away from his or her civilian job and deploy for a year.

“There’s nothing comfortable about boot camp. Training. A high operational tempo. Deployment.

“The men and women of the United States military choose this life anyway.

“They sacrifice personal comfort and convenience in service of a cause greater than themselves – the safety and security of the United States. The preservation of our freedoms.

“And it is a privilege to be invited to spend time with them.

“They inspire me always.

“Mr. President, there’s another thing that always strikes me when I attend events like the recent welcome-home and deployment ceremonies.

“And that is the families gathered there to support their loved one in uniform.

“They also serve.

“Being in the military is a tough job – so is being married to the military.

“Having a husband or wife – a dad or mom, a son or daughter – in uniform asks for sacrifice.

“If your spouse or parent is active duty, you have to pull up stakes on a regular basis and move to a new state or country and a new community.

“Leave friends and family behind. Enroll in a new school. Learn a new city or town – only to leave it again a couple of years later.

“And then, of course, there are deployments.

“All of a sudden, the spouse left at home has to shoulder all of the business of life – from home maintenance to car upkeep to bill payments.

“If you’re the parent left behind, you have to be both mom and dad for months – sometimes many months – at a time.

“You miss time with your loved one.

“There are birthdays and Christmases and Thanksgivings and Easters where husband or wife, mom or dad, isn’t there.

“And on top of this, there is always the fear in the back of your mind.

“The fear that your husband or wife, dad or mom, son or daughter will never come home.

“And this isn’t a theoretical fear.

“Military families have seen other families go through injury or loss.

“They know intimately what could happen to their loved one.

“But they serve anyway, shouldering the burden of that knowledge along with all the practical work that needs to be done to support their individual in uniform.

“It’s Military Family Appreciation Month, Mr. President.

“And Thanksgiving next week.

“And as we count our blessings – as we reflect on the free country that we live in and the liberty that we enjoy – at the top of our list should be those who secure those freedoms for us.

“Those who secure these freedoms for us, and their families.

“Mr. President, I want to wish a very happy Thanksgiving to our men and women in uniform and their families.

“Thank you – all of you – for your service.

“And may God bless you.”

title: Warner, Collins, Padilla, McConnell Introduce Bipartisan Legislation to Strengthen Election Security
text:
WASHINGTON— U.S. Sens. Mark R. Warner (D-VA), Vice Chair of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, Susan Collins (R-ME), Alex Padilla (D-CA), Ranking Member of the Senate Committee on Rules and Administration, and Mitch McConnell (R-KY), Chair of the Senate Committee on Rules and Administration, introduced the bipartisan Election Infrastructure Security Act (EISA) to provide states and localities with a more reliable source of funding to secure American elections. The legislation would repurpose the largely unused Presidential Election Campaign Fund (PECF) to support critical election security needs, including cybersecurity improvements, voting equipment upgrades, and protections for voter registration systems.

State and local election officials are on the front lines of protecting American elections, but they too often lack the consistent federal resources needed to maintain secure and reliable election systems. Currently, federal election security funding is limited and unpredictable, forcing election officials to rely on already-strained state and local budgets to address evolving threats, replace aging equipment, and maintain critical infrastructure. By establishing a dedicated source of funding, this legislation would allow election officials to make long-term security improvements, proactively address vulnerabilities, and avoid costly emergency upgrades.

“Free and fair elections are the foundation of our democracy. As Vice Chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee, I’ve seen firsthand the threats facing our election systems and the critical role that state and local officials play in defending against them,” said Sen. Warner. “Keeping our elections secure requires more than sporadic funding; it requires sustained investment. This bipartisan legislation would put an outdated, largely unused federal program to work strengthening election security by providing election officials with reliable funding to modernize voting infrastructure, address evolving threats, and ensure every eligible American can cast their ballot with confidence.”

“Protecting the integrity of our elections is essential to maintaining public confidence in our democratic process,” said Sen. Collins. “This bipartisan legislation would support that goal by providing a reliable source of funding to strengthen election security, modernize outdated equipment, and help ensure that our elections remain safe and secure.”

“American elections are safe and secure, but in a time of rising threats at home and abroad we will ensure they stay that way with the right investments in our election infrastructure,” said Sen. Padilla. “Our bill would rededicate an existing, but widely unused, voluntary fund to ensure that localities have the resources to support election needs – like improved cybersecurity and voting equipment upgrades. As Ranking Member of the Senate Rules Committee and California’s former Secretary of State, I recognize that robust and reliable federal funding for elections is a top priority, and I’m proud to support this commonsense, bipartisan legislation that will help further build up the strength of our democracy.”

“Election security is a fundamental responsibility of government, and states and local election officials need the resources to carry it out,” said Sen. McConnell. “This bipartisan legislation would put an outdated federal fund to better use by providing a dedicated source of funding to strengthen election infrastructure, improve cybersecurity, and modernize voting equipment. It is a practical approach that supports state and local election administration without creating a new federal spending program.”

The PECF was established to provide public financing to eligible presidential candidates through voluntary taxpayer contributions made on federal income tax returns. However, participation has declined significantly as candidates have increasingly relied on private fundraising. No major-party presidential candidate has used the program since 2008, leaving the fund largely obsolete. Congress has already begun redirecting portions of the fund toward other priorities, including election security. In fiscal years 2024, 2025, and 2026, a combined $80 million from the PECF was directed toward election security grants. The Election Infrastructure Security Act would build on this approach by permanently converting the PECF into a dedicated Election Security Fund, providing states with a more predictable source of support to protect and modernize their election systems.

Specifically, the Election Infrastructure Security Act would:

Establish a dedicated Election Security Fund by converting the existing PECF into a program supporting state and local election security. States would receive a guaranteed minimum of $3 million annually, while territories would receive at least $600,000. At least 67 percent of the fund would be directed to local election jurisdictions, except in states that centrally administer federal elections.

Support critical election security improvements by allowing funds to be used for broad purposes, including modernizing election technology, strengthening cybersecurity, upgrading voting equipment, protecting election infrastructure, reimbursing prior security investments, improving election administration, and shortening wait times. Funds cannot be used for litigation.

Require transparent spending plans and accountability by directing states to develop plans outlining how funds would be used, tracked, and monitored, subject to a public notice and comment process.

Modernize the voluntary taxpayer contribution system by increasing the federal income tax checkoff from $3 to $5 for individuals and from $6 to $10 for married couples filing jointly, with adjustments for inflation.

Place administration of the fund under the Election Assistance Commission (EAC), which already oversees federal election assistance grants under the Help America Vote Act.

Strengthen oversight by requiring annual state reports on expenditures, equipment purchases, and program outcomes, as well as periodic EAC audits to ensure funds are used appropriately.

In recent years, the PECF has received approximately $21 million to $25 million annually through voluntary taxpayer contributions, a reduction from historic numbers due to the defunct status of the program. The Bipartisan Policy Center estimates that the proposed reforms could generate approximately $200 million annually for election security grants, providing a significant boost to state and local election officials working to protect election infrastructure.

The bill is endorsed by the Bipartisan Policy Center and 23 state and local election associations, including the Arizona Recorder Association, California Association of Clerks and Election Officials, Colorado County Clerks Association, Connecticut Town Clerks Association, Florida Supervisors of Elections, Georgia Association of Voter Registration and Election Officials, Kentucky County Clerks Association, Louisiana Registrar of Voters Association Inc., Maine Town & City Clerks Association, Massachusetts Town Clerks Association, Michigan Association of Municipal Clerks, Nevada Association of County Clerks and Election Officials, New Hampshire City and Town Clerks Association, New Jersey Association of Election Officials, Ohio Association of Election Officials, Oregon Association of County Clerks, Rhode Island Town and City Clerks’ Association Elections Committee, Texas Association of County Election Officials, Clerk and Auditor Association of Utah, Vermont Municipal Clerks’ and Treasurers’ Association, Washington State Association of County Auditors, West Virginia Association of County Clerks, and Wisconsin County Clerks Association.

“The Election Infrastructure Security Act is a critical first step in ensuring that state and local officials across the country have the funding and resources they need to keep our elections secure and accurate. It turns a defunct box on a form into an opportunity for Americans to direct sustainable support to the dedicated people who keep elections running. This bipartisan legislation helps fund our elections like the essential infrastructure they are, and I commend the leaders of this bill for putting forward this innovative solution,” said Sam Oliker-Friedland, Chief Executive Officer of Responsive Gov Action.

“Secure elections require modern infrastructure. This legislation provides a fiscally responsible way to ensure election officials have the tools, technology, and cybersecurity protections necessary to administer elections safely and efficiently. Thank you, Senators, for your steadfast work in a solution that does not increase the deficit or impose new federal mandates, but ensures our elections are safe and secure,” said Sarah Hague, Executive Director of the Project for Election Infrastructure.

“Bipartisan action to better fund elections is one of the most meaningful steps federal lawmakers can take to protect the security, accessibility, and accuracy of our elections. We’re asking election officials to run elections in increasingly complex threat environments, with fewer resources than ever before. Defending against these evolving threats requires continuous vigilance and sustained investment. This legislation would provide the stable, long-term funding election officials need to continuously strengthen the security and resilience of our elections,” said Kathy Boockvar, former Pennsylvania Secretary of State.

“Confidence that election results reflect the will of the voters is the thread that holds our democracy together. This initiative would improve elections across America with no additional net federal spending, helping the tens of thousands of dedicated workers who run our elections to update outdated voting equipment, invest in cyber and physical security, and improve the accuracy of voter rolls,” said Former U.S. Sen. and Secretary of State Roy Blunt (R-MO).

“The threats facing our elections are increasingly complex and constantly evolving – and election officials are on the front lines of confronting those challenges. They need reliable funding to stay ahead of the latest threats, strengthen election infrastructure, and communicate effectively with voters. The Election Infrastructure Security Act is a timely and, importantly, bipartisan investment in our election infrastructure. This is a consequential way we can support the dedicated public servants in Virginia and across the country who work year-round to administer secure, transparent, and accessible elections,” said Chris Piper, former Virginia Chief Election Official and Commissioner of the Virginia Department of Elections.

Sen. Warner has long advocated for stronger federal support for election security, including sustained funding and cybersecurity assistance for state and local election officials. He has also raised concerns about the Trump administration’s reduction of federal election security assistance, including cuts to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s (CISA) election-related support. The legislation builds on Sen. Warner’s long-standing efforts to protect American elections, including his recently introduced Guaranteeing Universal Access to Cybersecurity Act, which would expand access to cybersecurity resources and monitoring for state and local governments, including election offices.

title: Warnock Statement on Permitting Reform Bill
text:
Washington, D.C. – Today, U.S. Senator Reverend Raphael Warnock (D-GA) released the following statement on his decision to vote ‘NO’ on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) unless the legislation is further amended.

title: Welch Escalates Call for Answers from DOD on Violent U.S. Joint Counternarcotics Operation with Ecuadorian Military
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Senator Peter Welch (D-Vt.) today led six colleagues in escalating their demand for answers about a violent joint counternarcotics operation carried out with the Ecuadorian military in March 2026. The letter comes three months after Senators Welch and Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.) led a push for answers about the operation from DOD Secretary Pete Hegseth and former Ecuadorian Ambassador Cristian Espinoza. To date, the Senators have not received a response to either letter.

Between March 1 and March 6, 2026, Ecuadorian and United States armed forces carried out a violent counternarcotics operation in the remote village of San Martin, located on the banks of the San Miguel River bordering Colombia and consisting of about two dozen impoverished families. The operation is the subject of multiple reports by journalists and human rights organizations who either visited the site or spoke and toured the property remotely with the registered owner, an Ecuadorian farmer who raised cows, pigs, and chickens.

The Senators wrote: “On August 11, 2026, we wrote to you about a reported counternarcotics operation carried out jointly by the United States and Ecuador in the remote village of San Martin on the banks of the San Miguel River bordering Ecuador and Colombia. In that letter, a copy of which is attached, we asked several questions and we are waiting to receive your answers. As Members of Congress, we have a responsibility to oversee U.S. military activities and ensure that taxpayer dollars are used lawfully and effectively.”

The Senators requested answers from Secretary Hegseth on the following questions, in addition to the questions posed in their previous letter, by December 11, 2026:

What specific intelligence led to this operation?

Which U.S. or Ecuadorian officials selected and approved each of the targets?

Where was the operation planned—in the United States, Ecuador, or another location?

Did the Department determine that each target could be lawfully attacked? If so, on what factual and legal basis did the Department determine that each target could be lawfully attacked?

Was a civilian-harm or collateral-damage estimate conducted before the strikes? If so, please provide a copy of those estimates. If not, why not?

How many U.S. personnel, if any, were in Ecuador for the operation, what U.S. units or agencies were involved, and where were they located?

What did U.S. military personnel do before, during, and immediately following the operation?

Which Ecuadorian military units were involved, and what did they do?

Is there an impact report or investigation of what the operation achieved? If so, please provide a copy. If not, why not?

Joining Senators Welch and Shaheen on this letter are Sens. Tim Kaine (D-Va.), Adam Schiff (D-Calif.), Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.), Jacky Rosen (D-Nev.), and Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.).

Read and download the Senators’ full letter to Secretary Hegseth.

title: Welch Presses Judicial Nominee on Derogatory Remarks Calling First Responders Injured by Corporate Negligence “Lottery” Winners
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — U.S. Senator Peter Welch (D-Vt.), a member of the Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Antitrust, Competition Policy, and Consumer Rights, this week pressed Arkansas Supreme Court Justice James Hiland, nominee to be United States Circuit Judge for the Eighth Circuit, for answers about his remarks demeaning first responders who suffered debilitating injuries as a result of corporate negligence as “lottery” winners in the case of Old Dominion Freight Line, Inc. v. McMillion.

“I mean, this is pretty astonishing: This company that had a billion dollars in profit did not find it necessary to give a heads-up to first responders, who are among the best people in all of our communities. In Arkansas and in Vermont, those folks show up. And to deny them the heads-up that they’re going to walk into a place where they’re breathing and it’s going to cause permanent damage is really concerning to me. So, the judicial philosophy question here is what’s at the heart of my concern with you having this lifetime appointment,” said Senator Welch. “So, I’d just like you to explain how you square the—I think—derogatory language that you used towards the plaintiffs: ‘Powerball winners,’ when they had these very severe injuries that were all avoidable by a simple heads-up by an incredibly wealthy and successful corporation.”

Watch the Senator’s full remarks below and on his YouTube channel:

In 2026, Hiland dissented from the majority decision in Old Dominion Freight Line, Inc. v. McMillion, which considered a jury verdict awarded to six first responders who assisted with an accident involving a tractor-trailer carrying formic acid. The first responders alleged that Old Dominion negligently failed to inform them of the presence of hazardous material when they arrived on scene and complained of ongoing health issues due to the exposure, including breathing issues. After a trial, a jury found Old Dominion liable and awarded the first responders $75 million in compensatory damages for pain and suffering.

The appellate court affirmed the jury’s finding regarding Old Dominion’s liability but ordered a new trial on damages; the Arkansas Supreme Court then vacated that opinion and affirmed the judgment. In Hiland’s dissent, he argued that the $75 million verdict was “excessive” and wrote: “The law does not permit juries to convert transitory or moderate injuries into generational wealth…[the judgment] transforms our civil justice system into something far more arbitrary—an institutionalized lottery, dispensing windfalls.”

Read key excerpts from Senator Welch’s exchange with Justice James Hiland, nominee to be United States Circuit Judge for the Eighth Circuit:

Sen. Welch: One of the rights that injured people have is the tort system. They can present their case to a jury, the jury—as you know—makes a determination: A, is there liability; B, what should be the damages. I understand there was a case involving Old Dominion where first responders who showed up got toxic injuries. There was a tractor-trailer that carried formic acid, and that’s an apparently very extremely dangerous substance. And the individuals who were the first responders got health problems, according to the majority opinion. They suffered reactive airway dysfunction—a very brutal injury, it’s like you’re breathing through a straw.

The jury considered all the evidence, found Old Dominion liable, because it knew that this formic acid was there, but did not give a heads-up to the first responders. A simple heads-up to allow them to protect themselves. In your dissent, you said that, “the law does not permit juries to convert transitory or moderate injuries into generational wealth.” First of all, how is it that you describe these injuries as “transient or moderate” when the jury found that they were quite extreme?

Justice Hiland: Senator, I’m in a tough position on—first of all, you’re taking the position that my friends on the majority took, so I understand. That case just went down. I don’t think the mandate has been issued in that case. There could be procedural opportunities for a re-hearing and some other things. Senator, respectfully, I would just hate to comment on that knowing that it could be coming back to the court. If the mandate had gone down, I’d be happy to talk about my position on that.

Sen. Welch: Here’s what does concern me. There are fewer and fewer ways for people who are injured as a result of corporate bad conduct—I mean, this is pretty astonishing…So, I’d just like you to explain how you square the, I think, derogatory language that you used towards the plaintiffs: “Powerball winners,” when they had these very severe injuries that were all avoidable by a simple heads-up by an incredibly wealthy and successful corporation.

Justice Hiland: Senator, again, I would love the opportunity to talk to you about that case, and visit with you about it and the rationale—

Sen. Welch: Well, you’ve got the opportunity right now.

Mr. Hiland: But again, we have ethical considerations from the Arkansas Code of Judicial Conduct, and that mandate has not been issued, at least of night. So, it just is something that I shouldn’t discuss in public.

###

title: Young, Banks Urge NASA to Consider Indiana for United States Space Academy
text:
WASHINGTON – Today, U.S. Senators Todd Young (R-Ind.) and Jim Banks (R-Ind.) sent a letter to NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman expressing strong support for Indiana’s proposal to host the United States Space Academy, a proposed NASA-supported federal academy that will educate the next generation of American leaders in space.

In the letter, the senators highlighted Indiana’s longstanding contributions to America’s space program, its leading research institutions, and its growing defense manufacturing sectors.

“American leadership in space is critical to our national security. As our adversaries invest in capabilities intended to challenge the United States, we must ensure our country has the scientists, engineers, and military and civilian leaders necessary to maintain our advantage,” the senators wrote.

Indiana Governor Mike Braun submitted the state’s bid to host the brand-new United States Space Academy earlier this week. The state’s proposal includes a partnership among Indiana University, Purdue University, the University of Notre Dame, and Ivy Tech Community College to support the Academy’s academic workforce development needs.

The Space Academy, established by Presidential Commission in August 2026, is expected to welcome its first class of 300 cadets in fall 2028 and grow to 1,200 students by 2031. Officials anticipate this number could eventually reach 4,000 or more, with graduates expected to go into the Space Force, to NASA or the civilian sector.

Full text of the letter is available here and below.

Dear Administrator Isaacman:

We write in strong support of the State of Indiana’s response to NASA’s Request for Information regarding the establishment of the United States Space Academy.

American leadership in space is critical to our national security. As our adversaries invest in capabilities intended to challenge the United States, we must ensure our country has the scientists, engineers, and military and civilian leaders necessary to maintain our advantage. President Trump’s vision for the United States Space Academy recognizes that our future success in space will depend as much on developing talented Americans as it will on advancing new technologies.

Indiana has a long history of contributing to America’s space program, from the earliest days of NASA through today’s missions. Our state is home to leading research universities, major defense installations, advanced manufacturers, and companies developing technologies important to our national security.

We are particularly encouraged by the leadership and collaboration among Indiana University, Purdue University, the University of Notre Dame, and Ivy Tech Community College. These institutions have come together to address the Academy’s immediate academic needs while also developing an additional approach to producing more of the highly skilled Americans NASA and the Department of War will need in the years ahead. This partnership demonstrates Indiana’s ability to bring together its academic resources to address a national challenge. All of these institutions are led by Presidents who support their institutions’ engagement with our national security and defense apparatus through research and workforce development. Particularly noteworthy, Purdue University announced this month that Retired Lt. Gen. Jay B. Silveria will be the next President of the University. His past role as Superintendent of the US Air Force Academy will bring familiarity to the role of the Academy, its operations, and end goals.

Indiana’s response also identifies multiple locations capable of supporting the Academy and its long-term growth. Each offers access to academic, military, research, and industry assets that can contribute to the Academy’s success.

As Indiana’s United States Senators, we have worked closely with Governor Braun, our congressional delegation, and leaders across the state to strengthen Indiana’s role in our national defense. Our work to advance unmanned systems, military testing, microelectronics, and defense manufacturing reflects a shared commitment to ensuring Indiana continues to contribute to America’s military readiness and technological superiority. The United States Space Academy would build on that work while helping prepare the next generation of Americans to serve our country.

We strongly support Indiana’s response and respectfully urge you to give it full and fair consideration. We stand ready to work with NASA, the Administration, and our state partners to support this important national mission.

title: Young, Coons, Lee Reintroduce JUDGES Act to Address Judicial Shortages
text:
WASHINGTON – Today, U.S. Senators Todd Young (R-Ind.), Chris Coons (D-Del.), and Mike Lee (R-Utah) reintroduced the Judicial Understaffing Delays Getting Emergencies Solved (JUDGES) Act. The legislation would address judicial shortages by adding 69 federal district judgeships in overburdened courts across the country, including in the Southern District of Indiana.

“Federal courts across the country, including in Indiana, are facing overwhelming caseloads and a shortage of judges,” said Senator Young. “These delays can prevent Americans from receiving timely justice. Our bipartisan legislation would help address these shortages and ensure Hoosiers and Americans across the country can have their day in court without unnecessary delays.”

“Lower courts across the country, including in Delaware, are struggling to keep up with growing caseloads,” said Senator Coons. “Congress must ensure the federal judiciary is able to give every litigant their day in court, keeping our justice system accessible to all. This bipartisan bill will address this access-to-justice crisis.”

“A lack of federal judges and a backlog of filings affects the lives of too many Americans,” said Senator Lee. “The Judges Act will help shape the federal judiciary for years to come, adding district judgeships for the first time in twenty-five years, and circuit judgeships for the first time in nearly four decades. Our bill will provide faster hearings and decisions for Americans seeking justice.”

Background:

Senator Young first introduced the JUDGES Act in 2020 and reintroduced the bill in 2021 and 2023. The legislation has previously passed out of both chambers of Congress. Young also highlighted the need for additional federal judges in an op-ed in the IndyStar.

In March 2025, the Judicial Conference of the United States, the nonpartisan policymaking body for federal courts, recommended creating 69 new permanent district court judgeships, including one in the Southern District of Indiana, and 2 new permanent Ninth Circuit judgeships to address growing caseloads and judicial shortages.

The JUDGES Act would address these shortages by authorizing additional federal judgeships phased in over multiple presidential administrations. Congress last enacted a comprehensive expansion of federal judgeships in 1990, despite growing caseloads and repeated recommendations from the federal judiciary.

In addition to Sens. Young, Coons, and Lee, the bill is cosponsored by Senators Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.), Ted Cruz (R-Texas), Andy Kim (D-N.J.), Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.), John Hickenlooper (D-Colo.), James Lankford (R-Okla.), Cory Booker (D-N.J.), Mike Crapo (R-Idaho), and Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-Del.).

title: Young Supports Permitting Reform Legislation
text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. Senator Todd Young (R-Ind.) voted for the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, bipartisan legislation to reform our nation’s permitting and environmental review processes and make life more affordable for American families. The bill passed the Senate last night by a vote of 62-33.

The legislation aims to streamline the federal permitting process, reduce regulatory delays, and accelerate critical infrastructure and energy projects across Indiana and the country. It also requires data centers to pay their fair share of electricity infrastructure costs, helping protect families and small businesses from higher utility bills.

“It costs too much and takes too long to build things in our country,” said Senator Young. “Indiana has billions of dollars in potential investment tied up in the federal permitting process. The simple reforms in this bill will help cut unnecessary red tape, move critical infrastructure projects forward, and create more opportunities for Hoosier workers and businesses. It’s long past time to modernize our permitting process, and I am pleased the Senate passed this bipartisan bill.”

According to an estimate provided by the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, approximately $31.4 billion in Indiana projects are currently tied up in the federal permitting process, representing an estimated $57.6 billion in potential economic impact. Major infrastructure projects, including Interstate 69 and the I-69 Ohio River Crossing, have faced permitting challenges that contributed to delays and increased costs.

title: Rep. Young Kim Leads Bill to Cut Red Tape, Help More American Families Attain Homeownership
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Today, Congresswoman Young Kim (CA-40) and Congresswoman Nikema Williams (GA-05) introduced the bipartisan Housing Process Parity Act to cut federal red tape and increase the supply of available homes, helping more American families achieve the dream of homeownership.

Under current law, federal requirements can force lenders to navigate lengthy and expensive court proceedings before foreclosed homes return to the market. These unnecessary delays leave homes sitting vacant for extended periods of time, driving up costs and even further straining an already limited housing supply.

The Housing Process Parity Act streamlines this process for certain Federal Housing Administration (FHA) loans, helping return homes to the market faster. The bill also directs the Government Accountability Office (GAO) to study the feasibility of offering FHA-insured mortgages with no down payment, including potential benefits for homebuyers and risks to taxpayers.

“Homeownership is a cornerstone of the American Dream, but for too many families, that dream is slipping out of reach,” said Rep. Kim. “I’ve been proud to champion bipartisan legislation to alleviate the housing crisis and put the American Dream back within reach. My Housing Process Parity Act will build on these efforts by getting homes back on the market faster and exploring new pathways to homeownership for everyday Americans.”

“Homeownership is a powerful tool for building generational wealth and economic opportunity, however there simply aren’t enough affordable homes available for families to purchase,” said Rep. Nikema. The bipartisan Housing Process Parity Act cuts unnecessary barriers to get homes back on the market faster and expand housing supply. Every family, no matter their ZIP code or bank account, deserves a fair shot at building wealth for the next generation.”

“MBA commends Representatives Young Kim (R-CA) and Nikema Williams (D-GA) for their bipartisan leadership in introducing this legislation, which advances important Federal Housing Administration (FHA) program improvements, provides parity across government-insured mortgage programs, and supports broader efforts to expand access to sustainable homeownership,” said Bill Killmer, Senior Vice President of Legislative and Political Affairs at the Mortgage Bankers Association.

title: Rep. Smith Statement on Detainment at Sea-Tac Airport
text:

title: Rep. Smith Statement on GEO Group's $453 Million Sale of NWIPC to ICE
text:
On Wednesday, GEO Group, a private prison corporation, sold the Northwest ICE Processing Center (NWIPC) in Tacoma to the U.S. Department of Homeland Services for $453 million. I am deeply alarmed by this move and indications this is an attempt by the Trump administration to limit Washington state’s ability to conduct oversight of the facility. NWIPC has a documented history of poor sanitation, insufficient medical care, inadequate food, and issues with access to legal counsel, and any attempts to limit transparency and oversight must be vigorously pushed back against.

I am also concerned by reports ICE may have overpaid for this facility, given that the City of Tacoma valued the property at only $72.6 million. GEO Group has publicly stated net proceeds will be used to fund stock buybacks. This is an absolute misuse of federal funds, as NWIPC joined a list of privately operated facilities now owned by ICE.

title: DelBene Statement on Detainment at Sea-Tac Airport

title: Smucker’s Bipartisan Claiming Age Clarity Act Signed Into Law
text:
WASHINGTON – Rep. Lloyd Smucker (PA-11) announced that his bipartisan Claiming Age Clarity Act, H.R. 5284, has been signed into law by President Trump.

Smucker introduced the legislation with Rep. Don Beyer (VA-08) to help Americans better understand how the timing of their decision to claim Social Security affects their monthly retirement benefit. The law requires the Social Security Administration to replace confusing terminology with clearer language explaining how claiming age affects monthly benefits.

“This law will make it easier for Americans who have worked hard their entire lives to make informed decisions about their Social Security retirement benefits. The confusing government terminology will now be replaced with straightforward language that better explains how the age at which someone claims Social Security affects their monthly benefit. I thank Rep. Don Beyer for joining me in introducing this legislation, our colleagues for supporting this legislation, and President Trump for signing it into law,” said Rep. Lloyd Smucker.

“Thanks to our bill, now signed into law, seniors and older workers will now be better informed as they approach crucial decisions about retirement,” said Rep. Don Beyer. “I commend Rep. Smucker for his leadership on the Claiming Age Clarity Act, sorely needed legislation that will help seniors navigate financial choices going forward.”

The Claiming Age Clarity Act modernizes terminology used by the Social Security Administration to better reflect how claiming age affects an individual’s monthly benefit:

“Early Eligibility Age” will become “Minimum Monthly Benefit Age” — age 62, the earliest age at which an individual can begin receiving retirement benefits, with permanently lower monthly benefits than those received at standard benefit age.

“Full Retirement Age” and “Normal Retirement Age” will become “Standard Monthly Benefit Age” — generally age 66 or 67, depending on an individual’s birth year.

“Delayed Retirement Credits” will become “Maximum Monthly Benefit Age” — age 70, the latest age someone can begin receiving benefits. Electing to delay receiving benefits by a year increases an individual's benefits, up to a maximum of 24% more than the standard benefit.

The bipartisan legislation was supported by AARP, Bipartisan Policy Center Action, and AMAC Action.

Sens. Bill Cassidy (R-LA), Chris Coons (D-DE), Susan Collins (R-ME), and Tim Kaine (D-VA) introduced companion legislation in the Senate.

title: Bennet, Hickenlooper, Colleagues Introduce Resolution to Commemorate Transgender Day of Remembrance
text:
Washington, D.C.— Colorado U.S. Senators Michael Bennet and John Hickenlooper joined Senator Mazie Hirono (D-Hawaii) and 13 of their Senate colleagues to introduce a resolution commemorating November 20, 2026, as Transgender Day of Remembrance (TDOR).

“On Transgender Day of Remembrance, we stand united against the discrimination and attacks faced by the transgender community in Colorado and across the nation,” said Bennet. “We honor the memory of those lost and recommit to protecting the rights and safety of the transgender community to ensure that everyone can live with dignity and respect.”

“We’ve experienced years of rising discrimination and hate, specifically anti-transgender hate, across the country. We will not accept it. Transgender rights are human rights,” said Hickenlooper. “Everyone has the right to be who they are without being targeted.”

“As anti-transgender hate continues to rise nationwide, bolstered by the Trump regime’s harmful rhetoric, supporting and protecting transgender and gender-nonconforming individuals is critical. This resolution honors the lives of those who were lost to violence and educates communities about the dangers and discrimination transgender people face,” said Hirono. “Transgender rights are human rights, and I remain committed to defending everyone’s right to live openly, safely, and without fear.”

Transgender and gender-nonconforming people continue to face disproportionately high rates of violent crime. Following the still-unsolved murder of Rita Hester, a transgender woman of color, Gwendolyn Ann Smith founded TDOR to honor Hester and other transgender people whose lives were lost to violence. This year’s resolution also commemorates Stonewall veteran and longtime transgender advocate, Victoria Cruz, who passed away in June. Ms. Cruz dedicated her life to helping victims of domestic violence, police violence, and rape in the LGBTQ+ community.

Bennet is an ardent supporter of the LGBTQ+ community. In June 2026, Bennet introduced a resolution recognizing June as Pride Month. In July 2025, Bennet and Hickenlooper reintroduced the bipartisan Refund Equality Act to ensure that married same-sex couples can amend their tax returns back to the date of their marriage. In June 2025, Bennet introduced the No Place for LGBTQ+ Hate Act, which would ensure that President Trump’s executive orders targeting LGBTQ+ Americans have no force or effect, and would ensure that no federal funds are used to implement, administer, enforce, or carry out those executive orders. In April 2025, Bennet reintroduced a resolution to designate March 26, 2025 as “Clela Rorex Day” in honor of Clela Rorex, the Boulder County Clerk who issued the first marriage license to a same-sex couple. June 2023, Bennet reintroduced the Equality Act, which bans discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity in housing, education, employment, public accommodations, federal funding, and more. In June 2020, Bennet spoke on the Senate floor to urge his colleagues to support the Respect for Marriage Act to protect marriage equality. In December 2022, Bennet joined then-President Joe Biden at the White House for its signing.

title: Slotkin Statement on Voting Yes on Permitting Reform Bill
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Senator Elissa Slotkin (D-MI) released the following statement after voting in support of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) on the Senate floor.

“Last Thursday, I voted for the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. This bipartisan bill has both strengths and shortcomings, as with nearly every bill. I am grateful to the Michiganders who have reached out to share their concerns and perspectives, on this issue — both for and against.

“The central problem this Congress must face is the existential threat to America’s middle class. Michiganders of all political persuasions are demanding we do something to lower their costs. And we cannot meaningfully lower utility costs without legislation that reforms federal permitting laws. This bill does just that. Current laws mean it can often take four years to get permission to build or upgrade projects — which drives up the cost of these projects, particularly projects to bring cheaper and cleaner energy online.

“This bill will help decrease monthly utility costs for Michiganders by cutting the red tape around building new energy projects and allowing supply to keep up with demand. Importantly, this bill also puts in place the first federal guardrails on data centers to prevent them from passing on electrical costs to Michigan ratepayers, providing an estimated tens of billions of dollars in new revenue that can be used to lower energy bills for Michigan residents.

“Voting yes wasn’t simple. I pushed for amendments to address concerns about the bill’s impact on the Clean Water Act and its impact on tribal sovereignty. I am disappointed that fellow Democrats killed consideration of those amendments to try and tank the entire bill. I remain committed to addressing those concerns moving forward.

“Michigan families have been feeling the burden of their monthly utility costs, and we cannot delay easing that pressure. That is the bottom line, and it’s why I voted to pass this bill.”
